topics.title: Starter Components & Motor Parameters
topics.zh: 起动器元件与电机参数

sections.b:
• Push buttons — start/stop the motor. Start is normally green, stop is red.
  • Interlocking push buttons — give a mechanical interlock in control circuits.
  • Contactor — an electrically controlled switch for a power circuit; supplies the motor. Parts: coil (energises it), main contacts / poles (carry motor current), auxiliary contacts (control and signalling).
  • Timer relay — on-delay: output turns ON after time t once input is applied (input removed to reset). Off-delay: output ON with trigger; when trigger is removed, output stays ON for time t then turns OFF (re-trigger during t resets the delay).

Inside a contactor

Protects the motor from overload. Every overload relay must: (1) sense motor current, (2) have a time delay, (3) be split into a current-sensing section (in series with the motor, 120–600 V) and a contact section (in the control circuit, typically 240 V).

Set to trip at 115–125 % of full-load current. It must not trip instantly or the motor could never start (starting current is high).

Bimetal strip type: motor current → heat → bimetal strip bends and opens the contacts (the melting-alloy type uses the same heat principle).

Bimetal strip overload relay

DeviceHow it works
RCCB / RCDCompares phase and neutral current. If they differ (current leaking to earth), trips within ~30 ms. Still protects if the earth wire is faulty.
ELCBSenses current flowing back through the earth wire only. Misses faults that do not return via the main earth — hence replaced by RCCB.
MCBMiniature CB, rated ≤ 100 A, thermal or thermal-magnetic.
MCCBMoulded-case CB, rated up to 1000 A, thermal or thermal-magnetic.

Safe body limit is about 30 mA·s. With body resistance 500 Ω at 230 V: I = 230/500 = 460 mA, so the device must trip within 30 mA·s ÷ 460 mA ≈ 0.065 s (65 ms).

The slide writes this as "500/230 = 460 mA" and "0.65 ms". The correct working is 230 ÷ 500 = 0.46 A and 0.03 ÷ 0.46 ≈ 0.065 s.

• Voltage & frequency — run at the rated voltage; 50 or 60 Hz.
  • Current & connection — e.g. 400 V mains → star, 27.5 A; 230 V mains → delta, 48.7 A.
  • Power — kW or HP. 1 HP = 0.746 kW; 1 kW = 1.34 HP.
  • Speed — full-load rpm at rated output.
  • IP rating — protection of the enclosure against solids and liquids.
  • Efficiency — output mechanical power ÷ input electrical power.
η = Po / Pi × 100 %
Unitsη — percent (%)Po, Pi — watt (W)
T = 60·Po / (2πN) = 9.55 · Po / NT in N·m, P in W, N in rpm
UnitsT — newton-metre (N·m)Po — watt (W)N — revolutions per minute (rpm) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use

sections.h: Timer relays on a timing chart
sections.b:
On-delay (delay-on-make): the output waits time t after the input is applied, then switches ON. Removing the input turns the output OFF immediately and resets the timer. If the input is removed before t has passed, the output never comes on. Use: the star → delta changeover, delayed start of a second conveyor.

Off-delay (delay-on-break): the output switches ON immediately with the trigger. When the trigger is removed the output stays ON for time t, then turns OFF. Re-triggering during t restarts the delay. Use: a cooling fan that keeps running after the motor stops, stair lighting.

Exam tip: on a timing chart, look at which edge is delayed. Rising edge delayed = on-delay. Falling edge delayed = off-delay.

sections.h: Setting the overload relay — step by step
sections.b:
1. Read the motor's full-load current (FLC) from the nameplate for the connection actually used (star or delta).
  2. Choose an overload relay whose adjustment range includes that FLC.
  3. Set the dial to the FLC. The relay is built not to trip at the set current, and to trip — after a time delay — once the current rises to roughly 115–125 % of the setting. A larger overload trips it faster (inverse time).
  4. Test with the test button, then reset. Choose manual reset where an automatic restart would be unsafe.

If the nameplate is missing, estimate the FLC from the power:

IFL = Pout / (√3 · VL · cos φ · η)P in W, V in V
UnitsIFL — ampere (A)Pout — watt (W)VL — volt (V)cos φ, η — no unit
Star–delta starters: the overload relay normally sits in the winding (phase) circuit after the main contactor, so it carries the winding current. Set it to FLC ÷ √3 ≈ 0.58 × FLC.

Torque is the twisting or turning moment of a force about an axis. It is the product of force × radius at which the force acts. The unit for torque is the newton-metre (Nm).

Voltage and frequency on the nameplate: the voltage tells you at which voltage the motor is made to operate; used at other voltages, its performance will be affected. Input frequency is 50 or 60 Hz. If more than one frequency is marked, the other parameters that differ at each frequency have to be indicated on the nameplate as well.

Output 14 450 W at 800 rpm. Torque?
Exercise 1 — 1460 rpm, 23.5 N·m output, 280 V, 14.1 A. Efficiency?
Exercise 2 — DC motor input 18 600 W, output 14 850 W at 1000 rpm. Efficiency and torque?

A star–delta started motor has FLC 30 A. The overload relay is in the winding circuit. What setting?
worked.s:
Winding current = FLC ÷ √3 = 30 ÷ 1.732 = 17.3 A
Set the relay to 17.3 A

topics.title: AC Motor Starters
topics.zh: 交流电机起动器

sections.b:
On full voltage a motor draws 2–6× its running current (DOL on a cage motor: 6–7× full-load current). Large starting current damages driven machinery and causes line disturbances for other motors.

  • Small motors that can take the shock → DOL.
  • Motors larger than 2.2 kW → reduced-voltage starting.

Requirements for control: reduced starting torque, reduced starting current, under-voltage protection, over-current protection. CP5 adds: isolation for the installation, protection against under-voltage, and permissible voltage drop.

• DOL — motor connected straight across the line. Press START → contactor coil energises → main contacts close (motor runs) and an auxiliary NO contact seals in (holds) the coil after the button is released. STOP (NC) or overload trip breaks the coil circuit.
  • Overload warning lamp — wired via the overload relay's NO contact so the operator sees that the motor tripped on overload.
  • Jog / inch — motor runs only while the button is held (no seal-in). Used for positioning/setting up.
  • Forward–reverse — two contactors swap two phases. Electrical interlock: an NC auxiliary contact of each contactor in series with the other contactor's coil, so both can never be ON together.

DOL forward-reverse starter — control circuit

For large motors where torque must build gradually and high current would pull down line voltage.

Star–delta — four states:

  1. OFF — all contactors open.
  2. STAR — Main + Star closed. Motor gives ⅓ of DOL torque at ⅓ of DOL current.
  3. OPEN — Main closed, Star and Delta open (no current, transition gap).
  4. DELTA — Main + Delta closed → full line voltage.

The changeover timer is an ON-delay timer.

Primary resistance — resistors in series drop the voltage at start; after a time they are shorted out by another set of contacts → full voltage.

Auto-transformer — a transformer steps the voltage down at start, reducing line current; the timer then bypasses it.

Start pressed → contactor energises but motor does not run. Possible faults: a main contact (pole) burnt or not closing, open overload heater element, loose/broken power wiring to motor, blown power fuse on one or more phases, open motor winding, seized motor or jammed load.

Which starter gives it? Any starter built on a magnetic contactor with a hold-in (seal-in) auxiliary contact — so all the starters above: DOL (including jog and forward–reverse), star–delta, primary resistance and auto-transformer. The DOL starter is the standard example.

How it works:

  1. The contactor coil is what holds the main contacts closed.
  2. If the supply voltage drops too low or fails, the coil cannot produce enough magnetic pull, so the contactor drops out.
  3. The main contacts open → the motor stops.
  4. The hold-in auxiliary contact also opens, so the coil circuit is broken.
  5. When the voltage returns, the motor does not restart by itself — the operator must press START again.

Why it matters: (1) a motor running on low voltage draws excessive current and overheats; (2) a machine that restarts by itself after a power cut can injure someone. It is listed in the notes as a requirement for the control of AC motors and is also required by CP5.

Exam answer: A contactor-type starter such as the DOL starter provides under-voltage (no-volt) protection: the coil drops out when the voltage falls, and the hold-in contact prevents automatic restart when the supply returns.

sections.h: Why star–delta starting gives ⅓ current and ⅓ torque
sections.b:
The same motor windings are connected two different ways:

  • Star (start): each winding gets VL/√3 — 230 V on a 400 V supply.
  • Delta (run): each winding gets the full VL — 400 V.

Current: lower winding voltage means winding current also falls by √3. In delta, the line current is √3 × the winding current; in star, line current equals winding current. Putting both together, line current in star is (1/√3) × (1/√3) = ⅓ of the delta (DOL) value.

Torque: torque is proportional to the square of the voltage on each winding, so (1/√3)² = ⅓ of DOL torque.

What this means in practice: the motor must start on a light load (the starting torque is low), and it must be a motor rated to run in delta at the supply voltage (e.g. 400 V Δ), with 6 terminals brought out to the terminal box.

sections.h: DOL control circuit — wire by wire
sections.b:
Terminal numbers follow the IEC/EN standard, so they are the same on every brand of contactor:

TerminalsMeaning
1-2, 3-4, 5-6Main power contacts (poles) L1/L2/L3 → T1/T2/T3
F2Control-circuit fuse — protects the control wiring, buttons and coil from a short circuit
A1-A2Contactor coil
13-14 (x3-x4)Auxiliary NO contact — the second digit 3-4 means NO
21-22, 11-12 (x1-x2)Auxiliary NC contact — the second digit 1-2 means NC
95-96Overload relay NC contact — in series with the coil
97-98Overload relay NO contact — trip lamp / alarm
Press S1 Start
Current flows F2 → 95-96 → S0 → S1 → coil KM1 A1-A2
KM1 pulls in: main contacts 1-2/3-4/5-6 close → motor runs
KM1 13-14 closes → bypasses S1 = seal-in; KM1 23-24 → H1 running
Release S1 — the coil stays energised through 13-14
Stop pressed, overload trips, or supply fails?
Any of these breaks the coil circuit → KM1 drops out → motor stops and 13-14 opens. It will not restart by itself.
Overload trip: 97-98 closes → H2 overload lamp on. Find the cause, then reset.

sections.h: Star–delta starter — power connections and sequence
sections.b:
ContactorConnectsClosed during
KM1 MainL1→U1, L2→V1, L3→W1Star and delta
KM3 StarJoins U2, V2, W2 together (the star point)Star only
KM2 DeltaL1→W2, L2→U2, L3→V2 (makes U1–W2, V1–U2, W1–V2)Delta only
KT timerOn-delay, starts with KM1Star period
Press Start: KM1 + KM3 close → motor starts in star (≈⅓ current, ⅓ torque)
KT (on-delay) times while the motor accelerates
Time t up: KT opens the KM3 circuit → KM3 drops out
Short gap: only KM1 closed, windings open = open transition
KM3 NC auxiliary re-closes → KM2 closes → motor runs in delta at full voltage
Stop / overload: KM1 and KM2 drop out
Interlocks: KM2 and KM3 must never be closed together — that would short-circuit the supply through the star point. Each has an NC auxiliary contact in series with the other's coil (electrical interlock), and many starters add a mechanical interlock as well.

Setting the timer: long enough for the motor to reach close to full speed in star — typically a few seconds (often 5–10 s), depending on the load inertia. Change over too early and the current surge on delta is nearly as large as a DOL start.

worked.q: A motor has a full-load current of 20 A. DOL starting current is 6 × FLC. What line current flows at the instant of starting in star?
worked.s:
DOL starting current = 6 × 20 = 120 A
Star–delta = ⅓ of DOL = 120 ÷ 3 = 40 A

worked.q: A star–delta starter: KM2 (delta) is found welded closed when KM3 (star) pulls in. What happens and what prevents it?
worked.s:
With KM2 and KM3 both closed, L1/L2/L3 are joined at the star point through W2/U2/V2 → a line-to-line short circuit; the fuses or breaker trip.
Prevention: NC auxiliary of KM2 in series with KM3 coil and NC of KM3 in series with KM2 coil (electrical interlock), plus a mechanical interlock.

topics.title: 3-Phase Induction Motor Construction
topics.zh: 三相感应电机结构

sections.b:
• Stator — 3-phase winding in the slots of a laminated steel core, coils spaced 120° apart, connected star or delta; 3 or 6 leads to the terminal box.
  • Rotor — ~90 % of induction rotors are squirrel cage: laminated cylindrical core, heavy copper/aluminium bars brazed/welded/bolted to two heavy short-circuited end rings.
  • Skewed rotor slots — (1) quieter running, less magnetic hum; (2) reduce the rotor's locking (cogging) tendency.
  • Two end shields house the bearings that support the shaft.

1. Current in a coil produces magnetic flux.
  2. 3-phase supply to the stator sets up a flux of constant magnitude rotating at synchronous speed.
  3. The flux crosses the air gap and cuts the rotor conductors; the relative speed induces an EMF in them.
  4. The rotor bars form a closed loop, so current flows. It opposes the relative motion, so the rotor turns in the same direction as the field, trying to catch it.

Uses: lathes, pumps, industrial drives, fans and blowers, conveyors.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Simple, rugged, almost unbreakableSpeed cannot be varied without losing efficiency
Cheap and reliableSpeed falls as load rises
High efficiency, good power factorPoor starting torque, high starting current
Minimum maintenance (no brushes)
Starts easily, often without extra equipment

Same stator; the rotor has a 3-phase winding (usually star) brought out to slip rings with brushes connected to an external star-connected rheostat (secondary resistance).

Starting: full voltage on stator, full rotor resistance in → limited rotor current, high torque. Resistance is cut out step by step; at full speed the rings are shorted and it runs like a cage motor. Large motors add brush-lifting gear. Rotor resistance can also control speed down to about half synchronous, but wastes power.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
High starting torque with low starting currentMore maintenance than cage
Speed controllablePoorer efficiency and power factor
High overload capacity, smooth accelerationPoor speed regulation with rotor resistance in

Applications: hoists, elevators, compressors, lifts and pumps needing speed control.

sections.h: How three phases make a rotating magnetic field
sections.b:
1. The three stator windings are placed 120° apart around the stator.
  2. They are fed by three currents that are 120° apart in time (the three phases).
  3. At every instant, the three winding fields add up to one resultant field. Its strength stays constant (1.5 × the peak field of one phase).
  4. As each phase current rises and falls in turn (A → B → C), the peak of the resultant field moves from winding to winding — the field rotates.
  5. For a 2-pole stator it makes one revolution per supply cycle: 50 Hz → 50 rev/s = 3000 rpm (synchronous speed).

Reversing the motor: swap any two of the three supply lines. This reverses the phase sequence (A → C → B), so the field — and the rotor — turn the other way. This is exactly what the forward–reverse starter and plugging do.

topics.title: Synchronous Speed & Slip
topics.zh: 同步转速与转差率

sections.b:
• Frequency — cycles per second; f = 1/T.
  • Poles vs pole pairs — a 4-pole stator has 2 pole pairs (p = poles ÷ 2).
  • Synchronous speed (N) — speed of the rotating field; depends on pole pairs p and supply frequency f.
  • Rotor speed (Nr) — actual load speed. Always below N: if it caught up, no relative motion → no induced EMF → no torque.
  • Slip speed — N − Nr.

N = 60 f / p (rpm)p = pole pairs
UnitsN — revolutions per minute (rpm) †f — hertz (Hz)p — no unit† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
Slip speed = N − Nr
Unitsslip speed, N, Nr — revolutions per minute (rpm) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
s = (N − Nr) / N × 100 %standstill: s = 1 (100 %)
Unitss — percent (%)N, Nr — revolutions per minute (rpm) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
Nr = N (1 − s)
UnitsNr, N — revolutions per minute (rpm) †s — no unit† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
fr = s · fstandstill: fr = f
Unitsfr, f — hertz (Hz)s — no unit
PolesPole pairs pN at 50 Hz
213000 rpm
421500 rpm
631000 rpm
84750 rpm

This curve shows the torque a cage induction motor produces at every speed from standstill (slip = 1) to synchronous speed Ns (slip = 0).

  • Starting torque — torque at standstill. It must be larger than the load torque or the motor will not start.
  • As the motor speeds up, torque dips a little (pull-up torque), then rises to the breakdown (maximum) torque.
  • Normal running is on the steep right-hand part between breakdown and Ns. Here torque rises almost in proportion to slip: more load → slightly more slip → more torque, so speed stays nearly constant. Full-load slip is typically a few per cent.
  • If the load torque is larger than the breakdown torque, the motor stalls and draws starting current — the overload relay must trip.
  • At Ns torque is zero: the rotor would not cut any flux, so no current is induced.
T ∝ V2torque varies with the square of the supply voltage
UnitsT — newton-metre (N·m)V — volt (V)

A 10 % voltage drop leaves only 0.9² = 81 % of the torque at every speed. This is why star starting (V ÷ √3) gives ⅓ torque, and why a long, undersized cable can stop a loaded motor from starting.

worked.q: Slide example: a 3-phase, 6-pole squirrel-cage induction motor is connected to a 3-phase, 50 Hz supply. The motor speed is 970 rpm on load. Calculate both the synchronous and slip speeds of the motor.

No. of pole pairs p = 3, f = 50 Hz
Synchronous speed N = 60 × f / p = 60 × 50 / 3 = 1000 rpm
Rotor speed Nr = 970 rpm
Slip speed = N − Nr = 1000 − 970 = 30 rpm

topics.title: Single-Phase Induction Motors
topics.zh: 单相感应电机

sections.b:
Used where only a single-phase supply exists and the power needed is small (fractional horsepower).

A single winding gives a pulsating (not rotating) flux, so the motor is not self-starting. It is temporarily made into a 2-phase motor by adding a starting (auxiliary) winding in parallel with the running winding, with currents displaced up to ~90°.

• Stator: starting winding — thin wire, high resistance, low reactance; running winding — low resistance, high reactance.
  • Rotor: same as a 3-phase cage rotor.
  • Centrifugal switch: stationary part on the end shield, rotating part on the rotor. Cuts out the starting winding at about 75 % of rated speed.
  • Low/moderate starting torque.

Split-phase motor circuit diagram

TypeCapacitorCentrifugal switchCharacter
Capacitor-startElectrolytic, in series with starting windingYesHigh starting torque, up to 4× rated
Permanent split (PSC)Oil / pyranol, always in circuitNoHigh efficiency, high power factor
Two-value capacitorElectrolytic (start) + oil (run)YesGood start torque and near-unity PF

Split-phase and capacitor-start motors have lower power factor and efficiency than polyphase motors; capacitor start-and-run designs overcome this.

Capacitor-start motor circuit diagram

• Split-phase (low start torque): fans, blowers, centrifugal pumps.
  • Capacitor-start (high start torque): compressors, pumps, refrigeration, air-conditioning.
  • Capacitor start-and-run (quiet): oil burners, metal-working machines.

sections.h: Why the capacitor helps — and how to reverse a single-phase motor
sections.b:
To start, the motor needs two fields that peak at different times. The bigger the time (phase) difference between the two winding currents, the stronger the starting torque — the best is 90°.

  • Split-phase: the running winding is mostly inductive (its current lags a lot), the starting winding is mostly resistive (its current lags little). The difference is only modest, so starting torque is moderate.
  • The Week 6 slide calls the phase difference large (90°). In a real split-phase motor it is closer to about 30° — that is exactly why the capacitor-start version, which gets near 90°, has so much more starting torque.
  • Capacitor-start: the capacitor makes the starting-winding current lead the voltage, bringing the difference close to 90° — much higher starting torque.

Reversing: swap the two leads of the starting (auxiliary) winding (or of the running winding), not both. Swapping the two supply leads does not reverse the motor, because both windings are reversed together.

Centrifugal switch faultWhat you see
Stuck openMotor hums but does not start (it will run if spun by hand)
Stuck closedMotor starts, but the starting winding overheats and burns out

Switch ON
Main (run) winding and start winding are both energised through the closed centrifugal switch
Start winding has higher resistance (or a series capacitor) → its current is shifted in time from the main current
Two shifted fields at 90° in space → a rotating field → starting torque
Motor accelerates
Speed about 70–80 % of synchronous?
No: keep accelerating with both windings
Centrifugal switch opens → start winding disconnected
Runs on the main winding only
If the centrifugal switch sticks closed, the start winding stays on; it is only rated for a few seconds, so it overheats and burns out. If it sticks open, the motor only hums at switch-on and will not start (but will run if spun by hand).

topics.title: AC Braking & AC Drives
topics.zh: 交流制动与交流驱动

sections.b:
MethodHowNotes
MechanicalFriction between rotating parts and brake drumCan hold the load at rest
Dynamic (DC injection)Disconnect AC, inject DC into stator windingsStationary field brakes the rotor
RegenerativeMotor runs as a generator, energy returned to supplySlows rather than holds; hoists, traction, descending lifts
PluggingSwap 2 of the 3 phases → reverse torqueFastest; needs a sensor (e.g. zero-speed switch) to disconnect at standstill or it reverses

Dynamic (DC injection) braking

An AC drive controls the speed of an AC motor by:

  1. Pole changing — Nr = N(1 − s); switch between e.g. 4- and 6-pole windings. Cage motors only; needs switching.
  2. Varying voltage (slip control) — line-voltage control (works for 1-phase, not 3-phase); rotor-resistance control (wound rotor); rotor-voltage control.
  3. Varying frequency (VFD) — variable voltage and frequency supply.

• Variable voltage & frequency — simplest: transformer → controlled rectifier → filter (variable DC) → variable-frequency inverter.
  • PWM — most complex, most efficient: switches the DC bus into pulses; wider pulse = higher output voltage.
  • Cyclo-converter — converts a higher frequency/voltage directly to a lower variable frequency/voltage.
  • Flux vector PWM — microprocessor + closed-loop feedback, DC-motor-like control: excellent speed/torque control, fast response; the motor's parameters must be programmed or auto-tuned.

Inverter: DC → variable AC. Converter: higher frequency → lower frequency.

sections.h: Inside a variable frequency drive (VFD) — and the V/f rule
sections.b:
A VFD has three stages:

  1. Rectifier — diodes turn the incoming AC into DC.
  2. DC bus — capacitors smooth the DC (a braking resistor may be fitted here to absorb energy when the motor slows a heavy load).
  3. Inverter — fast transistors (IGBTs) switch the DC on and off in pulses (PWM) to build a new AC output of any frequency and voltage.

Why frequency changes speed: synchronous speed N = 60f/p. A 4-pole motor runs near 1500 rpm at 50 Hz, near 750 rpm at 25 Hz.

The V/f rule: the motor's magnetic flux is proportional to V/f. If the drive lowered the frequency but kept full voltage, the flux would rise, the iron would saturate and the motor would draw too much current and overheat. So the drive lowers the voltage in proportion to the frequency, keeping V/f constant and the torque available:

V/f = 400 V ÷ 50 Hz = 8 V/Hzat 25 Hz → 200 V
UnitsV — volt (V)f — hertz (Hz)V/f — volt per hertz (V/Hz)
  • At very low speed a small extra voltage (torque boost) makes up for the winding resistance.
  • Above 50 Hz the voltage cannot go higher than the supply, so flux and available torque fall (field weakening).

Benefits: smooth soft start with low current, adjustable ramp-up/ramp-down times, large energy savings on fans and pumps, and built-in DC injection braking.

1. Rectifier — a diode bridge turns the fixed 50 Hz AC into DC (still rippled).
  2. DC bus (link) — large capacitors smooth the DC. The slide’s diagram shows a 480 V three-phase input giving a DC bus of +650 Vdc.
  3. Inverter — IGBT transistors switch the DC bus on and off thousands of times a second (PWM). By varying the pulse widths the drive builds an AC output of any chosen frequency and voltage.
Ns = 120 f / Pspeed follows frequency
UnitsNs — revolutions per minute (rpm) †f — hertz (Hz)P — no unit† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
V / f = constant400 V ÷ 50 Hz = 8 V/Hz keeps the flux constant
UnitsV — volt (V)f — hertz (Hz)V/f — volt per hertz (V/Hz)

topics.title: Motor Installation & Maintenance
topics.zh: 电机安装与维护

sections.b:
First rule: follow the manufacturer's manual.

  1. Cables sized to carry full-load current continuously without overheating.
  2. Overload relay set to the machine's full-load current.
  3. Voltage drop from consumer terminals to motor terminals ≤ 4 % of nominal.
  4. Means of isolation and switching.
  5. Overcurrent protection (machine + fire hazard).
  6. All metal frames of controllers earthed.

1. Mount rigidly on a solid foundation (noise, vibration).
  2. Align couplings and set belt tension correctly (bearing wear).

Power transmission: direct coupling (shafts joined end to end) or belt drive (parallel shafts, pulleys, flexible belt).

EnclosureUse
Open drip-proofIndoors, fairly clean air, little splashing
Totally enclosed non-ventilatedCorrosive or harmful environments
Totally enclosed fan-cooled (TEFC)Corrosive, dirty or moist surroundings
Explosion-proofFlammable/hazardous areas: oil & gas, chemical

• Preventive — physical inspection to keep parts in good condition.
  • Corrective — least desired; replace worn/damaged parts.
  • Planned — regular schedule; good overview of reliability.

Bearing lubrication: right grade and amount. Under-lubrication → pitting; over-lubrication → grease splashes on windings and damages insulation.

  • Mineral/synthetic — general and high-speed use.
  • Silicone — wide temperature range, stable viscosity; not for high load/speed.
  • Food-grade — food & beverage hygiene; resists wash-out.

Use a torque wrench where bolt tightness is critical; check sprocket/belt alignment; vacuum dust from windings (dust → overheating); check motor speed.

The voltage drop from the consumer's terminals to the motor terminals must not exceed 4 % of the nominal voltage (the figure in the notes).

Supply4 % allowed dropMinimum at the motor
400 V 3-phase400 × 0.04 = 16 V384 V
230 V single-phase230 × 0.04 = 9.2 V220.8 V

How to check: with the motor running at full load, measure the voltage at the main switchboard and at the motor terminals at the same time. The difference is the drop. A large drop causes low torque (T ∝ V²), slow starting, high current and overheating. Cures: a larger cable, a shorter route, or a supply closer to the motor.

sections.h: Operation, back EMF and armature reaction
sections.b:
Field and armature currents each make a magnetic field; their interaction produces torque. As the armature turns, its conductors cut the field and an EMF is induced opposing the supply — the back EMF Eb.

Armature reaction — the armature's own field distorts the main-pole flux, causing sparking at the brushes.

  • Interpoles (small motors) — small poles between main poles, in series with the armature, so compensation tracks load.
  • Compensating windings (large motors) — in slots in the pole faces, in series with the armature, current opposite to armature current, cancel reaction around the whole periphery.

sections.h: How a DC motor produces torque (motor action)
sections.b:
A conductor carrying current in a magnetic field feels a force:

F = B · I · LB = flux density (T), I = current (A), L = conductor length in the field (m)
UnitsF — newton (N)B — tesla (T)I — ampere (A)L — metre (m)

Direction — Fleming's left-hand rule (for motors): hold the first three fingers of your left hand at right angles.

  • First finger → Field (N to S)
  • Second finger → Current
  • Thumb → Motion (force)

Conductors under a N pole and conductors under a S pole carry current in opposite directions, so their forces push the armature the same way round — that is the torque.

The commutator's job: as each coil passes the neutral zone between poles, the brushes move onto the next commutator segments and the coil current reverses. Without this, the torque would reverse every half turn and the armature would just rock back and forth.

Reversing a DC motor: reverse either the armature current or the field current — not both (reversing both keeps the same direction).

Why large DC motors need a starter: at standstill the back EMF is zero, so the only thing limiting armature current is the small armature resistance: Ia = V / Ra. A starting resistor limits this current until the motor speeds up and builds back EMF.

worked.q: A 220 V DC motor has Ra = 0.5 Ω. Find the armature current at the instant of starting (no starter), and when running with Eb = 210 V.
worked.s:
Start: Eb = 0 → Ia = 220 / 0.5 = 440 A
Running: Ia = (220 − 210) / 0.5 = 20 A
The starting current is 22 × the running current → a starting resistor is needed.

topics.title: Shunt, Series & Compound Motors
topics.zh: 并励、串励与复励电机

sections.b:
Field winding in parallel with the armature.

V = Eb + IaRaI = Ia + IfIf = V / Rf
UnitsV, Eb — volt (V)I, Ia, If — ampere (A)Ra, Rf — ohm (Ω)

Speed falls as field current rises (N ∝ 1/Φ). Speed–torque curve is nearly flat — almost constant speed from no load to full load.

Uses: constant speed (drill press); several selectable speeds each held constant (lathes).

Field winding in series with the armature.

V = Eb + I(Ra + Rs)I = Ia
UnitsV, Eb — volt (V)I, Ia — ampere (A)Ra, Rs — ohm (Ω)

Very high speed at no load → never start without a load. Very high starting torque.

Uses: hoists, cranes, trains; loads directly coupled whose torque rises with speed (fans).

Short-shunt compound motor

Long-shunt compound motor

Has both shunt and series fields. Short-shunt: shunt field across the armature only. Long-shunt: shunt field across armature + series field.

Uses: large starting torque where load may drop so low a series motor would overspeed; fluctuating loads (stamping press); fluctuating supply voltage (traction).

Eb = 2PΦNZ / (60c)P = pole pairs, Φ = flux/pole (Wb), Z = conductors, c = parallel paths
UnitsEb — volt (V)Φ — weber (Wb)N — revolutions per minute (rpm) †P, Z, c — no unit† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use

CurveShapeWhy
Shunt: speed vs field currentFalls as field current rises (steep at low If)N ∝ 1/Φ
Shunt: speed vs torqueAlmost flat — speed drops only slightly from no load to full load (typically about 5–10 %)Only the small IaRa drop increases with load
Series: speed vs torqueFalls steeply; very high at light loadFlux rises with load current, so speed falls as load rises
CompoundBetween shunt and seriesHas both fields

Torque and current:

  • Shunt motor: flux is constant, so T ∝ Ia.
  • Series motor: flux ∝ Ia (until the iron saturates), so T ∝ Ia² — this is why it has such high starting torque.
Safety: never open the field circuit of a running shunt motor. With the flux almost gone, the motor either races to a dangerous speed or draws a very large armature current.

sections.h: Series motor braking and when to use each speed method
sections.b:
The slides show these as diagrams — here is what each one does:

  • Rheostatic (dynamic) braking: disconnect the supply and connect the armature and series field across a braking resistor. The field connections are reversed relative to the armature, so the current the motor now generates still flows through the field in the original direction. If they were not reversed, the generated current would cancel the field and the braking would collapse.
  • Plugging: reverse the armature connections (the field stays the same) and add a current-limiting resistor. The armature sees V + Eb, giving strong reverse torque. Disconnect at standstill or the motor runs in reverse.
  • Regenerative braking: not possible with a plain series motor — as speed rises, Eb cannot exceed V while the field is fed by the same current. For regeneration (e.g. in traction) the field is reconnected to be separately excited.
Shunt speed methodSpeed rangeNotes
Field control (field rheostat)Above rated speedEfficient — the field current is small
Armature resistance controlBelow rated speedWasteful — the full armature current heats the resistor
Armature voltage control (DC drive)Below rated speed, smoothEfficient; used by SCR drives and choppers

topics.title: DC Drives
topics.zh: 直流驱动

sections.b:
A DC drive is a speed-control system that supplies the motor voltage for the desired speed. Raising or lowering the applied voltage changes the speed — up to rated voltage.

  • Power diodes — robust diodes for high forward current / high reverse voltage where small-signal diodes would overheat.
  • SCR (thyristor) — conducts once a small gate pulse is applied; stays on until the AC voltage crosses natural zero, then turns off until the next gate pulse. Used to turn fixed AC into variable DC.

1. 1-phase half-wave rectifier — one diode; simple and cheap, but uses only half the waveform → low average voltage.
  2. 1-phase half-controlled — diodes + SCRs, phase-controlled DC output.
  3. 1-phase fully-controlled — all SCRs.
  4. 3-phase fully-controlled bridge — large motors, smoother DC.
  5. DC chopper — SCR/transistor chops DC into pulses.
V0 = Ton/(Ton+Toff) · Vs = (Ton/T)·Vs = A·VsA = duty cycle
UnitsV0, Vs — volt (V)Ton, Toff, T — second (s)A — no unit
The slide says "3 electronic circuits" but lists five; learn all five.

sections.h: How an SCR varies DC motor speed (firing-angle control)
sections.b:
The idea: with the field held constant, a DC motor's speed follows its armature voltage (N ∝ Eb/Φ, and Eb = V − IaRa). More average armature voltage → higher speed. The SCR drive's whole job is to turn fixed AC into an adjustable average DC voltage.

How an SCR behaves:

  • Three terminals: anode, cathode and gate.
  • It turns ON only when the anode is positive and a short pulse arrives at the gate.
  • Once on, it latches — the gate pulse can be removed and it keeps conducting.
  • It turns OFF only when its current falls below the holding current. On AC this happens by itself when the supply passes through zero (natural commutation).

Controlling the pulse = controlling the voltage. A firing circuit, synchronised to the AC supply, waits an angle α (the firing or delay angle) after each zero crossing before sending the gate pulse. The SCR then conducts only from α to the end of that half-cycle, so the motor receives only that slice of each wave.

  • Small α (fire early) → wide slice → high average voltage → high speed.
  • Large α (fire late) → narrow slice → low average voltage → low speed.
  • α = 180° → the SCR never fires → no voltage → motor stops.
Half-wave (1 SCR): Vdc = Vm(1 + cos α) / 2π
UnitsVdc, Vm — volt (V)α — degree (°) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
Half-controlled bridge: Vdc = Vm(1 + cos α) / π
UnitsVdc, Vm — volt (V)α — degree (°) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
Fully controlled bridge (continuous current): Vdc = 2Vm cos α / π
UnitsVdc, Vm — volt (V)α — degree (°) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
3-phase fully controlled: Vdc = 1.35 · VL · cos αVm = √2 × Vrms
UnitsVdc, VL, Vm, Vrms — volt (V)α — degree (°) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use
With a fully controlled bridge, α above 90° makes the average voltage negative. The converter then works as an inverter, sending the motor's energy back to the AC supply — this is how SCR drives perform regenerative braking.

sections.h: Closed-loop control and the chopper (pulse-width) method
sections.b:
Closed-loop speed control: the set speed (from a potentiometer or PLC) is compared with the actual speed measured by a tachogenerator or encoder. The difference (error) goes to a controller, which moves the firing angle automatically. If load increases and the motor slows, the error grows, the controller reduces α, the voltage rises and the speed recovers. A current-limit loop stops the armature current from getting too high when starting.

Chopper on a DC supply: when the supply is already DC (e.g. a battery), the switch is turned fully ON for Ton and OFF for Toff, hundreds or thousands of times a second. This is pulse-width modulation: V0 = (Ton/T)·Vs. Wider ON pulses → higher average voltage → higher speed. The armature's inductance and the motor's inertia smooth the pulses into steady rotation.

Turning the SCR off in a chopper: DC never passes through zero, so an SCR cannot switch itself off. Chopper SCRs need a forced-commutation circuit — usually a charged capacitor that briefly reverse-biases the SCR. This is why modern choppers mostly use transistors (MOSFET or IGBT), which switch off with just a gate signal.

Phase (firing-angle) controlChopper (pulse-width) control
SupplyAC mainsDC (battery or rectified DC)
What is variedFiring angle αDuty cycle Ton/T
How the SCR turns offNaturally at each zero crossingForced commutation circuit
Typical useMains-fed DC drives, large motorsBattery vehicles, forklifts, small drives

worked.q: Chopper: Vs = 220 V, Ton = 3 ms, Toff = 2 ms. Output voltage?
Half-controlled bridge on a 230 V AC supply. Find V<sub>dc</sub> at α = 0°, 60° and 90°.
The motor runs at 1500 rpm on 207 V (α = 0°). Roughly what speed at α = 60°? (Ignore IaRa, field constant.)
worked.s:
N ∝ V

Firing 60° later cut the speed by about a quarter.

topics.title: Servo Motors & Encoders
topics.zh: 伺服电机与编码器

sections.b:
A servo = motor + encoder + driver. The driver compares the position command with encoder feedback and controls drive current — an automatic closed-loop system.

Hobby/position servo control: 3 wires (+, ground, control). A PWM pulse every 20 ms; pulse width sets shaft angle:

Pulse widthShaft position
1.0 ms−90° (anticlockwise)
1.5 ms0° (neutral)
2.0 ms+90° (clockwise)
  • DC servo — usually separate DC supplies for field and armature; control by field or armature current, chosen by application.
  • AC servo — built-in encoder, high accuracy; robotics, automation, CNC.

An encoder converts motion into an electrical signal (position, count, speed, direction) for a controller such as a PLC.

  • Optical — LED shines through a code disk; opaque lines interrupt it; photodetector makes pulses (light = on).
  • Magnetic — magnet on shaft, field sensor gives absolute position. Robust, simple, economical (no battery/gear), compact.
AbsoluteIncremental
OutputUnique code for every positionPulse each time the shaft moves
At power-upKnows position immediately; nothing lost when offStarts counting from zero — needs homing (battery backup helps)
VariantsSingle-turn (short travel), multi-turn (long/complex)Channels A, B in quadrature
CostHigherSimpler, cheaper
Good forExact machine positionSpeed, direction, pulse counting

Resolution — smallest measurable step, given in pulses per revolution (PPR); fixed at manufacture. Accuracy — difference between true and reported position; depends on consistent width and spacing of the lines. They are independent.

sections.h: The servo drive (amplifier) — what boosts voltage and current
sections.b:
A motion controller (a PLC or motion card) only sends out a small command signal — a few volts and a few milliamps, far too weak to turn a motor. The driver, also called the servo amplifier or servo drive, sits between the controller and the motor:

  1. It receives the command (position, speed or torque) from the controller.
  2. It compares the command with the encoder feedback to find the error.
  3. It amplifies the result into the high voltage and current the motor windings need, using power from its own supply.
  4. It keeps correcting until the error is zero — this is the closed loop.
Exam answer: The amplifier (servo driver) increases the amplitude of the voltage and current of the motion controller's signal so it can drive the motor.

The same idea appears elsewhere in the course: the stepper driver delivers current to the correct winding, and a PLC output module has an amplifier stage before its output terminals.

Servo motorStepper motor
Control loopClosed loop (encoder feedback)Usually open loop (no feedback)
If the load is too heavyError is detected and correctedSteps are missed without warning
Torque at high speedMaintained wellFalls off as speed rises
Cost and complexityHigherLower, simpler
Typical useRobots, CNC axes, fast precise motionPrinters, plotters, light positioning

sections.h: Encoders — more points from the slides
sections.b:
• Absolute encoder: able to determine the exact position of a machine and control over the storage of electronic data; multiple interface options — analog, Ethernet, fieldbus, parallel, serial; optical and magnetic measuring principles.
  • Incremental encoder: each time it is powered on it begins counting from zero, regardless of where the shaft is or its previous position; it stores the data in an external buffer or counter; battery backups can help eliminate the need for re-homing after planned or unplanned shutdowns; typically simpler to use and cheaper than absolute encoders.
  • Direction: incremental encoders often output on two channels, A and B, offset by 90 degrees (in quadrature). Generally, if channel A is leading the direction is taken to be clockwise; if channel B is leading, counterclockwise.
  • Magnetic encoder advantages: robust and durable; mechanically simple and economical — no battery, no gear; compact design for installation in small spaces.

terms: 伺服放大器（伺服驱动器）
recap: A servo consists of a ___, an ___ and a ___.
A servo is controlled by a ___ signal on the control wire.
___ encoders give unique position values from switch-on.
For speed and direction monitoring we could use the ___ encoder.
Consistent ___ and ___ of the lines is key to incremental accuracy.

topics.title: Stepper Motors
topics.zh: 步进电机

sections.b:
• Electromagnetic device that rotates in discrete steps; converts digital pulses into shaft motion.
  • Each pulse → a small fixed angle. Shaft angle ∝ number of pulses; speed ∝ pulse frequency.
Step angle θ = 360° / steps per revolution
Unitsθ — degree (°) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use

1. Permanent magnet — most basic type.
  2. Variable reluctance — soft-iron rotor; coils energised in opposite pairs attract the rotor.
  3. Hybrid — permanent magnet + variable reluctance features.

Advantages: digital control; simple open-loop (no feedback); brushless; positional error is non-cumulative; speed set by signal frequency.

Applications: robots, printers, plotters, disk drives, photocopiers, scanners.

• Full-step — rotor pulled by two stator coils each step → high torque.
  • Half-step — an extra step with only one winding on between full steps → double the steps, twice the resolution, with somewhat less torque.

Driver: generates the pulse train, controls frequency/width, sequences the windings and delivers current to the correct winding from the positioning command.

Full-step operation — the rotor is pulled each time by the field of two stator coils.

Half-step operation — an additional step is put between each two full steps by switching on only one winding.

The two windings are A–A′ and B–B′. The driver energises them in a fixed order; running the order backwards reverses the motor.

ModeSequence (one cycle)Steps per cycleTorque
Wave drive (one phase on)A → B → A′ → B′4Lowest
Full step (two phases on)AB → BA′ → A′B′ → B′A4Highest
Half stepA → AB → B → BA′ → A′ → A′B′ → B′ → B′A8Between (alternates)

Half-stepping mixes one-phase-on and two-phase-on states, so it gives twice as many steps per revolution — the resolution doubles without changing the motor.

sections.h: Full-step drive on a timing chart
sections.b:
In two-phase-on full step, both coils are energised all the time and the controller reverses one coil current at each step. Each step moves the rotor field 90° electrical, which is one mechanical step (1.8° on a 200-step motor). Four steps complete one electrical cycle, then the pattern repeats.

  • To reverse, run the same table backwards.
  • The speed is set by the pulse rate; the distance by the number of pulses.
  • With both coils on, torque is about √2 times one-coil-on (wave) drive.
rev/s = pulses per second × step angle / 360°
Unitsspeed — revolutions per second (rev/s) †pulse rate — pulses per second (pulses/s)step angle — degree (°) †† not an SI unit, but it is the unit your notes use

worked.q: 32 steps per revolution. Step angle?
Printer motor, 96 steps/rev. Step angle?
Step angle 7.5°. Steps for two revolutions?
worked.s:
Steps/rev = 360/7.5 = 48
Two revs = 96 steps

worked.q: 256 rpm stepper with an 8:1 step-down. Output speed?
A 1.8° stepper (200 steps/rev) runs in half-step mode. Find the new step angle, steps per revolution, and pulses needed to turn 90°.
worked.s:
Half step → step angle = 1.8 ÷ 2 = 0.9°
Steps/rev = 360 ÷ 0.9 = 400
90° → 90 ÷ 0.9 = 100 pulses

worked.q: A 1.8° stepper is driven at 2000 pulses/s in half-step mode. Find the speed in rpm.
worked.s:
Half step angle = 1.8 ÷ 2 = 0.9°
rev/s = 2000 × 0.9 ÷ 360 = 5 rev/s
rpm = 5 × 60 = 300 rpm

topics.title: DC Motor Maintenance
topics.zh: 直流电机维护

sections.b:
TaskInterval
Wipe off dust, dirt, oil externallyMonthly
Clean vent screens and fansQuarterly
Lubricate bearings (if applicable)Semi-annual
Vacuum dust/abrasives from windingsSemi-annual
Check commutator, brushes, leadsSemi-annual
Check brush spring tensionSemi-annual
Test field coils and armature windingsSemi-annual
Check electrical connectionsSemi-annual

High-wear parts: the commutator and brush assembly — spend extra time inspecting, repairing or replacing them. Also inspect bearings; replace worn/noisy ones; lubricate if not sealed.

1. Motor fitted with sensors that collect data continuously.
  2. Data sent to a local database.
  3. AI raises alerts when data deviates from normal — it continuously scans for problems.

Detectable faults: overload, supply problems, misalignment, bearing problems, cooling problems, structural problems.

Isolate the motor, lock off and tag, and prove dead with a tester
Disconnect the motor cables from the drive / controller — never megger through a VFD or DC drive; the test voltage can destroy the electronics
Clean and dry the terminals. Note the winding temperature.
Choose the test voltage: 500 V DC is usual for low-voltage motors (up to about 1 kV rating)
Test each winding (armature, field, or each phase) to frame/earth, and between windings. Hold the test for 1 minute, then read.
Reading acceptable?
No → dry the winding (low heat) and retest; if still low, the insulation is damaged or contaminated — rewind or replace
Discharge the winding to earth after each test — it stores charge like a capacitor
Record the reading, the test voltage and the temperature. Compare with earlier records.

Judging the result: many sites use 1 MΩ as the absolute minimum for a low-voltage motor; the IEEE 43 guide recommends at least 5 MΩ for windings rated below 1 kV. A clean, dry, healthy motor usually reads hundreds of MΩ or more. The trend matters most: a reading that keeps falling from one test to the next shows the insulation is deteriorating, even if it is still above the minimum.

Polarisation index (PI) = reading at 10 min ÷ reading at 1 min. A PI of about 2 or more indicates clean, dry insulation; close to 1 indicates moisture or contamination.

topics.title: DC Motor Troubleshooting
topics.zh: 直流电机故障排除

sections.b:
CauseTypeCheck
Open fuseElectricalMultimeter
Dirty brushesElectricalInspect; replace periodically
Open armature circuitElectricalMultimeter
Shorted or grounded fieldElectricalMegger
Shorted armature or commutatorElectricalGrowler
Worn bearingsMechanicalInspect; replace
Grounded brush holderElectricalMultimeter
OverloadMechanicalCheck load
Defective controllerElectricalCheck output

SymptomCauses
Runs slowlyShorted armature/commutator (E), worn bearings (M), open armature coils (E), overload (M), wrong voltage (E)
NoisyWorn bearings, high or low commutator bars, rough commutator, unbalanced armature — all mechanical
Runs hotOverload (M), sparking (E — brushes, shorted coil), shorted coils (E — growler/multimeter), too much brush pressure (M — alignment)

sections.h: Fault-finding flowchart: DC motor fails to run
sections.b:
DC motor will not run
Supply and fuses OK at the controller input?
No → replace the fuse, then find out why it blew (short, overload)
Controller giving armature and field output voltage?
No → defective controller / drive (check its fault display, enable signal, speed reference)
Voltage reaching the motor terminals?
No → loose or broken cable, bad connection
Field circuit OK (continuity and field current)?
No → open or shorted field. Never run a shunt motor with an open field — it can overspeed.
Armature circuit continuous (through brushes)?
No → worn or sticking brushes, weak spring, grounded brush holder, open armature coil
Shaft turns freely by hand?
No → worn or seized bearings, or jammed / overloaded machine
Test armature and commutator for shorts (growler) and insulation to frame (megger)

topics.title: Automating with a PLC
topics.zh: 用PLC实现自动化

sections.b: First developed at General Motors in 1968 to replace complex relay control. IEC 61131-1 definition: a digitally operating electronic system for industrial environments, using programmable memory to store user instructions for logic, sequencing, timing, counting and arithmetic, controlling machines/processes through digital or analogue I/O. In short: a computer tailored for control. Examples: Festo FEC, Mitsubishi FX0, Siemens S7-300.

PLC advantages: easier to program than to wire relays; reprogrammable; less floor space; easier maintenance, higher reliability; connects to plant computers easily; shorter installation/commissioning.

Reasons for automating: productivity, high labour cost, labour shortage, safety, high raw-material cost, quality, shorter lead time.

Hard-wiredPLC
CostCheap for few pointsCheaper for many points
WiringMoreLess
DeviceSpecific purposeGeneral purpose
ScaleSmall–mediumMedium–large
ChangesDifficult, space limitsEasy, flexible
Power useHighLow
ReliabilityContact problemsFewer contact problems
TroubleshootingDifficultEasy; self-diagnostics

vs relay: fast, easy install, compact, flexible, reliable, simple maintenance. vs computer: low cost, simple to program, modular, error-checking, suits industrial environments.

Since 1992 an international standard defines PLC design/functionality and programming languages so users can move between brands. Supported by ABB, GE Fanuc, Mitsubishi, Moeller, OMRON, Schneider, Siemens.

topics.title: Components of a PLC
topics.zh: PLC的组成

sections.b: Input module · Output module · Processor (CPU) · Memory · Power supply · Programming device.

Connects limit switches, push buttons, sensors. Functions: reliable signal detection, adjust control voltage to logic voltage, protect electronics from external voltages, screen signals.

Optocoupler — passes the signal by light → electrical isolation (up to ~5 kV).

Positive switching — PLC input is a current sink; sensor supplies the voltage (1-signal). Negative switching — PLC input acts as the source.

Signal → optocoupler → short-circuit monitoring → amplifier → output, driving motors, valves, lamps.

Relay outputs work with different output voltages. Transistor outputs switch much faster and last longer.

CPU — the "brain"; microprocessor(s) execute the program against input states to set outputs.

Memory (1 K to 48 K+): program memory (user program) and data memory (I/O states, timer/counter values — change as program runs).

TypeKey fact
RAMRead/write, easy to change, volatile — needs backup battery
EPROMFast, low cost, non-volatile
EEPROMElectrically erasable and rewritable; widely used application memory

Power supply — AC → low-voltage DC for CPU logic (and sometimes I/O). Programming device — hand-held or PC; enters programs, shows timers/counters and diagnostics.

topics.title: Operation of PLCs
topics.zh: PLC的运行

sections.b:
Programmable internal relays replace hard-wired control relays. Inputs switch input relays; the program sets output relays, grouped in modules of 8/16/32. The CPU only knows addresses (e.g. inputs start at 0.00, then 0.01, 0.02 …; outputs start at 1.00, then 1.01, 1.02 …); timers, counters and internal relays all have addresses too.

Input path: PB closes → LED in opto-isolator lights → phototransistor conducts → input relay energises. Output path: CPU energises output relay 0.5 → contact closes → external supply powers the load (the relay isolates).

Cycle: (1) read inputs, (2) execute program, (3) set outputs, with housekeeping (diagnostics) between. Scan time depends on I/O count, program length and instruction types — typically 10 ms per 500 instruction words, so the PLC appears simultaneous.

Sensor outputs: AC or DC; relay or solid-state (2-, 3-, 4-wire). 3-wire is most popular; 4-wire adds both NO and NC outputs. Solid state is NPN (sinking) or PNP (sourcing).

Matching rule: NPN sensor → source-type (common positive) input module. PNP sensor → sink-type (common negative) input module.

Outputs are "dry" — the load's power comes from an external supply; the module is just an isolated switch. Choose by load current, AC/DC, and switching speed.

Output typeLoadCurrentResponse
RelayAC/DC2 A typ10 ms
Triac (solid-state relay)AC1 A typ1 ms
Transistor (NPN/PNP)DC1 A typ0.3 ms
The source table lists the transistor output load as "AC"; transistor outputs switch DC loads.

sections.h: Sinking and sourcing — follow the current
sections.b:
Conventional current flows from + to −. Ask: which device supplies the +24 V to the input signal wire?

PNP sensor (sourcing)NPN sensor (sinking)
What the sensor switchesConnects its output to +24 VConnects its output to 0 V
Current path+24 V → sensor → PLC input → input common (0 V)+24 V → input common → PLC input → sensor → 0 V
PLC input module neededSink type (common = 0 V)Source type (common = +24 V)
Memory aid: PNP switches the Positive; NPN switches the Negative. The PLC input must be the opposite type so a complete loop is formed.

3-wire sensor colours (IEC standard): brown = +24 V, blue = 0 V, black = signal output.

If the types are mismatched (e.g. NPN sensor on a sink input), there is no complete current path — the sensor's own LED may light, but the PLC input never turns on.

topics.title: Material Handling Systems
topics.zh: 物料搬运系统

sections.b:
Move materials point to point; advantages: safety and productivity.

  • Roller — rollers in frames; powered for heavy loads; non-powered need an incline (gravity) or manual push.
  • Belt — powered at one end, idler at the other; baggage handling, packaging.
  • Overhead — ceiling-mounted, lighter loads, saves floor space; garment lines, parts that must cool/dry/cure.

Driverless vehicles moving raw materials, pallets, containers. Advantages: efficiency, productivity.

NavigationPath changes
Wire in floor slotFixed; costly to change
Guide tape (magnetic/coloured)Fixed; easier to change
Laser target (reflectors)Easy — move reflectors / update program
Vision (cameras)No changes to environment needed

ASRS — highly automated store/retrieve in a fixed facility; narrow aisles, tall racks. Consider volume, standard vs odd loads, space. Advantages: minimal unneeded stock, better organisation, inventory tracking.

Material handling robots — consider payload, work envelope, space. Uses: part transfer, packing, palletising, pick-and-place. Advantages: versatility (swap end effector), accuracy and repeatability.

sections.h: 4.1 What a material handling system does
sections.b:
A material handling system (MHS) moves, stores and keeps track of materials — raw materials coming in, work-in-progress between machines, and finished products going out. Every one of the four technologies in this chapter does one or more of these jobs:

JobTechnology in this chapter
Move material along a fixed routeConveyors (roller, belt, overhead)
Move material along a flexible routeAGV
Store and retrieve materialASRS
Pick, place, pack, stackMaterial handling robots

Where the PLC fits. Each of these systems is run by a controller. A PLC typically starts and stops conveyor motors (through contactors or VFDs), reads the photo-eyes and proximity sensors along the line, controls diverters and stoppers, talks to AGVs and robots through handshake signals, and controls the cranes in an ASRS. Above the PLCs, a warehouse or production computer decides what should move where; the PLCs make it happen safely.

Why automate material handling? Moving material adds cost but no value to the product. Automating it cuts manual labour, reduces injuries from lifting and forklifts, reduces damage, and gives an accurate record of where every item is.

sections.h: 4.2 Conveyors in detail — roller, belt and overhead
sections.b:
Roller conveyors

  • Gravity (non-powered): installed on a slight downward slope so the load rolls by itself, or level so an operator pushes it. No motor, no electricity — cheap and simple, but the speed cannot be controlled and loads need a flat, rigid bottom (cartons, totes, pallets).
  • Powered: rollers are driven by a chain, a belt or a line shaft under the rollers, or each zone has a motor-driven roller (MDR) — a small 24 V DC motor built inside one roller. Used for heavier loads and where loads must be stopped, spaced or queued.
  • Zero-pressure accumulation: a powered roller line is split into zones, each with a sensor. A zone only runs if the zone in front is empty, so loads queue up without touching each other — no crushing of cartons.

Belt conveyors

  • A continuous belt runs round a head (drive) pulley at one end and a tail (idler) pulley at the other, as in the notes. The motor and gearbox drive the head pulley.
  • Carrying idlers (or a flat slider bed) support the loaded top run; return idlers support the empty bottom run.
  • A take-up keeps the belt tight so the drive pulley does not slip; the belt must also be tracked (kept centred).
  • Good for small, soft or irregular items that would fall between rollers, and for inclines (with a rough or cleated belt). Typical uses: baggage handling, packaging, bulk materials.

Overhead conveyors

  • Mounted to the ceiling, so the floor space stays free. Loads hang from hooks or carriers.
  • Monorail (chain) type: trolleys run on an overhead track, pulled by a continuous chain — every carrier moves together.
  • Power-and-free type: carriers can be released from the moving chain to stop, wait or be switched to another track, while others keep moving.
  • Used for garment lines and for parts that must hang while they cool, dry or cure — e.g. passing slowly through a paint oven.

sections.h: PLC control of a conveyor line
sections.b:
A typical PLC-controlled belt conveyor has these field devices (see the diagram above):

DevicePLC signalPurpose
Motor contactor or VFDOutput (run) + input (running / fault)Drive the head pulley
Photo-eyeInputDetect a product at a position — count, stop, or trigger the next action
Zero-speed (motion) sensorInput (pulses)Prove the belt is really moving; detects a broken or slipping belt
Pull-cord switchHard-wired safety + inputAnyone along the conveyor can stop it
Belt misalignment switchInputBelt running off the pulleys
Diverter / stopperOutput (solenoid valve)Send product to another line / hold it

Typical program functions

  • Jam detection: if a photo-eye stays blocked longer than the time a product normally needs to pass (an on-delay timer), the PLC stops the line and raises an alarm.
  • Motion check: if the motor is commanded ON but no pulses arrive from the zero-speed sensor within a few seconds, the belt has slipped or broken → stop and alarm.
  • Counting: a counter on the photo-eye counts products, e.g. 10 per carton, then triggers the packing step.

Starting and stopping a line of conveyors

START pressed
Sound the start-up warning horn / beacon for a few seconds
Start the last (downstream) conveyor first
Is it proven running (motion sensor)?
No → stop the sequence, alarm "conveyor 3 not running"
Start the next conveyor upstream, and so on back to the first
STOP: stop the first (upstream) conveyor first, let the others run empty, then stop them in order
Why this order? Starting downstream first means every conveyor has somewhere to put its load, so nothing piles up at a transfer point. The same idea in reverse empties the line when stopping.

An automated guided vehicle (AGV) is a driverless, battery-powered vehicle that carries loads between fixed points in a facility. Main parts:

  • Drive and steering — electric motors on the wheels; steering by turning a wheel or by running the left and right wheels at different speeds.
  • Battery and charging — the AGV goes to a charger when its battery is low, or charges briefly at stations during idle time ("opportunity charging").
  • Navigation sensors — find where the AGV is (see the table).
  • Safety devices — a safety laser scanner and/or bumpers in front: the AGV slows when something is ahead and stops before contact. Emergency stop buttons on the vehicle.
  • Load transfer — tugger (tows carts), unit-load (carries a pallet or tote on a deck or roller top), or forklift AGV (lifts pallets from the floor or racks).
  • Fleet management system — a central computer that gives each AGV its jobs and controls traffic at junctions, over Wi-Fi.

Navigation methods (from the notes) — how each one works

MethodHow it senses the pathPath change
WireAn AC current in a wire buried in a floor slot makes a magnetic field. Two pick-up coils on the AGV compare the signal strength left and right and steer to keep them equal.Fixed; costly — new slot must be cut
Guide tapeMagnetic tape is read by magnetic sensors; coloured tape is read by optical sensors under the AGV.Fixed; easy — lift and re-lay the tape
Laser targetA rotating laser on the AGV measures the angles to reflectors on walls and poles. From several reflectors it calculates its position (triangulation) and follows the route stored in memory.Easy — move reflectors / update the program
VisionCameras record the route during training; the AGV then recognises its surroundings and follows the stored path.Easy — no tape, wire or reflectors needed
AGV vs AMR. A classic AGV follows a defined path and stops when something blocks it. An autonomous mobile robot (AMR) builds a map of the building and plans its own route, driving around obstacles. Vision and laser navigation are the bridge between the two.

When an AGV delivers a pallet to a conveyor station, the AGV and the station PLC exchange simple ON/OFF signals (through an optical I/O link or Wi-Fi) so the load is only moved when both sides are ready:

AGV arrives and stops at the station
AGV → PLC: "In position"
Station conveyor empty and ready?
No → PLC keeps "Ready" OFF; AGV waits (time-out → alarm to fleet manager)
PLC → AGV: "Ready to receive"
Both run their rollers in the same direction → pallet transfers
Station photo-eye sees the pallet fully on → PLC → AGV: "Transfer complete"
AGV drops "In position" and drives away to its next job

The same handshake idea is used between a PLC and a robot, and between conveyors and an ASRS P&D station: request → ready → do the transfer → confirm → release.

An automated storage and retrieval system (ASRS) puts away and fetches loads automatically. As the notes say, space is used very efficiently: aisles are narrow (only wide enough for the crane) and racks are tall.

Main parts

  • Storage racks — rows of storage locations on both sides of each aisle.
  • Storage/retrieval (S/R) machine or stacker crane — runs on a floor rail along the aisle (x), lifts its carriage up the mast (y), and extends its forks or shuttle into the rack (z). Its PLC positions the crane using encoders or laser distance sensors.
  • Pick-up and deposit (P&D) station — where loads enter and leave the system, usually fed by conveyors or AGVs.
  • Computer control — a warehouse management system records which load is in which location and sends move orders to the crane controllers.

Common types

TypeStoresTypical use
Unit-loadFull palletsWarehouses, cold stores
Mini-loadTotes, trays, cartonsSmall parts, order picking
Vertical lift module (VLM)Trays in a tall cabinetSpare parts and tools stores
Carousel (horizontal / vertical)Bins that rotate to the operatorSmall parts picking
Shuttle systemTotes, one shuttle per levelHigh-throughput e-commerce

Single and dual command cycles

  • Single command: the crane makes one trip for one job — store or retrieve — and returns empty.
  • Dual command: on one trip the crane stores a load, travels to another location and retrieves a load on the way back. Two jobs per trip → higher throughput.
AdvantagesLimitations
Very high storage density (narrow aisles, tall racks)High capital cost
Unnecessary stock kept to a minimum (notes)Less flexible — loads must fit the rack and crane
Better organisation and inventory tracking (notes)Needs skilled maintenance; a crane breakdown blocks its aisle
Fewer handling errors and less damage; can run with lights offBest when volume is high (notes)

Robot types used for handling

TypeMovementBest for
Articulated (usually 6-axis)Rotary joints like a human armGeneral handling, machine loading, palletising heavy loads
SCARAFast horizontal moves in one plane + vertical strokeFast small-part pick-and-place, assembly
Cartesian / gantryStraight X–Y–Z axesLarge work areas, heavy palletising, overhead transfer
Delta (parallel)Three light arms from an overhead baseVery fast picking of light items from a conveyor
Collaborative (cobot)Force-limited, works beside peopleLight packing and handling without full guarding

End effectors — the reason robots are versatile

  • Mechanical gripper (2- or 3-finger, pneumatic or electric) — rigid parts with surfaces to grip.
  • Vacuum gripper — suction cups and a vacuum generator. Ideal for flat, smooth, non-porous items (sheets, boxes, glass).
  • Magnetic gripper — ferrous (steel) parts only.
  • Fork / clamp / bag gripper — palletising sacks and cartons.

Changing the end effector (for example from a gripper to a vacuum cup, as in the notes) changes what the robot can handle without buying a new robot.

Selecting a robot (factors in the notes, explained)

  • Payload — the rated mass includes the end effector, not just the part.
  • Work envelope / reach — every pick and place point must be inside the volume the robot can reach.
  • Space constraints — floor, wall or ceiling mounting, and room for safety guarding.
  • Also: repeatability (how exactly it returns to the same point), speed / cycle time, and the number of axes needed.

A PLC-controlled pick-and-place cell

Robot at home, cell guards closed, safety circuit healthy
Conveyor brings a part; photo-eye stops it at the pick position
PLC → robot: "Part present" + program number; robot → PLC: "Busy"
Robot picks the part (gripper closes / vacuum ON), checks it is held (gripper or vacuum sensor)
Part held?
No → robot retries once, then stops and signals "Fault"
Robot places the part, returns, sends "Done"
PLC releases the next part
Safety: guard doors, light curtains and area scanners are wired to a safety relay or safety PLC that stops the robot. Signals such as "part present" are for sequencing only — never for protecting people.

ConveyorAGVASRSRobot
RouteFixedFlexibleInside the storeWithin its reach
Floor spaceTakes a permanent strip (overhead saves floor)Shares aisles with peopleVery little per item storedSmall cell + guarding
ThroughputVery high, continuousMedium, per tripSet by crane cyclesSet by cycle time

worked.q: A belt conveyor: motor 1440 rpm, gearbox 24:1, head pulley Ø200 mm. Cartons are spaced every 0.5 m. Find the belt speed and the cartons per hour.
worked.s:
Pulley speed = 1440 ÷ 24 = 60 rpm
Belt speed v = π × D × N ÷ 60 = π × 0.2 × 60 ÷ 60 = 0.628 m/s
Cartons per second = 0.628 ÷ 0.5 = 1.257
Cartons per hour = 1.257 × 3600 ≈ 4520

worked.q: Same conveyor: 100 kg of cartons on a slider-bed belt, friction coefficient 0.3, gearbox efficiency 80 %. Estimate the motor power (simplified — belt weight and pulley losses ignored).
worked.s:
Friction force F = μ × m × g = 0.3 × 100 × 9.81 = 294 N
Power at the belt P = F × v = 294 × 0.628 = 185 W
Motor power = 185 ÷ 0.8 = 231 W
Choose the next standard size up, e.g. 0.37 kW

worked.q: A route is 120 m each way. AGV speed 1 m/s, loading + unloading 60 s per trip, AGVs are available 85 % of the time. How many AGVs for 40 deliveries per hour?
worked.s:
Travel = 240 m ÷ 1 m/s = 240 s
Trip time = 240 + 60 = 300 s
Trips per AGV per hour = 3600 ÷ 300 = 12
Allowing 85 %: 12 × 0.85 = 10.2 trips/h
AGVs = 40 ÷ 10.2 = 3.9 → 4 AGVs

worked.q: An ASRS crane takes 90 s for a single-command cycle and 150 s for a dual-command cycle. Compare the transactions per hour.
worked.s:
Single: 3600 ÷ 90 = 40 cycles × 1 job = 40 transactions/h
Dual: 3600 ÷ 150 = 24 cycles × 2 jobs = 48 transactions/h
Dual command gives 20 % more throughput

worked.q: A part of 8 kg is handled by a gripper of 4 kg. Is a robot rated 10 kg payload suitable?
worked.s:
Total payload = part + end effector = 8 + 4 = 12 kg
12 kg > 10 kg → NOT suitable
Choose a larger robot (e.g. 20 kg) or a lighter gripper

worked.q: Vacuum cups Ø40 mm at 0.6 bar vacuum (60 kPa) must lift a 5 kg flat sheet horizontally with a safety factor of 2. How many cups?
worked.s:
Cup area A = π × 0.02² = 1.257 × 10⁻³ m²
Force per cup F = 60 000 × 1.257 × 10⁻³ = 75.4 N (theoretical)
Required = 5 × 9.81 × 2 = 98.1 N
Cups = 98.1 ÷ 75.4 = 1.3 → 2 cups (150.8 N)

topics.title: PLC Programming Languages
topics.zh: PLC编程语言

sections.b:
GroupLanguageCharacter
GraphicalLadder Diagram (LD)Like relay ladder logic
GraphicalFunction Block Diagram (FBD)Blocks wired like circuits; popular in Europe
TextInstruction List (IL)Low-level, assembly-like; one operation per line
TextStructured Text (ST)High-level, English/BASIC-like
Flow chartSequential Function Chart (SFC)Steps and transitions

Contacts pass power left → right; coils store the result in Boolean variables. Bounded by power rails (left always ON; right optional). Parallel branches = wired-ORs. An LD network needs at least one coil and a left rail. Connectors tidy large networks; jumps go to labels; returns go back to the calling POU. LD variables are always Boolean.

FBD — functions/blocks linked by lines; outputs cannot be connected to outputs.

IL — each line: operator + operand (with optional modifiers); comments in (* … *).

LD S1 AND B1 ST T_Start

ST — statements end with a semicolon; expressions evaluated by operator precedence.

Y1 := TOF_Y1.Q; RS_Y2( S := R_TRIG_B2.Q & B3, R1 := B4 );

Steps (boxes with actions) linked by transitions (conditions). A network always has one initial step; simultaneous or alternative branches allowed. When a transition is TRUE the next step becomes active and previous steps are no longer executed.

Advantage: only active steps are scanned; program is segmented. Disadvantage: alarms cannot be monitored. Good for batch sequencing.

sections.b: Bistable flip-flop with preferred state 1. S1 = 1 sets Q1. R resets Q1 only if S1 = 0. Both 1 → Q1 = 1.

Preferred state 0. R1 = 1 resets Q1 regardless of S. S sets Q1 only if R1 = 0. Both 1 → Q1 = 0.

Example: sensor B1 (error) sounds horn H1; push button S1 silences it even while B1 stays 1 → RS_H1 with S := B1, R1 := S1.

SRSR outputRS output
00holdhold

Often the moment of change matters, not the level — one reaction per button press however long it is held.

  • Rising edge — 0 → 1 (NO push button pressed). Block R_TRIG: Q = 1 for one scan when CLK goes 0→1.
  • Falling edge — 1 → 0 (button released). Block F_TRIG: Q = 1 for one scan when CLK goes 1→0.

Example: press S1 once → furnace door opens; press again → closes (R_TRIG toggling an RS flip-flop).

sections.h: Storage operations, SR and RS — your notes’ wording
sections.b:
“Storage operations form part of the elementary PLC operations and apply in cases where a briefly occurring signal status is permanently stored. Typical examples of storage operations are the permanent setting or resetting of output signals. The standard function blocks SR and RS are available for the realization of storage functions.”

SR — set dominantRS — reset dominant
What it containsa dominant setting flip-flop (bistable memory with preferred status 1)a dominant resetting flip-flop (bistable memory with preferred status 0)
Inputs / outputS1 (set dominant), R (reset) → Q1S (set), R1 (reset dominant) → Q1
Set input = 1A 1-signal at set input S1 sets the flip-flop, i.e. the value of Q1 becomes 1.A 1-signal at set input S sets output Q1 to 1 only if a 0-signal simultaneously applies at the R1 input.
