sections.h: Edges, R_TRIG and F_TRIG — your notes’ wording
sections.b:
• “A 1-signal applies for as long as a push button is pressed, otherwise a 0-signal is received.”
  • “In many cases, however, it is not the signal itself which matters, but the exact instant during which the signal changes. This type of signal change is termed Edge.”
  • “Rising edges mark the instants in which a signal level changes from 0 to 1.”
  • “Falling edges mark the exact instants when a signal level changes from 1 to 0.”
  • “A push button (normally open contact), for instance, creates a rising edge the moment it is pressed and a falling edge the moment it is released.”
BlockDetectsOutput Q (from the notes)
R_TRIG (rising)rising or positive edges“Its output Q has the value 1 from one execution of the function block to the next, if its input CLK changes from 0 to 1.”
F_TRIG (falling)a falling or negative switching edge“If a change has taken place at input CLK from 1 to 0, output Q assumes the value 1 for one processing cycle.”

Why edges are needed (notes, 8.4.1): “only ever one single reaction per push button actuation may be triggered irrespective of how long the 1-signal applies. This prevents a process from being put in motion repeatedly by the controller, should a push button be actuated for too long.”

R_TRIG example: actuation of push button S1 causes the door of a furnace to be opened; a repeat actuation of S1 causes the door to be closed. F_TRIG example: used to monitor a garage.

Memory. A push button only gives a 1 while your finger is on it. SR and RS remember that it was pressed, so the output stays on after you let go — the same job as a holding (latching) contact in a relay circuit.

Dominant = who wins when both are pressed. The two blocks behave the same in every case except one: both inputs at 1.

Set inputReset inputSR (set dominant)RS (reset dominant)
00no change — remembersno change — remembers
10onon
01offoff
11on (set wins)off (reset wins)

Memory aid: read the name — the dominant word tells you the result when both are high. Set dominant → output set (on). Reset dominant → output reset (off). In the block symbol, the dominant input is the one with the “1”: S1 on SR, R1 on RS.

Level vs edge. A level is the state (0 or 1) and lasts as long as the button is held. An edge is the instant of change and happens once per press or release. R_TRIG and F_TRIG turn that instant into a 1 that lasts one cycle only.

Common mistakeCorrect
“Falling-edge trigger: output comes on when the button is pressed.”Pressing gives a rising edge. A falling-edge trigger reacts when the button is released (1 → 0).
“RS with both inputs high → output unchanged.”RS is reset dominant → output is turned off. “Unchanged” is what happens when both inputs are 0.
Mixing up the namesSR = Set dominant. RS = Reset dominant. The first letter is the winner.
“The trigger output stays on while the button is held.”It is 1 for one cycle only, however long the button is held.

worked.q: For a Reset-Set (Reset Dominant) function, when both inputs are set to High, the output is — blinking / unchanged / turned off / turned on.
worked.s: Turned off. Notes, 8.3.1: “If 1-signals apply both at inputs S and R1, output Q1 is reset.” Reset is dominant, so reset wins.

worked.q: For a Set-Reset (Set Dominant) function, when both inputs are set to High, the output is — ?
worked.s: Turned on. Notes, 8.2.1: “If a 1-signal applies both at the S1 and the R input, output Q1 is set.”

worked.q: When a push button is pressed, the signal changes from 0 to 1. This change is known as — rising edge / setting edge / falling edge / resetting edge.
worked.s: Rising edge. Notes, 8.4: “Rising edges mark the instants in which a signal level changes from 0 to 1”; a push button “creates a rising edge the moment it is pressed”.

worked.q: True or false: for a falling edge trigger function, when the input button is pressed, the output lights up.
worked.s: False. Pressing the button changes the signal from 0 to 1 — a rising edge. A falling edge (1 to 0) occurs the moment the button is released; F_TRIG’s output Q becomes 1 “if a change has taken place at input CLK from 1 to 0” (8.4.4).

topics.title: Timers & Counters
topics.zh: 定时器与计数器

sections.b:
• TON (on-delay) — output goes 1 only after the preset time PT has elapsed with the input ON; drops when input goes 0. Omron style: TIM 0000 #0100 = 10.0 s (units of 0.1 s).
  • TOF (off-delay) — output goes 1 with the input; after the input returns to 0 it stays 1 for PT, then 0. Example: stamping cylinder retracts 30 s after button release.
  • Accumulative (retentive) timer — keeps elapsed time when input drops and resumes when it returns; output when the total reaches PT.
The notes title the accumulative timer "TOF"; it is a separate retentive timer, not the off-delay TOF.

Timer example from your notes

• CTU (count up) — reset to 0; +1 each rising edge; output 1 when PV ≥ SV.
  • CTD (count down) — reset loads SV; −1 each rising edge; output 1 when PV reaches 0.
  • CTR (reversible) — increment and decrement inputs; PV moves between 0 and SV.

Standard counters are not time-critical. High-speed counters (above ~50 Hz) need dedicated modules because input delays and scan time limit counting rate — e.g. workpiece positioning.

Counter example from your notes

worked.q: Two timers T25 and T30 (3 s each), T30 NC contact resets T25. What does output 1.07 do while 0.00 is ON?
worked.s:
T25 times 3 s → 1.07 ON and T30 starts
T30 times 3 s → its NC contact opens, resetting T25
T25 off → 1.07 OFF (and T30 resets) → cycle repeats
Result: 1.07 flashes 3 s OFF / 3 s ON

topics.title: Developing a PLC Program
topics.zh: PLC程序开发

sections.b: Each rung: inputs left, output right; output ON if power can flow left → right. The PLC reads all inputs, solves rungs top to bottom, then updates outputs.

ModeWhat happens
RunMachine operates; I/O active; program scanned
EditChange the program. Off-line: not scanning. On-line: while outputs run — take extreme care, changes can cause hazardous operation
WriteEnter program; operation stopped and outputs inhibited (test/simulation modes similar)

Typical convention: I for inputs, O for outputs, plus a number. Contacts of I/O, timers, counters can be used any number of times.

InputDeviceOutputDevice
0.06Enable switch1.07Light
0.07Count switchCNT4 / CNT5Counters

Workflow: create program → compile → download.

Figure 16-1 in the notes shows the whole procedure in three phases. The shaded bands above show which steps belong to each phase:

  • Creating the program — plan the logic, assign the I/O addresses and enter the program.
  • Compiling the program — the software checks it, and you simulate and debug it without the real machine. Any mistake → correct and simulate again.
  • Downloading the program — the program is transferred to the PLC and tried on the real machine with the field devices connected. Any mistake → correct and trial-run again. When it is right, store it and switch to RUN.
There are two test loops: one in simulation (cheap and safe — nothing moves) and one on the real machine (real wiring, real timing). Catch as many mistakes as possible in the first loop.

StepWhat you doWhy / watch out
1 Prepare flow chart or ladder diagramWrite down the sequence: what starts it, what each output does, what stops it, interlocks and safetyA clear flow chart makes the ladder logic straightforward
2 Assign I/O terminal addressesMake the I/O assignment table (10.5): every switch, sensor, lamp, coil and counter gets an addressAssumes the PLC has enough I/O points — otherwise add an expansion module
3 Write program into the PLCEnter the ladder with a programming device: a hand-held programmer for small "micro" PLCs, or a computer running the programming software (10.1). The PLC is in Write mode — outputs are inhibitedThe programming device also shows the program, sets timer/counter values and displays diagnostic messages
4 Simulate operation and debugCompile, then run the program in test/simulation mode; switch inputs on and off and watch each rungCompiling catches syntax errors (e.g. missing END, double coils); simulation catches logic errors
5 Is the program correct?Compare the simulated behaviour with the flow chartNo → program correction, then simulate again
6 Connect external devicesWith the power OFF, wire the field devices to the addresses in the I/O table; check each input LEDWiring mistakes look like program mistakes — check the I/O first
7 Trial runDownload and run the program on the real machine, carefully (low speed, E-stop ready, one cycle at a time)Real timing and real sensors behave differently from a simulation
8 Is the program correct?Check every step of the sequence, every interlock and every fault conditionNo → program correction (off-line editing preferred; on-line editing only with extreme care), then trial-run again
9 Store programSave the finished program in the PLC's memory and keep a backup copyMost PLCs store the keyed-in program automatically
10 RunSwitch to Run mode for normal productionKeep the I/O table and program printout as documentation

worked.q: Apply the procedure to the 10.5 example: an enable switch (0.06) lets a count switch (0.07) be counted by CNT4; when the count is reached, the light (1.07) comes on.
worked.s:
1 Flow chart: Enable ON → each press of the count switch adds 1 → count = set value → light ON. Enable OFF → reset the counter, light OFF.
2 I/O table: 0.06 enable switch, 0.07 count switch, 1.07 light, CNT4 counter.
3 Write the ladder: 0.07 → CNT4 count input; NOT 0.06 → CNT4 reset; CNT4 contact → 1.07.
4–5 Simulate: force 0.06 ON, toggle 0.07 and watch the counter value rise; check 1.07 turns on at the set value and resets when 0.06 goes OFF.
6 Wire the two switches to inputs 0.06 and 0.07 and the lamp to output 1.07 (power off).
7–8 Trial run with the real switches; check one press = one count (no contact bounce double-counting).
9–10 Store the program and switch to Run.

topics.title: Power Requirements
topics.zh: 电源需求

sections.b:
Total consumption of all units in a rack must not exceed the power supply unit's rating. Add currents per supply rail, then P = V × I.

P = Σ(I5V) × 5 V + Σ(I24V) × 24 V
UnitsP — watt (W)I5V, I24V — ampere (A)

sections.h: Why the power must be calculated — your notes’ wording
sections.b:
• “It is vital to calculate the power requirements of the entire PLC system. This is to ensure that every device that is connected has enough power to operate properly.”
  • “The amount of current/power that can be supplied to the Units mounted in a Rack is limited by the capacity of the Rack’s Power Supply Unit.”
  • “Refer to the product’s tables when designing your system so that the total power consumption of the mounted Units does not exceed the maximum power for the Power Supply Unit.”
Key factFrom the notes
Total power consumption of the mounted units must not exceed…the maximum (supply) power of the Power Supply Unit
Internal logic voltage5 V DC
Relay voltage24 V DC
Power formulaP = I × V — watts (W), amperes (A), volts (V)
Where the current figures come fromthe product’s tables

sections.h: The example in your notes — units mounted to a CPU rack
sections.b:
UnitQuantity5 V DC (each)24 V DC (each)
CPU Unit10.910 A—
I/O Control Unit10.020 A—
Input Units20.080 A—
Input Units20.090 A—
Output Units20.090 A0.048 A
Special I/O Unit10.120 A—
CPU Bus Unit10.350 A—
  1. 5 V DC (internal logic): 0.910 + 0.020 + (0.080 × 2) + (0.090 × 2) + (0.090 × 2) + 0.120 + 0.350 = 1.92 A
  2. 24 V DC (relays): 0.048 × 2 = 0.096 A
  3. Power consumption (P = I × V): (1.92 A × 5 V) + (0.096 A × 24 V) = 9.60 W + 2.304 W = 11.904 W
  4. Compare: 11.904 W is within the 25 W of the Power Supply Unit.

The idea: the Power Supply Unit is like a wallet with a fixed amount in it. Every unit on the rack — CPU, input units, output units, special units — spends some of it all the time. If the units together try to spend more than the wallet holds, the supply is overloaded and the units no longer get enough power to operate properly.

Why there are two voltage groups

  • 5 V DC — internal logic. This powers the electronics inside every unit (the CPU and the circuits that talk to it), so every unit in the table has a 5 V figure.
  • 24 V DC — relays. This drives the relay coils in the output units, so only the output units have a 24 V figure.

Method — the same four steps every time

  1. From the product tables, list each unit’s current in each voltage group.
  2. Multiply by the quantity, then add up the current within each voltage group.
  3. Convert each group to power with P = I × V, then add the groups to get the total in watts.
  4. Compare with the maximum power of the Power Supply Unit. Total ≤ maximum → acceptable. Total > maximum → overloading; use a larger power supply or move units to another rack.
Common mistakeWhy it is wrong
Adding 5 V amps and 24 V amps togetherCurrents at different voltages are not the same amount of power. Convert each group to watts first, then add.
Forgetting the quantityTwo input units draw twice the current: 0.080 A × 2, not 0.080 A.
Comparing amperes with wattsThe limit in the example is in watts (25 W), so the total must be in watts too.
Choosing “24 V” for internal logic24 V is for the relays. Internal logic is 5 V.

In the example the rack uses 11.904 W of 25 W — less than half. Spare capacity is useful: it leaves room to add units later.

worked.q: The total power consumption of the mounted units of a PLC system must not — exceed total output power / exceed the processor power / exceed total input power / exceed maximum supply power.
worked.s: Exceed maximum supply power. Notes, 11.2: “…so that the total power consumption of the mounted Units does not exceed the maximum power for the Power Supply Unit.”

worked.q: In a PLC system, the internal logic voltage is normally rated at — 10 V / 12 V / 5 V / 24 V.
worked.s: 5 V. The example in the notes is headed “5 V DC (Internal Logic)”. 24 V DC is the relay voltage — the tempting wrong option.

worked.q: True or false: when total power consumption in a PLC system exceeds the maximum supply power, overloading will occur.
worked.s: True. The current/power available to the units is limited by the capacity of the rack’s Power Supply Unit, which is why the total must not exceed its maximum power. (The notes do not use the word “overloading”; it follows from 11.2.)

worked.q: Practice: a rack holds 1 CPU unit (0.50 A at 5 V), 2 input units (0.10 A at 5 V each) and 1 output unit (0.10 A at 5 V and 0.05 A at 24 V). The power supply unit is rated 10 W. Is it enough?
worked.s: 5 V group: 0.50 + (0.10 × 2) + 0.10 = 0.80 A → 0.80 × 5 = 4.0 W 24 V group: 0.05 A → 0.05 × 24 = 1.2 W Total = 4.0 + 1.2 = 5.2 W — does not exceed 10 W, so the supply is enough.

topics.title: Electro-Pneumatic Systems
topics.zh: 电气气动系统

sections.b:
Pneumatics: air pressure on a piston/valve does work. Electro-pneumatics uses electrical signals and solenoid valves. Extra parts: 24 V DC supply, switches, contacts, relays, solenoid valves, sensors. Uses: packaging, stamping/shearing/embossing, sorting, stacking.

Drawing rules: pneumatic circuit flows bottom to top; cylinders and valves drawn horizontally, cylinders acting left → right. Electrical circuit flows top to bottom.

• Latching — separate start (NO) and stop (NC); relay's own contact holds it on. Safety: machine won't restart by itself after a power failure.
  • Interlocking — NO/NC contacts of the same relay ensure only one rung is powered at a time.
  • Reciprocating cylinder — two latches: S1 latches Y1 (extend), S2 drops Y1 and latches Y2 (retract), S1 resets Y2. Only one solenoid on at a time → continuous reciprocation.

1. Study the process; determine the sequence of operation.
  2. List all output and input devices.
  3. Assign a PLC address to each.
  4. Order output rungs by the sequence.
  5. Use the input that confirms one step to trigger the next.

• Single-acting cylinder: air pushes the piston out; a spring returns it.
  • Double-acting cylinder: air pushes it both ways — needs a valve with two outputs.

5/2 valve = 5 ports, 2 positions. Port numbers: 1 supply, 2 and 4 outputs to the cylinder, 3 and 5 exhausts; 12 and 14 are the pilot / solenoid sides.

Single-solenoid (spring return)Double-solenoid
When the coil is switched offSpring returns the valve → cylinder returnsValve stays where it is (it "remembers")
PLC program needsA latch (seal-in) to hold the output onOnly a short pulse to each coil
Watch outPower failure → cylinder returnsNever energise both coils at once — use an interlock

This is why the Ch12 reciprocating example uses two latches with interlocking: Y1 and Y2 are the two coils of a double-solenoid valve, and the program makes sure only one is on at any time.

sections.h: Worked project: A+ B+ A− B− — task, sequence and I/O
sections.b:
Task. Two double-acting cylinders, A (clamp) and B (punch), each driven by a 5/2 double-solenoid valve. Press START: A extends and clamps, B extends and punches, A retracts, B retracts. Switch S2 selects single cycle (0) or continuous (1). STOP finishes the cycle and stops at home. An E-stop removes power from all valve coils.

Y_B_Ret%QX0.32Y2valve B retract coil
H_Run%QX0.4green lampcycle running
H_Fault%QX0.5red lampwatchdog fault
Step0–Step4%MX0.0–0.4markersexactly one is TRUE
Run%MX0.5markercycle requested
Fault%MX0.6markera step took > 5 s

• Inputs: 24 V DC, sinking PLC inputs with PNP (sourcing) 3-wire cylinder sensors: brown +24 V, blue 0 V, black signal to the input.
  • Stop is NC (input = 1 when healthy). A broken wire then looks like "Stop pressed" — the machine fails safe.
  • E-stop is hard-wired. S3 drops relay K0; K0's power contact removes +24 V from the PLC output supply (1L+), so every valve coil loses power even if the program is wrong. K0's auxiliary contact only tells the PLC (EStop_OK) — the PLC input is for information, not for safety.
  • Flyback diodes across each 24 V DC valve coil (or valves with built-in suppression) clamp the voltage spike when the transistor output switches off.
Important with 5/2 double-solenoid valves: removing coil power does not move the cylinders — the valve stays in its last position (it has "memory"). After an E-stop, pressurised cylinders hold where they are. If the risk assessment requires the air to be removed as well, add a safety dump (exhaust) valve on the air supply.

PROGRAM AB_Sequence      (* A+  B+  A-  B-   IEC 61131-3 Structured Text *)
VAR
  (* ---- inputs : 24 V DC, PNP (sourcing) sensors ---- *)
  S0       AT %IX0.0 : BOOL;  (* Stop button, NC   -> 1 = not pressed      *)
  S1       AT %IX0.1 : BOOL;  (* Start button, NO  -> 1 = pressed          *)
  A_Ret    AT %IX0.2 : BOOL;  (* 1S1  cylinder A fully retracted          *)
  A_Ext    AT %IX0.3 : BOOL;  (* 1S2  cylinder A fully extended           *)
  B_Ret    AT %IX0.4 : BOOL;  (* 2S1  cylinder B fully retracted          *)
  B_Ext    AT %IX0.5 : BOOL;  (* 2S2  cylinder B fully extended           *)
  S2       AT %IX0.6 : BOOL;  (* Mode: 0 = single cycle, 1 = continuous   *)
  EStop_OK AT %IX0.7 : BOOL;  (* K0 aux 13-14 -> 1 = E-stop circuit healthy *)
  (* ---- outputs : 24 V DC transistor ---- *)
  Y_A_Ext  AT %QX0.0 : BOOL;  (* 1Y1  valve A, extend coil  *)
  Y_A_Ret  AT %QX0.1 : BOOL;  (* 1Y2  valve A, retract coil *)
  Y_B_Ext  AT %QX0.2 : BOOL;  (* 2Y1  valve B, extend coil  *)
  Y_B_Ret  AT %QX0.3 : BOOL;  (* 2Y2  valve B, retract coil *)
  H_Run    AT %QX0.4 : BOOL;  (* green lamp: cycle running *)
  H_Fault  AT %QX0.5 : BOOL;  (* red lamp: watchdog fault  *)
  (* ---- step markers ---- *)
  Step0    AT %MX0.0 : BOOL;  (* home / wait for start *)
  Step1    AT %MX0.1 : BOOL;  (* A+ *)
  Step2    AT %MX0.2 : BOOL;  (* B+ *)
  Step3    AT %MX0.3 : BOOL;  (* A- *)
  Step4    AT %MX0.4 : BOOL;  (* B- *)
  Run      AT %MX0.5 : BOOL;  (* cycle requested *)
  Fault    AT %MX0.6 : BOOL;  (* a step took longer than 5 s *)
  (* ---- internal, non-retentive ---- *)
  Init : BOOL;
  T1, T2, T3, T4, T5 : BOOL;
  WD_In   : BOOL;
  R_Start : R_TRIG;           (* rising edge of S1 *)
  WD      : TON;              (* step watchdog     *)
END_VAR

(* 1. first scan after power-up: go to the home step *)
IF NOT Init THEN Step0 := TRUE; Init := TRUE; END_IF;

(* 2. calculate ALL transitions first (one step per scan) *)
R_Start(CLK := S1);
T1 := Step0 AND R_Start.Q AND S0 AND EStop_OK
            AND A_Ret AND B_Ret AND NOT Fault;
T2 := Step1 AND A_Ext;
T3 := Step2 AND B_Ext;
T4 := Step3 AND A_Ret;
T5 := Step4 AND B_Ret;

(* 3. move the active step *)
IF T1 THEN Step1 := TRUE; Step0 := FALSE; Run := TRUE; END_IF;
IF T2 THEN Step2 := TRUE; Step1 := FALSE; END_IF;
IF T3 THEN Step3 := TRUE; Step2 := FALSE; END_IF;
IF T4 THEN Step4 := TRUE; Step3 := FALSE; END_IF;
IF T5 THEN
   Step4 := FALSE;
   IF Run AND S2 THEN Step1 := TRUE;              (* continuous: go again *)
   ELSE Step0 := TRUE; Run := FALSE; END_IF;      (* single cycle: home   *)
END_IF;

(* 4. Stop or E-stop cancels the cycle request (finish at home) *)
IF NOT S0 OR NOT EStop_OK THEN Run := FALSE; END_IF;

(* 5. watchdog: any active movement step older than 5 s = fault *)
WD_In := (Step1 OR Step2 OR Step3 OR Step4) AND NOT (T2 OR T3 OR T4 OR T5);
WD(IN := WD_In, PT := T#5s);
IF WD.Q THEN Fault := TRUE; END_IF;

(* 6. fault reset: press Stop (S0 opens) -> back to home step *)
IF Fault AND NOT S0 THEN
   Fault := FALSE; Run := FALSE;
   Step1 := FALSE; Step2 := FALSE; Step3 := FALSE; Step4 := FALSE;
   Step0 := TRUE;
END_IF;

(* 7. outputs: written ONCE, from the step markers *)
Y_A_Ext := Step1 AND NOT Fault;
Y_B_Ext := Step2 AND NOT Fault;
Y_A_Ret := ((Step0 AND NOT A_Ret) OR Step3) AND NOT Fault;   (* Step0 = homing *)
Y_B_Ret := ((Step0 AND NOT B_Ret) OR Step4) AND NOT Fault;
H_Run   := Run;
H_Fault := Fault;
END_PROGRAM

1. Step chain. Five step markers Step0–Step4; exactly one is TRUE at a time. This makes the program easy to read and to debug: look at %MB0 and you know which step the machine is in.
  2. Transitions first, then moves. All transitions T1–T5 are calculated from the step states before any step changes. So the sequence can advance only one step per scan, and two steps can never be active together.
  3. Start on an edge. R_TRIG means holding START down (or a jammed button) cannot start a second cycle by itself.
  4. Permissives. T1 also needs Stop healthy, E-stop healthy, both cylinders home and no fault.
  5. Stop. Pressing Stop clears Run. The current cycle finishes (so nothing is left clamped half-way) and the chain returns to Step0 at the end of step 4.
  6. Watchdog. WD_In is TRUE while a movement step is waiting. Every transition drops it for one scan, restarting the 5 s timer. If a cylinder never reaches its sensor (no air, stuck valve, failed sensor), WD.Q sets Fault, all outputs go OFF and the red lamp lights.
  7. Reset. With a fault present, pressing Stop clears it and returns to Step0. Step0 then drives any cylinder that is not home back in.
  8. Outputs written once, at the end, from the step markers. No output is ever SET in one place and RESET in another, so there are no double-coil problems.
StateIB0 (inputs)MB0 (markers)QB0 (outputs)

Step 1, A just left home16#91 = 1001 000116#22 = Step1 + Run16#11 = 1Y1 + H_Run

IB0 at rest: bit 7 EStop_OK = 1, bit 4 B_Ret = 1, bit 2 A_Ret = 1, bit 0 S0 (NC) = 1 → 1001 0101 = 16#95.

1. Power off: check wiring against the I/O table; check every coil has suppression; check the E-stop removes 1L+.
  2. Power on, air off, PLC in STOP: operate each sensor by hand (magnet or move the cylinder) and watch its input LED and address change.
  3. Force outputs one at a time (air still off) — check the right valve's coil LED lights.

sections.h: 12.1–12.2 Electro-pneumatic systems and reading the circuits
sections.b:
A pneumatic system does work with compressed air pushing on a piston or valve. An electro-pneumatic system uses the same air power, but its signals are electrical: switches and sensors feed relays or a PLC, and solenoid valves turn those electrical signals into air flow. The extra parts are a 24 V DC supply, electrical switches, contacts, relays, solenoid valves and sensors. Typical uses: packaging, stamping/shearing/embossing, sorting and stacking.

  • Pneumatic circuit — drawn from the bottom up, following the signal flow: air supply (port 1) → valve 1.1 → cylinder 1.0. Cylinders and valves are drawn horizontally, with the cylinder moving left → right.
  • Numbering: 1.0 is actuator (cylinder) no. 1 and 1.1 is the valve that controls it. Valve ports: 1 supply, 2 and 4 outputs to the cylinder, 3 and 5 exhausts.
  • Electrical circuit — drawn from the top down, between +24 V and 0 V, in three zones: signal input (S1, S2), signal processing (relay K1) and signal output (solenoid Y1). The current paths are numbered 1, 2 … across the top.
What happensWhy
S1 and S2 are both pressedThey are in series in path 1 — an AND condition
Relay coil K1 energisesCurrent flows +24 V → S1 → S2 → K1 → 0 V
K1 contact in path 2 closes → Y1 energisesThe relay contact switches the solenoid
Valve 1.1 shifts → port 1 to 4 → cylinder 1.0 extendsThe crossed-arrow box of the valve is now active
Release either button → K1 and Y1 drop out → spring returns the valve → cylinder retractsSingle-solenoid, spring-return valve

sections.h: 12.3 Ladder program for a reciprocating cylinder
sections.b:
A double-acting cylinder with a 5/2 double-solenoid valve (Y1 = extend, Y2 = retract) reciprocates using two latch circuits. S1 is the limit switch at the retracted end and S2 at the extended end.

MomentS1S2Y1Y2What happens
Rod retracted10ONoffS1 latches Y1 → cylinder starts to extend
Rod moving out00ONoffS1 opens, but Y1 is held by its own latch contact
Rod reaches S201offONNC S2 breaks the Y1 rung; NO S2 latches Y2 → retract
Rod moving in00offONY2 held by its latch
Rod reaches S110ONoffNC S1 breaks the Y2 rung; S1 latches Y1 again → repeats

Because each coil's rung contains the other limit switch as an NC contact, only one of Y1 or Y2 is ever on, and the cylinder reciprocates continuously. In a real machine add Start/Stop control — see the worked design below.

Event000002 (Start, NO)000003 (Stop)000500Explanation
Press Start10ONCurrent flows through 000002 and the closed 000003 to the coil
Release Start00ONThe coil's own contact 000500 (in parallel with Start) now carries the current — the circuit "latches"
Press Stop01offThe NC contact 000003 opens and cuts the rung; the latch contact opens too
Release Stop00offStays off until Start is pressed again
Power failure, then power returns00offThe latch was lost with the power, so the machine does not restart by itself
  • This is why a latching (start/stop) circuit is a safety feature: an operator must deliberately press Start after any power interruption.
  • A latch can also keep one section of a bigger program powered for as long as it is needed.
NC contact vs NC button. The ladder's NC symbol 000003 passes power while input 000003 is OFF. That matches a stop button wired NO. Many installations wire the physical stop button NC so that a broken wire also stops the machine; the input is then ON in normal use, and the program must use an NO contact for it. Always check how the button is wired before choosing the contact.

• Each rung is a latch (0.01 latches 1.03; 0.04 latches 1.04).
  • Each rung also contains an NC contact of the other output. Whichever output turns on first opens the other rung, so the second one cannot turn on — even if its button is pressed.
  • Typical uses: motor forward/reverse contactors, the extend and retract coils of a double-solenoid valve, two conveyors that must never run together.
Event1.031.04Why
Press 0.01ONoff1.03 latches; its NC contact in rung 2 opens
Press 0.04 while 1.03 is onONoffRung 2 is blocked by NC 1.03 — the interlock
(1.03 switched off)offoffRung 2 is free again
Press 0.04offON1.04 latches and now blocks rung 1
The notes' example has no stop contact, so once an output latches nothing can turn it off. A real circuit adds a common NC stop in each rung. For motor contactors, also fit a hard-wired electrical (and often mechanical) interlock — the PLC interlock cannot stop a welded contactor contact.

For a process to work properly, its steps must happen in an orderly sequence: each device must finish its task fully, at the correct moment, and only after the previous task is complete. The flowchart below is the procedure for designing such a program.

  • Steps 1–6 — understand the job: what moves, in what order, which device does each task, and which input tells you each output has finished (e.g. a limit switch shows the cylinder is fully out).
  • Steps 7–8 — the I/O assignment table: one PLC address per input device and one per output device.
  • Step 9 — write one rung per output, in the order of the sequence.
  • Step 10 — in each rung, use the input that confirms the previous output has operated as the condition that triggers the next output. This is what makes the sequence wait for each step to finish.
Corrections to the figure in the notes: "Identify hardware device for each task" is printed twice, and "Assign a PLC input address to each input device" is also printed twice. The second one should read output address to each output device, as 12.6 point 4 says ("PLC input and output address has to be assigned to each device"). Cut-off text is completed: "Study process or scenario" and "List all input devices for the operation".

sections.h: Worked design: reciprocating cylinder with Start and Stop
sections.b:
Applying the 12.7 procedure to the 12.3 cylinder, adding a Start button and a Stop button:

StepResult
1 StudyA cylinder must extend and retract continuously after Start; Stop must finish the stroke and park it retracted
2 SequenceA+ → A− → repeat while running
3 HardwareDouble-acting cylinder, 5/2 double-solenoid valve, two limit switches, Start (NO) and Stop (NC) buttons
4 OutputsY1 extend coil, Y2 retract coil
5 InputsStart, Stop, S1 (retracted), S2 (extended)
6 RelateStart/Stop → running memory; S1 + running → Y1; S2 → Y2
7 Input addresses0.00 Start, 0.01 Stop (NC button), 0.02 S1, 0.03 S2
8 Output addresses1.00 Y1, 1.01 Y2; internal relay 2.00 = RUN
9 Order the rungsRUN latch, then Y1 (A+), then Y2 (A−)
10 Confirm inputsS1 confirms A− is complete and triggers A+; S2 confirms A+ is complete and triggers A−
  • Rung 1: Start latches RUN (2.00). The Stop button is wired NC, so input 0.01 is ON in normal use and is programmed as an NO contact — pressing Stop (or a broken wire) drops RUN.
  • Rung 2: Y1 turns on when the rod is home (S1) and RUN is on, latches, and is cut by S2 at the end of the stroke.
  • Rung 3: Y2 turns on at S2, latches, and is cut by S1 when the rod is home.
  • Stop: RUN drops and Y1 goes off — but the double-solenoid valve stays where it is, so the rod still reaches S2, retracts, and then stays home because Y1 cannot restart without RUN.

worked.q: In the 12.4 latching circuit, the operator presses Start, releases it, then the power fails and returns. Is 000500 on? Explain.
worked.s: No. While power was on, 000500 was held by its own seal contact. The power failure de-energised the coil and opened the seal contact. When power returns, Start (000002) is not pressed and the seal contact is open, so the rung has no path — 000500 stays OFF until Start is pressed again.

worked.q: In the 12.5 interlock circuit, 1.04 is ON. The operator presses 0.01. What happens to 1.03, and why?
worked.s: Nothing — 1.03 stays OFF. Rung 1 contains the NC contact of 1.04. While 1.04 is ON that contact is open, so pressing 0.01 cannot complete rung 1. 1.04 must be switched off first.

TypeArrangementProsCons / notes
Through-beamSeparate emitter and receiverLongest range; reliable; small objects far away; harsh environments; good positioningTwo units + wiring; not for fully transparent objects; emitter failure reads as "object present"

Examples: through-beam — broken drill bit check; diffuse — workpiece position; retro — counting / build-up monitoring.

• Capacitive — RC oscillator; any material (metal, plastic, glass, wood, water) changes capacitance. Depends on distance, size and dielectric constant. Detects matt black objects, liquid level through thin plastic/glass walls. Compensating electrode cancels humidity.
  • Inductive — LC oscillator + ferrite core; a conductive target sets up eddy currents that damp oscillation. Only metals. E.g. sensing a cylinder piston rod, metal pallets on a conveyor.
  • Reed switch — ferromagnetic (Fe-Ni) blades sealed in a glass tube with inert gas (nitrogen); a magnet pulls them together. Cylinder switches, speed, counting, door switches.

Reed switch

sections.h: Sensors — two more points from your notes
sections.b:
• Retro-reflective sensor: interruption of the light beam must not be compensated by direct or diffuse reflection of an object. Transparent, bright or shiny objects may in some cases remain undetected. Mirroring objects must be positioned in such a manner that the reflecting beam does not impinge on the receiver.
  • Capacitive sensor — detection of fluid levels: when detecting filling levels of fluids through thin walls of plastic containers, inspection glass etc., the wall thickness must be limited so that the capacitive proximity sensor responds to the contents alone.

topics.title: Sensor Calibration
topics.zh: 传感器校准

sections.b: Most have a sensitivity adjustment. If a target isn't detected: move the sensor closer, or increase sensitivity.

Sensitivity = how much change in light the receiver needs; set with a gain potentiometer.

  1. Set the Lt/Dk switch to Lt (LED on when it sees light).
  2. Turn the pot fully anticlockwise (minimum gain).
  3. Align emitter and receiver far enough apart that the LED stays off.
  4. Slowly turn clockwise until the LED turns on.
  5. Higher sensitivity → detection at a greater distance.

sections.h: Calibration, adjustment and sensitivity — what each word means
sections.b:
In plain words — what are you actually adjusting?
• Sensitivity (the potentiometer) = how far the sensor can reach. It sets how weak a signal the sensor will still accept, so turning it up lets it detect from further away. It does not move anything and it does not aim the sensor. On a photo-electric sensor it changes the receiver’s gain — how hard the receiver “listens” — not how strongly the emitter shines.
• How near = the mounting distance. You move the sensor itself closer to or further from the target.
• Left / right / up / down = alignment. You turn or shift the sensor so it points at the target (or the emitter points at the receiver).
• Calibration = doing all three until the sensor switches correctly, then testing it.

WordWhat it meansOn the sensor
CalibrationSetting the sensor up on the real machine so that it works at the level the system needs: it must switch every time the real target is there, and never when it is not.The whole job — positioning, setting, then testing.
AdjustmentThe thing you physically change to get there.① the position, distance and alignment of the sensor · ② the sensitivity potentiometer · ③ the Lt/Dk switch
SensitivityHow small a signal is enough to make the sensor switch. For a photo-electric sensor your notes define it as the amount of change in light intensity the receiver needs to detect a target.Set by the potentiometer, which changes the gain (amplification) of the receiver circuit.

Gain and sensitivity go together: more gain → the receiver amplifies the light signal more → a weaker light signal is enough → higher sensitivity → the emitter can be detected from further away.

SettingWhat happensWhat you see
Too lowThe signal from the target never reaches the switching point.Target is missed; no output even when the part is there.
CorrectClear difference between “target present” and “target absent”.Output changes cleanly every time.
Too highThe sensor reacts to things that are not the target — the background, a shiny surface, or (through-beam) light that still passes a thin or translucent object.False signals, or the beam never looks “blocked”.

Sensitivity is not the only fix. Your notes give two ways to make a sensor see a target it is missing: move the sensor nearer to the target, or increase its sensitivity setting. Moving nearer is the safer first choice, because raising sensitivity also makes the sensor more likely to react to unwanted objects.

sections.h: The sensitivity setting, step by step — and why
sections.b:
The five steps in your notes, with the reason for each one.

Step (from your notes)Why you do it
1 · Turn the Lt/Dk DIP switch on the receiver to LtLt = light-on: the indicator LED turns on when the receiver senses light. This turns the LED into your “light received” indicator for the rest of the procedure. (Dk = dark-on: the opposite.)
2 · Turn the sensitivity potentiometer fully counter-clockwiseThis is the minimum gain setting. You start from the lowest point so that you approach the switching point from below and cannot overshoot it without noticing.
3 · Align emitter and receiver at a distance where the LED stays offAlignment comes first: the beam must point at the receiver. LED off confirms that at minimum gain the light arriving is not yet enough.
4 · Slowly turn the potentiometer clockwise until the LED turns onGain rises until the received light is just enough. The point where the LED comes on is the switching point for this distance. Turn slowly so you can stop exactly there.
5 · More sensitivity → emitter detected at a greater distanceThe same light gets weaker as distance grows, so a longer distance needs more gain.

Check afterwards (good practice, not a step in your notes): put the real target in the beam — the LED should go off; remove it — the LED should come back on. Repeat a few times. If the result is not the same every time, re-align first, then repeat the setting.

Proximity sensors follow the same idea. Your notes say most sensors have an adjustment feature that varies the strength at which they detect a target, and that at a medium setting a sensor may not detect a target located a distance away. Fix: move it nearer, or raise the sensitivity. For a capacitive sensor reading a liquid level through a container wall (Ch 13), the aim is that it responds to the contents alone, not to the wall.

sections.h: Key terms — match the term to the notes’ exact wording
sections.b:
Quiz questions on this chapter reword one sentence from your notes and ask which term it describes. Learn each term with its sentence.

TermThe sentence in your notesKey words to spot
Adjustment“Most sensors have an adjustment feature that varies the strength at which they are able to detect a target.”varies the strength · detect a target
Sensitivity“Sensitivity is a measure of the amount of change in light intensity required by the Receiver to detect a target.”measure · change in light intensity · Receiver
Calibration“Calibration is sometimes necessary so that the devices can operate at an optimal level as required by the system.”operate at an optimal level · required by the system
ProximityA type of sensor (capacitive, inductive, reed switch — Ch 13), not a setting.a sensor type, so usually the distractor

Easy to mix up: “varying the strength of sensors to detect a target” describes what the notes put under the heading 14.1.1 Calibration of Proximity Sensors, so the term asked for is most likely Calibration; the sentence itself calls the feature an “adjustment”. “A measure of … light intensity” → Sensitivity. Calibration is the overall reason you adjust; adjustment is the feature you use; sensitivity is what you measure and set on a photo-electric receiver.

More facts from the notes that get asked:

  • The Receiver has a potentiometer that varies its sensitivity by changing the gain of its electronic circuitry.
  • Lt position of the Lt/Dk DIP switch → the indicator LED turns on when it senses light.
  • Fully counter-clockwise = minimum gain; turn clockwise until the LED turns on.
  • Increasing sensitivity → the Emitter light can be detected at a greater distance.
  • Two ways to detect a target a distance away: move the sensor nearer, or increase its sensitivity setting.

worked.q: Which one of the following terms refers to varying the strength of sensors to enable them to detect a target? — Proximity / Adjustment / Calibration / Sensitivity
worked.s: Most likely Calibration. The matching sentence is in section 14.1.1 Calibration of Proximity Sensors: “Most sensors have an adjustment feature that varies the strength at which they are able to detect a target.” Varying the strength so the sensor can detect the target is what that section calls calibrating the sensor; “adjustment” is the name of the feature used to do it. Both words appear, so check the answer your quiz marks as correct.

worked.q: What is a measure of the amount of change in light intensity required by the Receiver to detect a target? — Calibration / Proximity / Sensitivity / Adjustment
worked.s: Sensitivity. Notes, 14.1.2, word for word: “Sensitivity is a measure of the amount of change in light intensity required by the Receiver to detect a target.”

worked.q: The Receiver’s sensitivity is varied by changing the ______ of its electronic circuitry, using a ______.
worked.s: gain; potentiometer. Notes, 14.1.2: “The Receiver has a potentiometer that can be adjusted to vary its sensitivity by changing the gain of its electronic circuitry.”

worked.q: When performing the sensitivity setting, which way is the potentiometer turned first, and why is the Lt/Dk switch set to Lt?
worked.s: First fully counter-clockwise — its minimum gain setting. The switch is set to Lt so that the indicator LED turns on when the Receiver senses light. Then the potentiometer is slowly turned clockwise until the LED turns on.

topics.title: PLC Maintenance & Safety
topics.zh: PLC维护与安全

sections.b:
StrategyTriggerNotes
Preventive (scheduled)Fixed time or usagee.g. bulbs every 3 months; oil every 10 000 km
PredictiveMonitored actual conditionCostly equipment/skills but reduces maintenance time and downtime
Corrective (breakdown)After failureLeast efficient — investigation, waiting for parts, lost production; last resort

Predictive maintenance — explained two ways

1 · In the notes’ words (step by step). It is a two-step strategy: first, try to predict when the system is likely to fail; second, carry out the maintenance just before it actually fails. To predict well, the system must be constantly monitored. So the trigger is the actual operating condition of the system — not the calendar and not a usage counter. It costs a lot to set up, because the monitoring equipment and the skilled, experienced engineers are expensive. Used effectively it saves cost in the long run, because time spent on maintenance is reduced and production downtime is reduced.

2 · As an everyday comparison (my own example, not from the notes). Think of the tyres on a car. Preventive: change them every 3 years, whether they are worn or not. Predictive: check the tread depth regularly and change them when the tread is almost at the limit — just before they become unsafe. Corrective: keep driving until a tyre bursts. Predictive gets the most use out of each tyre without waiting for the failure, but only works if you keep measuring.

One line to remember: preventive asks “has enough time or usage passed?”; predictive asks “what condition is it in right now?”

Robust construction, electrostatic screening, opto-isolated I/O against surges, battery-backed RAM or EPROM keeps the program after power loss.

Fault distribution: sensors ≈ 45 %, actuators ≈ 30 %, I/O ≈ 15 %, wiring and CPU make up the small remainder. Most faults are outside the PLC.

Internal faults — self-tests; critical faults stop the CPU until cleared. Fix by swapping suspect cards with known-good ones. External faults — faulty I/O device, wiring, comms link, power interruption/noise.

No controller is 100 % reliable, so safety must be hard-wired, independent of the PLC. Normal start/stop can go through the PLC, but emergency stops must be hard-wired — a series chain of NC push buttons mounted near the machine. Once pressed, nobody can restart until the local button is reset.

sections.h: The three maintenance strategies — your notes’ wording
sections.b:
Why maintain? “Maintenance is often necessary to ensure that a piece of equipment or machine remains in a specific operating condition to maintain optimal performance. … qualified personnel must conduct the required functional checks, service, repair, or even replacement of the necessary components or devices in the system.”

PreventivePredictiveCorrective
Also known asScheduled maintenance; a type of planned maintenance—Reactive, unplanned or breakdown maintenance
When it is doneOn a fixed schedule, while the system is still operationalJust before the system actually failsWhen the system has already failed
What triggers itTime or usage (fixed intervals)The actual operating condition of the systemA breakdown
What it needsThe necessary checks and replacementsConstant monitoring to predict when the system is likely to failDiagnosing the cause after the failure
Result (notes)“helps to lessen the likelihood of failure”Cost can be high (monitoring equipment, skilled and experienced engineers) but it saves costs in the long run“very inefficient” — use “only as a last resort”
Example in the notesTime: replacing light bulbs in a building every three months. Usage: changing engine oil after 10,000 km.—A car broken down along the road; calling a mechanic to diagnose the cause
  • Predictive is a two-step strategy: (1) try to predict when the system is likely to fail; (2) carry out the maintenance just before it actually fails.
  • Why predictive saves cost in the long run: time spent to maintain the system is reduced; production downtime is reduced.
  • Problems with corrective maintenance: time spent investigating what caused the breakdown; time spent waiting for new/spare parts; lost production hours.
  • “While breakdowns cannot be avoided entirely, they can be reduced through effective planning (preventive and predictive maintenance).”

sections.h: Maintenance of PLC systems — reliability, faults and safety in your notes’ wording
sections.b:
Why PLCs are reliable (16.2). “PLCs are made to operate reliably for long periods of time in adverse industrial environments, for example, temperature, humidity, etc. This is one of the main advantages over both traditional electromechanical relays and microcomputer-based controllers.”

Design featureWhat it protects against
Robust electronic construction and effective electrostatic screeningPlaces that are both physically and electrically hostile
Opto-isolated circuits on all I/O linesHigh damaging surges
Battery-backed RAM or EPROM holding the applications softwareProgram loss or corruption after a plant power failure

Distribution of faults (16.2.1). “High reliability does not mean that the control system will not fail.”

Internal PLC faults (16.2.2)External PLC faults (16.2.3)
WhereInside the PLCOutside the main unit — “a large proportion of system failures”
ExamplesSelf-test failures, system status errorsFaulty I/O device · faulty wiring · faulty communication link · power supply interruption (noise or break in supply)
What happensCritical faults cause the CPU to stop; others let the controller continue, displaying an error. After a self-test failure it cannot be restarted until the fault is cleared and the system re-started.The PLC itself is healthy; the fault is in the sensors, actuators, wiring, power supply or software around it.
How to find itUse the error message listings; replace suspected faulty items in the rack with known good cards.Check the devices and wiring outside the PLC.

Safety (16.2.4 – 16.2.5). “There is no controller that is 100% reliable, therefore the only way to ensure a safe system is by using hardware safety circuits.” These safety circuits “must be wired independently from the PLC”.

  • Normal start and stop push buttons can be connected through the controller I/O units (i.e. detected by software).
  • Emergency stop switches and push buttons must be hard-wired.
  • A common approach: a series of normally-closed push-button switches which open when pushed.
  • They should be mounted locally and close to the moving machinery.
  • Once an emergency stop button is activated, no one can start the machine again until the local button is reset.

Telling the three strategies apart — ask “what makes me do the maintenance?”

If the answer is…It is…Picture it as
The calendar or a counter says so (every 3 months, every 10,000 km)PreventiveServicing a car on schedule, whether or not anything feels wrong
Measurements show it is about to failPredictiveWatching a part’s condition and changing it just before it gives up
It has already brokenCorrectiveCalling the mechanic from the roadside

Preventive vs predictive is the pair that gets confused. Both are planned and both happen before failure. The difference is the trigger: preventive follows fixed intervals of time or usage; predictive follows the actual condition, so it needs constant monitoring. That monitoring is why predictive costs more to set up, and also why it wastes less: parts are not replaced early and the plant is stopped less often.

Why corrective is “very inefficient”: the breakdown chooses the time, not you. Production stops immediately, then you still have to find the cause and wait for parts.

Using the pie chart when fault-finding. Sensors (45 %) and actuators (30 %) together are three-quarters of all faults, and I/O adds another 15 %. So when a machine stops, look at the field devices and their I/O first, and suspect the CPU last.

Why the emergency stop is not just a PLC input. A program can only stop the machine if the PLC itself is working. If the CPU has stopped on a critical fault, a stop button read by software does nothing. A hard-wired circuit does not depend on the PLC at all. Using normally-closed buttons in series means any one button opens the whole circuit; a broken wire also opens the circuit, so that failure stops the machine too.

Common mistakeCorrect
“Preventive maintenance is done after the machine fails.”That is corrective. Preventive is done on a fixed schedule while the system is still operational.
“Predictive and preventive are the same thing.”Predictive depends on the actual operating condition; preventive depends on time and usage.
“Most PLC system faults are in the CPU.”The CPU is the smallest share. Sensors are the largest at 45 %.
“The emergency stop can be wired to a PLC input like any other button.”Emergency stops must be hard-wired, independently from the PLC.
“Emergency stop buttons are normally open.”They are normally closed and open when pushed.

worked.q: Which maintenance strategy is also known as scheduled maintenance? — Predictive / Preventive / Corrective / Breakdown
worked.s: Preventive. Notes, 16.1.1: “Also known as Scheduled Maintenance, it is a type of planned maintenance…”

worked.q: Changing the engine oil of a car after it has been driven for 10,000 km is an example of ______-triggered ______ maintenance.
worked.s: Usage-triggered preventive maintenance (16.1.1). Replacing light bulbs every three months is the time-triggered example.

worked.q: Which maintenance strategy is carried out when the system has already failed, and what are its other names?
worked.s: Corrective maintenance — also known as reactive, unplanned or breakdown maintenance (16.1.3). It should only be used as a last resort.

worked.q: True or false: predictive maintenance depends on time and usage factors.
worked.s: False. Predictive maintenance “depends of the actual operating condition of the system”. It is preventive maintenance that “depends on time and usage factors” (16.1.2).

worked.q: According to the fault distribution chart, which part of a PLC system has the most faults, and what percentage?
worked.s: Sensors — 45 %. Then actuators 30 % and I/O 15 %; wiring and CPU share the rest (16.2.1).

worked.q: What protects a PLC from high damaging surges on its I/O lines, and what keeps the program after a power failure?
worked.s: Surges: opto-isolated circuits. Program: battery-backed RAM or EPROM (16.2).

worked.q: True or false: emergency stop push buttons can be connected through the PLC’s I/O units like normal start and stop buttons.
worked.s: False. “Normal start and stop push-buttons can be connected through the controller I/O units … but emergency stop switches and push-buttons must be hard-wired”, independently from the PLC, using a series of normally-closed push buttons (16.2.5).

worked.q: What happens to the CPU when a critical internal fault occurs, and how do maintenance personnel locate the fault?
worked.s: Critical faults cause the CPU to stop; it cannot be restarted until the fault is cleared and the system re-started. The fault is located with the error message listings, and by replacing suspected items in the rack with known good cards (16.2.2).

topics.title: Relay Control Circuits & PLC (China textbook view)
topics.zh: 继电器控制线路与 PLC（中国教材的讲法）

sections.b:
About this page. This is a study guide written in my own words. Its structure follows the tables of contents of representative books in your folder of Chinese textbooks; it is not a translation of any one book. Chinese practice follows GB standards, which can differ from what Singapore uses (SS 638, IEC) — for anything you do in the workshop, follow your lecturers and the Singapore rules.

The “Electrical and PLC Control Technology” textbooks in the folder nearly all follow the same two-part plan. The first part is relay–contactor control; the second is the PLC that replaces it.

PartTypical chaptersLinks to your ITE modules
1 · Relay–contactor controlCommon low-voltage apparatus → basic control circuits → control circuits of ordinary machine tools → designing a control systemDrives & Motor Control W2–W3
2 · PLCPLC overview → one PLC family in detail (often Mitsubishi FX or Siemens S7) → basic logic instructions → step (sequence) instructions → function instructions → programming software → special modules → designing a PLC control systemPLC & Automation Ch 1–12

The order matters: every PLC ladder rung is a relay circuit drawn in software, so the books teach the hard-wired circuit first.

Low-voltage apparatus are devices that switch, control, protect or regulate circuits, working at up to AC 1200 V or DC 1500 V. They are grouped by job.

DeviceChineseLetter code*Job
Circuit breaker断路器QFSwitches the supply and trips on short circuit or overload
Isolator / knife switch隔离开关 / 刀开关QSGives a visible break for maintenance; not for breaking load current
Fuse熔断器FUShort-circuit protection
Contactor接触器KMSwitches the motor’s main circuit, operated by its coil
Thermal overload relay热继电器FROverload protection (bimetal strip)
Intermediate (control) relay中间继电器KAMultiplies and passes on control signals
Time relay时间继电器KTDelayed contacts (on-delay or off-delay)
Push button按钮SBOperator start / stop
Limit (travel) switch行程开关SQDetects that a moving part has reached a position
Indicator lamp指示灯HLShows the state of the circuit

* The older Chinese letter codes (GB 7159), still used in most of these textbooks. Your ITE notes use IEC-style labels such as F1, F2 and KM1; the idea is the same.

Distribution apparatus (breakers, isolators, fuses) carry and protect the supply. Control apparatus (contactors, relays, buttons) decide when the load runs.

sections.h: The basic control circuits (基本环节)
sections.b:
The books call these the “basic links”: small circuits that every larger machine circuit is assembled from.

CircuitChineseHow it works
Jog (inching)点动Motor runs only while the button is held; no holding contact
Self-holding (latching)自锁A normally-open auxiliary contact of the contactor is wired in parallel with Start, so the coil stays on after Start is released
Interlock互锁A normally-closed contact of contactor A is wired in series with coil B, and the other way round, so the two can never be on together
Forward–reverse正反转Two contactors swap two of the three phases; always interlocked
Star–delta start星—三角起动Start in star to cut the starting current to one third, then a time relay changes over to delta
Sequence control顺序控制Motor 2 can start only after motor 1 is running (a contact of KM1 in the KM2 rung)
Braking制动Plugging (reverse-connection) or dynamic (energy-consumption) braking to stop quickly

Protection that every motor circuit needs

ProtectionChineseProvided by
Short-circuit短路保护Fuse or circuit breaker
Overload过载保护Thermal overload relay
Under-voltage / loss-of-voltage欠压 / 失压保护The contactor itself: it drops out when the voltage falls, and the self-holding contact opens, so the motor cannot restart by itself when power returns

The chapters on lathes, grinders, drilling machines and milling machines all teach the same reading method.

  1. Know the machine first: what moves, which motor drives it, and what the operator does.
  2. Main circuit: for each motor, find its contactors, protection, and whether it reverses or changes speed.
  3. Control circuit: for each contactor in turn, find the rung that feeds its coil, then trace what makes that rung complete: start button, holding contact, interlocks, limit switches.
  4. Auxiliary circuits: lighting, indication, and the control transformer.
  5. Whole picture: go through one full working cycle of the machine and check that every interlock makes sense.

Diagrams are always drawn with every device in its un-operated, de-energised state.

sections.h: PLC as taught with Mitsubishi FX — compared with your Omron notes
sections.b:
Many of these books use the Mitsubishi FX series, so the names differ from your Omron notes while the ideas are identical.

IdeaMitsubishi FX (these books)Omron (your notes)
Input / output relaysX0, X1 … / Y0, Y1 … (numbered in octal)0.00, 0.01 … / 1.00, 1.01 …
Internal (auxiliary) relayMwork bits
TimerT, set with a K value: T0 K50 = 50 × 0.1 s = 5 sTIM, set with # value: #0050 = 5 s at 0.1 s base
CounterCCNT
Load a normally-open / normally-closed contactLD / LDILD / LD NOT
Series contactAND / ANIAND / AND NOT
Parallel contactOR / ORIOR / OR NOT
Join two blocks in series / parallelANB / ORBAND LD / OR LD
Output coilOUTOUT
Latch and unlatchSET / RSTSET / RSET (or KEEP)
One-scan pulse on rising / falling edgePLS / PLFDIFU / DIFD
End of programENDEND

Step (sequence) programming. For machines that work in a fixed order of steps, the books draw a sequential function chart (SFC): one box per step, one transition condition between steps. Only the active step’s outputs are on. On the FX this is entered with the step-ladder instructions STL and RET.

Scan cycle. The PLC repeats three phases: read all inputs → run the program from top to bottom → write all outputs. An input that changes during the scan is not seen until the next scan.

sections.h: Designing a PLC control system — the steps the books give
sections.b:
1. Analyse the process: write down every action, its conditions and its interlocks.
  2. List the I/O: count the inputs (buttons, switches, sensors) and outputs (contactors, valves, lamps); add 10–20 % spare.
  3. Choose the PLC: I/O count, output type (relay or transistor), memory, special modules.
  4. Assign addresses and draw the I/O wiring diagram.
  5. Write the program: from experience (adapting the basic circuits), or from a sequential function chart for step sequences.
  6. Simulate and debug without the load connected.
  7. Commission on the machine, then complete the documents: I/O table, wiring diagram, commented program.

Hard-wired safety stays hard-wired. Emergency stops and the interlock between forward and reverse contactors are wired outside the PLC as well as programmed inside it — the same rule as Chapter 16 of your PLC notes.

Books in the folder for this subject (14): 电气与PLC控制技术 (4 different authors), 电气与PLC控制技术及应用, 电气与PLC综合控制技术, 电气与可编程控制器原理及应用, 电气与可编程控制器综合应用实训, 西门子PLC高级应用实例精解, and others — see the catalogue on the Extra tab.

recap: A contactor’s normally-open auxiliary contact wired in parallel with the Start button gives ___.
A normally-closed contact of one contactor in series with the other contactor’s coil gives ___.
On a Mitsubishi FX, T0 K50 with a 0.1 s time base gives a delay of ___ s.

topics.title: Electrical Drawings & Symbols
topics.zh: 电气制图与图形符号

sections.b:
About this page. This is a study guide written in my own words. Its structure follows the tables of contents of representative books in your folder of Chinese textbooks; it is not a translation of any one book. Chinese practice follows GB standards, which can differ from what Singapore uses (SS 638, IEC) — for anything you do in the workshop, follow your lecturers and the Singapore rules.

About 45 books in the folder are about drawing and reading electrical diagrams. They all start by separating the kinds of drawing, because each answers a different question.

DrawingChineseQuestion it answers
System / block diagram系统图 / 框图What are the main parts and how do they relate?
Circuit (schematic) diagram电路图 / 电气原理图How does it work? Shows every component and connection by function, not by position
Wiring (connection) diagram接线图Which wire goes to which terminal?
Terminal diagram / table端子接线图 / 表What is connected on each side of each terminal block?
Layout (location) drawing布置图 / 位置图Where is each device mounted in the panel or room?
Parts list元件明细表What exactly is each item: type, rating, quantity?

The books written for power stations add two more ideas. The primary diagram (主接线图, single-line) shows the equipment that carries the power: generators, transformers, breakers, busbars. The secondary diagrams (二次回路图) show what measures, controls and protects that equipment.

Chinese standardWhat it coversInternational counterpart
GB/T 4728Graphic symbols for electrical diagramsIEC 60617
GB/T 6988Rules for preparing electrical documents and diagramsIEC 61082
GB 7159 (older)Letter codes for devices, e.g. KM, FR, SBReplaced in newer practice by reference designations to IEC 81346

This is why the folder has several “old and new symbols compared” handbooks: textbooks and factory drawings from different years use different symbols and letter codes for the same device. When you read a drawing, check which standard it was drawn to.

DeviceOlder Chinese codeTypical IEC 81346 letterOn your ITE drawings
ContactorKMQKM1 / K1
Circuit breakerQFQQ1
FuseFUFF2
Thermal overload relayFRFF1
Control relayKAKK1
Time relayKTKKT / K1T
Push buttonSBSS1, S2
Limit switchSQBS / B
Indicator lampHLPH1
MotorMMM1
TransformerT / TCTT1

The letters in the IEC column are the usual ones; exact sub-letters vary between companies.

• Normal state. Every contact is drawn as it is with the device de-energised and un-operated: coils off, buttons not pressed, limit switches not touched.
  • Layout. The main (power) circuit is drawn on the left or at the top, usually in thicker lines. The control circuit is on the right or below, between two supply rails, with each coil at the end of its rung.
  • Reading direction. Left to right, top to bottom, in the order the machine operates.
  • Detached representation. The parts of one device are drawn where they act, not together. The coil of KM1 is in the control circuit, its main contacts are in the power circuit, and its auxiliary contacts are in other rungs. They all carry the same designation, KM1.
  • Cross-references. Under each coil a small table lists where its contacts are; larger drawings are divided into numbered columns or a grid so that a contact can be found quickly.
  • Terminal and wire numbers. Every terminal and every wire is numbered. Wires joined directly have the same number; the number changes after each component.

sections.h: Conductor marking and colours — China and Singapore differ
sections.b:
ConductorMarkingChina (GB)Singapore (current, harmonised with IEC)
Phase 1L1 (older: A)YellowBrown
Phase 2L2 (older: B)GreenBlack
Phase 3L3 (older: C)RedGrey
NeutralNLight blueBlue
Protective earthPEGreen-and-yellowGreen-and-yellow
Motor terminalsU, V, W——

Never assume a conductor’s function from its colour alone, especially on equipment made in another country or installed years ago. Test before touching.

sections.h: A method for reading any diagram
sections.b:
1. Title block and notes: what the drawing is, its standard, its revision.
  2. Supply: voltage, number of phases, where it comes in, what protects it.
  3. Loads: motors, heaters, valves — what the circuit is for.
  4. Main circuit of each load: from the supply through protection and contactor to the load.
  5. Control of each contactor: one rung at a time; ask “what must be closed for this coil to get power?”
  6. Interlocks and protection: find every normally-closed contact and ask what it prevents.
  7. One full cycle: start, run, stop, and what happens on a fault.

From the schematic, move to the wiring diagram to find the real terminals, and to the layout drawing to find where the device is mounted.

Books in the folder for this subject (45): 电气制图 (4), 电气制图与识图 (4), 电气制图与读图 (3), 电气原理图识读, 电气识图一看就会, 电气图形符号手册, 电气图用新旧图形符号对照, 电气制图国家标准汇编, and others — see the catalogue on the Extra tab.
