Semi-enclosed porcelain plug-in (RC1A)Porcelain cover carrying the element plugs into a porcelain base; the space between them forms the arc chamberAC 380 V; bodies 5–200 A; breaking capacity 250 A (5 A size) to 3000 A (60–200 A sizes); element of soft lead wire, copper wire or stamped copper stripLighting and small loads, overload or short-circuit protection
Unfilled enclosed tube (RM7)Element sealed in a fibre tube with no filler, held in knife-clip basesAC 380 V / DC 440 V; bodies 15–600 A; breaking capacity 2000 A (15 A), 5000 A (60 A), 20 000 A (100 A and above)Power stations, substations, motor protection; easy element change
Filled enclosed tube (RT0)Tube filled with quartz sand, which cools and quenches the arc; a red indicator pops out when it has blownAC 380 V / DC 440 V; bodies 50–1000 A; breaking capacity 50 000 A at AC 380 V, 25 000 A at DC 440 VSupply lines and plant with high fault levels
Screw type (RL1)Porcelain base, screw cap and a cartridge filled with quartz sand; an indicator in the cap drops when blownAC 500 V; bodies 15, 60, 100, 200 A; breaking capacity 2000, 3500, 20 000, 50 000 AMachine-tool control panels; compact and safe to change
Fast-actingSilver element shaped to melt very quickly—Protecting semiconductor devices such as thyristors
Self-resettingMetallic sodium vaporises on a fault and becomes high-resistance, then condenses and conducts again—Limits the current; used with a breaker

• Screw fuse wiring. Supply to the centre contact of the base, load to the screw shell. Then the shell is dead while you unscrew the cap. (“Low in, high out.”)
  • Plug-in fuse. The insulation of the incoming wires must go right into the porcelain base with no bare conductor showing. In a switchboard, guard against vibration shaking the cover out and causing a short between phases.
  • Find the cause first. When a fuse blows, analyse and clear the fault, then fit a new element. Never trace a fault by fitting fuse after fuse.
  • Replace with the supply off. The one exception in the book is the RT0 with its insulated handle, which may be changed live once the load has been removed.
  • Same rating, proper element. Do not change the element rating casually, do not use an element of unknown rating, and never substitute copper or iron wire.

worked.q: A fuse element is rated 20 A. About how long does it take to melt at 40 A, at 60 A and at 160 A?
worked.s: Work out the multiple and read the table. 40 A ÷ 20 A = 2.0 → 30–40 s. 60 A ÷ 20 A = 3 → 4.5 s. 160 A ÷ 20 A = 8 → 1 s. (Values from the book’s Table 1.8.)

worked.q: Why is the supply connected to the centre contact of a screw fuse?
worked.s: The screw shell is the part your fingers can reach when you change the cartridge. With the supply on the deep centre contact, the shell is connected only to the load side and is dead once the cap is out.

worked.q: A fuse blows. A colleague fits a larger element “so it will hold”. What is wrong with this?
worked.s: Two things. The fault has not been found, so it is still there. And the larger element no longer protects the cable and equipment it was chosen for: they can now overheat before the fuse melts. Find and clear the fault, then fit the same rating.

worked.q: Under the national standard quoted in the chapter exercises, what colours must the stop and start buttons be?
worked.s: Stop: red. Start: green. (Exercise 1.1(10).)

worked.q: True or false: (a) the protection characteristic of a fuse is inverse-time; (b) travel switch, limit switch and end switch are the same kind of switch.
worked.s: (a) True. (b) True: the same device, named after its job. (Exercises 1.2(9) and (15).)

recap: A fuse is connected in ___ with the circuit it protects.
The larger the current through a fuse element, the ___ the melting time.
Pressing a combination button opens the NC contact ___ the NO contact closes.
The filler in an RT0 fuse is ___ sand.

topics.title: Circuit Breakers, Isolators & Changeover Switches
topics.zh: 低压断路器、隔离器与转换开关

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 1, “Common low-voltage apparatus”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.), one of the books in your folder. Written in my own words; curves and block diagrams are redrawn. Type numbers such as CJ20, JR16 or DZ20 are Chinese product series: learn what each one is, not the number. Ratings are quoted from the book’s tables and are for study, not for selecting equipment.

A low-voltage circuit breaker is also called an automatic air switch. It is used in low-voltage power circuits and does two jobs: it is a hand-operated switch, and it opens by itself on under-voltage, loss of voltage, overload and short circuit. In effect it combines a knife switch, fuse, thermal relay, over-current relay and under-voltage relay in one device. Unlike a fuse, it is simply reclosed after the fault is cleared.

Four parts: contact system, operating mechanism, protective elements (releases) and arc-extinguishing system. The main contacts are of arc-resistant alloy such as silver-tungsten and use grid-plate arc chutes. The mechanism is worked by a handle or by an electromagnet or motor.

Redrawn as a block diagram from the structure the book shows in its Fig. 1.29.

The main contacts are closed by hand or electrically, and the free-trip mechanism latches them closed against their opening springs. Each release can knock the latch away:

ReleaseConnectedTrips whenProtection given
Over-current (electromagnetic)Coil in series with the main circuitShort circuit or severe overload: the armature snaps in at onceShort-circuit, instantaneous
ThermalHeater in series with the main circuitSustained overload: the bimetal bends upOverload, inverse-time
Under-voltageCoil in parallel with the supplyVoltage sags or is lost: its armature, normally held in, is releasedUnder-voltage and no-voltage
ShuntCoil normally de-energised, fed through a push buttonThe button is pressed and the coil is energisedNone: it is for remote tripping

sections.h: Types, ratings and the type code
sections.b:
TypeAlso calledUseSeries named
Frame typeUniversal breakerInfrequent starting of 40–100 kW motor circuits, with short-circuit, overload and under-voltage protectionDW10, DW15
Moulded-caseEnclosed breakerProtective switch for distribution lines; control switch for motors and lightingDZ5, DZ10, DX10, DZ12, DZ15, DZX19, DZ20
Modular miniatureMCBSupply switch and overload / short-circuit protection for final circuits and small AC motors. Width in multiples of 9 mm; clips onto a DIN railC45, DZ47, S, DZ187, XA, MC
DC fast-acting · current-limitingSpecial duties—
RatingMeaning
Rated voltageWorking voltage, insulation voltage and impulse voltage
Rated currentThe rated current of the over-current release
Making and breaking capacityLargest current it can make and break at the stated voltage under stated conditions
Breaking timeTime taken to clear a fault current

DZ20 code letters. Breaking-capacity class: Y general, J higher, G highest, C economy, S four-pole. Operation: no letter for a direct handle, P motor-operated, Z rotary handle. Duty: no code for distribution, 2 for motor protection.

DZ20 frame (AC 380 V / DC 220 V)Release rated currents IN, AInstantaneous release setting
100 A16, 20, 25, 32, 40, 50, 63, 80, 100Distribution 10 IN · motor protection 12 IN
225 A100, 125, 160, 180, 200, 225Distribution 5 IN or 10 IN · motor protection 12 IN
400 A250, 315, 350, 400Distribution 10 IN · motor protection 12 IN
630 A400, 500, 630Distribution 5 IN or 10 IN

Why 12 IN for motors? The instantaneous release must not trip on the motor’s starting current, which is several times the rated current, so it is set higher than for a distribution feeder.

1. Before first use, wipe the anti-rust grease off the pole faces of the release electromagnets, or it will hinder their action.
  2. Set the thermal and electromagnetic releases to the required currents before putting the breaker into service. Do not alter the settings casually during maintenance.
  3. After a certain number of operations (about one quarter of the mechanical life), lubricate the moving parts.
  4. Clean off dust regularly to keep the insulation good, and check the release settings regularly.

After the breaker has cleared a short circuit, inspect the contacts and the arc chute before returning it to service.

A knife switch is the simplest hand-operated device: an operating handle, knife-blade moving contacts, clip-type fixed contacts and an insulating base. It is used in low-voltage switchboards to make and break AC or DC circuits by hand and not often, or as an isolator that gives a visible break for safe maintenance.

Classified by poles (one, two, three), by construction (flat-panel or bar type), by operation (direct handle, lever mechanism, motor-operated) and by throw (single-throw or double-throw).

Open-type load switch (HK)Enclosed load switch (HH)
Other namesMoulded-base knife switch, porcelain-base switch with coverIron-clad switch
ConstructionPorcelain base, knife contacts, fuse wire, moulded coverOperating mechanism, knife contacts, porcelain plug-in fuses, steel enclosure
Speed of contact movementDepends on your handA spring and cam mechanism snaps the contacts over, independent of handle speed, which helps put out the arc
Safety featureCover over live partsMechanical interlock: the cover cannot be opened with the switch closed, and the switch cannot be closed with the cover open
UseAC 50 Hz, up to 380 V; lighting, heating, irrigation and small motors; infrequent manual switching with short-circuit protectionHeavier duty; infrequent starting of motors
HK ratingPolesLargest motor it may control, kW
15 A2 · 31.5 · 2.2
30 A2 · 33.0 · 4.0
60 A2 · 34.5 · 5.5
75 A (HK2)37.5
100 A (HK2)313

Two-pole switches are the 220 V versions and three-pole the 380 V versions. HK2 also has a 10 A two-pole size for 1.1 kW.

Installing an HK switch.

  • Mount it vertically, fixed contacts at the top connected to the supply, moving blades at the bottom connected to the load. Never upside-down or flat: a loose blade could fall and close the circuit by itself.
  • Open and close it quickly. Keep the arc cover intact, the lever mechanism free, all connections tight and the base clean.

Installing an HH switch.

  • Mount it vertically, handle up to close. Operate it with one hand, standing to the side, and move it briskly. Outdoors it needs protection from rain.
  • No bare conductor may show at the terminals; the wire insulation must sit inside the enclosure. The steel case must be reliably earthed.

A changeover switch, also called a combination switch, is a rotary switch. Moving and fixed contact blades are mounted in several stacked layers of insulating wafer. Turning the shaft makes or breaks all the layers together. It is for making and breaking a circuit by hand, not often.

The book’s example is the HZ10: long life, reliable, simple. A torsion-spring energy store in the mechanism snaps the contacts over quickly, which improves its switching ability. It is used on AC 50 Hz up to 380 V and DC up to 220 V to:

  • make or break a circuit by hand, or change over supplies or loads;
  • measure three-phase voltages (voltmeter selector);
  • change heaters between series and parallel;
  • control forward–reverse running of a small induction motor.

It must not be used as a hand switch for frequent operation. In the type code HZ10-□□/□, the figures give the rated current and number of poles, and a letter gives the type: P two-way changeover, S three-way changeover. Circuit code: QS.

A universal changeover switch is a master device that controls many circuits in several positions. It is a stack of identical switch units. It is used for closing and tripping control of breaker operating mechanisms, for changing over circuits in electromagnetic control stations, and for starting, reversing and changing the speed of small motors.

Three parts: cam mechanism, contact system and positioning (detent) device. Turning the handle turns the cams; cams of different radius push the contacts so that they make and break in the designed order. The detent and stop make sure each position is exact and reliable.

Series named: LW2, LW5, LW6. The LW6 works in control circuits up to AC 380 V or DC 220 V at up to 5 A, and can control small induction motors up to 2.2 kW if not switched often. Mechanical life 1 000 000 operations; rated operating frequency 120 per hour.

LW6 typeContact decksContact pairsLW6 typeContact decksContact pairs
LW6-113LW6-8824
LW6-226LW6-101030
LW6-339LW6-12 (double row)1236
LW6-4412LW6-16 (double row)1648
LW6-5515LW6-20 (double row)2060
LW6-6618

Reading its two diagrams. Each deck has three contact pairs, so pairs = decks × 3.

  • Graphic symbol. A dashed vertical line is drawn for each handle position (I, II, III …). A black dot under a contact on one of those lines means that contact is closed in that position.
  • Contact table. Rows are contacts, columns are positions. × means closed; a blank means open.

worked.q: Which devices does a low-voltage circuit breaker replace, and which release does each job?
worked.s: Knife switch → the hand-operated main contacts. Fuse and over-current relay → the over-current (electromagnetic) release for short circuits. Thermal relay → the thermal release for overloads. Under-voltage relay → the under-voltage release. The shunt release adds remote tripping.

worked.q: A DZ20 breaker for motor protection has a release rated I<sub>N</sub> = 40 A. At about what current does its instantaneous release operate? What if it were a distribution breaker?
worked.s: Motor protection: 12 × 40 A = 480 A. Distribution: 10 × 40 A = 400 A. (Multiples from the book’s Table 1.13, 100 A frame.)

worked.q: Why must an HK knife switch be mounted with the supply at the top and the blades at the bottom?
worked.s: So that gravity can only open it. If it were mounted upside-down, a blade that worked loose would fall into the fixed contacts and switch the circuit on by itself while someone was working on it. And with the supply on the fixed contacts, the blades and fuse wire are dead when the switch is open.

worked.q: An LW6 universal changeover switch has 5 contact decks. How many contact pairs does it have, and what is its type?
worked.s: 5 decks × 3 pairs = 15 pairs; it is the LW6-5.

worked.q: True or false: (a) a low-voltage circuit breaker is also called an automatic air switch; (b) it has loss-of-voltage protection; (c) a universal changeover switch has various protections of its own.
worked.s: (a) True. (b) True, through the under-voltage release. (c) False: it is only a command switch with no protective function. (Exercises 1.2(5), (10), (16).)

recap: The ___ release of a breaker trips on overload; the over-current release trips on short circuit.
The coil of the under-voltage release is connected in ___ with the supply.
Two switches for making and breaking a circuit by hand, not often, are the knife switch and the ___ switch.
The steel case of an HH enclosed load switch must be reliably ___.

topics.title: Electronic Apparatus: Electronic Timers, Proximity Switches & Solid-State Relays
topics.zh: 电子电器：半导体时间继电器、接近开关和固态继电器

sections.h: What electronic apparatus is, and its trade-offs
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 1, “Common low-voltage apparatus”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.), one of the books in your folder. Written in my own words; curves and block diagrams are redrawn. Type numbers such as CJ20, JR16 or DZ20 are Chinese product series: learn what each one is, not the number. Ratings are quoted from the book’s tables and are for study, not for selecting equipment.

Electronic apparatus is built mainly from electronic components. Examples are leakage, short-circuit and phase-loss protectors, and detectors for all kinds of electrical and non-electrical signals. It comes in two forms:

  • Fully electronic — keeps the outline and function of the contact device it replaces but has no contacts: proximity switch in place of limit switch, electronic over-current protector in place of thermal relay.
  • Hybrid — combines contacts and electronics. A hybrid relay uses an electronic circuit to sense and time, and a small electromagnetic relay as its output. A hybrid contactor has a bidirectional thyristor in parallel with each main contact: the thyristor conducts just before the contact closes and just after it opens, so the contact itself makes and breaks without an arc.
AdvantagesDetail
High operating frequencyA thyristor can switch more than 100 times a minute
Long lifeWithin its ratings a semiconductor does not wear
ToughWorks where there is vibration, dirt or hazardous gas
FastA high-power thyristor turns on in not more than 10 µs and off in not more than 30 µs
Tiny control powerA field-effect or MOS input stage draws almost nothing from the signal source
Multi-functionCan also give soft starting, speed control and regenerative braking
DisadvantagesDetail
Leakage currentA thyristor that is off still passes a few milliamps, so it does not isolate
Low overload capacityFor motor starting it often has to be sized for the starting current
Circuit complexityTemperature drift and noise must be designed against
BulkA conducting thyristor drops about 1–2 V, so it needs a large heat sink
CostThe thyristors themselves are expensive

Signal path left to right; the rectifier and regulator feed all stages.

BlockJob
Sensor (sensing mechanism)Converts between electrical and non-electrical signals, usually into a signal that can be measured
Conversion circuitTurns the signal from a passive sensor into a voltage or current
AmplifierRaises the weak signal to improve sensitivity, accuracy and reliability
DetectorA smoothing filter: turns the amplified modulated signal into a steady level
Amplitude discriminatorA comparator: decides whether the input has reached the set value
Delay circuitDelays the action once the set value is reached or passed
Output circuitFinal stage: supplies the required output level and power, with good switching behaviour
Rectifier and regulatorSupply the working voltage
ParameterMeaning
Operate valueInput that makes the output go high
Release valueInput at which the output goes from “1” back to “0”
DifferentialOperate value − release value
Return coefficient KFRelease value ÷ operate value
Supply voltageRated working voltage, sometimes a range
Output voltageHighest allowed “0” level and lowest (book: highest) allowed “1” level
Frequency responseHighest rate of input change it can follow
Ambient temperatureAffects electronics strongly; check the working conditions
OthersAltitude, pollution, explosion protection, vibration limits

Two families: RC transistor timers and digital timers. Both give a wide delay range, good accuracy, small size and reliable working.

RC transistor timer (book’s example: JS20). A hybrid of contactless timing and a contact output. It is based on the voltage across a capacitor rising gradually as it charges through a resistor.

  1. The supply is rectified, smoothed and regulated.
  2. A capacitor charges through a fixed resistor and an adjustable potentiometer. Its voltage rises along an exponential curve.
  3. When that voltage exceeds the peak-point voltage of a unijunction transistor, the transistor fires and gives a pulse.
  4. The pulse triggers a small thyristor, which energises the output relay K. Its contacts switch the outside circuit.
  5. One NO contact of K short-circuits the capacitor so it discharges quickly, ready for next time. Another contact lights a neon lamp to show that the delay has finished.
  6. Switching off the supply releases K and the circuit returns to its starting state.

The potentiometer sets the delay: more resistance, slower charging, longer delay. Versions exist with on-delay, on-delay plus an instantaneous contact (two relays, the timed one switched by a thyristor on the DC side of a bridge rectifier), and off-delay (a mechanically latched relay that a second electromagnet unlatches after the delay).

JS20 typeAC supply, VDC supply, VDelay ranges, s
On-delay36, 110, 127, 220, 38024, 48, 1101, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 600, 900
With instantaneous contact36, 110, 127, 22024, 48, 1101, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 600
Off-delay36, 110, 127, 220, 38024, 48, 1101, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 180

Repeat interval for the on-delay type: not less than 2 s. Minimum energised time for the off-delay type: not less than 2 s. Power taken: not more than 5 W.

Digital timers count pulses. By the source of the pulses they are mains-frequency dividing, RC oscillator or quartz dividing types. They give high accuracy, a very wide range, a digital display of the time elapsed and flexible delay modes; against that, the circuit is complex and the price higher.

A proximity switch is a contactless limit switch. It gives its signal when an object comes within a set distance. Nothing touches it and no force is needed, which is the difference from a mechanical limit switch. Its uses go beyond travel control and limit protection: level control, metal detection, size checking, and as a contactless push button.

The metal absorbs the oscillator’s energy; no touch and no force are needed.

The usual (inductive) type has an oscillator, a detector circuit, a switching transistor or thyristor, and an output.

  1. No target. With the supply on, the oscillator runs. The detector output is low, the transistor is cut off, only the small current that keeps the oscillator going flows, and the load does not operate.
  2. Metal target inside the sensing distance. The metal absorbs the oscillator’s energy and the oscillation stops. The detector output goes high, the transistor conducts, load current flows and the load operates.
  3. Target moves away. The oscillator restarts and the switch returns to its first state.

A two-wire AC proximity switch is simply connected in series with the load across the supply, like a contact.

It offers a high operating frequency, long life, resistance to shock, vibration and damp, and it tolerates harsh surroundings.

A solid-state relay (SSR) does a relay’s job with electronic components and no moving parts, with its input and output isolated from each other. It is a contactless switch made of solid-state semiconductor devices. Result: small control power, fast switching, high operating frequency, long life, good noise immunity and reliable action.

Classified byKinds
Load switchedDC-SSR · AC-SSR
IsolationOptocoupler isolation · magnetic (transformer) isolation
TriggeringZero-crossing · random turn-on (phase-control type) · active trigger · passive trigger
MountingPanel-mount · solder-in · plug-in

Four terminals: two input, two output.

How a zero-crossing AC-SSR works. It is a four-terminal device: two input terminals, two output terminals, and an isolating element between them.

  1. An input signal lights the LED of the optocoupler; its phototransistor conducts. Nothing electrical crosses the gap, only light.
  2. A transistor stage watches the mains voltage through a resistor divider. The divider is chosen so that this transistor is held saturated except when the mains is near zero (roughly ±10 to ±25 V). Saturated, it blocks the trigger.
  3. So, whenever the input arrives, a small thyristor is triggered only near the next zero crossing. Through a bridge rectifier it fires the output bidirectional thyristor (triac), and the switch closes.
  4. When the input is removed, the triac goes on conducting until the load current next falls to zero, then turns off.
  5. An RC snubber across the output absorbs voltage spikes.

Why zero-crossing? Switching on at the voltage zero avoids a sudden step of voltage and current, so it causes less electrical interference and less stress on the load.

GT-series SSR (book’s Table 1.17)Input voltageTurn-off voltageInput currentTurn-on currentLoad voltageLoad currentInsulation voltage
Small3–12 V DC1.5 V DC≤ 25 mA5 mA220 V AC / 380 V AC0.5–2 A≥ 2000 V AC
Medium3–12 V DC1.5 V DC≤ 25 mA5 mA220 V AC / 380 V AC1–3 A≥ 2500 V AC
Large3–32 V DC1.5 V DC≤ 25 mA5 mA220 V AC / 380 V AC10–60 A≥ 2500 V AC

Using an SSR.

  • Choose it for the type of load and provide effective over-voltage protection.
  • Fit an RC surge absorber or a non-linear varistor across the output to absorb transients.
  • For over-current protection use a breaker that acts in less than 10 ms, or a fast-acting fuse made for semiconductors.
  • Mount it on a heat sink with good contact and with the heat sink earthed.
  • Never short-circuit the load side: that destroys the relay.

worked.q: In an RC timer the potentiometer is turned to a higher resistance. What happens to the delay, and why?
worked.s: The delay gets longer. The capacitor charges through the resistance; more resistance means a smaller charging current, so the capacitor voltage takes longer to reach the level that fires the unijunction transistor.

worked.q: Give three differences between a proximity switch and a mechanical limit switch.
worked.s: (1) It is operated without contact or force; the limit switch must be struck. (2) It has no contacts to wear, so longer life and a much higher operating frequency. (3) It stands vibration, damp and dirt better. Against that, it needs a supply, and the common inductive type senses only metal.

worked.q: Why can a solid-state relay not be relied on to isolate a circuit for maintenance?
worked.s: A thyristor that is off still passes a leakage current of a few milliamps, and the snubber adds more. The load terminals can therefore still be at a dangerous voltage. Isolation needs a real air gap: an isolator or breaker.

worked.q: An electronic relay operates at 5.0 V and releases at 4.0 V. Find its differential and return coefficient.
worked.s: Differential = 5.0 V − 4.0 V = 1.0 V. KF = 4.0 V ÷ 5.0 V = 0.8 (no unit). My own example for practice.

worked.q: True or false: a solid-state relay is a contactless relay.
worked.s: True. (Exercise 1.2(20).)

topics.title: How to Read a Machine’s Control Circuit
topics.zh: 怎样分析机床电气控制线路

sections.h: Why learn to read whole-machine circuits
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 3, “Analysis of the electrical control circuits of ordinary machine tools”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. The book’s full-page schematics are not reproduced; the control logic is redrawn here as simplified ladder circuits and step sequences built from the book’s written explanation. Device codes are the book’s. The machines are Chinese models; the point is the method and the circuit ideas, which carry over to any machine.

The electrical control system is the part of a production machine that makes it follow the process: it sets the running states, coordinates the movements, keeps the machine safe and automates the work. Chapter 2 taught the basic links. This chapter puts them together on four real machines: a lathe, a surface grinder, a radial drill and a milling machine.

The aim is fourfold: to read schematics fluently, to understand how mechanical, electrical and hydraulic or pneumatic control work together, to find and clear common electrical faults, and to prepare for designing, installing and maintaining such circuits.

Machines differ in movement and process, so their circuits differ in complexity. Two methods of reading are used:

MethodAlso calledIdea
Direct readingLine-tracing methodFollow the current path through the diagram, device by device. This chapter uses it
Indirect readingLogic-algebra methodWrite each coil as a logic expression of its contacts and analyse the expressions

1 · Know the machine first. Before looking at the circuit, find out what the machine is for: its basic structure, its movements, its machining process, how it is operated, and what it demands of the electrical control, including the protections and interlocks it needs. Modern machines combine mechanical, electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic drives, with the electrical control as the link between them. Keep the whole picture in mind and watch how the parts coordinate.

2 · Main circuit first, auxiliary circuits second; break the whole into parts. Any control system divides into a main circuit and auxiliary circuits; the auxiliary circuits divide again into control, indication, lighting and protection circuits. Read the main circuit first, because the control circuit exists only to serve it.

1 · Main circuit
How many motors? What type and job has each? How is each started, is it reversed, braked, speed-controlled?
2 · Control circuit
Take the letter code of each main contact and find its coil in the control circuit. Split the control circuit into one local circuit per motor
In each local circuit read top to bottom, link by link. Press each button in your mind and trace which coils change, and what their contacts then do
3 · Auxiliary circuits
Supply and status indication, lighting, fault alarm. Most are driven by contacts from the control circuit, so look back at it
4 · Interlocks and protection
Find every electrical interlock and every protective device and ask what each is there to prevent
5 · Overall check
Put the parts back together. Read the whole diagram once more and make sure every device’s role is understood

The drawing convention helps: the control circuit of one motor is drawn in adjacent columns, and rungs are arranged in the order they act.

The tracing method for step 2, in three moves.

  1. Start from the actuator (the motor). In the main circuit, see which contacts control it and how they are combined.
  2. In the control circuit, use the letter codes of those main contacts to find the related control links and how the links connect.
  3. Start from the start button. Trace the line, see how each contact controls the next device, and how the actuator finally moves the machine. Write the sequence down as you go.

worked.q: Which methods are used to analyse a schematic, and what are the steps for a machine tool? (Exercise 3.1)
worked.s: Methods: direct reading (line tracing) and indirect reading (logic algebra). Steps: (1) main circuit; (2) control circuit, split into local circuits and traced from the start button; (3) auxiliary circuits; (4) interlocks and protection; (5) overall check. Before all of these, find out the machine’s purpose, structure, movements and control requirements.

worked.q: Why is the main circuit read before the control circuit?
worked.s: The control circuit exists to switch the devices in the main circuit. Once you know how many motors there are and how each must start, reverse, brake or change speed, you know what to look for in the control circuit and can read it with a purpose.

topics.title: The CA6140 Lathe
topics.zh: CA6140 型卧式车床

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 3, “Analysis of the electrical control circuits of ordinary machine tools”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. The book’s full-page schematics are not reproduced; the control logic is redrawn here as simplified ladder circuits and step sequences built from the book’s written explanation. Device codes are the book’s. The machines are Chinese models; the point is the method and the circuit ideas, which carry over to any machine.

The lathe is the most widely used metal-cutting machine. It turns outside diameters, faces, bores and threads, and can also drill, ream and counter-bore. There are horizontal, vertical, turret and facing lathes; the horizontal lathe is the commonest.

Parts: bed, headstock (spindle gearbox), change-gear box, feed box, apron (carriage), tool post, tailstock, feed rod and lead screw.

MovementWhat movesNotes
Main (cutting)The workpiece rotates, driven by the spindle through a chuck or centresCutting speed must suit material, size, tool and cooling, so the spindle needs a wide speed range: more than 70 : 1 on a horizontal lathe. It must also reverse for thread cutting
FeedThe tool post moves in a straight line, lengthwise or crosswiseTaken from the headstock output through change gears, feed box and feed rod or lead screw to the apron. For threads, the feed must keep a strict ratio to spindle rotation
AuxiliaryRapid movement of the apron, moving the tailstock, clamping and releasing the work

Type code CA6140: C = lathe · A = structural feature code · 6 and 1 = group and series (horizontal lathe) · 40 = main parameter.

1. One motor drives both the main and the feed movement, to keep their ratio exact. For economy and reliability it is a squirrel-cage induction motor.
  2. Speed is changed mechanically through a gearbox between motor and spindle. Some lathes combine a pole-changing motor with the gearbox; heavy lathes use a DC motor for stepless speed.
  3. Reversing for thread cutting: small lathes reverse the motor; larger ones use a friction clutch and the motor runs one way.
  4. Starting: small and medium spindle motors start direct-on-line; larger ones use star–delta. Stopping is usually by mechanical or electrical braking to save time.
  5. A coolant pump is needed. Its motor runs one way only, may start only after the spindle motor, and must stop when the spindle motor stops.
  6. A separate rapid-traverse motor, jog-controlled, moves the tool post quickly to save effort and time.
  7. The circuit needs proper protection and signal lamps.
  8. Local lighting must be at a safe voltage.

Three squirrel-cage motors: M1 spindle and feed, M2 coolant pump, M3 rapid traverse of the tool post. All three are small enough to start direct-on-line and all run in one direction.

110 V control supply. SQ1 is closed only while the belt cover is shut. Simplified from the book’s description.

Supply. Power enters through circuit breaker QF. A control transformer TC steps 380 V down to 110 V for the control circuit, 24 V for the work lamp and 6 V for the indicator lamp. Before starting, the key switch SA2 is turned to the right with its key and QF is then closed.

Spindle motor M1. Press the green button SB1. Current flows through fuse FU6, the belt-cover safety switch SQ1, the emergency-stop button SB2, SB1 and the thermal-relay contact FR1 to the coil of KM1. KM1 closes its main contacts and M1 runs; its auxiliary NO contact across SB1 holds the circuit. To stop, press the red mushroom button SB2. It latches down; turn it to the right to release it. Spindle reversing is done by the mechanical friction clutch, not electrically.

Coolant pump M2. Turn rotary switch SA1. Current flows through SA1, an NO contact of KM1 and FR2 to KM2. Because of the KM1 contact, the pump can run only while the spindle motor is running, which is what turning actually needs.

Rapid traverse M3. Set the apron handle to the direction wanted, then press SB3, which is built into the handle. KM3 pulls in and M3 runs for as long as the button is held: jog control. An over-running clutch lets the rapid drive take over from the feed drive and hands back when the button is released.

Lamps. Work lamp EL: 24 V, switched by its own lamp switch, fused by FU5. Indicator HL: 6 V, fused by FU4, wired straight to the transformer, so it lights whenever QF is closed and warns that the machine is live.

ProtectionProvided by
Short circuit, whole machineFuses FU at the incoming supply and breaker QF
Over-current, overload, under-voltage and loss of voltage, whole machineBreaker QF
Short circuit, coolant pump M2FU1
Short circuit, rapid-traverse motor M3FU2
Short circuit, control transformer primaryFU3
Short circuit, indicator circuitFU4
Short circuit, lighting circuitFU5
Short circuit, 110 V control circuitFU6
Overload, M1 and M2Thermal relays FR1 and FR2
Loss of voltage, motorsContactor KM1 with self-holding

Safety interlocks.

  • Belt-cover switch SQ1. Opening the headstock belt cover opens SQ1. KM1, KM2 and KM3 all lose their supply and every motor stops.
  • Control-cabinet door switch SQ2 and key switch SA2. Their contacts are wired to the trip coil of QF. If SA2 is turned to the left, or the cabinet door is opened, the contact closes, the QF coil is energised and QF trips. Even if someone tries to close it again, it trips within 0.1 s.
  • Working live in the cabinet. For authorised live testing, the actuating rod of SQ2 is pulled out so that its contact opens and QF can be closed. When the door is shut again the rod resets and protection is restored.

Three features to remember. (1) All three motors are small, start at full voltage and run one way; one of them is jogged. (2) The coolant pump is interlocked with the spindle motor. (3) Personal protection is thorough: key-operated supply switch, latching emergency stop, belt-cover switch and cabinet-door switch.

CodeDeviceRatingJob
M1Induction motor Y132M-4-B37.5 kW, 1450 r/minSpindle and feed
M2Coolant pump AOB-2590 W, 3000 r/minCoolant supply
M3Induction motor AOS5634250 W, 1360 r/minRapid traverse

KM2 · KM3Intermediate relays JZ7-44Coil 110 VControl M2 · M3
FU1 · FU2Fuses1 A · 4 A elementsShort circuit of M2 · M3
FU3–FU6Fuses1 A, 1 A, 2 A, 1 ATransformer primary, indicator, lighting, control

SB2Push buttonRed mushroom, latchingStop M1
SB3Push buttonJog M3
SA1 · SA2Rotary switchesSA2 with keyM2 control · supply lock
SQ1 · SQ2Limit switchesBelt-cover · cabinet-door safety

QFCircuit breaker20 ASupply

The pump and rapid-traverse motors are so small that intermediate relays switch them in place of contactors.

SymptomLikely causes

No motor will startBelt cover not shut, SQ1 not closed · control fuse FU6 blown or loose · if HL is dark too, transformer primary fuse FU3 · no supply voltage

Motor hums and will not start on pressing SB1One phase missing: a supply fuse blown in one phase, one KM1 main contact not making, a broken motor lead or an open winding. Switch off at once or the motor will burn out
Motor stops when SB1 is releasedNo self-holding: the KM1 holding contact is dirty or its wire is loose
Motor will not stop on pressing stopKM1 main contacts welded or jammed by debris, or residual magnetism holding the armature · stop button contact stuck · stop button insulation broken down
Coolant pump will not startSpindle not started · SA1 not making · FU1 blown · FR2 tripped · KM2 coil open · pump motor damaged
Rapid traverse will not startStop button SB2 not released · SB3 not making · KM3 coil open · FU2 blown · M3 damaged
Work lamp darkBulb · lamp switch · FU5 · transformer winding burnt
Indicator darkBulb · loose lamp-holder wire · FU4

worked.q: What are the features of the CA6140 lathe control circuit? (Exercise 3.2)
worked.s: (1) Three small motors, all started at full voltage and all running one way; the rapid-traverse motor is jogged. (2) The coolant pump is interlocked with the spindle motor and can start only after it. (3) Thorough personal protection: key-operated supply switch SA2 with QF, latching emergency stop SB2, belt-cover switch SQ1 and cabinet-door switch SQ2.

worked.q: Which protections does the CA6140 have, and which devices give them? (Exercise 3.3)
worked.s: Short circuit: supply fuses FU and QF for the machine; FU1 for M2, FU2 for M3, FU3 for the transformer, FU4 indicator, FU5 lighting, FU6 control circuit. Overload: FR1 for M1, FR2 for M2. Over-current, under-voltage, loss of voltage: QF; the self-holding contactor also gives loss-of-voltage protection. Personal safety: SQ1, SQ2, SA2 and the emergency stop SB2.

worked.q: On the CA6140 the spindle runs but the coolant pump will not. The indicator lamp is lit. List what you would check, in order.
worked.s: The pump rung is SA1 → KM1 contact → FR2 → KM2 coil, and its motor is fed through FU1. Check: (1) Is SA1 turned on and making? (2) Has FR2 tripped? Reset and find why. (3) Does KM2 pull in? If not, its coil or the KM1 auxiliary contact. (4) If KM2 pulls in but the pump is still, FU1 or the pump motor itself.

worked.q: Why are the coolant-pump and rapid-traverse motors on the CA6140 switched by intermediate relays?
worked.s: They are tiny: 90 W and 250 W. Their currents are well inside the contact rating of an intermediate relay (about 5 A), so a contactor with an arc chute is not needed.

recap: On the CA6140 the coolant pump can run only after the ___ motor has started.
The rapid-traverse motor of the CA6140 uses ___ control.
Opening the belt cover opens limit switch ___ and stops all three motors.
A motor that hums and will not start has probably lost one ___.

topics.title: The M7130 Surface Grinder & Its Electromagnetic Chuck
topics.zh: M7130 型平面磨床与电磁吸盘

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 3, “Analysis of the electrical control circuits of ordinary machine tools”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. The book’s full-page schematics are not reproduced; the control logic is redrawn here as simplified ladder circuits and step sequences built from the book’s written explanation. Device codes are the book’s. The machines are Chinese models; the point is the method and the circuit ideas, which carry over to any machine.

A grinder is a precision machine that cuts with the rim or face of a grinding wheel. It machines ordinary metals and also hard materials that cutting tools cannot touch, such as hardened steel and cemented carbide. It gives high accuracy and a fine finish, so it is used for finishing. In industrial countries grinders make up about 13–27 % of all metal-cutting machines.

Kinds: surface, cylindrical, internal, centreless and special-purpose grinders. The example is the M7130 horizontal-spindle, rectangular-table surface grinder. Its parts are the bed, worktable, electromagnetic chuck, wheel head, cross slide and column.

MovementWhat movesHow
MainThe wheel rotates. Rim speed is about 30–50 m/sWheel motor, directly
Longitudinal feedThe table moves back and forth along the bedHydraulic drive: smooth reversal and easy speed adjustment. Dogs on the table strike a hydraulic reversing valve on the bed
Cross feedThe wheel head moves in or out along the slide, one step per table stroke, or continuously when dressing the wheelHydraulic, or by handwheel
Vertical feedThe slide moves up or down the column to set the depth of cutHandwheel through a mechanical drive

Coolant from a pump carries away heat and swarf so that the work does not distort. Large work is bolted or clamped to the table; small work is held on the electromagnetic chuck.

Type code M7130: M = grinder · 7 = surface · 1 = horizontal spindle, rectangular table · 30 = table working width 300 mm.

sections.h: Requirements, main circuit and control circuit
sections.b:
Requirements.

  1. The wheel needs no speed control, so a three-phase squirrel-cage motor will do. Wheel, hydraulic-pump and coolant-pump motors all run one way only.
  2. The coolant pump runs only after the wheel motor has started.
  3. Protection: short circuit, motor overload, zero voltage, and under-voltage (weak-field) protection of the chuck.
  4. The chuck must have a demagnetising control.
  5. Lighting and signal lamps.

Main circuit. Supply through the main switch QS. Three motors share fuse FU1 for short-circuit protection.

MotorJobSwitched byOverload protection
M1Grinding wheelKM1FR1
M2Coolant pumpKM1 as well, through plug and socket X1None of its own: it is small
M3Hydraulic pumpKM2FR2

The coolant tank stands apart from the bed, so M2 is connected through a plug X1. Pull the plug when coolant is not wanted.

KM1: grinding wheel (and coolant pump). KM2: hydraulic pump. The first three elements are common to both rungs.

Control circuit. Supplied at 380 V, protected by FU2.

  • Wheel: SB1 start, SB2 stop, KM1 with self-holding.
  • Hydraulic pump: SB3 start, SB4 stop, KM2 with self-holding.
  • Common condition: neither can be energised unless there is a path through point 6–8. That path is closed either by the NO contact of the under-current relay KA (chuck energised and holding) or by a contact of the chuck changeover switch (chuck deliberately not in use).

The book labels the chuck changeover switch SA2 in some places and SA3 in others. These notes call it “the chuck switch”.

The chuck holds the work by magnetic attraction for grinding.

Compared with mechanical clamping
AdvantagesFast to clamp, quick and simple to use, does not mark the work, holds several small parts at onceThe work is free to expand as it warms, so it does not distort
LimitsHolds only magnetic materials such as steel and ironAluminium and copper cannot be held

Construction. The body is a steel box. Raised cores inside it carry the coil. The steel top plate is divided into many strips by non-magnetic material. With the coil energised, neighbouring strips become N and S poles. A workpiece laid across them completes the magnetic circuit, and the flux through it holds it down firmly.

Why DC? The chuck coil must be fed with direct current. On AC the workpiece would vibrate and the iron core would heat up from eddy currents. So the circuit includes a rectifier.

380 V AC
Transformer TC steps down to 127 V AC
Bridge rectifier VC gives 110 V DC
Chuck switch, three positions: HOLD · RELEASE · DEMAGNETISE
Under-current relay KA coil in series · chuck YH through plug X2
Chuck YH, with discharge resistor R3 across it
Chuck switch positionWhat it connectsResult
HoldChuck across the 110 V DC in the forward directionWork is held. KA pulls in and its NO contact (6–8) allows the motors to run
ReleaseChuck disconnectedCoil off. But residual magnetism still grips the work: it is hard to lift off, and the process often does not allow the part to stay magnetised
DemagnetiseChuck reversed, through series resistor R2A small reverse current cancels the residual magnetism. Then return the switch to Release and take the work off

DeviceJobWhy it is needed
Under-current relay KAIts coil is in series with the chuck. If chuck current is lost or too weak, KA drops out, contact 6–8 opens and KM1 and KM2 are de-energised: all motors stopIf the chuck lost its grip during grinding, the work could be flung out by the fast-spinning wheel and cause an accident
Discharge resistor R3, across the chuckGives the coil a path through which to release its stored magnetic energy as heatThe chuck is a large inductance. At the instant it is switched from hold to release, the coil generates a high self-induced voltage that could break down its insulation and would arc and burn the switch contacts
R1 and C, across the rectifier inputAbsorb over-voltageSurges from the supply, and the switching of the DC circuit, produce transient high voltage on the transformer secondary that could damage the rectifier diodes. C absorbs the peak; R1 damps the oscillation between C and the transformer inductance
R2Limits the demagnetising currentSo that the reverse current is small and the work is not re-magnetised the other way
FUsShort circuit protectionSupply, control, chuck and lighting circuits each have their own

Grinding without the chuck. When the work is clamped mechanically, pull out the chuck plug X2 and set the chuck switch to the demagnetise position. Its contact 6–8 is then closed, so the motors can be started even though KA is released.

Lighting. A lighting transformer steps 380 V down to a safe 36 V. One side of lamp EL is earthed, the switch is in the other side, and FU4 protects the circuit.

Thorough demagnetising. Where the part must be very clean of magnetism, pass it over a separate AC demagnetiser plugged into a socket on the machine.

SymptomLikely causesAction
No motor will startKA contact 6–8 dirty, oily or its wire loose · chuck-switch contact 6–8 not makingSet the switch to Hold and check that KA’s contact makes. Set it to Demagnetise, pull the chuck plug and check the switch contact. Repair or replace
Wheel motor thermal relay FR1 tripsFront bearing bush of the wheel motor worn: the motor is partly stalled and draws a heavy current · depth of cut too great, same effect · replacement relay of the wrong size or badly setRepair or replace the bush · choose a sensible depth of cut · select and set FR1 to the motor’s rated current
Coolant pump will not startSocket damaged · pump motor damagedRepair socket · replace motor
Hydraulic pump will not startSB3 or SB4 contact bad · KM2 coil burnt · motor burntRepair contacts · replace coil · repair or replace motor
Chuck has no pullA fuse in the supply, chuck or control circuit has blown · chuck plug X2 not making · two adjacent diodes of the bridge short-circuited (the shorted diodes and the transformer run hot; output is zero) · two adjacent diodes open (output is zero) · chuck coil openReplace fuse · repair plug · replace diodes · repair coil
Chuck pull is weakChuck coil partly short-circuited: the chuck was not sealed, coolant got in and ruined the insulation. No-load rectifier voltage is high, but it falls far below 110 V when the chuck is connected · one diode open: output falls to halfReplace the chuck coil · replace the diode
Work hard to remove after demagnetisingDemagnetising circuit open: chuck switch not making or R2 damaged · demagnetising voltage too high · demagnetising time too long or too shortCheck switch and R2 · adjust R2 to give 5–10 V · different materials need different times: learn the right time

worked.q: Why does the M7130 hold work on an electromagnetic chuck, and why must the chuck coil be fed with DC and not AC? (Exercise 3.4)
worked.s: Compared with mechanical clamping the chuck is fast and simple, does not mark the work, holds several small parts at once, and lets the work expand freely as it warms so that it does not distort. The coil must have DC because AC would make the work vibrate and would heat the iron core through eddy currents.

worked.q: Why does the chuck circuit include under-current relay KA, and what does it do? (Exercise 3.5)
worked.s: KA’s coil is in series with the chuck, and its NO contact is in the supply to both contactor coils. If the chuck current is lost or falls too low, the grip is unsafe; KA drops out, its contact opens, and the wheel and hydraulic pump stop before the work can be thrown off by the wheel.

worked.q: List the protections in the M7130 circuit. (Exercise 3.6)
worked.s: Short circuit: FU1 (supply), FU2 (control), a fuse for the chuck circuit, FU4 (lighting). Overload: FR1 (wheel), FR2 (hydraulic pump). Zero-voltage: the self-holding contactors. Chuck weak-field: under-current relay KA. Over-voltage on the rectifier: R1 and C. Coil over-voltage on switching off: discharge resistor R3.

worked.q: The bridge rectifier normally gives 110 V DC. One diode goes open-circuit. What voltage does the chuck now get, and what will the operator notice?
worked.s: A bridge with one open diode works as a half-wave rectifier, so the average output halves: about 110 V ÷ 2 = 55 V. The operator notices weak holding force, and KA may drop out and stop the motors.

recap: The electromagnetic chuck coil is supplied with ___ current.
Residual magnetism is cancelled by passing a small ___ current through the chuck.
The ___ relay KA stops the motors if the chuck loses its current.
Demagnetising voltage should be adjusted to about ___ V.

topics.title: The Z3040 Radial Drilling Machine
topics.zh: Z3040 型摇臂钻床

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 3, “Analysis of the electrical control circuits of ordinary machine tools”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. The book’s full-page schematics are not reproduced; the control logic is redrawn here as simplified ladder circuits and step sequences built from the book’s written explanation. Device codes are the book’s. The machines are Chinese models; the point is the method and the circuit ideas, which carry over to any machine.

A drilling machine makes holes: drilling, enlarging, reaming, tapping and spot-facing. There are upright, bench, radial and special drills. The radial drill is flexible and convenient, and suits single or batch work on large parts with many holes. It is found in every general machine shop.

Parts: base, inner column, outer column, radial arm, headstock (spindle box) and worktable.

  • The inner column is fixed to the base. The hollow outer column fits over it and can turn round it.
  • One end of the arm is a sleeve on the outer column. A lead screw moves the arm up and down the outer column; arm and outer column cannot turn relative to each other, so they swing round the inner column together.
  • The headstock rides on horizontal ways along the arm.

So the spindle can be put over any point of a large workpiece without moving the work. Before cutting, three things are clamped: headstock to arm, outer column to inner column, and arm to outer column. Before moving, they are released.

MovementWhat movesDriven by
MainThe spindle rotates the drillSpindle motor
FeedThe spindle moves down and upSpindle motor, through the feed gearbox in the headstock
AuxiliaryHeadstock along the arm · arm up and down the outer column · arm with outer column round the inner columnBy hand · arm-lift motor · by hand
ClampingArm, column and headstock clamp and releaseHydraulic pump motor

The arm’s release and clamp happen automatically as part of every lift: release first, then move, then clamp again at the new height. Swinging the arm and sliding the headstock are done by hand, but the column or headstock must be released first. The column and headstock clamps work together from one hydraulic mechanism.

Type code Z3040: Z = drill · 3 = radial · 0 = series · 40 = largest drilling diameter 40 mm.

1. There are many moving parts, so to simplify the transmission several motors are used: four in all.
  2. Tapping needs the spindle to reverse. This is done mechanically, by a hydraulically operated forward–reverse friction clutch, so the spindle motor runs one way only.
  3. The arm is raised and lowered by reversing the arm-lift motor. For easy positioning it is jog-controlled.
  4. The oil for clamping and releasing headstock, column and arm comes from the hydraulic pump motor running forward or in reverse. The clamps are self-locking mechanically, so the pump is jogged too.
  5. A coolant pump motor, running one way, switched directly.
  6. Interlocks, protection, lighting and indicator lamps.
MotorJobContactorsOverload protection
M1Spindle (and its gear pump for clutch, brake and gear-change oil)KM1FR1
M2Arm up and downKM2 up · KM3 downNone: it runs for short periods only
M3Hydraulic pump: release and clampKM4 forward = release · KM5 reverse = clampFR2
M4Coolant pumpChangeover switch directlyNone: very small

Supply through the changeover switch QS; FU1 is the main short-circuit protection. The control circuit is fed at 110 V from transformer TC.

The book’s printed schematic for this machine (its Fig. 3.7) repeats the grinder diagram by mistake, so the sequence below follows the book’s written explanation, which is complete.

sections.h: Spindle and arm-lift control, step by step
sections.b:
Spindle. Press SB2: KM1 pulls in and holds itself, M1 runs, and lamp HL3 lights. Press SB1: KM1 releases and M1 stops. On overload FR1 opens and KM1 releases.

Raising the arm (lowering is the same with SB4 and KM3). The devices involved: time relay KT, solenoid valve YV, and limit switches SQ2 (arm fully released) and SQ3 (arm fully clamped).

Press and hold SB3 (up)
KT is energised. Its instantaneous NO contact energises KM4: hydraulic pump M3 runs forward and delivers oil
KT’s other contact energises solenoid valve YV: the oil is directed into the arm’s release chamber
The arm releases. The release mechanism presses limit switch SQ2
SQ2 NC opens → KM4 off, pump stops. SQ2 NO closes → KM2 on, lift motor M2 raises the arm
Arm reaches the height wanted: let go of SB3
KM2 and KT are de-energised. M2 stops and the arm stops rising
KT is an off-delay relay. After 1–3 s its delayed-closing NC contact closes → KM5 on, pump M3 runs in reverse
SQ3’s NC contact is still closed, so YV stays energised: oil goes to the arm’s clamp chamber
The arm clamps. The mechanism presses SQ3: its NC contact opens → KM5 and YV off, pump stops
Lift complete, arm clamped
DeviceIts job in the sequence
SQ2Makes sure the arm moves only when fully released. If the arm is not released, SQ2 does not operate, its NO contact stays open, and KM2 / KM3 cannot be energised
KTMakes sure clamping begins 1–3 s after KM2 / KM3 has dropped out, when the lift motor has come to rest
SQ3Stops the pump when clamping is complete
SQ1A combined limit switch for the top and bottom of travel. At the upper limit the dog opens SQ1-1 in series with SB3: KM2 releases and the lift stops, but SQ1-2 in the down circuit is still closed, so SB4 can bring the arm down. The lower limit works the other way round
FR2If the hydraulics fail and the arm cannot clamp, or SQ3 is badly set, SQ3’s NC contact never opens and the pump motor would run on under load. Although M3 is a short-time motor it therefore has overload protection

sections.h: Headstock and column clamps, lamps and parts
sections.b:
Headstock and column are released or clamped together.

ActionPressWhat happensLamp
ReleaseSB5 (jog)KM4 on, pump M3 forward. Unlike the arm sequence, YV is not energised, so the oil goes to the headstock and column release cylinders. Limit switch SQ4 is let go and its NC contact closesHL1 “released” lights
ClampSB6 (jog)KM5 on, pump M3 reverse. SB6’s NC contact keeps YV off, so the oil goes to the headstock and column clamp cylinders. SQ4 is pressed: its NC contact opens and its NO contact closesHL1 goes out, HL2 “clamped” lights

The solenoid valve YV is the selector. YV energised: oil goes to the arm cylinders. YV de-energised: oil goes to the headstock and column cylinders.

Lamps. HL1 released, HL2 clamped, HL3 spindle running; fed from a tapping on a transformer secondary. Work lamp EL: 24 V from another secondary, switched at the lamp head, one side earthed for safety, fused by FU4.

CodeDeviceCodeDevice
M1Spindle motorFR2Thermal relay, hydraulic pump motor
M2Arm-lift motorQFSupply breaker
M3Hydraulic pump motorSA2Coolant pump switch
M4Coolant pump motorSQ1Limit switch, end-of-travel protection
KM1Contactor, spindleSQ2Limit switch, pressed when arm is released
KM2 · KM3Contactors, arm up · downSQ3Limit switch, pressed when arm is clamped
KM4 · KM5Contactors, release · clampSQ4Limit switch, pressed when column and headstock are clamped
KTTime relayFU1Fuse, main supply
YVSolenoid valveFU2Fuse, M2, M3 and control circuit
SB1 · SB2Spindle stop · startFU3 · FU4Fuses, indicator · lighting
SB3 · SB4Arm up · down (jog)HL1 · HL2 · HL3Released · clamped · spindle running
SB5 · SB6Headstock and column release · clamp (jog)EL · SA1Work lamp and its switch
FR1Thermal relay, spindle motorTCControl transformer

SymptomLikely causes
FU1 blows the moment the spindle motor startsDrill jammed by swarf · feed too heavy, spindle stalled
Arm will not go up or downSQ2 is not being pressed. Possible reasons: (a) supply phase sequence reversed — pressing “up” then runs the pump backwards, so the arm clamps instead of releasing and SQ2 is never pressed; (b) SQ2 has shifted, so the released arm does not reach it; (c) a hydraulic fault, so the arm does not release fully · Lift motor does not start although the arm has released: KM2 or KM3 main contacts dirty or coil burnt
Arm does not clamp after movingSQ3 set wrongly: it is pressed too early, before clamping is complete, so the pump stops too soon · hydraulic fault
Arm limit protection does not workSQ1 damaged so its contacts cannot operate · SQ1 contacts dirty · SQ1 contacts welded. Repair or replace SQ1
Headstock and column will neither clamp nor releaseSB5 or SB6 wiring loose, circuit open · KM4 or KM5 coil lead open or main contacts dirty · hydraulic fault

Lesson. On a machine with hydraulic sequences, the electrical fault is often a limit switch out of position, and after any work on the supply the phase sequence must be checked, because a reversed pump turns “release” into “clamp”.

worked.q: During an arm lift on the Z3040, how do the hydraulic pump motor and the arm-lift motor work together? (Exercise 3.7)
worked.s: Pump first, lift second, pump again. Pressing the button runs the pump forward to release the arm. When the arm is fully released SQ2 stops the pump and starts the lift motor. Releasing the button stops the lift motor; after KT’s 1–3 s delay the pump runs in reverse to clamp the arm, and SQ3 stops it when clamping is complete. The two motors never drive at the same time.

worked.q: What is each of the limit switches SQ1–SQ4 on the Z3040 for? (Exercise 3.10)
worked.s: SQ1: upper and lower end-of-travel protection for the arm. SQ2: signals “arm released”; stops the pump and permits the lift. SQ3: signals “arm clamped”; stops the pump and the solenoid valve. SQ4: signals whether headstock and column are clamped, and switches the indicator lamps HL1 and HL2.

worked.q: On the Z3040, when are KT and YV energised, and what do KT’s contacts do? (Exercise 3.11)
worked.s: KT is energised for as long as an arm up or down button is held. Its instantaneous contact starts the pump forward (KM4); its off-delay contact holds off clamping until 1–3 s after the button is released, then starts the pump in reverse (KM5). YV is energised throughout the arm’s release and clamp, to send oil to the arm cylinders; it is not energised when the headstock and column are released or clamped.

worked.q: The arm of a Z3040 can go down and clamps afterwards, but it will not release and go up. Where is the fault? (Exercise 3.9(2))
worked.s: Lowering works, so the pump, YV, KT, SQ2 and the clamping sequence are all healthy. The fault is in what only the up path uses: the up button SB3, the upper-limit contact SQ1-1 in series with it, or contactor KM2 and the KM3 interlock contact in its coil circuit.

worked.q: Why does the hydraulic pump motor have a thermal relay when the arm-lift motor, also a short-time motor, has none?
worked.s: The lift motor runs only while a button is held. The pump motor is stopped by a limit switch, SQ3. If SQ3 is out of adjustment or the hydraulics fail, the pump keeps running under load, so it needs FR2.

recap: On the Z3040 the arm can be raised only after limit switch ___ shows that it is fully released.
Time relay KT delays clamping by ___ s after the lift motor is switched off.
If the supply phase sequence is reversed, pressing “up” makes the arm ___ instead of release.
With solenoid valve YV de-energised, oil goes to the headstock and ___ cylinders.

topics.title: The X62W Universal Milling Machine
topics.zh: X62W 型万能铣床

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 3, “Analysis of the electrical control circuits of ordinary machine tools”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. The book’s full-page schematics are not reproduced; the control logic is redrawn here as simplified ladder circuits and step sequences built from the book’s written explanation. Device codes are the book’s. The machines are Chinese models; the point is the method and the circuit ideas, which carry over to any machine.

A milling machine cuts with a rotating multi-tooth cutter. It machines flat and formed surfaces and grooves of many kinds, and even bodies of revolution. With a dividing head it cuts spur gears and helical surfaces; with a round (rotary) table it cuts cams and curved slots. Kinds include horizontal, vertical, toolroom, planer-type and copy millers. The most used are the horizontal and vertical knee-type universal millers: the X62W (horizontal spindle) and X53K (vertical spindle). Their electrical control is similar; the X62W is the example.

PartWhat it does
Base and bed (column)The box-shaped bed is fixed on the base and carries everything else. Inside are the spindle drive and speed-change mechanism. On top are horizontal ways; on the front, vertical ways for the knee
Overarm and arbor supportCarry the outer end of the cutter arbor; the other end is in the spindle. The support slides on the overarm and the overarm slides on the bed
KneeMoves up and down the front ways on a screw. The feed motor and feed gearbox are inside it
Saddle (cross slide)On the knee’s horizontal ways; moves across, parallel to the spindle axis
TableOn the saddle; moves lengthwise, at right angles to the spindle. A swivel between saddle and table lets the table turn, usually ±45°, so that it can feed at an angle for helical grooves
MovementWhat moves
MainThe spindle rotates the cutter
FeedThe table moves in a straight line in three mutually perpendicular directions: left–right, front–back, up–down. By hand or power
AuxiliaryRapid straight-line movement of the table in the same three directions

Spindle and table have separate motors. The feed motor and feed gearbox are both in the knee, and rapid movement is taken from the feed motor through a fast drive chain. A flywheel on the spindle evens out its speed and reduces vibration in cutting.

Type code X62W: X = milling machine · 6 = horizontal · 2 = No. 2 size (0, 1, 2, 3 give the table size) · W = universal.

sections.h: Requirements, the clutch, and the main circuit
sections.b:
1. Spindle and feed motors must both reverse, for climb (down) milling and conventional (up) milling. Both also need a speed-change pulse so that gears mesh when the speed is changed.
  2. For accurate stopping and easy cutter changing, the spindle has an electromagnetic brake.
  3. An electromagnetic clutch in the feed drive switches between rapid traverse and normal feed.
  4. Thorough electrical interlocks for safety.
  5. Two sets of buttons so that the machine can be controlled from two places.
  6. Interlocks and protection; lighting and indication.

Electromagnetic clutch. A clutch is an actuator that passes torque between two rotating parts by friction, under electrical control. It can be operated from a distance, needs little control power, and acts fast and reliably. Kinds: friction-plate, magnetic-powder and slip types. Machine tools commonly use the multi-plate friction type.

How the multi-plate type works: driving plates are splined to the driving shaft and can slide along it; driven plates are interleaved with them and keyed by lugs to a sleeve fixed to the driven gear. Energising the DC coil pulls the armature towards the core and squeezes the plates together. Friction then carries the driven plates, sleeve and gear round with the driving shaft. De-energising the coil lets ring springs between the plates push armature and plates apart, and no torque passes.

MotorJobSwitched byOverload
M1SpindleKM1. Direction is pre-selected before starting with changeover switch SA5: forward · stop · reverseFR1
M2FeedKM3 forward · KM4 reverseFR2
M3Coolant pumpFed from after the KM1 main contacts, so it can run only while M1 runs; switched by SA3FR3

Supply through the changeover switch QS; FU1 is the main short-circuit protection. Control voltage is 110 V from transformer TC1.

SB1 and SB2 are compound stop buttons: the NC half drops KM1, the NO half picks up KM2. Not shown: SQ7 also has an NO contact that pulses KM1 during a speed change.

  • Starting, from two places. One button set is on the front of the table, the other on the side of the bed. First turn SA5 to the direction wanted. Then press SB3 or SB4: KM1 pulls in and holds itself, and M1 drives the spindle. The NC contacts of FR1 and FR3 are in series in this circuit, so an overload on either the spindle motor or the coolant pump stops both.
  • Stopping with braking. Press SB1 or SB2. Its NC contact opens and KM1 releases, but the spindle keeps turning by inertia. The button must be pressed right down. The speed-relay contact for the running direction (KS-1 forward, KS-2 reverse) is closed, so KM2 pulls in and connects M1 to a reversed supply. The motor is braked hard; near standstill the KS contact opens and KM2 releases.
  • Speed-change pulse. Pull the speed-change handle forward, turn the dial to the speed wanted, then push the handle back. As it goes back, a cam linked to it briefly presses limit switch SQ7. SQ7’s NO contact closes for an instant, KM1 pulls in for an instant and M1 gives a short kick. The gears turn slightly and slide into mesh. The spindle need not be stopped first: pulling the handle forward also presses SQ7, whose NC contact opens and drops out KM1, so the motor stops by itself.
  • Brake for cutter changing. Before changing the cutter, set switch SA2 to the “cutter change” position. One contact cuts off the control circuit, for personal safety; another energises the spindle brake clutch YC1, which holds the spindle still. Afterwards return SA2 to “work”: YC1 is released and the control circuit is restored.

The book describes both braking arrangements: reverse-supply braking through KS in its circuit walk-through, and the electromagnetic brake clutch for cutter changing.

The feed motor can start only after QS is closed and KM1 has pulled in and held: the feed control circuit takes its supply through a KM1 contact.

Principle only. The real circuit also routes each branch through the NC contacts of the other handle’s switches, of SQ6 and of the round-table switch SA1.

The idea that makes this circuit unusual: the operator does not press buttons for the feed. He moves a handle. The handle does two things at once: it mechanically engages the feed drive with the right lead screw, and it electrically presses a limit switch that starts the feed motor in the right direction.

HandlePositionLimit switch pressedContactorMotor M2Table moves
Longitudinal handle (two, mechanically linked: one at the centre front of the table, one at the lower left of the base)RightSQ1KM3ForwardRight
LeftSQ2KM4ReverseLeft
CentreNoneNoneStoppedStopped
Cross-and-vertical “joystick” handle (two, linked, on the left side of the table front and back; five positions)Down or ForwardSQ3KM3ForwardDown or forward
Up or BackSQ4KM4ReverseUp or back
CentreNoneNoneStoppedStopped

The joystick’s mechanism decides which screw the motor is coupled to: the vertical screw of the knee for up and down, the cross screw under the saddle for forward and back. Each switch has an NO contact that energises its contactor and an NC contact used for interlocking.

End-of-travel protection. Stop dogs are fixed at each end of the table. When the table reaches one, the dog knocks the handle back to centre, the limit switch is released and the feed stops. Moving a dog changes the stroke.

Rapid traverse. With the spindle running and the feed handle set, the table creeps in that direction. Press SB5 or SB6 (one at the table front, one at the bed side): KM5 pulls in and energises the rapid-traverse electromagnet YA. Through a lever it engages the friction clutch and takes the reduction gearing out of the drive, so the table moves fast in the same direction. Release the button: KM5 and YA drop out, the clutch opens, and the table carries on at feed speed. It is jog control.

Feed speed-change pulse. Start the spindle first, so that KM1’s contact prepares the circuit. Pull the mushroom-shaped feed speed dial out, turn it to the speed wanted, then push it back in. On the way the stop piece briefly presses SQ6: its NC contact opens and its NO contact closes for a moment, KM3 pulls in briefly and M2 gives a kick so that the gears mesh.

Round table. The round table is an accessory driven by the feed motor through the longitudinal drive. Set its switch SA1 to “on” and put both feed handles at centre. Start the spindle: KM1 pulls in, then KM3, and M2 turns the round table. Only KM3 is used, so the round table turns in one direction only.

Contact of SA1Round table ONRound table OFF
SA1-1OpenClosed
SA1-2ClosedOpen
SA1-3OpenClosed

InterlockWhyHow the circuit does it
Feed only after spindleIf the table fed with the cutter stationary, work and cutter would collide and the machine would be damagedThe feed control circuit gets its supply only through a KM1 contact. If the spindle motor stops during work, the feed motor stops with it
Only one feed direction at a timeFeeding in two or more directions at once easily causes an accidentMechanically, each handle can select only one direction. Electrically, the NC contacts of SQ1 and SQ2 are in series in one branch and the NC contacts of SQ3 and SQ4 in series in another; the two branches are in parallel and feed KM3 and KM4. With one handle moved, one branch opens and the other still carries the current. With both handles moved, both branches are open: neither contactor can pull in and M2 stops
No feed during a feed speed changeSafety: the table must not move when the gears are being pulsedThe pulse circuit passes through the NC contacts of SQ1, SQ2, SQ3 and SQ4 in series. If either handle is off centre, one of them is open and KM3 cannot pulse
Round table and normal feed never togetherThe round table and the straight feeds share the feed motorWith SA1 at “on” the supply to KM3 passes through the NC contacts of all four handle switches in series. Move either handle and KM3 drops out: the round table stops
Forward and reverse contactorsBoth together would short-circuit the supplyEach of KM3 and KM4 has an NC contact in the other’s coil circuit; KM1 and KM2 likewise

Lighting. A separate transformer TC2 gives a safe 24 V. The lamp is switched by SA4, one side is earthed, and FU3 protects the circuit.

CodeDeviceCodeDevice
M1 · M2 · M3Spindle · feed · coolant pump motorsSA1Round-table switch
KM1Spindle startSA2Master switch: spindle brake and release (cutter change)
KM2Spindle reverse-supply brakingSA3Coolant pump switch
KM3 · KM4Feed forward · reverseSA5Spindle direction switch
KM5Rapid-traverse electromagnetYARapid-traverse electromagnet / clutch
TC1 · TC2Control · lighting transformersSQ1 · SQ2Feed right · left
FR1 · FR2 · FR3Thermal relays for M1 · M2 · M3SQ3Feed down and forward
FU1 · FU2 · FU3Fuses: supply · control · lightingSQ4Feed up and back
QFSupply breakerSQ6 · SQ7Feed · spindle speed-change pulse
SB1 · SB2Spindle stop-and-brake buttonsSB3 · SB4Spindle start buttons
SB5 · SB6Rapid-traverse buttonsELWork lamp
SymptomLikely causes
Spindle motor will not startControl fuse blown · cutter-change switch SA2 left in the brake position · direction switch SA5 at “stop” · contacts of SB1–SB4 dirty · NC contact of spindle pulse switch SQ7 not making · FR1 or FR3 tripped
No spindle speed-change pulseSQ7 has shifted, been knocked out of place or has a broken wire
Spindle will not brakeFuse in the brake circuit blown · spindle brake clutch coil burnt
Spindle does not stop on pressing stopUsually the main contacts of KM1 have welded
Table will not feed at allFuse blown · spindle motor not started · KM3 or KM4 coil open or main contacts dirty · NC contacts of SQ1–SQ4 dirty, or wiring loose · FR2 tripped · NC contact of SQ6 open · both handles off centre
No feed speed-change pulseSQ6 shifted, knocked out of place or wire loose · a feed handle is not at centre
Feeds left, right and down correctly, but not up or backNO contact of SQ4 open: SQ4 is the switch for up and back
Cross and vertical feeds work, longitudinal does notAn open circuit through the NC contacts of SQ6, SQ4 and SQ3 that the longitudinal branch uses
No rapid traverseFuse blown · SB5 or SB6 contact dirty or wire loose · KM5 coil burnt · rectifier diode damaged · rapid clutch YA damaged

Method. Use the table of handle positions backwards. A direction that fails points to one switch; a group of directions that fail together points to what they share.

worked.q: What is the purpose of the speed-change pulse on the X62W? (Exercise 3.13)
worked.s: After a speed change the new gears may sit tooth-against-tooth and will not slide into mesh. A brief pulse of the motor (spindle: SQ7 and KM1; feed: SQ6 and KM3) turns the gears slightly so that they engage easily, without running the machine up to speed.

worked.q: Explain how the X62W prevents the table from feeding in two directions at once. (Exercise 3.14)
worked.s: Mechanically, each handle selects only one direction. Electrically, the NC contacts of SQ1 and SQ2 (longitudinal handle) form one series branch and those of SQ3 and SQ4 (joystick) another; the two branches are in parallel in the supply to KM3 and KM4. One handle moved: one branch opens, the other still conducts, the feed runs. Both handles moved: both branches open, KM3 and KM4 cannot be energised, M2 stops.

worked.q: On an X62W the table feeds up, down, left, right and forward, but not back. Find the fault. (Exercise 3.15(3))
worked.s: “Up” and “back” both use SQ4 and KM4, and “up” works, so SQ4, KM4 and the motor are healthy. Only the mechanical selection differs: the joystick linkage that couples the motor to the cross screw in the back direction, or the handle not fully engaging in that position. Look at the linkage and at whether SQ4 is fully pressed in the “back” position.

worked.q: Why is the feed motor allowed to start only after the spindle motor?
worked.s: If the table fed while the cutter was not turning, the work would be driven into a stationary cutter, breaking the cutter and damaging the machine. Taking the feed circuit’s supply through a KM1 contact also stops the feed at once if the spindle stops during a cut.

worked.q: The round table is in use and the operator bumps the longitudinal feed handle. What happens, and why is that the right behaviour?
worked.s: The handle presses SQ1 or SQ2, whose NC contact is in the series chain feeding KM3 in round-table mode. KM3 drops out and the round table stops. That is correct: round-table rotation and straight table feed must never happen together.

recap: On the X62W the direction of the spindle is pre-selected with changeover switch ___.
Pushing the longitudinal handle to the right presses SQ1 and energises contactor ___.
The feed motor can be started only after contactor ___ has pulled in.
The round table can turn in ___ direction(s) only.
Rapid traverse on the X62W is a ___ control.

topics.title: Design Principles, Choosing the Drive, and Rules for a Sound Control Circuit
topics.zh: 设计原则、拖动方案的确定和控制电路的一般要求

sections.h: Principles and what a design contains
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 4, “Design of electrical control systems”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, with figures redrawn. Selection rules and multipliers are the book’s rules of thumb for study. Real equipment must be selected to the current standards and the maker’s data.

Design has two halves: the schematic design, which makes the machine do what the process needs, and the construction (process) design, which lets the control gear be built, used, run and repaired.

Four principles.

  1. Meet the demands of the machine and the process as fully as possible.
  2. Having met them, keep the system simple, economical and sensible; easy to operate, easy to repair, safe and reliable.
  3. Choose components that are correct and suitable, so the system works normally.
  4. Leave some margin in capacity for later process changes.
Schematic designConstruction design
1 · Draw up the design brief1 · Design the overall arrangement; draw the general assembly and general wiring diagrams
2 · Choose the drive scheme and control method2 · Draw the layout and wiring diagram of each assembly, showing how parts are mounted and connected
3 · Fix the motor type, model, rating and speed3 · Write the operating and maintenance instructions
4 · Design the schematic
5 · Select the components and make the parts list
6 · Write the design calculations

First choose the kind of drive and the number of motors from the process and the machine’s structure. Then choose how speed is to be varied from the speed range each mechanism needs, so that every motor is fully used.

Single or separate drive. One motor for the whole machine, or one motor per mechanism. The trend is for the motor to move ever closer to the working mechanism, giving multi-motor drives.

Speed control. The options are gearboxes, hydraulic variable-speed units, two-speed or multi-speed motors, and electrical stepless speed control.
