  • Heavy or large machines: stepless control wherever possible for the main and feed movements.
  • Precision machines (jig borers, precision grinders, CNC machines): electrical stepless control, for accuracy and for automatic control.
  • Ordinary small and medium machines with no special needs: the cheap, simple, reliable three-phase cage motor with a gearbox. A two-speed or multi-speed cage motor simplifies the gearbox and widens the range.

Match the motor’s speed-control character to the load. Mechanisms differ: on a machine tool the main movement is a constant-power load and the feed is a constant-torque load. Choose a speed-control method of the same character, or the motor will be either oversized or overloaded over part of the range.

What the machine needsKind of motor
No speed controlInduction motor first: simple, cheap, little maintenance
Long-running machine with a periodically fluctuating loadA motor with a flywheel to level the peaks. A wound-rotor induction motor suits this, considering starting and full use of the flywheel
Power-factor correction and a steady speedSynchronous motor
Only a few fixed speeds, no continuous controlMulti-speed induction motor
High starting torque and constant-power speed control (electric vehicles, traction)DC series motor
Demanding starting, speed control and brakingDC motor, or an induction motor with a speed controller
Very wide speed rangeCombined mechanical and electrical speed control
EnvironmentEnclosure
NormalProtected type; open type only where people and plant are safe
Much dust in the airTotally enclosed
Hot-humid region or damp placeTropicalised type; an ordinary motor only with moisture protection
OutdoorsOutdoor type; enclosed or protected if sheltered
Hot workshopInsulation class to suit the ambient temperature, plus better ventilation
Explosion risk or corrosive gasFlameproof or corrosion-proof type
  • Rated speed. For the same power, a faster motor is smaller and cheaper, but the faster the motor, the larger the reduction ratio and the more complex the transmission. Weigh the two.
  • Rated voltage. Equal to the supply voltage.
  • Rated power. Practice shows it is right to choose a motor with rated power about 10 % above what the driven machine needs.

Use the standard control voltages and keep the number of different voltages and currents in the control circuit as small as possible.

Kind of control circuitUsual voltages, VSource
Simple AC drive controlAC380, 220The mains directly
More complex AC drive controlAC110, 127, 48Control transformer
Lighting and signal circuitsAC48, 36, 24, 6Control transformer
Control of DC drivesDC220, 110Rectifier or DC generator
Control of DC electromagnets and electromagnetic clutchesDC48, 24, 12Rectifier

This is what the four machines of Chapter 3 showed: the simple grinder used 380 V directly, the others a 110 V transformer, and every lamp a safe low voltage.

sections.h: Keep the circuit simple and cheap
sections.b:
1. Shorten and reduce the connecting wires. Think about where each device is mounted. Buttons are on the operator’s desk and contactors in the cabinet, so every connection between a button and a contactor is a wire run between desk and cabinet. Wire the start and stop buttons to each other first, then take the group to the cabinet: three wires are needed where a careless arrangement takes four.
  2. Fewer kinds, sizes and numbers of components. Devices doing the same job should be the same make and model.
  3. Fewer contacts. Every contact is a possible fault. Contacts doing the same job can be merged. Before merging, check that no other branch is affected and that the remaining contact can carry the combined current.
  4. Fewer devices energised. In running, keep as few coils energised as possible. This lengthens life, saves energy and reduces faults.

KT is needed only to bring in KM2, yet it stays on all the time.

Fewer devices energised: longer life, less energy, fewer faults. My redrawing of the principle in the book’s Fig. 4.3.

sections.h: Keep the circuit safe and reliable
sections.b:
RuleWrongRight, and why
Connect coils correctlyTwo AC coils in seriesCoils in parallel, each across the full control voltage. In series the voltage divides according to impedance, and the impedance of an AC coil changes sharply when its armature closes. The first to close takes most of the voltage and the other never pulls in
A large DC electromagnet coil directly in parallel with a small relay coilGive the relay its own contact path. When the supply is cut, the large coil’s stored energy discharges through the relay coil and can hold the relay in, or pull it in again, wrongly
Connect contacts correctlyThe NO and NC contacts of one limit switch wired to different potentials of the supplyWire both to the same potential. The two contacts sit very close together; if an arc is drawn when one opens it can flash over to the other and short-circuit the supply. The same-potential wiring also needs three leads to the switch where the other needs four
Prevent parasitic (sneak) circuitsIndicator lamps across the coils of a forward–reverse circuit with the thermal relay contact placed after the lamps and coilsPlace the thermal relay contact so that when it opens it isolates the whole control circuit. A parasitic circuit is a path that conducts unintentionally during operation: here, when FR opens, current can still creep through a lamp and the other coil, so the contactor may not release reliably and the protection fails
Arrange control contacts sensiblyOne coil that needs a long chain of other relays’ contacts in series before it can pull inFeed each coil through as few contacts as possible, taken as directly from the supply as the logic allows
Allow for making and breaking capacityA contact working beyond its ratingTo raise making capacity, put several contacts in parallel. To raise breaking capacity, put several in series
Avoid races and hazardsA circuit that depends on which of two contacts moves firstChoose devices with short operating times, or use a time relay to fix the order. Every device takes a definite time to act; when the circuit changes state, contacts “race” and several different outcomes are possible. A hazard is a brief wrong output caused by a release delay
Double interlockElectrical interlock alone on a reversing circuit that operates oftenAdd a mechanical interlock between the forward and reverse contactors as well

And before any of this: talk to the mechanical designers. Understand the machine’s performance, structure and process; study similar products; then propose the control scheme, with the interlocks and protection it needs.

worked.q: State the design principles for an electrical schematic. (Exercise 4.2(1))
worked.s: (1) Meet the requirements of the machine and process as fully as possible. (2) Within that, keep the system simple, economical, easy to operate and repair, safe and reliable. (3) Choose components correctly and sensibly. (4) Leave capacity margin for process improvement.

worked.q: Two 220 V AC contactor coils are connected in series across 440 V “to share the voltage”. Why does this fail?
worked.s: An AC coil’s impedance is small with the armature open and large once it has closed. The two never close at exactly the same instant. The first to close has the higher impedance and takes most of the voltage; the other is left with too little to pull in, and its coil, with the armature open, carries a heavy current and overheats. Coils go in parallel at their rated voltage.

worked.q: A machine’s feed is a constant-torque load. Its spindle is a constant-power load. What does this say about choosing speed control for each?
worked.s: Choose a method whose character matches. For the feed: constant-torque control, such as varying armature voltage on a DC motor or constant V/f on an induction motor. For the spindle: constant-power control, such as field weakening on a DC motor, or a multi-speed motor with a gearbox.

worked.q: A driven machine needs 5 kW at its shaft. About what rated motor power does the book’s rule of thumb suggest?
worked.s: About 10 % more: 5 kW × 1.1 = 5.5 kW, which is a standard motor size.

recap: To increase the breaking capacity of contacts, connect several in ___.
Two AC coils must never be connected in ___ in one control branch.
An unintended path that conducts during operation is called a ___ circuit.
A motor’s rated power is usually chosen about ___ % above the power the machine needs.

topics.title: Design Methods and a Worked Design: the Material Trolley
topics.zh: 设计方法与设计举例：送料小车

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 4, “Design of electrical control systems”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, with figures redrawn. Selection rules and multipliers are the book’s rules of thumb for study. Real equipment must be selected to the current standards and the maker’s data.

MethodHow it worksStrengths and limits
Analytical (experience) methodStarting from the process requirements, pick proven typical basic links for each requirement, extend them step by step, then add interlocks and protection until the links form a complete circuitSimple and direct; nothing new to learn. The result depends on the designer’s experience and is not necessarily the most economical circuit, so it must be checked carefully
Logic methodUse logic algebra. Treat contact states as input logic variables and coils as output variables. Write each output as a logic function of the inputs, simplify with the laws of logic algebra, then draw the circuit from the simplified expressions and check and optimise itGives a circuit with fewer contacts and a more nearly ideal design. Harder to carry out on a large circuit

In the logic method, the relation between inputs and outputs is the logic function, and it is the structure of the circuit: contacts in series are AND, contacts in parallel are OR, a normally-closed contact is NOT.

sections.h: Five steps of the analytical method
sections.b:
1 · Main circuit
Design it from the starting, braking, reversing and speed-control requirements of the process
2 · Basic links of the control circuit
From the main circuit, design the basic control links: the start, brake, reverse and speed-control circuits the requirements call for
3 · Special links
From how the movements must cooperate and interlock, decide the control parameters (travel, time, speed, current) and design the special parts of the circuit
4 · Protection
Analyse the faults that could occur in operation and add the necessary protection
5 · Review
Check carefully that the circuit acts correctly. Test key links if necessary. Refine and simplify

sections.h: The task: a trolley serving three stations
sections.b:
One cycle has four runs; then it repeats. Limit-switch labels follow the book’s sketch.

A trolley is driven by a three-phase cage motor rated 7.5 kW, 1470 r/min, AC 380 V, 13.5 A. Required sequence:

  1. Started at station A, it runs to B and stops by itself. It waits t₁ to be loaded, then returns by itself.
  2. Back at A it stops by itself, waits t₂ to be unloaded, then starts again by itself.
  3. This time it passes B without stopping, runs on to C and stops. It waits t₃, takes on another material, then returns by itself.
  4. Returning, it passes B without stopping and stops at A. One working cycle is complete.

After the wait t₂ at A it starts again, runs to B and stops, and the whole cycle repeats automatically.

Step 1 · Main circuit. The trolley must run both ways and hold its position when stopped, so the main circuit is a forward–reverse circuit with a power-off holding brake: isolator QS, fuses FU1, contactors KM1 (forward) and KM2 (reverse), thermal relay FR, and an electromagnetic brake YB connected across the motor terminals. With the motor energised the brake is lifted; with the motor off, springs apply it.

Step 2 · Basic links. Start with the known forward–reverse circuit: start buttons, a stop button, self-holding, and KM1 / KM2 interlocked with each other.

Step 3 · Special links. Now turn each sentence of the task into a device.

RequirementControl parameterDevice and use
Stop at A, B and CTravelThree limit switches, one per station. The NC contact of each opens the running contactor’s coil circuit
Wait t₁, t₂, t₃, then move by itselfTimeThree time relays KT1, KT2, KT3. Each is started by the limit switch at its station; its delayed contact then energises the contactor for the next run
Stop at B on one trip, pass it on the nextMemory of which trip this isAn intermediate relay KA. It is set when the trolley returns to A from B and reset when it returns from C. One of its contacts bridges the B limit-switch contact on the trips that must not stop at B
Do not restart by itself after a supply failureVoltageA voltage relay KV with self-holding gives under-voltage and loss-of-voltage protection: after the supply returns, the start button must be pressed again

Step 4 · Protection. Short circuit: FU1 in the main circuit, FU2 in the control circuit. Overload: FR. Under-voltage and loss of voltage: KV. Interlock: NC contacts of KM1 and KM2 in each other’s coil circuits.

Step 5 · Review. Trace one whole cycle on paper, then ask the awkward questions. What if the supply fails halfway between stations? What if a limit switch sticks? What if a timer is set to zero? Simplify where a contact turns out to be unnecessary.

The book’s finished schematic (its Fig. 4.11) is not reproduced; the table gives the reasoning that leads to it.

sections.h: Parts list, layout drawing and wiring diagram
sections.b:
CodeDeviceRatingQty
M1Three-phase induction motor7.5 kW, 380 V, 13.5 A, 1470 r/min1
KM1 · KM2AC contactors CJ20-25Coil 220 V2
FR1Thermal relay JR16-20Heater rated 16 A1
KT1 · KT2 · KT3Time relays JS-20Coil 220 V3
KVVoltage relayCoil 220 V1
SQ1 · SQ2 · SQ3Limit switches LX19-1113
SB1 · SB3 · SB4Push buttons5 A, green3
SB2Push button5 A, red1
QSSupply switchThree-pole, 15 A1
FU1 · FU2FusesWith the switch, 15 A · 500 V, 2 A element1 each
KAIntermediate relay JZ7-44Coil 220 V1

Notice how the list applies Chapter 4’s rules: one coil voltage (220 V) throughout, two identical contactors, three identical time relays, three identical limit switches.

Layout drawing. Shows the real position of every device and gives what is needed to build and install the control gear. It is often combined with the wiring diagram. For the trolley panel: QS, FU1, FU2, the resistor and KV along the top; KM1, KM2 and KA in the middle; FR and the three time relays below; terminal block XT1 along the bottom and XT2 at the side. Buttons, limit switches, motor and brake are outside the panel.

Wiring diagram. Serves installation, wiring and fault repair. It uses the standard symbols but shows each device in its relative physical position with all its parts drawn together, and shows the actual connections. Proportion and size are not strict. Wires that leave the panel are drawn to the terminal block. Every wire number and device code is the same as on the schematic.

worked.q: What is an electrical layout (installation position) drawing for, and how is it related to the wiring diagram? (Exercise 4.2(2))
worked.s: The layout drawing shows the real position of every component and gives the information needed to manufacture and install the control gear. The wiring diagram shows the actual connections between those components, drawn in the same relative positions. The two are often combined on one sheet, and both use exactly the device codes of the schematic.

worked.q: In the trolley design, why is an intermediate relay needed? Could limit switches and timers alone do the job?
worked.s: No. At station B the trolley must do two different things on different trips: stop on the first, pass on the second. A limit switch gives the same signal every time it is struck. Something must remember which trip is in progress; that is the job of KA, which bridges the B switch when the trolley must not stop.

worked.q: The trolley uses a power-off holding brake. Why is that kind chosen and not a power-on brake?
worked.s: It fails safe. If the supply is lost, or the motor is switched off anywhere along the track, the springs apply the brake at once and the loaded trolley cannot roll. A power-on brake would release exactly when the power failed.

worked.q: Write the logic expression for a contactor KM that is started by SB2, held by its own contact, and stopped by SB1 or by FR.
worked.s: KM = (SB2 + KM) · SB1 · FR. The parallel pair (start button OR holding contact) is in series with (AND) the two normally-closed contacts (NOT).

recap: The two design methods are the analytical (experience) method and the ___ method.
In logic design, contacts in series represent AND and contacts in parallel represent ___.
On the wiring diagram every wire number must be the same as on the ___.
The trolley’s main circuit is a forward–reverse circuit with a power-___ holding brake.

topics.title: Selecting Control Components, and Building & Commissioning the Panel
topics.zh: 常用控制电器的选择，电气控制的施工与调试

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 4, “Design of electrical control systems”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, with figures redrawn. Selection rules and multipliers are the book’s rules of thumb for study. Real equipment must be selected to the current standards and the maker’s data.

ChooseRule
TypeAC or DC contactor according to the current the main contacts switch. If the system is mainly AC and the DC loads are small, AC contactors may be used throughout, but with a larger rated current
Utilisation categoryBy the duty of the load. General duty (starting a cage motor, switching it off while running): AC-3. Heavy duty (inching, plugging, reversing): AC-4
Rated voltageMain-contact rated voltage not less than the rated voltage of the load circuit
Rated currentMain-contact rated current not less than the rated current of the controlled circuit. Where starting, braking and reversing are frequent, derate: choose a size larger
Coil voltageThe same as the control-circuit voltage

For a motor load the rated current can be estimated from the nameplate power:

IN = PN × 10³ ÷ (√3 × UN × cos φ × η)

IN: motor rated current, in amperes (A) · PN: rated power, in kilowatts (kW) · UN: rated line voltage, in volts (V) · cos φ: power factor (no unit) · η: efficiency (no unit).

RelayHow to select and set
Over-voltage relay (AC)Parameters: rated voltage and operating voltage. Set the operating voltage at 1.1–1.2 × the circuit’s rated voltage. DC circuits do not normally suffer over-voltage, so there is no DC over-voltage relay
Under-voltage relayAC: an ordinary AC electromagnetic voltage relay will do. DC: pick-up set at 0.3–0.5 × rated voltage, release at 0.07–0.2 ×
Over-current relayAC and DC types; used mainly for motors that start often or under heavy load. Rated current not less than the motor’s rated current. Operating current: AC, 1.1–1.3 × the motor’s starting current according to duty; DC, 1.1–3.0 × the motor’s rated current
Under-current relayDC only; for weak-field protection of DC motors and electromagnetic chucks. Rated current not less than the rated field current. Release current about 0.85 × the minimum field current
Intermediate relayTwo points. Coil current type and voltage must match the control circuit. Type, number and rating of contacts must meet the circuit’s needs
Thermal relay — formStar-connected motor: a two-element or three-element relay. Delta-connected motor: a three-element relay with phase-loss protection
Thermal relay — currentMotor not started often, starting current about 6 × rated and starting time not over 6 s: heater rated current = motor rated current. Motor with poor overload capacity, if starting allows: 60–80 % of its rated current. Repeated short-time duty: first find the relay’s permitted operating frequency, then choose by starting time, starting current and duty factor
Time relay(1) Current type and voltage to match the control circuit. (2) Delay mode: on-delay or off-delay. (3) Contact form and number. (4) Accuracy: air-damped where accuracy is unimportant, motor-driven or electronic where it matters. (5) Delay time long enough. (6) Operating frequency not too high, or life suffers and it may misoperate

Choose the element first, from what the circuit needs, then the fuse body to hold it. The element’s rated current must not exceed the body’s rated current.

  • Type: by the circuit’s requirements, the place of use and the mounting. Its protection characteristic should match the overload capacity of what it protects.
  • Breaking capacity: not less than the largest short-circuit current that can occur at that point. Only then is the protection reliable.
  • Rated voltage: not less than the working voltage. Rated current: not less than the element fitted.
LoadElement rated current IFU
Lighting, heating: no inrush currentIFU ≥ IN
One motor, long runningIFU ≥ (1.5 to 2.5) × IN
One motor, started oftenIFU ≥ (3 to 3.5) × IN
Several motors on one fuse, long runningIFU ≥ (1.5 to 2.5) × IN,max + Σ IN

All currents in amperes (A). IN: rated current of the load or motor · IN,max: rated current of the largest motor · Σ IN: sum of the rated currents of all the other motors.

The multiplier exists because a motor’s starting current is several times its rated current; the element must ride through it. Use the lower end for light or no-load starting and the upper end for heavy starting.

Fast-acting fuses for rectifiers: rated voltage above the normal working voltage of the circuit; rated current not less than that of the element inside. The element is chosen from the rated average current of the rectifier device. A small rectifier may use an ordinary fuse, but then with a reduced element: generally not more than two-thirds of the rectifier device’s rated current.

DeviceSelection rules
Knife switchChoose by place of use, kind of supply, voltage, load and number of poles. (1) Construction by its job and mounting position: for isolating only, a type without arc cover; for breaking load, a type with arc cover and lever operation. (2) Rated voltage not less than the circuit’s; rated current not less than the load’s, and larger still when the load is an induction motor, to allow for its starting current. (3) Poles to match the circuit
Combination switch(1) Choose by kind of supply, voltage, number of contacts needed and motor capacity. (2) It cannot break a fault current. (3) Do not operate it too often. (4) When it reverses a motor, the motor must have stopped completely before the opposite direction is switched in. (5) It has no overload, short-circuit or under-voltage protection of its own
Circuit breaker(1) Rated voltage and current not less than the normal working voltage and current. (2) Ultimate breaking capacity not less than the largest short-circuit current of the circuit. (3) Under-voltage release rated voltage equal to the circuit’s rated voltage. (4) Thermal release setting equal to the circuit’s rated current. (5) Instantaneous (over-current) release setting, see below

Instantaneous release setting. For a cage induction motor: 8–15 × the motor’s rated current. For a wound-rotor motor: 3–6 ×. Or calculate:

IZ ≥ K × IS

IZ: instantaneous setting of the over-current release, in amperes (A) · IS: peak current in the circuit, in amperes (A); for a motor load it is the starting current · K: safety factor (no unit) allowing for setting error and variation in starting current. K = 1.35 when the breaker’s operating time is over 20 ms; K = 1.7 when it is under 20 ms.

Choose by the primary and secondary voltages and by the capacity needed.

  1. Primary voltage to match the AC supply; secondary voltages to match the control circuit and the auxiliary circuits.
  2. Long-term running. The capacity must cover the largest working load:
ST ≥ KT × Σ PXC

ST: transformer capacity needed, in volt-amperes (VA) · Σ PXC: total power needed by all the devices energised at the heaviest load, where PXC is each device’s holding power, in watts (W) · KT: reserve factor (no unit), usually 1.1 to 1.25.

  1. Starting. The capacity must also be enough for devices already pulled in to stay in while others are starting, and for the starting ones to pull in reliably:
ST ≥ 0.6 × Σ PXC + 1.5 × Σ Pst

Σ Pst: total pull-in power of the devices that start at the same moment, in watts (W). Take the larger of the two results and round up to a standard size.

The second formula exists because an AC coil draws several times its holding power at the instant of pull-in. A transformer sized only for the steady load would sag in voltage at that instant and could drop out the contactors already holding.

Overall arrangement. Shown as a general assembly drawing and a general wiring diagram: in outline, where the main assemblies of each part sit, how the parts connect to one another, the routing of the wiring and the conduit required.

Laying out the cabinet.

  1. Large or heavy devices at the bottom.
  2. Heat-producing devices at the top, kept apart from temperature-sensitive ones.
  3. Power and control (strong and weak current) separated. The weak-current part should be shielded and isolated against interference from the power part and from outside.
  4. Tidy, good-looking and symmetrical.
  5. Leave space between devices for wiring, connection, repair and adjustment.
  6. Terminal blocks: those linking adjacent cabinets at the two sides; those for devices outside the cabinet at the bottom, not lower than 200 mm from the floor of the cabinet.

Drawing the wiring diagram.

  1. Follow the national standard for wiring diagrams.
  2. Relative positions of devices as actually mounted.
  3. All live parts of one device (coil, contacts) drawn together, inside one thin-line box.
  4. Device codes and terminal wire numbers identical to the schematic.
  5. Drawn throughout in thin lines.
  6. Mark the type, size, cross-section and colour of the connecting wires.

Wiring the cabinet. Inside: different colours for circuits of different nature and purpose; no joints anywhere along a wire. Outside: insulated multi-strand wire with no joints, and every wire outside the cabinet laid in a wiring duct or conduit. Cross-section chosen from the largest steady current in normal working, with allowance for ambient conditions.

Inspect, adjust, trial run
1 · Check the wiring diagram
2 · Check the components against the parts list
3 · Check that the wiring is correct
4 · Carry out the insulation test
5 · Check and adjust the circuit until it acts correctly

worked.q: Estimate the rated current of a 7.5 kW, 380 V three-phase cage motor. Take cos φ = 0.85 and η = 0.87 (typical values that I have assumed; the book’s exercise gives none).
worked.s: IN = PN × 10³ ÷ (√3 × UN × cos φ × η) = 7500 W ÷ (1.732 × 380 V × 0.85 × 0.87) = 7500 ÷ 486.7 = 15.4 A. A quick check: the 7.5 kW lathe motor in Chapter 3 has its thermal relay set at 15.4 A.

worked.q: That 7.5 kW motor starts on no load and is protected against short circuit by a fuse. Choose the element. (Exercise 4.5)
worked.s: One long-running motor: IFU ≥ (1.5 to 2.5) × 15.4 A = 23.1 A to 38.5 A. No-load starting is light, so take the lower part of the range: a 25 A or 30 A element. From the Chapter 1 table, an RL1-60 screw fuse (60 A body) accepts both.

worked.q: Two motors do not start at the same time. Their rated currents are 14.8 A and 6.47 A. Choose the rated currents of the element and of the fuse for their common short-circuit protection. (Exercise 4.2(4))
worked.s: IFU ≥ (1.5 to 2.5) × 14.8 A + 6.47 A = 22.2 A + 6.47 A to 37.0 A + 6.47 A = 28.7 A to 43.5 A. Choose a standard element in that range, for example 35 A or 40 A, in a 60 A fuse body.

worked.q: A breaker protects the same 7.5 kW cage motor (I<sub>N</sub> = 15.4 A). In what range should its instantaneous release be set?
worked.s: 8 to 15 times the rated current: 8 × 15.4 A = 123 A to 15 × 15.4 A = 231 A. So between about 123 A and 231 A. The thermal release is set at the rated current, 15.4 A.

worked.q: The devices energised at the heaviest load of a control circuit need 60 W in total to hold. At the worst moment, devices needing 80 W to pull in start together while devices needing 40 W are already holding. Size the control transformer. (My own figures, to practise both formulas.)
worked.s: Running: ST ≥ KT × Σ PXC = 1.25 × 60 W = 75 VA. Starting: ST ≥ 0.6 × 40 W + 1.5 × 80 W = 24 + 120 = 144 VA. Take the larger, 144 VA, and round up to a standard size such as 150 VA.

worked.q: Fill in: when choosing a contactor, the rated voltage of its main contacts should be ___ the voltage of the load circuit, their rated current ___ the load current, and the coil’s rated voltage should ___ the control circuit. (Exercise 4.1(2))
worked.s: Greater than or equal to · greater than or equal to · be the same as.

recap: A current coil is connected in ___ with the load; a voltage coil is connected in parallel across the circuit being measured.
A delta-connected motor needs a three-element thermal relay with ___ protection.
For one long-running motor, the fuse element is chosen at ___ to 2.5 times the motor’s rated current.
Heat-producing devices are mounted at the ___ of the cabinet.
No wire in a control cabinet may have a ___ along its length.

topics.title: PLC: Origin, Definition, Features, Uses, Classes & Trends
topics.zh: PLC 的产生、定义、特点、应用、分类和发展

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 5, “Overview of the PLC”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, figures redrawn. The book dates from the 2000s, so its “latest trends” and market remarks describe that period. Your ITE PLC module (Sem 4) covers the same ideas with a different PLC family; where the two agree, this is useful second reading.

Before the PLC, industrial control was dominated by relay control. A relay system works through a sequence fixed by its wiring. To change the sequence you must change the wiring, so such systems are neither general-purpose nor flexible.

In the 1960s computers began to appear in industry, but price, mismatched input and output circuits, difficult programming and poor tolerance of harsh surroundings kept them out of general control work.

In 1968 General Motors, needing to retool its car lines every model year, asked for a new controller that was more reliable than relays, more capable and faster. From the user’s side it set out ten conditions, the “GM ten”:

  1. Easy to program; the program can be changed on site.
  2. Easy to maintain; plug-in construction.
  3. More reliable than a relay panel.
  4. Smaller than a relay panel.
  5. Data can be sent directly to a management computer.
  6. Competitive in cost with a relay panel.
  7. Inputs can be mains voltage (115 V AC).
  8. Outputs can be mains voltage, 2 A or more, able to drive contactors directly (115 V AC, 2 A).
  9. Can be expanded with the least change to the existing system.
  10. User memory of more than 4 KB.

The idea behind the list: join the relay system’s strengths (easy to understand, easy to use, cheap) to the computer’s (complete functions, flexible, general-purpose), and turn hard-wired logic into software logic.

In 1969 Digital Equipment Corporation built the first programmable controller, the PDP-14. It was tried on a GM production line with good results. Japan began making PLCs in 1971 and Europe in 1973.

GenerationDevicesCapability
1st1-bit microprocessorLogic control
2nd8-bit microprocessor and memoryProducts made in series
3rdHigh-performance 8-bit microprocessors and bit-slice processorsFaster; moving towards multiple functions and networking
4th16-bit and 32-bit microprocessors, high-performance bit-slice processorsLogic, motion, data handling and networking: truly multi-function

Name. The first products were called Programmable Logic Controller, PLC: they replaced relay logic. By 1975–76 integrated circuits and microprocessors had widened what they could do, and “logic” no longer described them. In 1980 the US National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) gave the new name Programmable Controller, PC. But “PC” had become the name of the personal computer, so to avoid confusion the old abbreviation PLC is still used. It does not mean the device does logic only.

NEMA’s definition (1980), in substance: a digital electronic device that uses a programmable memory to store instructions for functions such as logic, sequencing, timing, counting and arithmetic, and controls machines or processes through digital or analog inputs and outputs. A digital computer used to do a PLC’s job counts as one; drum and mechanical sequencers do not.

IEC’s definition (drafts of November 1982, January 1985 and February 1987), in substance: an electronic system operating digitally, designed for use in an industrial environment. It uses a programmable memory for the internal storage of user-oriented instructions for logic, sequencing, timing, counting and arithmetic operations, and controls various machines or processes through digital or analog inputs and outputs. The controller and its peripherals are designed to be easily integrated into an industrial control system and easily expanded.

Phrase in the definitionWhat it tells you
“Electronic system operating digitally”It is a computer
“Designed for an industrial environment”Strong noise immunity and wide adaptability. This is what separates it from an ordinary microcomputer system
“User-oriented instructions”Easy to program
“Easily integrated … easily expanded”Built to join a larger system and to grow
“Programmable”The real difference from drum and mechanical sequencers: the behaviour is changed in software

FeatureWhy
1 · Highly reliable, strong noise immunityUsually the first thing a user asks for. Makers take a whole series of hardware and software measures against interference, so a PLC can be installed directly on the shop floor. Mean time between failures is far above the IEC figure of 100 000 hours (about 4166 days, roughly 11 years). For special duties some PLCs add redundant and diverse designs
2 · Adaptable, flexibleProducts are made in series with a full range and mostly modular hardware. They are easy to combine and expand, so systems of any size and function can be built
3 · Easy to program and useThe ladder diagram language looks very like a relay circuit: direct and easy to understand, welcomed by site electricians. The sequential function chart (SFC) makes programming simpler still
4 · Easy to design, install and commissionA PLC contains large numbers of “soft” devices equivalent to intermediate relays, time relays and counters. The program (soft wiring) replaces hard wiring, so there is far less installation wiring. The designer needs only the PLC to design the system, and it can be simulated and debugged in the laboratory
5 · Easy to maintainFull self-diagnosis, fault history and monitoring. It displays its own working state, communication state, abnormal state and the state of every I/O point, so the cause of a fault is found quickly
6 · Complete functionsBeyond logic, timing, counting and arithmetic: with special modules, point-to-point positioning, PID, process control and numerical control. It communicates with a host computer for plant management and controls distant equipment through remote modules

“Wherever there is a factory and something to control, there is a use for the PLC.”

PLCs are used in metallurgy, oil, chemicals, building materials, machine building, power, cars, light industry, environmental protection and entertainment. As performance for the price has risen, use has spread from industrial plant and machines to small process-control systems, remote maintenance services, energy-saving monitoring and equipment connected with daily life.

Kind of useWhat the PLC doesExamples
1 · Discrete (on/off) logic controlIts most basic and widest use: replaces relay sequence controlSingle machines, groups of machines, automatic production lines; special machine tools, lifts, assembly lines
2 · Process controlPID instructions or PID modules, even fuzzy-control modules, with A/D and D/A conversion, give closed-loop control of analog quantitiesTemperature, pressure, flow
3 · Motion controlPositioning modules control one axis or severalPositioning and interpolation; simple CNC functions
4 · Data processingPLC sequence control and computer numerical control merge: CNC with a built-in PLC, PLC with built-in CNC. With configuration (SCADA) software it forms control-and-management systemsMachining centres, plant data collection
5 · Communication and networkingPLC to PLC, PLC to host industrial PC, PLC to other intelligent devices such as variable-speed drives and CNC. Makers offer fieldbus systems (FCS), for example Siemens PROFIBUS and Mitsubishi CC-Link, forming distributed control systems (DCS) of “centralised management, distributed control”Factory automation (FA), flexible manufacturing systems (FMS)

PLC and DCS are growing into each other and the line between them is blurring: the PLC has spread from discrete manufacturing into continuous process industries.

By I/O pointsNumber of I/O points
SmallFewer than 256. Fewer than 64 is super-small or micro
Medium256 to 2048
LargeMore than 2048. More than 8192 is super-large

These limits are not fixed; they move as PLCs develop.

By constructionHow it is builtFeatures
Compact (unit) typePower supply, CPU and I/O all in one case. A system is a base unit (main unit) plus expansion units or expansion modules, joined by flat cable. The base unit has the CPU, I/O, an expansion port and a port for the programmer or EPROM writer. An expansion unit has I/O and a power supply but no CPU; an expansion module has I/O only and is powered from the base unit. Special function units (analog, position control) can be addedCompact, small, cheap. Small PLCs are usually built this way
Modular typeEach part is a separate module: CPU module, I/O modules, power module, function modules. Modules plug into sockets on a rack or baseplateFlexible configuration, easy to assemble, expand and repair. Medium and large PLCs are usually built this way
Stackable typeCombines the two. CPU, power and I/O are separate modules, but they are joined by cable and stacked layer on layerFlexible and still compact
By functionWhat it can doUsed for
Low-endLogic, timing, counting, shifting, self-diagnosis, monitoring; perhaps a little analog I/O, arithmetic, data transfer and comparison, communicationStand-alone machines with logic control, sequence control or a little analog
Mid-rangeAll of the above with stronger analog I/O, arithmetic, data handling, number conversion, remote I/O, subroutines, networking; some add interrupts and PIDComplex control systems
High-endAdds signed arithmetic, matrix operations, bit-logic operations, square root and other special functions, table making and transfer; stronger networkingLarge-scale process control and distributed network systems: factory automation

sections.h: Makers, and where the technology was heading
sections.b:
The PLC joins three kinds of electrical engineering (control, instrumentation, drives) in one general-purpose industrial controller with a computer’s abilities. It is one of the three pillars of modern industrial automation: PLC, robots, CAD/CAM.

RegionMakers named in the book
EuropeSiemens (Germany), Telemecanique (France)
USAAllen-Bradley (A-B), General Electric (GE)
JapanMitsubishi Electric, OMRON, Fuji. Japan concentrates on small and medium PLCs: advanced small machines, compact and cheap

Trends the book lists.

  1. Faster, larger memory. Scan speeds of around 0.1 ms per thousand steps; scan speed has become an important performance figure. Memory up to tens of megabytes.
  2. Towards both extremes. Super-large machines with up to 14 336 I/O points, 32-bit processors and several CPUs in parallel. Small machines becoming modular; micro machines with as few as 8–16 I/O points.
  3. Intelligent modules and stronger networking. High-speed counter, temperature control, remote I/O, communication and operator-interface modules, each with its own CPU and memory. Two kinds of networking: PLC to PLC on each maker’s own fieldbus, and PLC to computer. Makers are agreeing common communication standards.
  4. Better detection of external faults.
  5. More programming languages, moving towards standardisation; “soft PLCs” and PC-based control; the programmable automation controller (PAC).
Where faults occur in a PLC control system (book’s statistics)Share
CPU5 %
I/O interfaces15 %
Input devices (switches, sensors)45 %
Output devices (contactors, valves)30 %
Wiring5 %

Read the table. Only 20 % of faults are inside the PLC, where its own hardware and software can detect them. 80 % are outside it: sensors, actuators and wiring. When a PLC-controlled machine stops, look at the field devices first.

worked.q: State the definition of a programmable controller. (Exercise 5.1)
worked.s: In substance (IEC): an electronic system operating digitally, designed for use in an industrial environment. It uses a programmable memory to store user-oriented instructions for logic, sequencing, timing, counting and arithmetic, and controls machines or processes through digital or analog inputs and outputs. It and its peripherals are designed to integrate easily into an industrial control system and to be easily expanded.

worked.q: What are the features of the PLC, and where is it mainly used? (Exercise 5.3)
worked.s: Features: (1) high reliability and noise immunity; (2) adaptable and flexible; (3) easy to program and use; (4) easy to design, install and commission; (5) easy to maintain; (6) complete functions. Uses: discrete logic control, process control, motion control, data processing, and communication and networking.

worked.q: How are PLCs classified by I/O points and by construction? (Exercise 5.4)
worked.s: By I/O points: small (under 256; micro under 64), medium (256–2048), large (over 2048; super-large over 8192). By construction: compact (unit) type, modular type and stackable type.

worked.q: A machine has 40 inputs and 28 outputs. What class of PLC is that, and what construction would you expect?
worked.s: 40 + 28 = 68 I/O points. That is under 256, so a small PLC (just above the 64-point micro limit). Small PLCs are normally the compact type: a base unit plus an expansion unit.

worked.q: A PLC-controlled conveyor stops. Using the book’s fault statistics, where should you look first, and why?
worked.s: At the field devices and wiring. Input devices account for 45 % of faults, output devices 30 % and wiring 5 %: 80 % in all are outside the PLC. The CPU (5 %) and I/O interfaces (15 %) are the least likely, and the PLC’s self-diagnosis would usually flag them anyway.

topics.title: Inside a PLC: CPU, Memory, I/O Interfaces & the Rest
topics.zh: PLC 的基本组成：CPU、存储器、输入/输出接口及其他

sections.h: A PLC is an industrial computer
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 5, “Overview of the PLC”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, figures redrawn. The book dates from the 2000s, so its “latest trends” and market remarks describe that period. Your ITE PLC module (Sem 4) covers the same ideas with a different PLC family; where the two agree, this is useful second reading.

PLCs come in many types, but their construction and working principle are much the same. A PLC is in essence an industrial computer. Compared with an ordinary computer it has stronger interfaces to the industrial process and a programming language made for control work.

Its hardware is: central processing unit (CPU), memory (ROM and RAM), input and output units, power supply and programmer, plus interfaces for expansion, communication and peripherals.

sections.h: The CPU and its five tasks
sections.b:
As in any computer, the CPU is the core. It directs the PLC, step by step, according to the functions given to it by the system program.

  1. Receive and store the user program and data entered from the programming tool, and show the program contents and memory addresses on the display.
  2. Check the user program. As a program is entered it is checked; a syntax error raises an alarm at once and input stops. If an error is found while the program is running, the alarm is raised or the program is stopped.
  3. Receive and recall field information. Data from the field inputs is stored, and fetched and sent where it is needed.
  4. Execute the user program. In run mode the CPU reads, interprets and executes the instructions one by one in the order they are stored, completes the operations they specify, and sends the results to the output ports to drive the external loads.
  5. Diagnose faults. It diagnoses the power supply and the PLC’s internal circuits, and shows information according to the type of fault or error, so that the user can clear it in time.

Different PLCs use different CPU chips. Some use general-purpose chips (the book names the 8031, 8051, 8086 and 80286); others use chips designed by the maker. The chip decides how well and how fast the PLC handles control signals: the more bits, the more information the system handles and the faster it computes.

MemoryHoldsKind of chipWho can change it
System program memoryThe system program written by the makerROMNobody: it is fixed in ROM
User program memoryThe application program the user writes, in the PLC’s programming language, for the control taskRAM kept alive by a lithium battery; or EPROM; or EEPROM; in newer PLCs, flash ROM, which needs no backup battery and keeps its data with the power offThe user, freely
Working data memoryWorking data: ON/OFF states and numerical values used by the user programRAMThe running program

The system program largely decides the PLC’s performance. It has three parts:

  • System management program — controls the running of the PLC so that it works step by step in good order.
  • User instruction interpreter — turns the PLC’s programming language into machine-language instructions for the CPU to execute.
  • Standard program modules and system calls — many subroutines of different functions. The PLC’s actual work, such as input, output and special operations, is done by these; how many there are decides how powerful the PLC is.

The working data area contains the device image registers and data tables.

  • The image registers hold the ON/OFF state of the inputs and outputs and of internal devices such as timers, counters and auxiliary relays.
  • The data tables hold values: variable parameters used when the program runs, numbers from A/D conversion, and the results of arithmetic.
  • The part of this area that keeps its data when the PLC loses power is the data retention area.

The sizes of the user program memory and the data memory decide how long a program can be and how many internal devices there are. They are important figures of a PLC’s performance.

The I/O interfaces are where the PLC meets the outside world. Inputs are of two kinds: switch (digital) signals from buttons, selector switches, limit switches, relay contacts, proximity switches, photoelectric switches and thumbwheel switches; and analog signals from potentiometers, tacho-generators and transmitters.

Digital input interface. It turns a field on/off signal into the standard signal the PLC handles internally. By the kind of supply the external signal uses, there are three forms:

FormExternal supplyFront end of the circuit
DC input24 V DCSeries resistor, filter, optocoupler
AC/DC inputEitherBridge rectifier first, so polarity does not matter, then filter and optocoupler
AC inputACCapacitor and resistors to drop and filter the voltage, then an optocoupler with two back-to-back LEDs

Every digital input circuit contains two things:

  • A filter: for noise immunity. (It is also why an input takes a few milliseconds to respond.)
  • An optocoupler: isolation between the field wiring and the internal electronics, and conversion to the internal standard signal.

The book draws the input supply outside the input port, as in a separate-supply arrangement. In an ordinary compact PLC the input circuits are fed from the PLC’s own DC supply and no external supply is needed.

Analog input interface. It converts a continuously varying field signal into a digital signal of several binary bits that the PLC can process. It accepts standard analog signals, voltage or current: the internationally used values are 4–20 mA DC and 0–10 V DC (or 0–5 V). Field signals are rarely standard, so they normally pass through a transmitter first. Inside: filter and level conversion → multiplexer → A/D converter → memory → optical isolation → bus logic → data bus.

Outputs connect the actuators of the controlled plant: contactors, solenoid valves, indicator lamps, and analog devices such as control valves and variable-speed drives.

Digital output interface. It turns the PLC’s internal standard signal into the on/off signal the field device needs. By the switching device used inside the PLC there are three types:

TypeSwitching deviceLoad supplySwitching frequencyNotes
RelayA small relay with a real contactAC or DCLowThe most adaptable; the contact wears, so life is limited
TransistorTransistor behind an optocouplerDC onlyHighFast, no wear; for pulse outputs and frequent switching
Thyristor (triac)Bidirectional thyristor behind an optocouplerAC onlyHighFast AC switching, no wear
  • Every type has an isolating coupling circuit.
  • The output interface supplies no power itself. The load supply is external. When choosing that supply, consider both the load and the type of output device.
  • Protective parts appear in the circuits: a diode across a DC inductive load, an RC network and varistor across the thyristor.

Analog output interface. It converts the several-bit digital result of the PLC’s arithmetic into a corresponding analog signal for continuous control of the process. Inside: data latch and address decoding → optical isolation → D/A converter → multiplexer → sample-and-hold → voltage or current output. Analog input and output interfaces are usually built into special analog units.

Intelligent I/O. For harder control work there are intelligent units: PID unit, high-speed counter unit, temperature control unit, position-control unit. Most are independent units. Unlike ordinary I/O, each has its own CPU and its own processing power. In every scan cycle the intelligent unit exchanges information once with the main CPU, and together they do the job. Many newer PLCs have PID and high-speed counter inputs built in, but usually a little weaker than the special units.

worked.q: What are the main parts of a PLC’s hardware and what is each for? (Exercise 5.7)
worked.s: CPU: executes the system and user programs, handles data, diagnoses faults. Memory: stores the system program, the user program and the working data. Input interface: brings field signals in, filtered and isolated. Output interface: drives the actuators. Power supply: feeds the internal circuits and gives 24 V DC for sensors. Programmer: for writing, editing, debugging and monitoring the program. Also expansion and communication interfaces.

worked.q: What forms do PLC digital input circuits take, and what types of digital output are there? (Exercises 5.8 and 5.9)
worked.s: Inputs: DC input, AC/DC input and AC input; all have a filter and an optocoupler. Outputs, by the switching device: relay type (AC or DC loads, low frequency), transistor type (DC loads, high frequency) and thyristor type (AC loads, high frequency).

worked.q: Which output type suits (a) a 220 V AC contactor coil switched a few times an hour, (b) a 24 V DC solenoid valve cycled several times a second, (c) a 220 V AC heater switched every second? (After Exercise 5.10)
worked.s: (a) Relay: AC load, low frequency. (b) Transistor: DC load, high frequency, where a relay contact would wear out quickly. (c) Thyristor: AC load, high frequency. The root difference: the relay has a moving contact and handles either supply slowly; the two semiconductor types are contactless and fast, but each handles only one kind of supply.

worked.q: Why is an optocoupler used in every input and output circuit?
worked.s: It passes the signal as light, so there is no electrical connection between the field wiring and the PLC’s internal electronics. Noise, voltage spikes and faults on the field side cannot reach the CPU, and the low internal voltage is kept apart from the higher field voltage.

worked.q: A user program is stored in battery-backed RAM. What happens if the lithium battery is flat when the PLC is switched off, and how do newer PLCs avoid this?
worked.s: RAM keeps its contents only while powered, so the program and retained data are lost. Newer PLCs store the user program in flash ROM (or EEPROM), which needs no backup battery.

topics.title: How a PLC Works: the Scan Cycle, Interrupts & the Five Languages
topics.zh: PLC 的工作原理：扫描周期、中断和五种编程语言

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 5, “Overview of the PLC”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, figures redrawn. The book dates from the 2000s, so its “latest trends” and market remarks describe that period. Your ITE PLC module (Sem 4) covers the same ideas with a different PLC family; where the two agree, this is useful second reading.

A relay control system is a hard-wired logic system. Take three branches: KM1 with a self-holding contact, KM2, and time relay KT. Press SB1 and KM1 is energised and holds itself; the coils of KM2 and KT are energised at the same moment. A relay system works in parallel.

A PLC is an industrial computer. It works by executing a user program that expresses the control requirement. But the CPU handles its tasks by time-sharing: at any instant it can do only one thing. So the program is executed in order, instruction by instruction, and the actions happen one after another: a serial way of working. Because the CPU is very fast, the devices seem to act together. In reality the response of the inputs and outputs lags slightly.

In the PLC version of that circuit, SB1 and SB2 are wired to inputs X0 and X1, the coils of KM1 and KM2 to outputs Y0 and Y1, and the thermal-relay contacts are in series with the coils outside the PLC. The time relay disappears: it becomes a timer inside the program.

In a sentence: a PLC works by scanning in a never-ending cycle. The time for one scan is the scan cycle (scan time). The CPU starts at the first instruction, executes the user program in order to the end, then goes back to the first instruction and begins again.

Redrawn from the book’s Fig. 5.10.

The running of a PLC has three parts.

  1. Power-up processing. Once, at switch-on: the system is initialised. This includes hardware initialisation, a check of the I/O module configuration, setting the power-failure retention range and other initialisation.
  2. The scan. After power-up the PLC enters the scan. In order: input processing; communication with other peripherals; update of the clock and the special registers. In STOP mode it then goes to self-diagnosis. In RUN mode it also executes the user program and does the output processing, then goes to self-diagnosis.
  3. Error handling. Once every scan the PLC runs a self-diagnosis to confirm that it is working properly: CPU, battery voltage, program memory, I/O, communication. If something is abnormal the LED on the CPU panel and the abnormality relay come on and an error code is stored in a special register. On a fatal error the CPU is forced into STOP and all scanning stops.

How long is a scan? It depends on the CPU’s speed, the number of I/O points, the length of the user program and how the program is written. Makers usually quote the time to execute 1K (1000) instructions: typically 1–10 ms per K. Different instructions take different times, from a fraction of a microsecond to over a hundred microseconds, so the same number of steps does not always give the same scan time. For a high-speed system, shorten the scan through both software and hardware.

During phase 2 the program reads inputs only from the image register, never from the terminals.

Leave aside remote I/O, special modules and other communication, and the scan reduces to three phases. (This is the usual case of batch input and batch output.)

1 · Input sampling. The PLC scans all the input terminals and stores the state of each in the corresponding cell of the input image register. The image register is now refreshed. Then the PLC moves on. During program execution and output refresh the input image register is cut off from the outside world: however the input signals change, its contents stay the same until the input-sampling phase of the next scan.

2 · Program execution. Following the scanning rule for ladder programs, the PLC scans the statements left to right, top to bottom. If it meets a jump instruction, whether it jumps depends on whether the jump condition is met. When an instruction involves an input or output state, the PLC “reads” the input state that was captured in phase 1 from the input image register, and “reads” the present state of the device (the “soft relay”) from the device image register. It does the logic and writes the result into the device image register. So for every device except the inputs, the state in the image register changes as the program runs.

3 · Output refresh. When all instructions have been executed, the states of all the output relays in the device image register are transferred, in this phase, to the output latch, and from there, through the output circuits, drive the external loads.

What follows from this.

  • A change at an input is not seen until the next input sampling. An input pulse shorter than one scan can be missed altogether.
  • An output computed early in the program does not reach its terminal until the end of that scan.
  • Within one scan, a rung lower down sees the results of the rungs above it; a rung higher up sees what a lower rung did only on the next scan. The order of rungs matters.
  • Worst-case response from input to output is roughly the input filter delay plus up to two scan times plus the output device’s delay.

Two ways to collect inputs. Sampled input: at the start (or end) of the scan all input signals are collected into the input image register; the program takes its input states from there, not from the terminals. Immediate input: as the program runs, when it needs a particular input it reads the state straight from the input terminal or module, as an “immediate input instruction” does. The input image register is not altered; it changes only at the next batch sampling.

Two ways to send outputs. Batch output: results are not sent out one by one as they are obtained. All are first stored in the output image register and sent together to the output ports once the program has finished, so that the output devices act together. Immediate output: as soon as the program obtains a result it is sent to the output port, as an “immediate output instruction” does, and the output image register is updated as well.

Some PLCs offer an I/O refresh instruction: placed where needed, it re-reads all or some of the inputs that are ON to refresh the input image register, or sends the output result out at once. Some also have input and output inhibit functions, which switch off the transfer service: the input signals are not read in and the outputs are not sent out.

Interrupts. Because external signals enter through the scan, a “logic lag” is unavoidable. Can a PLC use interrupts, as a computer does, breaking off the running program to run an interrupt routine? It can, and the idea is the same as in a general computer, but there are three particular points.

PointIn a PLC
When it respondsAn ordinary CPU checks for an interrupt request at the end of every instruction. A PLC checks after the relevant program block has ended and while it is executing the user program. If the user program is built of blocks, it checks at the end of each block or when a block is called, and handles the interrupt promptly
Order and nestingInterrupt information enters through input points, and the PLC scans input points in number order, so the order of interrupt sources is simply the order of the input numbers. The system keeps an “interrupt handling table” in a special memory area and stores the requests in sequence. Several sources can be queued by priority, but there is no nesting: a new interrupt, whatever its priority, waits until the routine now running has finished. So interrupts are not closed automatically on entering a routine, and need not be re-opened
Getting the result outIn scanning, normal output happens at a fixed phase of the cycle, which makes fast peripheral response difficult. Interrupt input solves the fast response on the input side. The information produced by the routine should then reach the peripheral as soon as possible, not wait for the output phase. So part of the I/O must work outside the scan cycle: by special hardware modules (fast-response I/O modules) or by special instructions that make certain I/O act immediately

PLCs have several programming languages: ladder diagram, Boolean mnemonic (instruction list), sequential function chart, function block diagram and structured text. Ladder and mnemonic are the basic languages. They are made of sets of instructions that cover most simple control: replacing relays, counters and timers for sequence and logic control, and, with extended instruction sets, other basic operations. SFC and structured text are higher-level languages. Languages can be used in combination.

LanguageWhat it isFeatures
Ladder diagram (LD)Describes the program with ladder graphic symbols. It expresses the conditions and results of events as cause and effect. Each rung is one cause-and-effect relation: conditions on the left, result on the right. It grew out of the description of relay logic control, which electricians know well, and is the most used(1) Corresponds to the electrical schematic: direct and intuitive. (2) Consistent with relay logic, so easy for electrical staff to learn. (3) Different from relay logic in one way: the “power flow” in a ladder is not a real current, and the relays inside are not real relays, so treat it differently in use. (4) One-to-one correspondence with the mnemonic language: easy to convert and check
Boolean mnemonic (instruction list, IL)Describes the program with Boolean mnemonics. Very like assembly language(1) Mnemonics are easy to remember. (2) The programmer’s keypad carries the mnemonics, so a program can be written on site with no computer. (3) One-to-one correspondence with ladder
Sequential function chart (SFC)Describes the program as a function chart. A more recent language. The control system is split into sub-systems by function, so that each operation has a clear meaning. It came from Petri nets; being graphical, it shows clearly the concurrent, complex phenomena of a system and analyses things such as deadlock and unsafe states(1) Function is the main thread: clear and easy to understand and discuss. (2) A large program can be divided among designers with a flexible structure, saving design and commissioning time. (3) Used for large systems with complex relations. (4) Only the commands of the active step are executed, and only the transitions after the active step are scanned, so the scan time is much shorter than for other programs
Function block diagram (FBD)Blocks represent functions. Each block has inputs and outputs, joined by “soft wiring” to other terminals to carry out the required operation or control. Blocks come in types; within a type, parameters adapt them to different uses(1) The function block is the unit: analysis starts from the control function and is easy to follow. (2) Graphical: very convenient to program and configure, easy to operate. (3) For large, complex systems the relations between functions are expressed clearly, so programming, configuration and commissioning take less time. (4) Each block takes program memory and execution time, so FBD is used on medium and large PLCs and in distributed control systems
Structured text (ST)Describes the program in structured statements, like a high-level computer language (BASIC, Pascal, C), but simplified in how statements are written and in the kinds of statement(1) High-level language: can do complex control computation. (2) Needs knowledge of high-level programming and programming skill, beyond most electricians. (3) Less intuitive and less easy to operate. (4) Used for control functions that are hard to realise with function blocks

terms: 立即输入 / 立即输出

worked.q: A PLC executes its program by cyclic scanning. What are the phases of each scan? (Exercises 5.11 and 5.12)
worked.s: Three: input sampling (all input terminals are read into the input image register, which is then frozen), program execution (rungs scanned left to right, top to bottom, reading the image registers and writing results to the device image register), and output refresh (output-relay states are transferred to the output latch and drive the loads). Around these, every scan also does internal self-diagnosis and communication.

worked.q: Compared with the parallel working of relay–contactor control, what are the characteristics of the PLC’s serial working? (Exercise 5.13)
worked.s: The PLC executes its instructions one at a time in a fixed order, so actions that are simultaneous in a relay circuit happen in sequence. Inputs are seen only at the sampling moment and outputs change only at the refresh, so there is a small response lag of up to about two scans. In return there are no contact races: the result is decided by program order, not by which relay happens to move first.

worked.q: A program has 4000 instructions and the PLC’s scan speed is 5 ms per K. Estimate the program execution time. A proximity sensor gives a 10 ms pulse: is it certain to be caught?
worked.s: Execution time ≈ 4 K × 5 ms/K = 20 ms, and the whole scan is a little longer. The 10 ms pulse is shorter than the scan, so it may rise and fall between two input samplings and be missed. Use an interrupt input, a high-speed counter or an input refresh instruction.

worked.q: Which programming languages does a PLC have, and what is the main feature of each? (Exercise 5.14)
worked.s: Ladder: graphical, like a relay circuit, the most used. Mnemonic / instruction list: like assembly, can be keyed in on a hand-held programmer, one-to-one with ladder. SFC: organises a sequence into steps and transitions; only active steps are executed. FBD: graphical blocks joined by soft wiring; for larger systems. Structured text: like a high-level language; for complex computation.

worked.q: In a ladder diagram, rung 2 uses a contact of an internal relay M0 whose coil is on rung 5. When does rung 2 see a change of M0?
worked.s: On the next scan. In the present scan rung 2 was evaluated before rung 5 changed M0 in the device image register. A rung below rung 5 would see the change in the same scan.

Three things the table teaches.

  • Common terminals limit the total. Four relay points on one common may carry 8 A between them. Four points at 2 A each just reach that limit; they do not exceed it. With the semiconductor types the shared limit (0.8 A) is far below four times the per-point figure.
  • Semiconductor outputs leak. A thyristor output that is “off” still passes about 1–2 mA. A very small load, such as a neon indicator or a sensitive relay, may stay on. This is the reason for the minimum-load figure.
  • Lamp and inductive loads are rated lower than resistive ones: a cold filament draws a heavy inrush current, and an inductive load produces a voltage spike when switched off.

sections.h: FX1N: performance, and how to compare PLCs
sections.b:
ItemFX1N

Processing timeBasic instructions 0.55–0.7 µs each; applied instructions a few µs to several hundred µs
Programming languagesRelay-symbol ladder and instruction list; step-ladder gives SFC-type programs

Number of instructionsBasic sequence 27 · step-ladder 2 · applied 89
Maximum I/O128 points in hardware (inputs up to 128 and outputs up to 128 can be addressed in software)

Five figures for comparing PLCs.

  1. I/O points. The largest number of input and output signals the PLC can take: the number of external terminals. It shows the largest system the PLC can build. Usually inputs outnumber outputs, and inputs and outputs cannot stand in for each other.
  2. Scan speed. The time to execute 1000 steps of instructions, in ms per thousand steps; or the time for one step, in µs per step.
  3. Memory capacity. System program memory, user program memory and data memory; the user can use the last two. Programs are stored by the step. One step takes one address, and one address generally takes two bytes. So a PLC with a capacity of 1000 steps has 2 K bytes of memory.
  4. Programming languages. Ladder, mnemonic, menu diagram, function block and statement description. A PLC may have one, two or all of them.
  5. Instruction set. The more kinds of instruction, the stronger the software and the easier the control task.

Also weigh expandability, conditions of use, reliability, ease of operation and economy.

worked.q: Explain the meaning of 48, E and R in the type FX2N-48ER, and state its numbers of inputs and outputs. (Exercise 6.1)
worked.s: 48: total I/O points. E: an expansion unit (mixed inputs and outputs). R: relay outputs. From the book’s table it has 24 inputs and 24 outputs.

worked.q: What is the difference between an expansion unit and an expansion module? (Exercise 6.3)
worked.s: Both add I/O points and neither has a CPU. An expansion unit has its own power supply. An expansion module has none and takes its supply from the base unit or an expansion unit; modules are also used to change the ratio of inputs to outputs.

worked.q: A PLC has a user program capacity of 8K steps. How many bytes is that?
worked.s: One step takes one address of two bytes: 8000 steps × 2 bytes = 16 000 bytes, that is 16 K bytes.

worked.q: Four relay outputs of an FX1N share one common terminal. Each drives a resistive load of 2.5 A. Is this acceptable?
worked.s: No, on two counts. Each point is limited to 2 A, so 2.5 A is too much for one point. And the four together would carry 4 × 2.5 A = 10 A, above the 8 A limit for four points on one common. Use interposing contactors or relays.

worked.q: A sequence has 20 inputs and 14 outputs. Choose an FX1N base unit from the table, leaving some spare.
worked.s: FX1N-40M has 24 inputs and 16 outputs: enough, with 4 inputs and 2 outputs spare. (FX1N-24M has only 14 inputs and 10 outputs: too few.) Choose FX1N-40MR for mixed AC and DC loads at low switching frequency, or FX1N-40MT for fast DC loads.

topics.title: FX Soft Devices 1: Input X, Output Y, Auxiliary M & State S
topics.zh: FX 编程元件（一）：输入继电器 X、输出继电器 Y、辅助继电器 M 和状态器 S

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 6, “Introduction to the Mitsubishi FX series PLC”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, with ladder examples redrawn. The book describes the older FX0S, FX0N, FX1S, FX1N and FX2N families. Device ranges differ from model to model and from the PLC used in your ITE lab, so use the numbers to understand the system, and take real ranges from the manual of the PLC in front of you.

Inside a PLC there are many devices with different functions: input relays X, output relays Y, timers T, counters C, auxiliary relays M, state devices S, data registers D. To distinguish them from real physical devices they are called soft devices. Each is really a location in memory.

That answers a standard question: why can a PLC contact be used any number of times? A “contact” in the program is not a piece of metal. It is an instruction to read one bit of memory, and a bit can be read as often as you like. A normally-closed contact simply reads the bit and inverts it.

The number, kinds, functions and numbering of soft devices differ between makers, between series, and between models of one maker. Before programming, get to know the devices of the PLC you have chosen.

FX numbering: a letter followed by a number. Input and output relays are numbered in octal (digits 0–7 only: after X007 comes X010). Everything else is numbered in decimal.

The input relay is the interface through which the PLC receives external switch signals. Its normally-open and normally-closed contacts can be used any number of times.

Numbering is octal: X000–X007, X010–X017, X020–X027, X030–X037 … up to 128 points.

An input relay receives the signal sent by the user’s input device. Its coil can be driven only by the external input signal. When the external signal is on, the corresponding input relay is energised. It cannot be driven by an instruction.

  • The coil of an input relay must never appear in the program. Only its contacts appear.
  • Its NO and NC contacts can be used without limit.
  • The numbers on the base unit are fixed. Expansion units and modules are numbered in sequence, starting from the one nearest the base unit.

Example. Base unit FX0N-40MR has inputs X000–X027 (24 inputs, octal). The next unit, FX0N-40ER, takes X030–X057. The module after that, FX0N-8EX, takes X060–X067.

The output relay passes signals to the external load. Numbering is octal too: Y000–Y177, up to 128 points.

Its coil can be driven only by the program inside the PLC, never by an external signal. The state of the coil is passed to the output unit, and the hard contact in the output unit drives the external load.

  • In the output unit each output relay has one normally-open hard contact. In the program, though, its NO and NC contacts may be used any number of times.
  • As with inputs, the base unit’s numbers are fixed; expansion units and modules are numbered in order from the nearest.

Example. Base unit FX1N-60MR has outputs Y000–Y027. Expansion unit FX2N-32ER takes Y030–Y047. Module FX2N-16EYR takes Y050–Y067.

In practice, how many input and output relays there are depends on how the system is configured.

Input relay XOutput relay Y

Contacts in the programUnlimitedUnlimited
Physical contactNone: it is the terminal circuit itselfOne NO hard contact per point
NumberingOctalOctal

The auxiliary relay is the most numerous relay in a PLC. It does the job of the intermediate relay in a relay control system. Like an output relay its coil is driven by program instructions, and each has unlimited NO and NC contacts for programming. But its contacts cannot drive an external load directly; a load is driven only through an output relay.

An M relay cannot drive an external load itself; only a Y relay has a hard contact.

When to use a latched relay. Where the machine must carry on from where it was after a power cut: for example, remembering which way a table was travelling.

Special auxiliary relays are in two classes.

  • Contact type. The coil is driven by the PLC system; the user may only use its contacts.
  • Coil type. The user’s program drives the coil; when it is energised the PLC performs a particular action.

Of the 256 numbers M8000–M8255, those the PLC has not defined must not be used in a user program. Different FX models define different numbers of them: check the manual.

The state device S is the key soft device for building an SFC (sequential function chart). It plays the main part in step-ladder sequence programs and is used with the step-ladder instructions described in Chapter 8. Each S stands for one step of the sequence.

worked.q: Why can the contacts in a programmable controller be used without limit? (Exercise 6.2)
worked.s: Because a soft device is a bit of memory, not a physical relay. A contact in the program is just an instruction to read that bit (and, for an NC contact, to invert it). Reading does not use anything up, so it can be done any number of times.

worked.q: An FX base unit has 24 inputs. What is the number of its last input, and what number does the first input of the next expansion unit take?
worked.s: Inputs are numbered in octal, eight to a group: X000–X007, X010–X017, X020–X027. That is 3 × 8 = 24 inputs, so the last is X027. The expansion unit starts at the next octal number, X030.

worked.q: A program contains the rung “X001 contact → X005 coil”. What is wrong?
worked.s: An input relay’s coil can be driven only by its external signal. The coil of an X relay may never appear in a program. If an internal result is wanted, use an M relay; if an external load is to be driven, use a Y relay.

worked.q: You want an indicator lamp on Y0 to flash once a second whenever the PLC is running. Which special relay does this in one rung?
worked.s: M8013, the 1 s clock pulse: “M8013 contact → Y0 coil”. Y0 is then on for half a second and off for half a second. (M8000 would light it steadily in RUN.)

worked.q: A counter must be cleared once, automatically, each time the PLC is switched to RUN. How?
worked.s: Use the initial pulse M8002: “M8002 contact → RST C0”. M8002 is ON for the first scan only, so the reset happens once and then releases the counter.

topics.title: FX Soft Devices 2: Timers, Counters, High-Speed Counters, Pointers, Constants & Registers
topics.zh: FX 编程元件（二）：定时器、计数器、高速计数器、指针、常数和寄存器

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 6, “Introduction to the Mitsubishi FX series PLC”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, with ladder examples redrawn. The book describes the older FX0S, FX0N, FX1S, FX1N and FX2N families. Device ranges differ from model to model and from the PLC used in your ITE lab, so use the numbers to understand the system, and take real ranges from the manual of the PLC in front of you.

A PLC timer does the job of an on-delay time relay, but it offers unlimited delayed NO and NC contacts for programming.

Each timer has three things, all under the same number:

  • a set-value register,
  • a current-value register,
  • one bit that stores the state of its output contact.

The same number, T2 say, therefore means different things in different places: as a coil or contact it is the bit; in a data instruction it is the current value.

Principle. A timer counts clock pulses. The clocks are 1 ms, 10 ms and 100 ms. When the count reaches the set value, the contact operates. The set value is given by a constant K or by the contents of a data register D, in the range 1–32 767.

delay = set value K × clock period

delay in seconds (s) · K is a pure number · clock period in seconds: 0.1 s for a 100 ms timer, 0.01 s for a 10 ms timer, 0.001 s for a 1 ms timer.

T2 is a 100 ms timer, so K123 means 123 × 0.1 s = 12.3 s.

Inside, the drive input passes through an AND gate with the clock pulses into a counter; a comparator compares the count with the set value K and switches the output contact when they are equal. Turning the drive input off resets the counter.

The set level is reached only when the on-time totals the set value.

General timerRetentive (accumulating) timer
If the input goes off, or power is lost, during timingThe timer resets: current value back to 0The timer keeps its current value. When the input comes on again it carries on from there
How it is resetAutomatically, when its drive input goes offOnly by an RST instruction
UseAn uninterrupted delayTotalling time that comes in pieces: running hours, total heating time
General timersFX0SFX1SFX0NFX1NFX2N (FX2NC)
100 msT0–T49T0–T62T0–T62T0–T199T0–T199
10 msT24–T49T32–T62T32–T62T200–T245T200–T245
