Ranges. 100 ms timer: 0.1–3276.7 s. 10 ms timer: 0.01–327.67 s. 1 ms timer: 0.001–32.767 s. On the smaller models the 10 ms timers share numbers with the 100 ms ones and are selected with special relay M8028.

The on-times add up: t1 + t2 = 12.3 s.

Timing error. Apart from interrupt-driven timers, the error from driving the coil to the contact operating lies between −α and +T₀, where α is one clock period (0.001 s, 0.01 s or 0.1 s) and T₀ is the scan time. In the worst case, if the program has the timer’s contact instruction before its coil instruction, the error can reach +2 T₀. The 1 ms timer is interrupt-driven and counts the 1 ms clock by interrupt, so it is the most accurate.

An internal counter counts internal signals (X, Y, M, S, T and so on) as the scan runs. Because it works inside the scan, both the ON time and the OFF time of the signal being counted must be longer than the scan time, or pulses are missed.

The set value is a constant K or, indirectly, a data register D.

On the 10th rising edge of X11 the C0 contact closes and stays closed until X10 resets the counter.

16-bit up-counter. Set value 1–32 767. Each rising edge of the count input adds 1 to the current value. On the count that makes it equal the set value, the contact operates. Further pulses change nothing. The contact stays operated until an RST instruction clears the counter: current value to 0, contact released. While the reset input is on, counting is blocked.

32-bit up/down counter (FX1N, FX2N, FX2NC only). Apart from its length, it differs in being able to count both ways. Set value −2 147 483 648 to +2 147 483 647.

  • Direction is set by the special relay with the matching number: counter C△△△ goes with M8△△△. Relay ON = count down, OFF = count up. Example: C200 with M8200.
  • Contact action. The contact turns ON when the current value rises from (set value − 1) to the set value, and turns OFF when it falls from the set value to (set value − 1). In the book’s example C210 has set value K−5: its contact comes on as the count goes from −6 up to −5 and goes off as it goes from −5 down to −6.
  • RST clears the current value to 0 and releases the contact.

An internal counter cannot count faster than the scan allows. A high-speed counter can.

  1. It counts by interrupt, so it is independent of the scan time.
  2. It counts only specific input terminals (X0–X3 on the FX0N).
  3. It is a 32-bit up/down counter, set value −2 147 483 648 to +2 147 483 647.
  4. It allows a far higher input frequency than an internal counter and is flexible in use. All high-speed counters are latched; a parameter can make them non-latched.
  5. There are three kinds: one-phase one-input, one-phase two-input and two-phase (A/B phase).
FX0N: one-phase, one count inputC235C236C237C238C241C242C244

X002U/DU/D
X003U/DRS
Direction relayM8235M8236M8237M8238M8241M8242M8244

U/D = up/down count input · R = reset input · S = start input.

  • C235–C238 have no start or reset terminal. They behave like the ordinary 32-bit counter, except that each has its own count input and counts by interrupt. Direction: its M82△△ relay ON counts down. An ordinary contact selects (enables) it; an RST instruction clears it.
  • C241 and C242 each have a count input and an external reset input.
  • C244 has a count input, a reset input and a start input. It counts X0 only when it is selected in the program and X3 is on. X1 resets it.

External start and reset terminals respond immediately, by interrupt, unaffected by the scan.

FX0N: one-phase, two inputsC246C247C249
X000UUU
X001DDD
X002RR
X003S
Direction monitorM8246M8247M8249

One input counts up, the other down. Each OFF → ON on X0 adds 1; each OFF → ON on X1 subtracts 1. The M relay now only shows the direction.

FX0N: two-phase (A/B)C251C252C254
X000AAA
X001BBB
X002RR
X003S
Direction monitorM8251M8252M8254

Two-phase counting takes the two outputs of an incremental encoder, A and B, which are 90° apart. The phase relation decides the direction: with A ON, B going OFF → ON counts up; with A ON, B going ON → OFF counts down. So the counter follows the encoder forwards and backwards without any direction signal.

sections.h: Pointers P / I and constants K / H
sections.b:
PointerUsed forForm
N — nestingNesting levels of the master-control instructions MC and MCRN0–N7: 8 levels
P — branchA label marking the target of a jump or subroutine-call instructionP0–P63 on FX0S, FX1S, FX0N · P0–P127 on FX1N, FX2N
I — input interruptMarks the start of an interrupt routine run when an input changesI□0■: □ = 0–5 is the input interrupt number (0–3 on FX0S and FX0N); ■ = 0 for a falling edge, 1 for a rising edge
I — timer interruptRuns a routine at a fixed intervalI□■■: □ = 6–8 is the timer interrupt number; ■■ = 10–99 is the interval in ms. FX2N and FX2NC only
I — counter interruptUsed with the high-speed counter set instructionI0□0: □ = 1–6. FX2N and FX2NC only

Examples. I000: when input X0 goes from ON to OFF (falling edge), the interrupt routine labelled I000 is executed, returning at the IRET instruction. I720: the routine labelled I720 runs every 20 ms and returns at IRET.

Constants. K marks a decimal number and H a hexadecimal number. A constant is treated as a device too, because it occupies memory.

Decimal KHexadecimal H
Written123 is written K123The number 345 is written H159

sections.h: Data registers D and index registers V / Z
sections.b:
For I/O processing, analog control and positioning a PLC needs many data registers to hold data and parameters. A data register is 16 bits, and the top bit is the sign bit. A 32-bit number is held in two registers together (written D1D0, for example).

TypeBehaviourFX0SFX1SFX0NFX1NFX2N (FX2NC)
GeneralAll cleared when the PLC goes from RUN to STOP. If special relay M8033 is set, the data is kept on RUN → STOPD0–D29D0–D127D0–D127D0–D127D0–D199
LatchedKeeps its data unless rewritten, whether power is on or off and whether the PLC runs or notD30, D31D128–D255D128–D255D128–D7999D200–D7999
SpecialMonitor the running of devices inside the PLC. Undefined ones must not be usedD8000–D8069D8000–D8255D8000–D8255D8000–D8255D8000–D8195
Special registerHolds
D8000Watchdog timer (WDT) setting; initial value 200 ms
D8001CPU type
D8020Input filter time for X0–X7; initial value 10 ms
D8030 · D8031Values of analog potentiometers No. 1 and No. 2
D8039Constant scan time, in ms

File registers (in the D1000 range and above) are special registers for storing large amounts of data: sampled data, statistics, sets of control parameters for several products. They occupy a block of the user program memory. They are written with the programmer or the programming software. While the PLC runs, the BMOV instruction can read file registers into general registers, but instructions cannot write to file registers.

Index registers V and Z are special-purpose data registers, like the index registers of a computer. They modify the number of a device (indexing). Both are 16-bit and are read and written like any register. For 32-bit work V and Z are used as a pair, Z the low word, V the high word.

Example. D0Z means “D(0 + Z)”. If Z = 10, D0Z is D10. Change Z and the same instruction works on a different register: that is how one piece of program handles a whole table.

Index registersFX0SFX1SFX0NFX1NFX2N (FX2NC)
V, ZV0–V7, Z0–Z7V, ZV0–V7, Z0–Z7V0–V7, Z0–Z7

worked.q: How do a general timer and a retentive timer differ? (Exercise 6.4)
worked.s: A general timer has no memory: if its input goes off or power is lost during timing, it resets to zero, and it resets by itself whenever its drive goes off. A retentive timer keeps its current value when the input goes off or power fails and carries on from there when the input returns; it is cleared only by an RST instruction.

worked.q: Timer T10 (a 100 ms timer) has set value K250. Timer T200 (a 10 ms timer on the FX1N) has set value K250. What delay does each give?
worked.s: T10: 250 × 0.1 s = 25 s. T200: 250 × 0.01 s = 2.5 s. The same K gives a delay ten times shorter on the 10 ms timer.

worked.q: You need a delay of 8 s using a 100 ms timer. What set value? And what is the longest delay one such timer can give?
worked.s: K = 8 s ÷ 0.1 s = K80. The largest set value is 32 767, so the longest delay is 32 767 × 0.1 s = 3276.7 s, about 54.6 minutes.

worked.q: What types of high-speed counter does the FX0N have, and how is the count direction of C251 set? (Exercise 6.5)
worked.s: Three types: one-phase one-input (C235–C238, C241, C242, C244), one-phase two-input (C246, C247, C249) and two-phase A/B input (C251, C252, C254). C251’s direction is not set by the program: it is decided by the phase relation of the A and B inputs. With A ON, B rising counts up and B falling counts down. M8251 only monitors the direction.

worked.q: A scan takes 15 ms. A sensor on X2 gives a signal that is on for 5 ms and off for 5 ms. Can an internal counter count it? What should be used?
worked.s: No. An internal counter needs the on-time and the off-time each to be longer than the scan, and 5 ms is much less than 15 ms, so most pulses would be missed. Use a high-speed counter on one of the special inputs: it counts by interrupt, independently of the scan.

worked.q: Z = 6. Which register does D10Z refer to? And what does the interrupt pointer I301 mean?
worked.s: D10Z = D(10 + 6) = D16. I301: input interrupt number 3 (input X3), triggered on the rising edge because the last digit is 1.

topics.title: FX Basic Instructions 1: Contacts, Coils, Edges and Blocks
topics.zh: FX 基本指令（一）：触点、线圈、边沿和电路块

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 7, “Basic logic instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. Ladder examples are redrawn; several are my own simplified versions of the book’s, and each instruction list here was written to match the ladder shown beside it. The instructions are Mitsubishi FX mnemonics. Other makers use different mnemonics for the same ideas.

The FX1N and FX2N have 27 basic instructions. They are used to write an instruction list, and each corresponds exactly to an element of the ladder diagram. To convert a ladder to a list, read it left to right, top to bottom, and write one line for each contact, block junction and coil.

GroupInstructionsJob
Start a rung, drive a coilLD, LDI, OUTTake a contact from the rail; drive a coil
Series contactAND, ANILogical AND
Parallel contactOR, ORILogical OR
Edge contactsLDP, LDF, ANDP, ANDF, ORP, ORFOn for one scan at a rising or falling edge
Block connectionORB, ANBJoin whole blocks in parallel or in series
StackMPS, MRD, MPPRemember a junction for several branches
Master controlMC, MCRA common series contact for a group of rungs
LatchSET, RSTSet and hold; reset
Pulse outputPLS, PLFOne-scan pulse on a rising or falling edge
OthersINV, NOP, ENDInvert; no operation; end of program

That is 3 + 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 27.

MnemonicNameFunctionDevicesSteps
LDLoadStart logic with a normally-open contactX, Y, M, S, T, C1
LDILoad inverseStart logic with a normally-closed contactX, Y, M, S, T, C1
OUTOutDrive a coilY, M, S, T, CY, M: 1 · T: 3 · C: 3 to 5
0  LD   X000     start at the rail, NO contact
1  OUT  Y000     drive the coil
2  LDI  X001     start at the rail, NC contact
3  OUT  T0  K19  drive a timer; the set value follows
6  LD   T0
7  OUT  Y001
  • LD and LDI take a contact from the left rail. They are also used, with ANB and ORB, at the start of a branch block.
  • OUT drives the coil of an output relay, auxiliary relay, state device, timer or counter. It cannot be used on an input relay X.
  • OUT may be used several times in a row: that is coils in parallel, all driven by the same logic.
  • After OUT for a timer or counter, the set value must follow: a constant K or the number of a data register.
  • Notice the step numbers jump from 3 to 6: the timer instruction occupies three steps.

MnemonicNameFunctionDevicesSteps
ANDAndOne NO contact in seriesX, Y, M, S, T, C1
ANIAnd inverseOne NC contact in seriesX, Y, M, S, T, C1
OROrOne NO contact in parallelX, Y, M, S, T, C1
ORIOr inverseOne NC contact in parallelX, Y, M, S, T, C1
0  LD   X002
1  AND  X000     series NO contact
2  OUT  Y003
3  LD   Y003
4  ANI  X003     series NC contact
5  OUT  M101
  • AND and ANI connect a single contact in series. There is no limit to how many may follow one another.
  • Follow-on (cascade) output. After an OUT, a further contact and another OUT may follow: for example OUT M101, then AND T1, then OUT Y004. As long as the order is right this can be repeated. Because of the width of programmer screens and printers, keep to about 10 contacts and one coil per line and not more than 24 lines in all.
  • If the order is the other way round (the coil that needs the extra contact comes first), a plain cascade will not work and the stack instruction MPS is needed.
0  LD   X004
1  OR   X006     parallel NO contact
2  ORI  M102     parallel NC contact
3  OUT  Y005
  • OR and ORI connect a single contact in parallel. They follow an LD or LDI, and the contact is paralleled back to the left rail, across everything from that LD up to this point.
  • There is no limit to the number of parallel contacts, though for the same screen-width reason keep it under 24 lines.
  • To parallel a branch that has two or more contacts in series, OR is not enough: use ORB.

MnemonicFunctionDevicesSteps
LDPStart logic on a rising edgeX, Y, M, S, T, C2
LDFStart logic on a falling edgeX, Y, M, S, T, C2
ANDPSeries, rising edgeX, Y, M, S, T, C2
ANDFSeries, falling edgeX, Y, M, S, T, C2
ORPParallel, rising edgeX, Y, M, S, T, C2
ORFParallel, falling edgeX, Y, M, S, T, C2

LDP, ANDP and ORP are contacts that detect a rising edge: they are on for one scan only, when the device changes OFF → ON. LDF, ANDF and ORF detect a falling edge: on for one scan when the device changes ON → OFF. In a ladder they are drawn as a contact with an upward or downward arrow.

0  LDP  X000     on for one scan when X000 comes on
2  ORP  X001     or when X001 comes on
4  OUT  M0
5  LD   M8000    always on in RUN
6  ANDP X002     and for one scan when X002 comes on
8  OUT  M1

In this example M0 is on for one scan whenever X000 or X001 changes OFF → ON, and M1 for one scan whenever X002 does. Replace the three with LDF, ORF and ANDF and the same happens on ON → OFF.

Two equivalent ways to write the same thing.

  • “LDP X010 → OUT M6” does the same as “LD X010 → PLS M6”: M6 is on for one scan when X010 rises.
  • An edge contact in front of an applied instruction, such as MOV, does the same as the pulse-execution form of that instruction (MOVP): the instruction is executed once when the input rises, not on every scan while it is on.

Two or more contacts in series form a series block. To connect series blocks in parallel: begin each block with LD or LDI, and finish it with ORB. ORB has no device number; it occupies 1 step.

RecommendedWorks, but not recommended
0LD X0000LD X000
1AND X0011AND X001
2LD X0022LD X002
3AND X0033AND X003
4ORB4LDI X004
5LDI X0045AND X005
6AND X0056ORB
7ORB7ORB
8OUT Y0068OUT Y006
  • Written the recommended way, with an ORB after each block, there is no limit to the number of parallel blocks.
  • Written with all the blocks first and the ORBs collected at the end, LD and LDI can be used only 8 times in succession, so ORB is limited to 8 as well.

Two or more contacts in parallel form a parallel block. To connect a parallel block in series with what comes before: begin the branch with LD or LDI, build the parallel block, then finish with ANB. ANB has no device number; 1 step.

0  LD   X000
1  OR   X001     first parallel block complete
2  LD   X002     start of the second block (branch start)
3  AND  X003
4  LDI  X004
5  AND  X005
6  ORB           end of a series block inside it
7  OR   X006     OR before ANB: parallels inside the second block
8  ANB           connect the second block in series with the first
9  OUT  Y007
  • Position of OR matters. An OR written before ANB parallels a contact inside the block being built. An OR written after ANB parallels a contact across everything so far, back to the left rail.
  • ANB can in principle be used without limit. But as with ORB, LD and LDI can be used only 8 times in succession, so batching the ANBs at the end limits them to 8.

A way to remember. ORB and ANB both mean “take the last two blocks you built and join them”. ORB joins them side by side; ANB joins them end to end.

worked.q: Draw (describe) the ladder for this instruction list, and write the logic expression for Y0: LD X0 · OR Y0 · ANI X1 · OR M0 · LD X2 · AND X3 · LDI X4 · AND X5 · ORB · ANB · OUT Y0. (Exercise 7.2, list 1)
worked.s: Work through it. LD X0, OR Y0: X0 in parallel with Y0. ANI X1: in series with NC X1. OR M0: M0 in parallel with all of that. That is the first block. LD X2, AND X3: a series block. LDI X4, AND X5: another series block. ORB: those two in parallel, making the second block. ANB: second block in series with the first. So Y0 = [(X0 + Y0) · X1 + M0] · (X2 · X3 + X4 · X5).

worked.q: Write the instruction list for: Y1 is on when (X1 AND X2) OR (X3 AND NOT X4) is true, and X5 is not on.
worked.s: LD X1 · AND X2 · LD X3 · ANI X4 · ORB · ANI X5 · OUT Y1. The two series blocks are joined by ORB; then one NC contact follows in series with ANI.

worked.q: Why can the instruction OUT X003 never appear in a program?
worked.s: An input relay’s coil is driven only by the external input signal. OUT may drive Y, M, S, T and C, but not X.

worked.q: A button on X0 must add 1 to a counter each time it is pressed. With “LD X0” in front of an increment instruction the count races up. Why, and what is the fix?
worked.s: While the button is held, X0 is on for many scans, and the instruction is executed on every one of them. Use a rising-edge contact, LDP X0 (or the pulse form of the instruction), so that it is executed once per press.

recap: The FX1N and FX2N have ___ basic instructions.
LDI starts a rung with a normally-___ contact.
After OUT for a timer, the set value ___ must follow.
LDP is on for one scan on a ___ edge.

topics.title: FX Basic Instructions 2: Stack, Master Control, SET/RST, Pulses and END
topics.zh: FX 基本指令（二）：堆栈、主控、置位复位、脉冲和 END

sections.h: MPS, MRD and MPP: the stack
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 7, “Basic logic instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. Ladder examples are redrawn; several are my own simplified versions of the book’s, and each instruction list here was written to match the ladder shown beside it. The instructions are Mitsubishi FX mnemonics. Other makers use different mnemonics for the same ideas.

MnemonicNameFunctionSteps
MPSPushStore the logic result at this junction on the stack1
MRDReadRead the top of the stack; the stack does not move1
MPPPopRead the top of the stack and remove it1

These three are for multiple-output circuits: several branches that leave from the same point after a contact. They store the junction so that it can be used for the branches that follow. None takes a device number.

The FX has 11 memory cells for intermediate results, called the stack.

  • MPS pushes the present result onto the top. What was there moves down one level.
  • MPP reads the top and everything moves up one level. The value read disappears from the stack.
  • MRD reads the top and leaves the stack as it is.
0  LD   X000
1  MPS           remember the junction after X000
2  AND  X001
3  OUT  Y000     first branch
4  MRD           read the junction again
5  AND  X002
6  OUT  Y001     middle branch
7  MPP           read it for the last time and clear it
8  AND  X003
9  OUT  Y002     last branch
  • First branch MPS, middle branches MRD, last branch MPP. With only two branches there is no MRD.
  • MPS and MPP must be used in pairs.
  • They may be nested: an MPS inside a branch gives a two-level stack, and so on. Used in succession, MPS may appear at most 11 times before an MPP: the depth of the stack.

MnemonicNameFunctionDevicesSteps
MCMaster controlStart of a master-control block: connects a common series contactMC N Y or M (not special M)3
MCRMaster control resetEnd of the blockMCR N2

In programming it often happens that several coils are controlled by one contact or one group of contacts. Putting the same contact in every rung wastes memory. The master-control contact solves this. In the ladder it is drawn vertically, at right angles to ordinary contacts. It is a normally-open contact connected to the rail and acts as a main switch for a group of rungs.

0  LD   X000
1  MC   N0  M100   when X000 is on, the rail below is live
4  LD   X001
5  OUT  Y000
6  LD   X002
7  OUT  Y001
8  MCR  N0         end of the master-control block
  • X000 ON: the instructions between MC and MCR are executed. Y000 and Y001 follow X001 and X002.
  • X000 OFF: the block is skipped as if every rung in it were false. Y000 and Y001 are off. But retentive timers, counters and devices driven by SET / RST keep the state they had when the master contact opened.
  • After MC the rail moves behind the MC contact, so every instruction inside the block starts with LD or LDI. MCR moves the rail back.
  • The same MC can be used many times by changing the device number (the M or Y).
  • Nesting. MC blocks can be nested up to 8 levels, N0 to N7. Going in, the level numbers increase (N0, then N1, then N2). Coming out, MCR releases from the largest level first (MCR N2, MCR N1, MCR N0). An MCR for a level also cancels all the levels inside it.

MC or MPS? Both feed several rungs from one condition. MPS is for a few branches in one rung. MC is for a whole section of program, and it costs steps only once however many rungs are inside.

MnemonicNameFunctionDevicesSteps
SETSetTurn a device on and keep it onY, M, SY, M: 1 · S, special M: 2
RSTResetTurn it off; clear a current value or a registerY, M, S, T, C, D, V, ZY, M: 1 · S, special M, T, C: 2 · D, V, Z, special D: 3
0  LD   X000
1  SET  Y000     X000 on: Y000 on, and it stays on when X000 goes off
2  LD   X001
3  RST  Y000     X001 on: Y000 off, and it stays off when X001 goes off
  • Once X000 has come on, Y000 is driven ON; even if X000 then goes OFF, Y000 does not go OFF. Once X001 has come on, Y000 is reset; even if X001 then goes OFF, Y000 does not come on.
  • For one device (Y000, M0, S0 …) SET and RST may be used several times, in any order. The last one executed in the scan wins.
  • RST also clears data. It zeroes a data register D or index register V, Z. It resets the current value and the contact of a retentive timer (T246–T255). It resets the output contact of a counter and clears its current value.

SET/RST against a self-holding rung. “Start OR hold, AND NOT stop → coil” and a SET/RST pair do the same job. With SET/RST the start and stop conditions can sit in different parts of the program, which is convenient, but it makes it harder to see at a glance what controls the output.

MnemonicNameFunctionDevicesSteps
PLSPulseOne-scan pulse on the rising edge of its driveY, M (not special M)2
PLFPulse fallOne-scan pulse on the falling edge of its driveY, M (not special M)2
0  LD   X000
1  PLS  M0       M0 on for one scan when X000 comes on
3  LD   M0
4  SET  Y000
5  LD   X001
6  PLF  M1       M1 on for one scan when X001 goes off
8  LD   M1
9  RST  Y000

With PLS, the device Y or M is on for one scan only after the drive input comes on. With PLF, it is on for one scan only after the drive input goes off. In other words, these instructions turn an input signal of any width into a trigger pulse exactly one scan wide, without changing the signal’s period.

In the example, Y000 is set at the moment X000 is pressed and reset at the moment X001 is released.

Special auxiliary relays cannot be used as the device of PLS or PLF.

MnemonicNameFunctionDeviceSteps
INVInverseInvert the logic result obtained so farNone1
NOPNo operationDo nothingNone; not drawn in a ladder1
ENDEndEnd of program: go to output processing and return to step 0None1

INV inverts the result of the logic that comes before it in the rung. It needs no device. “LD X000 → INV → OUT Y000” makes Y000 on when X000 is off. It cannot be connected directly to the rail like LD, nor used alone in parallel like OR.

NOP makes that step do nothing.

  • Putting NOPs into a program leaves room, so that later changes or additions cause less renumbering of steps.
  • An instruction already written can be replaced by NOP to change the circuit. But take care: replacing LD, LDI, ANB or ORB by NOP changes the structure a great deal and may make the circuit invalid.
  • When the whole program is cleared, every step becomes NOP.
Replace this by NOPEffect
AND or ANIThat contact is short-circuited (removed from the series chain)
ANBThe preceding circuit is short-circuited: an error is likely
ORThat parallel contact is cut out
ORBThe preceding parallel block is cut out: an error is likely
LDThe following contacts become joined to the previous rung’s OUT (a cascade output)

END marks the end of the program. A PLC works in a cycle of input processing, program execution and output processing. If no END is written, it scans from the first step right to the last step of program memory. With an END, the steps after it are not scanned and output processing begins at once. So END shortens the scan time.

END for debugging. Insert ENDs to split the program into sections. Test the first section; when it is right, delete its END and test the next; and so on.

terms: 进栈 / 读栈 / 出栈

worked.q: Write the instruction list for: after X0, three branches. Y0 directly; Y1 through X1; Y2 through X2.
worked.s: LD X0 · MPS · OUT Y0 · MRD · AND X1 · OUT Y1 · MPP · AND X2 · OUT Y2. (Simpler still: because Y0 needs no extra contact it can be written first as a cascade, LD X0 · OUT Y0 · MPS · AND X1 · OUT Y1 · MPP · AND X2 · OUT Y2.)

worked.q: Describe what this list does: LD X1 · MC N0 M10 · LD X2 · OUT Y0 · LD X3 · OUT Y1 · MCR N0 · LD X4 · OUT Y2 · END. (Exercise 7.2, list 2)
worked.s: X1 is a master switch for the two rungs between MC and MCR. With X1 on, Y0 follows X2 and Y1 follows X3. With X1 off, Y0 and Y1 are both off whatever X2 and X3 do. Y2 follows X4 always, because its rung is after MCR, outside the block. As logic: Y0 = X1 · X2, Y1 = X1 · X3, Y2 = X4.

worked.q: In one scan the program executes SET M0 (condition true) and, further down, RST M0 (condition also true). What is M0 at the end of the scan?
worked.s: OFF. For the same device the last instruction executed is the one that counts, and RST comes later in the scan.

worked.q: A master-control block is switched off by its MC contact. Inside it are an ordinary coil Y0, a retentive timer T250 and a relay M5 that was set with SET. What happens to each?
worked.s: Y0 goes off. T250 keeps its current value (it stops accumulating but is not cleared). M5 stays set. Devices driven by OUT drop out; retentive timers, counters and SET/RST devices keep their state.

worked.q: Why does writing END at the end of a short program shorten the scan time?
worked.s: Without END the PLC scans on through the whole program memory, including all the unused steps (which are NOPs). With END it stops there and goes straight to output processing.

recap: The first branch uses MPS, the middle branches use ___ and the last branch uses MPP.
Master-control blocks can be nested up to ___ levels.
For the same device, the ___ SET or RST executed in the scan is the one that takes effect.
PLF gives a one-scan pulse on the ___ edge.

sections.h: Eight rules for drawing a ladder
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 7, “Basic logic instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. Ladder examples are redrawn; several are my own simplified versions of the book’s, and each instruction list here was written to match the ladder shown beside it. The instructions are Mitsubishi FX mnemonics. Other makers use different mnemonics for the same ideas.

  1. Top to bottom, left to right. A sequence program is written, and executed, rung by rung from the top, and within a rung from the left.
  2. More on top, more on the left. A sensible order shortens the program. Put the branch with the most series contacts at the top: then no ORB is needed. Put the block with the most parallel contacts at the left: then no ANB is needed.
  3. Horizontal, never vertical. Contacts are drawn on horizontal lines only. A contact on a vertical branch, as in a bridge circuit, cannot be programmed. Redraw it: trace every path through the bridge and write each as its own series branch.
  4. No contact to the right of a coil. The coil is the last element in its rung. If a relay circuit has a contact after a coil, move the contact in front; where contacts lie between coils, program the coil that needs fewer contacts first.
  5. Avoid double coils. If one coil is driven in two or more places in a program, that is a double output. The earlier ones have no effect: only the last counts.
  6. A relay’s coil and its contacts share one number, and each device’s contacts may be used any number of times.
  7. A coil is never connected directly to the left rail. There must be at least one contact first. (To drive a coil always, use the M8000 contact.)
  8. No real current flows in a ladder. To follow the logic we imagine a “current” in it. It flows one way only: from left to right; and the rungs are taken only from top to bottom.
BeforeAfterSaves
LD A · LD B · AND C · ORB · OUT YLD B · AND C · OR A · OUT YThe ORB: the two-contact branch is now on top
LD A · LD B · OR C · ANB · OUT YLD B · OR C · AND A · OUT YThe ANB: the parallel block is now on the left

sections.h: Double coils, and how to cure them
sections.b:
Why a double coil goes wrong. Take three rungs: X001 → Y003; Y003 → Y004; X002 → Y003. Suppose X001 is ON and X002 is OFF.

  1. First rung: X001 is on, so the image of Y003 becomes ON.
  2. Second rung: Y003 is on, so Y004 becomes ON.
  3. Third rung: X002 is off, so the image of Y003 becomes OFF.
  4. Output refresh: the terminals get Y003 = OFF, Y004 = ON.

Y004 says Y003 was on; the Y003 terminal is off. The first rung’s result was used inside the program but never reached the outside.

A double output does not break any input rule of the programmer, but the behaviour is confusing. Cure: give each condition its own auxiliary relay, then drive the output once from the two in parallel.

LD  A          LD  M100
AND B          OR  M101
OUT M100       OUT Y000
LD  C
ANI E
OR  D
OUT M101

Other cures: use jump instructions, or step-ladder instructions, where each step may program the same output. But note: in a step-ladder program, if an output that appears in the main program is also programmed inside a state, it is treated exactly like a double coil.

sections.h: Analysing a program scan by scan; input timing
sections.b:
The I/O state analysis method. A PLC executes its program by cyclic scanning. Ignore the other phases of the scan and look only at the execution of the user program. From the order of the input signals, the image registers and the logic of the ladder, you can work out the state of every output in each successive scan. This is a way to check the control sequence of a program on paper.

  1. Draw a table: one row per scan, one column for each input and each output.
  2. Fill in the input states for every scan first.
  3. For each scan take the rungs in order. Use that scan’s inputs and the outputs left by the previous scan. As soon as a rung gives an output, write it in the table: the next rung uses it at once.

The book’s example. Rungs in order: (1) Y0 = X0 + Y0; (2) Y1 = X0 · Y2 + Y1; (3) Y2 = X0 · Y1, with X0 OFF in scan 1 and ON afterwards.

ScanX0Y0Y1Y2Why
10000X0 = 0, so nothing is on
21110Y0 = 1. For Y1: Y2 is still 0 from scan 1, so Y1 = 1. For Y2: Y1 is already 1 in this scan, so its NC contact is open and Y2 = 0
31110Y1 holds itself; Y2 stays 0

The lesson: Y1 and Y2 seem to compete, but there is no race. Y1 always wins because its rung comes first. Swap the two rungs and Y2 would win.

How long must an input signal last? The state of an input is detected only in the input-processing phase. If the signal is ON or OFF for too short a time it may not be detected. The ON time and the OFF time of an input must each be longer than the PLC’s scan time. Allowing for the input filter: with a filter delay of 8 ms and a scan of 8 ms, the ON or OFF time must be at least 16 ms. Higher-frequency signals are handled by the PLC’s high-speed instructions, or by interrupts.

Start, self-hold and stop is the most basic link of all. It is used on Y and on M.

Stop-priorityStart-priority
ExpressionY0 = (X0 + Y0) · X1Y0 = X0 + Y0 · X1
Both buttons pressedY0 offY0 on
UseThe normal choice: stop must always winWhere failing to start is the greater danger, such as a fire pump or an alarm

Keeping the state through a power cut. Use a latched auxiliary relay in place of Y0 in the holding rung, then drive Y0 from its contact. On the FX1N, M384–M511 are kept in EEPROM and M512–M1535 by capacitor. When power returns, the relay is in the state it had, and so is the output.

Interlock. Two outputs that must never be on together each carry the other’s NC contact. For a motor’s forward and reverse contactors the book is emphatic: besides the interlock in the program, there must also be an electrical interlock and a mechanical interlock outside the PLC. The reason: the PLC switches its outputs within one scan, far faster than a contactor’s arc goes out, and a welded contactor is invisible to the program.

Sequence interlock. When the result of one action is the condition for the next, put a normally-open contact of the first output in series in the start circuit of the second.

Every FX timer is an on-delay timer with a largest delay (3276.7 s for a 100 ms timer). Everything else is built from it.

1 · Long delay, timers in relay. The first timer’s contact starts the second, the second starts the third, and the last one’s contact does the job. The delays add.

2 · Long delay, timer with counter. T0’s own NC contact is in its coil rung, so T0 restarts itself: every 100 s its contact closes for one scan. The counter counts those pulses. Total delay ≈ timer setting × counter setting. Strictly it is (t₁ + Δt) × n, where Δt is one scan, which is small enough to ignore. X0 must stay on throughout; X1 resets the counter.

3 · Off-delay. Y0 comes on at once with X0 and holds itself. When X0 goes off, T0 starts; 3 s later its NC contact drops Y0.

4 · Double delay: delayed on and delayed off.

5 · One-shot (“inching” timer). Each time X0 comes on, Y0 gives one pulse of fixed width, set by a timer, however long or short the press. One way to write it: LD X0 · PLS M0; then LD M0 · OR Y0 · ANI T0 · OUT Y0; then LD Y0 · OUT T0 K50. Y0 is on for 5 s after each rising edge.

6 · Oscillator with adjustable on and off times. T2’s NC contact restarts the pair. T1 sets the off time and T2 the on time.

sections.h: Dividers, one-button control, edge pulses and counters
sections.b:
Divide-by-two. PLS turns each press of X0 into a one-scan pulse M0. The second rung is an exclusive-OR of M0 and Y0: when the pulse arrives Y0 becomes the opposite of what it was, and between pulses it holds. Two input pulses give one output pulse. The same circuit is a toggle (flip-flop).

One button for start and stop. Normally start and stop use two buttons and two inputs. To save an input, one button can do both. It is a divide-by-two again; here with a counter set to 2.

  • First press: M0 pulses, C0 counts 1. Y0 = (M0 + Y0) · C0 comes on and holds.
  • Second press: C0 counts 2 and its contact operates. Its NC contact drops Y0. On the next scan the C0 contact resets the counter.
  • M8002 clears the counter when the PLC starts.

Edge pulse without PLS. This works purely because of the scan order.

  • Scan in which X0 comes on: rung 1 sees X0 on and M1 still off, so M0 comes on. Rung 2 then turns M1 on.
  • Next scan: rung 1 sees M1 on, so M0 goes off. M0 was on for exactly one scan.
  • For a falling-edge pulse, make rung 1 “NC X0 AND NO M1 → M0”.

Counting beyond one counter. A 16-bit counter stops at 32 767.

In series: C1 counts only after C0 has reached 200, so Y0 comes on after 200 + 300 = 500 counts.

Multiplied: C0 resets itself each time it reaches 200 and gives C1 one count. Y0 comes on after 200 × 300 = 60 000 counts.

terms: 停止优先 / 起动优先

worked.q: A ladder has a branch “LD X1” in parallel above “X2 AND X3 AND X4”. Rearrange it to save a step, and give both lists.
worked.s: As drawn: LD X1 · LD X2 · AND X3 · AND X4 · ORB · OUT Y0: six instructions. Put the longer series branch on top: LD X2 · AND X3 · AND X4 · OR X1 · OUT Y0: five instructions, and no ORB.

worked.q: Can the ladder of Exercise 7.3 be programmed directly? (It has X1 · X2 · X3 → Y0 on the top line, with a lower branch X4 · X5 · X6 from after X1, and from within that a further branch X7 · X10 that rejoins after X6.)
worked.s: Not conveniently: branches leave and rejoin at points in the middle of the rung, so it needs stack instructions or cannot be entered at all, depending on how the joins fall. Apply the rules: write each complete path from rail to coil, group the common contacts, and put the block with the most parallel branches on the left and the longest series branch on top. The equivalent ladder then needs only LD, AND, OR, ORB and ANB.

worked.q: An input filter delays by 10 ms and the scan time is 12 ms. What is the shortest ON time an input signal should have to be sure of being detected?
worked.s: At least the filter delay plus one scan: 10 ms + 12 ms = 22 ms. The OFF time must be at least as long for the same reason.

worked.q: Design a delay of 2 hours using 100 ms timers and a counter.
worked.s: 2 h = 7200 s. One 100 ms timer reaches only 3276.7 s. Use a self-resetting timer of 600 s (K6000) and a counter of 12: 600 s × 12 = 7200 s. Rungs: LD X0 · ANI T0 · OUT T0 K6000; LD T0 · OUT C0 K12; LD C0 · OUT Y0; LD X1 · RST C0.

worked.q: In the oscillator circuit T1 is set to K5 and T2 to K15. Describe Y0.
worked.s: T1 is 0.5 s and T2 is 1.5 s. While X0 is on, Y0 is off for 0.5 s, then on for 1.5 s, repeating. Period 2 s; on for 75 % of the time.

worked.q: Why must a forward–reverse motor circuit have an interlock outside the PLC even though the program already interlocks Y1 and Y2?
worked.s: The program can switch Y1 off and Y2 on in the same scan, a few milliseconds apart at most, while the forward contactor needs longer to open and quench its arc. And if the forward contactor’s contacts have welded, the program cannot know. NC auxiliary contacts of each contactor in the other’s coil circuit, and a mechanical interlock, prevent a phase-to-phase short circuit in both cases.

recap: Put the branch with the most series contacts at the ___ of a parallel group.
If the same coil is driven twice in a program, only the ___ one takes effect.
The ON time of an input signal must be longer than the PLC’s ___ time.
Two timers in relay give a delay equal to the ___ of their settings.
A timer with a counter gives a delay equal to the ___ of their settings.

topics.title: Two Design Methods with Worked Programs: Quiz Buzzer and Traffic Lights
topics.zh: 两种编程方法与实例：抢答器和交通信号灯

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 7, “Basic logic instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. Ladder examples are redrawn; several are my own simplified versions of the book’s, and each instruction list here was written to match the ladder shown beside it. The instructions are Mitsubishi FX mnemonics. Other makers use different mnemonics for the same ideas.

The experience method designs a program from experience, your own or other people’s. Start from known typical ladder circuits. Then, following the control requirements, test and modify repeatedly, adding intermediate devices and contacts, until the result is satisfactory. Because it proceeds by trial, it is also called the trial-and-error method.

It requires that you know the standard building-block circuits well and have a grasp of the principles and tricks of ladder design, so that a known program can be turned into one that meets the real requirement.

1 · Analyse the control requirements; choose the control principle
2 · Decide the command devices, sensors and actuators; fix the inputs and outputs
3 · Design the program
4 · Check, modify and complete the program

Verdict. The experience method follows no fixed rule. It is tentative and arbitrary, and usually takes several rounds of change. The time taken and the quality depend heavily on the programmer; results are not standardised and differ from person to person. The ladder is hard to read and the system hard to maintain. It suits only programs with simple logic, where it is quick.

Requirement. Four teams. Whichever team presses first, a display shows that team’s number at once and a buzzer sounds. The others are locked out: their buttons have no effect. A reset switch clears it for the next question.

InputDeviceOutputDevice
X1Team 1 buttonY0Buzzer
X2Team 2 buttonY1Segment a
X3Team 3 buttonY2Segment b
X4Team 4 buttonY3Segment c
X0Reset switchY4Segment d
Y5Segment e
Y6Segment f
Y7Segment g

The book’s I/O table and its ladder number the buttons differently; these notes follow the ladder.

Thinking it through. The familiar self-holding and interlock circuits give the “first to press” logic. The hard part is the display. Work out which segments each number lights on a seven-segment display (a top, b upper right, c lower right, d bottom, e lower left, f upper left, g middle):

TeamSegments lit
1b, c
2a, b, d, e, g
3a, b, c, d, g
4b, c, f, g

If each button drove the segments directly, segment b would be driven from four places: a double coil four times over. The cure is the one from the previous topic: introduce auxiliary relays M1–M4 as flags for “this team was first”, then drive each segment once.

DeviceLogicMeaning
M1(X1 + M1) · X0 · M2 · M3 · M4Team 1 first: holds itself, locked out by any other flag, cleared by reset
M2(X2 + M2) · X0 · M1 · M3 · M4Team 2 first
M3(X3 + M3) · X0 · M1 · M2 · M4Team 3 first
M4(X4 + M4) · X0 · M1 · M2 · M3Team 4 first
Y0 buzzerM1 + M2 + M3 + M4Any team has buzzed
Y1 (a)M2 + M3
Y2 (b)M1 + M2 + M3 + M4
Y3 (c)M1 + M3 + M4
Y4 (d)M2 + M3
Y5 (e)M2
Y6 (f)M4
Y7 (g)M2 + M3 + M4
LD   X1          LD   M1          LD   M2
OR   M1          OR   M2          OR   M3
ANI  X0          OR   M3          OUT  Y1     (a)
ANI  M2          OR   M4          OUT  Y4     (d)
ANI  M3          OUT  Y0  buzzer  LD   M1
ANI  M4          OUT  Y2  (b)     OR   M3
OUT  M1                           OR   M4

Two outputs with the same logic (Y0 and Y2, or Y1 and Y4) are written as consecutive OUTs.

sections.h: The sequential-circuit method and the laws of contact logic
sections.b:
Most PLC control circuits are sequential circuits. From a timing diagram you can find how each output corresponds to the inputs and internal contacts, and simplify using the laws that contacts obey. In general this method should be used together with the experience method, or the logic becomes too complicated.

Let X, Y and Z be three contacts. “·” is series (AND), “+” is parallel (OR), and a bar is a normally-closed contact (NOT).

LawStatement
CommutativeX · Y = Y · X  ·  X + Y = Y + X
Associative(X · Y) · Z = X · (Y · Z)  ·  (X + Y) + Z = X + (Y + Z)
Absorption (identities)0 + X = X  ·  1 · X = X  ·  1 + X = 1  ·  0 · X = 0
IdempotentX · X · … · X = X  ·  X + X + … + X = X
DistributiveX · (Y + Z) = X · Y + X · Z  ·  X + Y · Z = (X + Y) · (X + Z)
ComplementX · X = 0  ·  X + X = 1
Double negationNOT (NOT X) = X
De MorganNOT (X + Y + Z) = X · Y · Z  ·  NOT (X · Y · Z) = X + Y + Z

Each law can be checked on a real circuit. The distributive law says: contact X in series with the parallel pair (Y, Z) behaves exactly like two branches in parallel, X–Y and X–Z.

1 · Assign inputs and outputs; also the internal relays, timers and counters needed
2 · Analyse the logic; draw the timing diagram
3 · From the timing diagram, write the logic expression for each output
4 · Draw the ladder from the expressions
5 · Verify. The expressions may not cover everything, so check them with the experience method too

sections.h: Example 2: traffic lights at a crossroads
sections.b:
Requirement. Press start button SB1. The north–south red comes on and the east–west green comes on. After 25 s the east–west green flashes for 3 s (three times, 0.5 s on and 0.5 s off) and goes out. The east–west yellow then lights for 2 s and goes out. As it goes out, the east–west red and the north–south green come on, and the same pattern follows the other way round. When the north–south yellow goes out the second cycle begins, and so on. Press stop button SB2: every lamp goes out.

AddressDeviceAddressDevice
X0Start button SB1Y0North–south green
X1Stop button SB2Y1North–south yellow
Y2North–south red
Y3Alarm: both greens on together
Y4East–west green
Y5East–west yellow
Y6East–west red

Each output drives the lamps of both directions of its road. A half-cycle is 25 s + 3 s + 2 s = 30 s, so each red is on for 30 s and the full cycle is 60 s.

Time in cycle, s0–2525–2828–3030–5555–5858–60
North–southRedRedRedGreenGreen flashingYellow

Software. Ordinary timers give the on-times; the flashing uses the one-second clock M8013 (0.5 s on, 0.5 s off).

DeviceSetLogicJob
M0(X0 + M0) · X1 · Y3Run flag: start, hold, stop; also dropped by the alarm
T0K300M0 · T130 s: north–south red time
T1K300T030 s: east–west red time. When it times out it resets T0, and the cycle restarts
T2K250M0 · T025 s: east–west green steady
T3K30T23 s: east–west green flashing
T4K20T32 s: east–west yellow
T5K250T025 s: north–south green steady
T6K30T53 s: north–south green flashing
T7K20T62 s: north–south yellow
Y2M0 · T0North–south red
Y6T0East–west red
Y4Y2 · T2 + T2 · T3 · M8013East–west green: steady, then flashing

Y0Y6 · T5 + T5 · T6 · M8013North–south green: steady, then flashing
Y1T6 · T7North–south yellow
Y3Y0 · Y4Alarm

How to read it. With the PLC in RUN, press SB1: M0 is energised and holds. Y2 and Y4 come on first: north–south red, east–west green. Then follow the timers down the table against the timing row above. Press SB2: M0 drops, its holding is released, every timer resets and every lamp goes out.

The safety rung. Two greens together would cause a collision, so Y3 detects that state, lights an alarm and stops the sequence.

worked.q: Three conveyor belts must start in the order A → B → C and stop in the reverse order C → B → A. From the book’s timing diagram: with switch X0 on, Y0 (belt A) runs at once, Y1 (B) 10 s later, Y2 (C) 20 s after X0. With X0 off, Y2 stops at once, Y1 10 s later, Y0 20 s after X0. Design the program. (Exercise 7.5)
worked.s: One solution (mine). On-delays from X0: LD X0 · OUT T0 K100 · OUT T1 K200. Belt C: LD T1 · OUT Y2 (T1 resets the moment X0 goes off, so C stops at once). Belt B: LD T0 · OR Y1 · ANI T2 · OUT Y1; and its stop timer LDI X0 · AND Y1 · OUT T2 K100. Belt A: LD X0 · OR Y0 · ANI T3 · OUT Y0; and LDI X0 · AND Y0 · OUT T3 K200. Check: start: Y0 at 0 s, Y1 at 10 s, Y2 at 20 s. Stop: Y2 at once; T2 runs 10 s and drops Y1; T3 runs 20 s and drops Y0. I/O: X0 run switch; Y0, Y1, Y2 the contactors of belts A, B, C.

worked.q: Extend the quiz buzzer to five teams. What must change? (Exercise 7.6)
worked.s: Add input X5 for team 5 and flag M5 = (X5 + M5) · NOT X0 · NOT M1 · NOT M2 · NOT M3 · NOT M4. Add NOT M5 to the rungs of M1–M4. The digit 5 lights segments a, c, d, f, g, so add M5 in parallel to Y1 (a), Y3 (c), Y4 (d), Y6 (f) and Y7 (g), and to the buzzer Y0. Segment b (Y2) is not lit for 5, so Y2 stays M1 + M2 + M3 + M4.

worked.q: Simplify Y = X · Z + X · NOT Z + Y1 · X and say which laws you used.
worked.s: Y = X · (Z + NOT Z) + X · Y1 (distributive) = X · 1 + X · Y1 (complement) = X + X · Y1 = X · (1 + Y1) (distributive) = X · 1 = X (absorption). Three branches reduce to one contact.

worked.q: In the traffic-light program, which timer makes the whole cycle repeat, and how?
worked.s: T1. T0 runs 30 s; its contact starts T1, which runs another 30 s. When T1 times out, its NC contact in T0’s rung resets T0. T0’s contact opens, which resets T1 and, through them, T5–T7; T2–T4 restart because NOT T0 is true again. One scan later T1’s NC contact has closed and T0 starts timing afresh.

worked.q: Why is the experience method not recommended for a program with a long sequence of steps?
worked.s: It has no fixed procedure: the program grows by adding interlocks and auxiliary relays until it works. For a long sequence the interlocks multiply, the ladder becomes hard to read and maintain, and different programmers produce quite different results. A long sequence is better designed with the step (sequential function chart) method of Chapter 8.
