topics.title: SFC and the Step-Ladder Instructions STL and RET
topics.zh: SFC 图和步进指令 STL、RET

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 8, “Step-ladder instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, with state diagrams redrawn. The instructions are Mitsubishi FX (STL and RET with state devices S). Other PLC families build the same step-by-step structure in other ways, and your ITE module calls the idea a sequential function chart.

A state transfer diagram, also called a sequential function chart (SFC), is used for programming complex sequences. It is more direct than a ladder diagram.

The idea: a control process can be divided into a number of stages. Each stage is a state (a step). States are separated by transition conditions. Neighbouring states do different things. When the transition condition between two states is satisfied, the transfer happens: the previous state’s actions end and the next state’s actions begin.

The state device S is the basic element. The FX1N has 1000 of them, S0–S999. The ten devices S0–S9 are initial states: the starting points of state diagrams.

SymbolMeaning
Box with a device numberA state. The initial state is drawn with a double box
Line between boxes, read top to bottom and left to rightThe order of transfer. Arrows in that normal direction may be left out
Short bar across the line, with a labelThe transition condition, written as text or a logic expression
Coil or box at the side of a stateThe outputs that state drives

A two-state example. While S20 is active, output Y5 is on and the program waits for X3. When X3 comes on, the state moves from S20 to S21 and Y5 goes off by itself.

The key property: when one state transfers to the next, the previous state is reset automatically. You never write the interlock that switches the old step off.

A mechanical hand moves a workpiece from point A to point B. Up, down, left and right are driven by double-coil two-position solenoid valves on air cylinders. Gripping and releasing use a single-coil valve: the gripper is clamped only while the valve is energised. The origin is at the upper left. The arm goes down, clamps, up, right, down, releases, up, left, in that order. It has manual and automatic modes; this is the automatic sequence.

StateOutput drivenActionTransition to the next state
S2 (initial)—Automatic mode readyM8041 (transfer start) and M8044 (origin condition) on
S20Y0DownX1: lower limit
S21SET Y1 · T0 K10Clamp, and wait 1 s for a firm gripT0
S22Y2UpX2: upper limit
S23Y3RightX3: right limit
S24Y0DownX1: lower limit
S25RST Y1 · T1 K10Release, and wait 1 sT1
S26Y2UpX2: upper limit
S27Y4LeftX4: left limit, then back to S2

Things to notice.

  • The clamp uses SET Y1 in S21 and RST Y1 in S25. An ordinary OUT would drop when the state is left, and the part would fall. SET keeps the grip through S22, S23 and S24.
  • Y0 (down) and Y2 (up) each appear in two states. In a step-ladder program that is allowed: only the active state is executed.
  • The two waits make sure the gripper has really closed or opened before the arm moves.
  • At the left limit the state returns to S2 and the next cycle can begin.

The FX has two step-ladder instructions: STL, step-ladder start, and RET, step-ladder end.

STL activates a state. In the ladder it appears as a state contact drawn from the rail (a contact with a doubled outline). STL sets up a sub-rail, so that everything belonging to that state is done on the sub-rail.

Each state has three elements:

ElementIn the example “STL S21 · OUT Y3 · LD X2 · SET S22”Required?
Drive the loadsOUT Y3Depends on the job: a state may drive nothing
Name the transfer targetSET S22Always
Name the transfer conditionLD X2Always
  • If the state is on (“activated”), its loads are driven and its transfer can take place.
  • If the state is off, neither can happen.
  • So, apart from the initial state, a state is switched on only when the state before it is active and the transfer condition holds. And once the next state is activated, the previous one is switched off automatically.

In terms of the scan. “Activated” means that section of the program is scanned and executed. “Off” means that section is skipped. This is why analysing a state program is so orderly: there are no tangled interlocks to think about. The book’s phrase for it: “do only your own job and take no thought for the others.” The program is easy to read, and trial running, debugging and fault-finding become very easy.

RET returns to the main rail. When the step sequence is finished, operations that are not part of it are done on the main rail again, which prevents logic errors. A state program must end with RET.

1. States are programmed with the step contact instruction STL. An STL contact is a normally-open contact connected to the left rail. When it is on, the state is the active step. Contacts that follow an STL contact use LD or LDI.
  2. The program must end with RET, which returns to the main rail.
  3. An STL contact may drive, directly or through other contacts, the coils of Y, M, S, T and C.
  4. The PLC executes only the circuit of the active step, so double-coil outputs are permitted with STL. But the same timer must not be used in two adjacent states.
  5. Inside a block driven by an STL contact, MC and MCR cannot be used. CJ (jump) can, but is not recommended.
  6. STL cannot be used inside interrupt routines or subroutines.
  7. During a transfer, two states are both on for one scan. To stop two outputs that must not be on together from being driven at the same time, provide the necessary interlocks, inside and outside the PLC.
  8. In one SFC a state number may not be used twice.
  9. Order within a state: drive first, then transfer. Never the other way round.
  10. A transfer that does not go to the next state in sequence must not use SET: use OUT.
  11. The initial state can be driven by another state, but at the start of running it has to be driven some other way, or the state flow cannot begin. Normally use the system’s initial conditions; if there are none, use M8002 (the initial pulse when the PLC goes from STOP to RUN). An ordinary state can be driven only by another state, never by an outside signal.
  12. To carry on from the same state after a power cut, use latched state devices.

sections.h: Designing an SFC: the shuttle trolley
sections.b:
Requirement.

  1. Press start button SB. The trolley motor runs forward and the trolley advances. When it strikes limit switch SQ1 the motor reverses and the trolley goes back.
  2. Going back, it strikes SQ2. The motor stops and the trolley waits 3 s. Then it advances again, strikes SQ3, and goes back again.
  3. When it strikes SQ2 on the way back this time, it stops.
  4. Press SB again and the whole thing repeats.

SQ1, SQ2 and SQ3 are normally on. They go off only while the trolley is touching them.

InputDeviceOutputDevice
X0Start button SB (normally open)Y1KM1: motor forward, trolley advances
X1Limit switch SQ1 (normally closed)Y2KM2: motor reverse, trolley goes back
X2Limit switch SQ2 (normally closed)
X3Limit switch SQ3 (normally closed)

The two contactors are also interlocked with each other’s NC contacts in the external wiring.

Step 1 · Break the process into stages and give each a state.

StageActionStateStageActionState
①InitialS0④Wait 3 sS22
②AdvanceS20⑤Advance againS23
③Go backS21⑥Go back againS24

S20 and S23 do the same thing, and so do S21 and S24. But they are different stages of the process, so they are different states with different numbers.

Step 2 · Decide what each state does. S0: ready after power-up. S20: Y1. S21: Y2. S22: timer T0, set to 3 s. S23: as S20. S24: as S21. A load may be driven directly by the state, or through a logical combination of other contacts.

Step 3 · Find each state’s transfer condition: under what condition is the next state activated? A condition may be a single contact or a series–parallel combination of several.

sections.h: From SFC to step ladder to instruction list
sections.b:
A state diagram converts to a ladder, and the ladder to an instruction list. The three correspond one to one.

0   LD   M8002      initial pulse
1   SET  S0         activate the initial state
3   STL  S0
4   LD   X0         start button
5   SET  S20
7   STL  S20        --- advance ---
8   LDI  Y2         interlock: not while reversing
9   OUT  Y1
10  LDI  X1         SQ1 struck (NC input goes off)
11  SET  S21
13  STL  S21        --- go back ---
14  LDI  Y1
15  OUT  Y2
16  LDI  X2         SQ2 struck
17  SET  S22
19  STL  S22        --- wait 3 s ---
20  OUT  T0   K30
23  LD   T0
24  SET  S23
26  STL  S23        --- advance again ---
27  LDI  Y2
28  OUT  Y1
29  LDI  X3         SQ3 struck
30  SET  S24
32  STL  S24        --- go back again ---
33  LDI  Y1
34  OUT  Y2
35  LDI  X2         SQ2 struck
36  OUT  S0         return to the initial state: OUT, not SET
38  RET
39  END

Read the pattern. Every state is the same four-line shape: STL the state · drive the load · the condition · SET the next state. Once you have the SFC, writing the list is mechanical.

  • The rungs “LDI Y2 · OUT Y1” are the interlock that rule 7 asks for. For one scan during a transfer, S20 and S21 are both on, and without it Y1 and Y2 could both be driven.
  • The last transfer goes back up to S0, which is not the next state in sequence, so it uses OUT S0.
  • Y1 appears in S20 and S23, and Y2 in S21 and S24: double coils, allowed here.
  • Because the limit switches are NC inputs, the conditions are written with LDI.

worked.q: What is the difference between the STL instruction and the LD instruction? Give an example. (Exercise 8.1)
worked.s: Both take a normally-open contact from the left rail. LD takes the contact of any device (X, Y, M, S, T, C) and simply starts a rung. STL works only on a state device S and does much more: it sets up a sub-rail for that state, the instructions after it are executed only while the state is active, and when the state transfers onward the state is reset automatically. Example: “LD S20 · OUT Y1” just makes Y1 follow S20 and S20 is used like an auxiliary relay; “STL S20 · OUT Y1 · LD X1 · SET S21” makes S20 a step that drives Y1, moves to S21 when X1 comes on and then switches itself off.

worked.q: Name the three elements of a state, and say which may be omitted.
worked.s: (1) Driving the loads; (2) naming the transfer target; (3) naming the transfer condition. The target and the condition are always needed. Driving a load may be omitted: a state can exist only to wait.

worked.q: In the mechanical-hand sequence, why is the gripper driven by SET Y1 and RST Y1, not by OUT Y1 in state S21?
worked.s: An output driven by OUT inside a state goes off when that state is left. The gripper must stay clamped through the up, right and down states that follow. SET latches Y1 in S21 and it stays on until RST Y1 in S25.

worked.q: Two adjacent states S21 and S22 each use timer T0. Why is that a fault, and what is the fix?
worked.s: During the transfer both states are on for one scan, so T0’s coil is driven without a break and the timer is never reset: in S22 it is already timed out and the state is left at once. Use different timers in adjacent states (T0 in one, T1 in the other). The same timer may be reused in states that are not adjacent.

worked.q: Write the instruction list for a three-state sequence: S0 waits for X0; S20 drives Y0 until X1; S21 drives Y1 for 5 s and then returns to S0.
worked.s: LD M8002 · SET S0 · STL S0 · LD X0 · SET S20 · STL S20 · OUT Y0 · LD X1 · SET S21 · STL S21 · OUT Y1 · OUT T0 K50 · LD T0 · OUT S0 · RET · END.

recap: When a state transfers to the next, the previous state is reset ___.
A step-ladder program must end with the instruction ___.
Within a state, first ___ the load, then make the transfer.
A transfer to a state that is not next in sequence uses ___, not SET.

topics.title: SFC Flow Forms: Single Sequence, Jumps, Selective and Parallel Branches
topics.zh: SFC 流程的形态：单流程、跳转、选择性分支和并行分支

sections.h: Single sequence, and transfers that are not “next in line”
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 8, “Step-ladder instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, with state diagrams redrawn. The instructions are Mitsubishi FX (STL and RET with state devices S). Other PLC families build the same step-by-step structure in other ways, and your ITE module calls the idea a sequential function chart.

A single sequence is one in which the states can follow each other in only one order. The trolley is an example: S0 → S20 → S21 → S22 → S23 → S24 → S0, with no other possibility.

Real sequences are not all like that. One with several possible paths is a branching sequence.

The programming principle of step control: drive the loads first, then handle the transfer. Both must come after an STL instruction, which guarantees that they are carried out on that state’s sub-rail.

A transfer to the next state in line uses SET. A transfer upward, or to a state further down that is not adjacent, or to another sequence, is a non-continuous transfer. It cannot use SET: it uses OUT (or RST). On the diagram it is shown by an arrow pointing to the target state number.

KindWhat happensInstruction
Repeat (loop)Transfer back up to an earlier state, to do part of the sequence againOUT
JumpTransfer down past one or more states, skipping themOUT
Jump to another sequenceTransfer to a state in a different flow, one that starts from another initial stateOUT
ResetThe state switches itself off and the flow ends thereRST

Example. “STL S23 · LD X5 · OUT S20” sends the flow back from S23 to S20 when X5 is on. “STL S23 · LD X6 · RST S23” ends the flow at S23.

If there are several paths and only one of them can be taken, that is a selective branch.

  • The diagram contains three separate flows: S20 → S21 → S22 → S50, S20 → S31 → S32 → S50, and S20 → S41 → S42 → S50.
  • S20 is the branch state. According to the condition (X0, X10 or X20) one flow is chosen. X0, X10 and X20 must not be ON at the same time.
  • S50 is the merge state. It can be driven by any one of S22, S32 or S42.
  • A selective structure can have at most 8 branches.

Programming principle: handle the branch state first, all together; then handle the merge, all together.

The branch state. First drive the branch state’s own load; then write the transfers in order.

STL  S20
OUT  Y0          drive
LD   X0
SET  S21         transfer to the first branch
LD   X10
SET  S31         transfer to the second branch
LD   X20
SET  S41         transfer to the third branch

The merge. First drive the loads of all the states before the merge, branch by branch. Then, in order, write the transfers into the merge state.

STL  S21         first branch
OUT  Y1
LD   X1
SET  S22
STL  S22
OUT  Y2
STL  S31         second branch
OUT  Y11
LD   X11
SET  S32
STL  S32
OUT  Y12
STL  S41         third branch
OUT  Y21
LD   X21
SET  S42
STL  S42
OUT  Y22
STL  S22
LD   X2
SET  S50         from the first branch into the merge
STL  S32
LD   X12
SET  S50         from the second branch into the merge
STL  S42
LD   X22
SET  S50         from the third branch into the merge

Notice that S22, S32 and S42 each appear in two STL instructions: once to drive their loads, and again, later, for the transfer to S50.

If there are several paths and all of them must be carried out at the same time, that is a parallel branch.

  • After S20 there are three branches. When X0 comes ON, all three start together: S21, S24 and S27 are all set.
  • The branches then run independently, each at its own pace.
  • Only when all three have finished (S23, S26 and S29 all active) and X7 is ON is S30 set. S23, S26 and S29 are then reset together.
  • A join that waits like this until every path has been completed is called a parallel join.
  • A parallel structure too can have at most 8 branches.

Programming principle: the same as before. Handle the branch state first, then the join.

The branch state. As for any state: drive, then transfer. All the transfers are written one after another under a single condition.

STL  S20
OUT  Y0          drive
LD   X0
SET  S21         to the first parallel branch
SET  S24         to the second
SET  S27         to the third

The join. Before the join, write the output handling of each last state separately. Then write the join, from left to right.

STL  S23
OUT  Y1          drive
STL  S26
OUT  Y2          drive
STL  S29
OUT  Y3          drive
STL  S23         consecutive STL instructions
STL  S26           mean “all of these states together”:
STL  S29           the parallel join
LD   X7
SET  S30

Selective branchParallel branch
How many paths runOne, chosen by a conditionAll, at the same time
Lines on the diagramSingle horizontal linesDouble horizontal lines
Where the conditions areOne at the head of each branch, below the split; one at the foot of each branch, above the mergeOne above the split; one below the join
Branch codeA separate “LD condition · SET” for each branchOne “LD condition”, then several SETs in a row
Merge codeEach branch on its own: “STL · LD condition · SET target”Several STLs in a row, then one “LD condition · SET target”
Does the merge wait?No: whichever branch was taken moves on when its own condition is metYes: it waits until every branch has reached its last state
RequirementThe conditions must be mutually exclusiveOutputs driven in different branches must not conflict
Maximum8 branches8 branches
Typical useDifferent products, sizes or modes: sorting, manual / automaticThings that happen side by side: two stations working at once, the two directions of a junction

Mixed structures. The two can be combined. A branch that follows immediately on a merge, with no state in between, cannot be programmed directly: insert an empty (dummy) state that drives nothing and transfers at once.

worked.q: A selective branch at S20 has two paths: X1 → S21 and X2 → S31. Write the code for the branch state, which drives Y0.
worked.s: STL S20 · OUT Y0 · LD X1 · SET S21 · LD X2 · SET S31. Drive first, then one “LD · SET” for each branch. X1 and X2 must not be on together.

worked.q: Two parallel branches end in S22 and S32. When both are active and X5 is on, the flow must move to S40. Write the join.
worked.s: STL S22 · STL S32 · LD X5 · SET S40. The two STL instructions in a row mean “S22 and S32 both active”.

worked.q: From state S25 the flow must return to S21 while X3 is on, or go on to S26 when X4 is on. Write the transfers.
worked.s: STL S25 · (drive its load) · LD X3 · OUT S21 · LD X4 · SET S26. Going back up is a non-continuous transfer, so OUT; going on to the next state uses SET.

worked.q: In a parallel structure one branch finishes long before the other. What does the finished branch do?
worked.s: It stays in its last state, still active and still driving whatever that state drives, and waits. The join takes place only when every branch has reached its last state and the join condition is on. So the last state of each branch should be one in which it is safe to wait.

worked.q: A sorting machine must take path A for a tall box and path B for a short one. A second machine must clamp a part and start a coolant pump at the same moment. Which branch type suits each?
worked.s: The sorter: selective branch, with the height sensor as the condition, because only one path is wanted. The second machine: parallel branch, because both things must happen together.

recap: On an SFC a parallel branch is drawn with ___ horizontal lines.
In a selective branch the transition conditions of the branches must not be ON at the ___ time.
A selective or parallel structure can have at most ___ branches.
Several STL instructions in a row mean a parallel ___.
A state that ends the flow by switching itself off uses the instruction ___.

topics.title: SFC Applications: Traffic Lights Two Ways, and a Ball Sorter
topics.zh: SFC 的编程应用：两种方法实现交通灯，以及大小球分拣

sections.h: Traffic lights as a single sequence
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 8, “Step-ladder instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words, with state diagrams redrawn. The instructions are Mitsubishi FX (STL and RET with state devices S). Other PLC families build the same step-by-step structure in other ways, and your ITE module calls the idea a sequential function chart.

The requirement, the I/O assignment and the timing are exactly those of the traffic-light example in Chapter 7: X0 start, X1 stop; Y0, Y1, Y2 north–south green, yellow, red; Y4, Y5, Y6 east–west green, yellow, red; Y3 alarm.

The idea. Treat the two directions together as one sequence. Divide the 60 s cycle into its six time intervals and give each a state. In every state exactly two things are lit: one output for the east–west lamps and one for the north–south lamps.

The rungs outside the state flow (on the main rail, before the first STL):

LD   Y0
AND  Y4
OUT  Y3            alarm: both greens on together
LD   X1            stop button
OR   M8002         or the first scan after RUN
ZRST S0   S24      reset every state S0 to S24: all lamps go out
LD   X0            start button
SET  S0

How it runs. Press SB1: X0 comes on and S0 is set. In S0, Y2 and Y4 are driven, so the north–south red and the east–west green light, and T0 runs for 25 s. Then the state moves to S20: Y2 is still driven, but Y4 is now driven through M8013, so the east–west green flashes; T1 runs 3 s. S21: Y2 and Y5, east–west yellow, for 2 s. S22: Y0 and Y6, north–south green and east–west red, for 25 s. S23: Y6, and Y0 through M8013, for 3 s. S24: Y6 and Y1, north–south yellow, for 2 s. Then T5’s contact sends the flow back to S0 and the cycle repeats, over and over.

Press the stop button SB2, or let the two greens come on together, and states S0–S24 are reset: all lamps go out.

Compare with Chapter 7. There, eight timers and seven output expressions had to be worked out and checked against each other. Here each state simply lists what is lit and for how long. Y2 appears in three states, Y6 in three, Y0 and Y4 in two: double coils, harmless in a state program.

sections.h: Traffic lights as two parallel branches
sections.b:
The same job can be seen another way: the east–west lamps and the north–south lamps are two sequences running side by side. Make the east–west lamps the left-hand parallel branch and the north–south lamps the right-hand one.

East–west branchDrivesForNorth–south branchDrivesFor
S20Y4 green · T0 K25025 sS30Y2 red · T2 K30030 s
S21Y4 through M8013 · T1 K303 sS31Y0 green · T3 K25025 s
S22Y5 yellow · T2 K202 sS32Y0 through M8013 · T4 K303 s
S23Y6 red30 s (waits for the other branch)S33Y1 yellow · T5 K202 s

Timer numbers follow my reading of the book’s diagram, where the same timer number appears in both branches; give each branch its own timers if you build this. The structure is what matters here.

S0 (initial), entered by the start button
Parallel split: S20 and S30 are set together
Left: S20 → S21 → S22 → S23  ·  Right: S30 → S31 → S32 → S33
Parallel join: S23 and S33 both active, and T5 timed out
Back to S0: the next cycle

What the join does here. The east–west branch reaches its last state, S23 (red), after 30 s and then simply waits there with the red on. The north–south branch takes the full 60 s. When its yellow time T5 ends, both branches are in their last states, the join condition is met, and the cycle restarts. The waiting property of the parallel join is what gives the east–west red its 30 s.

The rungs outside the flow are as before, with the reset widened to cover the new states: ZRST S0 S33.

Which version is better? The single sequence is shorter and easier to check. The parallel version keeps each road’s lamps together, which reads naturally and is easier to change if one road’s timing has to differ. Both give exactly the same lamps.

In production, products on a line often have to be sorted. This machine sorts large and small steel balls into two boxes.

How it works. The arm’s home (origin) is at the upper left, shown by lamp HL. A proximity switch SP detects that a ball is present. The arm then goes down with an electromagnet on its end.

How it tells large from small. The arm descends for a fixed time. If the magnet lands on a small ball, the arm gets all the way down and the lower limit switch SQ2 operates. If it lands on a large ball, the ball stops the arm short and SQ2 does not operate. So after the descent time, the state of SQ2 says which kind of ball it is.

After that: pick the ball up, go up, move right to the correct box, go down, release, go up, move left to the origin.

  • Left and right movement: motor M, forward for right and reverse for left.
  • Up and down: a double-acting air cylinder with a double-coil three-position solenoid valve. YY1 energised: arm down. YY2 energised: arm up. YY1 and YY2 must not be energised together: interlock them.
  • Gripping: electromagnet YA. Energised: holds the ball. De-energised: releases it.
InputDeviceOutputDevice
X0SP: proximity switch, ball presentY0YY1: arm down
X1SQ1: left limitY1YA: electromagnet
X2SQ2: lower limitY2YY2: arm up
X3SQ3: upper limitY3KM1: motor forward, arm right
X4SQ4: middle position, release point for small ballsY4KM2: motor reverse, arm left
X5SQ5: right limit, release point for large ballsY5HL: lamp, arm at origin

In the hardware, KM1 and KM2 are interlocked with each other’s NC contacts.

sections.h: A ball sorter: the state diagram
sections.b:
The process has two paths, chosen by the state of SQ2, that is by large or small. So this is a selective branch. The split comes after the arm has descended. The two paths pick up, rise and move right, each to its own box. They merge at “descend at the box”, and the rest is common.

StateDrivesActionTransfer condition → next
S0 (initial)—Ready. Entered by M8002X0 (ball present) AND Y5 (at origin: up, left, released) → S20
S20Y0 · T0 K20Arm down for 2 sT0 AND X2 (lower limit reached: small) → S21  ·  T0 AND NOT X2 (not reached: large) → S24
S21 (small)SET Y1 · T1 K10Pick up, wait 1 sT1 → S22
S22Y2UpX3: upper limit → S23
S23Y3 (through NC X4)RightX4: middle position, the small-ball box → S27
S24 (large)SET Y1 · T1 K10Pick up, wait 1 sT1 → S25
S25Y2UpX3: upper limit → S26
S26Y3 (through NC X5)RightX5: right limit, the large-ball box → S27
S27 (merge)Y0DownX2: lower limit → S28
S28RST Y1 · T2 K10Release, wait 1 sT2 → S29
S29Y2UpX3: upper limit → S30
S30Y4 (through NC X1)LeftX1: left limit → S0

Points worth copying.

  • The sensor decides the branch. The two conditions are “T0 AND X2” and “T0 AND NOT X2”. They can never both be true, which is exactly what a selective branch requires.
  • SET and RST for the magnet. The ball is held from S21 or S24 right through to S28.
  • A limit contact in the output rung. Y3 is driven through the NC contact of the limit it is travelling towards (X4 or X5), and Y4 through NC X1. The drive stops the instant the limit is reached, even before the state transfers.
  • The same T1 in S21 and S24 is allowed: those states are in different branches and are never adjacent in time.
  • The origin lamp Y5 is part of the start condition, so a cycle can begin only from the home position.
  • The program ends with RET and END.

worked.q: Write the instruction list for states S0 and S20 of the traffic-light single sequence. (After Exercise 8.2)
worked.s: STL S0 · OUT Y2 · OUT Y4 · OUT T0 K250 · LD T0 · SET S20 · STL S20 · OUT Y2 · OUT T1 K30 · LD M8013 · OUT Y4 · LD T1 · SET S21. The remaining four states follow the same pattern, and the last transfer is “LD T5 · OUT S0”, then RET and END.

worked.q: Write the instruction list for the branch state S20 of the ball sorter. (After Exercise 8.4)
worked.s: STL S20 · OUT Y0 · OUT T0 K20 · LD T0 · AND X2 · SET S21 · LD T0 · ANI X2 · SET S24. Drive first, then one condition and one SET for each branch.

worked.q: In the ball sorter, why is the decision between large and small made only after timer T0, and not as soon as the arm starts down?
worked.s: At the start of the descent SQ2 is off for both kinds of ball, because the arm has not arrived yet. Only after enough time for a full descent does “SQ2 still off” mean that a large ball has stopped the arm. T0 is that waiting time.

worked.q: A part is machined in three operations taking 2 s, 3 s and 4 s in turn, 9 s in all. A control switch X0 starts and stops the process, and each start begins with the first operation. Outline a state program. (Exercise 8.5)
worked.s: One solution (mine). Outputs Y1, Y2, Y3 for the three operations. S0 initial, entered by M8002; transfer on X0 to S20. S20: OUT Y1 · OUT T0 K20; on T0 → S21. S21: OUT Y2 · OUT T1 K30; on T1 → S22. S22: OUT Y3 · OUT T2 K40; on T2 → OUT S0. For stopping at any time: on the main rail, “LDI X0 · ZRST S20 S22” and “LDI X0 · SET S0”, so that switching X0 off clears the active state and returns to S0; the next start then begins at operation 1. While X0 stays on the cycle repeats, because S0 transfers to S20 again at once.

worked.q: In the parallel version of the traffic lights, what would go wrong if the two branches were joined as a selective merge?
worked.s: A selective merge moves on as soon as one branch meets its condition. The flow would restart when the first branch finished, and the other branch’s remaining states would be left active or cut short, so the lamps of the two roads would lose step with each other. A parallel join waits for both.

recap: In the single-sequence traffic-light program, each state lights ___ lamp outputs.
The instruction that resets a whole range of states, such as S0 to S24, is ___.
The ball sorter uses a ___ branch, chosen by the state of the lower limit switch.
In the ball sorter the electromagnet is switched on with SET Y1 and off with ___ Y1.

topics.title: Applied Instructions: Format, Operands, Data and the Full Instruction Map
topics.zh: 功能指令：格式、操作数、数据形式和指令总览

sections.h: What an applied instruction looks like
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 9, “Function instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. Program fragments are short listings I wrote to match the book’s explanations. These are Mitsubishi FX applied instructions; which ones exist depends on the model, so check the manual of the PLC you are using.

Applied (function) instructions are the mark of a PLC’s data-handling ability. They are far more involved than the basic logic instructions.

In the FX series each is numbered by function number, FNC00 to FNC250, and each also has a mnemonic. In a ladder it is drawn as a box at the right of the rung: the mnemonic first, then the operands.

LD    X0
MOV   K150   D20      when X0 is on, put the number 150 into D20

Most have one to four operands; a few have none.

SymbolMeaning
[S]Source operand: where the data comes from. Its contents are not changed
[D]Destination operand: where the result goes
[S·] [D·]The dot means the operand may be indexed with V or Z
n, mOther operands: usually constants K or H, or extra information about the source and destination
[S1·] [S2·] [D1·] [D2·]Numbered when there is more than one of a kind

Each instruction also takes a fixed number of program steps: typically 5 or 7 for a 16-bit instruction and 9 or 13 for the 32-bit form.

sections.h: Two letters that change everything: D and P
sections.b:
MarkWhereMeaning
DIn front of the mnemonic: DMOVThe instruction handles 32-bit data. Without it: 16-bit
PAfter the mnemonic: MOVPPulse execution: the instruction is executed once, when its condition changes OFF → ON. Without it: continuous execution, repeated on every scan while the condition is on
BothDMOVP32-bit, executed once

32-bit operands take two registers. “DMOVP D10 D12” means: when the condition rises, send the data in D11 and D10 to D13 and D12. The register you name is the low word; the next one is the high word. For that reason, use even-numbered registers as the first of each pair, so that pairs never overlap.

The 32-bit counters C200–C255 are 32 bits in one device. They cannot be operands of a 16-bit instruction.

Why P matters. For an instruction such as MOV it makes little difference: sending the same number again does no harm, only wastes time. For an instruction that changes its own data, such as INC, ADD with the same source and destination, or a shift, continuous execution repeats the change every scan, hundreds of times while a button is held. Those instructions almost always need the P form.

sections.h: Bit devices, word devices and KnM groups
sections.b:
Bit devices handle only ON/OFF information: X, Y, M and S. Word devices handle numbers: T, C, D and so on.

Bit devices can be grouped to make a word. Four bits are one unit (one hexadecimal digit). The general form is Kn followed by the first device, where n is the number of four-bit units.

WrittenMeansBits
K1M0M0–M34
K2M0M0–M7. M0 is the lowest bit8
K4M0M0–M1516
K8M0M0–M3132
K2Y0Y0–Y78
K2X0X0–X78

This is how a number is put onto outputs or read from inputs. “MOV HFF K2Y0” switches on all eight outputs Y0–Y7 at once; “MOV H0 K2Y0” switches them all off.

Data format. Inside an FX PLC, data is stored in binary (BIN), two’s-complement form, and all arithmetic is done in binary. The top bit is the sign bit: 0 for positive, 1 for negative. For more precise work the FX2N family also offers binary and decimal floating-point arithmetic.

Indexing. In transfer and compare instructions an index register V or Z modifies the address of an operand, and is used just like an ordinary data register.

LD    X0
DMOVP D10Z0  D12      if Z0 = 5:  (D16, D15)  →  (D13, D12)

Different FX models support different ranges. The low-end FX0S has few applied instructions; the FX2N has nearly all. The grouping by function number is the thing to learn: it tells you where to look.

FNCGroupInstructions

Of these, the FX1N has six move-and-compare instructions and only four of the rotate-and-shift group (SFTR, SFTL, SFWR, SFRD). It has integer arithmetic only; floating-point instructions are on the FX2N.

worked.q: Explain every part of the instruction “DMOVP D10 D12”, driven by X0.
worked.s: D in front: 32-bit. MOV: move. P behind: pulse execution, once on the rising edge of X0. Source: D10, meaning the pair (D11, D10). Destination: D12, meaning the pair (D13, D12). So when X0 goes OFF → ON, the 32-bit number in D11 and D10 is copied into D13 and D12, once.

worked.q: Which devices does K3M10 stand for, and how many bits is that?
worked.s: Three four-bit units starting at M10: M10 to M21, 12 bits, with M10 the lowest bit.

worked.q: The instruction “MOV H0F K2Y0” is executed. Which outputs are on?
worked.s: H0F is binary 0000 1111. K2Y0 is Y7 … Y0, with Y0 the lowest bit. So Y0, Y1, Y2 and Y3 are on and Y4–Y7 are off.

worked.q: A button on X1 drives “INC D0” in continuous form. The scan time is 10 ms and the button is held for 0.5 s. By about how much does D0 rise? How is it fixed?
worked.s: The instruction runs on every scan: 0.5 s ÷ 0.010 s = about 50 times, so D0 rises by about 50. Use the pulse form INCP D0, which adds 1 once per press.

worked.q: In which function-number group would you look for (a) an instruction to read a special analog module, (b) one to light a seven-segment display, (c) one to skip part of the program?
worked.s: (a) FNC 70–79, external I/O devices: FROM and TO. (b) FNC 70–79 as well: SEGD or SEGL. (c) FNC 00–09, program flow: CJ.

A P after the mnemonic means ___ execution.

Inside the PLC, numbers are stored in binary two’s-___ form.
[S] is the source operand and [D] is the ___ operand.

sections.h: What the flow instructions are for
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 9, “Function instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. Program fragments are short listings I wrote to match the book’s explanations. These are Mitsubishi FX applied instructions; which ones exist depends on the model, so check the manual of the PLC you are using.

The program-flow instructions (FNC00–FNC09) control the order in which the program is executed. Within one scan:

  • a jump makes the program skip over, or go across to, a section, so that sections can be selected;
  • a subroutine instruction calls a section that stands apart;
  • a loop instruction repeats a particular section several times;
  • interrupt instructions deal with subroutine calls caused by an interrupt signal.

They affect both the flow and the content of what is executed. They matter for arranging the structure of a program sensibly, for getting more out of it, and for certain programming techniques.

NameMnemonicFNCOperandSteps
Conditional jumpCJ, CJP00 (16-bit)Pointer P0–P127. P63 means END and needs no label. The pointer number may be indexedCJ: 3 · the label P: 1

Meaning. In every scan in which the jump condition is satisfied, the PLC no longer scans the program between the jump instruction and the pointer. It goes straight to the section whose entry is the pointer label and carries on from there. When the condition is no longer satisfied, the jump stops.

      LD   X0
      CJ   P5         X0 on: jump from here ...
      LD   X10
      OUT  Y10        (skipped while X0 is on)
P5    LD   X20        ... to here
      OUT  Y20

Rules for CJ.

  1. A jump selects sections of program. So if the same coil appears in two sections that can never be executed in the same scan because of the jump, it is not treated as a double coil.
  2. Several jumps may use the same label. But one jump may not have two labels: the same label must not appear twice in a program.
  3. The label is normally placed after its jump. It may be placed before. In that case take care: if jumping backwards makes the section run longer than the watchdog setting, an error results.
  4. CJP is the pulse form: the jump is made for one scan only. With M8000 as the condition, the jump becomes unconditional.
  5. Even if the drive conditions in the skipped section change, its coils (its results) keep the state they had before the jump.
  6. During a jump, timers and counters stop working, and carry on when the jump ends. But timers and counters that work by interrupt, such as T192–T199 and the high-speed counters C235–C255, go on running whether skipped or not.
  7. If the RST for a retentive timer or a counter is outside the skipped area, the reset still works even though the timer or counter coil itself is being skipped.

1 · Run an initialisation section once only.

      LD   M8000
      PLS  M0         M0 is on for the first scan only
      LDI  M0
      CJ   P5         from the second scan on, skip the next section
      ...             initialisation program
P5    ...             working program

In the first scan M0 is on, so its NC contact is open and CJ P5 is not executed: the initialisation program runs, then the working program. From the second scan on, M0 is off, the jump is taken and the initialisation program is passed over.

2 · Switch between manual and automatic programs.

      LD   X1
      CJ   P0         X1 on: skip the automatic program
      ...             automatic program
      LDI  X1
      CJ   P63        X1 off: jump to END, skipping the manual program
P0    ...             manual program
      END

X1 ON: the automatic program is jumped over and the manual program at P0 is executed. X1 OFF: the automatic program is executed, then the jump to P63 (END) skips the manual program.

Because only one of the two sections is ever scanned, the same outputs can be programmed in both without a double-coil problem. This is the usual way to give a machine manual and automatic modes.

NameMnemonicFNCOperandSteps
Subroutine callCALL, CALLP01 (16-bit)Pointer P0–P62, P64–P127. Nesting 5 levels. The pointer may be indexed3 · the label P: 1
Subroutine returnSRET02None1
Main program endFEND06None1

A subroutine is a relatively independent piece of program written for one particular control purpose. To tell it from the main program, the rule is: main program first, subroutines after it, with the main-program-end instruction FEND separating the two.

      LD   X0
      CALL P20        X0 on: run subroutine P20, then come back here
      ...             rest of the main program
      FEND            end of the main program
P20   ...             subroutine P20
      SRET            return to the step after the CALL
      END
  • The CALL is in the main program. X0 is the condition for running the subroutine: when X0 is ON, the subroutine labelled P20 is executed.
  • The subroutine is placed after FEND. Everything between the label P20 and SRET is the subroutine.
  • With several subroutines, write them one after another after FEND, each with its own label.
  • A label must not be repeated, and must not be the same as a label used by a CJ instruction.
  • Subroutines can call other subroutines, up to 5 levels deep.

FEND marks the end of the main program. On reaching it the PLC does its input and output processing, refreshes the watchdog timer, and returns to step 0.

  • Subroutines and interrupt routines go after FEND.
  • They must be written between FEND and END, otherwise an error results.

Subroutine or jump? A jump chooses whether a section runs. A subroutine lets the same section be used from several places, and keeps the main program short and readable.

NameMnemonicFNCOperandSteps
Interrupt returnIRET03None1
Enable interruptsEI04None1
Disable interruptsDI05None1

An interrupt routine is a kind of subroutine. Like the others it is placed after FEND. It starts at an interrupt pointer (such as I001) and ends at IRET. It is not called by the program: it is run when its interrupt occurs.

      EI              from here interrupts are allowed
      ...             main program: the section where interrupts may occur
      DI              from here they are not
      ...
      FEND
I001  ...             interrupt routine for input X0, rising edge
      IRET
      END
  • The part of the main program between EI and DI is the section in which interrupts are allowed.
  • If the main program has several interrupt routines, each interrupt label together with the nearest IRET after it forms one routine.
  1. If several interrupts occur one after another, they are taken in the order they occur. If several sources signal at the same moment, the lower the pointer number, the higher the priority.
  2. Turning M8050–M8058 ON disables the corresponding interrupts I0□□–I8□□. M8059 ON disables all counter interrupts.
  3. If interrupts never need to be disabled, use EI alone; DI is not required.
  4. While one interrupt routine is running, other interrupts are disabled, unless EI and DI are written inside the routine, which allows two levels of nesting.

Why interrupts at all? The scan sees an input only once per cycle. An interrupt input makes the PLC drop what it is doing at once and deal with an event that cannot wait, such as a registration mark on fast-moving material.

NameMnemonicFNCOperandSteps
Watchdog timer refreshWDT, WDTP07None1
Loop startFOR08 (16-bit)n: K, H, KnX, KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, Z. Nesting 5 levels3
Loop endNEXT09None1

The watchdog. The PLC has a watchdog (monitoring) timer. Its default setting on the FX is 200 ms, and it can be changed through D8000. It is restarted at the end of every scan. If a scan (from step 0 to END or FEND) takes longer than 200 ms, the watchdog times out: the CPU-E error lamp lights and the PLC stops. This protects the plant against a program that has hung.

WDT refreshes the watchdog from inside the program. If a program really does need longer, put WDT part-way through it. A program taking 240 ms, for example, is split by one WDT into two parts of 120 ms each, neither of which exceeds the limit.

  • If a later FOR–NEXT loop might run longer than the watchdog time, put WDT inside the loop.
  • If a CJ jumps backwards to a label placed before it, the program between them can be executed over and over, long enough to exceed the watchdog time. Put WDT between the CJ and its label.

The loop. FOR and NEXT always come as a pair. The program between them is executed n times within one scan, and then the program after NEXT continues.

FOR   K5              outer loop: 5 times
  FOR   D0Z0          inner loop: the number held in D0Z0
    ...               this section runs  n(inner) x 5  times
  NEXT
  ...                 this section runs 5 times
NEXT
  • n is from 1 to 32 767. If n is between −32 767 and 0 it is treated as 1.
  • Loops may be nested up to 5 levels on the FX2N.
  • A CJ can be used to jump out of a loop before it has finished.
  • FOR must come before NEXT, and NEXT before FEND and END, or an error results.

Loops suit operations that must be repeated, such as a weighted sum over a number of sampled values. Remember that the whole loop runs inside one scan: a long loop lengthens the scan.

terms: 允许中断 / 禁止中断

worked.q: After a jump has taken place, does the CPU still scan the section that was jumped over and execute it line by line? What state are the output relays, timers and counters in that section left in? (Exercise 9.1)
worked.s: No: the skipped section is not scanned or executed. Its output relays keep the state they had just before the jump, even if their drive conditions change. Its timers and counters stop where they are and resume when the jump ends, except interrupt-driven ones (T192–T199 and the high-speed counters C235–C255), which keep running. An RST placed outside the skipped section still resets a counter or retentive timer inside it.

worked.q: An alarm clock has one bell schedule for spring and winter and another for summer and autumn. Give two program structures that arrange the two schedules. (Exercise 9.2)
worked.s: Let X0 be a season switch. Structure 1, jumps: LD X0 · CJ P0 · (spring–winter schedule) · LDI X0 · CJ P63 · P0 · (summer–autumn schedule) · END. Only one schedule is scanned, so both may drive the same bell output. Structure 2, subroutines: main program LDI X0 · CALL P1 · LD X0 · CALL P2 · FEND; then P1 · (spring–winter schedule) · SRET · P2 · (summer–autumn schedule) · SRET · END.

worked.q: A program takes about 320 ms to scan. What happens, and what is the least that must be done?
worked.s: The watchdog is set to 200 ms by default, so it times out: the CPU-E lamp lights and the PLC stops. Insert WDT instructions so that no stretch between refreshes exceeds 200 ms. Two WDTs dividing the program into three parts of about 107 ms each would do; one WDT would leave two parts of 160 ms, which also passes. (Or raise the setting in D8000.)

worked.q: How many times is the innermost section executed in one scan by: FOR K4 · FOR K6 · (section) · NEXT · NEXT?
Two interrupt requests, I001 and I201, arrive at exactly the same instant. Which is served first? How would you disable I201 alone?
worked.s: I001: the lower the pointer number, the higher the priority. To disable interrupt I20□ alone, turn on special relay M8052.

topics.title: Move, Compare, Convert and Arithmetic Instructions, with Two Worked Machines
topics.zh: 传送、比较、变换和四则运算指令，以及两个应用实例

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 9, “Function instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. Program fragments are short listings I wrote to match the book’s explanations. These are Mitsubishi FX applied instructions; which ones exist depends on the model, so check the manual of the PLC you are using.

NameMnemonicFNCSourcesDestinationSteps
CompareCMP, CMPP10 (16/32)[S1·] [S2·]: K, H, KnX, KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, Z[D·]: Y, M, S: three consecutive bits7 · 32-bit: 13
Zone compareZCP, ZCPP11 (16/32)[S1·] [S2·] [S·]: as above[D·]: Y, M, S: three consecutive bits9 · 32-bit: 17

CMP compares source 1 with source 2 and shows the result on three bits, starting at the destination.

LD   X1
CMP  K100  C20  M0

  K100 >  C20   →  M0 on
  K100 =  C20   →  M1 on
  K100 <  C20   →  M2 on
  • You name only M0; the instruction uses M0, M1 and M2. Do not use those three for anything else.
  • Read it as “first compared with second”: M0 is “first is greater”.
  • When X1 goes off the instruction is not executed, and M0–M2 keep the states they had. To clear them use RST or ZRST.
  • The comparison is algebraic, with sign: −5 is less than 2. All source data is treated as binary.
  • An error results if operands are missing, if the wrong kind of device is used as the destination (X, D, T or C), or if a device number is out of range.

ZCP compares one value with a zone between a lower and an upper limit.

LD   X0
ZCP  K100  K150  C20  M10

  C20 < K100            →  M10 on
  K100 ≤ C20 ≤ K150     →  M11 on
  C20 > K150            →  M12 on
  • The lower limit [S1] must not be greater than the upper limit [S2].
  • All data is treated as binary values, and the three bits again hold their state when the instruction is not executed.

NameMnemonicFNCSourceDestinationSteps
MoveMOV, MOVP12 (16/32)K, H, KnX, KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, ZKnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, Z5 · 32-bit: 9
Block moveBMOV, BMOVP15 (16)KnX, KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, DKnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, Z · n: K, H, up to 5127
Binary → BCDBCD, BCDP18 (16/32)KnX, KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, ZKnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, Z5 · 32-bit: 9
BCD → binaryBIN, BINP19 (16/32)as BCDas BCD5 · 32-bit: 9

MOV sends the data of the source to the destination: [S] → [D]. “LD X0 · MOV K150 D20”: while X0 is on, the constant 150 is sent to D20. The constant is converted to binary automatically. When X0 goes off, the instruction is not executed and D20 keeps its data.

BMOV sends a block of n data words, starting at the source, to n words starting at the destination.

LD    X0
BMOV  D10  D9  K3       D10 → D9,  D11 → D10,  D12 → D11

When source and destination overlap, as here, the PLC chooses the order of copying automatically so that no word is overwritten before it has been read. If the devices run past the permitted range, only those inside it are transferred.

BCD converts the binary number in the source to BCD code and sends it to the destination. BIN is the reverse: it converts a BCD number in the source to binary.

LD   X0
BCD  D10   K2Y0         binary in D10  →  two BCD digits on Y7…Y0 (to a display)
LD   X1
BIN  K2X0  D13          two BCD digits on X7…X0 (from thumbwheels)  →  binary in D13
  • Why they are needed. The PLC calculates in binary. A seven-segment display or a thumbwheel switch works one decimal digit at a time, four bits per digit: that is BCD. BCD goes on the way out to a display, BIN on the way in from a switch.
  • A 16-bit BCD result must lie in 0–9999; a 32-bit one in 0–99 999 999. Outside that an error results.

sections.h: What moving and comparing are used for
sections.b:
1. Giving the program its starting data. A control program always needs initial data. It can be read from devices on the input ports and moved into internal registers; or it can be set by the program, moving constants straight into registers; or data stored somewhere in the PLC is moved to the working registers by an initialisation routine when the program starts.
  2. Managing data inside the PLC. In calculation, moving data about is unavoidable. A calculation may involve several working registers, and data has to pass between them. It may produce intermediate results that have to be parked somewhere suitable. Sometimes data has to be backed up. In any program that calculates, data management matters; so does conversion between binary and BCD.
  3. Sending results to the output ports. Results in the end control actuators through the outputs, or are displayed, or become working data for other equipment. Discrete devices on the outputs can be treated as a group: send the right number to the group, according to the state each port should take, and all the devices are controlled at once.
  4. Setting control points. On site, a particular value or range of a physical quantity often serves as a control point: switch on a heater below so many degrees, give an alarm when a speed is above or below a band. As a control “gate”, the compare instruction appears constantly in industrial programs.

sections.h: Machine 1: a feed car serving eight stations
sections.b:
Requirement. A workshop has 8 workstations. A feed car runs back and forth between them. Each station has an arrival switch SQ and a call button SB. At the start the car must be standing at one of the eight arrival switches. A run/stop switch QS controls the system.

  1. If the number of the station where the car is standing is greater than the number of the calling button, the car moves left and stops at the calling station.
  2. If it is smaller, the car moves right and stops at the calling station.
  3. If they are the same, the car stays where it is.
InputDeviceInputDeviceOutputDevice
X0–X7SQ0–SQ7: arrival at stations 0–7X10–X17SB0–SB7: call from stations 0–7Y0KM1: motor forward, car moves right
X20QS: run/stop switchY1KM2: motor reverse, car moves left

Call the car’s present station m and the calling station n. The requirement becomes: m > n, go left until SQn operates; m < n, go right until SQn operates; m = n, stay.

LD   X0                LD   X10
MOV  K0  D128          MOV  K0  D129
LD   X1                LD   X11
MOV  K1  D128          MOV  K1  D129
 ...                    ...
LD   X7                LD   X17
MOV  K7  D128          MOV  K7  D129
        position m              call n

LD   X20
CMP  D128  D129  M0       m > n: M0     m = n: M1     m < n: M2
LD   X20
AND  M0
ANI  M1
ANI  Y0
OUT  Y1                   car to the left
LD   X20
AND  M2
ANI  M1
ANI  Y1
OUT  Y0                   car to the right

How it works. The car’s present position is stored as a number in D128, and the calling station’s number in D129. Comparing the two decides the direction, and tells the car when it has arrived: as the car reaches station n, its arrival switch writes n into D128, the comparison becomes “equal”, M1 comes on and both outputs drop.

D128 and D129 are latched registers. So after a power cut and restart, the system returns automatically to the state it was in before the cut.

Sixteen MOV instructions is a lot of program for one idea. The next topic replaces them with two ENCO instructions.

sections.h: ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, INC, DEC and the logic instructions
sections.b:
A PLC has two kinds of arithmetic. Integer arithmetic has simple instructions, but the data must be whole numbers: anything else has to be made whole first, and a division gives a quotient and a remainder. For calculations needing high accuracy with integers, the parts before and after the decimal point have to be worked out separately and combined, and a division needs several further operations on the remainder, which makes the program tedious. Real arithmetic is floating-point and highly accurate. The FX1N has integer arithmetic only; the FX2N also has real arithmetic.

NameMnemonicFNCDoesSteps
AddADD, ADDP20 (16/32)[S1] + [S2] → [D]7 · 32-bit: 13
SubtractSUB, SUBP21 (16/32)[S1] − [S2] → [D]7 · 13
MultiplyMUL, MULP22 (16/32)[S1] × [S2] → [D], double length7 · 13
DivideDIV, DIVP23 (16/32)[S1] ÷ [S2] → quotient in [D], remainder in the next device7 · 13
Add 1INC, INCP24 (16/32)[D] + 1 → [D]3 · 5
Subtract 1DEC, DECP25 (16/32)[D] − 1 → [D]3 · 5
Word ANDWAND, WANDP26 (16/32)Bit-by-bit AND of [S1] and [S2] → [D]7 · 13
Word ORWOR, WORP27 (16/32)Bit-by-bit OR7 · 13
Word exclusive ORWXOR, WXORP28 (16/32)Bit-by-bit exclusive OR7 · 13

ADD and SUB. “ADD D0 D1 D2”: [D0] + [D1] → [D2]. The arithmetic is algebraic: 2 + (−3) = −1.

FlagSet when
M8020 zeroThe result is 0
M8022 carryThe result is above 32 767 (16-bit) or 2 147 483 647 (32-bit)
M8021 borrowThe result is below −32 767 (16-bit) or −2 147 483 647 (32-bit)
  • In 32-bit work the device named is the low 16 bits and the next device the high 16 bits.
  • Source and destination may be the same device. But then, with the continuous form ADD or DADD, the result changes on every scan. Use ADDP.

MUL. The product is twice as long as the factors.

  • 16-bit: “MUL D0 D1 D2” gives [D0] × [D1] → (D3, D2), a 32-bit product. If [D0] = 10 and [D1] = −10, then (D3, D2) = −100. The top bit is the sign: 0 positive, 1 negative.
  • 32-bit: “DMUL D0 D2 D4” gives (D1, D0) × (D3, D2) → (D7, D6, D5, D4), a 64-bit product.
  • If a group of bit devices is the destination, only the low 32 bits of a 64-bit result can be obtained. Move the data into word devices first.
  • Even in word devices a 64-bit result cannot be monitored as one number, only as its upper and lower halves. In a 32-bit operation Z cannot be the destination.

DIV. [S1] is the dividend and [S2] the divisor. The quotient goes to [D] and the remainder to the device after it.

  • 16-bit: “DIV D0 D1 D2”. If [D0] = 23 and [D1] = 4, then [D2] = 5 and [D3] = 3.
  • 32-bit: “DDIV D0 D2 D4”: (D1, D0) ÷ (D3, D2); quotient in (D5, D4), remainder in (D7, D6).
  • A divisor of 0 is an operation error and the instruction is not executed.
  • If a group of bit devices is the destination, the remainder is not obtained.
  • The top bits of quotient and remainder are sign bits. If either the dividend or the divisor is negative, the quotient is negative. If the dividend is negative, the remainder is negative.

INC and DEC. “INCP D0”: when the condition rises, the binary number in D0 is increased by 1. In the continuous form it is increased every scan.

  • They set no flags. In 16-bit work +32 767 plus 1 becomes −32 768; in 32-bit work +2 147 483 647 plus 1 becomes −2 147 483 648. Likewise −32 768 minus 1 becomes +32 767. The counter simply wraps round.

WAND, WOR, WXOR work on each pair of corresponding bits. AND with a mask clears chosen bits (WAND with H00FF keeps the low byte). OR sets chosen bits. Exclusive OR inverts chosen bits, and also shows which bits differ between two words.

Requirement.

  1. The machine takes 1-yuan, 5-yuan and 10-yuan coins. After putting the coins in, the customer presses confirm.
  2. If the total is 12 yuan or more, the food lamp lights. If it is 15 yuan or more, both the food and the drink lamps light.
  3. With the food lamp lit, pressing the food button selects food; pressing buy confirms. The food lamp goes out, the delivery lamp lights to show the goods being delivered, and after a while it goes out.
  4. The same for a drink, with the drink button.
  5. If the total is more than the price, the lamp at the coin-return slot lights to show that change is being given. When change has been given, the lamp goes out and the machine waits for the next sale.
InputDeviceOutputDevice
X01-yuan coinY0Change output
X15-yuan coinY1Delivery output
X210-yuan coinY2Food lamp
X3Food selectY3Drink lamp
X4Drink select
X5Buy
X6Confirm

The heart of the program is three ideas, each one instruction you have just met.

LD    M8002
ZRST  Y0   Y3              reset at power-up

LD    X0
ADDP  K1   D0   D0         a 1-yuan coin:  D0 = D0 + 1
LD    X1
ADDP  K5   D0   D0         a 5-yuan coin:  D0 = D0 + 5
LD    X2
ADDP  K10  D0   D0         a 10-yuan coin: D0 = D0 + 10

LD    X6                   confirm
CMP   K12  D0   M0         is the total at least 12?   (M1: equal, M2: 12 < total)
CMP   K15  D0   M3         is the total at least 15?   (M4: equal, M5: 15 < total)

LD    X3                   food chosen
SUBP  D0   K12  D1         change = total − 12
LD    X4                   drink chosen
SUBP  D0   K15  D1         change = total − 15
  • Totalling the money: ADDP with the same register as source and destination. Each coin adds its value to D0. The P is essential: without it the coin would be added again on every scan while its sensor was on.
  • Deciding what may be bought: CMP against the prices. “12 ≤ total” is “M1 OR M2”, which becomes the flag for the food lamp. “15 ≤ total” is “M4 OR M5”, the flag for the drink lamp.
  • Working out the change: SUBP. The difference goes into D1. A further compare, of 0 with D1, decides whether there is any change to give.

The rest of the book’s program is self-holding and interlock logic around these: flags that remember which item was selected, the buy button driving the delivery output Y1 for a time set by a timer, the change lamp Y0 flashing through M8013 for a time that depends on the amount of change (the book multiplies the change by a constant with MULP to get the timer’s set value), and finally ZRST instructions that clear the registers and flags for the next customer.

terms: 逻辑字与 / 或 / 异或

worked.q: Use CMP to do this: X0 is a pulse input. When the number of pulses is greater than 5, Y1 is ON; otherwise Y0 is ON. (Exercise 9.4)
worked.s: Count the pulses, then compare. LD X0 · OUT C0 K100 (a set value larger than will be needed). LD M8000 · CMP K5 C0 M0. Now M0 is “5 > count”, M1 is “5 = count” and M2 is “5 < count”. LD M2 · OUT Y1. LD M0 · OR M1 · OUT Y0. Add LD X1 · RST C0 to start again.

worked.q: A control program has to calculate y = x ÷ 20 − 10, where x is the binary number in D0 and the result y is kept in D1. Do it with the arithmetic instructions. (Exercise 9.6)
worked.s: LD X0 · DIVP D0 K20 D2 · SUBP D2 K10 D1. The division puts the quotient in D2 and the remainder in D3; the subtraction takes 10 from the quotient and stores it in D1. Check with x = 460: 460 ÷ 20 = 23, remainder 0; 23 − 10 = 13. This is integer arithmetic, so the remainder is discarded: x = 470 gives 23 as well.

worked.q: [D0] = 250 and [D1] = 400. After “MUL D0 D1 D2”, where is the result and what is it? Why are two registers needed?
worked.s: 250 × 400 = 100 000, held as a 32-bit number in (D3, D2). A single 16-bit register holds at most 32 767, and the product of two 16-bit numbers can need up to 32 bits.

worked.q: [D0] = 47 and [D1] = 6. What does “DIV D0 D1 D10” leave, and where?
worked.s: 47 ÷ 6 = 7 remainder 5. Quotient 7 in D10, remainder 5 in D11.

worked.q: A temperature value is in D5. A heater must be on below 180, off above 200, and an alarm must sound above 200. Use one instruction for the comparison.
worked.s: LD M8000 · ZCP K180 K200 D5 M20. M20 is on below 180: LD M20 · SET Y0 (heater on). M22 is on above 200: LD M22 · RST Y0 (heater off) and LD M22 · OUT Y1 (alarm). Between 180 and 200 only M21 is on and the heater keeps the state it had, which gives a dead band.

worked.q: A two-digit thumbwheel switch on X0–X7 shows 37. What is on the inputs, and which instruction puts the number 37 into D0?
worked.s: BCD: one digit per four bits. 3 is 0011 and 7 is 0111, so X7…X0 = 0011 0111. Read as plain binary that would be 55, which is wrong. Use BIN K2X0 D0, which converts the BCD digits to the binary number 37.

In “CMP K100 C20 M0”, M1 is on when the two values are ___.
The product of a 16-bit MUL is ___ bits long.

The zero flag is special relay ___.
