topics.title: Shift, FIFO, Zone Reset, Decode and Encode Instructions
topics.zh: 移位、先入先出、区间复位、解码和编码指令

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 9, “Function instructions”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words. Program fragments are short listings I wrote to match the book’s explanations. These are Mitsubishi FX applied instructions; which ones exist depends on the model, so check the manual of the PLC you are using.

The FX rotate-and-shift group contains bit shifts, rotations, word shifts and first-in-first-out (FIFO) instructions.

KindWhat it doesVariants
RotateThe bits move round within the word or double word: a circular movement. Nothing is lostWith or without the carry flag; left or right
Shift (non-circular)A straight-line movement. The bits shifted out are lost, and the bits shifted in come from other dataLeft or right
Word shiftMoves whole words, to adjust where word data sits in memoryLeft or right
FIFOManages a queue of dataWrite and read

Shifts can be used to multiply data by 2, to form new data, or to form a kind of control switch that steps along. The FX1N has only four of the group: SFTR, SFTL, SFWR and SFRD.

NameMnemonicFNC[S·][D·]n1n2Steps
Bit shift rightSFTR, SFTRP34 (16)X, Y, M, SY, M, SK, H: length of the shift registerK, H: bits moved each time9
Bit shift leftSFTL, SFTLP35 (16)X, Y, M, SY, M, SK, HK, H9

These shift a register of n1 bits, starting at [D], by n2 bits to the right or left, taking n2 new bits from [S].

Shift right: “SFTRP X0 M0 K8 K2”. The register is M7…M0 (8 bits). Each execution moves everything 2 places towards the low end.

M7M6M5M4M3M2M1M0
Beforehgfedcba
AfterX1X0hgfedc

M1 and M0 (b, a) overflow and are lost. X1 and X0 enter at the high end.

Shift left: “SFTLP X0 M0 K8 K2”. Everything moves 2 places towards the high end.

M7M6M5M4M3M2M1M0
Beforehgfedcba
AfterfedcbaX1X0

M7 and M6 (h, g) overflow and are lost. X1 and X0 enter at the low end.

  • With the pulse form the shift happens once, when the condition goes OFF → ON. With the continuous form the shift is done on every scan. Take great care: a shift almost always needs the P form, or an edge contact in front of it.
  • To shift one lamp along a row, use n2 = 1 and feed a 1 in once, then 0s. To fill a row progressively, feed 1s in continuously (source M8000, which is always on). To empty it progressively, feed 0s in (source M8001, always off).

sections.h: SFWR and SFRD: a first-in-first-out queue
sections.b:
NameMnemonicFNC[S·][D·]nSteps
Shift writeSFWR, SFWRP38 (16)K, H, KnX, KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, ZKnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, DK, H: 2 ≤ n ≤ 5127
Shift readSFRD, SFRDP39 (16)KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, DKnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, ZK, H: 2 ≤ n ≤ 5127

These two manage data on a first-in, first-out basis: the first item written is the first read out. A block of n registers is used. The first register is a pointer that counts how many items are stored; the other n − 1 hold the data.

SFWR writes. “SFWRP D10 D0 K8”: the block is D0–D7. D0 is the pointer and must be cleared to 0 beforehand.

  • First rise of the condition: the contents of D10 are stored in D1, and D0 becomes 1.
  • Change D10, then a second rise: D10 is stored in D2, and D0 becomes 2.
  • And so on, filling from the right. The pointer D0 always shows how many items are stored.
  • If the pointer would exceed n − 1, nothing is done and the carry flag M8022 comes on: the queue is full.
  • With the continuous form SFWR, a value is stored on every scan.

SFRD reads. “SFRDP D0 D20 K8”: the same block D0–D7.

  • On each rise of the condition, the contents of D1 are sent to D20, the pointer D0 is reduced by 1, and the data in D2–D7 moves one word to the right.
  • Data is always read from D1: the oldest item.
  • With the continuous form the data moves right one word on every scan.
  • When the pointer is 0 nothing is done and the zero flag M8020 comes on: the queue is empty.

A use. Products pass a reading station in order and leave at a second station some way along. As each arrives its code is written into the queue. As each reaches the exit, its code is read out, and it is the right one, because the products are still in the same order.

The board. Eight LED channels a–h on outputs Y0–Y7. The upper eight form a ring, the lower eight a straight line; upper and lower are driven together. One control switch K1 on X0.

Requirement. After the switch is turned on: (a) light up quickly in order, then go out in order; (b) light up quickly in reverse order, then all go out; (c) light up slowly in order, then go out in reverse order; (d) flash quickly; (e) flash slowly; (f) the system repeats by itself. When the switch is turned off everything goes out and is reset.

Analysis. Shift left (SFTL) gives lighting and extinguishing in forward order. Shift right (SFTR) gives reverse order. Move (MOV) gives flashing. Make each kind of action a state and run them as a single-sequence loop. Zone reset (ZRST) resets all the states.

StateClockInstruction on each clock pulseEffectLeaves the state when
S0M8012, 0.1 sSFTL M8000 Y0 K8 K1 (shift a 1 in at the low end)Fast: light in orderY7 is on
S20M8012SFTL M8001 Y0 K8 K1 (shift a 0 in at the low end)Fast: go out in orderY7 is off
S21M8012SFTR M8000 Y0 K8 K1 (shift a 1 in at the high end)Fast: light in reverse order; when Y0 lights, wait 1 s (T1), then ZRST Y0 Y7T1
S22M8013, 1 sSFTL M8000 Y0 K8 K1Slow: light in order; then wait 1 s (T2)T2
S23M8013SFTR M8001 Y0 K8 K1 (shift a 0 in at the high end)Slow: go out in reverse orderY0 is off
S24M8012MOV HFF K2Y0 while the clock is on · MOV H0 K2Y0 while it is offFast flashing for 3 s (T3), then ZRST Y0 Y7T3
S25M8013MOV HFF K2Y0 / MOV H0 K2Y0Slow flashing for 5 s (T4), then ZRST Y0 Y7T4 → back to S0
LDI   X0                   switch off ...
OR    M8002                ... or first scan
ZRST  S0   S25             reset every state
ZRST  Y0   Y7              all lamps out
LD    X0
SET   S0                   switch on: start

STL   S0
LDP   M8012                once per clock pulse
SFTL  M8000  Y0  K8  K1    shift a 1 in: one more lamp lights
LD    Y7                   the last lamp is on
SET   S20
 ...
RET
END

Why this example is worth studying.

  • A whole row of outputs is handled as one piece of data (Y0–Y7 as a shift register, or K2Y0 as a number). Without shift and move instructions, each lamp would need its own rungs.
  • M8000 and M8001 as sources: a permanent 1 and a permanent 0 to shift in.
  • The clock relays set the speed. The same instruction with M8012 or M8013 gives a fast or a slow effect.
  • The shift must happen once per clock pulse, so the clock contact is an edge contact (or the SFTLP form is used).
  • Applied instructions inside an SFC. The state structure gives the order; the applied instructions do the work in each state.

NameMnemonicFNC[D1·] [D2·]Steps
Zone resetZRST, ZRSTP40 (16)Y, M, S, T, C, D. The number of [D1] must not be greater than the number of [D2]5

Zone reset is also called batch reset. It resets every device from [D1] to [D2] in one instruction.

LD    M8002
ZRST  S0   S127        reset states S0–S127
ZRST  D0   D100        clear registers D0–D100
ZRST  Y0   Y7          switch off outputs Y0–Y7
  • [D1] and [D2] must be the same kind of device, and [D1]’s number must be less than or equal to [D2]’s. If [D1]’s number is the larger, only the device named by [D1] is reset.
  • It is a 16-bit instruction, but 32-bit counters may be named in [D1] and [D2]. They may not be mixed: a 16-bit counter in [D1] with a 32-bit counter in [D2] is not allowed.
  • Its commonest use is initialising a data area, or resetting all the states of an SFC at power-up or on an emergency stop.

sections.h: DECO and ENCO: decode and encode
sections.b:
NameMnemonicFNC[S·][D·]nSteps
DecodeDECO, DECOP41 (16)K, H, X, Y, M, S, T, C, D, V, ZY, M, S, T, C, DK, H: 1 ≤ n ≤ 87
EncodeENCO, ENCOP42 (16)X, Y, M, S, T, C, D, V, ZT, C, D, V, ZK, H: 1 ≤ n ≤ 87

DECO turns a number into a position. It reads an n-bit binary number, call it Q, and switches on bit number Q of the destination. All the other bits are cleared.

LD    X10
DECO  X0  M0  K3       source: X2 X1 X0 (3 bits)     destination: M7…M0 (2³ = 8 bits)

  X2 X1 X0 = 1 0 1   →   Q = 4 + 1 = 5   →   M5 on, all the others off
  X2 X1 X0 = 0 0 0   →   Q = 0           →   M0 on
  • Bit destination (Y, M, S): n = 1 to 8, and 2n destination bits are used. With n = 8 the destination is 2⁸ = 256 bits. n = 0 does nothing; n outside 0–8 is an error.
  • Word destination: “DECO D0 D1 K3” reads the low 3 bits of D0 and sets that bit of D1. If the low bits of D0 are 011, Q = 3 and bit 3 of D1 becomes 1. Here n is at most 4, because a word has 2⁴ = 16 bits.
  • When the drive input is off the instruction is not executed, and the bit that the last decode set stays as it was.
  • In the continuous form it is executed on every scan.

ENCO does the opposite: it turns a position into a number. It looks at 2n bits and writes the position number of the highest bit that is on into the destination.

LD    X3
ENCO  M0  D0  K3       source: M7…M0 (2³ = 8 bits)    destination: D0

  M5 is the highest bit that is on   →   D0 = 5
  • Bit source: n = 1 to 8; with n = 8 the source is 256 bits long.
  • Word source: “ENCO D1 D0 K3” looks at the low 2³ = 8 bits of D1. If the highest 1 among them is bit 6, then D0 = 6. Here n is 1 to 4.
  • If only bit 0 of the source is 1, the destination gets 0. If no bit at all is 1, an operation error results.
  • When the drive input is off the last result is kept.

The feed car again. The sixteen MOV instructions of the earlier program did nothing but turn “which switch is on” into a number. That is exactly what ENCO does.

LD    X20
ENCO  X0   D128  K3       which of X0–X7 is on  →  position m
ENCO  X10  D129  K3       which of X10–X17 is on →  call n
CMP   D128 D129  M0       then the two output rungs, as before

Three instructions replace seventeen. That is the point of the applied instructions: one of them does the work of a page of contacts.

worked.q: M7…M0 contain 0011 0101 (M7 on the left). X0 is ON. What do they contain after one execution of “SFTLP X0 M0 K8 K1”? And after one execution of “SFTRP X0 M0 K8 K1” from the same starting pattern?
worked.s: Left: every bit moves one place towards M7, the old M7 is lost and X0 (1) enters at M0: 0110 1011. Right: every bit moves one place towards M0, the old M0 is lost and X0 (1) enters at M7: 1001 1010.

worked.q: A queue uses “SFWRP D10 D0 K5”. How many items can it hold? After three writes of the values 7, 9 and 4, what do D0–D4 contain? What does one “SFRDP D0 D20 K5” then do?
worked.s: n = 5: one pointer and 4 data registers, so 4 items. After three writes: D0 = 3 (pointer), D1 = 7, D2 = 9, D3 = 4, D4 = 0. The read sends D1, the oldest value 7, to D20; the pointer D0 becomes 2; the data moves down one word, so D1 = 9 and D2 = 4.

worked.q: Use SFTL as a shift register to control a flashing sign. Four lamps HL1–HL4 light the four characters. Steps, 1 s each: 1 HL1 · 2 HL2 · 3 HL3 · 4 HL4 · 5 all four · 6 none · 7 all four · 8 none; then repeat. (Exercise 9.7)
worked.s: One solution (mine). Use an eight-bit step register M0–M7 with exactly one bit on, advanced once a second, and build the lamps from the steps. Start: LD M8002 · SET M0. Advance: LDP M8013 · SFTL M7 M0 K8 K1. Taking the source from M7 feeds the bit that leaves the top back in at the bottom, so the single 1 circulates for ever. Lamps: HL1 (Y0) = M0 + M4 + M6. HL2 (Y1) = M1 + M4 + M6. HL3 (Y2) = M2 + M4 + M6. HL4 (Y3) = M3 + M4 + M6. Steps 6 and 8 (M5, M7) light nothing.

worked.q: “DECO D0 M10 K3” is executed with D0 = 6. Which relay comes on? How many relays does the instruction use?
worked.s: M10 is bit 0, so bit 6 is M16. With n = 3 it uses 2³ = 8 relays, M10–M17, and clears the other seven.

worked.q: Use DECO to control a fountain with three groups of jets: group 1 for 1 s, group 2 for 2 s, group 3 for 3 s, all three together for 4 s, all off for 5 s, then repeat. Outline the program. (Exercise 9.9)
worked.s: One solution (mine). Keep a step number in D0 (0 to 4) and decode it: LD M8000 · DECO D0 M0 K3 gives exactly one of M0–M4 on. Outputs: Y0 (group 1) = M0 + M3; Y1 (group 2) = M1 + M3; Y2 (group 3) = M2 + M3; step 4 (M4) is the pause. Timing: each step runs its own timer, LD M0 · OUT T0 K10; LD M1 · OUT T1 K20; LD M2 · OUT T2 K30; LD M3 · OUT T3 K40; LD M4 · OUT T4 K50. Advance: LD T0 · OR T1 · OR T2 · OR T3 · INCP D0. Wrap round: LD T4 · MOVP K0 D0. Start: LD M8002 · MOV K0 D0.

worked.q: In the feed-car program with ENCO, what would happen if two arrival switches were on at once, say X2 and X5?
worked.s: ENCO reports the highest bit that is on, so D128 would be 5 and the car would be taken to be at station 5. On a real machine that would be a fault to detect separately, since the car cannot be in two places.

recap: SFTR shifts towards the ___ end of the register.
In a FIFO data area the first register is the ___.
ZRST resets every device from [D1] to ___.
DECO with n = 3 uses ___ destination bits.
ENCO writes the position of the ___ bit that is on.

topics.title: Programming Tools and the FXGP/WIN-C Workflow
topics.zh: 编程工具和 FXGP/WIN-C 的使用流程

sections.h: What a programming tool does, and the three kinds
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 10, “Programming tools and their use”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words; no screenshots are reproduced. The software described (FXGP/WIN-C, GX Developer, GX Simulator) is old and has been replaced by newer packages. What carries over to any PLC software, including the one in your ITE lab, is the workflow: write, check, download, monitor, test, document.

A PLC needs a special programming tool to write the user program into its user program memory. That tool is called a programmer. It is one of the PLC’s important peripherals. It does two things:

  • it writes, reads and edits the program in the PLC;
  • it checks the program, and monitors, tests and diagnoses the running PLC.
KindDescriptionFX example
Hand-held programmerSmall and light, portable. Works in instruction-list form on a small keypad and displayFX-20P-E
Graphic programmerA more expensive unit with a screen, working directly in ladderGP-80FX-E
Personal computer with programming softwareThe most convenient: programming, monitoring and simulation on a PCMELSEC-F FX series and MELSOFT GX series software

Some of Mitsubishi’s matching touch screens (GOT) also have programming functions.

sections.h: FXGP/WIN-C: what it is and what it needs
sections.b:
FXGP/WIN-C is programming software for the FX series that runs under Windows. With it you can write a PLC program as a ladder diagram, as an instruction list or with SFC symbols, create comment data and set register data. A program you have created can be communicated to the PLC over a serial link, transferred as a file, monitored in operation and put through various tests. It can also be saved as a file and printed.

The system consists of the software itself, the operating manual, the software registration card, an interface unit and a cable.

ItemFor
RS-232C / RS-422 converter, portable typeBetween the PC’s RS-232C port and the PLC’s RS-422 port
RS-232C / RS-422 converter, built-in typeThe same job, fitted inside
RS-232C cables, 3 mPC side: different cables for different PC connectors (25-pin, 14-pin, 9-pin D-type)
RS-422 cable, 1.5 mPLC side, for the smaller FX models
RS-422 cables, 0.3 m and 1.5 mPLC side, for the older FX1, FX2 and FX2C models

The key point is the converter. A PC’s serial port is RS-232C; the PLC’s programming port is RS-422. They cannot be joined directly: the specified converter and cables must be used.

The PC it asked for shows the software’s age: an IBM PC/AT compatible with a 486 processor or better, 8 MB of memory (16 MB recommended), and a display of 800 × 600 in 16 colours or more.

Starting. Installing the software puts an icon on the desktop; double-click it to open. File → Exit closes it. File → New creates a new user program: a dialog asks for the PLC type, and you must choose the model you are actually using before confirming. File → Open opens an existing file. The main window has a title bar, menu bar, tool bar, a function-key bar, a status bar (showing the edit mode, step numbers and so on), and windows for SFC editing, list editing and ladder editing.

Its main functions are ladder editing, instruction-list editing, SFC editing, comment editing, register editing, and file printing, PLC operation, monitoring, testing and help.

OperationMenu pathWhat it does
CutEdit → Block select, then Edit → Cut (Ctrl+X)Removes the selected circuit block and keeps it on the clipboard
PasteEdit → Paste (Ctrl+V)Pastes the block. The data comes from the last cut or copy
Delete lineEdit → Delete line (Ctrl+Delete)Deletes the circuit line the cursor is on
Insert lineEdit → Insert lineInserts a line at the cursor
Device nameEdit → Device nameGives a device a name. Letters, digits and symbols, not more than 8 characters; names may not be duplicated
Device commentEdit → Device commentAttaches a comment to a device. Not more than 50 characters
Coil commentEdit → Coil commentAttaches a comment to a coil or an applied instruction
ContactTools → Contact → the symbol wantedEnters an NO contact, an NC contact, a rising-edge or a falling-edge contact. A dialog asks for the device
CoilTools → CoilEnters an output coil. A dialog asks for the device
FunctionTools → FunctionEnters an applied-instruction box. A dialog asks for the instruction; a “reference” button opens a description for further settings
WireTools → Wire → vertical, horizontal, invert, or deleteDraws vertical and horizontal lines, enters an invert, or deletes a vertical line

Why bother with names and comments? A program is read far more often than it is written, and often by someone else, with the machine stopped and production waiting. “X003” says nothing; “guard closed” says everything. Comment as you write.

sections.h: Finding, replacing, views, and changing a running program
sections.b:
OperationMenu pathWhat it does
Find device nameFind → Device name findSearches for a device name in the text. The cursor moves to it
Find contact or coilFind → Contact / coil findFinds any contact or coil you name
Go to stepFind → Go to stepMoves the cursor to a given program step
Change device numberFind → Change device numberReplaces device addresses. Example: to replace X10–X15 by X20–X25, enter X10 to X15 as the devices to be replaced and X20 as the start of the replacements. Replacement can be one at a time or all at once, and comments and applied-instruction operands can be moved too. Only devices of the same kind can be exchanged
Change bit deviceFind → Change bit deviceSwaps A contacts and B contacts, that is NO and NC, over a chosen range
Ladder viewView → Ladder viewOpens or activates the ladder window
Instruction list viewView → Instruction list viewOpens or activates the list window
Change program while runningPLC → Change program in RUN (Shift + F4)Changes part of the program in a PLC that is running and connected
Ladder monitorMonitor/Test → Start monitorShows the PLC’s operating state on the screen: the display changes from edit mode to monitor mode and shows which contacts and coils are ON

Changing a program in RUN: the conditions. This alters a PLC that is controlling a live machine, so confirm the change carefully first.

  • The PC’s RS-232C port and the PLC must be joined by the specified cable and converter.
  • The PLC’s program memory must be RAM.
  • Only one circuit block can be changed at a time, and it is limited to 127 steps.
  • The block being changed must not contain a high-speed counter instruction or a label.

Monitoring. In ladder monitoring only ON/OFF states are shown. To watch current values, or the set values of registers, timers and counters, use the device registration monitor.

sections.h: Files, printing and transferring to the PLC
sections.b:
OperationMenu pathNotes
New fileFile → New (Ctrl+N)Creates a new application program; choose the target PLC type in the dialog
OpenFile → Open (Ctrl+O)Opens a program from the file list, together with its comment data. A program and its comments under the same file name are collected as one set
SaveFile → Save (Ctrl+S)Saves the program, comments and other data under the same file name. The first time, a “name and save” dialog appears
Save asFile → Save asSets the file name and path. The extension is added automatically
PrintFile → Print (Ctrl+P)Prints the program and comments in an existing format. Comment printing and other conditions are set in a dialog; Cancel or Esc stops it
Print allFile → Print allPrints ladder, instruction list, SFC, register data and other data in one batch, in an order you set

PLC → Transfer. Sends the program between PC and PLC in one batch.

ChoiceDirectionEffect
ReadPLC → PCBrings the program in the PLC into the computer. The program now open is replaced by what is read, so set the PLC type first
WritePC → PLCSends the program in the computer to the PLC
VerifyComparesCompares the program in the computer with the one in the PLC
  • The PC’s RS-232C port and the PLC must be connected with the specified cable and converter.
  • For Write, the PLC must be stopped, and the program must be written with the memory protect of the RAM or EEPROM switched off. Verify afterwards.

Register transfer works the same way for register data: read, write and verify. The PLC type set in the computer must agree with the PLC connected.

PLC memory clear initialises the program and data in the PLC. Three things can be cleared:

  • PLC memory: the program becomes all NOP and the parameters return to their defaults.
  • Data device memory: the values in the data file buffer are set to zero.
  • Bit device memory: X, Y, M, S, T and C are reset.

Special data registers are not cleared.

sections.h: Monitoring, forcing and the options menu
sections.b:
OperationMenu pathWhat it does
Device monitorMonitor/Test → Device monitorOpens a window in which you register the devices to watch, and shows their states and values
Force Y outputMonitor/Test → Force Y outputForces an output terminal ON or OFF. Set the address and ON or OFF, then Run
Force ON/OFFMonitor/Test → Force set / resetForces a bit device set or reset. SET works on X, Y, M, special M, S, T, C. RST works on X, Y, M, special M, S, T, C, D, special D, V, Z. Resetting T or C clears its contact and its current value; for D, V or Z only the current value is cleared
Change current valueMonitor/Test → Change current valueChanges the present value of a word device
Change set valueMonitor/Test → Change set valueChanges the set value of a timer or counter, with the cursor on its output instruction in the monitored circuit. If the set value is given by a data register, or the cursor is on an applied instruction whose operand is D, V or Z, the function works too: then the device number can be changed

Changing a set value works only if the program in the PC agrees with the program in the PLC and the PLC’s memory is RAM or EEPROM, and only while the circuit is being monitored.

Forcing is powerful and dangerous. A forced output drives the real contactor or valve whatever the program says, and bypasses every interlock written in the program. Before forcing anything, know what it will move and make sure nobody is near it.

Options → Program check. Checks the program and shows the result.

  • Syntax check: instruction codes and their format.
  • Double-coil check: repeated use of the same device as an output.
  • Circuit check: faults in the ladder circuit.

An error from the double-coil or circuit check does not necessarily mean the PLC or the machine will misbehave. In particular, a double coil is not always a mistake: in a step-ladder program it is allowed and sometimes used deliberately.

Options → EPROM transfer. Transfers the program to a ROM writer connected to the PC’s RS-232C port: set-up (the transfer format, which must match the writer), read, write and verify. The ROM writer must support RS-232 transfer in the right format.

terms: 读入 / 写出 / 校验

worked.q: List, in order, the steps to take a new ladder program from an empty screen to a running, checked machine.
worked.s: (1) File → New, and choose the right PLC type. (2) Enter the ladder: contacts, coils, functions and wires; add device names and comments. (3) Options → Program check: syntax, double coil, circuit. (4) Save. (5) Connect the PC to the PLC with the proper converter and cable; put the PLC in STOP. (6) PLC → Transfer → Write, then Verify. (7) Put the PLC in RUN and start the monitor. (8) Test each input and output, using device monitor and, with care, forcing. (9) Print the program and comments for the machine’s documents.

worked.q: Why must the PLC be in STOP when a program is written to it, and why verify afterwards?
worked.s: Writing replaces the program in memory. If the PLC were running, the machine would for a moment be controlled by a half-old, half-new program. Verifying compares what is now in the PLC with what is in the computer, so a transfer error or a write-protected memory is caught before the machine is started.

worked.q: A PC’s serial port cannot be plugged straight into an FX PLC’s programming port. Why not, and what is needed?
worked.s: The PC port is RS-232C and the PLC’s programming port is RS-422: different electrical standards. An RS-232C / RS-422 converter with the specified cables is needed.

worked.q: You want to change, without stopping the machine, a rung of 20 steps that contains a jump label. Can the “change program in RUN” function do it?
worked.s: No. The block is small enough (the limit is 127 steps) but it contains a label, and a block containing a label or a high-speed counter instruction cannot be changed in RUN. Stop the PLC and transfer the program normally.

worked.q: The program check reports a double coil on Y3. Is the program wrong?
worked.s: Not necessarily. In an ordinary ladder program a double coil usually is a mistake, because only the last one takes effect. In a step-ladder program, or in sections that jumps prevent from running in the same scan, the same output may properly appear several times. Look at where the two coils are before deciding.

A device name may not be longer than ___ characters.

topics.title: GX Developer, GX Simulator and the MELSOFT Family
topics.zh: GX Developer、GX Simulator 和 MELSOFT 软件家族

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 10, “Programming tools and their use”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words; no screenshots are reproduced. The software described (FXGP/WIN-C, GX Developer, GX Simulator) is old and has been replaced by newer packages. What carries over to any PLC software, including the one in your ITE lab, is the workflow: write, check, download, monitor, test, document.

As equipment becomes more advanced and programs larger, the work of developing a program grows with them. MELSOFT is Mitsubishi’s general name for its integrated factory-automation software, covering design, operation and maintenance. It has three parts.

SeriesJob
GXProgramming the PLC and simulating off-line
GTCreating the screens of a human–machine interface and simulating them off-line
MXRich communication functions, and data sharing with Office, Visual Basic, Visual C++ and other software

Highly integrated, the software gives on one personal computer a simulation and debugging environment combining SCADA, PLC and HMI: debugging without the equipment. Once the system has been designed, the user can go straight to debugging, which greatly shortens the time spent on site.

The GX series consists mainly of GX Developer, for programming the PLC, and GX Simulator, for simulation and debugging.

1. Operating environment. Microsoft Windows 95, 98, 2000, Me and NT Workstation 4.0.
  2. One package for all families. It programs every Mitsubishi MELSEC PLC of the time: the Q, QnA, A, Motion and FX series. A “change PLC type” function lets data already written or being edited be converted for use on a different PLC.
  3. Languages. Besides ladder and instruction list it supports SFC, and structured programming with labels and function blocks.
  4. Standard Windows editing. Cut, copy and paste make it more convenient; data written elsewhere can be reused. Comment data, for example, can be edited beforehand in Word or Excel and pasted straight into the comment window.
  5. Monitoring. It supports device monitoring, monitoring of the buffer memory of special modules, and several other kinds. Using several windows (for example, different programs in the same file) makes monitoring quick and easy. Bit devices can be set and reset, and device values changed, with mouse and keyboard.
  6. Network parameters. Ethernet, MELSECNET/10(H) and CC-Link parameters are set inside it, so no separate network-setting software need be bought. Ethernet and CC-Link parameters that once needed program code are now set on parameter screens, which shortens the program and makes the settings easier to read.
  7. Diagnosis. MELSEC network diagnosis, CC-Link diagnosis, Ethernet diagnosis, PLC self-diagnosis and system monitoring.
  8. Old data is not lost. It reads existing data from the CPU module, and converts data made with the earlier DOS and Windows packages directly into its own format.
  9. On-line programming. Besides off-line programming it supports on-line programming, that is changing the program on line: during commissioning the program can be modified without stopping it. Programs can be uploaded and downloaded through the CPU module directly, or through a network: Ethernet, MELSECNET/10(H), CC-Link, a telephone line.
  10. Password registration protects the program and data in the PLC.

Programming with GX Developer is done in much the same way as with FXGP/WIN-C.

GX Simulator adds a simulation function to the GX Developer package. Besides the Q series it can be used with the CPUs of the A, QnA, Motion and FX series. A sequence program written in GX Developer does not have to be written into a real PLC: it can be simulated on the personal computer. And if the intelligent-function-module package GX Configurator is added, the initial parameter settings and auto-refresh settings of intelligent modules (A/D conversion, D/A conversion, communication modules) can be simulated too.

  1. No PLC needs to be connected. The action of a program can be confirmed at once on the computer on which it was written.
  2. It recognises automatically the PLC type the program was written for (Q, QnA, A, FX, Motion) and starts a virtual CPU.
  3. With simple settings it simulates the mechanical inputs and outputs. For example, one setting can say: “when X0 is OFF and X1 is ON, then 1 s later X2 goes ON”. The simulator behaves as the machine would, so the program can be exercised as if limit switches were really being struck.
  4. Debugging can begin at the design stage. Used together with the program-modularising function of the Q CPU (writing several programs, each for a control purpose, and running them together), debugging can be done module by module, which raises its efficiency and shortens the time spent adjusting on site.
  5. It supports the PLC’s basic and applied instructions.
  6. While simulating, besides watching the ON/OFF states of devices and the present values of numbers, you can force ON/OFF and change present values. ON/OFF states and values can also be shown as a timing chart, so the sequence of the control can be checked.

What simulation is good for, and what it is not. It proves the logic: that the sequence is right, the interlocks work and the timers and counters behave. It cannot prove the wiring, the sensors’ settings, the real speeds of actuators, or electrical noise. Simulate first, then commission on the machine; the first makes the second shorter and safer.

Besides GX Developer and GX Simulator, used for creating, managing, simulating and debugging programs, other packages can run alongside them to make programming and maintenance more efficient.

PackageKindJob
GX ConverterData conversion softwareLets comments created in CSV form (text files, Excel data) be used
GX ConfiguratorSetting and monitoring software for intelligent function modulesMakes it easy to set and monitor the parameters and data of intelligent modules, which simplifies the program. It shows the check of each module in the system at a glance, and helps restore operation quickly after a fault
GX ExplorerProject management toolLike a file browser. From it GX Developer can be started, the PLC’s project data read and written, and PLC diagnosis done
MX LinkBasic communication support toolSupports many forms of connection and communication with the CPU module, and provides a library of special instructions
MX MonitorMonitoring toolStrengthens support for Visual Basic
MX ChartExcel communication support toolExchanges data between the PLC and Microsoft Excel with no extra PLC program

The shape of a modern tool chain. One tool to program, one to simulate, one to configure special modules, one to build operator screens, and tools that pass plant data to office software. Every maker’s software today has the same shape, whatever the names.

worked.q: Name the three parts of the MELSOFT family and the job of each.
worked.s: GX: programming the PLC and off-line simulation. GT: creating human–machine interface screens and simulating them. MX: communication, and sharing data with Office, Visual Basic and Visual C++.

worked.q: A program was written for an FX1N. The machine is to be rebuilt with an FX2N. Must the program be retyped?
worked.s: No. GX Developer’s “change PLC type” function converts data already written to another PLC type. Afterwards check any instructions and device ranges that differ between the two models.

worked.q: You have no PLC at home but want to test a sequence program with three limit switches. How does GX Simulator help?
worked.s: It runs the program on a virtual CPU in the PC. Its input/output simulation settings can stand in for the machine, for example “1 s after Y1 goes on, turn X2 on”, so the limit switches seem to operate at the right moments. The device monitor and the timing chart then show whether the sequence is right.

worked.q: Give three things simulation cannot check, so that on-site commissioning is still needed.
worked.s: (1) The wiring: whether each sensor and actuator is connected to the terminal the program expects. (2) The real behaviour of the machine: actuator speeds, sensor positions and settings, mechanical play. (3) The electrical environment: noise, earthing, voltage drop. Also the timing of real fast signals against the real scan.

worked.q: Which package would you use to set up an analog input module without writing program code for it?
worked.s: GX Configurator, the setting and monitoring software for intelligent function modules.

Changing a program without stopping it is called ___ programming.

topics.title: Expansion Devices, FROM/TO, and the Analog Modules FX2N-2AD and FX2N-2DA
topics.zh: 扩展设备、FROM/TO 指令与模拟量模块 FX2N-2AD、FX2N-2DA

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 11, “Special function modules of the PLC”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words; the conversion graph is redrawn and program fragments are short listings written to match the book’s explanation. Module data are the book’s figures for the Mitsubishi FX2N family. For a real installation use the module’s own manual. This topic sits beside your ITE PLC Chapter 11 (expansion modules and power budget).

The FX series has four kinds of expansion device: the expansion unit, the expansion module, the special function module (special block) and the function expansion board.

  • Expansion units and modules add I/O points (Chapter 6).
  • Special function modules do special jobs: A/D conversion, D/A conversion, high-speed counting, positioning and so on. Their hardware is complete and some have their own CPU. They are mounted outside the base unit.
  • Function expansion boards fit inside the base unit and take no space beside it. They add communication, extra I/O, or analog I/O to the base unit.

The special modules fall into six groups: (1) analog input/output, (2) high-speed counter, (3) positioning, (4) rotary-angle detection, (5) communication interface, (6) human–machine interface.

sections.h: Configuring an FX2N system: four limits
sections.b:
When a system is expanded, first solve the configuration problem. An FX2N system must satisfy all of these:

  1. The system’s total digital I/O must not exceed 256 points.
  2. If special modules are fitted, the digital I/O must satisfy n ≤ 256 − k, where k is the sum of the I/O points that the special modules occupy.
  3. No more than 8 special function modules per base unit.
  4. Current budget. The internal 5 V DC current drawn by all expansion devices must not exceed what the base unit or powered expansion units can supply; and the external 24 V DC current drawn must not exceed what the base unit or expansion units supply at 24 V.

Numbering. Each special module has a module number so that the PLC can address it. Number from the module nearest the base unit, 0 to 7; the number may not exceed 7. Expansion units and I/O modules are not counted, only special modules.

Position from the base unitDeviceModule No.
Base unitFX2N-32MR—
1FX2N-2AD0
2FX2N-16EYR (output module)not counted
3FX2N-2DA1
4FX2N-20GM2
5FX0N-8EX (input module)not counted

sections.h: FROM and TO: talking to a module’s buffer memory
sections.b:
Every special module has a buffer memory (BFM): numbered 16-bit words #0, #1, #2 … Settings are written into BFMs, and results are read out of them. Communication between the base unit and a special module is done only through two instructions.

NameMnemonicFNCm1m2DatanSteps
BFM readFROM, FROMP78 (16/32)K, H: module No. 0–7K, H: first BFM 0–31[D·]: KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, ZK, H: 1–32 words9 · 32-bit: 17
BFM writeTO, TOP79 (16/32)K, H: 0–7K, H: 0–31[S·]: K, H, KnX, KnY, KnM, KnS, T, C, D, V, ZK, H: 1–329 · 32-bit: 17
LD    X3
FROM  K2  K20  D0  K3       module 2: BFM #20, #21, #22  →  D0, D1, D2
LD    X1
DTO   K1  K10  D0  K2       D1 D0 (32-bit)  →  module 1: BFM #10, #11 (two words)
  • FROM reads from the module into the PLC. When X3 is off, FROM is not executed and D0–D2 keep their data.
  • TO writes from the PLC into the module. When X1 is off, BFM #10 and #11 keep their data.
  • Read the order of the operands as: which module, which BFM, where in the PLC, how many.
  • M8028 decides about interrupts. OFF: interrupts are disabled while FROM/TO run, and FROM/TO may be used in an interrupt routine. ON: interrupts are allowed during FROM/TO, and FROM/TO may not be used in an interrupt routine.

Analog modules bring voltages and currents into the PLC and send them out. Used with PID modules or the PID instruction they give closed-loop control of temperature, pressure, flow and so on; with the PLC’s arithmetic, fuzzy-control and other algorithms can also be programmed.

The FX2N-2AD is a 2-channel, 12-bit analog input module. It converts 0–10 V DC, 0–5 V DC or 4–20 mA DC into a digital value and sends it to the PLC.

2.5 mV per count for voltage; 4 µA per count for current. With 4–20 mA, zero on the digital side is 4 mA, not 0 mA.

ItemVoltage inputCurrent input
Input range0–10 V or 0–5 V DC (input resistance 200 kΩ). Adjusted at the factory to 0–10 V → 0–4000. For 0–5 V, re-adjust offset and gain. Above −0.5 V or +15 V may damage the module4–20 mA (input resistance 250 Ω). Below −2 mA or above +60 mA may damage the module. Re-adjust the zero when used for current
Digital output12 bit
Resolution2.5 mV (10 V ÷ 4000); 1.25 mV (5 V ÷ 4000)4 µA ((20 − 4) mA ÷ 4000)
Overall accuracy±1 % of full scale±1 % of full scale
Conversion speed2.5 ms per channel (the sequence program and conversion run together)
SupplyAnalog: 24 V DC ±10 %, 50 mA · Digital: 5 V DC, 20 mA (from the base unit)
IsolationOptocouplers between the analog and digital circuits; DC/DC converter from the base unit. No isolation between channels
I/O points occupied8 (counted as inputs or outputs)
  • The two channels share the same offset and gain, so one channel cannot be voltage and the other current.
  • For current input, link terminals VIN and IIN.
  • If the voltage input fluctuates or is noisy, connect a 0.1–0.47 µF, 25 V capacitor across it.
  • Use shielded twisted-pair cable.
BFMb15–b8b7–b4b3b2b1b0
#0—Current value of the input data (low 8 bits)
#1————Current value (high 4 bits)
#17————A/D startA/D channel
#18–#31—

BFM #17: b0 = 0 selects CH1, b0 = 1 selects CH2. Changing b1 from 0 to 1 starts the A/D conversion. The 12-bit result is split: low 8 bits in #0, high 4 bits in #1.

sections.h: Reading the 2AD in a program, and averaging
sections.b:
LD    X0                  CH1 conversion
TO    K0  K17  H0  K1     select channel 1 (b0 = 0)
TO    K0  K17  H2  K1     b1: 0 → 1 starts the conversion
FROM  K0  K0  K2M100  K2  read BFM #0 and #1 into M100–M115
MOV   K4M100  D100        assemble the 12 bits: CH1 value in D100

LD    X1                  CH2 conversion
TO    K0  K17  H1  K1     select channel 2 (b0 = 1)
TO    K0  K17  H3  K1     b1: 0 → 1, channel 2
FROM  K0  K0  K2M100  K2
MOV   K4M100  D101        CH2 value in D101

The module is No. 0 here. My listing follows the book’s sequence; the book uses the values H0/H2 for CH1 and H1/H3 for CH2.

  • Why read into M100–M115 first? BFM #0 holds 8 bits and #1 holds 4 bits. Reading two words into K2M100 puts the low 8 bits in M100–M107 and the high bits in M108–M111; K4M100 then reads them back as one number.
  • From X0 or X1 turning on to the value being in the data register takes about 2.5 ms per channel.
  • On an FX0N the read is written differently (the book gives a modified circuit using FROM K0 K0 K4M100 K2 and MOV K2M116 K2M108).

Averaging. If the input is unsteady, add a routine that averages several samples. In the book’s example: at start (M8002) and each time the averaging is complete (M133), clear the totals and count with DMOV K0. Each scan (M8000): DINC the sample count D118; DADD the CH1 value D100 into the total D114 and the CH2 value D102 into D116; DCMP the count with K20, setting M133 when 20 samples have been taken; then DDIV D114 by D118 to get the CH1 average in (D111, D110), and D116 by D118 for the CH2 average in (D113, D112). The number of samples can be from 1 to 262 144.

The FX2N-2DA is a 2-channel, 12-bit analog output module: it converts a 12-bit digital value into two analog outputs, voltage or current.

ItemVoltage outputCurrent output
Output range0–10 V or 0–5 V DC (load resistance 2 kΩ to 1 MΩ)4–20 mA (load resistance 500 Ω or less)
Factory setting0–4000 gives 0–10 V. For 0–5 V or current, re-adjust offset and gain with the potentiometers
Digital input12 bit
Resolution2.5 mV (10 V ÷ 4000); 1.25 mV (5 V ÷ 4000)4 µA
Accuracy±1 % of full scale
Conversion speed4 ms per channel
SupplyAnalog: 24 V DC ±10 %, 85 mA · Digital: 5 V DC, 20 mA (from the base unit)
IsolationAs 2AD: optocouplers; channels not isolated from each other
I/O points occupied8
  • If 13 bits or more are input, only the last 12 bits count; the higher bits are ignored. Use digital values in 0–4095.
  • For voltage output, short IOUT and COM.
  • If the voltage output fluctuates or is noisy, connect a 0.1–0.47 µF, 25 V capacitor at the load.
BFMMeaning
#16Digital value to be converted, for the channel chosen in #17. Written as low 8 bits, then high 4 bits
#17 b01 → 0: start D/A conversion on channel 2
#17 b11 → 0: start D/A conversion on channel 1
#17 b21 → 0: hold (latch) the low 8 bits
LD    X0                    channel 1
MOV   D100  K4M100          spread D100 over M100–M115
MOV   K2M100  K2M116        low 8 bits  →  M116–M123
TO    K0  K16  K2M116  K1   write the low 8 bits to BFM #16
TO    K0  K17  H4  K1       b2 = 1 …
TO    K0  K17  H0  K1       … then 0: low 8 bits held
MOV   K2M108  K2M116        high 4 bits  →  M116–M123
TO    K0  K16  K2M116  K1   write the high 4 bits
TO    K0  K17  H2  K1       b1 = 1 …
TO    K0  K17  H0  K1       … then 0: D/A on channel 1

Channel 2 is the same with D101 and H1 in place of H2. From X0 or X1 to the analog output takes about 4 ms per channel.

The FX2N also has other analog modules: the 4-channel FX2N-4AD and FX2N-4DA, and temperature input modules with a built-in sensor amplifier, FX2N-4AD-PT for platinum resistance sensors (PT-100) and FX2N-4AD-TC for thermocouples, to which the sensor connects directly.

worked.q: An FX2N-2AD on 0–10 V reads a sensor giving 6.2 V. About what digital value appears? What is the resolution?
worked.s: Resolution = 10 V ÷ 4000 = 2.5 mV per count. Value = 6.2 V ÷ 0.0025 V = 2480.

worked.q: The same module on 4–20 mA reads 2000. What is the current?
worked.s: Each count is (20 − 4) mA ÷ 4000 = 0.004 mA. Current = 4 mA + 2000 × 0.004 mA = 4 + 8 = 12 mA, the middle of the range.

worked.q: An FX2N-2AD is in position No. 3. Both channels are 4–20 mA. Sample 10 times and store the averages starting at D100. Outline the program. (Exercise 11.1)
worked.s: Module No. = K3. Each scan: TO K3 K17 H0 K1 · TO K3 K17 H2 K1 · FROM K3 K0 K2M100 K2 · MOV K4M100 D10 (CH1), and the same with H1/H3 into D11 (CH2). Add D10 to a total D20 and D11 to D22 (DADD), INC the count D24, compare the count with K10; when it reaches 10, DDIV D20 by D24 → D100 (CH1 average) and D22 by D24 → D102 (CH2 average), then clear the totals and the count. Wiring: link VIN and IIN on each channel, and re-adjust the zero for current input.

worked.q: A system has an FX2N-2AD, an FX2N-16EYR output module and an FX2N-2DA, in that order after the base unit. What module numbers do the two analog modules take?
worked.s: Only special modules are counted. 2AD is the first: No. 0. The 16EYR is not counted. 2DA is the second special module: No. 1.

worked.q: Why must the two channels of an FX2N-2AD be the same type of input?
worked.s: The two channels share one offset and gain setting. Voltage and current inputs need different adjustments, so one channel cannot be voltage and the other current.

Data is read from a module’s buffer memory with the ___ instruction.
The FX2N-2AD converts a 0–10 V input into the digital range 0–___.
For voltage output on the FX2N-2DA, short IOUT and ___.

topics.title: Data Links and Communication: 232BD, 485BD, N:N Networks, Positioning and HMI Modules
topics.zh: 数据链接与通信：232BD、485BD、N:N 网络、定位与人机界面模块

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 11, “Special function modules of the PLC”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.). Written in my own words; the conversion graph is redrawn and program fragments are short listings written to match the book’s explanation. Module data are the book’s figures for the Mitsubishi FX2N family. For a real installation use the module’s own manual. This topic sits beside your ITE PLC Chapter 11 (expansion modules and power budget).

As factories have demanded more automation, central control by one big controller can no longer meet the need for “passing information, dispersing control, centralising management”. So every maker has brought out its own PLC network. Mitsubishi, for example, offers networks at several levels: company-level Ethernet, control-level MELSECNET/H, field-bus-level CC-Link, sensor-level CC-Link/LT, and other communication modules, for different levels of communication and network control. PLC networks are moving towards higher speed, more levels, larger capacity, higher reliability and openness.

So the FX series supports: (1) N:N links; (2) parallel links; (3) computer links (data transfer with a dedicated protocol); (4) no-protocol communication (data transfer with the RS instruction); and (5) an optional programming port.

The FX2N-232-BD is an RS-232C communication board that fits inside an FX2N base unit. It cannot be used together with an FX2N-485-BD or FX2N-422-BD; when two or more RS-232C units are needed, use the special RS-232C module. It lets the PLC exchange data with RS-232C devices such as a personal computer, a bar-code reader or a printer. The communication format (baud rate, parity, data length) is set in the special data register D8120.

Book’s example: printing from the PLC. A printer’s RS-232 port is joined by a serial cable to the FX2N-232-BD, and the PLC sends text to be printed.

Sequence: switch on the PLC and the printer and put the PLC in RUN; turn X0 on, which drives RS; then each time X1 turns on, the contents of D200–D210 are sent and the printer prints “test line” (the book’s sample text).

Points. CR (H000D) returns the print head and LF (H000A) feeds the paper; write them at the end of each message so the next one prints on a new line. Set the printer’s own DIP switches to the same format.

sections.h: FX2N-485-BD: RS-485 and the N:N network
sections.b:
With the FX2N-485-BD (“485BD”) fitted in the base unit, the PLC can be connected over shielded twisted pair for these uses:

  1. No-protocol or dedicated-protocol data transfer. With no protocol, through an RS-485 (422) converter, data passes between devices that have RS-232C units, such as a PC, a bar-code reader or a printer; the data is sent and received through the registers named in the RS instruction. With the dedicated protocol, data passes on a 1:N basis over RS-485 (422). With the 485BD the whole system may extend 50 m (without it, 500 m); with the dedicated protocol, including A-series PLCs, up to 16 stations.
  2. Parallel link between two PLCs. Two FX2N PLCs exchange the states of 100 auxiliary relays and 10 data registers on a 1:1 basis. The system may extend 50 m with the 485BD (500 m without); with a 485BD in the system, 10 m.
  3. N:N network. Up to 8 FX2N PLCs exchange data. With the 485BD the system may extend 50 m (without it, 500 m), up to 16 stations.
ItemSpecification
StandardRS-485 and RS-422
Distance50 m or less
LEDsSD flashes fast when sending; RD flashes fast when receiving
MethodsN:N network · dedicated protocol (format 1 or 4) · half duplex · parallel link
Baud rateDedicated and no protocol: 300–19 200 bit/s · parallel link: 19 200 bit/s · N:N network: 38 400 bit/s
IsolationNone
Current5 V DC, 60 mA (from the PLC)

Wiring. One twisted pair or two, depending on the use. For the no-protocol single-pair half-duplex link and the parallel link, one pair is recommended; for the N:N network, one pair is permitted, two pairs also work.

  • A terminating resistor of 330 Ω (marked R in the book) goes across SDA–SDB and RDA–RDB at the two ends of the line.
  • Earth the shield of the twisted pair (earth resistance 100 Ω or less). With the parallel link, earth both ends; with no protocol or the dedicated protocol, earth one end.
  • Connect terminal FG to the PLC’s earth terminal, earth resistance 100 Ω or less.

sections.h: An N:N network of three FX2Ns, worked through
sections.b:
Three FX2N PLCs, each with a 485BD, form an N:N network: master station No. 0, slave No. 1, slave No. 2.

Parameters, written into special registers in the master only, on the M8038 (parameter setting) contact:

RegisterMasterSlave 1Slave 2Meaning
D8176K0K1K2Station number (the master needs 0; range 0–7)
D8177K2——Total number of slaves: 2 (range 1–7)
D8178K1——Refresh range: mode 1 (32 bit devices and 4 word devices)
D8179K3——Retries: 3
D8180K5——Time-out: 5 × 10 ms = 50 ms

Error handling. A station cannot recognise its own communication error, so an alarm program for network errors is needed, though not every station must have one. In the book’s example: M8183 (master error) drives Y0, M8184 (slave 1 error) drives Y1, M8185 (slave 2 error) drives Y2, and M8191 (data communication error) drives Y3.

The tasks, and how each is done. In mode 1 each station has its own range of shared relays and registers: the master M1000–M1031 and D0–D3; slave 1 M1064–M1095 and D10–D13; slave 2 M1128–M1159 and D20–D23. A station writes into its own range; every other station can read it.

RequirementHow
Master’s inputs X0–X3 appear on Y10–Y13 of slaves 1 and 2Master: MOV K1X0 K1M1000. Each slave: MOV K1M1000 K1Y10
Slave 1’s X0–X3 appear on Y14–Y17 of the master and slave 2Slave 1: MOV K1X0 K1M1064. Others: MOV K1M1064 K1Y14
Slave 2’s X0–X3 appear on Y20–Y23 of the master and slave 1Slave 2: MOV K1X0 K1M1128. Others: MOV K1M1128 K1Y20
The master’s D1 sets counter C1 in slave 1; C1’s contact (via M1070) shows on the master’s Y5Master: MOV K10 D1. Slave 1: OUT C1 D1, then C1 drives Y5 and M1070. Master: M1070 drives Y5
The master’s D2 sets counter C2 in slave 2; its contact (via M1140) shows on the master’s Y6The same pattern with D2, C2, M1140
D10 of slave 1 and D20 of slave 2 are added in the master into D3Master: ADD D10 D20 D3
D10 of the master and D20 of slave 2 are added in slave 1 into D11Slave 1: ADD D0 D20 D11 (as the book writes it)
D10 of the master and D10 of slave 1 are added in slave 2 into D21Slave 2: ADD D0 D10 D21

Every read of another station’s data is guarded by an NC contact of that station’s error flag (M8184, M8185 …), so that a broken link does not feed stale data into the program.

Position control is the control of where a working position is. A PLC system can act as one control link in a whole position-control system; with a servo amplifier or driver and a stepper or servo motor, position control can be handled together with logic and sequence control.

Advantages of position modules on a PLC. (1) Full use of the PLC’s hardware and software; they are widely used in flexible manufacturing (FMS), computer-integrated manufacturing (CIMS) and factory automation (FA). (2) The user can configure the system flexibly, which lowers cost and suits each case. (3) Reliable and easy to maintain.

ModuleWhat it does
FX2N-1HC high-speed counterCounts high-speed signals from sensors such as rotary encoders
FX2N-1PG and FX2N-10PG pulse outputExchange data with FX1N, FX2N and FX2NC PLCs by FROM/TO. Each controls one axis independently; one PLC can take up to 8, giving several independent axes. Maximum output frequency 100 kHz (1PG) and 1 MHz (10PG)
FX2N-10GM (1 axis) and FX2N-20GM (2 axes) positioning unitsRun independently of the PLC. Besides their own positioning language they have a programming language and can process data at a higher level. The 20GM can interpolate straight lines and arcs on 2 axes, giving two-axis coordinated motion
F2N-1RM-E-SET programmable cam switchCombines CPU, supply, input and output programmer; detects rotation angle with a dedicated resolver for accurate angular position control

HMI modules (data access units) range from simple text displays (FX-10DU-E, FX-20DU-E, FX-10DM-E) used for monitoring states and setting parameters, to touch screens. A touch screen is tough, responsive, small and easy to talk to: touch a graphic or a word on the screen with a finger to control the plant. Mitsubishi’s graphic operator terminals (the 900 series) range from small to large HMIs and PC-based SoftGOT; the GOT-F900 series is the one usually paired with FX PLCs.

worked.q: In the printer example (Example 11-5), the printer must be set to 7-bit data at 9600 bit/s. What changes? (Exercise 11.3)
worked.s: Only the communication format in D8120. b0 = 0 for 7 bits; (b7, b6, b5, b4) = (1, 0, 0, 0) for 9600 bit/s; the rest as before (even parity, 1 stop bit, no protocol). That is 0000 0000 1000 0110 = H0086: MOV H0086 D8120. Set the printer’s DIP switches to match, and switch the PLC off and on after the change.

worked.q: How is an N:N network built from FX2N PLCs, and how many master and slave stations can it have? (Exercise 11.4)
worked.s: Fit an FX2N-485-BD (or 485 adapter) to each PLC and join them with shielded twisted pair, with terminating resistors at the two ends. Set the station number in D8176 of each PLC, and the number of slaves, refresh mode, retries and time-out in D8177–D8180 of the master. One master (No. 0) and up to 7 slaves: at most 8 PLCs.

worked.q: If the N:N network of Example 11-7 is changed to five FX2Ns, with the rest unchanged, how are the parameters and programs changed? (Exercise 11.5)
worked.s: In the master: D8177 = K4 (four slaves). In the two new PLCs: D8176 = K3 and K4. The new stations’ shared areas in mode 1 continue the pattern: slave 3 from M1192 and D30, slave 4 from M1256 and D40. Add error alarms for the new stations (M8186, M8187) and guard reads of their data with those flags. Keep or extend the data-exchange rungs as required.

worked.q: An FX2N-2DA is module No. 2. Channel 1 must give 4–20 mA from D10, channel 2 must give 0–5 V from D20. What must be done? (Exercise 11.2)
worked.s: Hardware: set channel 1 for current and channel 2 for voltage, re-adjust offset and gain on each with the module’s potentiometers, and short IOUT to COM on channel 2. Program: as the book’s routine with module number K2; for CH1 spread D10 over M100–M115 and write low 8 bits, then high 4 bits, to BFM #16, with #17 = H4 → H0 and then H2 → H0; for CH2 the same from D20 with H1 → H0 at the end.

worked.q: Why are terminating resistors fitted at the two ends of an RS-485 line?
worked.s: An RS-485 line is a long pair of conductors carrying fast signals. Without a matching resistor at each end, the signal reflects back along the line and corrupts the data. The 330 Ω resistors absorb the signal at the ends.

topics.title: Designing a PLC Control System: Steps, Hardware Choices and Programming Methods
topics.zh: PLC 控制系统的设计：步骤、硬件选择和编程方法

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 12, “Design and application of PLC control systems”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.), the last chapter of the book. Written in my own words. Installation figures are the book’s for the Mitsubishi FX series; follow the manual and your local wiring regulations on a real installation.

PLC technology is about engineering application. How to design a sensible PLC control system from real requirements, using everything learned so far, is the core of the subject. The general method below is a frame; the key is to explore, sum up and generalise through real projects.

Main contents of a system design.

  1. Draw up the technical conditions of the design, usually as a design brief. It is the basis of the whole design.
  2. Choose the electrical drive and the actuators: motors, solenoid valves.
  3. Choose the PLC model.
  4. Draw up the I/O assignment table, or draw the I/O terminal wiring diagram.
  5. Write a software specification from the requirements, then write the program in a suitable language (usually ladder).
  6. Understand and follow the user’s way of thinking, and pay attention to the operator interface: make man and machine work well together.
  7. Design the operator desk, the cabinet and any non-standard parts.
  8. Write the design description and the user instructions.

Depending on the job, these can be adjusted.

1 · Understand the plant and its requirements
2 · Decide the input and output devices
3 · Choose a suitable PLC
4 · Assign the I/O points
5 · Design the ladder program ‖ in parallel: design and build the cabinet, install and wire
6 · Enter the program into the PLC
7 · Test the software (check, debug; repeat until right)
8 · Commission the whole system on site (repeat until right)
9 · Write the technical documents, and hand over
  1. Understand and analyse the plant. The plant is the machine, the electrical equipment, the production line or the process being controlled. The requirements are the basic way it works, the actions to be done, how the automatic cycle is made up, and the necessary protection and interlocks. Split a complex job into several independent parts: break the whole into pieces, which helps programming and commissioning.
  2. Decide the I/O devices from the functions required. Typical inputs: push buttons, selector switches, limit switches, sensors. Typical outputs: relays, contactors, indicator lamps, solenoid valves.
  3. Choose the PLC from the I/O devices, counting the inputs and outputs: the model, the memory, the I/O modules and the power supply.
  4. Assign the I/O points. Make the I/O assignment table, or draw the I/O terminal wiring diagram. Then PLC programming can go on, and so can the cabinet and the site work, at the same time.
  5. Design the ladder from the function chart or the state diagram. This is the key step and the hardest. To design a good ladder you must first know the requirements thoroughly, and have some practical experience of electrical design.
  6. Enter the program. With a simple programmer, first convert the ladder to mnemonics. With programming software on a computer, download through the cable.
  7. Test the software. Mistakes are hard to avoid in writing a program. Before connecting the PLC to the plant, test the software to remove errors; it also lays the ground for commissioning and shortens it.
  8. Commission the whole system. When software, hardware, cabinet and site work are complete, run the whole system. If it has several parts, commission each, then the whole. If the program has many steps, commission it section by section and then together. Fix problems as they appear, until it works.
  9. Write the technical documents: description, schematic, layout drawing, parts list and the PLC ladder.

Before deciding the control scheme, understand the plant’s requirements in detail, and decide whether to use a PLC at all, and which. A PLC is very necessary where the logic is complex (many intermediate relays, time relays and counters needed), the process and product change often, data handling and information management are needed (analog control, PID regulation), the system must be highly reliable and stable, and factory automation and networking are planned.

There are many PLC series from many makers at home and abroad, and the user can be dazzled. Weigh the advantages and disadvantages and choose sensibly for economy and practicality. Generally, choose for the functions the system needs. Do not chase size and completeness for their own sake; that wastes investment and equipment.

ConsiderationGuidance
1 · I/O pointsChoosing too many is waste. Count the total I/O the system needs, then add 15–20 % spare (for system changes and the like) before deciding the PLC’s points. On some high-density modules, only about 60 % of the inputs may be ON at once. Each output’s current capacity is limited, and the allowed output current falls as the ambient temperature rises. Outputs come with common terminals, in groups, or isolated. Isolated outputs allow each group to use a different supply type and voltage, but cost more per point; use them only where isolation is needed
2 · MemoryOnly a rough estimate is possible. For purely on/off control: total inputs × 10 words per point + total outputs × 5 words per point. Counters and timers: 3–5 words each. Arithmetic: 5–10 words each. With analog I/O: 80–100 words per analog input or output. For communication: about 200 words or more per port. Finally allow 50–100 % margin; beginners should allow plenty
3 · Response timeThe PLC’s I/O response time includes the input circuit delay, the output circuit delay and the delay due to scanning (generally 2–3 scans). For on/off control, the response time generally meets the plant’s needs, and need not be considered. For analog systems, and especially closed-loop systems, consider it
4 · Output loadsDifferent loads need different output types. A frequently switched inductive load needs a transistor or thyristor output, not a relay. Relay outputs have many advantages: low voltage drop, isolation, relatively cheap, can stand momentary over-voltage and over-current, a wide range of load voltage (AC or DC). So where the AC or DC loads are switched infrequently, choose relay outputs
5 · On-line or off-line programmingOff-line: the PLC and the programmer share one CPU. A selector chooses program, monitor or run; in program mode the CPU serves only the programmer and does not control the plant. Dedicated programmers work this way. On-line: PLC and programmer each have a CPU. The PLC’s CPU controls the plant; at the end of each scan it talks to the programmer, which sends the modified program, and the PLC runs it from the next scan. Computer-aided programming can be off-line or on-line, but needs a computer and software
6 · NetworkingIf the system is to join a factory automation network, the PLC must have networking: interfaces to other PLCs, host computers and CRTs. Medium and large machines all have it; most small ones now do too
7 · ConstructionFor the same functions and I/O, the compact (unit) type is cheaper than the modular. But the modular is flexible to expand, easy to maintain (change a module) and easy to diagnose. Choose by need

sections.h: Assigning I/O, and four ways to design the program
sections.b:
I/O assignment. Generally inputs correspond one to one with input signals and outputs with output controls. After assignment, number them according to the system’s channels and contacts, and give each input signal and each output signal its number.

  • Sometimes, to save points, two signals can share one input: connect the contacts in series or parallel outside, according to the logic, before taking them to the input.
  • Know the channel ranges. Different PLC models have different I/O ranges. Choose according to the model and look it up in the manual; never “put Zhang’s hat on Li’s head”. (Do not assume one model’s numbers apply to another.)
  • Internal auxiliary relays give no outputs and cannot connect to outside devices. They work as intermediate relays, storing intermediate states or processing data. Unused I/O areas, and unused link relay areas, can also be used as auxiliary relays. List in the design description what each auxiliary relay is for, so that nothing is used twice.
  • Timers and counters: check the numbers available in the manual.
Programming methodHow it worksBest for
Ladder methodWrites the program in the ladder language, which imitates relay control: its graphics and even the names of devices are close to relay circuits. A relay control circuit can be carried over almost directlyPeople familiar with relay control: the easiest way
Logic flow-chart methodShows the program’s execution as logic blocks: how inputs and outputs relate. The process is expressed as a logic flow chart, showing the logic links and interlock conditions clearly. The program’s structure is clear, easy to analyse, to find faults, and to commission and maintain. When a complex program is hard to write straight in instruction list or ladder, draw the logic flow chart firstComplex programs, as a first step
Timing flow-chart methodFirst draw the timing diagram of the control system (what must happen at each moment). From it draw the program block diagram of the control tasks, and from that write the PLC programSystems controlled on a basis of time
Step-sequence methodDesigns a complex program with the step-sequence instructions. A complex program can be split into simple sections; each section is one step. Viewed this way, a complex system’s control is made up of steps, and the task is to make each step happen at the right time and the right place. Many makers provide step-ladder instructions; draw the state flow chart and then write the programSequences
Experience methodUses your own or others’ experience: choose a “trial program” close to your process, modify it step by step until it fits. The experience may be your own or from others’ designs; collect it over time and learn from it
Computer-aided programmingUses PLC software on a computer for programming, off-line or on-line, simulation, and saving and protecting the programEverything, today

1 · Split the system into tasks
2 · Draw the logic relationship diagram of the control system
3 · Draw the circuit diagrams
4 · Write the PLC program and simulate it
5 · Build the operator desk and cabinet
6 · Commission on site
7 · Write the technical documents, and run on site
  1. Split into tasks. The purpose is to divide a complex project into several simpler small tasks: a complex big problem made into several simple small problems. This makes programming easier.
  2. Logic relationship diagram. From it you can see what a given logic relation produces, and what actions that result then leads to. The relations may be based on the control actions, or on the timing of the whole activity. The diagram shows the order of control and the relations between the controlled objects’ activities, as well as between inputs and outputs.
  3. Circuit diagrams. Here the system’s inputs and outputs are linked with the addresses and names designed. This step is critical. For the PLC input circuit, consider not only whether the connection points match their names, but whether the voltages and currents at the inputs suit, and the reliability and stability of working in special conditions. In particular, take care that high voltage is never brought into the PLC’s inputs, or the PLC will be damaged. For the output circuit, consider not only whether connection points match names, but the driving ability and voltage withstand of the output modules. Also consider the supply’s output power and polarity. Throughout, follow the principle of thrift, but make the design careful and complete. So in drawing the circuits, be meticulous about where each wire goes and where each switch is placed.
  4. Write the program and simulate it. When programming, besides being correct and reliable, the program should be concise, save time, and be easy to read and modify. Write a block, simulate it; this finds problems early and corrects them promptly. Do not finish the whole program before testing.
  5. Build the desk and cabinet. After the circuit and the program, the operator desk and cabinet can be made; when time is short, this can go on alongside programming. Choose switches, buttons, relays and other devices carefully: their quality and specifications must meet requirements. The installation must be safe and reliable, and shielding, earthing and high-voltage isolation must be properly handled.
  6. Commission on site. This is an important link in completing the control system. No program can be used without on-site commissioning, however good its design. Only on site can you find where the control circuit and program fail the system, and where the circuit and the program conflict. Only by commissioning and finally adjusting the circuit and program on site can the system suit the requirement.
  7. Write the documents, and run. Once the site commissioning has confirmed the circuit and program, and the hardware and software have no problems, put all the technical documents in order: circuit diagrams, PLC program, user instructions and help files. The work is then complete.

worked.q: Describe the general steps in designing a PLC control system. (Exercise 12.1)
worked.s: (1) Study the plant and its requirements. (2) Decide the input and output devices. (3) Choose the PLC: model, memory, I/O modules, power supply. (4) Assign the I/O points and draw the I/O wiring. (5) Design the ladder program; in parallel, design and build the cabinet and do the site wiring. (6) Enter the program. (7) Test the software. (8) Commission the whole system on site, part by part and then together. (9) Write the technical documents and hand over.

worked.q: How is the memory capacity of a PLC estimated? A machine has 40 on/off inputs, 24 on/off outputs, 6 timers, 2 analog inputs and one communication port. Estimate it. (Exercise 12.2)
worked.s: My working, using the book’s rules of thumb (10 words per input, 5 per output). On/off: 40 × 10 + 24 × 5 = 400 + 120 = 520 words. Timers: 6 × 5 = 30 (upper end of 3–5). Analog: 2 × 100 = 200 (upper end of 80–100). Communication: about 200. Total ≈ 950 words. With 50–100 % margin: about 1.4K to 1.9K words; choose a PLC of 2K or more.

worked.q: A machine needs 48 inputs and 30 outputs. With the book’s 15–20 % spare, how many points should the PLC have?
worked.s: Total 78. Adding 15–20 %: 78 × 1.15 ≈ 90 to 78 × 1.2 ≈ 94. Choose at least about 90–94 points, split so that inputs and outputs each have spare: for example at least 56 inputs and 36 outputs. (Inputs and outputs cannot stand in for each other.)

worked.q: A solenoid valve (an inductive load) is switched on and off every second. A relay-output PLC is proposed. What is your advice?
worked.s: Use a transistor (DC valve) or thyristor (AC valve) output. A relay contact switching an inductive load every second would wear out in a short time. Relay outputs suit loads switched infrequently.
