topics.title: Installing, Wiring, Maintaining and Troubleshooting a PLC
topics.zh: PLC 的安装、接线、维护与检修

sections.h: Where a PLC may be installed
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on Chapter 12, “Design and application of PLC control systems”, of 《电气与PLC控制技术》 (Cai Hongbin, ed.), the last chapter of the book. Written in my own words. Installation figures are the book’s for the Mitsubishi FX series; follow the manual and your local wiring regulations on a real installation.

The PLC is a new kind of general automatic control device. It has many advantages, and many measures are taken in its design and manufacture so that it suits the industrial environment. But the industrial site is often harsh. To keep a PLC control system working stably and reliably, still give the PLC as good working conditions as possible, and take the necessary measures against interference.

Environment. For reliability and the longest life, the place must meet these:

  1. Ambient temperature 0–55 °C.
  2. Relative humidity 35–85 %.
  3. No flammable or corrosive gas.
  4. Not too much dust or metal particles.
  5. No excessive vibration or shock.
  6. Not in direct sunlight or where water can splash.

Other precautions.

  1. Install or remove every unit of the PLC only with the power off.
  2. To protect the PLC’s parts from static electricity, before touching the PLC, first touch an earthed metal object with your hand to discharge any static on your body.
  3. Take care of the ventilation and heat dissipation around the PLC, and do not let wire ends, iron filings and the like fall into the unit through the vents.

Mounting. Two ways for the FX series:

  • Panel mounting. Through the holes at the four corners of the case, fix the control unit, expansion units, A/D and D/A units and I/O link units to a base plate with M4 screws.
  • DIN rail mounting. Clip the units onto a DIN rail with the rail clip on the back. Push the unit onto the rail, aligned, from below upward. To remove a unit from the rail, pull the clip lightly down with a flat-blade screwdriver.

Power wiring. The FX takes a 24 V DC, 100–120 V AC or 200–240 V AC industrial supply. Its external supply terminals are the two at the left of the output terminal block. Use twisted pair of 2 mm diameter.

  • Excess noise and voltage fluctuation on the supply may make the CPU misbehave and the whole control system fail. To avoid such accidents, use an isolation transformer or other filter on the supply, and route the supply lines of the PLC and its I/O separately from those of motor equipment.
  • The FX PLC must start working only after all outside devices are powered. To ensure this: switch the external devices on first, then switch the PLC’s mode selector from STOP to RUN; or program the FX PLC so that it does no I/O until the external devices are powered.
  • When the control unit is joined to other units, their power lines should be switched on and off together.
  • A power cut of less than 10 ms does not affect the PLC’s normal working.
  • To avoid a system breakdown or irrecoverable accident caused by a fault, add an emergency stop circuit.
  • Where two actions are opposites, add an interlock circuit between the PLC and the controlled equipment.

Earthing. Good earthing is a condition for the PLC to work normally.

  1. Use a dedicated earth wire of at least 2 mm diameter.
  2. Earth resistance less than 100 Ω.
  3. The PLC’s earth must not be shared with other equipment, still less connected to a large metal structure of the building.
  4. The earth wires of all the PLC’s units are joined together.

Input terminals. The FX control unit’s input terminal block is a removable board with two-headed screws. All external switches connect to the PLC through it.

  1. Keep input wires as far as possible from output wires, high-voltage wires and motor wires, to avoid interference.
  2. Do not connect input devices to the terminals marked “•” (empty terminals).
  3. The internal DC supply output of an AC-powered PLC can be used for the inputs. If the DC supply of a DC-powered PLC is not enough, an external supply can be used.
  4. Never connect an external supply to the output terminals of the AC-powered PLC’s internal DC supply.
  5. Never connect the supplies used for the inputs in parallel with each other, and still less connect them in parallel with other supplies.

Output terminals. Also a removable board; the PLC and its output devices connect through it.

  1. Keep output wires as far as possible from high-voltage and power lines.
  2. Do not connect output devices to “•” terminals.
  3. Each “COM” terminal is independent, so the outputs can be independent or share a common. If the loads use different voltages, use independent outputs; if they use the same voltage, they can share a common.
  4. When several loads are on the same supply, link their “COM” terminals with short wires.
  5. If an output drives an inductive load, connect a protective circuit suited to the load. On an AC inductive load, connect an RC snubber across the load. On a DC inductive load, connect a diode across it. On an output with a low-current load, connect a bleed resistor across the load so that leakage current does not interfere.
  6. There is no fuse in the PLC’s output circuits. To prevent a load short circuit from damaging the output circuit, put a fuse in the external output circuit, or design an emergency-stop circuit.

Analog modules.

  • A/D: use shielded twisted pair against electromagnetic induction and noise on the input signal; earth the shield to the frame earth (FG). If terminals need shorting, short them directly on the terminal board, not with leads pulled out. Keep the input wiring away from high-voltage lines. Feed the control unit and the A/D unit from the same supply line.
  • D/A: shielded twisted pair against induction and noise on the output; earth the shield at the load end. The voltage output and current output of one channel cannot be used together; leave unused outputs open. Keep the output wiring away from high-voltage lines. Feed the control unit and the D/A unit from the same supply.

If the I/O points are not enough, the base unit can be connected to other expansion units. The configuration differs between models; read the user manual before expanding.

The main parts of a PLC are semiconductor devices. Because of the environment, they age with time, so regular inspection and maintenance are essential. Have a skilled team who know the equipment and the PLC’s working principles to look after it day to day.

Set up a system of inspection, check on schedule, keep the equipment in its best condition. Each PLC needs a definite inspection interval, generally every 6 months to 1 year; shorten it where the outside conditions are poor.

No.ItemWhat to checkStandard
1SupplyMeasure the voltage at the supply terminals: is it within the specified range?Fluctuation 85–110 % of the supply voltage
2EnvironmentTemperature · humidity · dust0–55 °C · 35–85 % RH, no condensation · no dust build-up
3I/O suppliesMeasure the voltage at the I/O terminals: within the standard?As specified for the I/O
4InstallationIs each unit firmly fixed? · Are the connecting cables’ connectors fully home? · Are any external wiring screws loose?Not loose · not loose · nothing abnormal
5Parts with a lifeBattery, relays, memoryBy the life of each part

ProblemCauseRemedy
Output does not workAn electrical surge on the output has damaged the controlled deviceIf the load is inductive, a surge suppressor is needed
Program errorCorrect the program
Loose or wrong wiringCheck the wiring; correct it if wrong
Output overloadedCheck the output load
Output being forcedCheck the CPU for forced I/O
CPU-E (system fault) lamp litUser program errorFor a program error, check the use of FOR, NEXT, jump and compare instructions
Electrical interference(1) Check the wiring. Good earthing of the control panel, and keeping high-voltage and low-voltage wiring from running in parallel, matter a great deal. (2) Connect the M terminal of the 24 V DC sensor supply to earth
Damaged componentFind the cause, then replace the component
Power supply damagedOver-voltage on the supply lineConnect a power analyser to the system and check the magnitude and duration of the over-voltage spikes; fit a suitable surge suppressor accordingly
Electronic interferenceUnsuitable earthing · cross wiring in the control cabinet · fast input signals without input filters configuredCorrect the earthing system. Correct bad earthing and unreasonable wiring of high and low voltage. Connect the M terminal of the 24 V DC sensor supply to earth. Increase the input filter delay in the system data block
Communication network damaged when an external device is connected (computer interface, PLC port or PC/PPI cable damaged)If all the non-isolated devices (PLC, computer and others) on a network have no common reference point, the communication cable gives an unwanted current path, which can cause communication errors or damage circuitsCheck the communication network. Use isolated PC/PPI cables. When connecting machines with no common electrical reference point, use an isolated RS-485 to RS-485 repeater
Communication problems—Check the network communication information
Error handling—Check the error code information

The book’s closing advice. The PLC is a highly reliable, stable controller. If it is installed and used to the technical rules, the chance of a fault is very small. But when one does occur, check and deal with it following the steps above. In particular, if damage was caused by an external device’s fault, find out the cause first, and only after the fault has been cleared try running again. Otherwise the new PLC (or the new module) goes the same way.

worked.q: If a PLC output drives an inductive load, what measures are generally taken? (Exercise 12.3)
worked.s: Fit a protective circuit across the load to absorb the voltage spike when the output switches off. For an AC inductive load (a contactor coil): an RC series circuit (snubber) across the coil. For a DC inductive load (a DC solenoid): a diode across the coil, cathode to the positive side (a freewheeling diode). If the load is switched often, choose a transistor or thyristor output. Also fit an external fuse, since the output circuit has none.

worked.q: Describe the types of earthing in a PLC control system and their purpose. (Exercise 12.4)
worked.s: The book’s rules give the main ones. (1) The PLC’s own protective earth: a dedicated wire of at least 2 mm diameter, earth resistance under 100 Ω, not shared with other equipment, all units’ earth wires joined: for personal safety and to give the PLC a clean reference. (2) The shield earth of signal cables: analog input shields to the frame earth FG, analog output shields at the load end; RS-485 shields earthed at one or both ends as the link type requires: to drain interference picked up on the shield. (3) The 0 V (M terminal) of the 24 V sensor supply, connected to earth to reduce interference. (4) Terminal FG of communication boards to the PLC earth. Purpose overall: safety, and keeping interference out of the PLC.

worked.q: Why must a PLC start running only after all its external devices are powered, and how is that ensured?
worked.s: If the PLC ran first, it would read inputs from sensors that are not yet working (giving wrong signals) and drive outputs before the equipment was ready, causing false actions. Ensure it by switching the external devices on first and then moving the mode switch from STOP to RUN, or by programming the PLC to do no I/O until the external devices are confirmed powered.

worked.q: An output of a PLC no longer works after a short circuit in the load wiring. What should be done before fitting a replacement PLC or module?
worked.s: Find and clear the cause: repair the short circuit in the load wiring and check the load. Fit a fuse in the external output circuit, because the PLC’s output circuit has none. Only then fit the replacement and test. Otherwise the new unit would be damaged in the same way.

worked.q: A PLC’s CPU-E lamp lights at random times, worst when a large motor starts. What is likely, and what should be checked?
worked.s: Electrical interference. Check the earthing of the control panel and that the PLC has its own earth; check that high-voltage and low-voltage wiring do not run in parallel or cross in the cabinet; connect the M terminal of the 24 V sensor supply to earth; supply the PLC through an isolation transformer, separately from the motor; and increase the input filter delay if fast spurious signals are being picked up.

topics.title: Primary Equipment in Power Stations and Substations: Ratings and Model Codes
topics.zh: 发电厂、变电所的一次设备：参数与型号

sections.h: Primary equipment and the main wiring diagram
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

In a power station or substation, the equipment that directly takes part in producing, carrying and distributing electrical energy is called primary equipment: generators, main transformers, circuit breakers, disconnectors, busbars, power cables, overhead lines, instrument transformers, surge arresters and so on. Primary equipment connected together in a definite way forms the primary circuit. The drawing that shows how it is connected is the primary wiring diagram, also called the main electrical wiring diagram (main one-line diagram).

The main wiring diagram is one of the essential drawings of every station. It shows the principle of how the primary equipment is connected and arranged. It is the basis for designing the electrical plant, for installing primary equipment, for ordering equipment, for working out the relay protection scheme, and for running the plant and dealing with accidents. Some stations post an enlarged copy on a prominent wall; others use a mimic board. The open/closed state of the switches on the mimic diagram corresponds to the real switches. When the operating arrangement is changed, after the switching operation the mimic is changed at once, so that it always matches what is really running.

Operators must know their own station’s main wiring thoroughly, and be able to make the mimic diagram from it: recognise the graphical and letter symbols, know what the model, specification and main ratings of each piece of equipment mean, and know its use, performance, switching steps and maintenance and inspection items, so as to supply power safely.

By function, primary equipment falls into four groups: energy conversion equipment, switching equipment, conductors, and devices that limit over-current and over-voltage.

Equipment that converts between electrical and mechanical energy: generators, transformers, motors, instrument transformers.

The synchronous generator is the main equipment of a power station, converting mechanical energy into electrical. In thermal and nuclear stations it is a turbo-generator (steam-turbine driven); in a hydro station, a hydro-generator (water-turbine driven).

RatingMeaning
Rated capacity SN or rated power PNThe guaranteed output: the electrical power delivered at the terminals
Rated voltage UNThe highest voltage for long-term safe running. Chinese turbo-generators are rated 0.4, 3.15, 6.3, 10.5, 13.8, 15.75, 18, 20 kV, and so on
Rated current INThe largest continuous working current, normally given as line current
Rated power factor cos φNRated power ÷ rated capacity
Rated frequency fN50 Hz in China
Rated efficiency ηNOutput power ÷ input power at rated conditions

Model codes (read left to right):

ModelLetters and fields
QF□□–□–□Q = (steam) turbine; F = generator; then cooling (blank = air; Q or N = hydrogen-inner-cooled; S or SS = double water-inner-cooled; QS = stator water-inner, rotor hydrogen-inner, core hydrogen); design number; rated capacity (MW); number of poles
TQC–□□–□T = synchronous; Q = turbo-generator; C = Czech-pattern type (仿捷式), air-cooled; then core-diameter number, core-length number; poles
TQN–□–□T = synchronous; Q = turbo-generator; N = hydrogen-inner-cooled; rated capacity (MW); poles
TS□–□/□–□T = synchronous; S = hydro-generator (水); cooling (S = water-inner; blank = air); stator core outer diameter (cm) / stator core length (cm); poles

Example in my words: QFS-300-2 = turbo-generator, double water-inner-cooled, 300 MW, 2 poles (a 3000 r/min machine at 50 Hz).

The power transformer is important equipment in stations and substations. It raises or lowers voltage, and so allows power to be carried economically and distributed sensibly.

Classified byKinds
PhasesSingle-phase, three-phase
Windings per phaseTwo-winding, three-winding
Voltage regulationOff-load tap changing, on-load tap changing
CoolingDry type, oil-immersed (oil-natural, oil + forced air, forced oil circulation)
ConductorCopper winding, aluminium winding

Main ratings. Rated capacity SN (kVA): the guaranteed apparent output in the rated state on the nameplate; for a three-phase transformer, the total of the three phases. Rated voltage UN (kV): U1N is the voltage specified for the primary; U2N is the open-circuit secondary voltage when the primary is at U1N. Rated current IN (A): I1N and I2N, the largest allowed currents in normal working. Rated frequency 50 Hz.

Single-phase: SN = UN IN Three-phase: SN = √3 UN IN

S in kVA, U in kV, I in A.

Model code □□□□–□/□: phases (D = single-phase; S = three-phase; O = auto-transformer, placed first for step-down, last for step-up); cooling (F = forced air; W = water; P = forced oil circulation; D = forced directed oil); L = aluminium winding (copper not shown), S = three-winding (two-winding not shown); design number; rated capacity (kVA) / high-voltage winding rated voltage (kV).

Induction motors turn electrical energy into mechanical. Rated voltage UN: the line voltage applied to the stator at rated conditions. Rated current IN: the stator line current at rated voltage with rated torque on the shaft. Rated frequency 50 Hz. Rated power PN: mechanical output on the shaft. Rated efficiency ηN, rated power factor cos φN, rated speed nN: rotor speed at rated voltage, frequency and output.

PN = √3 UN IN cos φN ηN

Model code Y□□–□□–□: Y = AC induction motor; then S = double squirrel cage, R = wound rotor, O = enclosed, D = multi-speed, Z = crane; Q = high starting torque (2nd letter) or reinforced insulation (3rd letter); design number; frame number; core number; poles.

An instrument transformer is a special transformer that changes the large current or high voltage of the primary circuit into a small current or low voltage. There are current transformers (CT) and voltage transformers (VT). Their uses:

  1. Meters, relays and other secondary equipment can be made small and standard.
  2. The secondary side is electrically isolated from the high voltage of the primary, for the safety of workers.
  3. Low-voltage control cables of small cross-section can be used, which helps measurement and control over long distances.
  4. When the primary circuit is short-circuited, the current coils of secondary equipment are protected from the large current.

Current-transformer connections to meters and relays (after Fig. 1-1 of the book, redrawn).

ConnectionUsed for
(a) Single-phaseA three-phase balanced system: current measurement, overload protection
(b) Three-phase starThree-phase systems: three-phase current, energy, over-current protection
(c) Two-phase incomplete star (V)Three-phase systems: current measurement, energy, over-current protection
(d) Two-phase current differenceThree-phase systems: over-current protection (the relay sees I₁ − I₃)
CTs are classified byKinds
PlaceIndoor (20 kV and below generally) and outdoor (35 kV and above generally)
MountingPost type, wall-bushing type, built-in type, busbar type
InsulationDry, cast-resin, oil-immersed (oil-immersed for outdoors)
Primary turnsSingle-turn, multi-turn
CoresSingle-core, multi-core (each core has its own secondary)
RatiosSingle ratio, multi-ratio

CT model L□□□□–□/□: L = current transformer; 2nd letter: Q = coil type, D = single-turn through type, A = wall-through, B = post, R = built-in, M = busbar, F = multi-turn through, Y = low-voltage, C = porcelain-bushing, X or J = for zero-sequence earth-fault protection; 3rd: W = outdoor, C = porcelain insulation, S = fast-saturating, J or Z = cast-resin, K = plastic-case, G = improved, L = cable-capacitor type (M = busbar, Q = coil); 4th: B = protection class, D = differential protection, Q = strengthened, J = increased capacity; 5th: L = aluminium conductor, D or C or B = for differential protection; then rated voltage (kV) / rated primary current (A).

VTs are classified byKinds
PlaceIndoor, outdoor
PhasesSingle-phase, three-phase (three-phase types are not made for 35 kV and above)
WindingsThree-winding, two-winding. The third winding of a three-winding VT is for insulation monitoring or earth-fault protection
InsulationDry (6 kV and below), cast-resin (3–35 kV indoor), oil-immersed (outdoor), gas-filled (in SF6 fully-enclosed switchgear)

VT model □□□□–□: 1st: J = voltage transformer, Y = capacitor type; 2nd: D = single-phase, S = three-phase, C = single-phase cascade three-winding; 3rd: J = oil-immersed, C = porcelain, Z = cast-resin, G = dry, R = capacitor voltage divider; 4th: J = earth protection, B = with compensating winding, W = three-phase five-limb; then rated voltage (kV).

Connection (book Fig. 1-2)Used for
(a) Single-phase35 kV and below small-earth-current systems where only one line voltage is needed; or a synchronising check (or no-voltage check) signal for the line side that has a source
(b) V–V (open delta, two VTs)Meters and relays connected across each line voltage of a three-phase three-wire system; widely used in small-earth-current systems
(c) Y–y0Meters and relays needing line voltage, and insulation-monitoring voltmeters needing phase voltage
(d) YN, yn, d (“universal” connection)The secondary in yn feeds meters, relays and insulation-monitoring voltmeters that need line voltage; the auxiliary secondary in open delta feeds a voltage relay. Widely used at every voltage level

Why open delta detects an earth fault (my explanation): in a healthy system the three phase voltages add to zero, so the open-delta winding gives almost nothing. When one phase is earthed, the three no longer balance and a residual (zero-sequence) voltage appears across the open corner, operating the voltage relay.

Switching equipment changes the on/off state of a circuit. By function: HV circuit breakers, disconnectors (isolators) and HV fuses.

HV circuit breaker. In normal running it makes and breaks normal load current; on overload it breaks the overload current; on a fault it quickly breaks the short-circuit current. Generator, transformer and line circuits all have breakers, for effective control.

RatingMeaningSelection rule
Rated voltage UNStandard voltage for long-term normal working; describes its insulationUN ≥ UWN (working voltage)
Rated current INLargest current allowed continuouslyIN ≥ Ig max (largest working current)
Rated breaking current IbrNLargest short-circuit current it can reliably break at rated voltage; describes breaking ability. (Rated breaking capacity SbrN is also used)IbrN ≥ I″; SbrN ≥ S″k
Rated making current IcNLargest short-circuit current it can close onto at rated voltage—
Dynamic stability current imaxLargest peak current it can withstandimax ≥ ish(3) (largest three-phase impulse short-circuit current)
Thermal stability current ItCurrent of the t-second thermal test at the factoryIt² · t ≥ Qk (heat effect of the largest short circuit)
Opening time toffFrom the contacts parting to the arc being fully extinguished: inherent opening time + arcing time—
Closing time tonFrom the mechanism receiving the close signal to the moving contact touching the fixed contact—

Breaker model □□–□□/□□□: type (D = bulk-oil, S = minimum-oil, K = air-blast, L = SF6, Z = vacuum, Q = gas-generating, C = magnetic-blow-out); place (N = indoor, W = outdoor); design number; rated voltage (kV); supplementary feature (G = improved, F = separate-phase operation, I, II = form codes); rated current (A); rated breaking current (kA); special-environment code.

Disconnector uses: (1) isolates equipment or lines to be repaired from the supply, for the safety of the repair staff; (2) switches circuits where there is equal potential; (3) makes and breaks permitted small-current circuits, such as a small unloaded transformer, a short unloaded line, a VT circuit. Its ratings: UN ≥ UWN, IN ≥ Ig max, thermal It² t ≥ Qk, dynamic imax ≥ ish(3). It has no breaking-current rating, because it must not break load current. Model G□□–□□/□: G = disconnector; N indoor / W outdoor; design number; rated voltage (kV); special (K = fast-break, G = improved, D = with earthing blade); rated current.

HV fuse: the simplest protective device, connected in series, for short-circuit and overload protection. Indoor fuses are current-limiting; the RN2 and RN6 series, rated 0.5 A, are used only in VT circuits. Outdoor fuses: post type (current-limiting) and drop-out type (non-current-limiting: when the element melts, the tube drops, giving a visible break). Ratings: UN ≥ UWN; IN (of the holder and current-carrying parts) ≥ Ig max; fuse-element rated current IbN must not exceed the fuse’s IN; breaking current IbrN ≥ I″ (current-limiting) or IbrN ≥ Ich (non-current-limiting). Model R□□–□/□: R = fuse; N indoor / W outdoor; design number; rated voltage (kV); rated current (A).

sections.h: Conductors, and over-current and over-voltage limiting devices
sections.b:
Conductors carry electrical energy: busbars and insulators. Busbars collect and redistribute energy; insulators keep conductors insulated from earth and from other equipment.

Busbar materials are copper, aluminium and aluminium alloy. Aluminium or aluminium alloy is generally used; copper is limited to places with a large continuous current where the layout size is especially restricted, or where pollution around the busbar corrodes aluminium badly but copper lightly.

Busbar working currentBusbar used (generator-voltage hard bare busbars)
Up to 2000 AOne rectangular bar per phase
2000–4000 A2 or 3 rectangular bars per phase
4000–8000 AChannel-section busbar
Over 8000 ATubular busbar; water or air can pass inside for cooling

Step-up (collecting) busbars used to be mostly flexible stranded conductors; now 35–500 kV can all use rigid tubular busbars. Insulators holding hard busbars: post insulators and wall bushings.

Limiting devices. Reactors limit short-circuit current: current-limiting reactors are generally NKL series aluminium-wire concrete reactors or FFL series aluminium-wire split reactors. Lightning protection: lightning rods (wires) protect the station’s equipment from direct strokes; surge arresters limit over-voltage on equipment, including induced over-voltage and incoming lightning waves.

Arrester typeUse
Expulsion (tube) arresterIn stations and substations, only for incoming-line protection
Ordinary valve type FSEquipment in small 6–10 kV distribution installations
Ordinary valve type FZTransformer-class equipment in stations and substations
Magnetic-blow valve FCZPower stations
Magnetic-blow valve FCDProtecting rotating machines
Zinc-oxide (metal-oxide)The most advanced over-voltage protection at present; gapless and gapped kinds

Earthing installation: metal earth electrodes buried in the soil plus earthing conductors. Connecting part of a piece of equipment to the earth electrode with a metal conductor is called earthing. Purposes: working earth (the transformer neutral in a solidly earthed system), protective earth (metal enclosures of equipment), lightning-protection earth (lightning rods, arresters).

sections.h: Symbols and letter codes on main wiring diagrams
sections.b:
Table 1-1 of the book gives the graphical symbols; I describe how each looks, since you will meet them on every drawing.

Note the duplicates in the book’s table: GA is listed for both AC generator and induction generator, MA for both AC and induction motor, and TA for both auto-transformer and current transformer. On real drawings, TA almost always means a current transformer.

worked.q: A three-phase transformer is rated 10 000 kVA, 110/10.5 kV. Find the rated primary and secondary currents.
An induction motor: 380 V, 15 kW, cos φ = 0.88, η = 0.89. Find its rated current.

At a 10 kV point the largest working current is 600 A and the initial short-circuit current I″ is 18 kA. Breakers available: 10 kV 630 A 16 kA, and 10 kV 1250 A 25 kA. Which passes the voltage, current and breaking checks?
worked.s: UN = 10 kV ≥ 10 kV: both pass. IN ≥ 600 A: both pass (630 and 1250 A). IbrN ≥ 18 kA: 16 kA fails; 25 kA passes. Choose the 1250 A, 25 kA breaker (and then also check dynamic and thermal stability).

worked.q: Why is a disconnector not used to open a loaded circuit, and what may it switch?
worked.s: It has no arc-quenching ability and so no breaking-current rating; opening load current draws an arc that can burn the blade and injure the operator. It is used to give a visible isolation gap for repair, to switch where there is equal potential, and to make or break the permitted small currents: a small unloaded transformer, a short unloaded line, a VT circuit.

(a) Three-phase, forced-oil-circulation forced-air (F … P) cooled, aluminium winding, 120 000 kVA, HV 220 kV. (b) Current transformer, porcelain-bushing type (C), outdoor (W), for differential protection (D), 110 kV. (c) Voltage transformer, single-phase, oil-immersed, 10 kV. (d) Disconnector, indoor, design 19, 10 kV, 630 A. (My examples, decoded by the book’s tables.)

recap: Equipment that directly takes part in producing and carrying electrical energy is called ___ equipment.
The letter code for a current transformer is ___.

topics.title: Main Wiring: Requirements, Busbar Schemes and Switching Sequences
topics.zh: 电气主接线：基本要求、母线接线形式与倒闸操作

sections.h: Four basic requirements: safe, reliable, economical, convenient
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

The basic requirements for a main wiring scheme can be summed up in four words (eight characters in Chinese): safe, reliable, economical, convenient.

Safety shows mainly in correctly placing disconnectors and correctly drawing their connection. First, a disconnector must be fitted wherever one should be, with none left out. Second, when a disconnector is operated, the time its moving blade is live should be as short as possible: the supply connects to the moving-blade side (book Fig. 1-3(a) correct, (b) wrong).

Reliability. Consider the station’s place and role in the system and the nature and class of its loads. Analyse: (1) when each breaker is under repair, how much is cut off and for how long; (2) when a busbar is faulted or repaired, how much is cut off and for how long; (3) whether the whole station could lose supply. Higher reliability needs more investment and running cost, but loses less through outages, so weigh the funds available against the cost of outages. Reliability can be analysed qualitatively or calculated quantitatively; for reading main wiring diagrams a qualitative analysis is generally enough.

Economy is relative and usually conflicts with reliability and convenience. With ample funds, the economic demand can be relaxed. If two schemes are similar in reliability and convenience, choose the more economical by a concrete economic comparison.

Convenience has three parts. Operation: simple wiring, few switching steps, so mistakes are unlikely; but generally the more reliable the scheme, the more complex the steps, so do not judge a scheme by ease of operation alone; reliability comes first. Dispatching: in normal running the operating mode can be changed easily as dispatch requires, and faults can be cleared quickly. Extension: besides funds and land, whether a station can be extended depends on its wiring; a station that will be extended must have a scheme that allows it.

Of the four, safety is absolute; the other three are related to one another and must be weighed together when analysing a main wiring scheme.

sections.h: Single busbar, and the standard switching sequence
sections.b:
Main wiring forms fall into two groups: with busbars (single busbar, double busbar) and without busbars (unit, bridge, polygon). The busbar (collecting bar) collects and distributes energy.

Unsectioned single busbar (after Fig. 1-4).

Unsectioned single busbar. All sources feed one busbar; all outgoing lines take power from it. Every circuit has a breaker, which makes and breaks it normally and trips it automatically on a fault. There is a disconnector on each side of the breaker, for safety when the breaker is repaired. If there is no source at the far end of a line, the line-side disconnector QS2 may be omitted. The earthing blade QE on the line disconnector can replace a temporary earth when the line is repaired.

Advantages: simple and clear, little equipment, economical, easy to operate and extend, suits packaged switchgear; disconnectors are used only for isolation, not as operating devices, so mal-operation is unlikely. Disadvantages: low reliability, inflexible dispatch: any circuit fault or breaker repair cuts off that circuit; a busbar fault or repair cuts off the whole station; sources can only run in parallel, and a line-side short circuit gives a large current. It must not be the only supply of class I loads. Used for: 6–10 kV switchgear with no more than 5 outgoing lines; 35–60 kV with no more than 3; 110–220 kV with no more than 2.

9. Hang “Do not close — men working on line” on the handle		1. Return the work permit; remove temporary safety measures

The golden rule these show (my summary): to switch off, breaker first, then line-side disconnector, then bus-side; to switch on, the reverse: bus-side, line-side, then breaker. Disconnectors never make or break load current. Opening the line-side one first means that if the breaker were wrongly still closed, the arc is on the line side, where the line protection trips this breaker alone rather than the whole busbar.

sections.h: Sectionalised single busbar and transfer (bypass) busbar
sections.b:
Sectionalised single busbar (after Fig. 1-5).

To avoid a total station outage, the busbar can be divided by a breaker into 2–3 sections, according to the number of sources and their size. The bus-section breaker QFd has a disconnector on each side for its own repair.

Operating modeHow it behaves
Section breaker closed (sections in parallel)A fault on one section: protection trips the section breaker and the source breaker of the faulted section; the healthy section keeps supply. But relay settings become very complex. If one section loses its source, its circuits are fed from the other section through the section breaker
Section breaker open (sections separate)A fault on one section: protection trips that section’s source breaker; the other section works normally. If a section’s source is lost, all its circuits lose supply. To limit short-circuit current, separate running is generally used, with an automatic standby-supply switching device on the section breaker

Advantages: fairly simple, easy to operate, more reliable, easy to extend, more flexible dispatch. Disadvantages: supply reliability still fairly low: repair or fault of any circuit cuts that circuit; repair or fault within a section cuts every circuit on that section. Used widely in 6–10 kV of small and medium stations and in 6–220 kV substations: 6–10 kV with 6 or more outgoing circuits, each section carrying no more than 25 MW; 35–60 kV with 4–8 circuits; 110–220 kV with 3–4 circuits.

Single busbar with transfer busbar (book Fig. 1-6). So that repairing a feeder breaker does not interrupt that circuit, a transfer (bypass) busbar WBP is added, with a bypass breaker QFP and a bypass disconnector QS1P on each feeder. A sectionalised busbar can also have one, needing two bypass breakers; to save money, the section breaker can double as the bypass breaker or vice versa (Fig. 1-7). It raises reliability but takes ground space, adds breakers and disconnectors, lowers economy and complicates operation. Fit it only where feeder breakers may not be taken out for repair: (1) 6–10 kV outdoor switchgear with many overhead lines whose users will not accept an outage for breaker repair; (2) 35 kV generally has none, since important users are mostly double-fed; if needed with a sectionalised busbar, mostly the section breaker doubles as bypass; (3) 110–220 kV sectionalised single busbar should generally have a transfer busbar, preferably with a dedicated bypass breaker.

Substituting the bypass breaker for the line breaker (QFP’s protection already set to WL₁’s settings): (1) check QF₁ of WL₁ closed; (2) fit QF₁’s operating fuse; (3) check QFP open; (4) fit QFP’s closing fuse; (5) close QFP’s bypass-bus-side disconnector QSP2; (6) close its working-bus-side disconnector QSP1; (7) fit QFP’s operating fuse; (8) close QFP to charge the transfer busbar (this tests it: if it is faulty, QFP trips); (9) close WL₁’s bypass disconnector QS1P; (10) open QF₁; (11) check QF₁ open. Note: QS1P is closed while both ends are at equal potential, which a disconnector may do.

Unsectioned double busbar (simplified from Fig. 1-8).

Unsectioned double busbar: two busbars that can back each other up, joined by a bus-coupler breaker, so that repair within the busbar area does not shut down the whole installation. Three operating modes: (1) one busbar working, the other standby, all sources and feeders on the same busbar; (2) the two run separately, sources and feeders spread evenly, coupler open: like a sectionalised single busbar running separately; (3) the two run in parallel, coupler closed: like a sectionalised single busbar running in parallel.

Features: (1) high reliability: apart from a circuit being off for a long time while its breaker is repaired, other repairs or faults cause only partial or total short interruptions; (2) easy dispatch, many flexible modes; (3) easy extension without cutting existing circuits; (4) when needed, a single circuit can be put alone on the standby bus to work or be tested; (5) poorer economy: an extra busbar, twice as many bus disconnectors; (6) operation is complex: changing busbars takes many steps, and a mistake could make or break load current with a disconnector.

Used for: 6–10 kV switchgear when short-circuit current is large and feeders need reactors; 35–60 kV with more than 8 outgoing circuits, or many sources and heavy load; 110–220 kV with 5 or more outgoing circuits, or 4 circuits but an important place in the system.

Working bus: running → repair (bus I running, bus II on hot standby; coupler disconnectors closed, operating fuse in)Double bus in parallel: one bus running → repairBus: repair → running

Why remove the coupler’s operating fuse while changing buses? (my explanation, consistent with the steps): while the bus disconnectors are swapped, the two buses must stay at equal potential through the closed coupler, so that the disconnectors open and close without current. Removing the fuse prevents the coupler from tripping in the middle, which would leave a disconnector breaking load current.

Sectionalised double busbar (Fig. 1-9): the working busbar is split into sections I and II, sources and feeders spread evenly. A standby busbar is always available, so reliability and flexibility are high; but more breakers, poorer economy and complex bus-changing. Widely used for 6–10 kV generator-voltage busbars of small and medium stations; for 220 kV with 10–14 circuits in total, one bus can be sectioned (three sections); with 15 or more, both (four sections); 330–500 kV EHV switchgear with very high reliability needs and 6 or more circuits may also use three or four sections.

Double busbar with transfer busbar (Fig. 1-10): a bypass breaker can replace a feeder breaker under repair. It can be a dedicated bypass breaker, a bypass breaker doubling as coupler, or a coupler doubling as bypass. A sectionalised double bus with transfer bus needs two bypass breakers. Flexible and reliable, but complex, uneconomical and complex to switch. 330–500 kV sectionalised double buses generally have a transfer bus.

sections.h: One-and-a-half breaker, unit, bridge and polygon schemes
sections.b:
One-and-a-half-breaker connection, two strings (after Fig. 1-11).

One-and-a-half breaker (Fig. 1-11): each circuit connects to one busbar through one breaker; between the two circuits on the two busbars is a tie breaker, so three breakers form a “breaker string” between the buses. Two circuits share three breakers, hence “three-halves” or “one and a half breakers per circuit”. Circuits are generally crossed: one incoming and one outgoing on each string, so that if the tie breaker fails, two source circuits are not cut off together. Very reliable and flexible, easy to operate, dispatch and extend; but less economical, a tie-breaker fault interrupts two circuits briefly, and protection is complex. Generally used in 500 kV step-up and step-down substations.

Unit connection. Different main elements (generator, transformer, line) are first connected in series as a unit, which is then paralleled with others. Less reliable and flexible than each element on its own, but it simplifies wiring and layout, reduces protection, and suits construction and commissioning in stages; popular when the system has enough reserve capacity.

  • Line–transformer unit (Fig. 1-12): a substation with only one line and one transformer, no HV busbar; very simple. HV side: a disconnector; a disconnector plus drop-out fuse; or a breaker plus disconnector. Used for rural and customer substations; also line–three-winding-transformer units at 110–220 kV terminal substations (Fig. 1-13).
  • Generator–transformer unit (Fig. 1-14): generator and transformer directly form one unit connected through a breaker to the HV bus; only an auxiliary branch at the generator outlet, no busbar. Simple and economical, small short-circuit current on the generator and transformer LV side; but if either fails or is repaired, the whole unit stops. With many generators, many transformers would be needed, increasing space and cost and complicating layout. Used for sets with high load-utilisation hours, no generator-voltage feeders and large capacity.
  • Extended unit (Fig. 1-15): two generators with one transformer (two-winding, split-winding, or split reactor plus two-winding). Each generator has its own breaker and disconnector, so one can keep running when the other is repaired or faulted. Drawback: if the main transformer fails or is repaired, no generator in the unit can send power. Used with 4 or fewer generators, no or unimportant generator-voltage load, and a unit capacity that is a small share of the system.

Bridge connections (after Fig. 1-16).

Bridge connection: only two transformers and two lines at the same voltage. Fewest breakers; more reliable and flexible than units; easily developed into a single busbar. Advantages: fewest breakers, simple switchgear, low cost, some reliability and flexibility.

Inner bridgeOuter bridge
DrawbackSwitching a transformer (or its fault) affects the line unit on the same side, briefly interrupting it: “inner bridge, inside inconvenient”. Breaker repair also affects the lineSwitching or a fault of a line affects the transformer unit on the same side: “outer bridge, outside inconvenient”. A line fault leaves half the station’s capacity unable to send out
UseHigh utilisation hours, base load in the system, transformers seldom switched, or lines long with a higher fault rate (hydro stations)Low utilisation hours, frequent start/stop, transformers often switched, large through-power, or both lines in a ring network

Polygon (mesh) (Fig. 1-17): the number of breakers equals the total number of source and outgoing circuits; the breakers form a ring, and each circuit connects between two breakers. Number of “corners” = number of circuits = number of breakers (quadrangle, triangle). Advantages: (1) one breaker fewer than a sectionalised single or unsectioned double busbar, yet reliability like a double bus; (2) no busbar faults; (3) a fault on any circuit trips only its two breakers; (4) easy operation, no disconnector mis-operation accidents. Disadvantages: (1) repairing any breaker opens the ring, and another breaker trip then disorders the supply; (2) currents differ greatly between open and closed ring; (3) protection is complex because the mode changes a lot; (4) hard to extend. Used in 110 kV and above switchgear with few circuits and no planned extension; also in small and medium hydro stations.

terms: 一台半断路器（二分之三接线）

worked.q: A 35 kV substation has 3 outgoing lines and supplies only class II and III loads. Suggest a busbar scheme and give the reason.
worked.s: An unsectioned single busbar fits the book’s limit for 35–60 kV (no more than 3 outgoing lines) and is cheapest; since there is no class I load relying on it alone, its low reliability is acceptable. If later a class I load is added, sectionalise the bus (or supply the class I load from two sources).

worked.q: A single-busbar line has QS₁ (bus side), QF, QS₂ (line side). An operator wants to open QS₁ first to take the line out. What is wrong?
worked.s: The breaker QF must be opened first; disconnectors must never break load current. After QF is opened and proved open, open QS₂ (line side) before QS₁ (bus side). If QF were wrongly still closed, an arc at QS₂ is a fault on the line side, cleared by this line’s protection; an arc at QS₁ would be a busbar fault and could shut down the whole bus.

worked.q: Why, in a one-and-a-half-breaker scheme, are a source and a line placed on the same string?
worked.s: If two sources were on one string, a fault of the tie (middle) breaker would cut off both sources at once. Crossing them (one source, one line per string) means a tie-breaker fault cuts at most one source and one line.

worked.q: A hydro station has two transformers and two long 110 kV lines with a fairly high fault rate; the transformers are seldom switched. Inner or outer bridge?
worked.s: Inner bridge: the line breakers are on the line side, so a line fault is cleared by its own breaker without disturbing the transformers. The inner bridge’s weakness (switching a transformer disturbs a line) matters little because the transformers are seldom switched.

worked.q: A quadrangle (four-corner) scheme has 4 circuits. How many breakers? Compare with a sectionalised single busbar for the same 4 circuits.
worked.s: Quadrangle: 4 breakers (corners = circuits = breakers). A sectionalised single busbar needs 4 circuit breakers + 1 section breaker = 5. So the polygon uses one fewer, as the book states, while giving double-bus-like reliability.

topics.title: Reading Real Main Wiring Diagrams: Hydro, Thermal and Substations
topics.zh: 识读实际电气主接线图：水电站、火电厂和变电所

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

  1. A hydro station is built where the water resource is, usually far from the load centre; local load is small or nil, so most energy is sent far at high voltage. So there is often no generator-voltage busbar; generator–transformer unit or extended unit connections are used. Units reduce the switchgear area and make automatic control easier.
  2. The wiring should be as simple as possible, with as few HV switchgear and breakers as possible, laid out compactly to cut excavation and fill in narrow valleys.
  3. The number and size of units are mostly fixed once, and the HV switchgear is built at once without allowing for extension. So besides sectionalised single bus, double bus, double bus with transfer, and one-and-a-half breaker, bridge and polygon schemes are used a lot.
  4. Hydro units start quickly, with little extra loss in starting and stopping, so they often do frequency regulation, peak load and phase modification (synchronous condenser) duty; they start and stop often and operating modes change a lot, so the wiring must be flexible.
  5. Hydro units are easy to control and automate, so the wiring should avoid using disconnectors as operating devices.

sections.h: Reading a small hydro station with local load (book Fig. 1-18)
sections.b:
The book’s worked example: 4 × 1600 kW horizontal-shaft hydro units, a station of minor importance serving local towns and farms. Read it in this order (the method of Table 1-3 below):

What to readWhat the drawing shows
Generator voltageMany units, so a single busbar at 6.3 kV: meets supply needs and is simple and clear
Connections to the systemLines at 35 kV and 10 kV, through two main transformers. 35 kV: only one outgoing line, so a line–transformer unit (simpler, compact outdoor 35 kV switchgear). 10 kV: 3 lines feeding local load and linking the system, unsectioned single busbar, indoor switchgear
Main transformer LV breakersBoth transformers have LV breakers, so a fault on one does not stop the other
Station serviceTwo station-service transformers: one on the generator-voltage bus, one on the 10 kV bus: two independent supplies backing each other
CablesGenerator leads, the 10 kV transformer and station-service transformer leads are all cable
Voltage transformersA VT with residual (open-delta) winding on the 6.3 kV bus, on the 35 kV transformer HV side and on the 10 kV bus: metering, protection, synchronising, insulation monitoring. On each generator lead, two single-phase VTs in V–V: metering, protection, synchronising
Current transformersGenerator circuits: three-phase, for metering and protection (the CTs at the generator outlet and neutral are the same type; the maker’s CTs and excitation transformer serve excitation). 6–35 kV lines: generally two-phase (L1, L3); but a 35 kV line with distance protection (in an unearthed-neutral system) still needs three-phase CTs
ArrestersValve-type arresters on the 35 kV line and the 10 kV bus protect against incoming lightning waves

Some equipment labels on the drawing and how they decode: generator SFW1600-8/1730, 1600 kW, 6.3 kV, 183 A, cos φ = 0.8; breaker SN10-10Ⅰ/630 (minimum-oil, indoor, 10 kV, 630 A); disconnector GN19-10/400; CT LZZB-10 0.5/10P (cast-resin, two secondaries: class 0.5 for metering, 10P for protection); busbar LMY-80×6.3 (rectangular aluminium, 80 × 6.3 mm); main transformer SL9-6300/35, 38.5 ± 5 %/6.3 kV, Uk % = 7.5, Y,d11; 35 kV breaker DW13-35/400 (outdoor bulk-oil); disconnector GW4-35D/600 (outdoor, with earthing blade); VT JDJJ-35; fuse RW10-35; arrester FZ-35.

Check of the generator current (my calculation): I = P/(√3 U cos φ) = 1600/(1.732 × 6.3 × 0.8) ≈ 183 A, as on the label.

sections.h: Small hydro without local load; medium and large hydro
sections.b:
Without local load (Fig. 1-19): 3 × 3000 kW, fairly important in the local grid. Generator voltage: one generator with one main transformer as a unit, the other two with one transformer as an extended unit: simple, compact. Two 35 kV lines: one to a nearby small hydro station, one to a regional substation; the neighbour’s power passes through this station to the substation, so an outer bridge is used (through power). The bridge gives the fewest 35 kV devices, simple outdoor switchgear, and can later become a breaker-sectioned single bus. Two station-service transformers back each other: one on the generator-voltage branch of the unit, one on the common branch of the extended unit, both protected by HV fuses. A VT and valve arrester on each side of the bridge breaker allow the bridge breaker to run open; a single-phase VT on each 35 kV line for synchronising. (Generator label SF3000-22/3250, 3000 kW, 6.3 kV, 344 A, cos φ 0.8: 3000/(1.732 × 6.3 × 0.8) ≈ 344 A ✓.)

A medium hydro station (Fig. 1-20): 4 generators and 2 two-winding transformers form two extended units; the 2 transformers and 2 HV lines form a quadrangle. No busbar, so no busbar faults; repairing any breaker does not stop supply to the system, so reliability is high; changing mode needs breakers only, not disconnectors; one breaker fewer than sectionalised single bus or double bus, no busbar equipment, compact layout.

A large hydro station (Fig. 1-21, 6 × 200 MW): generators in units or extended units; in the extended units the main transformer has a low-voltage split winding taking two generators, which simplifies wiring and limits generator-voltage short-circuit current. 220 kV: double bus with transfer bus; 500 kV: one-and-a-half breaker. An auto-transformer ties the two HV levels; its third winding is the standby station-service supply.

By size and role, thermal stations are regional or local.

Regional thermal stationLocal thermal station
SizeLarge units and total: units mostly 200 or 300 MW, a few 600 MW; total up to 1000 MW, even 2000 MW and moreSmall units and total
LocationAt large coal bases (“pit-head stations”) or where coal transport is easy (coast, river ports); far from load centresNear load centres (city edge)
Where the power goesAlmost all stepped up to a higher voltage and sent to the system; usually no generator-voltage busbarMuch sent at generator voltage (10 kV) to nearby users, some at 35 kV to users a bit farther, the rest stepped up to 110 or 220 kV for the system. If the station fails, the system can feed the local load back
Main wiringMostly generator–transformer units, stepped up to one or at most two voltages. 220–500 kV switchgear in reliable forms: double bus, double bus with transfer, double bus 4 sections with transfer, and one-and-a-half breakerThe generator-voltage bus is very important: sectionalised single bus, double bus, sectionalised double bus. A current-limiting reactor is usually in series with the section breaker; 10 kV feeders generally also have reactors so that light breakers can be used. Higher voltages: single bus, sectionalised single bus or double bus as needed

A medium combined heat-and-power station (Fig. 1-22): total 200–1000 MW, units 50–200 MW, also supplying steam and hot water; built in industrial centres or cities. Two generators on a 10 kV sectionalised double bus (high reliability; generators almost never stop for bus faults). The bus-section breaker has a bus reactor in series and each direct feeder a line reactor, limiting short-circuit current for internal faults and feeder faults, so that light breakers can be used. 10 kV users are nearby, so feeders are cables, avoiding lightning on lines reaching the generators directly. Two three-winding main transformers, each winding on a busbar of a different voltage. 220 kV: unsectioned double bus with a transfer bus on the line side and two dedicated bypass breakers: neither a bus fault nor a breaker repair causes a long outage of any line. The transformer HV breakers are generally repaired together with the transformers, so the transformer side has no transfer bus. 110 kV: sectionalised single bus, normally run separately; important users can be fed by two circuits on different sections.

A regional thermal station (Fig. 1-23): 4 generators each with its own transformer in 4 units: no outage from bus faults, simple generator-voltage wiring and layout. Two units on the 220 kV bus, two on the 500 kV bus. 220 kV: unsectioned double bus with transfer bus and a dedicated bypass breaker; no outage while a breaker is repaired, and not all off when a bus or bus disconnector is repaired. 500 kV: one-and-a-half breaker; much switchgear but far fewer outages. A three-winding auto-transformer ties the two HV levels; its LV winding is also the standby and start-up supply for station service. Overall very reliable, and the operating mode can be changed flexibly.

sections.h: Substations, and the reading report with marks
sections.b:
A 110 kV terminal substation (Fig. 1-24): 2 main transformers, 2 incoming lines, 110/10 kV step-down. 110 kV side: inner bridge; 10 kV side: sectionalised single bus. This is the usual scheme for a step-down substation with 2 transformers and 2 lines: simple, easy to operate, low cost. But a fault on one 10 kV bus section cuts some feeders, so important users must be fed by two circuits from different sections.

A 110 kV regional substation (Fig. 1-25): 110/10 kV, 2 main transformers, all regional load fed by 10 kV lines; the load is heavy, so 4 incoming 110 kV lines. 110 kV: sectionalised single bus. 10 kV: two sets of sectionalised single bus (looks like a four-section bus or a sectionalised double bus). To limit short-circuit current the 10 kV sections run separately, and a split reactor is fitted on each transformer’s LV side, its two arms feeding two sections. The loads on the 10 kV sections should be as equal as possible, so that the split reactor’s losses are not too large and the section voltages do not differ. If short-circuit current is still too large, reactors can be added on the feeders. This 10 kV scheme is used only when short-circuit current must be limited; it is seldom used, and is unsuitable where there are many important users.

Reading-analysis report (book Table 1-3), with its marking scheme: use it as your checklist for any main wiring drawing.

PartItem (weight)Standard

Equipment models (10 %)From each model on the drawing, state its features and ratings and judge briefly whether the choice is sensible
Basic facts of the station (10 %)Total and unit capacity; number and size of main transformers; generator voltage and higher voltages; number of incoming/outgoing circuits at each level; the station’s place and role in the system
Main wiring forms (20 %)Basic forms (20 %)Name the scheme at each voltage, and state its advantages and disadvantages
Equipment provision (20 %)Breakers (5 %)Every side of generators, main transformers, lines and busbars connected to a source must have a breaker
Disconnectors (5 %)(1) Fitted wherever needed (for repair work); (2) drawn correctly
Instrument transformers (5 %)(1) Fitted wherever needed; (2) correct number of CT phases and sets

Reliability (10 %)(1) Can the whole station lose supply? (2) Extent and time of outage when a breaker is repaired; (3) extent and time of outage for a fault or repair of a busbar or bus disconnector; (4) does it meet users’ supply requirements?
Economy (5 %)Given reliability, is the equipment minimal? Is the layout simple and compact?
Convenience (10 %)(1) Operation: are disconnectors used as operating devices; how many steps? (2) Dispatch: can modes be changed easily in normal running; can sources run separately; can faults be cleared quickly? (3) Extension: can generators and line units be added easily?

Reading exercise in the book (Fig. 1-26): the left-bank plant of the Three Gorges project on the Yangtze at Sandouping, Yichang, Hubei, 40 km upstream of Gezhouba. A dam-toe plant with left and right powerhouses, 26 units rated 777.8 MVA each (maximum 840 MVA): 14 on the left bank, 12 on the right. In the flood season it carries base and waist load; out of flood season, peak and waist load; in the dry season units start and stop often. It connects to the system at one level, 550 kV (500 kV class). Generator voltage: generator–transformer units, with 500 kV breakers on the transformer HV side; two unit connections combine into a joint unit, then go into a 500 kV one-and-a-half-breaker scheme. The bus has section breakers dividing the left bank into Left-1 (8 units, 5 lines at 500 kV; one string in the one-and-a-half scheme has double disconnectors) and Left-2 (6 units, 3 lines). Left-1 sends power to Wanxian (Chongqing) and the DC converter station; Left-2 to Jingzhou in central China. Try filling in Table 1-3 for it.

worked.q: Using the book’s method, give a short reading of a station with: 2 × 25 MW generators on a 10.5 kV sectionalised double bus with bus and feeder reactors, two three-winding transformers to 110 kV and 35 kV, 110 kV sectionalised single bus. What kind of station is it?
worked.s: A local thermal (CHP-type) station: generator-voltage bus with direct 10.5 kV feeders and reactors (local load near the plant), stepping the surplus up to 35 and 110 kV. Forms: 10.5 kV sectionalised double bus (very reliable; reactors limit short-circuit current so light breakers fit); 110 kV sectionalised single bus (simple, can run sections separately, important users double-fed from different sections). Check: breakers on every source-connected side; reactors and cables on feeders; VTs on each bus section.

worked.q: Why does a regional thermal station usually have no generator-voltage busbar, while a local one does?
worked.s: A regional station is far from load centres and sends almost everything into the system at high voltage, so generator–transformer units are simplest and avoid busbar faults. A local station supplies a large share directly to nearby users at generator voltage, so it needs a generator-voltage bus to collect and distribute that power.

worked.q: In the 110 kV regional substation with split reactors, why must the loads on the 10 kV sections be kept nearly equal?
worked.s: The split reactor’s two arms are magnetically coupled. With equal currents in the arms, their fluxes largely cancel, so the reactance seen by load current is small: low loss and voltage drop. With unequal loads the cancellation is incomplete, losses rise and the two section voltages differ. In a short circuit on one arm, the coupling is lost and the full reactance limits the current. (The first two sentences are my explanation of the book’s rule.)

worked.q: Using Table 1-3, how many marks are given for checking equipment provision, and what four items are checked?
worked.s: 20 %, 5 % each: breakers (every source-connected side of generators, transformers, lines, buses has one); disconnectors (fitted where needed for repair, drawn correctly); instrument transformers (fitted where needed, correct number of CT phases and sets); surge arresters (complete).
