sections.h: What auxiliary power is, and the loads in a power station
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Auxiliary power (自用电) is the electricity a power station, substation or hydro station uses itself in production and operation. For a power station it is called station service (厂用电) and its drawing the station-service wiring diagram; for a substation, substation service (所用电); for a hydro station, station auxiliary power (站用电).

A power station uses a great deal of energy itself: motors driving machinery that keep the main plant (generators, turbines, boilers) and auxiliary plant working, plus operation, control, testing, repair and lighting. The total is the station-service consumption.

Thermal station sectionMain loads
Coal handlingGrab cranes in the coal yard, bucket conveyors, conveyor belts, magnetic separators, impeller feeders, crushers, screens
BoilerCoal mills, pulverised-coal feeders, induced-draught fans, forced-draught fans, coal feeders, exhausters, flue-gas recirculation fans, rotary air pre-heaters
TurbineCondensate pumps, circulating-water pumps, feed pumps and their oil pumps, de-aerator transfer pumps, hydrogen-cooling water pumps, heating-network pumps, drain pumps, industrial water pumps
Ash handlingAsh-sluicing pumps, slurry pumps, slag crushers, dust-removal water pumps, electrostatic precipitators
ElectricalWater pumps for water-inner-cooling, transformer cooling fans and forced-oil circulation, water-cooling supply, battery charging and floating chargers, standby excitation supply
Chemical treatmentClear-water pumps, demineralised-water pumps, CO2-removal fans, brine pumps, tank stirrers
CommonMachine tools in the central repair shop, cranes, lighting
Hydro station sectionMain loads
Unit auxiliariesOil-pressure units, oil pumps for governing and bearing lubrication, water pumps for water-inner cooling, turbine head-cover drainage pumps, transformer cooling equipment, oil-leakage pumps
Whole-station commonPowerhouse cranes, fast gate hoists, tail-water gate cranes, battery charging and floating chargers, oil filters, air compressors, central repair shop tools, station lighting

By the role of the equipment in production, and how much a sudden loss of supply would harm production (i.e. by importance):

ClassDefinitionExamplesSupply
Class IA short outage (including the time to restore supply by manual switching) would endanger people or equipment, stop a unit or cut output sharplyThermal: motors of feed pumps, condensate pumps, pulverised-coal feeders. Hydro: unit bearing lubrication oil or water pumps, main-valve oil-pressure pumps or motors, turbine head-cover drainage pumps, cooling fans of thyristor rectifiersGenerally two sets backing each other, on two independent supplies; when one supply fails the other is put in automatically at once
Class IIA short outage is allowed, but a longer one could damage equipment or affect normal running of the unitThermal: coal handling, industrial water, drain and slurry pump motors, chemical treatment. Hydro: most auxiliary load of the main units and transformers, seepage drainage pumps, spillway gate hoists of run-of-river stationsGenerally from two bus sections, with manual changeover
Class IIIA long outage does not directly affect power productionCentral repair shop, laboratory, oil treatment roomGenerally one supply
Emergency (safety) loadMust still be supplied while the generator shuts down and for a time after, or equipment will be damaged, important automatic control lost, or people endangered(1) DC safety load from the battery, e.g. the generator’s DC lubrication oil pump. (2) AC safety load: normally from the AC station-service system; on loss of normal supply, generally a fast-starting diesel generator, e.g. turning-gear motors of 200 MW and larger unitsBattery; diesel set
Uninterruptible (UPS) loadNeeds continuous supply with constant frequency and voltage from start-up through running to shut-down and for a time afterReal-time computer controlA motor-generator set fed from a battery, or a static inverter with a static switch

Other features of station-service loads: by control location, local or from the control panel; interlock required or not; by duty, continuous regular, continuous irregular, short-time regular, short-time irregular, intermittent regular, intermittent irregular.

Station-service wiring must consider operation, maintenance and construction, adopt new technology and equipment actively but carefully, and be economical and technically advanced, so that units run safely and economically. Requirements:

  1. Each unit’s station-service system should be independent, especially for 200 MW and larger units: a unit tripping or a fault in its auxiliaries must not affect another unit, and the unit should be restorable in a short time.
  2. Consider supply during start-up and shut-down: generally provide a reliable start-up (standby) supply, with few switching operations during start, stop and accidents, able to run briefly in parallel with the working supply.
  3. Consider how the system runs during staged construction and continuous building: especially supply to common loads; transitions should be easy, with few wiring changes and little equipment replacement.
  4. 200 MW and larger units need an AC emergency safety supply of enough capacity; on total station blackout it must start quickly and switch in automatically. An AC uninterruptible supply of acceptable quality is also needed for loads like thermal instruments that may not be interrupted.
Motor rated voltage (V)2203803000600010 000
Capacity range (kW)< 140< 300> 75> 200> 200

Prefer the lower voltage where it meets the need; only a few large motors use high voltage. Station-service voltages should be few: generally two levels, low 0.4 kV (380/220 V) and high one of 3, 6 or 10 kV. Very large units (e.g. 600 MW) may use two high levels.

Generator (MW)Generator voltage (kV)Service voltage high/low (kV)Motor size high/low (kW)
60 and below10.53/0.38above 100 / below 100
above 606.36/0.38above 200 / below 200
100–20010.5, 13.8, 15.756/0.38above 200 / below 200
300 and above186/0.38above 200 / below 200
300 and above203 or 10/0.38200–1800 or above 1800 / below 200
Most small and medium hydro6.3, 10.5, 13.8—/0.38— / below 200; up to 245 where starting is not difficult

From practice: (1) 3 kV high voltage: thermal units of 60 MW and below at 10.5 kV; motors above 100 kW at 3 kV, below 100 kW at 380 V. (2) 6 kV: units 100–300 MW; motors above 200 kW at 6 kV, below at 380 V. (3) 3 kV and 10 kV: units above 300 MW, e.g. 600 MW; below 200 kW at 380 V, 200–1800 kW at 3 kV, above 1800 kW at 10 kV. (4) No high level: hydro stations have few, small auxiliary machines, usually only 380/220 V; if the dam area has large machines (gate hoists, ship locks or lifts), a dedicated dam-area transformer supplies 6 or 10 kV.

A substation uses far less than a power station of the same size. In a manned local substation the loads are: main-transformer cooling fans, battery chargers or rectified operating supply, ventilation and heating, water pumps, breaker oil heaters, lighting and maintenance power. For small and medium substations the total is generally about 20 kVA, usually one substation-service transformer connected Y, yn12, stepping 6–10 kV down to 380/220 V three-phase four-wire.

Large and medium regional substations, especially with large synchronous condensers, have more, and more important, loads: oil and water pumps of forced-oil-circulation transformer cooling, air compressors (with air-blast breakers), the transformer repair bay, condenser air-cooling and lubrication pumps. The total is generally 215–560 kVA, but reliability needs are high: two independent supplies.

  1. Hub substations, substations of 60 MVA and above total capacity, those with water-cooled or forced-oil-cooled main transformers, and those with synchronous condensers have two substation-service transformers. Substations with rectified operating supply or unmanned have two, on different voltage levels or two independent supplies. If a reliable 380 V standby can be brought in from outside, one transformer is enough.
  2. 500 kV substations have two working supplies; with two main transformers, one on the tertiary winding of each. The two transformers are of equal size, each chosen for the whole calculated load, backing each other. With a reliable outside supply, add a standby transformer of the same size; otherwise a self-starting diesel set as standby.
  3. Where there is a standby transformer, there is generally an automatic standby-supply switching device.

Thermal and hydro station service must be reliable: besides the normal working supply there must be a standby or start-up supply; stations with 200 MW and larger units also need an AC emergency safety supply.

Possible sources in a grid-connected hydro station: its own running units and the connected power system; also an outside distribution network (e.g. a construction supply kept on), a neighbouring station, even a dedicated small unit. Each must be reliable and big enough. The point where the station-service transformer’s HV circuit connects to the HV network is the tapping point (引接点). Reliability depends largely on the tapping point; the tapping point itself is not a source, but connects to one or more sources, so its reliability depends on them and on the main wiring and its operating mode.

One station-service transformer on a tapping point makes one supply. Any supply can fail (tapping point loses power, or the transformer fails), so there should be two: working and standby. The standby should normally be independent: through a different transformer from an independent tapping point. Two transformers taken from the same single bus section are not two independent supplies.

Standby modeHow it works
Open (explicit) standby 明备用The standby is de-energised in normal running and put in only when the working supply fails
Concealed (implicit) standby 暗备用Both supplies run normally, each carrying half the load, each keeping some spare capacity; if one fails the other takes the whole load. Mutual backup between two working supplies; the most widely used in small and medium hydro stations

Typical arrangements in small and medium hydro stations (Fig. 2-1), three kinds:

  1. Two station transformers, tapped from the generator-voltage bus groups or sections, through disconnectors and HV fuses, concealed standby (Fig. 2-1 (a), (b)); with open standby, breakers should be the operating and protective devices. Grouped or sectioned generator-voltage buses (except a single bus sectioned by a disconnector and run in parallel) are both normally live and cannot both be lost from one electrical fault: ideal independent tapping points. If one section’s units stop, the section can be back-fed from the main transformer; if all stop, both sections can be fed back by the two main transformers. To keep two independent supplies, both generator-voltage sections normally stay in service; both main transformers generally also; with a breaker-sectioned single bus, one main transformer may be taken out in a particular mode, e.g. units of section 1 with the main transformer of section 2.
  2. Two station transformers: one on a generator-voltage bus section (inner tapping point), the other on a transmission line to a reliable source (e.g. the grid) or the HV-side bus (outer tapping point), protected by fuses, concealed standby (Fig. 2-1 (c), (d)). Two fully independent supplies, the system back-feeding station service; for run-of-river stations that often shut down completely, this saves the main transformers’ no-load loss and reactive power.
  3. One station transformer on the inner tapping point as the working supply, the open standby taken directly from a nearby LV network. If that network is fed from a local transformer on the same generator-voltage bus section, it is not an independent standby; if fed from a local transformer on the step-up side or from another outside supply, it is independent, like (2). Check the LV network’s reliability so that it really works as a standby.

Working supply: keeps each station-service bus section working normally; it must be reliable and meet the section’s power and voltage needs. How it is tapped is closely tied to the main wiring.

  • HV working supply. With a generator-voltage bus: tapped from that bus (Fig. 2-2 (a)). A 12 MW unit on a 6 kV main bus whose feeders have no reactors: HV motors and LV service transformers may connect directly to the main bus without a separate HV service bus (Fig. 2-2 (b)); some tap from the generator outlet (Fig. 2-2 (c)). With generator–transformer units: from the main transformer’s LV side (Fig. 2-3 (a)–(f); (e) uses a split-winding service transformer, (f) two service transformers in parallel). With an extended unit: from the generator outlet or main-transformer LV side (Fig. 2-3 (g)).
  • LV working supply: from the HV service bus section through an LV service transformer. Without an HV service bus: from the generator-voltage main bus or the generator outlet. Where service buses are sectioned by boiler, each working transformer is fed from the matching HV section.

Standby (start-up) supply. The standby keeps station service supplied when the working supply is lost in an accident (also called the accident standby); it must be reliable and big enough. The start-up supply feeds the auxiliaries needed to start a unit quickly when the working supply is completely gone; it is really a standby with higher reliability demands. Only stations with units of 200 MW and above have a separate start-up supply that doubles as standby; with 125 MW and below, the standby doubles as start-up supply.

SituationWhere the HV standby is tapped
Generator-voltage bus, 6.3 kVGenerally directly from the main bus through a reactor; or from a 35 kV bus if there is one
Generator-voltage bus, 10.5 kV, with a 35 kV bus having two sourcesFrom the 10.5 or 35 kV bus. If no 35 kV bus, or only one source on it, from the 10.5 kV bus
Units, with two or three step-up buses (550 & 220, or 220 & 110, or 220, 110 & 35 kV)From the lowest-voltage bus connected to the system (Fig. 2-4 (a)). If the station 35 kV bus is not tied directly to the system but has two station sources or a link through three-winding transformers, still from the 35 kV bus (b), (c)
With a tie transformerFrom the tie transformer’s LV winding (d)
Only one or two step-up buses, and a reliable lower-voltage network nearby that can still supply when the whole station is downA dedicated line from that network; if needed a standby bus section feeding two or more standby transformers (e)
Generator–transformer–line unit to a regional substationA dedicated line from the substation’s lower-voltage bus (f)

Large units with generator-circuit breakers (Fig. 2-5): (1) if the generator breaker costs about the same as (or less than) a start-up transformer with its HV and LV switchgear, omit the dedicated start-up transformer: the main transformer feeds start-up power through the working service transformer (a); drawback: no standby. (2) No dedicated standby transformer; breakers at both generator outlets, working service transformers enlarged to back each other (b). (3) Two service transformers per unit, one serving as the other unit’s standby (start-up) supply and also feeding common loads (c). (4) Without a dedicated standby, a station-wide standby transformer can back several units. With two HV standby supplies, tap them from relatively independent sources: different bus sections of one voltage with different sources; buses of different voltages; or a bus and the tie transformer’s third winding.

LV standby: (1) avoid putting the LV standby transformer on the same HV service bus section as the LV working transformers it backs, or both lose supply when that section fails; (2) for 200 MW and above, take it from the normally energised HV standby (start-up) transformer; if the HV standby is a reactor, from the normally energised reactor; (3) if feeders on the generator LV bus have no reactors, it may be taken from that bus, but not the same bus as the working transformers it backs.

Emergency safety supply (large units, when both working and standby are lost, to shut down safely and restore supply quickly afterwards), three kinds: (1) a reliable outside independent supply: a dedicated line from the outside system, still reliable during a long total-station outage; usually high voltage, far away, costly. (2) A battery: independent and very reliable; supplies DC safety loads (lubrication oil pumps, hydrogen seal-oil pumps, emergency lighting) and, through an inverter or inverter-motor set, AC loads that cannot be interrupted (computers, thermal instruments, automatic devices); but present batteries are at most 1000 Ah, so they cannot carry much load and supply time cannot exceed 1 h. (3) A diesel generator set, widely used, sized for the safety loads; large sets need much cooling water, so a sufficient source must be ensured; maintain regularly, test-run periodically, always ready to start (Fig. 2-6: two working supplies through automatic switches to the 380/220 V safety bus, the diesel set as a third, DC 220 V via inverter to the 220 V instrument and automatic-device bus).

worked.q: A 300 MW unit has a 20 kV generator. Using the book’s Table 2-2, what station-service voltages would you expect, and at what voltage would a 1500 kW and a 2500 kW motor run?
worked.s: Table 2-2 row “300 and above, 20 kV”: service voltages 3 or 10 / 0.38 kV; motors 200–1800 kW on 3 kV, above 1800 kW on 10 kV, below 200 kW on 380 V. So the 1500 kW motor on 3 kV and the 2500 kW motor on 10 kV (if the two-level 3 + 10 kV arrangement is used).

worked.q: A hydro station has two station transformers, both connected to the same single (unsectioned) 6.3 kV bus. Do they give two independent supplies? What would you change?
worked.s: No. The book says two transformers from the same single bus section are not two independent supplies: a bus fault cuts both. Connect one to a different bus section or group, or to an outer tapping point (a line to the grid or the HV bus), or take an open standby from an independent LV network.

worked.q: Classify: (a) a thermal plant’s boiler feed pump; (b) the central repair shop; (c) a coal conveyor; (d) the turning-gear motor of a 300 MW unit; (e) the plant computer control system.
worked.s: (a) Class I; (b) Class III; (c) Class II; (d) AC emergency safety load (diesel set); (e) uninterruptible load (battery-fed inverter with static switch, or motor-generator set).

worked.q: Explain the difference between open and concealed standby, and say which is most used in small and medium hydro stations.
worked.s: Open standby: the standby supply is idle (de-energised) and switched in only when the working one fails. Concealed standby: both supplies work, each carrying half the load with spare capacity, and either takes the whole load if the other fails. Concealed standby is the most widely used in small and medium hydro stations.

Class ___ loads need two supplies with automatic changeover.
A small substation’s service load is about ___ kVA.

topics.title: Auxiliary Power Busbars, and Reading Real Auxiliary Wiring Diagrams
topics.zh: 自用电母线接线形式与实际自用电接线图的识读

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

  1. If the substation has a lower-voltage bus, 1–2 substation-service supplies are generally tapped from it (book Fig. 2-7 (a), (b)): economical and reliable. If two supplies can be taken from buses or lines of different voltage levels, uninterrupted substation service is better assured (Fig. 2-8 (a): one transformer on the 35 kV bus side through an HV line, the other on the 6–10 kV bus).
  2. With a transfer (bypass) busbar, one service transformer can be connected through a bypass disconnector to the transfer bus (Fig. 2-7 (c)): normally fed from the working bus; when the working bus is repaired or tested, changed over to the transfer bus.

Fig. 2-8 (b), a substation with a synchronous condenser: two 400 kVA, 10/0.4 kV service transformers, No. 1 from the main-transformer LV side (through a reactor) and No. 2 from a 10 kV line to a 110 kV substation; a separate 1250 kVA condenser-starting transformer.

Station-service busbars are usually single busbars. In a thermal station, boilers have many large auxiliaries, so the service buses are sectioned by boiler, each section feeding that boiler’s motors; the motors of the turbine in the same group are on the matching section. Both HV and LV service buses are sectioned by boiler. Benefits: (1) a fault on one section stops only one boiler; (2) a boiler’s auxiliaries and their motors can be repaired while the boiler is down; (3) sections run apart, limiting short-circuit current. Large boilers have two sections.

Boiler (t/h)HV service busLV service busMain-building lighting bus (independent)
65Two boilers share one section, split into two half-sections by a disconnectorTwo boilers share one section (where the boiler has no class I load), split in two by a knife switch—
120–220One section per boilerOne per boiler (with class I loads), split in two by a knife switchOne section per two units
400–670Two sections per boiler, fed by one transformer; the two sets of auxiliary motors split between themTwo per boiler; with few class I loads, one section split in two by a knife switchOne section per unit; each fed by one lighting transformer, two lighting transformers backing each other
≥ 1000Each HV level has two sectionsTwo per boiler, each fed by one transformerAs above

Common service sections. Large units have many and large common loads. With sensible centralised supply, separate the station-wide common loads from the units’ own loads and feed them from dedicated common sections: (1) strengthens the unit principle; (2) helps manage common loads centrally; (3) makes it easier to repair or stop a unit and its service switchgear. Common sections are generally on both HV and LV sides; with many units, two sections, plus special common sections for lighting, repair shop, coal yard, etc.

Basic requirements: safe and reliable, economical, easy to maintain and operate. Each section must have its own independent working supply and be connected to the standby, for reliability.

  • HV service buses (Fig. 2-9). (1) One HV section per boiler: sections may be unconnected, each linked to its working supply and to the standby (a); or two boilers’ sections may be joined by a breaker or disconnector to back each other (b), (c). (2) Two HV sections per boiler: each has its own independent working supply and standby (d); the two may also be joined by a breaker or disconnector (e), (f). Normally the standby breaker is open and an automatic standby-switching device is fitted.
  • LV service buses (Fig. 2-10). (1) One LV transformer per LV section: each section connected to the standby, with automatic switching (a); or manual switching without it (b); or no standby, the two sections tied by an automatic air circuit-breaker with automatic switching, backing each other (c). (2) One LV transformer with two LV sections: both sections connected to the transformer and to the standby, each section separately (d); or the two sections joined by a disconnector, one taking the LV transformer and the other the standby (e). The standby has automatic switching, which can be changed to manual.

sections.h: Small and medium hydro-station auxiliary wiring
sections.b:
Sectionalised single bus (Fig. 2-11 (a)): with two station transformers tapped from generator-voltage bus sections or groups, or one from a generator-voltage bus (inner tapping point) and one from a line to a reliable source or the HV bus (outer tapping point), a sectionalised single bus generally suits. The two transformers connect to the two independent tapping points through HV fuses and disconnectors; on the LV side, through automatic switches (like breakers in an HV circuit) and knife switches (like disconnectors), to the two main bus sections. The section automatic switch is normally open; if one supply is lost, it closes and the other supply takes the whole load: concealed standby. For urgent restoration of class I loads, an AAT (automatic standby-supply switching) device should be fitted, speeding the change and avoiding hasty manual mistakes. The two supplies must not be paralleled on the LV side.

Why fuses replace HV breakers: (1) with concealed standby, once the transformers are in service the HV side seldom needs operating, never under load; if needed, a transformer of 315 kVA or less can be switched off-load by the HV disconnector, load being switched by the LV automatic switch; (2) fuses meet the working and breaking capacity of small stations’ transformer circuits; (3) the primary circuit is simpler and no relay protection is needed; (4) small-section HV cable can be used with no thermal-stability problem.

CTs on the transformer LV side serve metering and over-current and overload protection. Besides over-current protection, the automatic switch is used to put load on and off the transformer in normal running, and, with AAT, to disconnect the dead transformer before the standby is put in, so that the LV side does not back-energise (step up into) the transformer.

Unsectioned single bus (Fig. 2-11 (b)): small stations, e.g. below 2000 kW, often have one station transformer on the inner tapping point; when the working supply fails, the open standby from the LV network is changed over manually.

Book figureWhat it shows
Fig. 2-12: medium hydro, 2 × 36 MW, LV onlyTwo generators share one step-up transformer (extended unit); two SJ-420/10 service transformers back each other. The station does peak-load duty, so to back-feed service from the system when the whole station is stopped, one transformer is tapped at No. 1 generator terminals and the other on the main-transformer LV side. All service load at 0.4/0.23 kV, no HV motors. Unit auxiliaries and important loads cross-fed from both sections; common loads directly from the service bus. Few units, so centralised supply with no unit-side panels; LV switchboards near the units on the generator floor
Fig. 2-13: 4 × 110 MW, two levels6 kV and 0.4 kV. Two HV service transformers (SGL-1800/15.75, 1800 kVA) from the main-transformer LV sides of the extended units, backing each other. Two LV unit-auxiliary transformers fed from 6 kV sections I and II supply the four unit-side panels, backing each other. Two more LV transformers feed 0.4 kV common sections I and II, also backing each other
Fig. 2-14: regional substation with synchronous condensers10, 110 and 220 kV; two 11 kV condensers G1, G2 on the LV sides of the two main transformers. A condenser is a synchronous machine built exactly like a generator but without a prime mover; it produces no active power, only reactive, balancing the network’s reactive demand and improving power factor; it has a motor for starting. Each condenser connects to a 10 kV section by two circuits, one with a reactor: when the starting condenser nears synchronous speed it is put on through the reactor, which is shorted once fully synchronised. Two HV service working transformers T1, T2 on the two 10 kV sections; HV service bus split by condenser into 6 kV sections I and II, joined by a normally open section breaker; condenser motors on each section, with LV working transformers T3, T4. Standby transformer T5 from the outside 35 kV system to 380/220 V sections I and II. Condenser auxiliaries are mostly LV motors fed from the 380/220 V buses
Fig. 2-15: medium thermal, 2 units, 3 boilers, 2 × 50 MW, 10.5 kV6 kV HV service bus single, sectioned by boiler into three, fed by three 5600 kVA 10.5/6.3 kV HV service transformers. Open standby: a dedicated No. 0 standby HV transformer, also 5600 kVA, normally off. Units not large, so no separate start-up or emergency supply. When a 6 kV working section loses supply, the AAT closes the corresponding breaker and the standby transformer takes over. 6 kV motors fed directly from the 6 kV bus; 560 kVA LV transformers feed 380/220 V sections I and II and the unit workshop panels

Book exercises (2.7): read Fig. 2-16, station service of a 4 × 100 MW thermal station; Fig. 2-17, substation service of a 110 kV substation; Fig. 2-18, station service of a 200 MW thermal unit (main building).

worked.q: In Fig. 2-12 (2 × 36 MW peak-load hydro station), why is one service transformer tapped at a generator terminal and the other on the main-transformer LV side?
worked.s: Because the station does peak-load duty it is often completely stopped. Tapping one transformer on the main-transformer LV side lets the system back-feed station service through the main transformer when all units are stopped, while the other at a generator terminal is supplied whenever that unit runs. The two taps are relatively independent, so they back each other.

worked.q: Why must the automatic switch on the LV side of a dead station transformer be opened before the AAT closes the standby?
worked.s: Otherwise the standby supply would feed back through the closed LV switch into the dead transformer, energising it from the LV side (“stepping up” into it) and possibly back to the HV side, with a large inrush and hazard. Opening the LV switch first isolates the dead transformer.

worked.q: A thermal station has 3 boilers of 220 t/h. Using Table 2-3, how many HV and LV service sections would you expect, and how is the main-building lighting bus arranged?
worked.s: 220 t/h falls in the 120–220 row: one HV section per boiler (3) and one LV section per boiler (3), each LV section split into two halves by a knife switch where class I loads are connected. Lighting: one section per two units.

topics.title: Switchgear Installations: Types, Safety Clearances and Indoor Layouts
topics.zh: 配电装置：类型、安全净距与屋内配电装置

sections.h: What switchgear installations are, and what they must achieve
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

A switchgear installation (配电装置) is the complete assembly, built to the main wiring diagram, of switching devices, protective and measuring devices, busbars and the necessary auxiliary structures. Normally it receives and distributes energy; on a fault it quickly cuts out the faulty part and restores normal running.

  1. Reliable running: choose equipment correctly, with sensible ratings; strengthen maintenance, repair, preventive testing and other safety measures for operation.
  2. Safety of workers: partition walls between adjacent circuits so equipment can be repaired safely; fences and safe distances against touching live parts; suitable safety exits; protective earthing of enclosures and bases; fire protection in the building structure.
  3. Easy operation and maintenance: operation concentrated, so an operator need not climb several floors or walk several corridors to operate one circuit; neat, clear structure and layout for patrol and repair; easy to move equipment.
  4. Economy: given the above, keep cost low, save land, steel, cement and non-ferrous metals; easy construction, less labour, shorter construction.
  5. Room to extend, if the station may be developed.

Classification: by location, indoor and outdoor; by assembly, site-assembled and packaged (metal-enclosed) switchgear assembled in the factory.

IndoorOutdoorPackaged (metal-enclosed)
Features(1) Small clearances allowed, can be built in storeys: small area. (2) Repair, operation, patrol done indoors, not affected by weather. (3) Polluted air does not affect equipment, less maintenance. (4) Building costs more; but 35 kV and below can use cheaper indoor-type equipment(1) Less civil work and cost, quick to build. (2) Easy to extend. (3) Large distances between equipment, convenient for live working. (4) Large area. (5) Equipment in the open, poorer conditions, needs stronger insulation. (6) Weather affects maintenance and operation(1) Equipment in closed or semi-closed metal cases; phase and earth distances can be reduced; compact, small area. (2) Much less site installation; quicker to build; easy to extend and move. (3) Reliable, easy to maintain. (4) More steel, higher cost

Where used: in large and medium power stations, 35 kV and below is generally indoor, packaged switchgear mostly indoors too; 110 kV and above mostly outdoor. In heavily polluted areas, 110 kV and even some 220 kV is built indoors. 3–35 kV packaged switchgear is widely used in large and medium stations and substations; 110–500 kV SF6 gas-insulated switchgear (GIS) is increasingly used.

LayoutFeaturesUsed for
Outdoor, ordinary low (medium) typeNo equipment under the busbars; easy to build, run and maintain; large areaMostly 330–500 kV; 110–220 kV where land is poor or seismic intensity is 8 or above
Outdoor, split-phase low typeOne set of bus disconnectors split into phases A, B, C, each placed under its busbar: no complex two-level gantries, clear layout, saves 20–30 % landCan be used for 220 kV generally; 110 kV gantries are low and single-column disconnectors scarce, so seldom used
Outdoor, semi-highBusbars raised, breakers, CTs and disconnectors under them; compact, saves land, but repair conditions poorer. Steel: about 5 % more than ordinary at 220 kV; at 110 kV saves compared with ordinary110–220 kV where land is scarce or space narrow; especially preferred for 110 kV
Outdoor, highTwo sets of busbars and bus disconnectors stacked one above the other; saves land, about 50 % at 220 kV; compact, easy patrol and operation; but much steel, construction and maintenance inconvenient, investment as ordinary110–220 kV where land is especially scarce
Indoor and packagedSaves much land, keeps out polluted air; needs damp, rust and small-animal protection; complex building; above 110 kV indoor costs more than outdoor; packaged switchgear very reliable6–10 kV widely indoor and packaged (low voltage); 35 kV generally indoor; 110 kV in class 2+ polluted areas or city areas; 220 kV where technically and economically sensible
SF6 GISArea greatly reduced, generally 2–10 % of ordinary low type; little maintenance, long repair interval, safe; free from pollution and altitude effects; but high investment, maintenance troublesome110–500 kV in city centres, underground, hydro stations, very narrow sites or very harsh environments

sections.h: Safety clearances A, B, C, D, E
sections.b:
The overall dimensions of an installation are set by the equipment sizes and by the safe distances needed for maintenance and transport. Clearances fall into five kinds, A, B, C, D, E (book Figs. 3-1, 3-2). The most basic is A: the smallest air distance between live parts of different phases, and between live parts and earthed parts, at which the air gap will not break down either at the highest normal working voltage or under internal or external over-voltage. The others are built on A by adding practical allowances.

SymbolIndoor table (mm) — rated kV: 3 · 6 · 10 · 15 · 20 · 35 · 60 · 110J · 110 · 220J
A1: live to earthed parts; mesh or solid fence extended up to 2.3 m from the ground, to live parts above the fence75 · 100 · 125 · 150 · 180 · 300 · 550 · 850 · 950 · 1800
A2: live parts of different phases; across the open gap of a breaker or disconnector75 · 100 · 125 · 150 · 180 · 300 · 550 · 900 · 1000 · 2000
B1: grille fence to live parts; crossing unfenced live parts not de-energised together for repair825 · 850 · 875 · 900 · 930 · 1050 · 1300 · 1600 · 1700 · 2550
B2: mesh fence to live parts (for a solid plate fence, 70 mm less)175 · 200 · 225 · 250 · 280 · 400 · 650 · 950 · 1050 · 1900
C: unfenced bare conductor to floor2375 · 2400 · 2425 · 2450 · 2480 · 2600 · 2850 · 3150 · 3250 · 4100
D: parallel unfenced bare conductors not de-energised together for repair1875 · 1900 · 1925 · 1950 · 1980 · 2100 · 2350 · 2650 · 2750 · 3600
E: outgoing bushing to the road of an outdoor passage4000 · 4000 · 4000 · 4000 · 4000 · 4000 · 4500 · 5000 · 5000 · 5500
SymbolOutdoor table (mm) — rated kV: 3–10 · 15–20 · 35 · 60 · 110J · 110 · 220J · 330J · 500J
A1: live to earthed; mesh or solid fence extended to 2.5 m, to live parts above200 · 300 · 400 · 650 · 900 · 1000 · 1800 · 2500 · 3800
A2: between phases; across breaker or disconnector gap200 · 300 · 400 · 650 · 1000 · 1100 · 2000 · 2800 · 4300
B1: outline of equipment during transport to unfenced live parts; crossing unfenced live parts not de-energised together; grille fence to insulators and live parts; live-working live part to earthed part950 · 1050 · 1150 · 1400 · 1650 · 1750 · 2550 · 3250 · 4550
B2: mesh fence to live parts300 · 400 · 500 · 750 · 1000 · 1100 · 1900 · 2600 · 3900
C: unfenced bare conductor to ground; to the top of buildings and structures2700 · 2800 · 2900 · 3100 · 3400 · 3500 · 4300 · 5000 · 7500
D: parallel unfenced bare conductors not de-energised together; live parts to the edge of buildings and structures2200 · 2300 · 2400 · 2600 · 2900 · 3000 · 3800 · 4500 · 5800

“J” means a solidly earthed neutral system. Distances used in practice are usually larger than these tables.

A pattern worth noticing (my own observation from the tables; it helps you remember them): B1 = A1 + 750 mm (the reach of an arm); B2 = A1 + 100 mm (a finger through the mesh); D = A1 + 1800 mm; C = A1 + 2300 mm indoors (a person’s reach upward) and A1 + 2500 mm outdoors. These hold for every column except outdoor 500 kV C (7500 mm), which is set by other factors.

sections.h: How an installation is made up, and its drawings
sections.b:
Bays. An installation is built like building blocks from many bays (配电间隔), the smallest unit. For safety and reliability bays must be relatively independent: with neighbouring bays live, any bay can be de-energised for repair of its main equipment; a fault in a bay should be confined to it and not spread. Bays correspond roughly to the connection units of the main wiring: the main ones are incoming and outgoing bays (sometimes all called outgoing bays); there are also extra bays such as VT–arrester bays, bus-section bays, bypass bays, de-icing bays. Main bays are sometimes called generator, transformer and line bays.

Arrangement. (1) Row arrangement: all bays in one row (single row: long and narrow) or two rows (double row: short and wide). Order: match the geography of the real incoming and outgoing lines to avoid crossing overhead lines; and reduce the current distribution along the collecting bus to cut heating. (2) Layers: equipment in each bay can be in layers: indoors on one, two or three floors; outdoors stacked using high gantries. (3) Passages routed according to the rows and layers.

Layout design: inside the bay, place the equipment, conductors and auxiliary items (gantries, supports, fences, cable trenches, internal passages) and fix their structure and dimensions; outside the bays, passages, entrances, doorways, lifting holes, cable trenches, buildings or walls, drainage: these “outside-bay facilities” affect safety, reliability and convenience and are a large share of the building area.

Drawings. (1) Arrangement (configuration) diagram (配置图): shows all bays in order (rows and order), each bay’s primary equipment (ratings and quantity) and connections, the layers, and the passages. Not to scale, no dimensions; equipment by graphical symbols, connections as single lines. Not a view but a special schematic; the step between the main wiring diagram and the layout drawings, used for ordering and site layout. (2) Layout drawings (布置图): engineering views by projection, to scale, showing the real layout; complex equipment may be simplified but outline and terminal positions kept to scale; the main dimensions in length, width and height marked. Mainly the plan and sections, with detail drawings where needed.

sections.h: Indoor switchgear, and two reading examples
sections.b:
The structure of an indoor installation depends on the main wiring form, voltage, busbar capacity, breaker type, number of outgoing circuits and how they leave, whether there are reactors, and on construction, maintenance, experience and habit. By arrangement: single-storey (everything on one floor, large area, usually packaged switchgear); two-storey (heavy items like line reactors and breakers on the ground floor, buses and bus disconnectors above; smaller area but complex and costly); three-storey (now seldom used in China).

Layout rules: (1) devices and conductors of one circuit in one bay, for safe repair and to limit faults; (2) put source incomers in the middle of each bus section so less current flows along the bus; (3) heavy equipment (reactors) on the lower floor; (4) use the bay space fully; (5) symmetrical, easy to operate; (6) easy to extend; (7) necessary passages: a maintenance passage for repair and moving equipment, an operating passage for operating breakers or disconnectors, an explosion-proof passage leading only to explosion-proof cells; (8) switchgear-room doors open outwards, with spring locks; doors between adjacent rooms open both ways; (9) “five preventions and one ventilation”: against fire, water, leaks, rain and snow, small animals, plus good ventilation.

ExampleReading (book’s analysis)
10 kV indoor switchgear of a small substation (Fig. 3-3)Basic facts: a 35/10 kV step-down substation with two SFL1-10 000 kVA transformers, built urgently for an industrial area; local, of ordinary importance, so modest reliability is acceptable; near the load and near a city, so construction must be quick. Arrangement: sectionalised single bus, 6 line units and 2 incomer (transformer) units spread evenly on the two sections, plus a bus-section unit and a VT unit on each section: 11 units; the section unit takes two bays, the rest one each: 12 bays in order (keeping bus current balanced). Overhead lines on the bus, so each section has an arrester, in the same bay as the VT. Operating passage in front, maintenance passage behind, exits at both ends. Type: indoor packaged switchgear, GG fixed open-type HV cabinets; 1.8 m operating passage in front, 1 m maintenance passage behind, exits at both ends; no fence behind. Evaluation: reliable (cabinets compact and dependable; 5 of 8 incoming/outgoing units by cable, avoiding direct lightning); safe (faults confined to the bay; a de-energised bay is separated from live ones by the cabinet body; passages wide enough; exits both ends); costly but quick to build, which fits its purpose; easy to operate and maintain
35 kV indoor switchgear of a substation (Figs. 3-4 incomer section, 3-5 outgoing section)Type: single bus; indoor, single storey; each bay split into front and back cells. Front: breaker and its mechanism (fence between them) and the disconnector mechanisms. Back, from top down: busbar, disconnector and CT. Incomer and outgoing bays differ in the direction of the line; the outgoing cell has one more disconnector. Maintenance passage behind, operating passage in front. Evaluation: safe (clearances met; 2 m high mesh fences in passages); reliability ordinary (no partition between busbar and disconnectors); economy poor (outdoor-type breakers, expensive). Suggestions: change the 35 kV breakers to indoor type; add a partition between bus and disconnectors, or give the disconnectors anti-mal-operation measures

worked.q: A 10 kV indoor switchroom (not packaged). What is the minimum (a) clearance from live parts to earth, (b) distance from a mesh fence to live parts, (c) height of an unfenced bare conductor above the floor?
worked.s: From Table 3-2, 10 kV column: (a) A1 = 125 mm; (b) B2 = 225 mm (155 mm for a solid plate fence: 70 mm less); (c) C = 2425 mm. (Practice uses larger values.)

worked.q: An outdoor 110 kV (solidly earthed) installation: how far must equipment being transported stay from unfenced live parts, and how high must unfenced bare conductors be above the ground?
worked.s: Table 3-3, 110J column: B1 = 1650 mm for transport outline to unfenced live parts; C = 3400 mm above ground.

worked.q: Why should the source incomers be placed in the middle of each bus section?
worked.s: Current flows from the incomer outward to the feeders on either side. With the incomer in the middle, each half of the bus carries only part of the load current, so the largest current along the bus, and its heating, is smaller than if the incomer were at one end and the whole load flowed along the bus.

worked.q: Name the three kinds of passage in indoor switchgear and what each is for.
worked.s: Maintenance passage: for maintaining and moving equipment. Operating passage: where operators operate breakers or disconnectors. Explosion-proof passage: leads only to explosion-proof cells.

topics.title: Outdoor Switchgear, GIS and the General Electrical Layout of a Plant
topics.zh: 屋外配电装置、GIS 与电气总布置

sections.h: Outdoor switchgear: low, semi-high and high types
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

By the height and overlap of equipment and busbars, outdoor installations are low (medium) type, semi-high and high.

Low type (中型): all devices on one horizontal level, mounted on foundations of a certain height (2–2.5 m) so that people can move safely on the ground. Advantages: clear layout, not easily mis-operated; reliable; easy to build and repair; low gantries, little steel, low cost. Disadvantage: large area.

High and semi-high: busbars and devices on several levels, overlapping. If one set of busbars is stacked over another, it is high; if only busbars are stacked over breakers, CTs, etc., it is semi-high. Both save much land and are widely used at 110 and 220 kV.

Reading example: 110 kV outdoor switchgear of a medium thermal station (Figs. 3-6 to 3-9)Book’s analysis
Station factsThree voltages, 10, 35 and 110 kV, with sectionalised double bus, sectionalised single bus, and sectionalised single bus with transfer bus respectively; two three-winding main transformers link the three buses. The station is fairly important; its 110 kV lines probably carry important through power
Overall arrangement (Fig. 3-6 arrangement diagram)Main wiring: sectionalised single bus with transfer bus: 2 main-transformer units, 4 line units, a bus-section-cum-bypass breaker unit, and a VT unit on each section. 10 bays in two rows: lines and section unit in the upper row, transformers and VTs in the lower. Different bays hold different equipment. One bay can serve as a spare. (Line bays also carry coupling capacitors and line traps for carrier communication)
Type (Figs. 3-7 to 3-9: plan, line-bay section, transformer-bay section)(1) Low-type outdoor switchgear. (2) A fence with a gate round the arresters. (3) Flexible busbars hung by suspension insulators from bus gantries; lines are overhead; transformers connected by overhead stretched conductors and jumpers. (4) Except the main transformers, all equipment on supports or foundations of some height. (5) Cable trench between breakers and disconnectors, also used as the patrol path. (6) A 2 m high wall round the whole installation
EvaluationSimple structure, clear layout, reliable, easy to operate and maintain, low cost; but a large area

220 kV ordinary low type (Fig. 3-10): double bus with transfer bus, combined bus gantries, breakers in a single row. GW4-220 disconnectors and minimum-oil breakers; all equipment except arresters on 2–2.5 m foundations. The outer phases of the main and transfer buses are far from the disconnectors, so post insulators are added on the down-leads. Dashed lines show the transformer incoming line raised to cross over.

Packaged switchgear is mass-produced in factories and can be put into service soon after arriving on site. Made by specialist makers, it has reliable quality, a compact sensible layout and lower cost. Widely used for 6, 10 and 35 kV switchgear in power stations and substations.

SF6 gas-insulated switchgear (Fig. 3-11, type ZF-220): a 220 kV installation with double busbars. Busbars, breaker, disconnectors, earthing switches, CTs and so on are all sealed in an enclosed metal housing and connected to outside circuits through cable heads. Each device is also sealed from the next, supported and separated by high-quality epoxy-resin basin (cone) insulators. The figure’s key: I, II main buses; 1, 2, 7 disconnectors; 3, 6, 8 earthing switches; 4 breaker; 5 CT; 9 cable head; 10 expansion joint; 11 basin insulator.

Advantages and disadvantages of SF6 GIS
(1) Saves a great deal of land and space
(2) Extremely reliable
(3) Factory-made, quick to install on site
(4) Repair interval can exceed 10 years
(5) The metal enclosure shields well, solving electrostatic induction, noise, radio interference and dynamic stability problems
(6) Good earthquake resistance
(7) Needs a special SF6 leak detector for monitoring
(8) Expensive

Especially suitable for city centres, underground, rugged mountain areas, caverns and other narrow spaces, and heavily polluted or harsh-climate areas, at 110–500 kV.

sections.h: The general electrical layout of a station
sections.b:
The general layout must balance long-term safe running, easy patrol and maintenance, saving land and construction cost, easy construction and a good working environment. Stations differ in role, building type, number and size of units, terrain and geology, so a sensible plan needs careful technical and economic comparison.

  1. Keep connections short between each stage of production (generator → generator-voltage switchgear → step-up main transformer → HV switchgear), and the layout compact, for patrol, maintenance and quick handling of accidents; this saves busbars, cables, structures and trenches, reduces area and space, and reduces losses and accident chances.
  2. Central control room (main control room) as near the generators as possible. It is the station’s control centre where operators watch instruments and start, stop and change units and switch lines; put it centrally so that its plan distance to each unit is shortest, for patrol and accident handling, and to shorten control cables. Also consider ventilation, lighting, vibration and sound insulation. In hydro stations it is usually beside the main powerhouse or between powerhouse and dam alongside the main transformers. In medium thermal stations with generator-voltage switchgear, the main control room is usually at the fixed end of that switchgear, linked to the turbine hall by a gallery bridge; large thermal stations mostly use unit control (machine, boiler, electrical together), sometimes with a separate network control room near the outdoor switchgear or with the first unit control room.
  3. Main transformers generally outdoors, close to the powerhouse, preferably at the same level as the erection bay, so that they can be pushed on laid rails to the erection bay and lifted by the powerhouse crane for overhaul; leave space for easy incoming and outgoing lines, good ventilation, and fire-protection requirements.
  4. Make full use of terrain and natural conditions and the station and project type, to place equipment sensibly and cut civil work.
  5. Avoid interference and crossing with construction facilities early in the station’s life; if needed, plan a staged transition.

Generator outlet busbars must be very reliable and economical. Common forms:

FormDescription
Open busbar bridgeGenerally rectangular or channel-section hard aluminium busbars; large current and long length, so the cross-section is chosen by economic current density
Composite conductorSeveral stranded conductors fixed on rings, hung between the generator hall and the switchgear wall (or a separate gantry). Rings keep the conductors evenly spaced, not rubbing and well cooled, one every 0.5–1 m; usually 2 steel-cored aluminium conductors at the two sides of the ring take the tension, the rest aluminium. Little skin effect, good cooling, reliable, little maintenance, low cost; can cross plant roads (span up to 30–35 m). For outlets of 6–125 MW units
CableCable is expensive and cable heads fail easily, so seldom used; only for small units (below 25 MW, i.e. 2.5 × 10⁴ kW) where the layout cannot use open busbars
Isolated-phase enclosed busbarIn China all outlet busbars of 200 MW and larger units use full-link isolated-phase enclosed busbars (Fig. 3-13, a 220 MW example)

sections.h: Hydro, thermal and substation layouts; the reading report
sections.b:
Hydro stations come in many types: diversion, river-bed, underground, in-dam and dam-toe; the layout depends strongly on terrain and the project layout. In large and medium hydro stations the generator-voltage switchgear is usually near the units, and the step-up transformers on the upstream side of the powerhouse or on the downstream tail-water platform, making the transformer–generator connections shortest. The dam area is narrow, so the switchyard is usually on the downstream bank, connected to the step-up transformers by overhead lines, or on the powerhouse roof to cut excavation and ease maintenance. The outdoor switchyard generally has a network relay room and a duty room. Fig. 3-14, a dam-toe hydro station: 8 units side by side in the powerhouse, main transformers right beside it, 220 kV and 110 kV switchyards on the right-bank slope.

Thermal stations: (1) generator-voltage switchgear near the generators; in medium stations it is next to the central control room, some distance from the main building (depending on circulating-water pipes and roads), the control room linked to the main building by a gallery bridge, which eases movement and reduces control-room noise. (2) Step-up transformers as close as possible to the generator-voltage switchgear; in large stations with generator–transformer units and no generator-voltage switchgear, close to the generator hall, to shorten the enclosed busbar. (3) The switchyard placed so that HV overhead lines can leave easily. (4) Main transformers and outdoor switchgear upwind of cooling towers (spray ponds) in the winter prevailing wind, and upwind of coal yards and chimneys in the prevailing wind all year, at the required distances, to reduce icing, dust and harmful gases. Fig. 3-15 shows (a) a layout with 6–10 kV generator-voltage switchgear and (b) a unit-connection layout, with keys: boiler house, machine–electrical–boiler control room, turbine hall, 6–10 kV service switchgear, generator-voltage switchgear, electrical main control room, gallery bridge, de-aerator bay, production office building, network control room, main transformers, HV station-service transformers.

Substations: Fig. 3-16, a 220/110/10 kV substation: the 10 kV indoor switchgear joined to the control building; 220 and 110 kV outdoor switchgear side by side in one row; one three-winding main transformer in the middle outdoors (another to be added on extension).

Report for switchgear and general layout drawings (Table 3-4)Item (weight)Standard
Basic items (20 %)Type of installation (20 %)Identify the type and state its main advantages and disadvantages
Reading the switchgear drawing (60 %)Main wiring scheme (20 %)From the layout drawings, work out the main wiring used, and draw the circuit
Equipment check (10 %)Identify the equipment each geometric shape represents
Connections (10 %)Explain from the layout how the equipment is connected
Power flow (20 %)Explain from the layout how energy is received, collected and distributed
Overall evaluation (20 %)Evaluation (20 %)Evaluate reliability, safety, convenience and economy

Book exercises (3.8): (1) read Fig. 3-17, a two-storey, two-passage, double-bus 6–10 kV indoor switchgear with cable outgoing lines and reactors (keys: 1, 2, 3 disconnectors; 4 minimum-oil breaker SN10-10; 5, 8 CTs; 6 minimum-oil breaker SN4-10G; 7 reactor); (2) read Fig. 3-18, a 110 kV single-bus, incoming and outgoing lines both with transfer bus, semi-high layout bay section (keys: 1 main bus; 2 transfer bus; 3, 4, 7 disconnectors; 5 breaker; 6 CT; 8 line trap; 9 coupling capacitor).

worked.q: Distinguish low, semi-high and high outdoor switchgear in one sentence each.
worked.s: Low (medium): all equipment on one level on 2–2.5 m foundations, nothing under the busbars. Semi-high: busbars raised and stacked over breakers, CTs etc. High: one set of busbars (and bus disconnectors) stacked over another.

worked.q: A 125 MW and a 300 MW generator need outlet connections. Which forms would the book suggest?
worked.s: 125 MW: within 6–125 MW, so a composite conductor (or open busbar bridge) is suitable. 300 MW: 200 MW and above, so a full-link isolated-phase enclosed busbar.

worked.q: Where should a thermal station’s main transformers and outdoor switchgear be placed relative to the cooling towers and the coal yard, and why?
worked.s: Upwind of the cooling towers (spray ponds) in the winter prevailing wind, and upwind of the coal yard and chimneys in the year-round prevailing wind, at the required distances, so that icing from the towers’ spray and dust and harmful gases do not foul the insulation.

topics.title: Secondary Diagrams: Forms, Item Designations, Circuit Numbers and How to Read Them
topics.zh: 二次图：图式、项目代号、回路编号与读图要领

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Besides primary equipment, stations contain a great deal of secondary equipment: auxiliary electrical devices that monitor, control, protect, signal and automatically regulate primary and mechanical equipment. The low-voltage circuits they form are secondary circuits: AC current circuits, AC voltage circuits, breaker control and signal circuits, relay protection circuits, automatic device circuits, and so on. A drawing that shows how secondary devices are connected, using their graphical and letter symbols, is a secondary wiring diagram. (Graphical symbols: book Appendices 1 and 2, old and new symbols for switches, control and protection devices, meters, lamps and signals; letter symbols: Appendix 3.)

Forms. Under the old standard, secondary drawings were schematic diagrams (integrated and expanded schematics), panel-front layout, panel-rear wiring diagrams and terminal-block diagrams. Under the new standard: circuit diagrams, location diagrams and connection diagrams (tables), linked together by item designations.

A circuit (schematic) diagram is drawn with standard graphical, letter and number symbols, arranged in working order, showing the full make-up and connections of a circuit, device or assembly in detail without regard to real positions; it lets you understand how the circuit works and analyse and calculate it. Representation may be attached (integrated), semi-attached or detached (expanded); semi-attached and detached may be combined. The book shows all three for a 10 kV line over-current protection in a GC5-10F cabinet (Fig. 4-1): (a) an integrated schematic, with relays drawn as whole devices beside the primary circuit; (b) attached representation within dashed device frames; (c) detached: current circuits, DC control circuit and signal circuit drawn separately, each device’s coil and contacts scattered to where they act, linked by the same label.

Fig. 4-1 equipment listNameTypeQtyNote

How it works (my reading of the detached diagram): CTs 1TA1, 1TA3 on phases L1 and L3 feed current relays KA1, KA2. On over-current either closes its contact and energises time relay KT from the control bus WC+ via fuse FU1. After the set delay KT’s contact energises signal relay KS and, through link XB, the trip coil Yoff via the breaker auxiliary contact QF1.1: the breaker trips. KS drops a flag and, from WS+, connects circuit 716 to the “flag not reset” bus WSR to give a signal.

Besides graphical symbols, a circuit diagram must show each device’s name, function, state, features, relationships and location: this uses letter symbols and item designations. An item is any basic part, component, functional unit, device or system shown by a graphical and letter symbol: assemblies (A), lines (W), relays (K), switching circuits (Q), control switches or buttons (S), transformers (T), terminals (X), etc. Beside each symbol, codes of different levels identify the item and give its hierarchy and real location.

Block1st2nd3rd4th
MeaningHigher-level designationLocation designationKind designationTerminal designation
Prefix=+−:

Book example (Fig. 4-2 (b)): relay K2 (the L3-phase current relay) in the relay compartment of the No. 1 line cabinet. The cabinet belongs to part 2 of the hydro station, No. 1 line switchgear: higher-level code =S2W1. The cabinet is in bay 3 of the 10 kV switchroom, and the relay is in component A2 (the relay compartment) numbered 2: location code +322. In compartment A2 it is relay K2: kind code −A2K2. Its terminal 2: :2. Full designation of terminal 2 of the L3 current relay: =S2W1+322−A2K2:2.

Not every designation on a drawing needs all four blocks. Where the real location is not needed, omit the location code; where every item shares the same higher-level code “=S2W1”, omit it with a note. The designation then simplifies to −A2K2:2. To keep drawings clean, the book shows only the letter symbol and number (the terminal number) beside each symbol.

To show the nature and use of circuits (DC, AC…) and help installation, construction, operation and maintenance, each circuit on the schematic is numbered: a number represents a connection between secondary devices. Numbers should be simple, easy to remember and clear. They are grouped by use, each group with its range; generally three digits or fewer. For AC circuits, letters L1, L2, L3 (or U, V, W), N (neutral) or Z (or PE) are added in front to show the phase. Some important common circuits have fixed numbers: positive supply 1, 101, 201…; negative 2, 102, 202…; closing 3, 103…; tripping 33, 133…; red-lamp 35, 135…; green-lamp 5, 105…; “flag not reset” 716.

Equipotential principle: (1) all wires joined to the same point have the same number; (2) wire sections separated by coils, resistors, capacitors, links, contacts or other voltage-dropping elements are different potentials and get different numbers.

DC numbering method: sections of the positive side are numbered with odd numbers in order, the negative side with even numbers; the number changes after each main voltage-dropping element (coil, resistor, capacitor). Start from the positive supply with odd numbers up to the last element with a voltage drop. If the last element is not connected directly to the negative but through a link, switch or relay contact, then number from the negative with even numbers backwards up to the point already numbered. AC circuits are numbered in order from the source, with no odd/even rule.

In real drawings not every section is numbered: only the cable cores brought to the terminal blocks (entering or leaving the panel). Devices on the same panel are marked on the panel-rear wiring diagram. In a detached schematic, if a contact is drawn on another sheet or in another “installation unit”, note “goes to”; for a circuit brought in from elsewhere, note “comes from”.

sections.b:

Cable numbers. Control cables: format (1) item (higher-level) code – sequence number by cable type and route; or (2) start location – end location – sequence number, taking the location with the smaller number as the start. Sequence numbers by route (Table 4-6), e.g. within the control room (including protection and automatic-device rooms) 101–119; control room to generator-voltage switchgear 121–129; control room to substation 131–139; control room to unit-side panels 141–149; within generator-voltage switchgear 201–229; within the substation (including its protection panels) 301–339; within unit-side panels 401–449; within a unit 501–559; within the excitation room 601–669; within station-service equipment 701–779; within the DC room 801–889; others 901–999. Parallel cables of one circuit share a number with suffixes a, b, c. Communication cables: standard abbreviations; for equipment with incoming and outgoing lines, odd 1 = in, even 2 = out; form: in/out – function letters – number /T, where “/T” marks a communication cable.

How to read a detached schematic:

  1. First learn the simple construction and operation of each control device and relay, and which contacts of the control switch close in which position.
  2. Know the standard graphical and letter symbols and what the devices do.
  3. All relay contacts and auxiliary contacts are drawn in the normal state: relay coil unenergised (or insufficiently energised), breaker open. A “make” (normally open) contact is open when the coil is unenergised and closes on operation; a “break” (normally closed) contact is closed and opens on operation. Some contacts are time-delayed (DS time relays, DZS intermediate relays), acting after some seconds, drawn with a different symbol: watch for them.
  4. The rule: “AC first, then DC; for AC look at the source, for DC find the coil; hold on to each contact and check them all one by one; top to bottom, left to right, and miss nothing outside the panel.” AC first: AC circuits are simpler; from the quantities and how they change in a fault, reason through to the DC circuits. AC from the source: find which CTs or VT feed each current and voltage circuit, what each relay measures, its symbol, and then its contact circuits. Hold each contact: having found a relay coil, find its contacts, which circuits each makes or breaks, and follow the changes until the whole logic is clear. Top to bottom, left to right: the order for DC circuit diagrams and for terminal and rear wiring diagrams, read together with the detached, attached and semi-attached schematics.
  5. Use the short text descriptions at the right of the drawing to learn each circuit’s nature and use; understand circuit numbers and small-busbar labels; follow “goes to” and “comes from” notes to the other drawings.

worked.q: A transformer has 1QF on the HV side and 2QF on the LV side. What numbers would the positive supply, trip circuit and red-lamp circuit of 2QF’s control circuit use?
worked.s: 2QF uses group 3 (201–299): positive supply 201, negative 202, trip circuit 233–249, red lamp 235 (and closing 203–231, green lamp 205).

worked.q: A generator has protection CTs 1TA and metering CTs 2TA, and a metering VT 1TV. Give the circuit numbers for L1 of each.
worked.s: 1TA: L1411–L1419; 2TA: L1421–L1429; 1TV: L1611–L1619 (neutrals N411…, N421…, N611…).

worked.q: In a DC circuit, from + through a contact, a relay coil, then a link to −: how are the sections numbered?
worked.s: From the positive supply (e.g. 101), odd numbers: + is 101; after the contact, the section up to the coil is 103 (a contact separates potentials). The coil is the last element with a voltage drop, but it reaches − through a link, so number from the negative backwards with even numbers: − is 102; the section between the coil and the link is 104.
