topics.title: Circuit-Breaker Control Circuits: Control Switches, Anti-Pumping, Position Lamps and Flashing Signals
topics.zh: 断路器操作回路：控制开关、防跳、位置指示灯与闪光信号

sections.h: Make-up of the control circuit, and control switches
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

The circuit breaker is the most important switching device in a station. It is installed in the HV switchgear, but controlled generally from the central control room. A breaker operating (control) circuit does this: the control switch in the control room and the operating mechanism in the switchgear, connected by control cables. Most stations now use computer monitoring, but some hydro stations still use strong-current, one-object-one-switch control.

Hydro stations mostly use LW2 series and LWX1-Z universal changeover switches as control switches. Read their contact tables like this:

  • LW2-W-2/F6 (book Fig. 4-3): in the contact table, the arrows show the handle position; 1–3 and 2–4 are contact numbers; “−” = open, “×” = closed. In the contact diagram, 0 = handle at its original position (before or after trip or close), F = trip operation position, N = close operation position; 1 and 2 are circuit numbers; a black dot on a dashed line under a contact means that contact is made in that position; the arrow shows which way the handle returns. Table: before/after position: 1–3 open, 2–4 open; close position: 2–4 closed; trip position: 1–3 closed.
  • LWX1-Z (Fig. 4-4): for applications where trip and close are each done in two steps, “prepare” then “operate”: positions F (trip position), N1 (prepare close), N2 (close operation), N (closed position), F1 (prepare trip), F2 (trip operation). Two-step operation prevents mal-operation accidents.

Basic requirements of a breaker control circuit: (1) breaker position signals, to monitor the breaker’s state, the integrity of the circuit and its supply; (2) after the operation is done, the trip or close circuit must be cut automatically; (3) both manual and automatic operation possible; each breaker’s control circuit has its own fuses; (4) where the mechanism has no mechanical anti-pump interlock, the control circuit must have an electrical anti-pumping device; (5) breakers needing synchronised closing must also have a synchronising interlock, to avoid non-synchronous closing; (6) wiring simple, reliable, easy to operate and as economical as possible.

sections.h: Basic trip and close circuit; anti-pumping
sections.b:
Basic trip and close circuit (book Fig. 4-5). Made up of control switch SAC, closing contactor 1KM, closing coil 1Yon, trip coil 1Yoff, breaker auxiliary contacts 1QF1 (make) and 1QF2 (break), protection output make contact 2KOU and automatic-device output make contact 1KOU. Control supply WC+ (1L+) / WC− (1L−) through fuses 1FU, 2FU; the closing coil is on a separate closing bus WON− through 3FU, 4FU, switched by 1KM1, 1KM2.

  • Functions: (1) the trip and close coils are energised only briefly, thanks to the breaker’s make and break auxiliary contacts; (2) manual and automatic operation; (3) no position indication, anti-pumping or self-supervision.
  • Manual close: turn SAC 45° clockwise to “close” → SAC circuit 1 contacts close → closing circuit made, 1KM energised → 1KM1, 1KM2 close → closing coil 1Yon energised, close command → breaker closes → 1QF2 (break) opens, 1KM drops out, circuit resets.
  • Manual trip: turn SAC 45° anticlockwise → SAC circuit 2 contacts close → trip coil 1Yoff energised → breaker trips → 1QF1 opens, 1Yoff de-energised, circuit resets.
  • Automatic: the automatic device or protection output relay operates; 1KOU or 2KOU closes in place of the SAC contacts; otherwise as manual.

Anti-pumping (trip-free) control circuit, after book Fig. 4-6, drawn as a ladder. The relay’s current coil KJL(I) (not drawn) is in series with the trip coil Yoff; KJL(U) is its voltage holding coil.

Electrical anti-pumping. During closing, if a breaker closes, trips, recloses and trips again repeatedly, that is “pumping” (跳跃). Fig. 4-6 adds an anti-pumping relay 1KJL to the basic circuit. Functions: manual and automatic operation, coils energised only briefly, and anti-pumping; but no circuit-integrity supervision or position indication. Principle: the handle is turned to “close” and held; 1QF closes and 1QF1 closes. If there is a short circuit, protection operates at once and 2KOU closes (or 2KOU is stuck closed): the trip circuit is made, the current coil of 1KJL and 1Yoff are energised together; 1Yoff trips the breaker; 1KJL operates, its break contact 1KJL1 opens the closing circuit, forbidding a second close command. At the same time 1KJL’s voltage coil holds it in through its own make contact until SAC is released; SAC circuit 1 opens, the voltage coil drops out, and the circuit resets.

Why the anti-pumping relay has two coils (a guide question in the book): the current coil in series with the trip coil makes it operate whenever a trip is carried out; the voltage coil, energised from the closing command through the relay’s own make contact, keeps it operated as long as the close command persists, even after the trip current has stopped. Only when the close command is removed does it reset. (My explanation of the circuit.)

To monitor the breaker’s state directly, red and green lamps on the control desk (panel) show its position. Lamps are steady or flashing.

Steady-light control circuit (Fig. 4-7): adds a red lamp HRd and a green lamp HGn (each with a series resistor) to the basic circuit. The green lamp is connected in parallel with the closing contacts (SAC 1 / 1KOU), in series with 1QF2 and 1KM; the red lamp in parallel with the trip contacts (SAC 2 / 2KOU), in series with 1QF1 and 1Yoff. Functions: manual and automatic, coils briefly energised, monitors circuit integrity and shows breaker position; but no anti-pumping.

  • Meaning of the lamps (steady only here). Breaker open: 1QF2 closed, green circuit made, green lit. A lamp current also flows through 1KM, but too small to pull in its armature, so no close command. Green lit means: (1) breaker open; (2) closing circuit intact; (3) control supply healthy. Likewise, breaker closed: red lit, 1Yoff carries a small current but does not trip; red lit means: (1) breaker closed; (2) trip circuit intact; (3) control supply healthy.
  • Close: SAC circuit 1 or 1KOU closes, short-circuiting the green lamp; 1KM gets full voltage, operates, close command, breaker closes → 1QF1 closes, red circuit made, red lit; 1QF2 opens, so the closing coil is energised only briefly.
  • Trip: similarly SAC circuit 2 or 2KOU short-circuits the red lamp: trip command, breaker opens, green lit.

Why a series resistor? (my explanation) It limits the lamp-circuit current so that the current through the closing contactor or trip coil stays well below their operating value, and so that a short-circuited lamp socket cannot operate the breaker.

sections.h: Control circuit with flashing signals; the flasher
sections.b:
Flashing-signal control circuit (Fig. 4-8), with an LW2-Z-1a, 4, 6a, 40, 20/F8 control switch. Contact table (× = made):

Position1–32–45–86–79–109–1210–1113–1414–1513–1617–1917–1818–20
After trip−×−−−−×−×−−−×
Prepare close×−−−×−−×−−−×−
Close−−×−−×−−−××−−
After close×−−−×−−−−××−−
Prepare trip−×−−−−××−−−×−
Trip−−−×−−×−×−−−×
  1. Open state: handle at “after trip”; SAC 10–11 made: green circuit on the DC bus WC+, green steady.
  2. Closing: turn the handle 90° clockwise to “prepare close”: 9–10 made, green circuit now on the flashing bus WFL(+): green flashes. Turn on 45° to “close”: 5–8 made, closing circuit made, 1KM at full voltage, close command, breaker closes; 1QF2 opens the closing circuit, green goes out; 1QF1 closes, red circuit ready; SAC 13–16 also made: red on WC+, red steady.
  3. Closed state: release; the handle springs back to “after close”; 13–16 still made, red steady.
  4. Tripping: turn 90° anticlockwise to “prepare trip”: 13–14 made, red on WFL(+), red flashes. Turn on to “trip”: 6–7 made, short-circuiting the red lamp, 1Yoff at full voltage, trip command, breaker trips; 1QF1 opens the trip circuit, red out; 1QF2 closes, green ready; 10–11 made, green on WC+, steady. Release: back to “after trip”, green steady.
  5. Automatic trip (protection): KOU closes, the trip circuit is put on WC+, 1Yoff at full voltage, breaker trips automatically; 1QF1 opens, red out; 1QF2 closes, green ready. The handle is still at “after close”, so SAC 9–10 is made: green on WFL(+), green flashes; at the same time SAC 1–3 and 17–19 make the signal circuit (WS+ – R – SAC 1–3 – 17–19 – 1QF2 – WS−), sounding the audible alarm. Turn the handle to “after trip” to silence it.

Meaning of the lamps: red and green can be steady or flashing; flashing helps find quickly which breaker has operated in an accident. Steady: as in the steady-light circuit. Red flashing: the breaker has closed automatically. Green flashing: the breaker has tripped on a fault. The flashing circuit is started by the “discrepancy” between the handle position and the breaker position: handle at “after close” (“after trip”) while the breaker is open (closed). Turn the handle to match, and the flashing stops.

Flasher with a flashing relay (Fig. 4-9): relay KEL contains intermediate relay K, capacitor C and a resistor. With the circuit made, C charges; when its voltage reaches K’s pick-up voltage, K operates: its make contact closes, short-circuiting K’s coil and resistor and putting WC+ directly on WFL(+); its break contact opens and C discharges through K’s coil. When C’s voltage falls below K’s drop-out voltage, K resets and C charges again. Repeated charging and discharging makes WFL(+) carry a periodically changing voltage. The white lamp HWh (with test button SBTE): (1) shows the control supply is healthy; (2) tests that the flasher works.

Breakers with spring operating mechanisms (Fig. 4-10). If the closing spring is not fully charged (not wound to position), the breaker must not close: closing speed could not be guaranteed and it might not close fully. So a contact of relay KC blocks the closing circuit.

  • Charging: with the mechanism uncharged, limit switch SP1’s break contact is closed. If the combination switch SAH is on, intermediate relay KC operates; its make contact KC1 closes and the motor starts, winding the spring. When the spring is wound, charging ends: SP1 opens, cutting the motor. At the same time SP2 closes and the white lamp HWh lights: the mechanism is charged. While the spring is not wound, contact SP3 is closed, giving a “spring not charged” signal.
  • Closing: when charging ends, KC2 closes. Then, if the mechanism is open, turning SAC to “close” energises closing coil Yon and the mechanism closes. During charging KC2 is open, so even with SAC at “close”, Yon cannot be energised and the breaker will not close. Note: close only after the white “charged” lamp lights.
  • The motor’s control supply can be DC or AC; Fig. 4-10 uses DC. Fig. 4-10 also has local and remote manual close (SBC, SAC) and trip (SBT, SAC), protection trip KOU, anti-pumping relay 1KJL with self-holding contact KJL3, and red/green position lamps. Manual tripping is as in the lamp-monitored circuit; anti-pumping as before.

terms: 合闸线圈/跳闸（分闸）线圈

worked.q: With the flashing circuit of Fig. 4-8, the operator sees a green lamp flashing and hears the horn. What happened, and what should be done?
worked.s: The breaker has tripped automatically on a fault: the handle is still at “after close” but the breaker is open (discrepancy), so the green lamp is on the flashing bus and SAC 1–3, 17–19 have made the audible-signal circuit. Check the protection signals and find the fault; turn the handle to “after trip” to make the handle agree with the breaker, which silences the horn and turns the green lamp steady.

worked.q: A breaker is closed but its red lamp is out (the green lamp is also out). What does this tell you?
worked.s: A lit red lamp means: breaker closed, trip circuit intact, control supply healthy. With the red lamp out, either the trip circuit is broken (e.g. 1QF1 or the trip coil open-circuit), the control fuse has blown or the supply is lost, or simply the lamp has failed. It must be found at once, because the breaker might not trip on a fault.

worked.q: Why must closing of a spring-mechanism breaker wait until the white lamp lights?
worked.s: The white lamp HWh lights through SP<sub>2</sub> only when the spring is fully charged. Until then KC<sub>2</sub> is open and closing is blocked; and a breaker closed with an under-charged spring might close too slowly or not fully, which is dangerous on a fault.

recap: Repeated close–trip–close–trip of a breaker is called ___.
A lit green lamp shows the breaker is open and the ___ circuit is intact.
A flashing red lamp shows the breaker has closed ___.
The LWX₁-Z switch operates in two steps: prepare and ___.

topics.title: Central Signal Circuits: Accident and Alarm Horns, Impulse Relays and Modular Systems
topics.zh: 中央信号回路：事故与预告音响、冲击继电器和模块式信号系统

sections.h: Central signals, and the simple non-repeating circuit
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Equipment in service must not only be watched by meters; signals must show whether it is running normally or abnormally. On a fault, besides the protection acting, the signal system must tell the duty staff at once so they can deal with it. Audible signals draw the staff’s attention; light signals show the nature and place of the fault or abnormal condition. The devices that show accidents or abnormal conditions are in the central control room and serve the whole station: hence the central signal system. Where computer monitoring is used, the host computer gives accident and fault messages, including voice messages, telling staff the type and place, and records the time and data automatically.

Central-reset, non-repeating important-accident audible circuit (book Fig. 4-11). When an accident or fault occurs, the relevant protection acts, the signal relay operates and drops its flag, lights the illuminated annunciator (光字牌, 1H … nH) showing the nature or object of the fault, and starts signal relay KS; a contact of KS makes the audible circuit and the horn (or bell PB) sounds. The duty operator hears it and presses the silence button SBAR: intermediate relay KC operates, its break contact opens the audible circuit and silences it; a make contact of KC holds it in until the signal relays KS are reset by hand, when KC resets and the whole signal circuit returns to its starting state. Between pressing SBAR and resetting KS, the accident or alarm signal cannot sound again: a second fault in that time would give no horn. SBTE is a test button (through resistor 1R); white lamp HWh supervises the supply. (Symbols in brackets in the book’s figure apply to fault/alarm signals.)

sections.h: Repeating audible circuits with impulse relays
sections.b:
A central-reset, repeating audible system is built round an impulse relay, the key element of the central signal system; how well it works decides how well the whole system works.

BC-4 impulse relay (Fig. 4-12). It acts not on the instantaneous change of annunciator current but on the change of average current, so it is not easily made to refuse or mal-operate by interference. Parts: R3, R4, C4 and Zener diodes VS1, VS2 form a simple stabilised supply; R0, R2, C1, C2, inductor L and potentiometers RP1, RP2 form the measuring part; small relay K and transistors VT1, VT2 form the output part.

  • A fault: the signal relay operates, the annunciator lights; current flows through R0, giving a voltage UR0. C1 charges through L, C2 through L and R2. C1’s charging circuit has a small time constant, so UC1 rises fast; C2’s is large, so UC2 rises slowly. The voltage on R2 is their difference, UR2 = UC1 − UC2. This difference turns VT1 from cut-off to conducting; relay K operates and its contact starts the following elements (the horn). When charging ends, both capacitors reach UR0 and UR2 = 0; but K holds through VT2, which has forward bias from the R6, R10 divider and saturates once K’s contact closes, even though VT1 is now off.
  • When an annunciator circuit opens, the reverse: UR0 disappears, C1, C2 discharge, C1 fast, C2 slowly, giving a difference of opposite polarity, which turns VT2 off: K resets, an automatic impulse reset.
  • With several annunciators switching on or off one after another, each step change of the average current through R0 gives a charge or discharge as above, and the relay starts or resets each time. When the number of lit annunciators stays the same, UR0 is constant and the relay state does not change, however many are lit. That is how it repeats: each new fault makes a new step.

JC-3 impulse relay (Fig. 4-13). When a fault occurs, the annunciator lights and a signal pulse enters at terminal ⑧ of KAI; the current increase Δi/Δt gives a voltage increase Δi·R0 across fixed resistor R0, turning the annunciator current into a voltage signal. It charges C2 through L and the polarised relay coils KPZ1, KPZ2; the charging current operates KPZ; its contact closes and stays closed after charging ends, starting intermediate relay KC, whose contact sounds the horn (or buzzer). Another contact of KC starts time relay KT; after the set time KT’s contact passes a reverse current through the polarised relay coil, forcing KPZ back within the set time and silencing the horn: ready for the next repeat. If the signal current suddenly decreases, a decreasing voltage on R0 discharges C2 through the coils and KPZ returns.

  • (a) Delayed automatic reset of the horn; KC2, KC3 sound horns 1EW (control room) and 2EW (machine hall); KK supervises the circuit. (b) Manual reset: the test button SB doubles as reset, because pressing and releasing it applies a sudden decrease pulse and the relay resets itself.
  • Annunciator check: with single lamps and a resistor in parallel, a test circuit (switch SAT) is added. SAT at “test”: WS+ → SAT ③–④ → SAT ②–① → WFA1 → left and right lamps of 1H → WFA2 → SAT ⑤–⑥ → SAT ⑧–⑦ → WS−: the lamps are in series, at half voltage, dim. SAT at “run”: WS+ → nKS → left and right lamps of nH → WFA1 and WFA2 → SAT ⑨–⑩ and ⑪–⑫ → KAI ⑧–⑯ → WS−: lamps in parallel, full voltage, bright. To simplify, the test circuit can be omitted: remove SAT and connect terminal ⑧ to WFA.
  • The alarm (pre-warning) signal device works and is wired basically the same; just replace the horn (or buzzer) with a bell PB (except type ZC-23).

sections.h: Signal-circuit supervision and modular low-voltage signal systems
sections.b:
Signal-circuit supervision (Fig. 4-14). The alarm signal device is generally fed through its own fuses, sometimes sharing fuses with the accident signal. To supervise the audible-signal circuits, a supervision relay KK is fitted: if the accident and alarm signal circuits lose supply, KK drops out, its break contact closes, the white lamp HWh lights and bell PB rings. While dealing with the fault, press silence button SBAR to stop the bell; SBAR’s coil then holds it in. The white lamp stays lit until the fault is cleared and KK is energised again; its break contact opens, releasing SBAR’s self-hold, and the whole circuit resets.

Low-voltage (weak-current) signal systems. The central signal system built round impulse relays is a strong-current system with many drawbacks: incomplete indication, limited number of operations, only about a dozen signals, awkward to connect to computer monitoring. A newer low-voltage system uses modules: choose several or a few dozen light boxes and one or two sound boxes as the job requires. Fig. 4-15 uses integrated circuits and miniature intermediate relays; binary elements use positive logic (high H = 1, low L = 0). Modules: I accident-signal, II alarm-signal, III audible, IV flasher, V remote-signalling; +48 V / −48 V supply.

  • A fault in the primary system: protection acts, its output relay’s NO contact KCO1 closes, relay K is energised; in accident module I, OR gate D1 and AND gate D8 get high inputs; D1 outputs high; after delay element D2 (adjustable) it starts monostable D3, AND D8 and AND D6. D8 output high closes S2’s NO contact, starting the automatic monitoring device (event recorder) and sending a group signal. D3 flips at once; its low output goes to bistable D4 and starts the audible module.
  • In audible module III, OR D1 output low makes bistable D2 output high, closing electronic switch S and sounding buzzer HAU1. In module I, after D4 flips its high output goes to AND D5 and, inverted, to AND D6. D5’s other input is the flasher source, so its output is intermittent; D6 outputs low; both feed OR D7, whose output is intermittent: switch S1 makes and breaks, and the red lamp RD flashes.
  • Press silence button SB1 in module III: D2 resets, S opens, sound stops. Press reset button SB1 in module I: D4 resets and outputs low; D5 outputs low; D6 now has two high inputs, outputs high, and through OR D7 keeps S1 closed: red steady.
  • When the accident is cleared, KCO1 opens; D8 outputs low, cutting the signal to the monitoring device; D6 outputs low; the red lamp goes out; module I resets.
  • Alarm module II is built and works the same, but with a longer delay and an amber (YE) lamp.
  • Several signal modules share one test button SB, one audible module and one flasher module. When SB is pressed, AND D8 has only one high input, so its output stays low: the test does not start the monitoring device or remote signalling.

worked.q: In the simple circuit of Fig. 4-11, a second fault occurs after the operator has silenced the horn but before resetting the signal relays. What happens, and how do impulse relays solve this?
worked.s: No horn sounds for the second fault: KC is held in (its break contact keeps the audible circuit open) until the signal relays are reset by hand. An impulse relay responds to each step change of annunciator current, so a newly lit annunciator gives a new step and the horn sounds again, regardless of how many are already lit.

worked.q: Why does the BC-4 impulse relay use two capacitors with different time constants?
worked.s: The relay must respond to a change of the annunciator current, not to its steady value. When UR0 steps up, C1 (small time constant) follows quickly and C2 (large) lags, so for a short time UR2 = UC1 − UC2 is large and operates VT1; when both have charged it falls to zero. A step down gives a difference of opposite polarity, which resets the output. A steady current, however large, gives no difference.

worked.q: With the SAT annunciator test switch at “test”, why do the lamps glow dimly?
worked.s: The circuit WS+ → SAT → WFA1 → left lamp → right lamp → WFA2 → SAT → WS− puts the two lamps of each annunciator in series, so each gets half the voltage. A lamp that does not light shows a burnt-out bulb. In “run” the lamps are in parallel at full voltage.

recap: Audible signals draw attention; ___ signals show the nature and place of a fault.
The key element of a repeating central signal system is the ___ relay.
The alarm signal device uses a ___ instead of a horn.
In the modular system the alarm module lamp is ___.

topics.title: Measuring and Monitoring Circuits: Meters, Power, Energy and AC Insulation Monitoring
topics.zh: 测量监察回路：仪表接线、功率、电能与交流绝缘监察

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Stations have many meters, mostly electrical instruments measuring voltage, current, active and reactive power, active and reactive energy, frequency, etc. (Common meter symbols: book Appendix 4.)

Current: an ammeter must be in series with the circuit (Fig. 4-16 (a)), its resistance small compared with the load. For DC, mind polarity: current in at “+”, out at “−”. To extend the range: a DC ammeter uses a shunt (Fig. 4-16 (b)); an AC ammeter uses a current transformer (c), its primary in series with the circuit and the ammeter in the secondary.

Shunt: I = K a, Rw = R0 / (K − 1) CT: I = KTA a

a = meter reading; K = shunt ratio; R0 = ammeter internal resistance; KTA = CT ratio. Ammeters used with CTs are all 5 A full scale, but scaled in primary current, so the reading is the circuit current directly.

Voltage: a voltmeter must be in parallel (Fig. 4-17 (a)), its resistance large compared with the load; DC: high potential to “+”. Range: DC uses a series (multiplier) resistor (b); AC uses a voltage transformer (c).

Multiplier: U = n b, Ra = RV (n − 1) VT: U = KTV b

b = reading; n = divider ratio; RV = voltmeter internal resistance; KTV = VT ratio. Voltmeters used with VTs are all 100 V full scale, scaled in primary voltage.

Power is measured with a wattmeter: active or reactive, single-phase or three-phase.

  • Single-phase active power (Fig. 4-18). In the wattmeter PW circle, the thick horizontal line is the current coil, the thin vertical line the voltage coil. The pointer’s direction depends on the phase relation of the currents in the two coils; reversing either coil reverses it. To prevent wrong connection, the terminals of the current coil and voltage coil that must go to the same supply pole are marked “*”, “·” or “+”: the generator end. Correct: the marked end of the current coil to the supply side, the other to the load side; the marked end of the voltage coil to the same pole as the marked end of the current coil, the other end across to the other side of the load. With CT and VT, mark the polarities of the instrument transformers and the meter correctly; then the pointer will not reverse.
  • Three-phase four-wire: three-wattmeter method (Fig. 4-19). Whether or not the load is balanced, total power P = P1 + P2 + P3.
  • Three-phase three-wire: two-wattmeter method (Fig. 4-20). Whatever the symmetry of voltages and loads, P = P1 + P2. If one wattmeter reverses during measurement, reverse one of its coils; its reading is then counted negative. In practice a three-phase two-element wattmeter combines two meters with their moving coils on one spindle and one pointer, showing three-phase power directly (Fig. 4-21: type 1D1-W, 380/100 V, 5 A, through TA1, TA3 and TV).
  • Delta load, artificial neutral (Fig. 4-22): two resistors equal to the wattmeter’s internal resistance and the meter itself, one in each phase, form an artificial neutral N′; three times the reading is the total power.

Three-phase reactive power is measured with active-power wattmeters:

  • 90° cross-phase connection (Fig. 4-23): current coils in L1, L2, L3; voltage coils on the voltages lagging uL1, uL2, uL3 by 90°, i.e. line voltages uL23, uL31, uL12. The sum of three readings is √3 times the three-phase reactive power. The Chinese 16D3-VAR three-phase varmeter is connected internally this way, its scale already allowing for the factor. In a balanced circuit with two wattmeters: Q = (√3/2)(P1 + P2).
  • Artificial neutral (Fig. 4-24): in a three-wire circuit there is no neutral, so no phase voltage; choose an extra resistor Ra equal to each wattmeter’s voltage-coil resistance and connect it in star with the two voltage coils, making an artificial neutral N. PW1 takes iL1 and uL3; PW2 takes iL3 and uL1. Balanced: Q = √3 (P1 + P2). The 1D1-VAR varmeter has this inside; only for balanced circuits.

sections.h: Energy meters, and a generator metering example
sections.b:
An instrument measuring energy is an energy meter (watt-hour meter, kWh meter). Symbol PJ (kW·h or kVA·h).

  • Active energy: connected on the same principle and in the same way as for active power, obeying the “generator end” rule; follow the connection diagram supplied with the meter. Fig. 4-25 shows common connections: (a), (b) single-phase direct and through a CT; (c), (d) three-phase three-wire direct and through instrument transformers; (e) three single-phase meters for three-phase four-wire, direct; (f), (g) DT-type three-phase four-wire meters, direct and through transformers. For a direct meter, energy (generated or used) = this reading − last reading. Through instrument transformers, multiply that by the CT ratio and VT ratio to get the real energy. If the dial shows a multiplier and matching transformers are used, use the stated multiplier.
  • Three-phase reactive energy, like reactive power, can be measured with the 90° cross-phase connection. Three-phase reactive energy meters are common, of two types: (1) DX1 with extra current coils; (2) DX2 with a 60° phase shift in the voltage coils. Both are three-phase two-element and use the 90° cross-phase connection. DX1 can be used in three-wire and four-wire circuits; DX2 usually only in three-wire. DX1 (Fig. 4-26): like a two-element active meter, but each element’s two current coils are fed from different phases; through the register it directly shows reactive energy; whether or not the load is balanced, as long as the voltages are symmetrical it meters correctly. DX2 (Fig. 4-27): same structure as the two-element active meter; a resistor in series with each voltage coil makes the current i lag the voltage u by 60°; through the register it measures three-phase reactive energy.

Example (Fig. 4-28): metering circuits of a small hydro-station generator, detached representation. The generator has: 2 voltmeters, 1 ammeter, 2 three-phase active-power meters, 1 three-phase reactive-power meter, 1 three-phase active-energy meter, 1 three-phase reactive-energy meter, 2 frequency meters. One voltmeter, one wattmeter and one frequency meter are on the control panel in the central control room; the other set on the unit-side panel. The current circuits come from CTs 4TAL1, 4TAL2, 4TAL3 and are numbered L1441–445, L2441, L3441–445, N441: each current coil in series in turn (PJ(W·h), PJ(VA·h), 1PW, VA, 2PW). The voltage circuits feed the same meters in parallel; voltmeter 1PV is switched across phases by SAM.

After an earth fault in a small-earth-current (unearthed or resonant-earthed) system, the healthy phases’ voltage to earth rises and earth current increases. Supply to users is not affected, but long running may break down a weak spot of insulation on a healthy phase, causing a phase-to-phase short circuit. So after a single-phase earth fault it is generally allowed to run on, but for no more than 2 h. To find a single-phase earth fault promptly, small-current systems have a dedicated insulation monitoring device that signals the fault and prompts operators to act (Fig. 4-29).

  • TV is three single-phase VTs, primaries in Y0 (neutral earthed), each with two secondaries: the secondary winding in Y for metering, protection and synchronising; the auxiliary winding in open delta, with voltage relay KIM across the open corner, for insulation monitoring. Normally the three phase voltages are symmetrical and the open corner has no voltage; KIM does not operate. When one phase is solidly earthed, the three voltages to earth are no longer symmetrical: about 100 V zero-sequence voltage appears at the open corner, KIM operates, its make contact closes the alarm-signal circuit: annunciator H lights and the alarm sounds.
  • The VT has HV fuses on the primary and LV fuses FU1–FU3 on the secondary, protecting the secondary in a phase-to-phase short on the LV bus. The secondary uses b-phase earthing, simplifying synchronising wiring; common in small hydro stations. The b-phase earth point is after FU2: if the secondary neutral becomes earthed, the b-phase winding is short-circuited and FU2 blows, protecting the winding. After FU2 blows the whole secondary has lost its protective earth, unsafe for equipment and people; so to stop HV from the primary entering the secondary, the secondary neutral is earthed through a breakdown fuse FD: a spark gap that does not conduct normally, but breaks down and conducts when the voltage exceeds a certain value, acting as a protective earth.
  • The open-delta circuit generally has no fuse: normally its voltage is zero, so a short across the corner would not blow a fuse; and an undetected blown fuse would stop the monitoring working; experience shows the circuit is simple and seldom faulty.
  • To prevent back-feeding from the secondary to the primary when the VT is out of service or under repair, all secondary leads except earthed b-phase go through auxiliary contacts QS of the VT’s disconnector: opening the disconnector cuts the secondary completely. Disconnector auxiliary contacts sometimes make poor contact, and a poor neutral contact is hard to detect, so the neutral uses two contacts in parallel.
  • Changeover switch SAM and voltmeter V monitor the network voltage. SAM has five positions: phase voltages of L1, L2, L3, the L1–L2 line voltage, and “off” (no voltage on V).

worked.q: An ammeter of 0.1 Ω internal resistance reads up to 1 A. A 20 A range is needed with a shunt. Find the shunt resistance.
worked.s: K = 20 / 1 = 20. Rw = R0 / (K − 1) = 0.1 / 19 ≈ 0.00526 Ω (5.26 mΩ). Then I = K a: a reading of 0.6 A means 12 A.

worked.q: A voltmeter of 10 kΩ internal resistance has a 100 V range. To measure up to 500 V, what series resistor is needed?
worked.s: n = 500 / 100 = 5. Ra = RV (n − 1) = 10 kΩ × 4 = 40 kΩ. Then U = n b.

worked.q: An energy meter on a generator is connected through 600/5 A CTs and 10 000/100 V VTs. Last month’s reading 3482.6, this month’s 3527.1 (no multiplier on the dial). Energy generated?
worked.s: Difference 3527.1 − 3482.6 = 44.5. Ratios: KTA = 120, KTV = 100, product 12 000. Energy = 44.5 × 12 000 = 534 000 kW·h.

worked.q: Two wattmeters measure a balanced three-wire load: P<sub>1</sub> = 6 kW and P<sub>2</sub> = 2 kW (both forward). Find P, and Q using the book’s two-wattmeter cross-phase relation, and say why you cannot use that formula carelessly.
worked.s: P = P1 + P2 = 8 kW. If the same two meters are connected in the 90° cross-phase scheme, Q = (√3/2)(P1 + P2). But that formula applies only to that cross-phase connection in a balanced circuit; for the ordinary two-wattmeter active-power connection, the standard textbook result is Q = √3 (P1 − P2) = √3 × 4 ≈ 6.9 kvar (this last relation is general circuit theory, not from this book). Always check which connection the readings come from.

worked.q: Why is the earth on the VT secondary b-phase placed after FU<sub>2</sub>, and what is FD for?
worked.s: If the secondary neutral becomes earthed by fault, the b-phase winding is then short-circuited through the earth, so FU2 blows and protects the winding. But after FU2 blows, the secondary has no protective earth; the breakdown fuse FD (a spark gap) on the neutral breaks down if a high voltage from the primary appears, earthing the secondary and protecting people and equipment.

Voltmeters used with VTs are rated ___ V.
A small-earth-current system may run with an earth fault for no more than ___ h.
An earth fault gives about ___ V across the open delta.

topics.title: Synchronising Circuits, Computer Monitoring, and Report Checklists for Secondary Diagrams
topics.zh: 同期回路、微机监控系统与二次图读图报告

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Paralleling generators with each other, or a generator with the power system, must be done with a synchronising device. By the order in which excitation is applied: self-synchronising and quasi-synchronising (accurate synchronising). By degree of automation: manual, semi-automatic and automatic.

Self-synchronising 自同期Quasi-synchronising 准同期
MethodBring the incoming generator up to near synchronous speed (slip S normally ±(1–2) %; in an emergency ±5 % or more), switch it into the system unexcited, then apply excitation: the generator pulls itself into stepRun the generator up to near synchronous speed and excite it; when its (or the incoming system’s) frequency, voltage phase angle and voltage magnitude are close to those of the running system, close the breaker
AdvantagesFast; simple; less chance of mis-operation; easy to automateSmall inrush current; system voltage does not dip; so widely used
DisadvantagesLarge inrush current, temporarily lowering system voltageTakes longer; operator error could cause non-synchronous paralleling
Where allowedTurbo-generators below 100 MW only when the periodic component of the largest inrush current does not exceed 0.74/x″d times rated current; hydro-generators of any size and synchronous condensers; never between two systemsGenerators to the system and between two systems; so substations all use quasi-synchronising

Synchronising points. When a breaker has tripped and both its sides are live, and the two sources may not be in step, closing it must be a synchronising operation: that breaker must be a synchronising point.

  • Large stations (Fig. 4-30): (1) generator outlet breakers and generator–two-winding-transformer unit breakers (each generator is normally paralleled with its own breaker); (2) all bus-coupler breakers: backup synchronising points for all sources on a bus; (3) all three-side breakers of auto-transformers or three-winding transformers: to reduce switching when paralleling, for quick reliable restoration after an accident; (4) tie-line breakers; (5) bypass breakers (they can replace the tie-line breaker); (6) incoming breakers of the 6 kV station-service sections III, IV, because the generator–transformer unit is on the 220 kV system while standby transformer TM is on 110 kV: not the same system. By contrast the incoming breakers of service sections I and II are not synchronising points.
  • Small hydro stations (Fig. 4-31): (1) generator breakers and the HV breakers of generator–transformer units: must have manual quasi-synchronising, and as needed automatic or semi-automatic quasi- and self-synchronising; (2) transformer breakers on each side (for a step-up or tie transformer, usually one side only); except unit HV breakers and LV breakers directly connected to generators, which follow the generator breaker’s method, the rest need only manual quasi-synchronising; (3) line breakers with a source at the far end, and bus-section (or bridge) breakers: generally manual quasi-synchronising only. (Figure key: 1 manual quasi; 2 automatic quasi; 3 self; 4 synchronism-check auto-reclosing.)

sections.h: Synchroscope wiring, synchronising interlock and angle-shifting transformers
sections.b:
Electromagnetic synchroscope (Fig. 4-32, type 1T1-S). It receives two sources: the generator (L1, L2, L3) and the system (L1, L2), from VT secondaries. The VT secondaries generally earth L2, so L2 of both sources is joined and earthed as a common L2: only four leads are needed. Small hydro stations generally use centralised synchronising (all synchronising done at one common panel), so these four leads are small buses, the synchronising buses: WSTL1, WSTL3, WOSL1 and WVBL2; WSTL1, WSTL3 and WVBL2 bring the generator’s three phases, WOSL1 and WVBL2 the system’s L1, L2.

  • SASC is the manual synchronising switch (LWZ-2, 2, 2, 2, 2/F4-8x) with positions “coarse”, “off” and “fine”. Voltmeters 1PV, 2PV and frequency meters 1PF, 2PF watch the two sources’ voltage and frequency; synchronism-check relay KSY has its two coils on the two sources.
  • To parallel the generator: SASC to “coarse”: contacts 2–4, 6–8, 10–12 made, the voltmeters and frequency meters connected; watch 2PV and 2PF and adjust the voltage and frequency by hand until close to 1PV and 1PF. SASC to “fine”: the odd contacts 1–3, 5–7 … made, and besides the meters the synchroscope S is connected; its pointer begins to turn. When it turns slowly (3–4 rad/min) from the “slow” to the “fast” direction (generator frequency below system) towards the red line, send the close pulse to the breaker: generator and system run in parallel. Each synchronising operation uses 1PV, 2PV, 1PF, 2PF and S, so these 5 meters are mounted on one small panel: the “synchronising panel”.
  • In “coarse”, SASC keeps S disconnected: S must not be energised too long or it may be damaged; and with too large a frequency difference S’s pointer jitters instead of turning, which could mislead the operator into thinking the frequencies are equal.
  • KSY prevents closing when the phase-angle difference is large, protecting the generator: its contact is in the breaker’s close-interlock circuit; with a large angle the contact is closed only very briefly, too briefly for the breaker to close.

Combined synchroscope MZ-10 (Fig. 4-33): small, cheaper than a synchronising panel, mounts directly on the control panel; widely used in new small stations. Terminals A, B, C via SASC to WSTL1, WVBL2, WSTL3; A0, A′0 to WOSL1; B0, B′0 to WVBL2. “Coarse”: A0, B0 made: frequency-difference and voltage-difference meters show the differences; when small, “fine”: A′0, B′0 made, the synchroscope works; the rest as before.

Synchronising interlock (Fig. 4-34). To avoid closing at a large angle, the manual quasi-synchronising close circuit has an interlock: the close circuit of breaker QF goes through the synchronising-interlock buses 1WSC, 2WSC, i.e. through the break contact of KSY. If the angle difference exceeds the setting, KSY’s break contact is closed only very briefly, so whatever SAC does, QF cannot close; only within the set range does it stay closed long enough. The interlock switch SAL in parallel with KSY’s break contact is used when one side is dead (e.g. a system split after an accident): no synchronising is needed, but KSY’s break contact cannot close because one coil is dead; operating SAL (1–3 made) completes QF’s control circuit so that QF can close.

Angle-shifting transformer (Fig. 4-35). For a two-winding Y, d11 transformer paralleled by its LV (delta) breaker, the synchronising voltages come from VTs on its HV and LV sides. The delta side leads the star side by 30°; both VTs are Y, y12, so their secondary voltages also differ by 30°: TV1’s secondary line voltage leads TV’s by 30°. So the VT secondaries cannot be used directly; an angle-shifting transformer TTA (D, y1) compensates: its Y side lags its Δ side by 30°, i.e. lags the main transformer’s Δ side by 30°, matching the voltage on the synchronising buses (WTAL1, WTAL3 auxiliary buses).

sections.h: Manual quasi-synchronising in a small hydro station
sections.b:
Fig. 4-36: manual quasi-synchronising system of a small hydro station. Four synchronising points; the main transformer’s point is on its LV side. Points needing no angle compensation: 1QF, 2QF, 5QF; needing compensation: 3QF.

Paralleling generator 2G with 1G (no compensation):

  1. Start the unit; adjust voltage and frequency to about those of the running system.
  2. Insert the synchronising handle into 2QF’s synchronising switch SAS and turn it to “on”. All 5 pairs of SAS contacts make: 1–3 and 5–7 put KSY’s break contact into the closing circuit; the other three bring the synchronising-bus voltages to the voltmeters and frequency meters, showing both systems’ voltage and frequency.
  3. Following the meters, adjust the unit’s voltage and speed to approach the running system’s.
  4. Turn synchroscope switch SASC to “fine”: 1–3, 5–7 bring the bus voltages to the synchroscope; 9–11 connect one coil of KSY to the running system’s synchronising bus.
  5. Fine-adjust voltage and frequency so that the synchroscope pointer turns slowly from slow to fast.
  6. When the pointer is about 30° before the red line, turn 2QF’s control switch SAC (not drawn) to “close”, sending the close command: 2G is paralleled with 1G.
  7. Turn 2QF’s SAS to “off” and remove the synchronising handle.

Line synchronising: no need to adjust voltage and frequency; just check that the conditions are met, i.e. only steps (4)–(7). Points needing angle compensation: paralleling at 3QF on the step-up transformer’s LV side, the 6.3 kV bus VT secondary voltage must go through the angle-shifting transformer; steps as for line synchronising.

All synchronising switches in the station share one handle, so that VT secondaries cannot be short-circuited on the synchronising buses, other breakers cannot be closed by mistake, and equipment under repair cannot be back-fed. After synchronising, return the handle to “off” at once. (Why closing ~30° early: my note, the breaker has an inherent closing time, so the command is given early so that the contacts touch near the red line.)

As stations and units grow, demands on safety, reliability and economy rise, and monitoring and control become stricter; many variables and much data. A computer monitoring system replaces conventional control equipment: start/stop of units, control of breakers and switchgear, optimised running, automatic generation control, on-line monitoring, limit alarms, logging and report printing, far better than conventional relay control.

It consists of the computer, peripheral (interface) equipment, external equipment and the controlled objects. Process parameters enter through the peripherals (sensors → transmitters → multiplexer → A/D → interface for analog inputs; switch-quantity inputs through interfaces); after calculation, analysis and judgment, outputs go back through peripherals (interface → D/A → multiplexer → actuators; switch-quantity outputs) to control the process, or to external equipment (printer, plotter, magnetic/optical disc, CRT) for printing, tabulating and display (Fig. 4-37).

Real-time control typeDescription
CentralisedOne computer controls the whole station; all electrical and non-electrical information is processed and commands given by it. If it fails, the whole station’s safe economic running may be affected
DistributedTwo levels: station management level (overall automation: economic running, generation control, safety control, automatic voltage control, monitoring and reports; generally a higher-grade microcomputer or minicomputer) and unit control level (basic control tasks per controlled object, generally microcomputers: data acquisition, monitoring, control and stable regulation for its object). Unit controllers are the foundation; they share some of the management level’s processing, reducing information flow and the demands on the management computer’s size, speed and reliability. Units take commands from the management level; the management level dispatches and supervises the whole plant

PLC-based hydro unit monitoring (Figs. 4-38, 4-39). Example: a generator electrical accident enters as a potential-free contact at terminal X2-15 (accident output), is processed by software, and output through intermediate-relay coils to close the guide vanes, trip the field-suppression switch and the generator breaker, and give an accident signal. The unit’s control logic is done by the PLC; relays serve only as intermediate relays, not for logic. Unit operating voltage is generally DC 220 V while the PLC is DC 24 V, and output modules cannot drive the unit directly and have limited power per channel; so outputs work through 24 V intermediate-relay coils. E.g. generator differential protection operates: an intermediate relay’s potential-free contact enters the PLC input module; after the PLC software logic, the output module drives a 24 V intermediate relay; its contacts in the DC 220 V turbine stop circuit and generator breaker auto-trip circuit trip, start the central audible system’s accident signal, give a voice message and send the signal to the host computer. (Fig. 4-38 inputs include breaker/switch positions, start, stop, emergency stop, speed relays at 0 %, 30 %, 80 %, 90 %, 140 % ne, temperatures, oil levels, protection outputs; Fig. 4-39 outputs include start/stop, technical water on/off, butterfly valve open/close, brake on/reset, field breaker on/off, excitation, auto-synchroniser on/off, governor emergency-stop valve, trip generator breaker, guide-vane limit and opening up/down, excitation up/down, unit accident and fault, indicator lamps.)

Fig. 4-40: a hydro complex with 21 units, total 2715 MW; distributed control combining division by function and by controlled object. The Dajiang plant uses distribution by controlled object; the Erjiang plant division by function. Dajiang’s host is two MICRO VAX-II computers, with microprocessors at the lower level replacing conventional control; Erjiang uses a PDP-11/24 minicomputer plus monitoring, regulating and display-recording devices (SXJ-2 event sequence recorder, SKT-1 control regulator, DJC-1 electrical monitoring), linked by Ethernet and optical cable to unit control terminals, switchyard and common-equipment terminals and the dispatch centre.

Book exercises (4.9): read Fig. 4-41 and Fig. 4-42, breaker control circuits with audible supervision. What is new in them (my reading of the figures): instead of lamps in series with the trip and close coils, a trip-position relay KTP (coil in the closing circuit, in series with 1QF2 and 1KM) and a close-position relay KCP (coil in the trip circuit, in series with 1QF1 and 1Yoff) supervise the circuits: KTP1 lights the green lamp HGn and KCP1 the red lamp HRd from WC+. If the control supply or both circuits fail, KTP and KCP both drop out; their break contacts KTP2 and KCP2 in series then connect WS+ to the alarm bus 1WAS/2WAS, lighting annunciator H and sounding the alarm: “control circuit broken”. The closing coil 1Yon is on the closing bus WON± via 1KM1, 1KM2. Fig. 4-42 also puts SAS (synchronising switch) contacts and the synchronising interlock buses 1WSC, 2WSC in the manual closing path.

worked.q: List the conditions for quasi-synchronising, and say what happens on the synchroscope when they are met.
worked.s: The incoming generator’s frequency, voltage phase angle and voltage magnitude must be close to the running system’s. Voltages are matched first by watching 2PV against 1PV and 2PF against 1PF; then in “fine” the synchroscope pointer turns slowly (3–4 rad/min); the close command is given as it approaches the red line (about 30° before it in the book’s procedure).

worked.q: Why does a Y, d11 step-up transformer paralleled at its LV breaker need an angle-shifting transformer?
worked.s: The LV (delta) side voltage leads the HV (star) side by 30°. The VTs on both sides are Y, y12, so their secondary voltages also differ by 30°, and a synchroscope fed directly would show a 30° error even when the two systems are in step. The angle-shifting transformer (D, y1) shifts the LV-side VT voltage back by 30° so that both voltages on the synchronising buses correspond.

worked.q: Why must all synchronising switches share one handle?
worked.s: So that only one synchronising point can be connected to the synchronising buses at a time: otherwise two VT secondaries could be paralleled or short-circuited on the buses, another breaker could be closed by mistake, or a de-energised piece of equipment under repair could be back-fed through the buses. After synchronising the handle goes to “off” at once.

worked.q: In a PLC-based hydro-unit monitoring system, why does the PLC not drive the unit’s trip circuits directly?
worked.s: The unit’s operating circuits are DC 220 V, the PLC DC 24 V; the output modules cannot control the unit directly and each output has limited power. So the PLC drives DC 24 V intermediate relays whose contacts switch the 220 V stop and trip circuits; the PLC does the logic, the relays only interpose.

topics.title: Operating Power Supplies: Battery DC Systems, DC Insulation and Voltage Monitoring
topics.zh: 操作电源：蓄电池直流系统、直流绝缘与电压监察

sections.h: What an operating supply is, and what it must do
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Operation, control, protection, signals and automatic devices of all equipment in stations need a reliable supply. It is so important that it is generally provided separately: the operating power supply (操作电源).

Basic requirements: (1) reliable: preferably an independent DC operating supply, so that AC system faults do not affect it; (2) enough capacity: on an accident blackout it must meet the station’s DC load, the largest impulse load and 1 h of emergency lighting; and keep the DC bus voltage within limits: in normal running bus voltage variation within ±5 % of rated; in an accident not below 90 %; after losing the floating-charge supply, at maximum load not below 80 %; (3) ripple factor below 5 %; (4) charging or a capacity-check discharge of the battery must not affect supply to DC loads; (5) long life, little maintenance, low cost, small area.

TypeDescription
DC (main kind): independentNot affected by outside conditions: the battery DC system, a rechargeable chemical source; many cells form a battery at a set voltage (usually 110 V or 220 V); independent of the power system’s state; even with total AC blackout it can feed important equipment for some time; the most stable and reliable DC supply, and the usual one in stations
DC: supply-converter type220 V AC rectified by thyristors to 48 V DC for the station’s 48 V operation, also floating-charging a battery; an inverter can turn DC back to AC and rectify to 220 V DC: a new multi-purpose independent supply, widely used in small and medium substations
DC: non-independent, compound rectifierInputs: secondary voltages of substation-service transformers and VTs, and secondary currents of CTs. Normally rectified service-transformer or VT voltage; in a fault, CT secondary short-circuit current turned into AC voltage by a ferro-resonant stabiliser and rectified as an accident supply for protection and breaker tripping. For substations with many lines, complex protection, large capacity
DC: non-independent, rectifier with capacitor energy storageRectifier plus capacitor bank. Normally station-service AC rectified as the operating supply, also charging the capacitors. In an accident, the capacitors’ stored energy feeds protection, automatic devices and breaker trip circuits. Only for substations of 35 kV and below, or 110 kV terminal substations with simple protection
AC operating supplyAC used directly for secondary circuits: CTs feed fault-sensing relays and breaker trip coils; service transformers feed closing coils; VTs (or service transformers) feed control and signals. Simple, easy to maintain, cheap, but technically not adequate for large and medium stations

Voltages: 220, 110, 48 and 24 V.

sections.h: Batteries and how a battery system runs
sections.b:
Lead-acid (acid)Alkaline
Electrolyte27–37 % sulphuric acid solution20 % potassium hydroxide solution
PlatesPositive lead dioxide, negative spongy leadPositive nickel hydroxide; negative cadmium (nickel-cadmium) or iron (nickel-iron)
FeaturesHigher cell voltage (2.15 V); large impulse discharge current, well suited to breaker trip and close impulse loads. Drawbacks: shorter life; gives off harmful gas when charging, so the battery room needs acid-proof and explosion-proof constructionSmall, long life, easy maintenance, no acid corrosion; but small accident discharge current. Stations commonly use nickel-cadmium
TypesFormerly GGF fixed acid-proof explosion-proof and GGM sealed types. Now widely used: maintenance-free solid gel (VRLA gel) batteries, with a special silica-gel electrolyte instead of liquid acid: high voltage, large capacity, stable, no leakage or spilled acid, long life, tolerant of over-charge and over-discharge, heat and cold resistant, little maintenance; no special battery room, can be put directly in the DC panel—

Operating modes:

  • Charge–discharge: a charged battery feeds the DC bus with the charger disconnected. When it has discharged to 75–80 % of capacity, discharge is stopped for reliability. It must be charged every 1–2 days and nights; operation is frequent, the battery ages and plates are damaged easily: rarely used.
  • Floating charge: the charged battery runs in parallel with a floating-charge rectifier; the rectifier normally carries the DC load and gives the battery a small current to make up its self-discharge, keeping it fully charged. A floating battery can take short impulse loads (breaker closing currents) and accident loads. It raises reliability and extends battery life: widely used; most battery DC systems now float.

sections.h: Reading a lead-acid battery DC system
sections.b:
Make-up (book Fig. 5-1): 2 chargers U1, U2; a battery; 3 voltmeters PV; 4 ammeters PA; 2 DC voltage monitors; 2 DC insulation monitors; 2 flashers; 4 sets of knife switches; 2 sets of DC buses (I and II, each + and −, with M100(+) flashing bus); fuses; feeders for control and signal, and for power. Each rectifier is fed from 380/220 V AC.

  • Silicon rectifier U1: the charger; while charging it supplies the battery and can carry all DC load on the bus. Double-throw switch QK3: contacts 2–3, 5–6 made = charge the battery; 1–2, 4–5 made = connect straight to the bus to carry DC load. Voltmeter PV2 and ammeter PA3 measure terminal voltage and charging current. To help discharge the battery, U1 should be a rectifier able to invert.
  • Rectifier U2: the floating charger; besides the normal bus load it floats the battery with a small current (about 0.03 QN/36 A) to make up self-discharge. QK4: 1–2, 4–5 = to the bus (normal load and floating); 2–3, 5–6 = charge the battery. PV3 and PA4 measure terminal voltage and floating current.
  • Battery circuit: 2 switches QK1, QK2, fuses, 2 ammeters PA1, PA2 and voltmeter PV1. QK1, QK2 can put the battery on either bus; fuses for short-circuit protection. PA1 is a centre-zero ammeter for charge and discharge current. PA2 measures floating current; it is normally shorted, and read by pressing SB to open contactor KM’s NC contact. PV1 measures battery terminal voltage. The end-cell regulator (端电池调整器) varies the number of cells n0 + n′ on the bus.

Charge–discharge operation (Fig. 5-2). Discharge handle S1 adjusts the number of cells connected as the battery voltage changes, keeping the DC bus at working voltage; charge handle S2 stops charging of already charged cells early.

  1. Start of discharge: S1 at the far left (between end cells and basic cells), QK3 open, QK1 closed (1–2, 3–4): battery on the bus carrying DC load.
  2. During discharge the terminal voltage falls; to keep the bus constant, move S1 gradually right to the far right, adding cells.
  3. Before charging: S1 at the far right, all cells working; put S2 at the far right too, so all cells get charged.
  4. Start charging: QK3 to charge (2–3, 5–6), QK1 still closed; start U1 with its terminal voltage 1–2 V above the bus, paralleling it with the battery. The slight excess makes U1 carry the whole bus load (I2) and also charge the battery (I1).
  5. As charging proceeds the battery voltage rises and the charging current falls; to keep the charging current constant, raise U1’s voltage; to keep the bus voltage normal, move S1 gradually left, reducing cells on the bus. Then the cells between the two handles carry (I1 + I2); having been connected later and discharged less, they are charged first; to prevent over-charge, move S2 gradually left, stopping charging of charged cells early.
  6. At the end, each cell is about 2.7 V; S1 at the far left; the cells on the bus are the basic cells, not used for regulation.

Floating operation (Fig. 5-1). Normally QK1, QK2 closed, QK4 normal (1–2, 4–5): battery kept fully charged; U2 in parallel with the battery. The battery’s internal resistance is very small, so its characteristic U = f(IL) is much flatter than U2’s: with a large impulse current, the bus voltage drops a little but most current comes from the battery. If the AC system fails or U2 is disconnected, the battery discharges, taking the whole DC load until AC returns; after it has been recharged by the charger, put U2 back for normal floating.

sections.h: Nickel-cadmium DC panels; DC insulation and voltage monitoring
sections.b:
Ni-Cd battery DC system (Fig. 5-3, BZGN-10S panel; Chinese factory-made Ni-Cd DC panels suit stations of 110 kV and below). Floating equipment: isolating transformer T1, single-phase bridge rectifier U1, lamp HL1, output voltmeter PV3, intermediate relay K2, voltage relay KV. Charging equipment: isolating transformer T2, charging-current regulator T, bridge rectifier U2, lamp HL2, voltmeter PV1, ammeter PA1. Battery GB switched between charge and float by double-throw switch QK5.

  • Charging: QK5 to charge (2–3, 5–6): U2 charges GB through current-limiting resistor R10; PV1, PA2 measure; adjust with regulator T and R10.
  • Floating: U1 feeds the control bus through voltage regulator V and switch QK4, carrying the regular load. V consists of 50 diodes (5 groups of 10 in series), selector SA and relay KC, giving about 35 V of adjustment. (1) Manual: if output is low, short the right number of diodes with SA (SA: LW5-15TG 5857/3). (2) Automatic: if the output (control bus voltage) falls to a set value, relay K1 drops out, its NC contact starts KC, whose NO contact shorts all the diodes: full output voltage (PV3, PV4); with S10 on, bell HAB rings; open S10 to silence; reset KC with SB. With QK5 at float (1–2, 4–5), U1 floats GB through R1, V1 and R10. If U1 loses AC, KV and K2 drop out; K2’s break contacts close, the control bus is fed without interruption from the battery; with S9 on, KV’s NC contact rings the bell; open S9 to silence.

DC insulation monitoring (Fig. 5-4). DC networks are widespread and work in poor conditions; insulation ages. Without monitoring, when insulation falls or a pole earths, no fuse blows; if not found and dealt with early, a second earth can make protection mis-operate or refuse, with serious results. Parts: a signal part (high-sensitivity, high-resistance signal relay KS, lamps; resistors R4, R5, each 1 kΩ, inside the relay) and a measuring part (voltmeter PV, control switch S2).

  • Normally S2 is at “bus” (middle): 2–5 made. The insulation resistances of + and − to earth, R+ and R−, with R4, R5 form the four arms of a bridge; KS’s coil is across the diagonal. With good insulation R+ = R−, the bridge is balanced, no current in KS.
  • When one pole’s insulation falls, the bridge unbalances and current flows in KS. At 220 V, when the resistance falls to 15–20 kΩ (at 48 V, to 1.5 kΩ), KS operates: annunciator H1 lights and the alarm sounds. Drawback: it cannot detect an equal fall of both poles’ insulation.
  • Measurement: after the alarm, measure the pole-to-earth voltages: turn S2 45° clockwise for U+, 45° anticlockwise for U−; with known voltmeter resistance RV:
R+ = ( (U − U+) / U− − 1 ) RV R− = ( (U − U−) / U+ − 1 ) RV

U = bus voltage; U+, U− = positive and negative pole voltages to earth; RV = voltmeter internal resistance.

Finding a DC earth. Method: momentarily cut the DC feeders in turn, the “flick-off” method; each cut generally no longer than 3 s. Principles: (1) check feeders “less important loads before important, outdoor before indoor”, then the battery, charger and DC bus; (2) less important feeders (emergency lighting, signals, closing) by flick-off; important feeders that cannot be interrupted even briefly (trip supply) first transfer their load, then flick-off. Order: (1) find the earthed pole and degree; (2) feeders of equipment under repair or just energised; (3) DC lighting and power circuits; (4) flasher and DC insulation monitor circuits; (5) control and signal circuits (first take the relevant protection out); (6) charger and battery; (7) if none found, the bus is earthed. Deal with it at once, de-energising if necessary. Precautions: (1) before cutting, take measures against mal-operation of protection and automatic devices; (2) never use a lamp to find an earth; use a high-resistance meter (220 V: RV ≥ 20 kΩ; 110 V: ≥ 10 kΩ); (3) never cause a short circuit or a second earth while searching.

DC voltage monitoring (Fig. 5-5). Too high a DC voltage damages or shortens the life of relays and lamps; too low may make protection and breaker mechanisms refuse. An under-voltage relay KV1< and an over-voltage relay KV2>, set at 0.75 Un and 1.25 Un. Beyond a setting, the relay contact makes the sound and light signal: annunciator H2 or H3 (on 5WAS, 6WAS) lights, bell rings.

Reports (Tables 5-1, 5-2): basic items 20 % (symbols); system 80 %: make-up 30 % and functions 50 % (operating mode; charging, discharging, floating operations) for a DC system; for a DC monitoring diagram, make-up 20 %, functions 30 % (insulation monitoring principle, what happens when it operates, voltage monitor) and handling 30 % (finding the earth; adjusting high or low voltage). Exercises: read Fig. 5-6, GZDW-I-21 DC system; Fig. 5-7, silicon-rectifier capacitor-storage DC supply.

worked.q: A 220 V DC system: after an earth alarm, U<sub>+</sub> = 150 V and U<sub>−</sub> = 50 V to earth, voltmeter R<sub>V</sub> = 100 kΩ. Find R<sub>+</sub> and R<sub>−</sub> with the book’s formula. Which pole is faulty?
worked.s: R+ = ((220 − 150)/50 − 1) × 100 = (1.4 − 1) × 100 = 40 kΩ. R− = ((220 − 50)/150 − 1) × 100 = (1.133 − 1) × 100 ≈ 13.3 kΩ. The negative pole has the low insulation (its voltage to earth has fallen to 50 V).

worked.q: Why must the voltage monitor relays be set at 0.75 U<sub>n</sub> and 1.25 U<sub>n</sub> on a 220 V system, and what voltages are those?
worked.s: 0.75 × 220 = 165 V (under-voltage: below this, protection and breaker mechanisms may fail to operate); 1.25 × 220 = 275 V (over-voltage: above this, relays and lamps are damaged or their life shortened).

worked.q: Why must a lamp never be used to find a DC earth?
worked.s: A lamp has low resistance; connecting it from a pole to earth can itself create a second earth path and pass enough current to operate protection or trip coils. Use a high-resistance meter (≥ 20 kΩ at 220 V, ≥ 10 kΩ at 110 V).

worked.q: In floating operation, why does the battery supply most of a breaker’s closing impulse current?
worked.s: The battery’s internal resistance is very small, so its voltage–current characteristic is much flatter than the rectifier’s. For the same bus-voltage dip the battery can give far more current, so it takes most of the impulse while the bus voltage drops only a little.
