topics.title: Relay Protection Diagrams I: Current Protection, Voltage Interlocks, Directional, Distance and Earth-Fault Protection of Lines
topics.zh: 继电保护图（一）：电流保护、电压闭锁、方向、距离与线路接地保护

sections.h: Purpose of relay protection; instantaneous and time-limited current quick-break
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

The main tasks of relay protection are to prevent accidents, cut out faulty equipment quickly, limit the extent of an accident and its losses, and raise the reliability of stations and the power system, keeping supply continuous and safe. Two tasks: (1) when protected equipment faults, automatically, quickly and selectively trip the breaker, and give the accident audible signal and the matching annunciator; (2) when it runs abnormally, give the alarm audible signal and annunciator so that operators can remove the condition. So protection must have selectivity, speed, sensitivity and reliability. To read protection drawings, besides the symbols you must know the characteristics of common relays and the make-up, principle and logic of basic protection. Current protection in principle suits hydro-generators, transformers and lines, as main or backup protection.

Instantaneous current quick-break (瞬时电流速断, Figs. 6-1, 6-2): the main protection against phase-to-phase short circuits on lines below 35 kV.

  • Task: quickly clear phase-to-phase faults on the first part of this line.
  • Parts: current relays 1KA, 2KA, signal relay KS, output relay KOU and link XB.
  • Operation: a phase fault near the line’s start makes the primary current a short-circuit current; CT secondary current rises; when it reaches the relay setting the current relay operates and these circuits make in turn: ① + → 1KA or 2KA make contact → KS coil → XB → KOU → −: protection starts; ② + → KOU make contact → QF1 contact → Yoff → −: “trip” command; ③ + → KS contact → signal: “accident signal” (audible and annunciator).
  • Reset: after the breaker trips, the fault current disappears, the current relays reset and the device resets. The signal relay holds its flag and must be reset by hand.
  • Why KOU: (1) its contacts have large capacity; (2) it rides through momentary phase short circuits (a short delay); (3) one output relay shared by the three-stage protection. XB: to put the protection in or out easily.

Time-limited current quick-break (限时电流速断, Figs. 6-3, 6-4): same primary and AC circuits; only the DC protection circuit differs.

  • Task: fairly quickly clear phase faults in the dead zone of the instantaneous stage. Its zone is the whole of this line, reaching a little into the start of the next line.
  • Parts: 1KA, 2KA, time relay KT, KS, KOU, XB.
  • Operation: ① + → 1KA or 2KA make → KT coil → −: starts; ② + → KT delayed make contact → KS coil → XB → KOU: “delayed” operation; ③ + → KOU make → QF1 → Yoff → −: trip; ④ + → KS contact → signal: accident signal. Reset as before.
  • Coordination with the instantaneous stage: (1) smaller operating current; (2) one time step longer.

Definite-time over-current (定时限过电流): near backup for this line and remote backup for the next line; wired like the time-limited stage. Task: when this line’s main protection, or the next line’s protection or breaker, fails to act, trip this line’s breaker to stop the accident spreading. Parts, operation, reset as for the time-limited stage; coordination with it: smaller operating current, longer operating time.

Connections of current relays to CTs (Fig. 6-5): (a) star (Y), three relays; (b) two-phase, two-relay incomplete star (V); (c) two-phase, one-relay current difference.

Current–voltage interlocked protection: under-voltage interlocked (started) over-current (for lines, generators, transformers), compound-voltage-started over-current (mainly generators and transformers), and current–voltage interlocked quick-break (current-blocked voltage quick-break, mainly lines).

Under-voltage interlocked over-current (Fig. 6-6). It stops over-current protection from mal-operating on overload: on overload the bus voltage is normal; on a short circuit it is a residual voltage, which an under-voltage relay can detect. Parts: KV1, KV2, KV3, KC, KA1, KA2, KT1, KS1, KOU, XB. Features: (1) the interlock is by intermediate relay KC controlled by the under-voltage relays; (2) if the VT secondary circuit breaks, the under-voltage relays operate but the current relays do not, so the device does not mal-operate; (3) it operates only when current rises (current relays act) and voltage falls (under-voltage relays act).

ConditionBehaviour
NormalNeither current nor under-voltage relays act
VT secondary brokenOnly the under-voltage relays act; their break contacts energise KC; KC1 closes giving an alarm (“voltage circuit broken”, audible and annunciator). KC2 also closes, but KA1, KA2 have not started: no mal-operation
Short circuitCurrent rises: KA1 or KA2 closes; voltage falls: one or more of KV1–KV3 act, their break contacts energise KC; KC2 closes; the protection starts and after the set delay trips and gives the accident signal

Current–voltage interlocked quick-break (Fig. 6-7): based on the basic feature of a short circuit, current up, voltage down. Without it, a short circuit on any line on a bus could trip all lines on that bus. Parts: KV1–KV3, KC, KA1, KA2, KS1, KOU, XB. Works basically like the under-voltage interlocked over-current, except that after starting it gives “trip” and “accident signal” without delay. Used only when the instantaneous quick-break is not sensitive enough.

Three-stage current protection, DC protection and trip circuits (after book Fig. 6-8 (b), as a ladder). Here 1KS, 2KS, 3KS stand for the signal-relay coils in series. Stage I acts at once; stages II and III through the delayed contacts of 1KT and 2KT. All share KOU.

Make-up (Fig. 6-8): stage I instantaneous quick-break: 1KA, 2KA, 1KS, 1XB, KOU (KOU shared by all three stages). Stage II time-limited quick-break: 3KA, 4KA, 1KT, 2KS, 2XB, KOU. Stage III definite-time over-current: 5KA, 6KA, 7KA, 2KT, 3KS, 3XB, KOU. The AC circuit from TA1, TA3 passes through 1KA/3KA/5KA and 2KA/4KA/6KA, with 7KA in the common return (a third relay in the stage III circuit). Signal circuit from WS+ (701) through the contacts of 1KS, 2KS, 3KS.

  • Stage I: quickly clears faults at the start of the line.
  • Stage II: fairly quickly clears faults over the whole line.
  • Stage III: when this line’s main protection, or the next line’s protection or breaker, fails, trips this line’s breaker with a longer delay, clearing the fault.

Why 7KA in the common wire? (my explanation) With CTs on phases L1 and L3 only, the current in the common return equals −(iL1 + iL3) = iL2 in a three-wire system. So 7KA sees phase L2 current, giving stage III a relay in every phase, which improves its sensitivity as a backup (for example for faults behind a Y, d transformer).

Why direction? In a double-source radial network or a single-source ring, selectivity cannot be obtained by time delay alone (Figs. 6-9, 6-10). For faults f1 and f2, the short-circuit power through breakers 2 and 3 flows in different directions: at f1, the power through breaker 3 flows out of the bus while through breaker 2 it flows into the bus; at f2 the reverse. If each protection has a direction element that tells whether current flows from bus to line or from line to bus, selectivity is solved. This element is the power-direction relay: it operates when short-circuit power flows from bus to line, and blocks the protection when it flows from line to bus. Time delays are still needed to guarantee selectivity. Its usual connection is the 90° connection (Fig. 6-11: 1KPD gets iL1 with uL2·L3, etc.).

Two-phase directional over-current (Fig. 6-12): KA1, KA2, KPD1, KPD2, KT, KS, KOU, XB. Current elements KA1, KA2 start the protection on a fault; direction elements KPD1, KPD2 judge whether the fault is in the protected direction. In each phase KA and KPD contacts are in series. Normal running: current elements below setting, no action. Three-phase fault in the forward direction outside the dead zone: KA1, KA2, KPD1, KPD2 all start; their make contacts energise KT; after the set delay it trips and gives the accident signal. Two-phase fault in the forward direction outside the dead zone: the elements of the affected phases start; the protection trips with delay and gives the accident signal.

Distance protection. In multi-source rings and heavily loaded long lines, current protection cannot give the needed selectivity and sensitivity. A distance protection responds to the distance from the relay location to the fault, and fixes its operating time by that distance: the nearer the fault, the shorter the time; the farther, the longer: selective clearing. Its measuring element is the impedance relay, measuring the impedance from the fault to the relay location (Zf = Z1 lf) and comparing it with the setting.

0° connection for phase faults (Table 6-1)UKIK
Relay 1UL12IL1 − IL2
Relay 2UL23IL2 − IL3
Relay 3UL31IL3 − IL1

With this connection every type of phase fault at one place gives the same measured impedance, proportional to the distance l. For earth faults, impedance relays need zero-sequence current compensation (Fig. 6-13), so that a single-phase earth fault at a place measures the same impedance as a phase fault there: relay 1: UL12 with IL1 + K·3I0; relay 2: U23 with IL2 + K·3I0; relay 3: UL31 with IL3 + K·3I0, where K = (Z0 − Z1) / 3Z1 (Z0 zero-sequence, Z1 positive-sequence impedance).

Three-stage distance protection, single-phase diagram (Fig. 6-14): 1KA, 2KPD, 3KI, 4KI, 5KT, 6KT, 7KS, 8KS, 9KS, 10KOU. ① Starting element 1KA (current relay) starts the whole device on a short circuit and is also the stage III measuring element; ② direction element 2KPD (power-direction relay, or a directional impedance relay) judges short-circuit power direction, preventing mal-operation for reverse faults; ③ measuring elements 3KI, 4KI (impedance relays) measure the impedance to the fault; ④ time elements 5KT, 6KT give each stage’s time; 6KT’s setting must be longer than 5KT’s for selectivity. Working: for a fault anywhere in the zone, 1KA starts; if forward, 2KPD operates, energising 6KT. (1) In stage I: 3KI and 4KI act, 3KI’s contact energises 7KS (signal) and 10KOU: trip. (2) In stage II: 3KI not, 4KI acts, energising 5KT; after its delay, 8KS (signal) and 10KOU: trip. (3) In stage III: neither 3KI nor 4KI acts; 6KT after its delay energises 9KS and 10KOU: trip.

The neutral earthing of the system directly affects protection. In China, networks of 110 kV and above have effectively earthed neutrals; 3–35 kV networks are generally not effectively earthed. A single-phase earth on a line: in the first case is a single-phase short circuit with a large earth-fault current; in the second (unearthed or arc-suppression-coil earthed) there is no short-circuit loop, and only capacitive current flows at the fault.

Effectively earthed networks: line earth protection is usually three-stage zero-sequence current protection, non-directional or directional. Only when the transformers at both ends of the line have earthed neutrals is zero-sequence directional current protection needed: zero-sequence instantaneous directional quick-break (zero-sequence stage I), time-limited directional quick-break (stage II) and directional over-current (stage III). Stages I and II together are the main protection for earth faults on this line; stage III is the backup. Fig. 6-15: non-directional three-stage zero-sequence current protection; KZC are zero-sequence current relays (1KZC, 2KZC, 3KZC in the neutral return of the CTs, after the phase-fault protection). Operation and reading are like the line three-stage current protection; besides responding to single-phase earth faults instead of phase faults, the main difference is the operating-current setting.

Non-effectively earthed networks:

  1. Non-selective insulation monitoring: uses the zero-sequence voltage that appears on an earth fault (see Project 4). It can only tell the type of fault and signal an earth fault; it cannot show which line. After the signal, operators open and reclose each line breaker in turn (the “pull-and-close” method): when the faulted line is opened, meters and signals return to normal at once. To shorten the user outage, an earth-test button with automatic reclosing AAR is widely used (Fig. 6-16): normally QF1-1 closed, QF1-2 open; button SB1 contact ① closed, ② open; AAR ready. To test a line, press SB1: ② closes the trip circuit, the breaker trips; then QF1-2 closes, QF1-1 opens; on release, ① closes at once (② opens), AAR operates and recloses the breaker, restoring supply quickly.
  2. Selective zero-sequence current protection: the zero-sequence current of the faulted line is larger than that of healthy lines; using a zero-sequence CT (core-balance CT) TA0 (Fig. 6-17, relay KZC).
  3. Zero-sequence directional protection: with few outgoing lines, the faulted and healthy lines’ zero-sequence currents may differ little, and selectivity and sensitivity are hard to meet; then use the different direction of zero-sequence current in faulted and healthy lines (Fig. 6-18: relay KZP with 3U0 from the VT open delta and current from TA0), acting on a signal.

worked.q: List the circuits that make in turn when the instantaneous quick-break operates.
worked.s: ① + → 1KA or 2KA make contact → KS coil → XB → KOU → −: the protection starts. ② + → KOU make contact → QF<sub>1</sub> auxiliary contact → trip coil Y<sub>off</sub> → −: trip command. ③ + → KS contact → signal: accident signal (audible and annunciator). After the breaker trips, the current relays reset; KS keeps its flag until reset by hand.

worked.q: How do the three stages of current protection coordinate with one another?
worked.s: Each later stage has a smaller operating current and a longer operating time: stage I (instantaneous) covers the first part of the line at once; stage II covers the whole line and a little of the next, one time step later; stage III, with the smallest setting and longest delay, backs up this line (near backup) and the next line (remote backup).

worked.q: In an under-voltage interlocked over-current protection, the VT fuse blows. What happens?
worked.s: The under-voltage relays lose voltage and operate; their break contacts energise KC; KC1 gives the alarm “voltage circuit broken”. KC2 also closes, but the current relays KA1, KA2 have not operated (no fault current), so the protection does not trip. Operators must repair the VT circuit.

worked.q: For a line with Z<sub>1</sub> = 0.4 Ω/km and Z<sub>0</sub> = 1.2 Ω/km, find the zero-sequence compensation factor K.
worked.s: K = (Z0 − Z1) / 3Z1 = (1.2 − 0.4) / (3 × 0.4) = 0.8 / 1.2 ≈ 0.67. Each earth-fault impedance relay gets IL + 0.67 × 3I0. (Magnitudes used for simplicity; in practice these are complex impedances.)

sections.h: Transformer faults, and the protection a transformer should have
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Transformer internal faults are inside the tank or outside the tank. Inside: phase-to-phase short circuits of windings, inter-turn short circuits, earth faults, core burning. These are very dangerous: the tank is full of oil, and the fault current makes the oil decompose violently into gas, possibly a large volume of flammable gas (“gas”, 瓦斯), which can easily burst the tank. Outside: phase and earth faults on the bushings and leads. Abnormal conditions: over-current from external phase faults and zero-sequence over-current from earth faults, overload beyond rated capacity, low oil level from tank leakage, over-voltage, over-excitation.

Protection (per the operating regulations)Where required, and what it does
Gas (Buchholz) protectionOil-immersed transformers of 800 kVA and above, and oil-immersed transformers in workshops of 400 kVA and above. Responds to internal short circuits and low oil level. Heavy gas trips the breakers on all source sides; light gas gives a signal
Longitudinal differential or current quick-breakDifferential: parallel-running transformers of 6300 kVA and above; single-running ones of 10 000 kVA and above; station-service working transformers of power stations; important industrial transformers of 6300 kVA and above. Transformers of 10 000 kVA and below: current quick-break, with over-current operating time more than 0.5 s. Above 2000 kVA, if quick-break is not sensitive enough, differential too. Responds to faults of windings, bushings and leads; trips all source-side breakers
Backup for phase faultsFor transformer over-current from external phase faults, and backup for gas and differential (or quick-break). Time graded by the current-protection step principle; delayed trip of all source-side breakers. Types: over-current or under-voltage-started over-current for small and medium step-down transformers; compound-voltage-started over-current for step-up and system tie transformers, and step-down transformers where over-current is not sensitive enough; for step-up transformers of 6300 kVA and above, negative-sequence current plus single-phase under-voltage-started over-current; for large step-up or tie transformers, impedance protection may be used
Zero-sequence protection for earth faultsTransformers in solidly earthed systems: earth faults on the HV (or MV) side and external elements. Neutral solidly earthed: zero-sequence current protection; neutral may or may not be earthed: zero-sequence current and voltage protection. Zero-sequence current: delayed trip of all source sides; zero-sequence voltage: delayed signal
OverloadTransformers above 400 kVA running in parallel or alone as standby for other loads. Usually in one phase; long delay; signal
OthersHV side 500 kV and above: over-excitation protection (excitation current rise from lower frequency and higher voltage). Temperature, tank pressure rise and cooling-system faults: as the current transformer standards require

sections.h: Reading a 35 kV step-up transformer protection diagram
sections.b:
Fig. 6-19, the complete protection of a 35 kV step-up transformer (two-winding, 35 kV / 6–10 kV). The protections and their parts:

ProtectionParts
GasKG, KS3, XBC, KOU (KOU is the common output relay of all protections)
TemperatureKθ, KS4, XB3
DifferentialKD1–KD3, KS2, XB2, KOU
Compound-voltage-started over-currentKV2> (negative-sequence voltage relay), KV<, KC, KA1–KA3, KT1, KS1, XB1, KOU
OverloadKA4, KT2; signal
Zero-sequence voltageThe open-delta circuit of the bus VT (not drawn)
  • Gas: a slight internal fault produces gas that lowers the oil in the gas relay, or oil leaks and the level falls: make contact KG1 closes, giving the alarm (audible and annunciator). A severe internal fault: a strong oil surge closes KG2, making the heavy-gas circuit: KOU trips the breakers on both sides; KS3 gives the accident signal. The changeover tab XBC is put to position “2” during tests, oil changes and earthquakes, so that gas protection cannot trip by mistake.
  • Temperature: temperature relay Kθ measures the comparison oil temperature; at 55 °C Kθ operates, its contact makes the temperature circuit; through KS4 it gives a signal or starts the cooling fans; at 45 °C Kθ resets.
  • Differential: on a fault in the zone, one or more of KD1–KD3 operate; their contacts make the differential circuit; KOU trips both sides; KS2 gives the accident signal.
  • Compound-voltage-started over-current:
    (1) Normal: bus at working voltage, load current: KA1–KA3 do not start; voltage symmetrical: KV2> does not act, its break contact closed, so KV<’s coil has normal voltage: KV< does not act; its make contact opens KC’s circuit; KC1, KC2 open; nothing moves.
    (2) Overload: maximum load current exceeds the KA setting and KA1–KA3 act; but overload is symmetrical, no negative-sequence voltage, KV2> does not act; as above KC2 is open, blocking the protection: no mal-operation.
    (3) Symmetrical fault: bus at residual voltage, short-circuit current: KA1–KA3 act, starting the device. No negative-sequence voltage, KV2> does not act; KV<’s coil has residual voltage: KV< acts, its make contact makes KC’s circuit; KC2 closes, making KT1; after the delay, KOU trips both sides; KS1 gives the accident signal.
    (4) Unsymmetrical fault: negative-sequence voltage appears, short-circuit current: KA1–KA3 act. The negative-sequence voltage operates KV2>; its break contact opens, removing voltage from KV<’s coil: KV< acts; then as above.
    (5) VT circuit broken: KV<’s coil loses voltage, KV< acts, its contact makes KC; KC1 gives an alarm. KC2 also closes, but KA1–KA3 have not started: no mal-operation.
  • Overload: current reaches KA4’s setting; KA4 makes the overload circuit; after KT2’s delay, an alarm.

Why compound voltage is better than plain under-voltage (my note): for unsymmetrical faults the negative-sequence relay KV2> is very sensitive (no negative-sequence voltage normally), and once it operates it also forces KV< to operate, so unsymmetrical faults far away are still detected.

Fig. 6-20: detached schematic of a three-winding step-up transformer (110 kV / 35 kV / 6–10 kV, breakers 3QF, 2QF, 1QF).

  1. Differential: 1KD, 2KD, 3KD, 1KS, XB, KOU (KOU is the common output; not repeated below): the main protection for windings and leads; trips the breakers on all three sides instantly. (A “sum-current” differential is used.)
  2. Gas: KG, 2KS, XBC: light gas gives a delayed signal; heavy gas trips all three sides instantly.
  3. Over-current: remote backup for external phase faults and near backup for internal phase faults; on all three sides (a two-winding transformer has it only on the main source side).
    (1) 110 kV side, compound-voltage-started over-current: 1KV<, 1KV2>, 1KVM, 1KA, 2KA, 3KA, 2KT, 5KS, 5XB; for faults in its zone it trips the HV breaker with delay.
    (2) 35 kV side, compound-voltage-started over-current, two sets: non-directional (2KV<, 2KV2>, 2KVM, 4KA, 5KA, 6KA, 3KT, 3KS, 1KC, 2KC, 2XB) and directional (1KPD, 2KPD, 2KV<, 2KV2>, 2KVM, 4KA, 5KA, 6KA, 4KT, 6KS, 6XB). The non-directional one is backup when differential refuses an internal fault, tripping all three sides via 3KT; 3KT’s delay exceeds the longest of 2KT, 4KT, 5KT. The directional one is backup for the 35 kV side; 4KT has two delays: the first trips the 35 kV bus coupler; if the fault persists, the second trips the transformer’s MV breaker.
    (3) 6–10 kV side over-current: 7KA, 8KA, 5KT, 7KS, 7XB: backup for LV external and internal faults; 5KT has two delays: first trips the 6–10 kV bus-section breaker, second the transformer LV breaker.
  4. Earth protection: KZC, KZV, 1KT, 4KS, 8KS, 2XB, 9XB: backup for earth faults in the 110 kV system. With two transformers in parallel, one neutral earthed and one not, a single-phase earth fault should first trip the unearthed transformer, then the earthed one: done by 1KT’s two delays.
  5. Temperature: temperature relay; signal.
  6. Overload: on all three sides (not drawn); signal. Also, broken 110 kV and 35 kV VT circuits give signals.

sections.h: Generator faults and a small hydro-generator protection scheme
sections.b:
Generator fault or abnormal stateProtection
Stator phase-to-phase short circuit: very large current, serious damage, even fireLongitudinal differential
Stator inter-turn short circuit: large circulating current, overheating, insulation ageing, even breakdown to earth or phase faults(Inter-turn protection)
Stator single-phase earth: the commonest generator fault; capacitive current through the stator core at the fault; if large or prolonged it melts the core locally, making repair very hardSensitive 100 % stator earth-fault protection covering every point of the winding
Rotor one-point and two-point earth: one point does no direct harm (no circuit), but a second makes a two-point earth, shorting part of the rotor winding, burning it, and upsetting the magnetic symmetry, causing violent vibrationRotor one-point and two-point earth protection
Loss of excitation: rotor winding open, excitation circuit fault or field breaker mis-trip; harms the generator and seriously affects system securityLoss-of-excitation protection
Over-current from external faults, non-synchronous closing, system swingsOver-current protection as backup for external and internal faults; 50 MW and above: negative-sequence over-current
Symmetrical or unsymmetrical overloadSymmetrical: overload signal protection in one phase; unsymmetrical: 50 MW and above, negative-sequence overload
Over-voltage on sudden load rejection, especially hydro-generators (large governor inertia) and large reheat turbo-generators (slow load-frequency control): speed rises sharplyOver-voltage protection on hydro and large turbo-generators
Turbine main steam valve suddenly closed while the generator breaker is still closed: the generator takes reactive power from the system and becomes a synchronous motor; turbine blades, especially last stages, may overheatReverse-power protection

To clear a generator fault, the protection trips the generator breaker and also acts on the automatic field-suppression switch, removing the generator’s excitation current.

Small hydro-generator protection (Fig. 6-21 layout; Fig. 6-22 detached diagram). Fitted: ① longitudinal differential; ② compound-voltage-started over-current; ③ over-voltage; ④ zero-sequence current; ⑤ low-frequency, low-voltage splitting; ⑥ loss of excitation; ⑦ overload; ⑧ rotor one-point earth. ① acts on “three-off” (三分: trip the generator breaker, trip the field switch, and stop the unit); ②–⑥ on “two-off” (二分: generator breaker and field switch); ⑦, ⑧ on a delayed signal.

ProtectionParts and action
(1) Differential1TA1–3, 4TA1–3, 1KD, 2KD, 3KD, KA, 1KS, 1KOU, 1XB. A broken CT secondary is signalled by KA. On an internal or outlet short circuit: instantly trips the generator breaker and field switch, and stops the unit
(2) Compound-voltage over-current3TA1–3, KV2>, KV<, KC, 2KA–4KA, 1KT, 2KS, 2XB, 2KOU (common). A broken VT secondary: KC blocks it and signals. For faults beyond the generator breaker, or if differential refuses: delayed trip of breaker and field switch. Because generator short-circuit current decays, to make the current elements hold reliably, an instantaneous make contact of 1KT is paralleled with the 2KA–4KA contacts
(3) Over-voltage1TV, KV>, 2KT, 3KS, 3XB, 2KOU: delayed trip of breaker and field switch
(4) Zero-sequence currentTA0, KZC, KLa, 3KT, 4KS, 4XB, 2KOU: on a single-phase earth of the stator winding or leads: “two-off”
(5) SplittingLow-frequency: 2TV, KHz<, 6KS, 6XB; low-voltage: 2KV<, 3KV<, 4KT, 5KS, 5XB: “two-off”
(6) Loss of excitationQfd·3, Qfd·4, QF2, KST, 6KT, 7KS, 7XB, 2KOU: when the field switch trips by mistake: “two-off”
(7) Rotor one-point earthA one-point earth in the excitation circuit: delayed signal (not drawn)
(8) Overload3TA, 1KA, 5KT: delayed signal

worked.q: A 3150 kVA oil-immersed transformer runs alone in an outdoor substation. Which of gas protection, differential, quick-break and overload does the book’s list require?
worked.s: Gas: yes (800 kVA and above). Differential: not required (below 10 000 kVA running alone, below 6300 kVA in parallel); instead current quick-break, with the over-current delay above 0.5 s; differential only if it is above 2000 kVA and quick-break is not sensitive enough. Overload: yes if it serves as standby for other loads (above 400 kVA). Plus phase-fault backup (over-current).

worked.q: During an oil change on a transformer, what must be done with the gas protection, and why?
worked.s: Turn changeover tab XBC to position “2” (signal/test), so that heavy gas does not trip the breakers. Oil changes, tests and earthquakes can disturb oil flow and the gas relay, causing a false trip.

worked.q: In the compound-voltage over-current protection, explain step by step why a heavy symmetrical overload does not trip.
worked.s: Overload current exceeds the KA setting, so KA<sub>1</sub>–KA<sub>3</sub> operate. But overload is symmetrical: no negative-sequence voltage, KV<sub>2></sub> stays reset and its break contact keeps normal voltage on KV<sub><</sub> (bus voltage is near normal), so KV<sub><</sub> does not operate; KC is not energised; KC<sub>2</sub> stays open and the time relay cannot be energised: the protection is blocked.

worked.q: What do “three-off” and “two-off” mean for a hydro-generator, and which protections use each?
worked.s: “Three-off”: trip the generator outlet breaker, trip the field-suppression switch, and stop the unit: used by the longitudinal differential (internal fault). “Two-off”: trip the breaker and the field switch only: compound-voltage over-current, over-voltage, zero-sequence current, splitting and loss-of-excitation protection. Overload and rotor one-point earth give delayed signals.

Light gas gives a signal; heavy gas ___.

The differential protection of a generator acts on “___-off”.

sections.h: Why microcomputer protection, and how it is built
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Features of microcomputer relay protection: ① easy maintenance and testing; ② high reliability; ③ high correct-operation rate; ④ extra functions easy to add; ⑤ performance easily improved; ⑥ flexible and convenient; ⑦ remote monitoring and control.

Its main part is the computer, which analyses and calculates power-system quantities, judges whether there is a fault, and decides whether to trip. Besides the computer it needs an input interface bringing information from the power system (signal processing, sampling and A/D conversion), an output interface sending control information (trip relays, contact outputs), and a man–machine interface (keyboard, printer) for entering settings and programs and outputting records for operators to analyse accidents (Fig. 6-23).

The book’s example is the WXH-822 microcomputer line protection and control unit (XJ Electric). Its protection: ① three-stage direction over-current with voltage interlock; ② zero-sequence over-current / network small-current earth-fault line selection; ③ three-phase single-shot auto-reclosing; ④ overload; ⑤ under-frequency load shedding; ⑥ accelerated protection before/after reclosing; ⑦ VT-broken alarm; ⑧ control-circuit abnormal alarm; ⑨ device fault alarm; ⑩ telemetering, telesignalling, telecontrol and teleadjusting pulse; ⑪ fault recording; ⑫ GPS time synchronisation; ⑬ network printing; ⑭ network communication.

How to read a logic diagram (my summary of the book’s method): each block is a gate: “&” = AND (all inputs 1), “≥1” = OR (any input 1), “=1” = exclusive-OR, a small circle = inversion, a box with T = time delay. Each protection has an enable input (“投/退”, set by a protection link or control word). Follow from the inputs on the left to the outputs on the right: trip, display and remote report, central signal.

WXH-822 has three-stage current–voltage directional protection; each stage’s voltage-interlock element and direction element can be put in or out individually, and each stage by its own protection link.

  1. Direction elements use the 90° connection, started per phase; to remove the dead zone the direction element has memory.
  2. The under-voltage element operates when any one of the three line voltages is below the setting, releasing the blocked protection; it prevents mal-operation on non-fault conditions such as motor back-feeding.
  3. The device calculates in real time and judges the three over-current stages with the same logic (Fig. 6-24). Operating conditions: ① measured phase current above the stage-n setting; ② after delay Tn (stage-n time); ③ the direction and under-voltage conditions of the over-current phase met (if required).

Worked logic, phase A (the book’s example): suppose an A–B phase fault in stage I’s zone, stage I in, voltage element in, VT normal, relevant protection in. Then AND D2’s output depends on OR D1; OR D4’s on D2; AND D8’s on OR D7. The fault is in the zone (forward), so AND D3 outputs 1 and OR D5 outputs 1; AND D6’s output depends on D4 and whether the A-phase current reaches its setting. The A–B line voltage is residual, below the voltage-element setting: OR D1 = 1, AND D2 = 1, OR D4 = 1. Phase A carries short-circuit current at or above setting: AND D6 = 1, OR D7 = 1, AND D8 = 1; after D9’s set delay the device trips and signals. If the VT is broken, AND D2 outputs 0, blocking the protection.

sections.h: Zero-sequence over-current, reclosing, overload, load shedding and acceleration
sections.b:
FunctionHow it works (WXH-822)
Zero-sequence over-current / small-current earth line selection (Fig. 6-25)One stage, put in/out by a protection link. The unit is for unearthed or small-current-earthed systems: earth-fault zero-sequence current is basically capacitive and small, so zero-sequence relays alone can hardly be selective. The units are networked and share information, so the faulted bay is found by network small-current earth line selection, then confirmed by an earth test-trip command sent over the network. In low-resistance earthed systems the earth current is larger: direct tripping, with one stage of zero-sequence over-current (control word “zero-sequence trip in” set to 0 = alarm only, 1 = trip). In some unearthed systems with many cable feeders and large capacitive current, direct tripping by zero-sequence relays can also be used. Logic: with a single-phase earth fault, “zero-sequence over-current in” and 3I0 ≥ setting make AND D1 = 1. If the “zero-sequence trip in” word is 1, AND D3 is blocked and D4 follows D1; after D2’s delay T0, D4 = 1: trip and signal
Three-phase single-shot reclosing (Fig. 6-26)Done in software on the existing protection hardware, by resource sharing: reclosing with no-voltage or synchronism check; put in/out by a link; Tar = reclosing time. (1) Starting: the device uses the breaker and post-close position contacts (KCT, KC) supplied by the external operating circuit to judge breaker position and post-close state. To ensure a single shot and no reclose after manual closing onto a fault, reclosing needs a preparation time: after manual or automatic closing it must “charge” for 15 s before it is effective. When the breaker trips on a fault or by mistake, it starts on the change from closed to trip position; if charged, reclosing starts. After a trip-position start, if reclosing conditions are not met within 10 s, it discharges. (2) Blocking: ① post-close relay KC reset; ② overload trip; ③ under-frequency shedding; ④ control circuit abnormal; ⑤ spring not charged; ⑥ reclosing blocked; ⑦ remote trip. (Figure also shows “no current < 0.3 A” and a 300 ms close pulse)
Overload (Fig. 6-27)Condition: every phase current above the setting. A control word selects trip or alarm; if set to trip, reclosing is blocked after the trip. TL = overload delay
Under-frequency load shedding (Fig. 6-28)With a switchable slip (df/dt) block; the frequency setting and time of shedding and of the slip block can be set separately. The slip-block stage is mainly for the first, fast shedding round: when a system fault makes frequency fall sharply, or a fault in the system or VT circuit distorts the voltage waveform transiently, the slip block tells apart fault conditions, motor back-feeding and a true active-power deficit; without slip block, it is used for later rounds. Conditions include Uab above the no-voltage setting, f ≤ frequency setting, and some current (I ≥ 0.3 A). Put in the appropriate stage by the feeder’s shedding round. Outputs: trip, signal, and block reclosing. Tf = shedding delay
Accelerated protection before/after reclosing (Fig. 6-29)An independent accelerated stage, selectable as pre-acceleration or post-acceleration. Since a fault may not appear at once after reclosing, the acceleration time setting can be lengthened a little, but not beyond 3 s; if no fault, the whole group resets. The manual-close acceleration circuit does not need a manual close-handle contact to start it, because many substations with integrated automation have removed control panels and no longer have manual handles, or only simple ones. Tacc = acceleration time
VT-broken alarm (Figs. 6-30, 6-31)(1) Bus VT: alarm when broken; from voltage (and combinations) and current it judges three-phase loss, two-phase or single-phase break. When voltage is normal again (line voltage > 80 V) the protection resets. Logic: current > 0.3 A with all U < 18 V, or any |Uab − Ubc| etc. ≥ 18 V; after 5 s alarm. (2) Line VT: for lines needing no-voltage or synchronism check, with the breaker closed the device checks that the line voltage is above the no-voltage value (30 V); otherwise “line VT broken” alarm
Control-circuit abnormal alarm (Fig. 6-32)The device takes the breaker’s trip position (KCT) and close position (KCC). With healthy control supply and auxiliary contacts there must be one and only one of trip or close position (exclusive-OR); otherwise after 3 s it alarms “control circuit abnormal” and discharges the reclosing, but does not block protection. (The figure’s timer box reads 5 s; the text says 3 s.)

Report (Table 6-3): basic items 20 % (symbols); reading the protection diagram 80 %: functions 20 % (which protections, against which faults or abnormal states), make-up 10 % (which secondary devices form each), logic 40 % (each protection’s operating logic), result 10 % (what each does). Exercises (6.8): read Fig. 6-33 transformer gas protection (KG, KS, XBC, KOU with KOU1, KOU2 tripping QF1, QF2; KG1 to the light-gas annunciator); Fig. 6-34 transformer under-voltage-started over-current (KV1–KV3, KC, KA1–KA3, KT, KS, XB, KOU); Fig. 6-35 transformer compound-voltage-started over-current (KV2>, KV<, KC, KA1–KA3, KT); Fig. 6-36 generator differential (1KD–3KD, KC for CT-circuit break, KOU1 trips QF, KOU2 to the field switch).

worked.q: Using the WXH-822 phase-A logic, what happens for a fault in the zone if the VT circuit is broken? Why is that the right behaviour?
worked.s: AND D2 outputs 0 (VT-broken input), so OR D4 loses the voltage-interlock release and the protection is blocked. With the VT broken the voltage element would see “low voltage” all the time, so it can no longer distinguish faults from overload or back-feeding; blocking (and alarming VT broken) avoids mal-operation.

worked.q: Why does the reclosing function need 15 s of “charging” after any close?
worked.s: To guarantee a single reclosure and no reclosure after manual closing onto a fault: if the breaker trips within 15 s of being closed, reclosing has not charged and does not act. After a successful reclosure it must charge again, so a second fault soon after does not cause repeated reclosing.

worked.q: The control-circuit alarm uses an exclusive-OR of KCT and KCC. When would it alarm?
worked.s: When both are 0 (e.g. control supply lost, or trip circuit and close circuit both broken) or both are 1 (auxiliary-contact fault). After 3 s the alarm is given and reclosing discharged; protection is not blocked.

topics.title: Automatic Devices: Automatic Standby-Supply Switching (AAT) and Auto-Reclosing (AAR)
topics.zh: 自动装置：备用电源自动投入（AAT）与自动重合闸（AAR）

sections.h: AAT: what it is and what it must do
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

The auxiliary supply is vital to safe, reliable station operation. Generally it must not be interrupted, so it has two or more independent sources: one working and one standby, or each backing the other. When the working station-service supply is opened by a fault, the standby must go in quickly and automatically, so that station service is not lost. The device that does this is the automatic standby-supply switching device, AAT (备用电源自动投入装置).

Basic requirements:

  1. AAT must operate when the working bus voltage disappears or falls severely.
  2. AAT may start only after the working-supply breaker has opened, and only if the standby voltage is high enough.
  3. The standby supply must have some overload capacity to allow motors to self-start.
  4. AAT’s operating time should be as short as possible, to ensure motor self-starting: generally 1–1.5 s.
  5. AAT may operate only once, so that a permanent fault on the bus does not hit the standby supply repeatedly and spread the fault. Use post-acceleration protection after AAT.

Fig. 7-1: AAT for a substation’s service transformers in concealed standby: sources 1 and 2 feed transformers 1T and 2T through 1QF, 2QF; on the LV side automatic air switches 1QK and 2QK feed bus sections I and II; section switch 3QK (normally open) joins them. Each AAT has two parts.

PartElements and roles
Under-voltage starting part: watches whether the working bus has lost voltage and whether the standby is normal, and starts the AATUnder-voltage relay 1KV (or 3KV): watches whether the working bus has lost voltage. Over-voltage relay 2KV (or 4KV): watches whether the standby supply voltage is normal; each has a break contact in series in the other AAT’s loss-of-voltage circuit, also blocking the AAT when a VT fuse blows. Time relay 1KT (or 2KT): sets the AAT delay. Signal relay 1KS (or 2KS): signals AAT operation
Automatic closing part: after the working supply is cut, closes the standby supply’s breakerIntermediate relay KC: its make contact closes instantly and opens with a 0.5–0.8 s delay, ensuring the AAT operates only once. Auxiliary contacts of automatic air switches 1QK, 2QK: ensure the working supply is cut first and the standby closed after. Signal relay 3KS: closing signal. Changeover switch BK: takes the AAT out by hand
  1. Working bus voltage normal: AAT ready. BK in; 1QF, 2QF, 1QK, 2QK in their post-close positions; 3QK open; bus I, II voltages normal: 1KV–4KV break contacts open, 2KV and 4KV make contacts closed; AAT not started; 1KT, 2KT not energised, their delayed make contacts open. KC is energised and its make contact closed, but the working supplies are cut off by 1QK and 2QK contacts, so no closing pulse. Lamp HL, supervising the 1QK, 2QK closed positions, is lit: AAT ready.
  2. Working bus loses voltage (bus I): 1KV and 2KV break contacts close. If the standby is normal, 4KV’s make contact is closed: start conditions met. 1KT operates; after its set delay (generally 1–1.5 s) it trips 1QK; 1KS signals AAT operation. When 1QK trips, its auxiliary contact 3–3 opens: KC de-energises, its contact opening after the 0.5–0.8 s delay. So for a short time 1QK’s auxiliary contact 4–4 and KC’s contact are both closed: a short closing pulse through 3KS’s coil to 3QK’s closing contactor YC: 3QK closes and bus I is fed from 2T; 3KS signals that 3QK has closed. Bus II losing voltage: the same with the corresponding elements.
  3. AAT unsuccessful: if the loss of voltage is due to a persistent fault on the bus itself, after the AAT closes 3QK the fault current starts 2T’s protection, which trips 3QK selectively. Because KC’s contact has already returned after the one closing pulse, AAT acts only once, and bus II’s normal supply is not affected.

When a line fault makes protection trip the breaker, a device that automatically and quickly recloses the breaker is an automatic reclosing device, AAR (自动重合闸装置).

Why fit AAR: (1) better supply reliability of lines, fewer losses from transient faults; (2) on double-end-fed HV lines, better stability of parallel operation, so more power can be sent; (3) faster recovery of system voltage after an accident; (4) makes up for a line’s reduced lightning withstand level; (5) corrects mis-trips of breakers.

Requirements: (1) fast: generally set at 0.5–1.5 s; (2) no reclosing after manual tripping: an operator tripping by the control switch or by telecontrol is normal operation, AAR must not act; (3) no reclosing after manual closing onto a faulty line when protection trips the breaker; (4) the number of reclosures set in advance; (5) after operating, AAR resets itself, ready for next time; (6) coordinated with protection; (7) easy to test and supervise; signal when it operates.

Types: (1) by working principle of its elements: mechanical and electrical; (2) by number of shots: single-shot, two-shot, multi-shot; (3) by line structure: single-source line AAR and double-source line AAR; (4) by how it acts on breakers: three-phase, single-phase, composite. The book covers only the single-source line, three-phase single-shot AAR.

sections.h: Three-phase single-shot AAR on a 35 kV line
sections.b:
Fig. 7-2: three-phase single-shot AAR with operating and protection circuits of a 35 kV line. Three parts: top, the AAR circuit; middle, the operating circuit (breaker control with flashing bus and lamp supervision, Project 4); bottom, the protection (current quick-break and over-current, Project 6).

Make-up. The core is the DH-2A (or DH-3) reclosing relay: time relay KT1, intermediate relay KC, charging resistor 4R, discharge resistor 6R, dropping resistors 5R, 17R, capacitor C and lamp H1. KT1 has an instantaneous break contact KT1·1 and a delayed make contact KT1·2, giving the AAR its delay. KC has two coils: a voltage coil (starting) and a current coil (self-holding); one break contact KC4 and three make contacts KC1, KC2, KC3. SAH puts AAR in or out (“in”: contacts ①–③ made). Control switch SAC (6 positions, 7 contact boxes): in “close operation” ⑤–⑧ and ㉕–㉘ made; in “after close” ㉑–㉓ made; in “prepare trip” and “after trip” ②–④ made; in “trip operation” ⑥–⑦ made. SBEY is the earth-check button.

  1. Normal running: SAH at “in” (①–③), SAC at “after close” (㉑–㉓); QF1 closed: its auxiliary contacts QF1·0, QF1·1 open, QF1·2 closed. C is charged through 4R (WC+ → 1FU → SAH ①–③ → 4R → C → 2FU → WC−); fully charged needs 15–20 s (“fully charged” = capacitor voltage equal to the DC operating voltage; chosen by 4R and C). Lamp H1 lights through 17R and KC4’s break contact (17R drops the voltage): lit means AAR is ready (C charging or charged).
  2. Transient fault: protection operates, KOU closes, QF1 trips. Now the breaker is “open” while SAC is “after close”: discrepancy. QF1·0 closes, starting KT1; KT1·1 opens at once, putting 5R in series with KT1’s coil to reduce its current so it does not overheat; after the set time (0.5–1.5 s) KT1·2 closes; C discharges into KC’s voltage coil; KC starts; the supply passes through the closed KC3, KC2, KC1, KC’s current self-holding coil, signal relay KS, changeover tab XBC (solid-link position), KJL’s break contact and QF1·1 to closing contactor KM: a closing pulse, QF1 recloses. After closing, QF1·0, QF1·1 open, KT1 and KC reset, C recharges (15–20 s), ready again.
  3. Permanent fault: after tripping and reclosing, protection operates again and trips; KT1 starts again and KT1·2 closes after 0.5–1.5 s, C discharges into KC’s voltage coil, but C has not had time to charge and its voltage is too low to start KC: no second reclosure. AAR acts only once.
  4. Manual trip by SAC: if SAH is first put to “off”, AAR is out and does not reclose. And since SAC and breaker positions now correspond, SAC’s ㉑–㉓ is open, cutting AAR’s starting circuit; SAC’s ②–④ closes, discharging C through 6R, further ensuring AAR loses the reclosing condition.
  5. Anti-pumping relay KJL and acceleration relay KAC: (1) when closing manually by SAC, they prevent breaker pumping (Project 4); (2) if after AAR operates KC’s make contacts weld and cannot return, and the fault is permanent, they also prevent pumping: on reclosure the acceleration relay KAC operates, protection immediately trips the breaker (post-acceleration), and KJL starts; its make contact makes KJL’s self-holding circuit and its break contact opens the closing contactor KM circuit: QF1 cannot close. To guard against welded KC contacts, the two make contacts KC1, KC2 are in series.
  6. Earth-check button SBEY: 35 kV and below networks have non-effectively earthed neutrals; single-phase earth faults are watched by insulation monitoring on the bus, which signals but does not show the line. To find the faulted line, press SBEY: its make contact trips the breaker, its break contact opens AAR’s starting circuit. After the operator reads the insulation monitor, releasing SBEY lets AAR start and restore supply.
  7. Lamp H1: when AAR operates, KC4 opens and H1 goes out briefly. If H1 is out, first check whether AAR has operated; if not, the lamp may be burnt out, the H1 circuit broken, a connection loose, the operating-supply fuse blown, or KC4 not closed: check and repair. AAR operation is recorded by signal relay KS dropping its flag.

Report for automatic device diagrams (Table 7-1)Item (weight)Standard
Basic items (50 %)Symbols (30 %)Name every symbol’s equipment and its role in the circuit
Make-up (20 %)Which secondary devices form the device
Circuit functions (50 %)Functions (20 %)Under what conditions it does what
Logic (30 %)AAT: the starting logic; the automatic closing logic. AAR: the logic when reclosing succeeds; how it achieves anti-pumping; why it does not act on manual closing; what to do when its lamp is out

Exercises (7.5):

  1. Fig. 7-3: AAT under-voltage starting part (QF1 control). Action chart: bus lost voltage (KV1, KV2 act, from 1TV) AND standby live (KV3 acts, from 2TV) → KT1 operates → KOU1 operates → trip QF1 and shed load → automatic closing part. Circuit: S1·1, QS1·1, KV1, KV2, KV3 in series to KT1; KT1·1 → KS1 → XB1 → KOU1; KOU1·1 → XB2 → QF1·1 → Yoff1; KOU1·2 → XB3 → load shedding.
  2. Fig. 7-4: a single-source three-phase single-shot AAR (KT with R5, KC voltage and current coils, C, R4, R6, HWh, acceleration relay KAT, anti-pumping KCF, trip-position relay KCT, close-position relay KCC; start circuit via SA ㉑–㉓, ST and KCT1; low-frequency and bus-protection inputs discharge C).
  3. Fig. 7-5: AAT automatic closing and post-acceleration part (QF2 control). Chart: QF1 opens → blocking relay KLA1 de-energised → after 0.5–0.7 s KLA blocks; meanwhile KOU2 operates → QF2 closes; if the bus has a permanent short circuit → KA acts → KOU3 operates → QF2 trips (post-acceleration). The slow-release relay KLA lets KOU2 give just one closing pulse in that 0.5–0.7 s window.

terms: 备用电源自动投入装置（AAT）

worked.q: In the AAT of Fig. 7-1, why does KC’s contact open with a 0.5–0.8 s delay instead of at once?
worked.s: When 1QK trips, its contact 3–3 de-energises KC, but KC’s make contact stays closed for 0.5–0.8 s. During that time 1QK’s contact 4–4 is already closed, so the two together give one short closing pulse to 3QK. After the delay KC’s contact opens, so even if 3QK is tripped by protection (permanent bus fault), no second pulse can be given: AAT acts only once.

worked.q: Why must AAT start only after the working breaker has opened?
worked.s: So that the standby supply is never paralleled onto a working supply or onto a fault fed from the working side; the working supply is cut first (1QK auxiliary contacts) and the standby closed after. Also, the bus voltage must really have gone, not just a VT fuse blown, which is why the over-voltage relays’ contacts also block the other AAT.

worked.q: Explain why the AAR of Fig. 7-2 recloses only once on a permanent fault.
worked.s: After the first reclosure, the capacitor C has just discharged into KC’s voltage coil and needs 15–20 s to recharge through 4R. The protection trips again within a short time; KT1 starts and after 0.5–1.5 s closes KT1·2, but C’s voltage is too low to operate KC, so no closing pulse is given.

worked.q: An operator trips a line breaker by SAC. Give two reasons the AAR does not reclose.
worked.s: (1) SAC is now at “after trip”, corresponding to the breaker’s open position, so SAC ㉑–㉓ is open and AAR’s starting circuit is cut. (2) SAC ②–④ closes, discharging C through 6R, so even if started, KC could not operate. (Also, SAH may be put to “off” beforehand.)

topics.title: Installation Wiring Diagrams: Location Diagrams, Connection Diagrams and Terminal Blocks
topics.zh: 安装接线图：位置图、接线图与端子排

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气原理图识读》 (Reading Electrical Schematic Diagrams), eds. Chen Fang and Li Jiakun, Yellow River Water Conservancy Press, 2010: a college textbook for power-station and substation work. Written in my own words; the figures are redrawn. Model codes and ratings are the Chinese (GB) ones the book uses.

Project 8’s tasks: from the location and connection diagrams, find every secondary device on the panel or cabinet; wire it from the connection diagram (table) and terminal diagram (table); and check the wiring with them.

A location diagram shows the real positions of the items in an assembly, device or installation. It is drawn to real size and to scale, with simple outline shapes. On a switchgear cabinet or protection panel it is the panel-front location diagram (屏面位置图); the old standard called it the panel layout diagram (屏面布置图).

ExampleWhat it shows
Fig. 8-1: No. 3 cabinet in a switchroom, type GC5-10(F) withdrawable (truck) HV cabinetOpen instrument door 1: the protective relays are in relay compartment 2 (KA1, KA2, KT in the top row; KS and XB below); terminal board 3 is at the left of the relay compartment. On instrument door 1: meters, red and green lamps, control switch. Above the relay compartment (cabinet top): DC small-bus compartment 9. Other parts: 4 maker’s plate, 5 truck compartment, 6 inspection window, 7 mimic diagram, 8 nameplate
Fig. 8-2: generator control panel (2360 mm high; columns 130/170/170/130 mm)Top to bottom: indicating meters (A, JW, 61A, VAR, 61V), watt-hour lamp 41WH, annunciators (1HL–63HL), synchronising switches (61SAM, 7SA), excitation remote-control board, insulation-check button, mimic line with the generator symbol, red and green lamps (1RD, 1GN, 51RD, 61RD …), control switches (1SA, 51SA, 61SA), field rheostat switches (41SA, 42SA)
Fig. 8-3: generator protection panel (800 mm wide, 2360 mm high)Top to bottom: relays needing little repair or adjustment at the top (current, voltage, time relays: 1KA–4KA, KV, KOU, KC, 1KT, 2KT, position relays 1KTP, 1KCP, 2KTP, 2KCP); directional, differential and reclosing relays in the middle (1KD, 2KD, 3KD; meters kW·h, kvar, kVA·h); at the bottom signal relays (KS–5KS), links (XB–4XB), test box TB, changeover tabs

sections.h: Connection diagrams: device marking, terminal designations and relative numbering
sections.b:
A connection diagram or table shows the connections of an assembly, device or installation, for wiring and checking. They can be used alone or together; in practice the connection diagram is used with the circuit and location diagrams. It generally shows the items’ relative positions, item designations (including terminal numbers) and wire numbers (circuit numbers). (Tables are simple; the book covers the diagram.) It can show the connections on the panel front or rear.

The devices’ relative positions and numbers must match the location diagram. In Fig. 8-1, the first relay on the left of the panel-front location diagram, KA1, is the first relay on the right of the panel-rear connection diagram Fig. 8-4 (a): the location diagram is a front view, the rear connection diagram a back view: positions agree top to bottom but are reversed left to right. Distances are already dimensioned on the location diagram, so the connection diagram need not be to scale; but each device’s internal wiring and terminal numbers must be drawn.

  • Device marking (Fig. 8-5): a circle above the device symbol (or internal wiring drawing), split into upper and lower halves: the upper half the device’s sequence number within the installation unit (e.g. 2), the lower half its letter symbol with the serial number among like devices (KA2, or 2KA). Or simply mark the number above the device, as in Fig. 8-4 (a).
  • Terminal designation: in secondary circuits, connections between devices inside a panel and outside or on the panel top, or between two units on one panel, go through terminals; several terminals together are a terminal block (terminal strip). The terminal designation is part of the full item designation. If the device’s terminals are marked, the designation must match; if not, assign numbers on the drawing. A terminal board is generally designated “X”, to distinguish it from device terminals. In Fig. 8-4 (a), terminal 2 of device 2 (relay KA2) is =S2W1+322−A2K2:2, simplified to 2:2. In Fig. 8-4 (b), terminal 1 of the terminal board is =S2W1+33−A2X:1, simplified to 33:1 or X:1.
  • Relative numbering (相对编号法): two ways of showing a wire between two devices: continuous lines or broken lines. With complex wiring, broken lines are clearer; their ends are marked by relative numbering. E.g. if terminal ① of KA1 connects to terminal ① of KA2, mark “2:1” (KA2 terminal ①) at KA1’s terminal ①, and “1:1” at KA2’s terminal ①. Because each end is marked with the other end, it is called relative numbering.
  • Rule: at most two wires on one terminal; conductor section not more than 6 mm².

Reading Fig. 8-4 (b), the left terminal board X of the cabinet: terminals 1–3 carry the CT circuits L1411, L3411, N411 (to relays 1:2, 2:2, 2:8; wires 34, 40, 41) from the cable compartment; 4, 5 WC+, WC− (fuses; 101, 102) from the small-bus compartment; 6 Yoff (102 → 3:8); 7, 8 signal circuits 701, 716 (49, 50; to 4:2, 4:4); 9–10 trip circuit 133 (52; to 5:2) to the truck compartment via a connecting test terminal; 11–13 spare.

A terminal consists mainly of an insulating base and a conducting strip. The base, generally of moulded bakelite, insulates the strip and holds the terminal in its fixing channel, and stops a wire touching the live part of the next terminal; a spring catch at the bottom fixes it in the rail.

Terminal type (by use)Model
(1) General terminal: ordinary connectionB1-1 or D1-10
(2) Connecting terminal: links adjacent terminalsB1-4 or D1-10L1, D1-10L2
(3) Test terminal: for testing current circuitsB1-2 or D1-10S
(4) Connecting-type test terminal: for testing current circuitsB1-3 or D1-10SL
(5) End terminal: fixes the terminals, or separates the blocks of different installation unitsB1-5 or D1-B
(6) Standard terminal: directly links wires inside and outside the panelB1-6
(7) Special terminal: in circuits that need to be opened easilyB1-7

Order on a terminal block, top to bottom: ① AC current and voltage circuits; ② DC control circuits; ③ signal and other circuits; ④ finally 2–5 spare terminals. End terminals fix the two ends of the board; they also separate the blocks of different installation units.

Drawing terminal-block diagrams: the view must agree with the connection diagram. Each terminal is marked by relative numbering. The diagram shows the number, type and order of terminals needed on the panel (cabinet), and their connections with the panel top, the panel body and external equipment; connections to external equipment go through the terminal block via control cables (Fig. 8-4 (b)). Fig. 8-6: terminal blocks with remote-end marks: each row shows the local item designation (with terminal number), the terminal, the remote item designation (with terminal), and for each cable: cable number + remote item (location) designation, type + cores × cross-section. worked.q: On a panel-front location diagram, relay KA<sub>1</sub> is the first on the left of the top row. Where is it on the panel-rear connection diagram, and why?
worked.s: The first on the right of the top row. The location diagram is a front view and the rear connection diagram a back view: positions are the same top to bottom but reversed left to right.

worked.q: Relay 3 (time relay KT) terminal ⑦ connects to relay 5 (signal relay KS) terminal ①. How are the two ends marked with relative numbering?
worked.s: At KT’s terminal ⑦ write “5:1” (device 5, terminal 1); at KS’s terminal ① write “3:7” (device 3, terminal 7). Each end shows where the other end goes.

worked.q: Arrange these on a terminal block in the correct order: spare terminals, CT circuits, signal circuit 701, DC control supply WC+, VT circuits.
worked.s: Top to bottom: CT circuits and VT circuits (AC current and voltage) → DC control (WC+) → signal and other circuits (701) → 2–5 spare terminals; with end terminals at both ends.

worked.q: Which terminal type would you use where a CT circuit must be tested on line, and why?
worked.s: A test terminal (B1-2 / D1-10S) or connecting-type test terminal (B1-3 / D1-10SL): they let a test instrument be inserted into the current circuit without open-circuiting the CT secondary.

topics.title: Electrical Accidents: Features, Patterns and Types
topics.zh: 电气事故：特点、规律与类型

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

  1. Great harm. They usually injure people and damage property; serious ones cause great economic loss and deaths, and they are an important cause of fires and explosions.
  2. The danger before an accident is hard to recognise. Over-current in conductors, hot connections and ageing insulation are not easy to see directly, so the accident comes as a surprise.
  3. They occur everywhere. Electricity is used in industry, farming and homes; wherever it is used an accident is possible, and almost everyone is a user. Society as a whole must spread safe-use knowledge.
  4. Prevention needs all of society: families, schools and employers spreading safety knowledge until safe habits form.

Most electrical accidents are repetitive and frequent; unforeseeable, unavoidable ones are very few. They follow patterns that can be learned. The organisational measures, technical measures and safety rules are the summed experience of fighting electrical accidents; using electricity by these rules, accidents can be avoided.

PatternReasons given in the book
1. More in hot, humid seasonsIn China, April–September, especially June–September: thin clothing and sweaty skin lower body resistance; wet ground conducts better and completes the current path; equipment insulation resistance falls, even breaking down; rural peak season increases use. In this season always wear proper insulating shoes and long-sleeved work clothes
2. More at low voltageFar more LV equipment and people in contact with it, many lacking safety knowledge; people are wary of HV and keep away
3. More with portable and mobile equipmentMoved often, poor conditions, frequent faults, cords break and leak; held tightly, so large contact area and low contact resistance, hard to let go; mostly single-phase, protective and working neutrals easily swapped. Plastic housings and RCDs have reduced these, but the supply cord remains a weak point
4. More at connection pointsTerminals, wrapped, crimped and soldered joints, cable heads, lamp holders, plugs, sockets, switches, contactors, fuses, breakers, disconnectors, branch lines, service drops: poor tightness, high contact resistance, heating, insulation failure
5. More in metallurgy, mining, construction, machineryDamp, hot sites; disorder; many temporary supplies and portable tools; metal conductive surroundings; cramped spaces
6. More in the countrysidePoor conditions and equipment, few qualified electricians, little knowledge, weak rules
7. More among young and middle-aged workers, non-electricians and temporary workersFront-line operators often near equipment, but inexperienced and lacking knowledge
8. More from mis-operation and rule-breakingIncomplete technical and management measures against mis-operation
9. More among maintenance electricians than duty electriciansNo fixed workplace or fixed equipment; temporary supplies and portable tools; both HV and much LV work; often at connection points
10. Most have more than one causeBy accident-causation theory: unsafe acts plus unsafe conditions. Control either: stop rule-breaking, or remove hazards and leakage

By the energy-transfer view, an electrical accident is electric energy acting unexpectedly on a person or a system. By the form of energy: electric-shock accidents, static electricity accidents, lightning disasters, electromagnetic field hazards and electrical system failure hazards.

Electric shock (电击): current through the body stimulates tissue, causing involuntary spasms of muscles; in severe cases it disrupts the heart, lungs and central nervous system, endangering life. Its severity depends on the current’s magnitude, kind, duration, path and the person’s condition. By the way of contact:

KindDescription
Single-phase contactBody touches earth or an earthed conductor while another part touches one live phase. Touching a normally live part = direct-contact shock; touching a part made live by a fault = indirect-contact shock. Over 70 % of all shock accidents are single-phase, so prevention focuses here. RCDs reduce single-phase shock but do nothing for two-phase contact
Two-phase contactTwo parts of the body touch two phases: the body takes the line voltage, 1.732 times the phase voltage: more dangerous
Step-voltage shockThe voltage between the feet of a person standing or walking near a point where current enters the earth (a fallen HV line, an earth fault). If caught in such an area, do not take long steps; hop out on one leg (or shuffle with feet together)

Electric injury (电伤): harm by the current’s heating, chemical and mechanical effects; usually large currents.

  1. Current burns: electrical energy turned to heat where current passes.
  2. Arc burns: direct (current passes through the body) or indirect (arc near the body, or splashes of molten metal). Opening a disconnector under load draws a strong arc; approaching HV parts closer than the flashover distance strikes an arc directly; severe arc burns can kill. Most arc-burn accidents happen to maintenance staff: wear long sleeves, fasten cuffs and collar, wear gloves and a helmet, preferably goggles.
  3. Electric marks (电烙印): a hard, dead, numb patch shaped like the contact.
  4. Skin metallisation (皮肤炭化): vaporised metal from an arc penetrating the skin; rough and tight.
  5. Mechanical injury: violent involuntary muscle contraction tearing tendons, skin, vessels, nerves; dislocations and fractures.
  6. Arc eye (电光眼): inflamed cornea and conjunctiva from infrared, visible and ultraviolet light of an arc.

sections.h: Static, lightning, RF fields and system failures
sections.b:
HazardWhat the book says
Static electricityCharges accumulate when materials move, touch and separate in processes and in operators’ movements. Voltages may reach tens to hundreds of kV but energy is usually small and not directly fatal. Hazards: (1) a static spark ignites flammable mixtures: explosion and fire; (2) a static shock startles a person into a secondary accident, e.g. a fall from height; (3) it hinders production, spoils product quality and damages electronics. Most likely in dry surroundings; quick movements in synthetic clothing generate it. Raising humidity and wearing pure cotton reduce it
LightningViolent discharge between charged clouds: very large current and voltage. (1) Direct strokes, secondary (side) flashes and the heat of lightning current cause fire and explosion; (2) direct strikes, side flashes, step voltage and the fires and explosions kill and injure; (3) huge current and voltage break down or burn equipment; strikes on generators, transformers, lines can cause large blackouts, and directly damage buildings
Radio-frequency fields (above 100 kHz)(1) The body absorbs radiated energy: excess causes central-nervous dysfunction (neurasthenia, autonomic disorder, abnormal heart rate and blood pressure), eye damage, testicular dysfunction, skin burns; (2) strong fields induce discharges that can set off electric detonators; a hazard in explosive or flammable areas; high induced voltages give noticeable shocks
Electrical system failuresLoss of control of energy in transmission, distribution or conversion: open circuits, short circuits, abnormal earths, leakage, wrong closing, wrong tripping, damaged equipment or components, mis-operation of electronics. (1) Fire and explosion: lines, switches, fuses, sockets, lamps and heaters can start fires; transformers and bulk-oil breakers can also explode. Electricity is the second cause of fires, after open flames. (2) Abnormal energisation: normally dead parts become live, e.g. an enclosure through poor insulation, step voltage near an HV earth fault. (3) Abnormal loss of supply: e.g. a crane pouring molten steel losing control; an operating theatre; a mine ventilation fan stopping, letting gas collect and explode; public places; computer systems

terms: 人的不安全行为/物的不安全状态

worked.q: Why are two-phase contacts more dangerous than single-phase, and why does an RCD not help?
worked.s: The body is across the line voltage (√3 = 1.732 times phase voltage), so more current flows. And an RCD trips on residual current (current not returning through the circuit conductors); in a phase-to-phase or phase-to-neutral contact the current goes out on one conductor and back on another, so the RCD sees the person as a normal load and does not trip.

worked.q: You find yourself near a fallen HV conductor with the ground live. What should you do?
worked.s: Do not take long strides (each step spans a large step voltage). Keep the feet together and hop on one leg (the book’s advice), moving away from the earth point until you are well clear.

worked.q: A maintenance electrician must operate a 400 V knife switch. What personal precautions against arc burns does the book give?
worked.s: Long-sleeved clothing with cuffs and collar fastened; gloves; helmet; preferably goggles. Operate side-on, keeping the face away from the switch; and never open a disconnecting device under load.

topics.title: Effects of Current on the Body, Body Impedance and Strategies Against Shock
topics.zh: 电流对人体的作用、人体阻抗与防触电策略

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Only one to a dozen or so milliamps of power-frequency current through the body causes numbness, tingling, pressure, blows and cramps; around 50 mA can cause ventricular fibrillation and death.

Left hand → right hand (Table 1-1): sensation5 % of subjects (mA)50 %95 %

LevelDefinitionValues
Perception currentSmallest current that can be feltAverage adult man 1.1 mA, woman about 0.7 mA. Not harmful in itself, but a startled reaction can cause a knock or fall
Let-go currentLargest current from which a person can free themselvesAverage man 16 mA, woman 10.5 mA; strong muscular people higher; weak people far lower, around 6 mA
Fibrillation currentSmallest current causing ventricular fibrillation: the heart quivers fast instead of pumping; death within minutes. Regarded as the lethal currentDepends strongly on duration: longer than one heartbeat: about 50 mA; shorter than one heartbeat: several hundred mA; under 0.1 s: only if the shock falls in the heart’s vulnerable period and is 500 mA or more, even several amperes

So: the shorter the shock, the less harm. Get the casualty off the supply as fast as possible.

sections.h: Duration, path, kind of current, personal condition
sections.b:
Duration. The longer the current flows, the more likely fibrillation, because: (1) energy accumulates, heating and chemical effects show fully, and the fibrillation threshold falls; (2) it is more likely to coincide with the heart’s vulnerable period; (3) body resistance falls (sweating, breakdown of high-resistance skin), so current rises; (4) central-nervous reflexes grow stronger, causing cardiac or respiratory arrest. Hence: free the casualty as quickly as possible.

Path. Any path through the heart, brain or central nervous system is extremely dangerous. The heart is least able to stand current, so paths with large current through the heart and short length are worst: chest → left hand most dangerous; chest → right hand next; left hand → both feet very dangerous but less; left hand → right hand is the least dangerous of the common paths, about half as dangerous as left hand → feet. Local paths (thumb to forefinger of one hand) do not cross the heart, but strong reflexes may still cause serious results or secondary accidents.

Kind of current. Almost all kinds harm the body, but power frequency (50–60 Hz) is the most harmful and lethal. DC is easier to let go of, its fibrillation current is higher, and DC systems are unearthed, so DC shock deaths are rare. With DC, the fibrillation current with the feet negative is twice that with the feet positive; DC from left hand to right hand is unlikely to cause fibrillation. For non-power-frequency AC, the further from power frequency, the smaller the threat to life.

Personal condition. More danger for people whose hands and feet sweat, with thin delicate skin (women, children), with heart, nervous-system or lung disease, and for weak, sickly people (poor let-go ability).

At a given voltage, the current depends only on body impedance; the higher it is, the smaller the current. Body impedance includes skin, blood, muscle, bone, tissue and their junctions, with resistance and capacitance. It is split into skin impedance and internal impedance (book Fig. 1-1): at each contact point a skin resistance Rp in parallel with a skin capacitance Cp forms the skin impedance Zp1, Zp2; the internal impedance Ri (body minus outer skin) has negligible capacitance and is treated as pure resistance. Total impedance ZT = Zp1 + Ri + Zp2.

Unlike a metal conductor, body impedance falls sharply as voltage rises. Table 1-3 (dry, large contact area 50–100 cm², left hand → right hand):

Touch voltage (V)5 % of subjects below (Ω)50 %95 %

50145026254375
75125022003500
100120018753200
125112516252875
220100013502125
