Asymptotic value650750850

Other factors lowering impedance: wet or sweaty skin, damaged skin, conductive dust (e.g. graphite). Skin wetted by a conductive solution: impedance halves; skin soaked for a long time (horny layer soft and full of water): skin impedance almost vanishes. Greater contact pressure and area lower it; longer current flow lowers it (sweating). Avoid these when operating or maintaining equipment.

Worked example (my calculation from Table 1-3): a 220 V touch, hand to hand, median person: 220 / 1350 Ω ≈ 163 mA, more than three times the 50 mA fibrillation level for long contacts. Even the most resistant 5 % (2125 Ω) would carry about 104 mA. That is why 220 V is lethal.

Overall, working strictly to the organisational and technical safety measures keeps work on electrical equipment safe. Large utilities and works do this, but small firms, villages and households often ignore them. So the book gives practical, individual strategies for low-voltage work:

  1. Safe working habits. ① One-hand working: while one hand works, keep the other hand and the rest of the body off any other part of the equipment; standing on dry wood, a rubber mat or in insulating shoes, even if the working hand touches a live part (220/380 V) no current flows through the body. ② Always wear insulating shoes for any electrical work or operation. In short: “work one-handed as a habit; always wear insulating shoes”.
  2. Work dead, plus: (1) isolate neighbouring live equipment: lock adjacent rooms, hang “Danger: live” signs, fence if possible, to stop entry into live areas, especially when starting and restarting after a break; if live parts are in the same area, guard them, supervise closely, keep movements small, use no long thin metal tools; if very close with risk of shorting, wear gloves, fasten cuffs and collar. (2) Prevent accidental re-energising, especially when the switch is not where you work: open the knife switch or remove the fuses, hang “Do not close — men working on line”, post a guard; if no guard, take the fuses with you, lock the mechanism, and at the work site short and earth all three phases that could become live. (3) Prove dead: test the voltage tester on a known live part first; in bright light a neon tester is hard to read, so confirm with a multimeter. Caution: on a 3-phase 4-wire system, measuring zero between the phases does not prove dead. The book’s case: one phase is still live while the other two are disconnected and floating; a meter between a live and a floating conductor has no return path and can read about zero, so AB, AC and BC can all read zero. Measure each phase to earth: only if all are zero is it dead.
  3. Close supervision. The “filter effect”: a person concentrating hard filters out everything unrelated, including hazards: e.g. hurrying to restore an important tripped machine, a fitter enters the wrong cubicle or touches a part known to be live. The most effective defence is a supervisor who knows about the filter effect and when it arises, and reminds the worker of the danger points repeatedly. Rules say the supervisor should be the most skilled and experienced; in reality, statistics from large steelworks show many fatalities involve team leaders, meaning the roles are often reversed.
  4. RCDs or isolating transformers. RCDs have clearly reduced shock deaths, but: (1) a correctly installed, healthy RCD can still let you be shocked: it trips only on single-phase contact, after current has already flowed; with contact across two phases or phase and neutral it treats the body as a load and does not trip; (2) never test an RCD by touching a live part: Chinese standard rated residual operating currents are 6, 10, 30, 100, 300, 500, 1000, 3000, 5000, 10 000, 20 000 mA … (15 levels); for a 30–1000 mA device the shock could be serious or fatal; (3) an isolating transformer (1:1, well insulated and screened) gives an unearthed supply: touching one conductor and earth passes no current. Like an RCD it does not protect against two-conductor contact; unlike an RCD, there is no current through the person and no need to trip, so other equipment keeps working. Drawbacks: cost and size.
  5. Safety extra-low voltage in high-risk places (inside metal vessels, on metal structures, damp, cramped, standing water), where RCDs are not enough. Chinese rated values: 42, 36, 24, 12, 6 V. Hand-held power tools in especially dangerous places: 42 V; hand lamps and local lighting where there is shock risk: 36 or 24 V; hand lamps inside metal vessels or very wet places: 12 V; underwater work: 6 V. Above 24 V, measures against direct contact are still required.
  6. Check the safety measures at the dangerous moments: starting, restarting after a break, moving to another work place, and near the end: confirm the cubicle number, the safety measures, prove dead (discharge if needed), check earths, know where nearby live parts are, guard against touching them.
  7. Follow the operating rules. Before re-energising: check for left tools, connections not remade, temporary earths and shorting links not removed; measure insulation resistance with an insulation tester and do not energise if it fails. Switch in the right order: energise: bus-side disconnector, then line-side disconnector, then breaker; de-energise in reverse; never make or break a disconnector under load. Wear insulating gloves and stand on an insulating mat when operating disconnectors. Prefer remote operation for trial energising; otherwise keep the body, especially the face, away: operate LV knife switches side-on with cuffs and collar fastened and gloves on.

worked.q: Using Table 1-3, estimate the current through a median person touching 50 V hand to hand, and compare with the let-go current.
worked.s: 50 V / 2625 Ω ≈ 19 mA, above the average man’s let-go current (16 mA): many people could not let go. With the least resistant 5 % (1450 Ω) it would be about 34 mA. (My calculation; this shows why even 50 V is not automatically safe in damp conditions.)

worked.q: On a 3-phase 4-wire circuit an electrician reads 0 V between L1–L2, L2–L3, L3–L1 and declares it dead. What is wrong?
worked.s: Line-to-line readings do not test against earth. If one phase is still live and the other two are open and floating, a meter between the live phase and a floating one has no return path and can read about zero, so all three readings can be zero while one phase is live. The book’s rule: measure each phase to earth; only if all are zero is the circuit dead. Also test the instrument on a known live source first.

worked.q: Choose the safety extra-low voltage for: (a) a hand lamp inside a steel boiler drum; (b) a hand-held drill in an especially dangerous place; (c) a lamp for underwater work.
worked.s: (a) 12 V (inside metal vessels); (b) 42 V; (c) 6 V.

topics.title: Protection Against Direct Contact: Insulation, Testing, Barriers and Safe Distances
topics.zh: 直接接触电击防护：绝缘、绝缘测试、屏护与安全距离

sections.h: Shock accidents and the five basic measures
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

A shock accident (触电事故) is one where a person touches a live part and current passes through the body. Current through the inside of the body is electric shock; local injury by heat, chemical and mechanical effects is electric injury, also a shock accident but generally less severe. At small currents and short times, ventricular fibrillation is the main cause of death; at even smaller currents a long time can also kill. Almost all electrocution deaths are by electric shock.

Three forms (Figs. 2-1 to 2-3): single-phase (standing on earth or an earthed conductor and touching one phase; its danger depends on the network: generally more dangerous in an earthed network than in an unearthed one); two-phase (touching two phases at once: very dangerous); step-voltage (between the feet near an earth point; HV line or equipment earth faults can produce high step voltages).

Basic measurePurpose
1 · InsulationEnclose live parts with insulating material so they cannot be touched. Never remove the insulation of equipment or lines; it must withstand electrical, mechanical, chemical and thermal effects
2 · Barriers (enclosures)Stop people approaching or touching live parts; also warn them that crossing is dangerous
3 · Safe distanceKeep accessible live parts out of arm’s reach, at a set distance
4 · Safety extra-low voltageRated value chosen for the work site
5 · RCDWhen the above fail (fault or carelessness), a current-operated RCD of 30 mA or less as supplementary protection. It does not replace basic protection and must be used together with one of the basic measures; experience shows it is an effective backup

Good insulation is a necessary condition for running equipment and lines, and the first condition for preventing shock. It must suit the network’s nominal voltage and the surroundings and operating conditions. Insulating materials generally have resistivity above 109 Ω·cm: porcelain, mica, wood, glass, rubber, bakelite, plastics, cloth, paper, mineral oil, etc.

Insulation performance is measured by insulation resistance, withstand voltage (dielectric strength), leakage current and dielectric loss. Insulation resistance is the most basic: enough of it limits leakage current to a very small value. It is measured by an insulation resistance tester (megohmmeter, “megger”): it applies a DC voltage, measures the leakage current and shows the converted resistance. Types: hand-cranked (a generator plus a two-coil ratio meter) and electronic. Terminals: E (earth), L (line), G (guard). E normally goes to earth or the equipment enclosure.

Connecting an insulation tester (after book Fig. 2-5, redrawn).

  1. Line to earth: E to earth, L to the conductor.
  2. Motor to earth: E to the motor frame, L to a motor terminal.
  3. Cable core to sheath: E to the sheath, L to the core, and to remove the error from leakage over the surface of the core insulation, G to the inner insulation layer under the sheath.

Electronic testers (e.g. the portable M-3121, M-3122, M-3123 HV models): a battery supply, DC/DC converted, output from E through the test object to L; the current is I/V-converted and divided to show the resistance on a dual scale or LCD. Features: (1) high output power, strong load and anti-interference ability; (2) an equipotential guard ring and active low-pass filter screen power-frequency and strong fields; on capacitive objects the output short-circuit current (above 1.6 mA) quickly raises the test voltage to its rating; low resistances are measured by a ratio method so voltage sag does not affect accuracy; (3) no cranking, battery powered, switchable ranges. Use: (1) zero: function switch “OFF”, set the pointer to “∞” with the zero knob; (2) battery check: “BATT. CHECK”, press test: pointer in or right of “BATT. GOOD”; do not hold or lock the test switch long; (3) measurement: set OFF, earth the circuit under test, connect the earth lead to the instrument’s earth terminal and the circuit’s earth; MΩ (M-3121/3122) or GΩ (M-3123); touch the probe, press test; green LED: read the outer (high) scale; red LED: inner (low) scale; at 5000 and 10 000 V read black and red scales (M-3123). After the test, release “PRESS TO TEST” and wait a few seconds before removing the probe to discharge the stored charge; (4) continuity: make sure no HV-sensitive components are connected.

Precautions: (1) crank steadily at about 120 r/min; check the tester before use; (2) choose the voltage: equipment of 100–1000 V: 500 V or 1000 V tester; above 1000 V: 2500 V or 5000 V; (3) test leads must be separate, not twisted pair, to avoid error; (4) if the pointer goes to “0”, the insulation is already faulty: stop, to avoid damaging the tester; (5) store electronic testers dry and ventilated, away from damp, dust, explosion, acids, alkalis and corrosive gas; (6) disconnect the supply before testing equipment that is normally live; there is high DC voltage between E and L when testing: touch nothing.

EquipmentMinimum insulation resistance (book)
Power cableVery high when good; follow the maker’s minimum; absorption ratio ≥ 1.3
AC motor below 1000 V≥ 0.5 MΩ at normal temperature (10–30 °C)
AC motor above 1000 VNear running temperature (75 °C): stator ≥ 1 MΩ/kV, rotor ≥ 0.5 MΩ/kV; absorption ratio generally ≥ 1.25–1.3
Hand-held power tool≥ 1 MΩ

Absorption ratio = R60s / R15s (the usual definition; the book uses the term without defining it here). A dry winding’s reading rises over the minute; a damp one stays flat, giving a ratio near 1.

Where live parts cannot conveniently be insulated, or insulation is not enough for safety, use screening (屏护): fences, covers, box lids separating live parts from the outside. Besides preventing shock, some also protect against arcs and make repair easier.

Fences do not touch live parts, so their materials need no special electrical properties, but must have enough mechanical strength and good fire resistance. Use with: (1) enough size and distance from live parts; (2) screened live parts clearly marked with the specified symbols or colours; (3) signs such as “Stop — high voltage danger”, “No climbing — high voltage danger”, “Beware of electric shock”.

Distances must be kept between live parts and the ground, other equipment and each other, to stop people touching or getting too close, to stop other objects striking them, and to avoid fire and short circuits. They depend on voltage and type of equipment.

  • Workshop LV distribution boxes: flush-mounted 1.4 m above floor, surface-mounted 1.2 m; LV operating handle centres generally 1.2–1.5 m; side-operated handles ≥ 200 mm from walls or other equipment.
  • Working distances: in LV work, body or tools ≥ 0.1 m from live parts. In HV work without barriers (Table 2-5): ≤ 10 kV 0.7 m; 20–35 kV 1.0 m; 110 kV 1.5 m; 220 kV 3.0 m. If less, fit temporary fences or other protection.

worked.q: Which tester voltage would you use for (a) a 400 V motor, (b) a 10 kV cable? What minimum insulation resistance would you expect for the motor?
worked.s: (a) 500 V or 1000 V tester (100–1000 V equipment); a 400 V motor should read at least 0.5 MΩ at 10–30 °C. (b) 2500 V or 5000 V tester (above 1000 V); judge by the maker’s minimum and an absorption ratio of at least 1.3.

worked.q: A 6 kV motor near running temperature measures 4 MΩ stator insulation. Is it acceptable by the book’s rule?
worked.s: Required: ≥ 1 MΩ/kV × 6 kV = 6 MΩ. 4 MΩ is below it: not acceptable; dry out and retest before running.

worked.q: Why connect the G terminal when testing a cable core to sheath?
worked.s: Current leaking across the surface of the core insulation (e.g. at a dirty or damp cable end) would otherwise flow through the meter and make the insulation look worse. G takes that surface current back to the tester’s source without passing through the measuring element, so only the current through the bulk insulation is measured.

worked.q: An electrician works without barriers near 35 kV live parts. What distance must he keep, and what if he cannot?
worked.s: At least 1.0 m (20–35 kV, Table 2-5). If that cannot be kept, fit temporary fences or other protection meeting the clearance rules, or de-energise.

sections.h: What indirect contact is, and the protective measures
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Indirect contact: exposed metal parts that are dead in normal service (enclosures, guards, frames) become live through a fault (leakage, a phase touching the case: a metallic earth fault), presenting a dangerous touch voltage; a person touching them is shocked. Indirect-contact protection aims to prevent shock deaths when equipment or lines are faulty, and usually also stops the fault growing into a worse equipment accident. Measures:

  1. Automatic disconnection of supply and earthing: suitable connections so that a fault automatically disconnects the supply within the specified time, preventing dangerous touch voltage: RCDs, protective earthing, insulation monitoring. Protective earthing limits the enclosure’s voltage to earth by connecting it directly to earth. Earthing or “zeroing” without a co-ordinated over-current device or RCD cannot give reliable indirect-contact protection.
  2. Class II equipment (double insulation): not only basic insulation, but also supplementary (or reinforced) insulation, so that if the working insulation fails, no dangerous voltage appears on accessible parts. Double insulation = working insulation plus protective insulation. Widely used: hand-held power tools, motors in very wet or corrosive surroundings.
  3. Electrical separation: an isolating supply separates a branch circuit from the whole system, making it an independent unearthed safe system. Conditions: (1) the source is an isolating transformer with a higher test voltage than ordinary transformers, meeting Class II requirements; the separated circuit voltage not above 500 V; (2) the separated circuit has no connection to other circuits, and especially must be insulated from earth.

sections.h: Earth potential, touch voltage and step voltage
sections.b:
Current Id entering the ground through an electrode spreads out hemispherically (Fig. 3-1). The hemisphere’s area grows with the square of the radius, so the soil resistance of each shell falls rapidly with distance. At 20 m the hemisphere’s area is already about 2500 m² and the soil resistance negligible: beyond 20 m the current makes no more voltage drop: the voltage is zero. “Earth” in electrical work means this ground beyond 20 m; “voltage to earth” is relative to it.

The electrode has the highest voltage; it falls with distance, fast at first then more slowly: the curve of voltage to earth is hyperbolic. Tests show about 68 % of the voltage drop within 1 m of the electrode, about 24 % from 2 m to 10 m, and about 8 % from 11 m to 20 m (Fig. 3-2).

  • Touch voltage Uc: when a person touches two points at different voltages, current flows through the body; the voltage across the body is the touch voltage. A person on the ground touching a leaking transformer bears the difference between the equipment’s voltage to earth Ud and the voltage of the spot where he stands.
  • Step voltage: the difference between two points on the ground under a person’s feet. It depends on the step: a person’s step is taken as 0.8 m, livestock 1.0–1.4 m. A person at the electrode bears the largest step voltage Ub1; one some distance away a much smaller Ub2; beyond 20 m it can be ignored.

The 68 % figure is why a person standing right at an earth electrode during a fault is at greatest risk, and why grading the ground near equipment (by burying the electrode or meshing) reduces touch voltage. (My note.)

sections.h: Protective earthing in an unearthed system
sections.b:
In an unearthed LV system (IT), when one phase touches the case, the earth current Id flows through the person and the network’s insulation impedance to earth (Fig. 3-3). With equal phase-to-earth impedances, the leaking equipment’s voltage to earth is:

Ud = 3 U Rr / | 3 Rr + Z |

U = phase voltage; Rr = body resistance; Z = each phase’s insulation impedance to earth (insulation resistance in parallel with distributed capacitance). If the insulation resistance is taken as infinite: Ud = 3URr / √(9Rr² + 1/ω²C²), C = each phase’s capacitance to earth.

With good insulation and a small network, Id and Ud are small; but with poor insulation or a large network (large capacitance), Ud can become dangerous. Then fit protective earthing (Fig. 3-4): the enclosure’s voltage now depends mainly on the earthing resistance Rb, which is in parallel with Rr and much smaller:

Ud ≈ 3 U Rb / | 3 Rb + Z |

The book’s example: a 380 V cable network 1 km long, body resistance 1500 Ω: a person touching leaking equipment bears 127 V, about 84.5 mA: very dangerous. With protective earthing Rb = 4 Ω, the voltage falls to 0.415 V and the current to 0.277 mA: no danger. (Check: 127 V / 1500 Ω ≈ 84.7 mA; 0.415 V / 1500 Ω ≈ 0.277 mA ✓.)

Where protective earthing applies: unearthed networks: in any surroundings, metal parts that may become live through insulation failure or other causes, unless otherwise specified: (1) bases and enclosures of motors, transformers, portable and mobile equipment; (2) drive gear of electrical equipment; (3) secondary windings of instrument transformers; (4) metal frames and enclosures of distribution boards, control desks, protection panels and cabinets; (5) cable supports, etc.

Earthing resistance of LV equipment: Rb ≤ 4 Ω; for distribution transformers not over 100 kVA (small network, smaller earth-fault current), Rb ≤ 10 Ω.

Most Chinese LV networks are solidly earthed-neutral 3-phase 4-wire, so TN systems are the most widely used. In a TN system one point of the source is directly earthed, and the exposed conductive parts of loads are connected to it by protective conductors: “protective zeroing” (保护接零). T = the source neutral directly earthed; N = equipment enclosures connected to the neutral (protective) conductor. If a phase touches the enclosure, a single-phase short circuit results and the line protection quickly disconnects.

The three TN arrangements (after book Fig. 3-5, redrawn; colours: phases blue, N orange, PE green, PEN yellow).

TypeArrangementUsed for (book)
TN-CProtective and working neutral combined throughout (PEN)Places of low explosion risk and good safety conditions
TN-SA dedicated protective conductor PE, separate from the working neutral NPlaces of greater explosion risk or higher safety requirements
TN-C-SPEN in the first part, then separated into N and PEWorkshops fed by a works LV incomer; civil buildings

In Singapore and IEC terms the same letters are used; LV installations in Singapore are generally TT or TN-S per SS 638 and the utility’s requirements, and a combined PEN conductor in final circuits is not permitted. Follow your lecturers on local practice. (My note for context.)

worked.q: Using the book’s 380 V example, verify that 4 Ω earthing makes the touch current safe, and say what remains necessary.
worked.s: Touch voltage 0.415 V over 1500 Ω: I = 0.415 / 1500 ≈ 0.28 mA, below the perception current (≈ 1 mA): safe. But earthing alone in an unearthed system does not disconnect the fault; a second fault on another phase would create a phase-to-phase fault through two enclosures, so insulation monitoring and prompt clearing of the first fault are still needed (and, per the book, earthing should be co-ordinated with an over-current device or RCD).

worked.q: What fraction of the voltage drop occurs within 1 m of an earth electrode, and what step is assumed for a person?
worked.s: About 68 % within 1 m; a person’s step is taken as 0.8 m (livestock 1.0–1.4 m). So most of the step-voltage danger is right beside the electrode.

worked.q: A workshop with fire and explosion risk is to be fed by TN. Which arrangement does the book recommend and why?
worked.s: TN-S: a separate PE conductor carries no load current, so no voltage drop on PE in normal service and no sparking where PE is bonded to metalwork; the book recommends TN-S where explosion risk or safety requirements are higher.

topics.title: Indirect Contact II: Protective Zeroing, Working and Repeated Earthing, Earthing Installations and Testing
topics.zh: 间接接触电击防护（二）：保护接零、工作接地与重复接地、接地装置及检测

sections.h: Protective zeroing, and why earthing alone fails in an earthed-neutral system
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Protective zeroing: in normal service, the dead metal enclosure of equipment is connected firmly to the network’s neutral (zero) conductor. In 380/220 V 3-phase 4-wire networks with solidly earthed neutral, it is the safety measure against shock from faulty equipment. Without any measure, a person touching faulty equipment would bear 220 V. With zeroing (Fig. 3-6), a phase touching the enclosure gives a phase-to-neutral short circuit; the short-circuit current Id makes the line protection (fuses etc.) operate quickly and disconnect.

Earthing alone is not safe in an earthed-neutral network (Fig. 3-7). With only a protective earth Rd on the motor and the neutral earth R0, a person (Rr) is in parallel with Rd:

Ur = U Rd Rr / (Rd R0 + R0 Rr + Rd Rr) ≈ U Rd / (R0 + Rd)

Since R0, Rd ≪ Rr. With R0 = Rd = 4 Ω: Ur ≈ 220 × 4 / 8 = 110 V: still very dangerous.

And the fault current Id = 220 / (4 + 4) = 27.5 A is too small to operate the line protection, so the dangerous voltage persists. For quick, reliable clearing, a breaker needs a fault current above 1.5 times its rated current, a fuse above 4 times. So in earthed-neutral networks, protective earthing reduces but does not remove the danger: the book says use protective zeroing, not earthing. In 380/220 V solidly earthed networks, in any surroundings, all metal parts that may become live through insulation failure must be zeroed; the parts that need or need not be zeroed are about the same as for earthing.

Working earth (工作接地): connecting the transformer LV neutral directly to an earthing installation. It reduces fault danger and stabilises the network’s potential.

  1. Reduces the danger of a phase-to-earth fault (Fig. 3-8). With an unearthed neutral, a phase touching earth draws little current; equipment keeps running and the fault may persist, while current through equipment and a person back to the neutral makes every zeroed device on that transformer dangerous. With a working earth, the earth current flows mainly through the fault’s earth resistance Rd and the working earth R0, and the zeroed equipment’s voltage to earth is U0 ≈ IdR0 ≈ U R0 / (Rd + R0). With R0 = 4 Ω and Rd = 10 Ω: U0 = 220 × 4/14 ≈ 63 V, much less dangerous.
  2. Reduces the danger of HV entering the LV side (Fig. 3-9): if transformer insulation fails and HV enters the LV side, the LV neutral rises to U0 = Id × R0. The rule: U0 ≤ 120 V, so R0 ≤ 120 / Id. For unearthed HV networks the earth current generally does not exceed 30 A, so R0 ≤ 4 Ω suffices (120 / 30 = 4).

Repeated earthing (重复接地): earthing the neutral again at one or more points (Rc, Fig. 3-10). It is an indispensable measure in zeroed networks:

  1. Lowers the voltage of faulty equipment: during the short time from the fault until the protection operates, the enclosure is live; its voltage equals the drop of the short-circuit current along the neutral, proportional to the neutral and phase impedances: the higher the neutral impedance, the higher the voltage. Repeated earthing lowers it.
  2. Reduces the danger of a broken neutral (Figs. 3-12, 3-13): without it, beyond the break, a case fault drives current through the person and the working earth; since the body’s resistance is far larger, the person bears almost the full phase voltage. With repeated earthing, the current flows mainly through Rc and R0, and the voltage beyond the break is less than phase voltage. Even with no case fault, a broken neutral plus unbalanced load can put a dangerous voltage on the neutral; repeated earthing reduces or removes it.
  3. Shortens fault duration: repeated and working earths form a parallel path with the neutral through the ground, increasing short-circuit current and speeding the protection; more marked on long lines.
  4. Improves lightning performance.

Requirements: (1) directly from the neutral or from zeroed equipment enclosures; (2) overhead lines: at the ends of mains and branches, and every 1 km along the line; (3) where cables and overhead lines enter workshops or large buildings, re-earth the neutral, or connect it indoors to the earthing of distribution and control panels; LV cables using the metal sheath as neutral also need repeated earthing; (4) inside workshops use a ring or repeated earthing, with at least two connections to the earthing installation: besides the incoming point, the nearest point on the opposite corner.

Protective earthingProtective zeroing
PrincipleLimits the faulty equipment’s voltage to earth to a safe valueTurns the fault into a single-phase short circuit so the line protection quickly disconnects
Where usedLV unearthed networks, and earthed LV networks with other safety measures; also HV unearthed networksLV networks with solidly earthed neutral
Line structureBesides phases, only a protective earth conductorBesides phases, a neutral is required; when necessary, protective and working neutrals separate
In commonBoth protect against indirect contact in LV networks; the same parts of installations need them; both need earthing installations (protective, working, repeated), built and connected in the same ways

An earthing installation = earth electrodes + earthing conductors; a zeroing installation = earthing installation + neutral conductor network. Artificial electrodes: metal deliberately buried for earthing. Natural electrodes: metal structures in direct contact with earth that serve as electrodes: buried metal pipes (not pipes for flammable or explosive media), metal well casings, building metal structures reliably connected to earth, metal pipes and piles of hydraulic structures. Use natural electrodes first (saves steel and cost and lowers resistance); add artificial ones if needed; substations always need designed artificial electrodes.

Ten safety requirements:

  1. Electrical continuity from equipment to electrode and to the transformer neutral; no breaks or poor contacts. Where building steel, crane rails or pipes are used as earthing conductors, fit bonding jumpers across expansion joints and joints. Do not use flexible conduit, metal jackets or mesh of pipe insulation, or cable metal sheaths, as earthing conductors.
  2. Reliable connections: generally welded. Flat steel lap length ≥ 2 × width, welded on at least three edges; round steel ≥ 6 × diameter; flat steel to pipe or angle: weld both sides plus a curved clamp of strip (or bend the strip round the pipe); weld jumpers across series metal parts used as conductors.
  3. Mechanical strength (with allowance for corrosion), minima of Table 3-1 below; large and medium power stations, 110 kV and above substations, and corrosive places: hot-dip galvanised steel or larger sections.
  4. Conductivity and thermal stability: with zeroing, the neutral must carry enough current to operate protection: if natural conductors are not used, the protective neutral’s conductivity ≥ half that of the phase conductor. In networks with large earth-fault current, check thermal stability for the single-phase earth-fault current.
  5. Protection from damage: where people are unlikely to touch them, yet visible for inspection.
  6. Corrosion protection: galvanised parts, bitumen on welds, paint on exposed conductors; in strongly corrosive soil, galvanised and larger section.
  7. Sensible underground distances: electrode to building ≥ 1.5 m; to the electrode of a free-standing lightning rod ≥ 3 m; keep away from pipes of flammable or explosive media.
  8. No series connection of branch conductors: each equipment earthing (or zeroing) branch connects separately to the main earthing conductor or electrode; the main conductor connects to the electrode at two points. A works substation earth is at once the transformer working earth, the HV protective earth, the LV repeated earth and sometimes the lightning earth: connect each part separately to the electrode.
  9. Burial depth: top of electrode ≥ 0.6 m and below the frost line.
  10. Resistance and protective devices as required: earthing resistance not above the specified value; in zeroed networks, fuse or breaker operating currents meet the zeroing requirements.
Table 3-1: minimum steel sizesAbove ground indoorAbove ground outdoorUnderground ACUnderground DC
Round steel diameter (mm)681012
Flat steel section (mm²)60100100100
Flat steel thickness (mm)3446

Table 3-2: exposed LV earthing conductors, minimum section (mm²)CopperAluminium
Bare conductor, surface run46

Portable equipment: earthing conductor of flexible stranded copper ≥ 1.5 mm².

Inspection and measurement: mainly visual checks, earthing resistance and adjacent circuits; interval per the preventive-testing rules, generally once a year, measured in March–April or when soil resistivity is highest (dry season).

Visual checks: (1) metal parts that could become live are actually earthed (or zeroed), especially new, temporary, mobile and portable equipment; (2) connections to equipment and main conductors tight, with spring washers, not loose; (3) welds sound, lap lengths right; natural conductors (conduit, busduct casings, crane rails) welded across sections without broken welds; (4) protection where conductors pass through walls and expansion joints; (5) corrosion of exposed conductors, anti-corrosion paint in corrosive places; (6) besides special checks, inspect with planned major and minor overhauls.

Earthing resistance measurement: earth testers: hand-cranked and clamp-on. The hand-cranked type generates its own AC test current, needs no external supply, is simple, portable and resists interference: widely used. Terminals E, P, C to the electrode under test, the potential probe and the current probe (Fig. 3-14); crank at about 120 r/min; read the resistance when steady. Disconnect the electrode under test from other electrodes (accuracy) and from the network (safety; no feeding the test voltage back into connected conductors; no error from stray currents).

Usual practice (not stated in this book): place the current probe C about 40 m away and the potential probe P about 20 m, in a straight line, i.e. at the “62 %” point; check by moving P a few metres either way: the reading should hardly change.

worked.q: In a 380/220 V network with an earthed neutral, a motor is only earthed (R<sub>d</sub> = 4 Ω) and the neutral earth is R<sub>0</sub> = 4 Ω. A phase faults to the frame. Find the fault current and the frame voltage. Would a 32 A breaker or a 20 A fuse clear it quickly?
worked.s: Id = 220 / (4 + 4) = 27.5 A; frame voltage ≈ 220 × 4/8 = 110 V. A breaker needs > 1.5 × 32 = 48 A: no. A fuse needs > 4 × 20 = 80 A: no. The 110 V persists: that is why the book requires zeroing (a metallic return to the neutral) in earthed-neutral networks.

worked.q: Why must the transformer working-earth resistance be ≤ 4 Ω for unearthed HV networks?
worked.s: If HV enters the LV side, the LV neutral rises to Id × R0, which must not exceed 120 V. The HV earth-fault current is generally ≤ 30 A, so R0 ≤ 120/30 = 4 Ω.

worked.q: A 40 mm wide flat-steel earthing conductor is lap-welded. What lap length and how many weld edges?
worked.s: Lap length ≥ 2 × width = 80 mm, welded on at least three edges.

worked.q: Give three reasons repeated earthing is needed in a zeroed network.
worked.s: (1) It lowers the voltage on faulty equipment before protection operates; (2) it reduces the danger when the neutral breaks (and under unbalanced load); (3) it increases fault current via the parallel earth path, so protection acts faster; and (4) it improves lightning performance.

topics.title: Low-Voltage Protective Devices I: Kinds of Protection and Residual-Current Devices (RCDs)
topics.zh: 低压保护电器（一）：保护的种类与漏电保护器

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

LV protective devices: the thermal release, electromagnetic over-current release and under-voltage (no-volt) release of LV circuit-breakers; the thermal relay, electromagnetic over-current relay and under-voltage release of magnetic starters; and all kinds of fuses. LV protection is generally divided into short-circuit, overload, under-voltage and shock/leakage (shock and earth-fault) protection.

ProtectionWhat it doesUsual devices
Short-circuitDisconnects quickly when a line or equipment short-circuits. In a solidly earthed 3-phase 4-wire system, if an enclosure becomes live, zeroing turns the leakage current into a short-circuit current, and the short-circuit protection must then disconnect quickly, protecting people and equipmentFuses, electromagnetic over-current relays, the electromagnetic release of LV breakers
OverloadDisconnects after a set delay when the load exceeds the allowed range. Many cases show equipment damage often leads to injury, so overload protection matters for safety tooThermal relays, over-current relays, the thermal release of LV breakers. Fuses are often used for lighting and other circuits without impulse loads
Under-voltage (no-volt)Disconnects automatically when supply voltage disappears or falls below a value: so that equipment does not restart suddenly when voltage returns (injury or damage), and does not struggle on at low voltage and get damagedUnder-voltage releases; the contactor itself in a start–stop circuit
Shock / leakageDetects residual (leakage) current and disconnectsRCDs (below)

sections.h: How an RCD works, and where it is required
sections.b:
Fitting RCDs (residual-current operated protective devices, 漏电保护器) in LV systems is an effective measure against shock, and against electrical fires and equipment damage from leakage. But prevention still comes first, and other measures must be taken too. The book applies them to 50 Hz, 220/380 V systems with solidly earthed neutral. The family includes RCD circuit-breakers, plugs and sockets with RCD, RCD relays, leakage fire alarms, and combined devices.

Parts: a detecting element (zero-sequence, core-balance CT), an intermediate stage (amplifier, comparator, release), an actuator (main breaker) and a test element (Fig. 4-1: TA zero-sequence CT, QF main breaker, TL shunt release coil).

Principle: with no leakage, by Kirchhoff’s law the phasor sum of the currents through the CT is zero: İL1 + İL2 + İL3 + İN = 0, so the core flux sum is zero and no EMF is induced: the RCD stays closed. With leakage or a person touching a live part, the sum is no longer zero: a residual current Ik sets up an alternating flux, the secondary winding produces an EMF; the signal is processed and compared; at the preset value, the shunt release coil is energised and QF trips.

UseRules
Direct contactOnly as supplementary protection to basic measures; use high-sensitivity, fast type, operating current not over 30 mA
Indirect contactMainly by automatic disconnection, so exposed parts of faulty equipment do not stay at a dangerous voltage; co-ordinate with the system earthing type. ① In TN systems, where an insulation fault current is below the over-current device’s operating current, fit an RCD. ② In TN systems with RCDs, exposed parts may be earthed separately, forming a local TT system. ③ In TT systems, RCDs should be the first choice for shock protection
Electrical fireRCDs (or leakage relays, alarms) giving audible and visual alarm or disconnecting when leakage exceeds a set value; graded with the final-circuit protection
GradingGenerally two levels, with co-ordinated rated residual currents and times; the one at the supply end should be low-sensitivity, time-delayed

Must have RCDs: (1) Class I mobile equipment and hand-held power tools; (2) equipment in damp, strongly corrosive or harsh places; (3) construction-site machinery; (4) temporary installations; (5) socket circuits in hotel and guest rooms; (6) socket circuits in offices, schools, enterprises and dwellings; (7) underwater lighting in swimming pools, fountains, baths; (8) supply lines and equipment installed in water; (9) medical equipment in direct contact with the body (type H per GB 9706.1); (10) other places requiring them.

Alarm-only RCDs where tripping would itself cause an accident or great loss: (1) passage and emergency lighting in public places; (2) fire lifts and equipment securing public safety; (3) supplies to fire equipment (fire alarms, fire pumps, escape lighting); (4) burglar-alarm supplies; (5) special equipment and places not allowed to lose supply.

Need not have RCDs: (1) equipment on safety extra-low voltage; (2) double- or reinforced-insulated equipment in ordinary surroundings; (3) equipment fed by an isolating transformer; (4) equipment in places with non-earthed local equipotential bonding; (5) equipment with no indirect-contact risk.

Protection classes (book footnote): products are Class 0, I, II, III. Class I relies not only on basic insulation but also on an additional measure: accessible conductive parts connected to the protective conductor of the fixed wiring, so they do not become live if basic insulation fails.

Choosing the rated residual operating current correctly matters: the RCD must operate selectively on a shock or excessive leakage, but not on normal leakage, avoiding needless supply interruption. Devices must meet GB 6829, carry the national certification mark, and match the protected circuit (book Appendix D).

Choice byRule
SupplySingle-phase 220 V: two-pole two-wire or single-pole two-wire. 3-phase 3-wire 380 V: three-pole. 3-phase 4-wire 380 V, or single- and three-phase loads on one circuit: three-pole four-wire or four-pole four-wire
Normal leakageConsider the normal leakage of lines and equipment (measure it if necessary). The rated residual non-operating current must be at least twice the maximum normal leakage
EnvironmentDegree of protection to suit; large supply-voltage deviation, very high or very low temperature: prefer electromagnetic (voltage-independent) types; frequent lightning: impulse-voltage non-operating type; flammable, explosive, damp or corrosive places: special-protection types or other measures
Operating valuesHand-held tools, mobile appliances, domestic socket circuits: ≤ 30 mA fast. A single motor: 30 mA up to below 100 mA, fast. Main protection for several devices: ≥ 100 mA fast
Special loads and placesHospital medical equipment: 10 mA fast. Damp places: 15–30 mA fast. Lighting in pools, fountains, water parks, bathrooms: 10 mA fast. Working on metal objects with hand tools or hand lamps: 10 mA fast. Equipment connected to outdoor overhead lines: impulse-voltage non-operating type. Main protection of a system with overhead lines: medium or low sensitivity, time-delayed

Installation: follow the maker’s instructions; consider the supply line, method, voltage and system earthing type; ratings (voltage, current, short-circuit breaking capacity, residual operating current, break time) must suit. Correct connections for single-phase, 3-phase 3-wire and 3-phase 4-wire in TT, TN-C, TN-S, TN-C-S are given in book Table 4-1. Note:

  1. A three-pole RCD’s CT passes only the three phases: suitable for loads needing no N, e.g. motors.
  2. A four-pole RCD for 3-phase 4-wire systems: if the system uses zeroing, from the RCD onward the 4-wire system must become 5-wire: N separate from PE, and N must not be re-earthed (TT or TN). PE must never pass through the RCD’s CT.

Requirements on the network: (1) the neutral on the load side must not be shared with other circuits; (2) with a high-sensitivity RCD, the separate earthing resistance of equipment may be relaxed up to 500 Ω, but the prospective touch voltage must be kept within limits; (3) leakage current of protected lines and equipment within limits (non-operating current ≥ 2 × max leakage); replace poorly insulated wiring if exceeded; (4) motors and other equipment protected by RCDs: insulation resistance ≥ 0.5 MΩ in normal running.

Construction: (1) connect line and load sides as marked, never reversed; (2) RCDs with short-circuit protection need enough arcing distance in the arc-blowout direction (maker’s value); (3) external control circuits of composite RCDs: copper, ≥ 1.5 mm²; (4) do not remove earthing after fitting an RCD, but check and adjust it; (5) operate the test button after installation; (6) acceptance: test button 3 times, operates correctly; switch on and off under load 3 times, no false operation; (7) keep N and PE strictly separate: the N of a 3-pole-4-wire or 4-pole RCD goes through it; N through the RCD must not be used as PE, re-earthed or connected to exposed parts; PE must not go through the RCD; (8) installed only by trained, certified electricians.

Operation and management: (1) keep an operating record (book Appendix E) and rules; (2) press the test button monthly with the supply on; more often in the thunderstorm season; (3) check after operating due to lightning or unknown causes; (4) regular characteristic tests: residual operating current, residual non-operating current, break time; (5) test before reuse of a removed RCD; (6) use certified test instruments only; never test by touching a phase to the earth electrode; (7) after a trip with no fault found, one trial re-energisation is allowed; if it trips again, find the cause, test if needed; never force repeated re-closing; never remove an RCD to force supply unless the RCD itself is proven faulty; (8) analyse records and replace faulty RCDs; (9) characteristics are set by the maker; do not alter them; (10) repairs only by specialists; (11) after a shock casualty within an RCD’s zone, check its operation and find why it failed; preserve the scene and do not disturb the RCD before investigation; maintain the breaker part per LV switchgear rules.

terms: 漏电保护器（剩余电流动作保护器）

worked.q: A group of hand tools on a site has a measured normal leakage of 8 mA. Can a 30 mA RCD with a non-operating current of 15 mA be used?
worked.s: The rule: rated residual non-operating current ≥ 2 × maximum normal leakage = 2 × 8 = 16 mA. 15 mA is just below: nuisance tripping is likely. Either split the tools over more RCDs or reduce leakage; for hand tools the operating current must stay ≤ 30 mA.

worked.q: Why must PE never pass through the RCD’s current transformer?
worked.s: Fault current returning on PE must be seen as residual current (it left on a phase and did not return through the conductors in the CT). If PE passed through the CT, the outgoing phase current and returning PE current would cancel, the RCD would see no residual current, and would not trip.

worked.q: An RCD on a workshop circuit trips; the electrician finds nothing wrong. What does the book allow?
worked.s: One trial re-energisation. If it trips again, find the cause (and test the RCD if needed); never keep forcing it in, and never remove or bypass the RCD unless the RCD itself is proven faulty.

worked.q: Choose rated residual operating currents for: (a) bathroom lighting; (b) a single 15 kW motor; (c) the incomer protecting several machines.
worked.s: (a) 10 mA, fast; (b) 30 mA up to below 100 mA, fast; (c) 100 mA or more, fast (for a supply-end device in a two-level scheme, low sensitivity and time-delayed).

recap: An RCD for direct-contact protection must operate at no more than ___ mA.
The RCD’s detecting element is a ___-sequence CT.
Press the RCD test button every ___.
After installation test the button ___ times.
With an RCD, separate earthing may be relaxed to ___ Ω.

topics.title: Low-Voltage Protective Devices II: Fuses, Thermal Relays, Relays, Contactors, Circuit-Breakers and Co-ordination
topics.zh: 低压保护电器（二）：熔断器、热继电器、电磁继电器、接触器、断路器及其配合

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

A fuse is a simple, effective current-protective device: when current exceeds a set value for some time, the element melts by its own heat and opens the circuit. It is connected in series with the protected circuit and is among the most widely used protective devices.

Construction: fuse element, body, base. The element’s material, size and shape set the characteristic. Low-melting materials (lead and lead alloys): melt easily, but high resistivity means a large section and much metal vapour: only for low breaking-capacity fuses. High-melting materials (copper, silver): do not melt easily, but low resistivity allows small sections and little vapour: for high breaking-capacity fuses. Shapes: wire or strip (LV elements also grid or plate); changing the cross-section shape changes the characteristic greatly. Materials: lead-tin alloy, silver-plated copper strip, zinc, silver. Fuses have an inverse-time characteristic: small overload, long time; large overload, short time; so a fuse does not melt if a moderate overload ends in time.

TypeDescription and use
Plug-in (rewirable)At line ends of 380 V and below, as short-circuit protection of branch circuits and equipment
Screw type (RL)Cartridge filled with quartz sand; the arc is driven into the sand and quenched quickly. A coloured indicator at one end pops out when the element melts, visible through the glass in the cap. Rated 5–200 A, large breaking current; circuits of 500 V and below, 200 A and below; branches with large short-circuit current or flammable gas; machine-tool control gear
Unfilled enclosed cartridge (RM)Fibre tube; zinc-alloy element of varying section; heat decomposes the fibre producing high-pressure gas that quenches the arc. Simple, good protection, convenient; usually with a knife switch as a fuse-switch; somewhat lower breaking capacity: 500 V and below, 600 A and below
Filled enclosed cartridge (RT)Current-limiting: porcelain tube with quartz sand, contacts and silver-plated copper grid element, on special bases (with isolating blades, or the fuse itself as the blade), operated by a handle; high breaking capacity; rated 50–1000 A; 500 V and below with large short-circuit currents or flammable gas
Fast-acting filled cartridge (RS)Same construction but silver narrow-section or mesh element; one-shot, not user-replaceable; for semiconductor rectifiers, which can stand overload only very briefly
Self-resettingSodium element: highly conductive cold; short-circuit heat vaporises it into a high-resistance gas that limits the current; it recovers when cool. It only limits current and cannot truly break the circuit; reusable

By breaking range: general-purpose fuses (from about 1.6–2 × rated current up to maximum breaking current; for transformers and general equipment); back-up fuses (from about 4–7 × rated current up to maximum; in series with a contactor, which breaks smaller overloads; mainly for motors); and full-range fuses. Special fuses: electronic fuses, thermal fuses.

Equipment can stand some overload for a time; beyond the allowed value the fuse must blow within a set time. Some equipment has large but short starting currents: the fuse must not blow on starting, yet must blow reliably on short circuits and on overloads beyond the allowance. Too large an element: no timely blowing on short circuit or long overload; too small: blows on normal load. The book’s rules (ranges allow for standard ratings):

LoadRated current of fuse element
Lighting circuit≥ sum of working currents of all lamps on the circuit
One direct-on-line motor(1.5–2.5) × motor rated current
Several DOL motors, common fuse(1.5–2.5) × sum of the motors’ currents
Reduced-voltage-start motor(1.5–2) × motor rated current
Wound-rotor motor(1.2–1.5) × motor rated current
Distribution transformer LV side(1.0–1.5) × transformer LV rated current
Shunt capacitor bank(1.43–1.55) × bank rated current
Welding set(1.5–2.5) × load current
Electronic rectifier elements≥ 1.57 × element rated current

Precautions: (1) the protective characteristic must suit the equipment’s overload characteristic; choose breaking capacity for the possible short-circuit current; (2) fuse rated voltage to suit the line; fuse (holder) rated current ≥ element rated current; (3) discrimination: each upstream element rating must be larger than the next downstream one; (4) use only the matching element; never fit a bigger element or substitute another conductor.

sections.h: Thermal relays, electromagnetic relays and AC contactors
sections.b:
Thermal (overload) relay: small, simple, cheap; widely used for motor overload protection. Current through the heater heats a bimetal strip (two metals with different expansion coefficients), which bends; at a certain bend it pushes a link, opens the control circuit, the contactor drops out and the motor is disconnected (Figs. 4-6, 4-7: setting cam, leaf springs, manual reset button, main bimetal, outer and inner guide plates, NC and NO contacts, lever, compensating bimetal, push rod; a differential mechanism gives phase-failure protection). Connect the heater in series with the equipment and the NC contact in series with the contactor coil; set the dial so that at rated current the push rod just touches the compensating bimetal without moving it. On overload the bimetal bends more, pushes the compensating bimetal, which opens the NC contact.

Setting: know the environment, starting current, load, duty and permitted overload. (1) The relay’s ampere-second curve should be as close as possible to (or below) the equipment’s overload characteristic, yet not operate on brief overloads and starting; (2) for continuous or intermittent-continuous duty, choose by rated current: setting 0.95–1.05 × rated current.

Electromagnetic relays: core, coil, armature, contact springs. Voltage on the coil → current → electromagnetic force pulls the armature against the return spring, and the moving contact closes onto the fixed (NO) contact; when the coil is de-energised, the spring returns the armature to the NC contact. NO: open when the coil is not energised; NC: closed. Testing: (1) contacts: with an ohmmeter, NC to common should read 0, NO to common infinite; (2) coil resistance (R×10 Ω range): checks for an open coil; (3) pick-up voltage and current: with an adjustable supply and series ammeter, raise slowly until it clicks in; repeat and average; (4) drop-out voltage and current: then lower until it releases. Drop-out is normally about 10–50 % of pick-up; if below 1/10 of pick-up it is unfit (unstable, unreliable). Choosing: know the control supply voltage and the maximum current it can give; the controlled circuit’s voltage and current; how many contacts of what kind; choose mainly by control-supply voltage, and make sure the control circuit gives enough current or pick-up will be unstable; then select model and specification.

AC contactor: frequently makes and breaks large control circuits or loaded main circuits, for remote automatic control (Fig. 4-8). (1) Contacts: double-break bridge contacts, usually three NO main contacts in the main circuit, plus NO and NC auxiliaries. (2) Magnet system: moving and fixed cores, coil, return spring; coil terminals carry colour-coded voltage labels to avoid burning a coil on the wrong voltage. (3) Arc quenching: large contactors (above 20 A): slot arc chutes and grid plates; small ones: double-break contacts, electrodynamic blow-out, interphase barriers, ceramic chutes. Operation: rated voltage on the coil gives a force exceeding the spring; the core closes; NC opens, NO closes, main circuit on; coil voltage removed: spring opens the contacts. Shading ring: AC flux passes through zero twice per cycle, so the pull pulsates and the armature chatters and hums; a short-circuited ring on part of the pole face carries an induced current whose flux lags the main flux (by up to 90°), so the total pull never falls to zero, reducing vibration and noise.

sections.h: LV circuit-breakers, and co-ordination of protective devices
sections.b:
The LV circuit-breaker combines control and several protections: besides making and breaking circuits it protects against short circuit, severe overload and under-voltage, and can start motors infrequently. Parts: operating mechanism, contacts, protective releases, arc-quenching system. The main contacts are closed by hand or motor and latched by the free-tripping mechanism. The over-current release coil and the thermal release heater are in series with the main circuit; the under-voltage release coil in parallel with the supply. Short circuit or severe overload: the over-current armature pulls in and trips the mechanism. Overload: the bimetal bends and trips it. Under-voltage: the under-voltage armature releases and trips it. The shunt release is for remote tripping: normally de-energised; pressing a button energises it and trips the breaker.

Classified byKinds
ConstructionMoulded-case, frame (air), current-limiting, DC high-speed, field-suppression, residual-current
PolesSingle, two, three
ProtectionElectromagnetic release, thermal release, combined release (common), no release
Total break timeOrdinary; fast (acting before the release mechanism, break within 0.02 s)

Advantages: safe, convenient, reliable, easy to install, no parts to replace after operating (unlike fuses). Its function sums up all or part of a knife switch, over-current relay, no-volt relay, thermal relay and RCD. Selection: (1) rated voltage ≥ network voltage; (2) rated current and over-current release rating > calculated maximum load current; (3) maximum breaking capacity > calculated maximum short-circuit current; (4) under-voltage coil rated voltage = network voltage; (5) for motors, the operating current and time must ride through the motor’s maximum starting current and time: at an overload current of 7 × motor rated current, the delay must exceed the motor’s real starting time; with reduced-voltage starting the starting current is much lower, so no trip; at a fault current of 8 × motor rated current or more, trip instantaneously.

Other fuse types by construction: open (element exposed in air on porcelain posts; LV outdoor; loud flash on breaking); semi-enclosed (element on a porcelain carrier in a porcelain box with metal sockets; LV indoor; flash contained); cartridge (sealed insulating tube with metal caps or blades; with quartz sand: current-limiting, high breaking capacity; vacuum or SF6 filled for better arc quenching; LV and HV); expulsion (element in a tube of gas-producing material such as fibre board or acrylic; the arc decomposes it into high-pressure gas that blows the arc out of the ends with a loud flash, extinguishing at current zero; a hinged tube that drops after operating is the drop-out fuse, for outdoor use above 6 kV). By use: transformer and general equipment, VT, capacitor, semiconductor, motor and domestic fuses.

Co-ordination: short-circuit protection by fuses or the electromagnetic release; overload by thermal relays, over-current relays or the thermal release; leakage by leakage relays or the breaker’s residual-current release. Short-circuit protection must act at once; overload protection is delayed according to severity: the heavier the overload, the shorter the time. For leakage, the whole LV network generally uses three levels: the main LV switch’s RCD (level 1), branch or feeder RCDs (level 2), individual equipment and household RCDs (level 3).

worked.q: A 15 kW, 380 V DOL motor has a rated current of 30 A. Choose a fuse element range and a thermal relay setting by the book’s rules.
worked.s: Fuse element: (1.5–2.5) × 30 = 45–75 A; choose a standard rating in that range, larger for heavy or long starts (e.g. 63 A). Thermal relay: 0.95–1.05 × 30 = 28.5–31.5 A, e.g. set at 30 A.

worked.q: A relay picks up at 9 V and drops out at 0.6 V. Is it fit for use?
worked.s: Drop-out / pick-up = 0.6 / 9 ≈ 6.7 %, below 1/10: by the book it is unfit, because it would hold in at very low voltage and make the circuit unreliable. (Normal range 10–50 %, i.e. 0.9–4.5 V here.)

worked.q: A circuit-breaker protects a 40 A motor started direct-on-line. What must its delay be at 280 A, and what at 320 A or more?
worked.s: 280 A = 7 × rated: the delay must be longer than the motor’s actual starting time, so it rides through starting. 320 A = 8 × rated or more: it must trip instantaneously.

worked.q: Why is a fast fuse (RS) used for thyristors instead of an ordinary fuse?
worked.s: Semiconductor devices can stand overload current only for a very short time; an ordinary fuse’s inverse-time characteristic is too slow and the device would be destroyed first. The RS fuse’s silver narrow-section or mesh element melts extremely fast. Size it at ≥ 1.57 × the element’s rated current.

recap: A thermal relay is set at 0.95–___ × rated current.
Contactors above ___ A use arc chutes with grid plates.
The device that reduces contactor hum is the ___ ring.
An LV network generally uses ___ levels of RCD protection.

topics.title: HV Switchgear I: Metal-Enclosed Switchgear and HV Disconnectors
topics.zh: 高压配电装置（一）：高压开关柜与高压隔离开关

sections.h: HV switchgear cabinets: types and features
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

A switchgear cabinet (packaged switchgear) is breaker-based: the maker assembles, to the main wiring diagram, the HV and LV devices (control, protective, measuring), busbars, conductors and insulators in a closed or open metal enclosure, as a unit for receiving and distributing energy; with a vacuum breaker inside it is an HV switchgear cabinet. Besides the breaker it holds a disconnector (isolation), an earthing switch (safety), CTs and VTs (measurement and protection), surge arresters or RC snubbers (over-voltage), secondary protection devices and wiring; cables or overhead lines can enter. Widely used in station switchyards, transmission substations and consumers’ substations.

Classified byKinds and features
Breaker mountingFixed: breaker fixed; disconnectors inside; roomy, easy to repair; easy to make, cheap; less safe. Semi-enclosed (e.g. GG-1A(F)Z) and box types are fixed. Withdrawable: breaker rolls out, easy to replace and repair; no disconnectors needed; compact; precise, more expensive. Compartmented (e.g. JYN) and armoured (e.g. KYN) are withdrawable; the newer mid-mounted type (中置柜) has a small, low truck, practically the vacuum breaker’s base with a few parts added
Main wiringBridge, single bus, double bus, sectioned single bus, double bus with transfer bus, sectioned single bus with transfer bus
EnclosureMetal-enclosed compartmented, metal-enclosed armoured, metal-enclosed box
PhaseColourVertical busbarsHorizontalDown-leads
AYellowTopFarLeft
BGreenMiddleMiddleMiddle
CRedBottomNearRight

Table 5-1: busbar position and phase sequence (Chinese practice). Singapore and IEC use brown, black, grey for L1, L2, L3 in LV wiring; follow local rules.

Main features: (1) defined primary and secondary schemes: one main-circuit and one auxiliary-circuit scheme per cabinet; combine several units if one cannot do it; (2) operating sequences with mechanical or electrical interlocks. Experience shows that missing or incomplete “five preventions” is a main cause of power accidents. The five preventions (五防): prevent wrong opening/closing of the breaker; prevent opening or closing disconnectors under load; prevent hanging an earth on live parts; prevent energising with earths still on; prevent entering a live compartment by mistake; (3) an earthed metal enclosure strong and rigid enough not to deform or break on an internal fault, keeping people from live and moving parts and protecting the interior; (4) internal-arc containment: an internal arc fault is confined to its compartment.

Inside (the book’s typical cabinet): steel sheets divide it into compartments: upper rear disconnector compartment, upper front relay compartment, middle breaker compartment (split front/back by the CT mounting plate; rear = outgoing cable compartment); mechanical interlock and lamps on the front. The breaker compartment holds a VT, arrester in front, CTs below, zero-sequence CT behind, an inspection window and lamp; the relay compartment has over-current, voltage and auxiliary relays; meters on the door. Interlocking linkages realise the five preventions. In the metal-enclosed design, an angle-steel frame is divided by steel sheets into five separate compartments: busbar, breaker, cable, protection/instrument, and control, separated by 3 mm aluminium plates; main busbars pass through bushings; breaker compartment at the front, cable compartment rear-lower (separated by earthed metal plates), busbar compartment rear-upper, instrument compartment front-upper, with a vent channel between busbar and instrument compartments. Any fault is confined locally.

sections.h: Common faults of switchgear, and operation and maintenance
sections.b:
Switchgear faults mostly concern insulation, current-carrying and mechanics.

FaultCauses
Failure to operate, or false operation (the main fault)Mechanical: mechanism and linkage binding, deformed, displaced or damaged parts, loose or sticking trip/close plungers, broken pins, trip failure. Electrical control and auxiliary circuits: poor secondary contacts, loose terminals, wrong wiring, trip/close coils burnt (because of binding mechanisms or faulty changeover switches), sluggish auxiliary switches; faults of the operating supply, closing contactor, micro-switches
Breaking and making faults (breaker itself)Minimum-oil breakers: oil ejection and short circuit, burnt arc chambers, insufficient breaking capacity, explosion on closing. Vacuum breakers: leaking interrupter and bellows, loss of vacuum, restrikes when switching capacitor banks, cracked ceramic envelopes
Insulation faultsExternal or internal flashover to earth, interphase flashover, lightning flashover; flashover, pollution flashover, breakdown or explosion of porcelain and condenser bushings; flashover of lifting rods; flashover, breakdown or explosion of CTs; broken insulators. (Insulation co-ordination balances the voltage on the insulation, the limiting measures and the insulation strength)
Current-carrying faultsAt 12–72 kV mainly poor contact of the cabinet’s isolating plug-in contacts, burning and melting them
External and otherForeign objects, natural disasters, small animals causing short circuits

Operation and maintenance: (1) keep the control circuits continuous and the trip and close coils and auxiliary switches reliable: it is a series circuit, so every switch, fuse and joint and the DC supply must be sound. A poorly insulated DC circuit with one or more earths may cause false operation; a poor connection or abnormal supply causes failure to operate; (2) the higher the voltage, the more attention to insulation level; at medium voltage a small extra cost for a slightly higher level makes running safer; (3) watch closely in the early period of service, at peak load and in hot summers, e.g. by infrared thermography, to catch hidden abnormal heating; (4) keep switchrooms free of damp, dust and small animals; (5) protect metal parts against rust (varnish or paint), lubricate moving parts, check screws, remove dust; (6) watch for overheating and discolouring, noises, poor contacts.

sections.h: HV disconnectors: what they may switch
sections.b:
The HV disconnector is an important switching device used with HV breakers. Indoor or outdoor; single-, double- or three-post. It has no arc-quenching device: it is mainly used to open circuits carrying no load current and to isolate the supply, giving a visible break in the open position for safe repair of other equipment. Closed, it carries normal load current and short-circuit current reliably. It cannot break load or short-circuit current, so it may be operated only after the breaker has opened the circuit; operating it under load is strictly forbidden. Directly switchable: VTs, surge arresters, unloaded transformers with magnetising current ≤ 2 A, unloaded lines with current ≤ 5 A. When closing, close the disconnector first, then the breaker.

By the rules, a disconnector may
1. Switch VTs and surge arresters
2. Switch the bypass (loop) current of a closed switch (where a parallel path keeps both sides at equal potential)
3. Switch the capacitive current of equipment on an unloaded busbar
4. Switch the transformer neutral earth; if an arc-suppression coil is on the neutral, only when the system has no fault
5. Switch unloaded transformers: up to 10 kV, not over 320 kVA; up to 35 kV, not over 1000 kVA
6. Switch unloaded lines up to 35 kV and within 5 km
7. Switch unloaded 10 kV lines within 5 km, but with a three-pole ganged disconnector

Outdoor disconnectors, often neglected because simple: (1) do not use excessive force when adjusting, or the gears mesh wrongly and the three phases become non-simultaneous; (2) check contact alignment and insertion depth, or poor contact causes heating; (3) the earthing blade’s long linkage needs more force: adjust its synchronism; apply solid lubricant to contacts against binding; (4) grease collects dust and sand that wears the contact faces, causing arcing and heating: clean, and dress worn faces flat; (5) three-phase closing non-simultaneity: ≤ 5 mm at 35 kV, ≤ 9 mm at 110 kV.

Order: de-energising: open the line-side disconnector first; energising: close the bus-side disconnector first; and before operating any disconnector, check that the breaker is really open.

  • Closing: by hand mechanism or insulating stick, quickly and decisively, but not too hard at the end (damage, deformed mechanism, cracked porcelain). Then check it is fully home in the fixed contact and making good contact.
  • Opening: slowly and carefully; but as the blade is about to leave the fixed contact, move fast, especially when breaking a transformer’s magnetising current, charging current of overhead lines and cables, small line loads or loop currents, to extinguish the arc quickly. Then check every phase is open and the blade pulled fully back.
  • Wrong closing: even if you close the wrong one and an arc appears, do not open it again: opening under load causes a three-phase arcing short circuit.
  • Wrong opening: if an arc appears as the blade begins to leave, close it again at once to quench the arc. If it is already fully open, never re-close it. With single-pole disconnectors, if one phase is found wrongly opened, do not operate the other two.

In service: patrol with the switchgear: (1) overheating of contacts; (2) porcelain cracks, damage, discharge marks, loose cemented joints; (3) blade locks of single-pole disconnectors on 10 kV overhead lines. Maintenance: (1) clean porcelain; check glaze loss, damage, cracks, flashover marks, iron–porcelain joints; replace if badly damaged; (2) clean blades and contacts with petrol; check for damage, oxidation, overheating, twisting; (3) fittings complete; (4) connections to bus and breaker tight, not overheated; (5) flexible connections not broken or stranded; (6) clean and lubricate mechanism and linkage; (7) clearance of linkage to live parts; positioners and brakes firm and correct; (8) base sound, earthing reliable.

Preventing mis-operation: (1) a mechanical interlock (linkage) between disconnector and breaker so the disconnector cannot open while the breaker is closed; (2) an electromagnetic lock on the disconnector handle controlled by the breaker’s auxiliary contacts; (3) where they are far apart, a key interlock: the disconnector’s key kept at the breaker (or on its control handle), released only when the breaker is open; (4) a mechanical interlock with the earthing conductor so the disconnector cannot close until the earth is removed; (5) check the interlock between main blade and earthing blade: the earthing blade must open before the main blade closes.

worked.q: List the “five preventions” of switchgear and give, for each, one way of achieving it.
worked.s: (1) Wrong breaker opening/closing: two-step control switch, KKS labels, interlock locks. (2) Disconnector under load: mechanical/electromagnetic interlock with the breaker. (3) Hanging an earth on live parts: earthing switch interlocked with the disconnector, voltage-indicator locks. (4) Energising with earths on: interlock so the disconnector cannot close until the earth is removed. (5) Entering a live compartment: doors interlocked with the earthing switch or truck position. (Examples from this chapter’s interlocks; the list of preventions is the book’s.)

worked.q: An operator opening a disconnector sees an arc as the blade starts to leave the contact. What should he do? And if he closed the wrong disconnector and an arc appeared?
worked.s: Opening: close it again at once to quench the arc (but if it is already fully open, never re-close). Wrong closing: do not open it again even if there was an arc: opening under load would cause a three-phase arcing short circuit; report and have the breaker opened first.

worked.q: May a 10 kV disconnector be used to de-energise an unloaded 400 kVA transformer?
worked.s: No. At 10 kV and below the limit is 320 kVA (unloaded). Use the breaker (or a load switch).

recap: In China, phase A is coloured ___.
Compartments in the metal-enclosed cabinet are separated by ___ mm aluminium plates.
A disconnector may switch an unloaded line current of up to ___ A.
Three-phase synchronism of a 110 kV disconnector: ≤ ___ mm.

topics.title: HV Switchgear II: HV Circuit-Breakers, Vacuum and SF₆
topics.zh: 高压配电装置（二）：高压断路器、真空断路器与 SF₆ 断路器

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Functions: (1) switch the no-load current of HV lines; (2) switch load current; (3) switch fault current; (4) with protection, quickly clear faults, keeping the system safe.

Arc quenching: mainly by cooling the arc to weaken thermal ionisation, and by blowing to lengthen it, strengthening recombination and diffusion of charged particles and blowing them out of the gap, so the gap’s dielectric strength recovers quickly. Breakers are chosen for normal working conditions and checked for thermal and dynamic stability under short circuit; environmental conditions (temperature, wind, humidity, pollution, altitude, seismic intensity, ice) beyond normal require measures.

Requirements: (1) work continuously at rated voltage and current; (2) enough breaking capacity, thermal and dynamic stability (breaking current, rated making current, peak withstand current, thermal current); (3) the shortest possible break time (less fault time, less damage, better stability); (4) simple, cheap, small, light, easy to install and repair.

Arc mediumFeatures
Oil (bulk-oil, minimum-oil)Insulating oil; being replaced by newer types, use falling
Air-blastCompressed air blows and cools the arc and at current zero sweeps ions away; complex, demanding, uses much non-ferrous metal; being replaced
SF6Excellent arc-quenching and insulating gas: high breaking capacity, fast, small; but uses much metal and is costly. Developing fast, especially as gas-insulated switchgear
VacuumArc burns in metal vapour from the contacts; ions and electrons diffuse rapidly; at current zero, when particles leave the gap faster than they are produced, the arc cannot be sustained. High breaking capacity, short break time, small, silent, clean, long life, frequent operation, long repair intervals: widely used in medium-voltage distribution in China

Parts: interrupting unit, intermediate transmission, operating mechanism, insulating support, base.

RatingMeaning
Rated (nominal) voltageInsulation strength; standard long-term working voltage
Rated currentLargest current it may carry continuously
Rated breaking currentBreaking ability: largest current it can reliably break at rated voltage
Dynamic stability (peak withstand) currentLargest peak it may carry closed or at closing, without damage by electrodynamic forces
Making currentA fault may already exist when closing: the short-circuit force opposes closing and pre-arcing may weld contacts. Rated making current = largest peak it can reliably close onto. Rated making current = dynamic stability current = 2.55 × rated breaking current

Why 2.55 (my note): the first peak of an asymmetrical short-circuit current reaches about 1.8 × √2 ≈ 2.55 times the symmetrical r.m.s. value at 50 Hz.

Vacuum insulates very well. With very thin gas, molecules travel far between collisions, so collision ionisation is not the main cause of breakdown; over small gaps (2–3 mm) vacuum insulates better than high-pressure air or SF6: that is why the contact gap of vacuum breakers is small. To keep the interrupter’s insulation, the vacuum must be no worse than about 4–10 Pa (as the book states).

Many makers and models; indoor ZN×-×× and outdoor ZW×-×× types; parts: frame, interrupter (“vacuum bottle”), operating mechanism. The arc is extinguished at current zero as the plasma diffuses rapidly in the high vacuum.

Operation, maintenance, testing: short arcing time, high insulation strength, long electrical life; small contact gap and stroke, little operating energy, so long mechanical life; little maintenance: check wear of moving parts and loose fasteners, clean insulating surfaces, grease moving parts. In preventive tests: compare contact (DC) resistance with history and act on changes; the power-frequency withstand test across the open contacts is an effective check for a leaking interrupter; on indoor breakers the colour of the flash inside the interrupter when breaking load gives a first indication: dull red = vacuum deteriorated; pale blue = vacuum good; when checking protection settings, do low-voltage trip and close tests to make sure it operates reliably when bus voltage is low during a fault.

A typical outdoor SF6 breaker: three vertical porcelain units, each with a puffer arc chamber; a spring operating mechanism with a single-box control cabinet; a frame and supporting structure; the three chambers filled with SF6 through a common pipe.
