Advantages: excellent breaking capacity; SF6 sealed from air, reliable insulation; spring mechanism needs no compressed air, much less maintenance; no gas exhaust, very quiet, usable in residential areas; simple, light, good seismic resistance. Drawbacks: high demands on sealing, machining precision and gas quality: expensive, maintenance harder.

SF6 gas: high dielectric strength, excellent arc quenching; inert, non-flammable, non-toxic, odourless, stable. Density about 5 times air; dielectric strength 2–3 times air. In the arc it captures free electrons, forming slow negative ions that recombine readily, so the gap recovers fast and the arc goes out easily: arc-quenching ability about 100 times air, better than compressed air. Arc-decomposed SF6 recombines in a very short time, over 99.9 %, leaving very few lower fluorides. But arc or corona heat, and lower fluorides reacting with traces of water, produce acids (SO2, SF2, HF, H2SO4), and contact erosion gives metal compounds (CuF2, WF6). These corrode metals and insulation, float as powder, or stick to insulating surfaces. With moisture, corrosive gases severely lower withstand: above 30 % RH the surface flashover voltage falls clearly; water condensed on surfaces (with impurities) drops it to 60–80 % of the dry value; severe moisture can cause breaking failure. So moisture must be strictly controlled.

Operation and maintenance: (1) follow DL/T 639-1997, safety rules for staff operating, testing and repairing SF6 equipment; (2) patrol checks: ① porcelain sound, clean, no flashover; ② pressure gauge (or density monitor) within limits on the temperature–pressure curve; record pressure and temperature regularly; alarm at 0.6 MPa, lock-out at 0.58 MPa; outdoor gauges read by the zone where the temperature curve meets the pointer: red = lock-out, green = normal, yellow = alarm; ③ position indicator correct, fully open or closed; ④ fasteners tight; ⑤ no abnormal noise from the charging motor or inside; ⑥ no burning smell, smoke or scorching of trip/close coils; ⑦ enclosure or frame well earthed; ⑧ enclosure and mechanism box complete, not rusted; ⑨ no damage, deformation or corrosion.

Although SF6 itself is non-toxic, its arc by-products are toxic and corrosive, and SF6 is heavier than air and can displace oxygen in low places: that is why the special safety rules exist. (My note.)

terms: 动稳定电流（极限通过电流）

worked.q: A 12 kV vacuum breaker has a rated breaking current of 25 kA. Find its rated making current and dynamic stability current by the book’s rule.
worked.s: Both = 2.55 × 25 = 63.75 kA peak (catalogues round to 63 kA).

worked.q: An indoor vacuum breaker shows a dull red flash in its interrupter when breaking load. What does it suggest, and how would you confirm?
worked.s: It suggests the vacuum has deteriorated (pale blue = good). Confirm by a power-frequency withstand test across the open contacts; also compare contact resistance with history. Replace the interrupter if it fails.

worked.q: An outdoor SF₆ breaker’s gauge shows 0.59 MPa at the reference temperature. What state is it in and what happens next?
worked.s: Between lock-out (0.58) and alarm (0.6): in the alarm (yellow) zone. The breaker still operates, but the leak must be found and gas topped up promptly; at 0.58 MPa it would lock out (red zone) and refuse to operate.

recap: Rated making current = ___ × rated breaking current.
SF₆ is about ___ times as dense as air.
SF₆ breaker alarm pressure is ___ MPa.
Outdoor vacuum breakers are type Z___.
A pale ___ flash shows a good vacuum.

topics.title: Electrical Measurement: Instruments, Multimeter, Insulation Tester, Clamp Meter
topics.zh: 电气测量：电工仪表、万用表、绝缘电阻表、钳形电流表

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Classified byKinds
Quantity measuredAmmeter, voltmeter, wattmeter, energy meter, phase meter, frequency meter, resistance meters (ohmmeter, insulation tester/megger, Wheatstone (single) bridge, Kelvin (double) bridge)
Working principleMoving-coil (magnetoelectric), moving-iron (electromagnetic), rectifier, electrodynamic
Current typeDC, AC, AC/DC
Accuracy class0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.5, 5.0: seven classes; the number is the relative rated (fiducial) error in %
Reading methodDirect-reading (ammeter, voltmeter, multimeter, megger: read the pointer on the scale) and comparison (bridges, earth-resistance tester: compare with a known standard)
DisplayPointer, light-spot, digital
UsePortable and panel-mounted

General rules: (1) choose the instrument for the kind of quantity (V, A, AC, DC), the range for its size, the class for the accuracy needed; (2) error differs across the scale and is largest at small deflections, so the reading should preferably be over half of full scale; (3) observe the stated conditions of use: position, ambient temperature, voltage withstand, magnetic shielding, vibration, electromagnetic environment; (4) connect correctly: a voltmeter in parallel, an ammeter in series. With a CT, its ratio must match the ratio marked on the ammeter; primary in series with the circuit, secondary to the ammeter; the CT secondary must never be opened (dangerous high voltage), and one end of it is earthed. With a VT, its ratio must match the voltmeter; primary in parallel, secondary to the voltmeter; the secondary must never be short-circuited, and one end is earthed against HV transfer. DC instruments have polarity; (5) read correctly: line of sight perpendicular to the dial; on multi-range meters and multimeters, scale reading and actual value may need converting.

Fiducial error (my note): a class 1.5 meter on a 100 V range may be off by ±1.5 V anywhere on the scale: at 90 V that is 1.7 %, at 20 V it is 7.5 %. That is why the reading should be above half scale.

Panel-mounted instruments (fixed ammeters, voltmeters on panels and cabinets): (1) calibrate and adjust periodically as the rules require; (2) handle gently: shock damages internal parts, especially pivots and hairsprings; (3) switch off before fitting or removing; when removing an ammeter or energy meter on a CT, short the current leads first; (4) mount where clean, dry, vibration-free, without strong magnetic fields; (5) mount in the working position marked on the dial, not too high or low; (6) use measuring leads of adequate size: current leads must not heat or drop much voltage, and be strong enough not to break open; (7) set the pointer zero and keep the meter clean.

Multimeter: measures AC and DC current and voltage, resistance, inductance, capacitance; made of a meter movement (a sensitive galvanometer), measuring circuits (convert each quantity to a small DC current for the movement) and a range switch.

  1. Sockets: red lead in “+”, black in “−” or “*”. For the “2500” socket (high voltage): red in “2500”, black unchanged; put the meter on a well-insulated surface and protect yourself against shock.
  2. Function: set the switch to the quantity; confirm it before measuring.
  3. Range: different ranges can give different readings (different internal resistance and deflection); choose a range slightly larger than the quantity.
  4. Leads: in parallel for voltage, in series for current. Measuring voltage on a current or resistance range can burn out the meter.
  5. Voltage: if unknown, start on the highest range then step down. Unknown DC polarity: highest DC range, touch briefly: forward deflection = red lead on positive; reverse = red on negative. Not known whether AC or DC: test on AC first, then DC; if the DC range reads nothing, it is AC.
  6. Resistance: switch off the circuit and disconnect one end of the resistor. Zero the meter (short the leads) on each range. Do not hold both ends with your hands (body resistance in parallel). The meter’s battery drives a current through the part: microammeter movements and low-voltage, low-current semiconductors can be damaged.
  7. Internal resistance: on low-power, high-resistance circuits (especially electronics) the meter shunts the circuit: the higher its internal resistance, the better.
  8. After use, set the switch to the highest AC voltage range or OFF.

The insulation-resistance tester (megohmmeter, megger) measures the insulation resistance and absorption ratio of equipment and lines, to judge insulation and decide whether they can go into service. Insulation resistance depends on the applied voltage, so a multimeter’s 9 V cannot show the true value under working voltage; meggers output typically 500–2500 V. The movement is usually a moving-coil ratio meter, supplied by a hand-cranked DC generator (≤ 2500 V); electronic HV testers use batteries and voltage-multiplier rectifiers to give 5000 V or 10 000 V DC. (Connections are drawn in Ch 2 of this book.)

  1. Terminals: E (earth), L (line), G (guard/screen). Equipment to earth: equipment to L, E to earth. Winding to frame: winding to L, frame to E. Phase-to-phase of a motor: L and E to the two windings. Cable core: core to L, sheath to E, the insulation wrapping to G.
  2. Choice: equipment rated below 500 V → 500 V or 1000 V tester (too high a voltage could break down the insulation); above 500 V → 1000 V or 2500 V tester.
  3. Check before use: leads open, crank: pointer to ∞; briefly short the leads: 0.
  4. Safety: never test live equipment. Capacitive HV equipment (HV cables, long HV lines, power capacitors) must be fully discharged after switching off, and again after testing. For a cable whose ends are apart, lock the far cabinet or post a person there.
  5. Technique: connect E to earth or frame first; crank to near rated speed (about 120 r/min); then connect L to the conductor; read when the pointer is steady. Keep cranking after reading until L is removed from the conductor, so stored charge does not feed back into the tester. The larger the capacitance (long HV cables), the longer it takes to settle; do not stop cranking before then; if you stop by mistake, remove the lead at once, discharge fully and test again.

Electronic HV testers: switch off, earth and fully discharge the equipment first; discharge it again after each test. Check the tester: battery state (low battery = data invalid); leads open → ∞, leads shorted → 0. L to the conductor, E to the enclosure or earth, G to the screen or a part not to be measured. G removes surface leakage current: e.g. for a cable in damp conditions with a dirty surface, wrap a metal guard ring on the insulation surface and connect it to G. Use separate single-core leads, not twin or twisted (their leakage causes errors). Wipe surfaces dry and clean. For capacitive equipment, after reading do not switch the tester off first (the charged object would discharge into it): disconnect the lead first, then switch off; do not touch conductive parts before full discharge. Record temperature, humidity and conditions for comparison.

sections.h: Clamp meter; measuring current and voltage safely
sections.b:
The clamp meter (tong tester) measures line current without breaking the circuit: a CT with a split core plus an ammeter; the conductor in the jaws is the primary (one turn), the many-turn secondary feeds the meter.

  1. Guard against short circuits and shock; never use a meter whose jaw insulation is damaged; wear PPE, especially insulating shoes, with a person supervising.
  2. Start on a large range, then step down so the reading is above two-thirds of full scale.
  3. Jaw faces must close tightly and align; if it buzzes, open and close a few times; if that fails, check for dirt or too large a gap.
  4. Below 5 A, wind the conductor several turns round the jaw and divide the reading by the number of turns. If one phase of a balanced three-phase load cannot be clamped, clamp the other two together: the reading equals the third phase current.
  5. After use, set to the highest range.
ChoosingAmmeterVoltmeter
TypeDC: moving-coil, moving-iron or electrodynamic. AC: moving-iron, electrodynamic or induction. For general maintenance a good multimeter is enoughA voltmeter is an ammeter with a large series resistance: same rules. For electronics, the higher the multimeter’s internal resistance the better
ClassCalibration and research: 0.1, 0.2, 0.5; industrial testing: 1.0, 1.5; maintenance multimeters: 1.5, 2.5Same
ConnectionIn series with the load; DC: mind polarity; AC: no polarity; large AC currents: via a CTIn parallel; DC: mind polarity; LV panel voltmeters directly on 380/220 V; AC HV: via a VT; DC HV: via a voltage divider

Safety when measuring: (1) portable measurements are done live: separate adjacent live parts with insulating material; stand on an insulating mat; wear insulating shoes, dry cotton or insulating gloves, long-sleeved overalls with cuffs and collar fastened; have a supervisor; hold both probes in one hand where possible, the other hand and body away from cabinets and metal enclosures; check case, probes and leads intact and plugs firm; move slowly and carefully so you do not short the circuit; (2) for panel meters on CTs and VTs measuring HV: prevent an open ammeter circuit (the CT secondary rises to a very high voltage, dangerous to equipment and people, and the CT core overheats and burns) and a shorted voltmeter circuit (blows the VT secondary fuses, disturbing metering and protection).

worked.q: A class 1.0 voltmeter with a 300 V range reads 220 V. What is the largest possible error, and the relative error of this reading?
worked.s: Max error = 1.0 % × 300 = ±3 V; relative error = 3 / 220 ≈ 1.4 %.

worked.q: A clamp meter on its lowest 10 A range is used on a 1.2 A control circuit. How can you get a better reading?
worked.s: Wind the conductor 6 turns through the jaws: the meter reads 7.2 A, above two-thirds of the 10 A range; divide by the turns: 7.2 / 6 = 1.2 A.

worked.q: Which tester for a 380 V motor, and how do you test its winding-to-frame insulation?
worked.s: Rated below 500 V → 500 V (or 1000 V) tester. Check ∞ and 0 first; motor isolated; winding to L, frame to E; crank at about 120 r/min, read when steady; remove L before stopping; discharge.

recap: The reading should preferably exceed ___ of full scale.
A CT secondary must never be ___.
Hand-cranked meggers are cranked at about ___ r/min.
The megger terminal that removes surface leakage is ___.

topics.title: Safe Operation and Maintenance of Transformers
topics.zh: 变压器的安全运行与维护

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

The transformer is a static machine based on electromagnetic induction: two or more mutually insulated windings on a common core, magnetically coupled but not electrically connected. The primary (formerly 原边) connects to the AC supply; its current sets up an alternating flux in the core, at the supply frequency, linking both windings and inducing EMFs; the secondary feeds the load. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: AC energy at one voltage becomes AC energy at another voltage, same frequency. Uses: power (step-up, step-down, distribution), special (furnace, rectifier, mining), instrument transformers, HV test transformers, regulators. By windings: two-winding, three-winding, multi-winding, auto; single- or three-phase. Most common in plants: 10 kV / 0.4 kV step-down; substation main transformers often three-winding.

Ratings: (1) rated capacity = rated apparent power (VA, kVA, MVA), normally equal on both sides; (2) rated voltages: the secondary rated voltage is the no-load secondary voltage with rated voltage on the primary; for three-phase, line voltages; (3) rated currents: line currents. The nameplate also gives impedance voltage, connection, tap positions and voltages, phases, diagram.

PartNotes
CoreMagnetic circuit and skeleton: limbs (carry the windings) and yokes; insulated-varnished silicon-steel sheets. Core and metal parts must be earthed against static-induced discharge, but the core at one point only: two or more earths form a loop, circulating current, local overheating
WindingsElectric circuit; paper-insulated copper; cylindrical, concentric: LV next to the core, HV outside; insulating cylinders between; oil ducts for cooling; taps on the HV winding for regulation
BushingsInsulate leads from the earthed tank: below 1 kV solid porcelain; 10–35 kV hollow gas- or oil-filled; 110 kV and above capacitor type; shed profile, more sheds for higher voltage; anti-pollution coating in bad environments
Tank and coolingTank: support, cooling, protection; filled with oil for cooling, insulation and arc quenching. Hot oil rises into the radiators’ top, cools, sinks and returns: natural circulation; larger units have fans on the radiators
ConservatorOn top; volume 8–10 % of the tank; less oil–air contact (less moisture and oxidation); takes up expansion; has a breather and an oil gauge (level and colour)
Pressure-relief valveOpens within 2 ms when an internal fault raises the pressure to the opening value; recloses at the closing pressure, keeping positive pressure (no air, water entering). Older: explosion diaphragm of glass or phenolic board, burst by a severe fault
ThermometerIn a pocket on the cover, filled with oil, measuring top-oil temperature; 35 kV units: signal and mercury thermometers. The signal thermometer’s bulb holds chloromethane; its vapour pressure moves the pointer; contacts set by the yellow and red pointers give alarms or start cooling
Gas (Buchholz) relayIn the pipe between tank and conservator. Gas from oil decomposition or an oil surge operates it. Light gas → signal (e.g. after topping-up: release the gas); heavy gas → trips the breaker. Colour and amount of gas help diagnose the fault
BreatherConnects the conservator to air, removes moisture and dirt; oil seal at the bottom; silica gel turns from blue (or white) to pale red when saturated: replace
Tap changerOff-load: both sides disconnected; 6–10 kV two-winding units, HV neutral-point taps, range ±5 %: primary high → +5 % (position I); low → −5 % (III); normal → II. Measure DC resistance before and after: it must not change. On-load (OLTC): changes taps under load; more taps, wider range, better supply quality; on substation main transformers

Site requirements (summary): lifting facilities and space for large and medium units; pressure relief must vent freely, not onto cable trenches, busbars or other equipment; numbered units with warning signs; oil level, top-oil temperature and gas relay safely visible, gas sampling safe (fixed ladder if needed); indoor units well ventilated; a remote signal if mechanical ventilation stops; ventilation not shared with other equipment; doors flame-retardant or non-combustible, locked, labelled, with a “Stop! High voltage” sign; fire-fighting and oil-catchment facilities for oil-filled units; for seismic intensity above 7: fix the base to rails, slack flexible connections, longer flexible links to rigid conductors, anti-seismic gas relay; limit short-circuit current; protection must operate faster than the short-circuit thermal withstand time.

Why temperature matters: losses (copper, iron, additional) become heat; temperature is higher on load than at no load, higher overloaded, and jumps on short circuit. Iron loss is about constant; copper loss ∝ I². Heat ages the insulation (it becomes brittle and cracks). The 8 °C rule: above the maximum allowed continuous temperature, every 8 °C rise halves the insulation life (10 °C for dry-type). Heat moves by conduction to the surfaces, oil convection to the tank and radiators, then radiation and convection to air; so the temperature order is winding → core → top oil → bottom oil. The rated winding hot-spot temperature is the normal-life temperature; its short-term maximum is the safety temperature; oil-filled units are watched by top-oil temperature. Class A insulation withstands 105 °C; class B 130 °C.

CoolingAmbientLong-term top oilMax top oilTop-oil rise (class A, 40 °C ambient, rated load)
ONAN / ONAF (natural oil, self- or fan-cooled)40 °C85 °C95 °C≤ 55 K
Forced oil, air-cooled40 °C75 °C85 °C≤ 45 K
Forced oil, water-cooled40 °C75 °C85 °C≤ 40 K (coolant max 30 °C)

Table 7-1 plus the rise limits. In service top oil is generally 75 °C, not over 85 °C (the book’s general statement). Watch both temperature and rise: “allowed temperature” reflects the insulation’s heat resistance, “allowed rise” the margin above the cooling medium.

The temperature relay: alarms when top oil exceeds its limit; starts and stops auxiliary coolers by top-oil range; if all coolers stop and top oil exceeds the limit, trips the transformer after a delay.

Protection, cooling, measuring: fuses must suit fault level, sensitivity and selectivity; a transformer with a gas relay and no built-in slope is installed with the cover rising 1–1.5 % towards the gas relay; forced-oil cooling needs two independent supplies with automatic changeover and a signal; coolers switched by temperature, standby cooler cut in automatically; a top-oil thermometer; oil-filled units of 800 kVA up to 1000 kVA (as the book writes the range) bring the signal thermometer to a remote signal; the thermometer pocket is filled with oil.

Cooling: ONAN small; ONAF medium; forced-oil large; forced directed-oil very large; dry-type by fans. ONAF: with top oil ≤ 65 °C it may carry rated load without fans. Forced-oil: coolers must run; number by load; not too many at light load; one auxiliary and one standby group enabled; on shutdown stop the transformer first, keep coolers running until oil temperature stops rising. Fan, pump motors: overload, short-circuit and phase-loss protection, and pump rotation monitoring. Water coolers: oil pump on the oil inlet side, oil pressure at least 0.05 MPa above water pressure so a leak cannot let water in; drain cocks to empty in winter. All coolers lost (forced-oil air-cooled): rated load allowed for 20 min; if top oil is still below 75 °C, run on until it reaches 75 °C; but never more than 1 h in total.

sections.h: Voltage, overvoltage, unbalance, loading and parallel operation
sections.b:
Voltage: below rating does no harm; above rating is harmful. Normal operating voltage must not exceed the tap’s rated voltage by more than 5 %; in special conditions never more than 10 %.

Overvoltage: atmospheric (lightning strikes or cloud discharges) and switching (internal: energy oscillation when switching). Both last only tens of µs but are large: switching 3.0–4.5 × rated, lightning 8–12 ×, and distributed very unevenly, the end turns taking very high voltage. Protection: surge arresters at the terminals (spark gap breaks down, surge discharged to earth; required for important and main transformers); reinforced insulation of the HV winding and the turns near its ends (worse cooling; used only up to 35 kV); interleaved (纠结式) windings to raise inter-turn capacitance and improve the initial voltage distribution. Consider it at ordering and installation.

Unbalance: single-phase loads (furnaces, welders), unbalanced lighting, or a phase out for repair. YNd, Yd, YNy, Yy may run unbalanced; large and medium YNyn0 units show neutral shift, so must not carry single-phase loads; neutral current per maker, generally ≤ 25 % of rated.

Load typeMeaning and rules
Normal cyclicPeriods of high ambient or over-rated current offset by periods below: thermally equivalent to rated load. Over-rated current allowed cyclically if the average relative ageing rate ≤ 1; not with defects (abnormal cooling, serious leaks, local overheating, abnormal gas analysis, insulation defects)
Long-time emergency cyclicWeeks or months over rating: units out for fault or repair, changed system arrangement, load growth before a new unit. Accelerates ageing, not an immediate danger; minimise time and overload factor, use standby coolers; record load and compute average ageing; not with defects
Short-time emergencyShort, large overload: hot spot may become dangerous, insulation strength temporarily lowered, relative ageing ≫ 1. Run all standby coolers, cut load, generally ≤ 0.5 h; not with serious defects; record and compute ageing

Parallel operation, three conditions: same connection group (same phase displacement and sequence), same voltage ratio, same impedance voltage. With different impedance voltages, raise slightly the secondary voltage of the one with higher impedance so both are fully used. New or re-connected units: check phase and sequence before paralleling. When a step-up transformer’s HV side trips, prevent serious overload of the station-service transformer; avoid non-synchronous switching of station supply.

Patrols: at least twice per shift each day and at least one night patrol a week; unattended substations at least weekly. Special patrols: new or repaired units and within 72 h after modification; serious oil defects; gales, fog, snow, hail, cold waves; thunderstorm season, especially after storms; hot season; peak load; emergency loading.

Patrol itemsPeriodic checks
Oil temperature and thermometers normal; conservator level matches temperature; no seepage or leaksTank and flange not abnormally hot
Bushing oil levels visible and normal; no cracks, heavy dirt, discharge marksEarthing sound; measure core and clamp earth currents if needed
Sound: an even hum, no other noisesAutomatic changeover test of forced-oil cooling
Coolers normalOLTC operating normally
Breather normal; silica gel not discolouredAll labels present; all protection complete and sound
Joints, busbars, cables not hot; flexible conductors not loose or broken-strandedFire-fighting facilities complete and sound
Pressure-relief valve intact; OLTC position and supply indication normal; no gas in the gas relay; control and terminal boxes closed and dry; doors, windows, lighting sound, no roof leaks, good ventilation, normal temperature

Energising and de-energising: (1) before energising, check unit and protection fit to be live: no foreign objects, temporary earths removed, tap position right, valves set right; in cold weather prevent the breather freezing up; (2) hot-standby units ready at any time; units out for long periods energised regularly with coolers; forced-oil units on no load: rotate some coolers, not more than the maker’s no-load number; (3) forced-oil: cut in coolers one by one by load; water coolers: start the oil pump, then the water; stopping: water first, then oil pump; drain in winter; (4) energise from the supply side, by breaker, with protection; de-energise load side first, then supply side; (5) with no breaker, a disconnector may switch an unloaded transformer up to 110 kV with current ≤ 2 A; for transformers of 20 kVA and above it must be three-pole ganged with arcing horns; indoors, arc-resistant barriers between phases; (6) fuses may switch unloaded distribution transformers and 66 kV station-service transformers; (7) after rewinding: 3 energising (inrush) tests; (8) after installation, overhaul, fault repair or oil change, standing time before voltage: 110 kV and below 24 h; 220 kV and below 48 h (as the book states); bleed air from bushing turrets, radiators, purifiers; for forced-oil units run the pumps to purge air, all sides earthed while the pumps run (oil-flow static electrification endangers staff); (9) in 110 kV+ effectively earthed systems, earth the neutral first when switching the transformer in or out; (10) protect dry-type units from damp when idle; (11) arc-suppression coils: tap set to system conditions; switch only with no earth fault; never remove with a disconnector when neutral displacement exceeds 0.5 × phase voltage; to move it between transformers, disconnect first; never two neutrals on one coil; (12) OLTC taps unused for long: cycle between highest and lowest a few times when there is an outage; fit a current block in the OLTC control, set ≤ 1.5 × rated current, so it does not change taps under heavy overload or short circuit.

terms: 气体继电器（瓦斯继电器）

worked.q: A transformer’s insulation runs 16 °C above its allowed continuous temperature for a long time. Estimate the effect on life by the 8 °C rule.
worked.s: Two steps of 8 °C → life × ½ × ½ = ¼ of normal.

worked.q: An ONAN transformer in 32 °C ambient has top oil at 90 °C. Is the top-oil rise within the limit?
worked.s: Rise = 90 − 32 = 58 K > 55 K limit → too high, even though 90 °C is below the 95 °C maximum. Reduce load or improve cooling.

worked.q: The forced-oil cooling of a loaded transformer fails completely; after 20 min top oil is 68 °C. How long may it continue?
worked.s: It may continue until top oil reaches 75 °C, but the total time without cooling must never exceed 1 h (40 min more at most).

worked.q: Two transformers to be paralleled: Dyn11 6 %, and Yyn0 6 %, same ratio. Allowed?
worked.s: No: the connection groups differ (11 vs 0: 330° vs 0° phase displacement), causing large circulating current. All three conditions must be met.

recap: The core may be earthed at ___ point only.
Off-load tap range on 6–10 kV units: ±___ %.
Neutral current of YNyn0 units: generally ≤ ___ % of rated.

topics.title: Safe Operation and Maintenance of Electric Machines
topics.zh: 电机的安全运行与维护

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Machines (generators and motors) convert energy; generators are the main plant of power stations; motors drive machine tools, cranes, fans, pumps, mills. Classification: by function generator / motor; by supply DC / AC; AC → synchronous and asynchronous (induction); induction → three-phase and single-phase; three-phase → squirrel-cage and wound-rotor (slip-ring); synchronous → motors and generators.

Type (steel-industry use)Notes
3-phase LV inductionMost used: simple, reliable, easy to maintain, cheap. Cage (Y, Y2 series) for pumps, fans, general machines; wound-rotor (YZR) good starting, smooth control, more complex and costly: cranes. Enclosure: generally IP44; important, outdoor or gas areas IP54, IP55; flammable/explosive areas flameproof (YB series)
3-phase HV inductionY, YR, YKK, YKOS series: large fans, pumps, air/oxygen/nitrogen compressors
3-phase HV synchronous motorRolling mills, air compressors of oxygen plants
3-phase HV synchronous generatorGenerating plant
DC motorFrequent speed control and reversing: wire and plate rolling mills

All work by the laws of electromagnetic induction and electromagnetic force; all rotating machines have a stator and a rotor. LV induction motor: stator = core, winding, end shields, frame (produces the rotating field, supports); rotor = core, winding (cage or wound), shaft (induced EMF, current, torque output). The difference between synchronous and induction motors: a synchronous rotor runs at exactly the synchronous speed fixed by supply frequency f and pole pairs p; an induction rotor always runs below it. HV motors: welded steel-plate frames, formed rigid coils with reinforced insulation; synchronous motors have concentrated field windings fed with DC, and a larger air gap.

DC motor: main parts stator, rotor (armature), air gap; auxiliaries base, end shields, brush gear. Stator: main poles (core, coil of thin wire with many turns, insulation); interpoles between adjacent main poles; compensating winding in slots of the main-pole faces (large motors, special loads). Adjacent poles have opposite polarity. Usually separately excited (independent field circuit); interpole, compensating and armature windings in series through the brushes. Rotor: slotted silicon-steel core, shaft, usually double-layer winding (wave, lap, frog-leg) connected to the commutator risers. Commutator: segments, risers, insulating sleeve, mica between segments; must be concentric and smooth, with no high or low segments or mica.

ns = 60 f / p

Synchronous speed in r/min (my note; the book states the relation in words). 50 Hz, 2 pole pairs → 1500 r/min.

ItemRequirement
Standard voltageHV motors 10 kV or 6 kV; LV 380 V
Voltage variation−5 % to +10 % of rated
Unbalance at rated outputVoltage difference ≤ 5 % of rated; current difference ≤ 10 % of rated, and no phase above rated
Temperature limits (ambient ≤ 40 °C)Class B windings 120 °C; class F windings 140 °C; slip rings 105 °C; DC commutator 120 °C; sleeve bearings 80 °C (hottest point; measured outside with an IR gun, site experience: ≤ 65 °C); rolling bearings 95 °C
TrendNot only below the limits: with steady ambient there must be no sudden change in any part’s temperature; investigate any jump
VibrationSteady at both bearings; investigate any sudden change in vibration velocity
DC commutation sparkingGrade < 1 in normal running; < 2 on short over-current; grade 3 briefly allowed at starting; should not change much: investigate
LubricationSleeve-bearing oil analysed every half year (change or filter); rolling-bearing grease topped up every half year

These winding limits are the book’s figures for whole-winding temperature; they sit below the class ratings (B 130 °C, F 155 °C) to allow for the hot spot. (My note.)

sections.h: Starting requirements, monitoring and emergency stops
sections.b:
Before starting a new or overhauled motor: test reports and repair data complete; insulation resistance per the rules; all work permits returned, temporary earths, signs, barriers removed; insulation of cables, bearings and oil-pipe insulating pads tested; labels correct; cable terminations and earth leads sound; motor normal, nobody working on the machine, wiring complete; switchgear sound, mechanism free; isolator and fuse bases good; fuses correct, all three the same, none missing; protection healthy, trip output links in; guards on fan and coupling, foundation bolts tight; driven machine ready; rotor turns freely by hand; coolers and air ducts clean; DC and wound-rotor motors: commutator, slip rings and brushes good, starting-resistor short-circuit handle in the start position; operators start and stop; for HV motors, governor oil pumps and DC oil pumps, inform the electrical duty staff first.

Cage-motor starting limitsRule
Cold (core below 50 °C)Two consecutive starts, at least 5 min apart
Hot (core above 50 °C)One start
ExceptionOne extra start only when handling an emergency, or for motors with start time ≤ 2–3 s
Dynamic-balancing testsBelow 200 kW ≥ 0.5 h between starts; 200–500 kW ≥ 1 h; above 500 kW ≥ 2 h
DefinitionsHot: run on load for more than half an hour. Cold: above 100 kW stopped 1 h; 100 kW and below stopped half an hour

Starting on load is not allowed in principle. After a trip on starting: inspect motor and machine, measure insulation, restart under supervision; on any abnormality press the emergency stop. Watch the start by ammeter, speed and sound. After starting, check: smooth running, no abnormal noise, vibration and end-float within limits; oil temperature and pressure, oil rings carrying oil, bearing temperatures; inlet/outlet air and body temperatures; direction of rotation after repair; clean air ducts or cooling-water system; brushes, rings, commutator; DC sparking acceptable.

Monitoring: duty staff record every hour; inspection (点检) staff do precision checks and trend analysis weekly; repair staff inspect, blow out and grease bearings on site every half year. Items: voltage and current; bearing sound and temperature; motor sound and temperature; brush gear; clean surroundings (no coal dust, steam, rags); measuring and protection devices; lubrication and cooling.

Stop immediately if: (1) the driven machine fails and must stop; (2) a personal accident involves the running motor; (3) smoke or fire; (4) bearing temperature rises abnormally fast; (5) current rises abnormally above rated; (6) abnormal heating and noise with abnormal speed; (7) violent vibration; (8) starting gear, lubrication, cooling or protection faults that affect safe running.

worked.q: A 75 kW cage motor tripped on its second cold start just now. May the operator try again immediately?
worked.s: No. Two cold starts are allowed, at least 5 min apart; and after a trip on starting the motor and machine must be inspected and insulation measured before a supervised restart. Also the motor is now nearly “hot”: only one more start once cleared.

worked.q: Phase currents of a motor at rated output are 98 A, 92 A, 100 A (rated 100 A). Within limits?
worked.s: Max difference = 100 − 92 = 8 A = 8 % ≤ 10 %, and no phase above 100 A → within limits.

worked.q: An IR gun shows a sleeve-bearing housing at 70 °C. Action?
worked.s: Above the 65 °C field guide (the 80 °C limit is for the hottest point inside): investigate oil level, oil rings, oil quality, alignment; if it rises fast, stop the motor.

recap: Motors may run at rated voltage −5 % to +___ %.
DC sparking in normal running: below grade ___.

topics.title: Cable Operation and Maintenance: Patrols and XLPE Cable Tests
topics.zh: 电缆运行维护：巡视检查与交联电缆试验

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Cable maintenance covers patrols and inspection, load monitoring, temperature measurement, corrosion prevention and preventive testing.

Staff: a strong sense of responsibility; the “three knows, three cans” (三熟三能): know the equipment of your lines (parameters, types), the defects and fault patterns, and the rules; can judge defects and hidden hazards correctly, do ordinary tests, build up operating records. Patrol, inspect and test to the set intervals, items and standards and record them; patrol carefully, watching changes in the surroundings, never just glancing from a distance; keep registers and defect records accurate, report defects promptly; take part in quality supervision and acceptance of new and overhaul work; patrol for faults and join fault handling and investigation.

Patrol itemRule
IntervalEvery week; excavated, exposed cables guarded by a person with special measures
Terminations (outage cleaning)Above 35 kV: once a year; 10 kV: twice a year
Buried routesSurface normal, no digging, route markers complete; no rubble, slag, building materials, heavy objects, acid/alkaline discharges or lime pits on the route
BridgesCable not pulled tight at the ends; protective pipes or troughs not detached or rusted through
PitsNo wear at duct mouths and hooks
Single-core cables with sheath protectorsSheath current measured monthly; protector discs/gaps checked at least yearly for breakdown or melting
Outdoor cable to overhead lineTerminations complete; lead joints not hot; protective pipes near ground undamaged
TunnelsCable positions normal, joint temperatures normal, no missing supports
XLPE cablesSurface and rain sheds not dusty; no ageing of insulation
RecordsEnter in the patrol book; schedule defect removal by severity
Extra patrolsBefore holidays, in bad weather, at peak load
TemperatureConductor temperature and ampacity within limits. For buried cables also measure soil temperature at the same section: thermocouple point at least 3 m from the cable trench, no other heat source within 3 m. Check in summer or at maximum load, where cables are densest or cooling worst

Commissioning (handover) tests check laying and installation quality before service; preventive tests periodically check insulation in service. Items for XLPE cables:

TestMethod and standardWhen
1. PhasingCheck with a phasing stick that cable phases match the networkHandover; when needed
2. Main insulation resistance2500 V tester, read after 1 min; discharge a cable in service fully before, and after every test with insulated tools. No marked change from the last test, otherwise investigateHandover; before withstand test; when needed
3. Oversheath and inner sheath insulationSteel armour to earth, copper screen to armour, 500 V tester: at least 0.5 MΩ per kmHandover; before withstand test; when needed
4. Screen-to-conductor resistance ratioKelvin bridge, DC resistance of copper screen and conductor at the same temperature. Ratio up vs pre-service → screen resistance up, screen possibly corroded; ratio down → contact resistance of conductor joints in the accessories may have risen. Limits set locallyHandover; after new terminations or joints; when needed
5. AC withstand of main insulationShort the sheath voltage limiters of single-core cables and temporarily earth that end’s screen. Handover: 0.1 Hz, 3U0, 60 min (≤ 35 kV); 20–300 Hz resonant, 2U0, 60 min (110 kV). Preventive: 0.1 Hz 2.1U0 5 min (≤ 35 kV); resonant 1.6U0 5 min (≤ 35 kV); resonant 1.36U0 5 min (> 35 kV)Handover; after new terminations/joints; every 3–6 years
6a. Cross-bonding: sheaths and insulating joints, DC withstand to earthDisconnect the limiters; earth all metal sheaths on the other side in the link box; 5 kV between each section’s screen or sheath and earth for 1 min, no breakdownHandover; 3 years; on a bonding-system fault
6b. Sheath voltage limiters1000 V tester: limiter and leads to earth ≥ 10 MΩHandover; 3 years
6c. Link boxesLinks in the right position; contact resistance by Kelvin bridge not over “20 MΩ” (as printed; a contact resistance is surely meant in µΩ)Handover; 3 years; on a bonding-system fault

U0 = rated voltage between conductor and screen (earth). E.g. an 8.7/15 kV cable: 3U0 = 26.1 kV at 0.1 Hz. (My note.)

Records: supervise and accept laying section by section. The contractor hands over: design description, route plan, maker’s test certificates, technical documents for special cables, civil and concealed-work drawings, post-laying test data. Completion tests: every core continuous; termination phasing; sheath insulation and limiter tests of single-core cables; tests per the handover and preventive test standard. Keep: network diagram, route drawings, cross-sections, line specifications, and the line file (design, installation data, acceptance, agreements, change records, operating and maintenance sheets, repair records, preventive test reports, fault-location records, load and temperature records, patrol records).

worked.q: On an XLPE cable, the screen-to-conductor resistance ratio is now higher than before service. What may be wrong?
worked.s: The copper screen resistance has risen: the screen may be corroded (e.g. water ingress through a damaged sheath). Check sheath insulation (500 V, ≥ 0.5 MΩ/km) and locate the damage.

worked.q: A 2.4 km cable’s oversheath reads 0.9 MΩ (armour to earth). Acceptable?
worked.s: Per km: 0.9 × 2.4 = 2.16 MΩ·km ≥ 0.5 → acceptable. (Insulation resistance of a longer cable is lower, so multiply by length to get the per-km value.)

recap: 10 kV terminations are cleaned ___ a year.
XLPE main insulation is tested with a ___ V tester.
Oversheath insulation must be at least ___ MΩ per km.
Soil thermocouple at least ___ m from the trench.

topics.title: Safety of Work on Power Lines: Organisational and Technical Measures
topics.zh: 电力线路工作安全：组织措施与技术措施

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Site: conditions and safety facilities to standards; safety tools tested and fit; PPE complete; workers told the hazards, precautions and emergency measures; with new techniques, processes, equipment, materials: safety measures approved by management. Equipment at 1 kV and above is HV; below 1 kV is LV. Workers: electrical knowledge and skills, safety and job training, know the site rules, passed strict exams; know first aid, especially for electric shock; anyone seeing a breach must stop it at once; anyone may refuse illegal orders and forced risky work, and in an emergency directly endangering people or plant may stop work or take emergency measures and leave, reporting at once.

Organisational measures: site survey; work permit; work licensing; supervision; interruption; completion and restoration of supply.

MeasureRules
Site surveyBefore line work, survey: the outage extent needed, live parts remaining, site conditions, environment and other hazard points. For dangerous, complex or difficult jobs, prepare organisational, technical and safety measures, approved by management
Work permits (工作票)Kinds: line first-type, cable first-type, line second-type, cable second-type, live-line work permit, line emergency repair sheet. First-type: work on de-energised lines or on de-energised circuits of multi-circuit towers; on wholly or partly de-energised distribution equipment; HV cable work needing an outage. Second-type: work on towers of live lines keeping minimum safe distances; on distribution equipment in service; cable work not needing an outage. Live-line permit: live work or work closer than the minimum safe distance to adjacent live equipment. Emergency repair sheet: equipment forced out by a fault and to be restored in a short time; non-continuous repair work uses a work permit
LicensingFirst-type: start only with permission from all permit issuers concerned. For line outages, the licenser gives the order only after opening every possible source and hanging the earths. No outage or restoration at pre-arranged times (禁止约时停、送电). Second-type: no licensing procedure
SupervisionAfter licensing, the person in charge and the dedicated supervisor brief the team on the work, safety measures and hazard points, with confirmation; work starts after the working earths are on. They stay on site throughout and correct unsafe acts; a dedicated supervisor does no other work. Changing the supervisor: by the person in charge; changing the person in charge: by the permit signatory; with formalities
InterruptionThunderstorms, gales or other threats: the person in charge or supervisor may stop work. Daytime breaks: earths stay; check all measures before resuming. Multi-day first-type permits: if earths are removed at the end of a day, re-hang them before resuming
Completion and restorationPerson in charge checks: no personal earths, tools, materials left on towers, conductors, insulator strings; everyone down; then orders the earths removed. Once the earths are off, the line is live: nobody climbs. Report to the licenser, who after all reports, checks with the log, then orders safety measures removed and supply restored. Completed permits, emergency sheets and task sheets kept one year

sections.h: Technical measures: isolate, prove dead, earth, personal earths, signs
sections.b:
Technical measures: switch off; prove dead; fit earths; use personal earthing leads; hang signs and fit barriers.

  1. Switch off: open the line-side switches and any switch that could back-feed from LV; a visible break at every end of the de-energised equipment, or, if it cannot be seen, electrical and mechanical indications of its state; lock mechanisms operable from the ground; hang signs on those that are not.
  2. Prove dead before fitting earths, with a tested contact-type detector of the right voltage. Test it first on live equipment (or with a power-frequency HV generator). Keep safe distance, with a supervisor; keep the effective insulating length of telescopic detectors. Indirect proving where direct proving is impossible, for HVDC, and outdoors in rain or snow: by mechanical position, electrical indication, live-line indicators, meters and telemetry: at least two indications, all changed correspondingly. Multi-level lines: LV before HV, lower before upper, near before far; phase by phase.
  3. Fit earths immediately after proving dead, short-circuiting all three phases; at each end of each team’s work section and on branches that could feed it; on lines de-energised in co-ordination, one earth near the work point is enough. Fit and remove under supervision; all working earths listed on the permit; work starts only when the person in charge confirms all are on. Positions may not be changed without the signatory’s consent, noted on the permit. Multi-level lines: LV before HV, lower before upper, near before far; remove in reverse. Earth sets: flexible multi-strand copper with a transparent sheath, not under 25 mm²; no other conductors; fixed with proper clamps, never by winding. Earth end first, then conductor end; remove in reverse; good contact; use insulating sticks or ropes; never touch an unearthed conductor. Cables: discharge each phase before earthing.
  4. Personal earthing leads (个人保安线): where adjacent, parallel, crossing or same-tower lines can induce voltage, use them when touching or approaching conductors: fit before starting such work, remove after leaving the conductor; earth end first; fitted and removed by the worker; flexible copper with transparent sheath, ≥ 16 mm², with insulated handle; never instead of the earths.
  5. Signs and barriers: on handles of every switch that would feed the work site: “Do not close — work on line” (禁止合闸，线路有人工作); partial outages of ground-level equipment: temporary barriers and “Stop! High voltage”; in busy areas or roads: barriers, signs, a guard if needed; around HV withstand tests: barriers with “Stop! High voltage” facing outwards; workers must not move or remove barriers and signs.

terms: 禁止合闸，线路有人工作

worked.q: A pole carries a 10 kV circuit on top and a 0.4 kV circuit below. In what order do you prove dead and fit earths, and remove them?
worked.s: LV before HV, lower before upper, near before far, phase by phase: prove dead and earth the 0.4 kV (lower) circuit first, near-side phases first, then the 10 kV. Remove in reverse: 10 kV first, then 0.4 kV.

worked.q: The crew lead removes the earths, then a lineman says he left a spanner on the crossarm. May he climb to get it?
worked.s: No. Once the earths are removed the line is regarded as live; nobody may climb. The check for tools must be made before ordering removal; now the spanner must wait for a new permit with proper measures.

worked.q: Why are earths connected earth end first?
worked.s: So that the conductor end is attached when the lead is already at earth potential: if the line is unexpectedly live or carries induced voltage, the current goes to earth instead of through the worker. Removal is in reverse for the same reason. (My explanation of the book’s rule.)

recap: Equipment at ___ kV and above counts as HV.
Earth sets must be at least ___ mm².
Personal earthing leads: at least ___ mm².
Indirect proving needs at least ___ indications.

topics.title: Fire Management of Substations and Cable Tunnels
topics.zh: 变电站与电缆隧道的消防管理

sections.h: Substation fire rules, extinguishers and inspections
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Basic rules: (1) a conspicuous fire-warning sign issued by the local fire authority at the substation (electrical room) gate; key fire points clearly marked with their name, the person in charge and the fire-responsible person; (2) teach operating, duty and gate staff the “three knows, three cans” of fire: know the fire hazards, the preventive measures, the extinguishing methods; can use extinguishers, put out an incipient fire, raise the alarm. Fire plans, fire-inspection system and post responsibilities: each key point has a responsible person, an extinguishing plan, planned and recorded inspections; hazards registered and corrected by a deadline; (3) fire equipment as the rules require, with a layout drawing on site; nothing piled round it; not used for other purposes; outdoor equipment in fire boxes; (4) no explosives stored; hot work only under a hot-work permit; (5) fire sand ample and dry; handles of fire boxes, buckets, shovels, axes painted red; sand turned and dried monthly; (6) extinguishers checked quarterly by fire specialists, labels renewed; automatic fire alarms tested weekly; (7) on fire: raise the alarm, cut off the supply, fight the initial fire per the plan.

EquipmentFor
Dry-powder extinguisherIncipient fires of flammable liquids (organic solvents), combustible gases and electrical equipment
CO2 extinguisherValuable equipment, archives, instruments, electrical equipment below 600 V, oils
Firefighter’s kitSpecial clothing, safety belt, hook, rope, breaking tools
Control rooms and storesEquipment per the national code for extinguisher installation; fire water supply assured

Equipment well distributed, easy to reach, well ventilated; outdoors in rain-proof boxes, away from oils, acids, alkalis; assigned keepers, tagged, never used for other purposes.

Inspections: monthly by the substation department with the fire authority; before New Year, May Day, National Day, Mid-Autumn, Spring Festival and major city events; station self-checks led by the station head (by area or jointly), results in the shift handover and fire log; check extinguisher location, movement, loss, use, damage, quantity and expiry; fire pools, hydrants, pump houses checked monthly (water flow, pressure, pump supply changeover, valves); HV equipment patrolled carefully (most fire risk comes from it); HV rooms, battery rooms and LV rooms: check rodent-proof mesh, gaps, doors shut; rodent prevention scheduled as a key safety activity; outside workers briefed, areas marked and barriered; stop illegal use of power, welding, open flames; LV wiring safe, fuses properly graded, never copper wire instead of fuse wire; check that each kind of equipment has the right type of extinguisher; check fire records. Rewards for good fire work; penalties, even criminal liability, for negligence causing fires.

Patrol and maintain cable tunnels strictly, correct problems promptly; ventilation, drainage, lighting and alarms complete.

  1. Fire compartments and fire-retardant measures; on every tray level, linear heat detectors laid in a sine-wave pattern with automatic temperature alarm; water-mist sealing and ventilation; water-mist extinguishing in high-risk, important zones; infrared surveillance at entrances.
  2. No oil, rubbish or combustibles in cable or drain trenches; waste oil only into dedicated containers.
  3. Holes and shafts where cables pass trenches, walls, floors into control rooms, cable spreading rooms, control, protection and instrument panels: sealed tightly with fire-resistant putty etc.; fire walls in trenches passing oil-filled equipment; covers sealed.
  4. Cables in spreading rooms and trenches leading indoors coated with fire-retardant; new cables on treated layers get the same treatment at once; 2–3 m each side of cable joints and on adjacent cables: fire-retardant paint or tape.
  5. Along the tunnel sides, fire barriers (rock wool) at intervals, with coating or retardant bags/tape on both sides next to them.
  6. In vertical cable shafts, a fire-stop layer every 7 m, sealing penetrations with fire putty and inorganic fire-stopping compound.
  7. Also fire pillows, fire-proof trays (troughs) and fire doors.
  8. Use flame-retardant or fire-resistant cables, prefabricated joints, measures against flame spread; protection clears faulted lines fast on overload or faults; no auto-reclosing on tunnel cable circuits.

Why no reclosing (my note): a cable fault is almost always permanent, so reclosing would only re-feed the fault arc inside the tunnel.

worked.q: A fire breaks out in a 400 V switchboard. Which extinguisher, and what first?
worked.s: First raise the alarm and cut off the supply; then a CO2 extinguisher (electrical equipment below 600 V, leaves no residue) or dry powder. Never water on live equipment.

worked.q: In a 30 m vertical cable shaft, how many fire-stop layers are needed at least?
worked.s: One every 7 m: 30 / 7 ≈ 4.3 → at least 4 intermediate layers (plus sealing at floor penetrations).

topics.title: Lightning I: Phenomena, Parameters, Hazards and Protective Devices
topics.zh: 雷电与防雷（一）：雷电现象、参数、危害与防雷装置

sections.h: How lightning forms; kinds and parameters
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Moist air heated at the ground rises, or cold and warm air masses meet, forming water drops or ice crystals in cumulus clouds; their motion separates charge; when enough accumulates, discharge occurs between oppositely charged clouds, or between a cloud and the ground (charged by electrostatic induction). A cloud may hold several charge centres, so repeated strokes are common, typically 2–3: after the first centre discharges, the next moves to the same channel and discharges at once, at intervals of hundreds of µs to hundreds of ms, each stroke’s current smaller than the last.

KindFeatures
Direct strokeField between a charged cloud and a projection on the ground reaches air breakdown strength. Largest energy and direct danger: 6000–10 000 °C locally (the Sun’s surface is about 6000 °C) and 5000–6000 N impact force; damages buildings, starts fires, kills
Electrostatic inductionA charged cloud induces opposite charge on the top of a projection; when the cloud discharges elsewhere, the freed charge travels off as a high-voltage surge
Electromagnetic inductionThe rapidly changing magnetic field of the lightning current induces very high EMF in nearby conductors
Ball lightningLuminous ball, usually orange or red (also yellow, green, blue, violet), enters through openings, doors, windows, chimneys or vents; mostly vanishes along live conductors; diameter about 10–20 cm (up to 1 m); lasts 3–5 s; silent or hissing; burns or explodes on meeting objects or equipment
ParameterValues (book)
PolarityNegative cloud to earth = negative flash (current from earth to cloud, negative polarity). 75–90 % of lightning currents are negative; induced overvoltages are mostly positive
ChargeMore charge, more energy and damage
Current amplitudeTens to hundreds of kA (the text prints “kV”); probability curve Fig. 10-1
Steepness (rate of rise)Up to 50 kA/µs; average about 30 kA/µs
WaveformShorter front → steeper → worse for inductive elements; longer tail → more energy. Direct strokes: front 1–4 µs, tail 10–200 µs
Direct-stroke overvoltageDepends on steepness and the impedance of the current path
U = I R + L · di/dt

I = current amplitude (kA), i = instantaneous current, R = earth resistance (Ω), L = inductance of the current path (H). (The di/dt term is lost in the printed formula; the definitions given show it is meant.) E.g. 30 kA through 10 Ω gives 300 kV from the resistance alone; 1.5 µH at 30 kA/µs adds 45 kV.

sections.h: Where lightning strikes, hazards and damage mechanisms
sections.b:
Most exposed places
Isolated structures in open country or over 20 m high: pavilions, big trees
Metal roofs; brick-and-timber buildings
Buildings by rivers and lakes, on hilltops
Low-lying areas, spring outlets, very damp places, slopes meeting paddy fields, ground over conductive ores or of low soil resistivity
Valley wind gaps
City chimneys, tall spires and steel towers
HazardDescription
Direct strokeHuge current (tens to hundreds of kA) through the object: tens of thousands of degrees inside it; burning; overhead conductors melted
Induced lightningOvervoltage induced on nearby conductors (the book gives “millions to tens of millions of volts”): flashover or breakdown of insulation, outages, HV entering LV systems, danger to LV equipment and people, fires and explosions
Incoming surgeLightning on an overhead line travels along it into substations or switchrooms, striking equipment or people

Damage mechanisms (combined): electromagnetic: destroys insulation, burns through wires, splits poles, causes electric shock; thermal: tens of thousands of degrees melt metal and ignite flammable and explosive materials; mechanical: twists, deforms, bursts or shatters the object.

A complete system = air termination (or arrester) + down-conductor + earthing. Arresters protect equipment; overhead earth wires protect lines; meshes and tapes protect buildings; rods protect outdoor substations, buildings and structures.

Air terminations sit on top and draw the stroke to themselves. Rods, wires, meshes, tapes; and metal roofs and members, for buildings other than Class 1. Strong, corrosion-resistant, thermally stable; galvanised, welds painted; replace when over 30 % of the section has corroded. Keep rod or wire at least 5 m from the protected object (induced overvoltage).

DeviceNotes
RodReally an “attracting rod”: intercepts the stroke and leads it safely to earth; it cannot stop or eliminate lightning
Overhead earth wireOne or two on the tower tops; 110–220 kV lines generally along the whole line. A stroke to a phase conductor gives overvoltages up to millions of volts, flashing the insulator string and tripping the line; the wire shields the conductors. A stroke to the tower or wire can still flash the string if tower-to-conductor voltage is too high (back-flashover): reduce tower earth resistance. Galvanised steel strand ≥ 35 mm²
TapeFlat strip instead of wire on buildings; fits the roof shape and decoration, wide effective protection on large buildings. Flat steel ≥ 48 mm², ≥ 4 mm thick
MeshAll roof projections (flagpoles, vents, ladders, chimneys, gutters) welded to it. Round steel ≥ 8 mm, flat steel ≥ 48 mm² × 4 mm
Tape and mesh installation
Expansion jointsBridging link with 10–20 cm slack
Flat roof with parapetWidth < 24 m: tape along the parapet only; > 24 m: add exposed connecting strips across the roof (strip spacing ≤ 20 m)
Tiled roof, slope 27–35°, length ≤ 75 mTape on the ridge only; hipped roofs: on every hip; protect eaves corners with short rods or by running the down-conductor round them. Eaves over 12 m high and length over 75 m: tape on ridge and eaves
Very large roofsMesh (exposed or concealed): the finer the mesh the more reliable; per importance
Roof projectionsShort rods or tapes on chimneys, parapets, vents, skylights, ornaments, bonded to the nearest tape; metal flagpoles, chimneys, ladders, cowls, vents welded to it
Down-conductorsAt least two per building (one if plan area < 50 m²), symmetrical (“一” or “Z” for two, “工” for four), ≤ 20 m apart, add one between if more

Down-conductors: preferably round steel ≥ 8 mm, or flat ≥ 48 mm² × 4 mm; on chimneys round ≥ 12 mm or flat ≥ 100 mm² × 4 mm; run exposed on the outer wall by the shortest path to earth; concealed only with round ≥ 10 mm or flat ≥ 80 mm². Fire ladders, steel columns may serve if electrically continuous. With several, fit a test (disconnect) clamp on each at 0.3–1.8 m above ground (not needed with reinforcement plus foundation earth; then connection plates for testing, extra earths and bonding; with reinforcement plus buried electrodes, a connection plate ≥ 0.3 m above ground on each). Protect from 1.7 m above to 0.3 m below ground where liable to damage or contact (concealed, galvanised angle, plastic or rubber pipe).

Earthing: like ordinary earthing but slightly larger minimum sizes; may be shared with other earths (except free-standing rods) if resistance is met. Vertical: angle, pipe or round steel; horizontal: flat or round. Round ≥ 10 mm; flat ≥ 100 mm², ≥ 4 mm; angle ≥ 4 mm; pipe wall ≥ 3.5 mm; joints welded and protected; in corrosive soil hot-dip galvanise or enlarge; earthing lead same section as horizontal electrode. Vertical rods 2.5 m long, spaced 5 m (vertical and horizontal), buried ≥ 0.5 m, away from kilns and flues. High-resistivity soil: radial extensions (not longer than the effective length), deeper low-resistivity layers, resistance-reducing compound, soil replacement. Electrodes ≥ 3 m from entrances and footpaths, or: bury ≥ 1 m deep locally, or wrap in 50–80 mm asphalt, or asphalt-gravel surface 50–80 mm thick extending 2 m beyond.

Impulse earth resistanceLimit
Direct-stroke protection; free-standing rod≤ 10 Ω
Induced-lightning protection≤ 5–10 Ω; less important Class 3 buildings up to 30 Ω
Incoming-surge protection≤ 5–30 Ω by class and level

Arresters protect equipment against lightning, switching and power-frequency transient overvoltages: when an incoming surge exceeds the arrester’s protective level, it discharges first and leads the current to earth, limiting the voltage below the equipment’s lightning impulse level.

TypeHow it worksNotes
Valve type (e.g. FS-6)Spark gaps + non-linear resistors in series. Non-linear: the larger the current, the smaller the resistance. Normally the gaps isolate the resistors; a surge breaks down the gaps, current flows through the resistors, which become very low: the voltage drop (residual voltage) stays below the equipment withstand. Afterwards the gaps carry power-follow current, limited by the now-high resistance, so the arc goes out at the first current zeroGaps: series of flat brass discs separated by mica washers, gap 0.5–1.0 mm; near-uniform field and pre-ionisation → small scatter, flat volt-time curve; many short gaps split the follow arc and quench it. Discs (valve blocks): SiC with some Al2O3, pressed with binder, fired
Magnetic-blow valve typeSame principle, with magnetically blown gaps (stronger arc quenching) and high-capacity resistorsRotating-arc gaps (2–15 kV): concentric electrodes, permanent magnet, arc spins and cools; breaks 300 A follow current. Arc-lengthening gaps (> 35 kV): horn electrodes in a ceramic or mica-glass chute with serrated grids; field from a coil carrying the follow current (so the arc moves the same way whatever the current direction); arc stretched tens of times; breaks 450 A, about 4× an ordinary gap
Expulsion (tube) typeInternal gap S1 in a gas-generating tube (fibre, plastic, rubber) + external gap S2 (isolates the tube normally). Both break down; follow-current arc decomposes the tube wall, tens to hundreds of atmospheres of gas blow out of the ring electrode, extinguishing the arc at first current zeroToo large a follow current → too much gas, tube may burst; too small → not enough gas: upper and lower limits marked in the type (GXS UN / Imax–Imin); the single-phase earth-fault current must lie within them. Drawbacks: steep volt-time curve (hard to co-ordinate), troublesome maintenance, steep chopped wave harmful to transformer insulation. Now only for special line sections: crossings, long spans, substation approach sections
Zinc-oxide (metal-oxide)Appeared in the early 1970s; ZnO blocks with small additions of bismuth, cobalt, manganese and antimony oxides, sintered. At normal voltage ZnO conducts only 10–50 µA (SiC: 200–400 A, so SiC needs series gaps): practically an insulator: no series gaps neededAdvantages: (1) simple, small, stable, unaffected by temperature, humidity, pressure and pollution; (2) no gap delay: better response, especially to steep surges; (3) practically no follow current: less energy, withstands many strokes, longer life; (4) large capacity: 4–5× SiC per unit area, residual voltage about ⅓ of SiC, even current sharing, can be paralleled; (5) simple to make, cheap
Protective gapSimplest: main gap + auxiliary gap in series (the auxiliary prevents mis-operation if a bird shorts the main gap); horn electrodes so the follow arc rises and stretches. Breaks down on a surge, shorting the line to earthNo arc quenching: follow current causes line tripping: use with auto-reclosing; only for less important places or where no suitable arrester exists
Rated kV36102035
Tube arrester external gap, min (mm)8101560100
GB1 (approach-section head) external gap, max (mm)———150–200250–300
Protective gap Table 10-2 (book’s column title “auxiliary gap”, values for 3 / 6–10 / 20 / 35 kV)510 (6–10 kV)—1520
Protective gap Table 10-3 “auxiliary gap” (mm)81525100210

Tables 10-1, 10-2, 10-3 as printed. The headings of 10-2 (titled “minimum main gap”, but its row says “auxiliary gap”) and 10-3 look swapped: in common practice the larger figures (8/15/25/100/210 mm) are the main gap and the smaller (5/10/15/20 mm) the auxiliary gap. The ZnO additives are printed as “Bi2O2, CO2O2, SbO3”; the usual oxides are Bi2O3, Co2O3, MnO2, Sb2O3. (My notes; check with your lecturer.)

worked.q: Lightning current 20 kA with steepness 30 kA/µs strikes a rod with earth resistance 10 Ω and down-conductor inductance 2 µH. Estimate the top voltage.
worked.s: U = IR + L·di/dt = 20 kA × 10 Ω + 2 µH × 30 kA/µs = 200 kV + 60 kV = 260 kV. Hence the 5 m clearance and low earth resistance.

worked.q: Why does a ZnO arrester need no series gap while a SiC valve arrester does?
worked.s: At normal voltage a ZnO block passes only 10–50 µA (practically insulating), so it can sit permanently on the line; a SiC block would pass 200–400 A and overheat, so gaps must isolate it until a surge comes.

worked.q: A building’s roof plan is 60 m × 30 m. How many down-conductors at least, by the 20 m spacing rule?
worked.s: Perimeter = 2 × (60 + 30) = 180 m; at ≤ 20 m spacing: 180 / 20 = 9 down-conductors at least (and at least two in any case). (My worked application.)
