Rods keep at least ___ m from the protected object.
Free-standing rod impulse earth resistance ≤ ___ Ω.
ZnO residual voltage is about ___ of SiC.

topics.title: Lightning II: Protection of Lines, Substations and People
topics.zh: 雷电与防雷（二）：线路、变配电所与人身防雷

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

MeasureBook’s points
Overhead earth wireThe most basic, most effective line protection; better and relatively cheaper the higher the voltage. 220 kV+: whole line; 110 kV: generally whole line; 35 kV and below: not whole line; usually 1–2 km at the substation approach, with good tower earthing. Also: shares the current (lower tower-top potential); coupling lowers the voltage across insulators; shielding lowers induced overvoltage. Shielding angle to the outer conductors small, generally 20–30°; earthed at every tower
Higher line insulationTall crossing towers attract more strokes, have higher top potential, more induced voltage and shielding failures: add insulator discs, increase conductor-to-earth-wire clearance in long spans
Lower tower earth resistanceLess potential rise when a tower is struck; works with earth wires. Use natural earthing in low-resistivity soil; in high-resistivity soil use radial or continuous counterpoise electrodes and resistance-reducing compound
Non-effectively earthed neutralIsolated or arc-suppression-coil earthed: most lightning single-phase earth faults clear themselves without phase-to-phase faults or tripping; with two- or three-phase strokes, the first phase to flash acts as an earth wire, raising coupling and lowering the voltage on the others
Line arresters, protective gapsGive a low-impedance path above a set level; protect the weakest points: very tall towers, guyed towers, crossings
Auto-reclosingLightning faults are arcs that go out when the breaker trips; one reclosure after 0.5 s or more usually succeeds. Success rates in China: 110 kV+ 75–95 %; 35 kV and below about 50–80 %

Lightning rods protect the whole substation from direct strokes. 35 kV and below: insulation is lower, so free-standing rods are required, clear of back-flashover. 110 kV and above: higher insulation, rods may stand on the switchgear structures; such structures get supplementary earth electrodes, connected to the station grid at least 15 m (electrical distance) from where the main transformer’s earth joins the grid, so the high potential decays along the grid before reaching the transformer. Never put a rod on the transformer’s gantry (weak insulation, key equipment).

The earth wire of the first line span may be brought onto the station gantry (cheaper than rods; current shares both ways so lower rise): 110 kV and above: allowed; in soil over 1000 Ω·m fit a concentrated earth. 35–60 kV: allowed where soil ≤ 500 Ω·m, with a concentrated earth; above 500 Ω·m the earth wire ends at the terminal tower and the last span is protected by rods.

Incoming surges: valve arresters or protective gaps on the incoming lines. FS series for small distribution installations; FZ series (printed “SFZ”) for medium and large substations; FCZ1 magnetic-blow for HV substation equipment. Purpose of approach-section protection: limit the arrester current and the surge steepness. A travelling wave arrives with amplitude equal to the line insulation’s 50 % impulse flashover voltage, far above station equipment withstand; so earth wires on the approach are the main measure; without them a close stroke can push over 5 kA through the arrester, too steep as well.

Transformer protection: an arrester as close as possible to the transformer, with the shortest leads (less drop); arrester earth bonded to the transformer tank and LV neutral, so the HV insulation sees only the residual voltage (not the earth-resistance drop). Then one common earth grid for safety and working earths, with extra electrodes under rods and arresters, or separate electrodes.

Buildings: the national design code for building lightning protection applies (not repeated in the book).

Unless work requires it, avoid going out during lightning; most deaths happen outdoors, so get indoors when storms approach. If caught outside:

  1. Lightning prefers tall objects and points: keep away from towers, chimneys, poles; never shelter under a big tree or in an isolated shed or hut (touch voltage, side flash, step voltage).
  2. A building or structure with a rod or tape protects its surroundings: if there is nowhere else, stay within the 45° cone below the air termination, but not close to the structure.
  3. Do not stand high or in open ground; no umbrella or long-handled tools; find low ground, stand on something dry, ideally insulating, crouch with feet together (no potential difference between the legs).
  4. Touch no metal (wires, pipes, rails); carry no metal objects (induction can burn the skin); do not huddle or run hand in hand; keep apart from each other.
  5. Keep away from water: strikes in and beside water are especially frequent.
  6. Indoors is only relatively safe; surges enter on power, signal and antenna lines: ① close doors and windows (direct strokes, ball lightning), keep away from them, balconies and outer walls; ② do not touch water, heating or gas pipes; no showers, especially from solar water heaters; no stray wires; ③ use no appliances (TV, computer, phone, fridge, washing machine, microwave): best to unplug power and signal leads; ④ keep floors dry and appliances and pipes well earthed.

worked.q: A 35 kV substation is planned in soil of 800 Ω·m. May the line earth wire be connected to the incoming gantry? How is the last span protected?
worked.s: No: for 35–60 kV it is allowed only where soil ≤ 500 Ω·m. The earth wire ends at the terminal tower, and the span into the station is protected by lightning rods (which, at 35 kV, must be free-standing).

worked.q: Why is the arrester earth bonded to the transformer tank and LV neutral?
worked.s: So the arrester’s earth-resistance drop appears on both sides alike: the HV winding-to-tank insulation sees only the arrester’s residual voltage, not residual voltage plus I·R of the earth.

worked.q: You are caught on an open field in a thunderstorm with a colleague. What do you do?
worked.s: Move to low ground away from trees, poles and water; drop umbrella and tools; keep a few metres from your colleague; stand on something dry, crouch with feet together; touch no metal.

recap: 220 kV lines carry earth wires along the ___ line.
35 kV lines: earth wire for ___ km at the approach.
Supplementary earth ≥ ___ m from the transformer earth point.
Safe zone below an air termination: a ___° cone.

topics.title: Electrical Safety Management I: Organisation, Inspections and Safety Equipment
topics.zh: 电气安全管理（一）：组织管理、安全检查与电工安全用具

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Electrical work is a special, dangerous trade: its quality affects the electrician, other people and plant; work is spread over many places with different duties, so supervision is hard. Set up a management body and staff to suit the plant’s equipment, the electricians’ make-up and the operating features; full-time managers need electrical and electrical-safety knowledge; departments co-operate.

Rules: sound rules (safety work rules, operation and maintenance rules, safety management systems) protect production; follow national, sector and local standards and write the plant’s own; safe working procedures for every trade, with electrical content in non-electrical ones; operation and installation rules suited to the plant; named responsibility for important equipment and for accident-prone items (wide-ranging or multi-circuit switchgear, temporary lines and equipment: set allowed length, period of use, installation requirements); work permits, supervision, licensing for repairs, especially HV.

Safety inspection items
Insulation aged, damp or damaged? Insulation resistance acceptable?
Exposed live parts guarded; barriers to requirements; clearances adequate
Protective earthing or neutralising correct and reliable; protective devices to requirements
Portable and local lamps on safety extra-low voltage or other measures
Safety tools and fire equipment complete
Equipment correctly selected, installed and sited; connections sound; temperatures of equipment and lines suitable
Fuse elements and other over-current settings correct
Maintenance and management systems complete; electricians trained and certified
Patrol system for main transformers and key equipment, with records
Periodic insulation resistance of equipment in use; earth resistance of earthing, connections and corrosion
Periodic checks or withstand tests of safety tools, arresters, transformer oil, protective devices
Strict acceptance of newly installed equipment

Training: raise awareness and teach basic knowledge and methods; new employees get three-level safety training (plant, workshop, team) and pass an exam; ordinary staff know general safe use; production workers using electrical equipment also the related rules; independent electricians know the safety requirements of installation, use, maintenance and repair, the safety procedures, first aid for shock and electrical fire fighting, and hold an operating certificate; newcomers, trainees and temporary workers: only after safety training, under supervision, never alone; staff from other units are briefed on the equipment, wiring and safety measures first.

Records: keep HV system diagrams, overhead-line and cable layouts, distribution plans and drawings; a file for each important item with every repair and test record; records of equipment and personal accidents; standards, codes and regulations kept up to date; domestic and foreign safety information sorted and kept; records complete and continuous, computerised where possible.

sections.h: Safety equipment: kinds, use, earths and signs
sections.b:
Insulating safety equipment: insulating sticks, insulating tongs, boots, gloves, mats, stands. Basic equipment withstands the working voltage for long and may directly handle live equipment; auxiliary equipment cannot and only reinforces the basic.

ItemClass and notes
Insulating stick, tongsBasic. Tongs only below 35 kV. Working, insulating and hand parts; insulating and hand parts of varnish-impregnated wood, hard plastic, bakelite or GRP, separated by a guard ring. Sticks with different heads: operate HV disconnectors and drop-out fuses, fit/remove temporary earths and arresters, measuring and testing. Tongs: fit/remove fuses. Minimum lengths of insulating and hand parts allow for internal overvoltage; metal hook of the working part not over 5–8 cm (avoid phase-phase or earth shorts)
Gloves, bootsRubber; auxiliary; but gloves are basic for LV work and boots are basic against step voltage. Gloves at least 10 cm beyond the wrist
Mat, standAuxiliary only. Mat: rubber ≥ 5 mm thick, ribbed non-slip surface, ≥ 0.8 × 0.8 m. Stand: wooden boards or slats, gaps ≤ 2.5 cm (heels), no metal parts, on support insulators ≥ 10 cm high, top not overhanging the insulators (tipping); ≥ 0.8 × 0.8 m, ≤ 1.5 × 1.0 m
Other electrician’s safety equipmentEquipment for work at height, portable voltage and current indicators, maintenance earths, barriers, signs, equipotential shielding (current-sharing) suits for live work

Signs: warning (do not approach or touch live parts), prohibition (do not operate this switch, protecting people working on dead circuits), permission (work here), reminder (remove temporary earths before energising).

Hanging temporary earths: (1) on every side that could feed the dead equipment (including branches) or where induced voltage may arise; visible from the work place; at safe distance from live parts; (2) electrically separate sections (e.g. sectioned busbars separated by disconnectors or breakers): prove dead and earth each; a step-down substation wholly dead: earth every possible feed side, not every section; (3) indoors, on places not painted with phase colours; (4) no switch or fuse between the earth and the work; (5) earth end first; reverse to remove; insulating stick or insulating gloves; (6) proper clamps, never by winding; (7) flexible bare multi-strand copper, sized for short-circuit current, minimum 25 mm² (printed “25 mm”); check before each use; (8) each set numbered and kept in a numbered place with matching numbers; record fitting and removal; hand over at shift change; (9) discharge capacitive equipment with a discharge stick first; (10) two people; with single-person duty only earthing switches may be used.

Management: safety equipment is for HV work only, kept in a cabinet or fixed place; insulating tools numbered and tested periodically per the safety rules; signs and barriers orderly and sufficient; earths numbered and kept in their places. Fire equipment kept in fire boxes, managed by the fire warden, not used otherwise; expired, ineffective or damaged items reported; duty staff do not casually open extinguishers.

Where signs go: “Do not close — men at work!” on handles of switches that would feed the work; “Do not close — work on line!” on switches controlling lines worked on outside the substation; “Stop! High voltage!” on barriers of adjacent and opposite bays, and on closed passages indoors; on fixed outdoor barriers in suitable numbers, facing inwards (words towards the inside).

Pattern to remember (my note): rigid tools (sticks, barriers, covers) yearly, 5 min; things worn or held by hand and detectors (gloves, boots, detectors, phasing tubes, ropes) every 6 months; gloves and boots for 1 min with a leakage limit.

worked.q: Which of these are basic safety equipment for 10 kV operation: insulating stick, insulating gloves, insulating mat, insulating boots?
worked.s: Only the insulating stick. Gloves, boots and mats are auxiliary for HV (gloves are basic only for LV; boots basic only against step voltage).

worked.q: HV insulating gloves were last tested 7 months ago. May they be used?
worked.s: No: the interval is 6 months. Send for test: 8 kV, 1 min, leakage ≤ 9 mA.

worked.q: A substation operator is on single-person duty and must earth a feeder. May he hang a portable earth set?
worked.s: No: hanging earths needs two people; on single-person duty only an earthing switch may be used.

topics.title: Electrical Safety Management II: Work Permits and Organisational Measures in Substations
topics.zh: 电气安全管理（二）：变电站工作票与保证安全的组织措施

sections.h: Permits: types, scope, filling-in and use
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Organisational measures for work on electrical equipment: work permit; work licensing; supervision; interruption, transfer and completion.

Substation first-type permitSubstation second-type permit
Work on HV equipment needing full or partial outageWork on control panels, LV switchboards, distribution boxes, supply mains
Secondary, lighting and similar circuits where HV equipment must be switched off or safety measures takenSecondary and lighting circuits not needing HV outage or safety measures
HV cables needing outageField circuits of running generators and synchronous condensers; rotor-resistance circuits of HV motors
Other work requiring HV outage or safety measuresNon-operating staff phasing with insulating sticks and VTs, or measuring HV current with a clamp meter
Work beyond the Table 11-1 distances, on enclosures of live equipment, and where live conductors cannot be touched
HV cable work not needing outage
Voltage (kV)≤ 1020, 3563 (66), 110220330500
Table 11-1: safe distance, equipment not de-energised (m)0.701.001.53.0——
Table 11-2: from normal working range to live equipment (m)0.35 (≤ 10, 13.8)0.601.503.004.005.00

Voltages not listed take the next higher level’s distance.

Filling in and issuing: in pen or ballpoint, in duplicate, correct and clear, no arbitrary alterations (standard correction marks). On switching sheets never write “open/shut” (开/关: ambiguous, “开灯” means switch on): use “分/合” (open/close the circuit). Computer-printed permits use the standard format, checked and signed (by hand or electronically) by the signatory. One copy at the work site held by the person in charge, the other with the licenser, handed over at shifts; the licenser logs number, task, licence and completion times. On one permit the signatory, person in charge and licenser must be three different people; the person in charge may fill it in. Issued by the equipment’s operating unit, or by approved maintenance, test or construction units whose signatory and person-in-charge lists are filed in advance. For first-type permits the signatory may use a master permit and sub-permits, issued together, per rules approved by the chief engineer. Contractors working in a customer’s substation: the permit is issued by that substation.

Use: one person in charge holds one permit at a time; work limited to one electrically connected section; several sections allowed on one permit if same voltage, same floor, energised and de-energised together and no live conductors can be touched; all safety measures completed at once before work. If a whole section or switchboard is dead, all work in different places may share one permit, main tasks detailed; for several teams, issue to an overall person in charge and list only team leaders. If some work is unfinished when supply must be restored and can continue without obstruction, a new permit per the energised state, with measures set up, before continuing. Successive same-type work without outage on several sections: one second-type permit; successive same-type live work in one substation: one live-work permit. Line or cable permits brought into a substation: extra copy for the substation licenser; lists filed. Changing team members: with the person in charge’s consent after a safety briefing. Changing the person in charge only if unavoidable: signatory agrees, licenser informed and records it; only once; handover of task and measures. Adding tasks within the outage area: with signatory and licenser consent, added on the permit; if measures change, a new permit and new licensing. If the signatory cannot be present, by telephone, noted in register and permit. First-type permits reach operations the day before (by hand, fax or LAN; with fax, licensing waits for the original); urgent work: hand to the licenser before starting. Second-type and live-work permits: on the day. Damaged permits: fill in a new one.

Validity: the approved maintenance period. Extension of first or second-type: requested by the person in charge to the shift leader before expiry (via the dispatcher for dispatched equipment); once only.

sections.h: People on the permit: qualifications and responsibilities
sections.b:
RoleQualificationsSafety responsibilities
Signatory (签发人)Knows staff skills, equipment and these rules, relevant experience: production leader, technician or approved person; names published in writing(1) Work is necessary and safe; (2) safety measures on the permit correct and complete; (3) person in charge and team suitable and sufficient
Person in charge (负责人)Relevant experience; knows equipment, team abilities and the safety rules; approved in writing by the area/company production leader(1) Organise the work correctly and safely; (2) check the permit’s measures and the licenser’s measures fit the site, add if needed; (3) brief every member on hazard points and safety and technical measures, confirm each knows; (4) enforce the measures; (5) supervise members to follow rules, use PPE, keep measures; (6) watch members’ fitness and changes
Licenser (许可人)Approved experienced operator, or approved operator of the maintenance unit; in customer substations a certified HV electrician(1) Check the permit’s measures are correct, complete and fit the site; (2) measures on site complete, add if needed; (3) check no risk of sudden energising; (4) ask the signatory about even the smallest doubt
Dedicated supervisor (专责监护人)Relevant experience; knows equipment and the rules(1) Know whom and what area to supervise; (2) brief them on measures and hazards; (3) see they follow rules and measures, correct unsafe acts
Team member—(1) Know the work, procedure, measures, hazards, and confirm; (2) obey rules and discipline, answer for own acts, look after each other, watch over the rules; (3) use safety tools and PPE correctly

sections.h: Licensing, supervision, interruption, transfer and completion
sections.b:
Licensing: after setting up the measures, the licenser, with the person in charge: (1) re-checks the measures on site, shows the actual isolation points, proves the equipment dead; (2) shows the live equipment and points of care; (3) both sign the permit. Operators may not change the running arrangement of equipment under repair; neither side may change measures alone; changes need the other’s consent, recorded in the shift log.

Supervision: after licensing, brief the team (work, division of labour, live parts, measures, hazards), confirm, then start; person in charge and supervisor stay on site throughout. Nobody (including the person in charge) may enter or stay alone in HV rooms or outdoor HV areas; where needed (polarity, continuity tests) and allowed, experienced members may work in other rooms after a detailed briefing. The person in charge may join the work in a full outage; in a partial outage only if measures are reliable and everyone is at one place with no risk of touching live parts. Add dedicated supervisors as conditions require; they do no other work; if they leave, the people supervised stop work or leave until they return. A person in charge leaving briefly appoints a competent deputy with handover, telling the team, and the same on return; for a long absence the signatory changes the person in charge, telling the team and licenser.

Interruption: the team leaves, measures stay, permit stays with the person in charge; resuming the same day needs no licenser. At the end of each day: clean up, reopen closed routes, return the permit to operations; next day: licenser’s permission, retrieve the permit, re-check measures, hold the site briefing, then work; nobody enters without the person in charge or supervisor. Until the permit is completed nobody may energise. In an emergency during an interruption, operators may energise without the permit returned only after telling the person in charge and getting the reply that everyone has left and supply may be restored, and then: ① remove temporary barriers, earths and signs, restore permanent barriers, change to “Stop! High voltage!”; ② post a person on every route to tell the team “equipment energised, do not continue”, staying until the permit is returned.

Trial energising before work ends: everyone out; all permits for that system returned; temporary barriers, earths, signs removed, permanent barriers restored; full check by person in charge and operators; operators apply the voltage. To continue: license again.

Transfer: moving between places within one section on one permit needs no transfer formalities if operators set all measures at the start; but the person in charge briefs the team on live areas and measures at each move.

Completion: team cleans and tidies; person in charge checks thoroughly, everyone leaves; tells the operators what was repaired, problems found, test results; they check together (state, nothing left behind, clean); end time written and both sign: work ended. The permit is completed when temporary barriers are removed, signs taken down, permanent barriers restored, and earths or earthing switches not yet removed reported to the dispatcher. Energise only when all permits for the dead system are completed and the dispatcher or shift leader orders it. Completed permits and emergency sheets kept one year.

worked.q: A worker must stand 0.5 m from live 10 kV busbars that are not de-energised. Is this allowed with barriers? Without?
worked.s: Table 11-2 (working range) for ≤ 10 kV is 0.35 m: 0.5 m is more, so allowed; but it is less than Table 11-1’s 0.70 m, so for 35 kV and below it requires insulating barriers or safety fences; without them the busbars must be de-energised.

worked.q: Can the shift operator be both licenser and person in charge on one permit, to save time?
worked.s: No: signatory, person in charge and licenser may not be combined on one permit. (The person in charge may fill in the permit.)

worked.q: Why must the operating instruction say “分/合”, not “开/关”?
worked.s: “开” is ambiguous: it can mean opening a breaker or switching something on (“开灯”). “分” (separate, open the contacts) and “合” (close the contacts) have one meaning only.

recap: Safe distance, ≤ 10 kV equipment not de-energised: ___ m.
The person in charge may be changed only ___.
First-type permits reach operations the day ___.

topics.title: Electrical Safety Management III: Technical Measures, Line Work, SF₆ Rooms and LV Work
topics.zh: 电气安全管理（三）：技术措施、线路作业、SF₆ 设备与低压工作

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Technical measures (carried out by operators or authorised persons): switch off, prove dead, earth, hang signs and fit barriers.

Equipment to switch off: (1) the equipment being repaired; (2) equipment closer than Table 11-2 to the normal working range; (3) at 35 kV and below, equipment farther than Table 11-2 but nearer than Table 11-1, with no insulating barriers or fences; (4) live parts behind, beside, above or below workers without reliable measures; (5) others needing outage. Disconnect every source (the neutral of any star-connected equipment in service counts as live). Never work on equipment isolated only by a breaker: open disconnectors, draw trucks to the test or maintenance position: a visible break on every side (except where it cannot be seen). Disconnect transformers and VTs connected to the dead equipment on all sides, against back-feed. Breakers and disconnectors on the equipment and possible feed sides: remove control and closing supplies; lock disconnector handles. Where full disconnection is hard, remove the connections between equipment and source.

Proving dead: a tested contact-type detector of the right voltage, each phase, at the places where earths will be fitted or earthing switches closed; test the detector on live equipment first (or an HV generator). On wooden poles, ladders or frames, if it cannot indicate without an earth, an earth lead may be fitted to the tail of the insulating stick, with permission. HV proving: insulating gloves; telescopic sticks fully extended; hand on the handle, not past the guard ring; safe distance; no direct outdoor proving in rain or snow. Indirect proving: disconnector mechanical position, electrical indications, meters and live-line indicators: at least two indications changed together; with remote operation, check disconnector status indication, telemetry, remote status signals and live-line indicators.

1. Earths fitted by two people (except approved single-person items and operators).
  2. Once proved dead, earth and short-circuit all three phases at once. Cables and capacitors: discharge each phase fully first; earth the star point of star capacitors; discharge series capacitors and capacitors separated from the bank one by one; discharge cases on insulated racks too.
  3. On every side that could feed: earths or earthing switches; allow for the earth lead swinging within safe distance.
  4. Induced voltage from parallel or nearby live equipment: extra earths (entered on the permit) or personal earthing leads (fitted and removed by the worker).
  5. Work on the line side of a gantry within 10 m of an earth: no extra earth needed even if outside it.
  6. Electrically separate sections: prove dead and earth each; a step-down substation fully dead: earth each possible feed side only.
  7. No breaker or fuse between earth (or earthing switch) and the work; if equipment design puts a breaker between, after closing both, ensure the breaker cannot open (sign “Do not open!”).
  8. Earths at designated points with paint scraped off and black marks; earth terminals connected to the grid at suitable points; three-phase short-circuit type earths, or a common three-phase earth terminal for single-phase sets.
  9. Earth end first; reverse to remove; insulating stick and insulating gloves; never touch the earth lead or unearthed conductors (induced shock).
  10. Transparent-sheathed flexible multi-strand copper ≥ 25 mm², also adequate for the fault current; no other conductors; clamps, never winding.
  11. Never move or remove earths without authority. Work needing some or all earths off (bus or cable insulation tests, line parameters, breaker contact simultaneity): ① remove one phase earth; ② remove earth, keep the short-circuit; ③ remove all earths or open the earthing switch: only with the operators’ (or dispatcher’s, for dispatcher-ordered earths) permission, restored immediately after.
  12. Earths numbered, kept in numbered places in the safety-equipment room; fitting and removal recorded and handed over.
SignWhere
Do not close — men at work!Handles of breakers and disconnectors that would feed the work; also on screen-operated switches
Do not close — work on line!Line breaker and disconnector handles when people work on the line
Do not open!The breaker between an earthing switch and the work, when both are closed
Stop! High voltage!Temporary barriers round live equipment within Table 11-1 in partial outages (barrier at least Table 11-2 from live parts; dry wood, rubber or tough insulation, firmly fixed); indoors on barriers of bays beside and opposite and on closed passages; on shutters of withdrawn trucks (shutters then never opened); outdoors on barriers round the work area, facing inwards; on all-round barriers enclosing the few remaining live items, facing outwards; on beams near live parts of outdoor structures
Enter and exit here!Entrance of the outdoor barrier, led to the nearby road
Work here!At the work place
Climb here!The steelwork or ladder workers use
No climbing — high voltage!Adjacent live structures that could be climbed by mistake

For 35 kV and below, if specially needed, insulating barriers of high insulation may directly touch live parts. Never cross barriers; never move or remove barriers and signs.

sections.h: Line work: measures in substations; SF₆ rooms; LV work
sections.b:
Substation measures for line work: line outages and restorations only on the dispatcher’s or line licenser’s order; no pre-arranged times; open all breakers, line and bus disconnectors that could feed the line, trucks to test/maintenance; prove dead; earths or earthing switches at every possible feed end; “Do not close — work on line!” on handles and on control-panel operating points. The dispatcher or licenser records the number of teams, persons in charge, places and tasks; at the end, gets completion reports from every person in charge (including customers), confirms all teams finished, earths removed, people off the line, checks the log, then orders the station measures removed and the line energised. Customer lines: outage only on the customer contact person’s written application, approved; restoration only on the same applicant’s completion report, recorded on tape and logged; contact lists filed with dispatch.

Work on SF₆ equipment (rules)
SF₆ switchrooms and gas laboratories: forced ventilation with intakes at the bottom of the room (SF₆ is heavy); exhausts not towards homes or pedestrians
Filling indoors: RH ≤ 80 %, ventilation on, no leaks into the work area; SF₆ in work-area air ≤ 1 mL/L
Gas-tight separation from the control room; holes to cable floors and tunnels below sealed; “Ventilate first” (注意通风) signs on doors; exhaust-fan switches outside the door
Alarm oxygen meters or SF₆ leak alarms in low areas, displays at entrances; tested regularly
No display at the entrance: ventilate 15 min and measure SF₆ with a leak detector first; avoid patrolling alone; never repair alone
Do not stand near SF₆ bursting discs; report abnormalities at once
Entering low areas or cable trenches: check oxygen (not below 21 %, as printed) and gas content
Work on opened equipment: specially trained staff with protective equipment
Before dismantling: analyse the gas; protective clothing, gas masks as needed; after opening, everyone leaves for 30 min; masks and gloves when removing adsorbent and dust
Never vent SF₆ to air: recover and purify; stand upwind. After evacuation, flush 3 times with high-purity nitrogen (10.1 × 104 Pa); soak adsorbent and metal powder in 20 % NaOH solution for 12 h, then bury deep
Cylinders: use a pressure reducer; stop when cylinder pressure falls to 10.1 × 104 Pa, close the valve, fit the cap
Major leaks: evacuate, start all fans; no entry without self-contained (isolating) gas masks; enter only after thorough ventilation. Burst disc: de-energise, wipe with petrol or acetone
Sampling and minor leaks: gas mask and ventilation. No work on the enclosure while the breaker operates. Shower after work; clean tools and PPE
Cylinders upright in a cool, dry, ventilated open store, away from heat and oil, out of sun, valves free of water and oil; handle gently

The 21 % oxygen figure is as printed; normal air is about 20.9 %, and many rules use 18–19.5 % as the minimum. (My note.)

De-energised LV switchgear and conductors: work on LV switchboards, distribution boxes and supply mains uses a second-type permit; LV motors and lighting circuits need no permit but a record, and at least two people (one works, one supervises). Measures: disconnect all sources and remove fuses; “Do not close — men at work!” on handles; prove dead before work; other measures as needed (insulating shoes, insulating mat). After replacing fuses with the supply off, wear gloves and goggles when restoring.

worked.q: A breaker has been opened to work on a 10 kV cable. The operator says “the breaker is open, go ahead.” What is missing?
worked.s: Never work on equipment isolated only by a breaker: open the disconnectors (or rack the truck out) for a visible break on every side, remove control and closing supplies and lock handles, isolate VTs against back-feed, prove dead each phase, discharge the cable phase by phase, earth and short-circuit, hang signs and barriers, license.

worked.q: To measure busbar insulation resistance during an outage, the earths are in the way. What may be done?
worked.s: With the operators’ permission (the dispatcher’s if the earths were ordered by dispatch): remove one phase earth, or remove the earth keeping the short-circuit, or remove all earths / open the earthing switch, as the test requires; restore immediately after.

worked.q: An SF₆ switchroom has no gas display at the door. A technician wants to go in alone to change a gauge. Allowed?
worked.s: No. First ventilate 15 min and measure SF₆ with a leak detector; repair work must never be done alone in an SF₆ room (and patrolling alone should be avoided).

recap: Never work on equipment isolated only by a ___.
No extra earth needed if within ___ m of an earth (gantry line side).
SF₆ in workroom air: not over ___ mL/L.
After opening SF₆ equipment, leave for ___ min.
LV switchboard work uses a ___-type permit.

topics.title: A Brief Analysis of Safety Psychology
topics.zh: 安全心理浅析

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Safety: “no danger means safe, nothing missing means whole” (无危则安、无缺则全), yet nothing is absolutely safe; the main task is preventive measures so that work causes no injuries or occupational diseases. Modern safety science covers all of life, production and survival, not just accidents at work. Early Chinese experience: Chao Yuanfang (Sui dynasty) recorded lowering a feather into old wells and deep caves first: if it whirled, toxic gas was rising, do not enter; Song Yingxing’s Tiangong Kaiwu (Ming) describes a hollowed bamboo pole driven into coal seams to vent firedamp. Safety management evolved from after-the-event (passively bearing losses), to rule-based management (rules and technical measures after accidents: the idea of prevention), to occupational health and safety management systems, the mark of modern management.

Maslow’s hierarchy, in the book’s seven-level form: physiological, safety, social (belonging), esteem, knowledge, aesthetic, self-actualisation. Safety comes second, so people whose physiological needs are not met pay little attention to safety: the book’s explanation of lower safety awareness in developing countries. Prof. Luo Yun’s statistics (as quoted): China’s occupational death rates per thousand workers, road deaths per 10 000 vehicles and deaths per million tonnes of coal far exceed developed countries; yearly accident losses could build 10 new Guangzhous, like three Boeing 747s falling every day; over 80 % of accidents come from rule-breaking. Accidents are preventable. People tire, err and slip, so the fundamental cure is inherent safety (mechanisation, automation, guards, better environment); since that costs money and is limited by technology, strong management fills the gap: “what hardware lacks, software makes up”.

Du Xunhe’s poem Jing Xi (Tang): where the stream is rocky and fierce people go carefully and no one capsizes all year; it is on smooth water with no rocks that one often hears of drownings. Lesson: “Know the danger and you are safe; forget it and you are in danger” (知其危则安，忘其危则危).

Heinrich’s law (300 : 29 : 1): from 550 000 machinery accidents in 1941 (1666 deaths and serious injuries, 48 334 minor injuries, the rest no injury), Heinrich found the ratio serious/fatal : minor : no-injury = 1 : 29 : 300: of every 330 incidents, 300 harm no one, 29 cause minor injury, 1 a serious injury or death. Behind every major accident lie 29 minor ones and 300 near-misses or hazards. The book’s case: a mechanic put a belt onto a running pulley by hand, without the belt pole, on a shaky plank, in a loose long-sleeved coat, and was drawn in and killed; he had done it for years and the first-aid log showed 33 arm grazes in four years. So prevention must target minor, near-miss and no-injury incidents, hazards and rule-breaking.

MindsetFeatures and remedy (book)
Chance-taking (侥幸)Knows the rules and is skilled, but breaks them knowingly: “breaking rules doesn’t always cause accidents, accidents don’t always injure, injuries don’t always hit me”; trusts luck, good motives, own skill, not being seen. Causes: wrong experience, wrong understanding. Stop and correct the first violation so no habit forms
Inertia (惰性, “energy-saving”)Saves effort, makes do, finds procedures a nuisance
Complacency (麻痹)Blind self-confidence (mostly veterans); reinforced by past success; mental fatigue or a careless personality; routine work feels safe, vigilance relaxes
Defiance (逆反)“The more you forbid, the more I do”: open (argues back, keeps breaking rules) or hidden (agrees outwardly, resists inwardly). Educate with tact, watching emotions
Showing off (逞能)Competitiveness plus vanity: over-confident, reckless; or long repetition of the same risky act unprotected
Larking about (凑趣)Joining in fun, horseplay at work, playing with equipment signals; can build team spirit but must be controlled by training
Risk-taking (冒险)Rational (“knowing a tiger is on the hill, go anyway”) or emotional (vanity, fear of losing face); mostly young new workers
Short-cut (捷径 = chance + risk)Sees safety rules, measures and equipment as obstacles: helmet strap undone, not using safety bridges and walkways, not following the permit system
Conformity (从众)Follows the group, willingly or under pressure; unsafe acts spread if no accident follows: point out the danger, build a culture of compliance
Indifference (无所谓)Doesn’t see the danger; thinks rules are for controlling people; “important in talk, secondary in work, forgotten in competition”; believes breaking rules is necessary to get work done
CuriosityTouching unfamiliar things leaves equipment unsafe
Emotional upset, distractionOverexcitement, confusion, losing track
Unskilled, panics in dangerCannot respond to sudden abnormalities
BoredomMonotonous repetitive work → mental fatigue
Illusion / subconscious errorRare but very serious; an illusion arises from a real stimulus and does not just vanish (unlike hallucination)
Mental slips“Inexplicable” violations caused by perceptual slips
Environmental interferenceTemperature, colour, noise, lighting beyond the senses’ range disturb judgement

Focus on the human factor, with measures to suit task, time, place, environment and person. Seven groups to watch: the “dangerous” (break rules, reckless), the “muddled” (blindly obey, make do), the “numb” (careless, chance-taking), the “hasty” (rush, flustered), the “output-minded” (production over safety), the “tired” (poor rest or health), and the “job-changers” (new trade, unfamiliar equipment).

The book ends the chapter with two topics. They are included so your notes match the book, but please read the notes in italics.

Temperament (book’s four types)Description
Choleric (胆汁质)Irritable, quick-tempered, sensitive, impatient, changeable; strong but short-lived feelings; warm, quick to help, explosive energy
Sanguine (多血质)Clever, quick, lively, sociable, not easily daunted, no grudges; promises readily and forgets; keeps balance but changes interests easily
Phlegmatic (黏液质)Quiet, cool reactions, slow; sincere and trustworthy; calm, not tense, casual
Melancholic (抑郁质)Steady but gloomy, nervous, broods; avoids socialising; loses balance under difficulty and recovers slowly
Cycle (book)LengthDays since birth ÷ length → remainderHigh / critical / low
Physical23 days< 11 high; 11, 12, 13 critical (prone to illness); > 13 low10 / 3 / 10 days
Emotional28 days< 14 high; 14, 15 critical (mood swings); > 15 low13 / 2 / 13 days
Intellectual33 days< 16 high; 16, 17, 18 critical; > 18 low15 / 3 / 15 days

My note: the four temperaments come from the ancient Greek humoral theory; they are a historical classification, not a modern psychological test. The book calls biorhythms a science taught at many universities and says Japanese firms use them; controlled studies have not found that these fixed 23/28/33-day cycles predict accidents or performance, so biorhythm theory is generally regarded as pseudoscience. Treat this part as background, not as a safety tool; real fatigue management uses rest, shift planning and fitness-for-work checks.

terms: 职业安全卫生管理体系

worked.q: A plant records 600 near-misses and unsafe acts in a year. By Heinrich’s ratio, what does that suggest?
worked.s: 600 / 300 = 2 → about 58 minor injuries and 2 serious or fatal accidents can be expected if nothing changes. The lesson: act on the near-misses now. (The ratio is a statistical tendency, not an exact forecast.)

worked.q: A senior electrician skips proving dead “because I switched it off myself, I’ve done this for 20 years.” Which mindsets?
worked.s: Complacency (veteran over-confidence, habit reinforced by success) and chance-taking; it is also a short-cut. The book’s remedy: stop it the first time, explain the danger, do not let it become a habit.

recap: Over ___ % of accidents come from rule-breaking (book).
In Maslow’s hierarchy safety is the ___ level.
Chance-taking plus risk-taking gives the ___ mindset.

topics.title: First Aid I: Electric Shock, Rescue and Resuscitation
topics.zh: 急救与逃生（一）：触电伤亡、脱离电源与心肺复苏

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Lethal current endangers life in a short time. Power-frequency AC over some tens of mA can cause ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest, or stop breathing; fibrillation occurs much earlier, so it is the main cause. At only 20–25 mA fibrillation is not caused directly, but if it lasts long the heart can stop through asphyxia (oxygen lack after breathing stops). Above several amperes the strong stimulus may stop breathing first, and severe burns can kill. Up to a few hundred mA the main cause of death is fibrillation, so the fibrillation current is regarded as the minimum lethal current.

Shock durationFibrillation current (book)
Longer than one heartbeat cycleAbout 50 mA
Shorter than one heartbeat cycleSeveral hundred mA
Below 0.1 s500 mA to several A, and only if it falls in the heart’s vulnerable period
Same current, longer than one cycleMay cause cardiac arrest

It also depends on current path, type, and the person’s tissues and heart. Small currents only tingle; below the let-go current you can still free yourself; near lethal levels the victim shows nerve paralysis, no breathing, no heartbeat, unconscious. This must be treated as apparent death (假死), with immediate and sustained rescue: people have been saved after 4 h or more of artificial respiration. Book’s figures: rescue starting 3 min after the shock: 90 % good results; 6 min: 10 %; 12 min: little chance. Speed is everything.

sections.h: Releasing the victim and resuscitation (book’s method)
sections.b:
Free the victim from the supply: HV: open the switch, disconnector or load switch quickly; if none is near, push or pull the victim with an insulating object. LV: open the nearest switch, flick the live conductor away with insulating material, or cut the wire with insulated-handle pliers. Then, by breathing and pulse, give artificial respiration or chest compressions.

General rules: keep going without stopping rashly, also on the way to hospital. Signs of success: skin from purple to red, pupils from large to small; lip, eyelid or swallowing movements: check for own heartbeat and breathing; stop ventilating when breathing returns, resume if it stops again. Stop only when lividity or rigor appears and a doctor declares the victim beyond help. Never inject adrenaline while the heart is still beating.

Book’s techniqueSteps and figures as printed
Mouth-to-mouthVictim on the back (on the side before starting, so vomit cannot block the airway); support the neck so the line from jaw to ear lobe is 90° to the ground, pad under the neck, loosen belt and cuffs; open the mouth, clear phlegm, blood, sand, dentures, bring the tongue forward; pinch the nose, blow in hard, watch the chest rise 3.5–5 cm; release the nose to let air out (press the chest if needed); one cycle every 5 s
Chest compression (breathing present, no heartbeat)Heel of one hand two fingers above the xiphoid, hands overlapped, heel along the sternum; shoulders’ weight vertically; depress 3.5–5 cm, release quickly, hand stays in place; even rhythm; about 60–80 /min; equal press and release times; not too violent
CPR (neither breathing nor heartbeat)Compressions : breaths = 5 : 1
RescuersVery tiring: change rescuer every 5–10 min

Important, my note: the book’s CPR figures are out of date. Current adult basic life support (e.g. Singapore’s national guidelines and international resuscitation guidelines) teaches: call for help and an AED at once; 30 compressions : 2 breaths; rate 100–120 per minute; depth about 5–6 cm, centre of the chest; full recoil; minimal interruptions; compression-only CPR is acceptable if you cannot give breaths; attach the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts. Follow your certified first-aid / CPR-AED course, not these book figures, and get trained before you need it.

InjuryBook’s first aid
Heavy bleedingPressure bandage; for pulsing or spurting arterial bleeding, finger pressure or a tourniquet above the wound, marked with the time. (The book says loosen every 20 min; see note)
FracturesSplint with whatever is to hand, to prevent further injury
Open head or abdominal wounds with protruding tissueDo not push it back; cover with a clean bowl and bandage; no food, drink or painkillers; hospital at once
Impaled object (stake etc.)Do not pull it out: saw off the outside part, leaving a stump; remove in hospital (it may be plugging a vessel)
Flail chestPad with clothing or cotton and bandage firmly; or lay the casualty on the injured side
Open chest woundHalf-sitting; seal the wound to turn an open pneumothorax into a closed one; hospital at once; trained rescuers may decompress a tension pneumothorax

My note: current first-aid teaching says a tourniquet, once applied, is not loosened by the first aider; note the time and leave it for medical staff. Follow your first-aid course.

worked.q: A worker collapses touching a 230 V appliance that is still live; the socket switch is 2 m away. What do you do first?
worked.s: Do not touch him. Switch off at the socket (or pull the plug / trip the breaker); if impossible, push the conductor or him away with a dry insulating object while standing on something dry. Then check response and breathing, call for help and an AED, and start CPR if he is not breathing normally.

worked.q: Why does the book call an unconscious shock victim “apparently dead”, and what follows?
worked.s: Because breathing and heartbeat may have stopped through fibrillation or paralysis without the body being beyond saving: prompt, sustained resuscitation can revive him. By the book’s figures, starting within 3 min gives 90 % good results, after 6 min only 10 %; so start at once and do not give up until medical staff take over.

recap: The fibrillation current (shock longer than one heartbeat) is about ___ mA.

topics.title: First Aid II: Escape from Fire, Crowds, Floods, Gas and Earthquakes
topics.zh: 急救与逃生（二）：火灾、踩踏、洪水、毒气与地震逃生

sections.h: Escape routes, doors and lifts; fire rescue
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气运行维检安全》 (Electrical Operation, Maintenance and Inspection Safety), eds. Li Qiuming and Zhang Wei, Handan Branch of Hebei Iron & Steel, China Machine Press, 2011: a training text for electrical operating and maintenance staff in steelworks. Written in my own words. The rules and numbers are the book’s, under Chinese standards; in Singapore follow SS 638, the Electricity Act and your workplace permit-to-work system.

Escape route: (1) from where you are to the stairs; (2) down the stairs; (3) from the stair foot out of the building. Fire doors slow the spread of fire and stop smoke and hot air early. Escape doors: open in the direction of escape (outwards); openable at any time (a door needing a key or remote release is not one); not revolving; wide enough with space to disperse.

Never take a lift in a high-rise fire or severe thunderstorm: the machine room on the roof may attract lightning if protection is poor; fire or lightning damage can make the lift fail and fall; the shaft collects smoke (stack effect). People carrying petrol, alcohol or fireworks should not ride lifts either.

Fighting a fire: right method and extinguisher; in a closed room on fire do not open doors or windows until enough extinguishers are ready; call 119 (China; in Singapore 995) giving place, extent, your name and number, and send someone to meet the fire engines at the road junction; if trapped, use the terrain and objects to protect yourself while waiting.

Most fire deaths are from toxic smoke (CO) by suffocation or poisoning, then burns, then crushing and falls. (1) Build fire awareness: in a new place, find exits, escape routes, stairs (locked?), hydrants and refuge equipment; (2) stay calm, judge danger and safe areas, go away from the fire by escape doors, emergency stairs or outside; (3) outdoors, go upwind (run against the wind, not with it); (4) smoke is lighter than air: to cross a fire zone, wrap in wet cloth, cover mouth and nose, keep low; no rushing, no stopping for belongings; (5) clothes on fire: don’t run: roll on the ground, jump into water, or smother with heavy cloth; (6) upstairs: escape downwards, once you know below is clear; if stairs are blocked and the floor is low, make a rope from sheets, curtains, carpets and climb down from windows, balconies or pipes; if high and blocked, go back in, close doors to the fire, seal gaps with wet cloth and keep wetting, call for help from a window away from the fire (torch or white cloth at night); never use the lift; do not jump rashly.

MethodHow (book)
1. RopeTie one end to a door or window frame or heavy object, climb down hand over hand, feet twisted round the rope; gloves or towels protect the hands. Keep a safety rope at work and at home
2. CrawlingSmoke gathers high: crawl or stoop low
3. Wet towel over noseCools and filters hot toxic smoke
4. Wet quiltSoaked quilt, blanket or cotton coat over you, then cross the fire fast; never a plastic raincoat
5. Fire barrierNail or clamp a blanket over the door and keep wetting it, to hold back flames and smoke while waiting for rescue high up
6. Knotted sheetsTear sheets, covers, curtains into strips, twist and join; tie firmly; climb down as with a rope
7. JumpingNever lightly! Only in the last resort, from low floors: choose the smallest drop, throw down mattresses and cushions, lower your centre of gravity, then jump
8. Sliding down pipesDrainpipes, poles, lightning down-conductors; not too many at once
9. Stair transferIf fire seals the stairs from below, climb through skylights to the roof and use another unit’s stairs
10. Bathroom refugeLast resort: seal the door gap with towels, wet the floor, or lie in a full bath; never hide under beds, in lofts or wardrobes (fuel and smoke collect there)

Crowd crush: (1) do not go towards a crowd out of curiosity; (2) if caught in one, obey marshals, move with the majority, never overtake or go against the flow, do not trip; (3) if someone falls, stop and shout to warn those behind; (4) if knocked down, get to a wall, curl up facing it, hands clasped behind the neck protecting the head, knees drawn up protecting the chest, then move towards the wall foot or the edges of the crowd.

sections.h: Floods, toxic gas, earthquakes and distress signals
sections.b:
Floods: stay calm, judge water and ground, move to high ground or buildings; if none, hold floating objects (tubs, chairs, boards) or climb a strong tree; not onto weak roofs (they collapse when soaked); sandbags (sand, earth, gravel) at door gaps and windowsills; store food, water, warm clothes and a kettle; if no longer safe, make a raft (bed boards, doors, boxes, with paddles) or rings from inner tubes; collect food and signalling items (whistle, torch, bright flags or sheets); if water is below head height and trees are dense, tie a rope inside, lead it tree to tree, winding it round each, to higher ground; before leaving eat high-energy food, drink hot drinks, turn off gas and the main switch.

Toxic gas leaks: protect yourself with whatever is at hand, raise the alarm, move upwind or crosswind, not into low places; or into civil-defence shelters with filtered ventilation; if you cannot leave, stay in a sound multi-storey building, seal gaps, switch off air-conditioning and fans, put out flames, stay on the sheltered side without doors or windows. Guide evacuees with posts along the route; check nobody is left in the zone. After leaving: remove contaminated clothes, decontaminate, see a doctor if needed. Protect breathing with wet towels or masks, gas masks; skin with raincoats, gloves, boots; eyes with goggles or swimming goggles.

Earthquakes: keep a clear head; never jump from buildings; on average only 12 s from feeling the shaking to building damage. (1) In a bungalow near the door: run out; in a multi-storey building: shut off gas and power, open the door to keep the exit clear, shelter in a small room with many load-bearing walls, or under a low, sturdy table holding its legs; protect your head; not onto balconies, into lifts or down stairs, not running about or with crowds; (2) at work: shelter under vehicles, machine tools, large equipment; key workers close flammable, explosive and toxic gas valves, reduce temperature and pressure of hot, high-pressure pipes, stop running machines; most leave, a few stay protected to watch and prevent secondary disasters; (3) after the first shock, everyone goes out to open ground (aftershocks), wary of falling glass, tiles, signs, light fittings, precast walls; head covered with a bag or soft object, away from poles and walls; (4) if buried: survival needs air (minutes without), water (about 7 days without), food (about 15 days with air and water), and space to move head and limbs. Keep breathing clear (move debris from head and chest, clear nose and mouth; wet cloth against gas or fumes); avoid unstable debris overhead; prop up the space with bricks and sticks against aftershocks; breathe at gaps, especially where light shows; save strength, tap on things that resonate rather than shouting; control emotions, rest; bandage wounds.

Distress signalMethod (book)
FiresThree equally spaced fires; at night light, by day add green grass for thick smoke
LightTorch or lamp flashed 6 times a minute, repeated
ColourBright clothes or hat on a prominent spot; hang bright clothing or quilts high
MirrorReflect sunlight about 6 times a minute: glass, tin lids, spectacle lenses
ObjectsLay out a large “SOS” with branches, stones, clothing; write it in snow
SoundShout if close, or knock on objects

In a fire, call from windows, balconies or roof, bang metal, throw soft objects; wave bright cloth by day, a torch or white cloth by night.

worked.q: Fire breaks out two floors below you in a 15-storey block; the stairwell is filling with smoke. What do you do?
worked.s: Do not take the lift or go up blindly. If the stairs below are impassable, stay in your flat: close the doors towards the fire, seal gaps with wet towels and keep them wet, call 995 (Singapore) giving your exact location, signal from a window on the side away from the fire. Keep low if smoke enters. Do not jump.

worked.q: Chlorine leaks at a plant; the wind blows from north to south. Where do you go?
worked.s: Upwind or crosswind: towards the north, or to the east or west, never south (downwind) and not into low places (chlorine is heavier than air). Cover nose and mouth with a wet cloth.

recap: Most fire deaths are caused by toxic ___.
Shaking to damage in a destructive quake: about ___ s.
Without water, survival is usually about ___ days.
Distress light: flash ___ times a minute.

topics.title: Electrical Testing I: Basic Principles — Transmission Lines, Megger, tan δ, Schering Bridge, AC Withstand
topics.zh: 电气试验（一）：基本原理——传输线、绝缘电阻表、介损、西林电桥、交流耐压

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QPoint
1.1 Transmission lineA wave-guiding structure that directs electromagnetic waves along a set path; also called a waveguide
1.2 Guided waveThe electromagnetic wave travelling along it
1.3 ModesField patterns that can exist alone in a waveguide; by longitudinal field components: TEM, TE, TM and hybrid
1.4 Wave impedance (TE, TM)Ratio of transverse electric to transverse magnetic field
1.5 Uniform waveguideUniform line assumed infinitely long, carrying only a travelling wave in the +z direction; real lines are finite, ending in a component or another line
1.6 Distributed parametersResistance R (Ω/m), conductance G (S/m), inductance L (H/m), capacitance C (F/m) per unit length
1.7 Lossless lineR and G negligible
1.8 Characteristic impedanceDepends on the line’s structure and frequency, with the dimension of impedance
1.9 Why ZC = U/I of one waveIt is analogous to wave impedance (Et/Ht of a wave in one direction), so ZC is the voltage-to-current ratio of a wave travelling one way. Voltage and current on a line are the sum of the incident wave (towards the load) and the reflected wave (towards the source)
ZC = √[(R + jωL) / (G + jωC)]

1.10 Wave speed on a lossless line = speed of light. Two-wire line (spacing D, wire diameter d): C = πε / ln[(D + √(D² − d²))/d], L = (μ/π) ln[(D + √(D² − d²))/d], so LC = με. Coaxial line (inner radius a, outer b): C = 2πε / ln(b/a), L = (μ/2π) ln(b/a) (printed “ln b/d”, a typo), so again LC = με. In vacuum μ0 = 4π × 10−7 H/m, ε0 = (1/36π) × 10−9 F/m:

v = 1/√(L0C0) = 1/√(μ0ε0) = c ≈ 3 × 108 m/s

Why it matters for testing (my note): travelling-wave fault location on cables and lines, and lightning-surge behaviour, rest on these ideas; on a cable the wave is slower (v = c/√εr, roughly half of c for XLPE).

sections.h: Insulation tester, leakage current and tan δ (Q11–17)
sections.b:
1.11 Hand-cranked megger movement (book Fig. 1-3): two coils L1 (current coil) and L2 (voltage coil), wound in opposite senses on one spindle carrying the pointer, with no hairspring, so with no current the pointer rests anywhere. Torques M1 = I1f1(α) and M2 = I2f2(α) oppose. Why two coils? Two opposing torques balance each other; one coil alone would just keep turning. L1 is the “current” coil because it is in series with the measured circuit (through the current-limiting resistor RI and Rx); L2 the “voltage” coil because it is across the generator (through RU). The L1–RI branch and the L2–RU branch are in parallel. (The deflection depends on the ratio I1/I2, so cranking speed hardly matters: a ratio meter.)

1.12 Tester capacity = ability to charge a capacitive object, measured by the short-circuit current (L–E shorted). A small-capacity tester charges a large capacitance slowly, so the test voltage builds up late, polarisation differs, and the apparent insulation resistance, absorption ratio and polarisation index differ: results on large-capacitance equipment are less accurate; take tester capacity into account when comparing results.

1.13 Leakage current: conduction current of the few charged particles in a dielectric under field; very small (hence “leakage”), measurable at high voltage.

1.14 tan δ is a property of the insulation, independent of its volume. Equivalent circuit: Rx ∥ Cx; δ is the angle between total current and the capacitive current. For a uniform dielectric, loss per unit volume is what tan δ shows: at a given working stress, thickness ∝ U; at a given thickness, area ∝ Cx ∝ ICx; so volume ∝ U·ICx, and

P = U IRx = U ICx tan δ = U² ω Cx tan δ (1-1)

tan δ against U (Fig. 1-5): flat until the ionisation inception voltage Uc, then rising.

1.15 Concentrated defects: the larger the insulation volume, or the smaller the defect, the smaller its share of total loss, and ICx hardly changes, so tan δ rises little: insensitive. So for machines and cables in service (large volume, faults usually from local defects) tan δ is generally not done in preventive tests; for bushings and instrument transformers (small volume) it is essential and effective, and can even reveal local defects.

1.16 Two dielectrics in series (C1, R1; C2, R2), tan δi = 1/(ωCiRi):

tan δ = [C1 tan δ2(1 + tan²δ1) + C2 tan δ1(1 + tan²δ2)] / [C1(1 + tan²δ1) + C2(1 + tan²δ2)]

1.17 n dielectrics in series: total loss = sum; same current through each; neglecting the small series resistances, Un/U = (1/Cn)/(1/Ctotal), so

tan δ = (tan δ1/C1 + tan δ2/C2 + … + tan δn/Cn) / (1/C1 + 1/C2 + … + 1/Cn)

Reading it (my note): each layer’s tan δ is weighted by the voltage it carries (∝ 1/C). A bad layer with large capacitance (thin, small share of voltage) hardly shows: another reason local defects are hard to detect by overall tan δ.

sections.h: Schering bridge, discharge, and the QS1 in practice (Q18–24)
sections.b:
QS1 high-voltage Schering bridge, normal connection (after book Fig. 1-8, redrawn). At balance Ig = 0 and Z3ZN = Z4ZX.

1.18 Balance condition: with Ig = 0, C and D are at the same potential: IX flows through ZX then Z3, IN through ZN then Z4; UCE = UDE gives IXZ3 = INZ4; UAC = UAD gives IXZX = INZN; dividing: Z3ZN = Z4ZX, where ZX is the test object, Z3 = R3, Z4 = R4 ∥ C4, ZN = CN (standard capacitor).

tan δ = ω C4 R4 CX ≈ CN R4 / R3

The two results above follow from Z3ZN = Z4ZX (my note, standard Schering-bridge results). In the QS1, R4 = 10 000/π Ω so that at 50 Hz tan δ reads directly as C4 in µF.

1.19 Non-self-sustained discharge: above an inception field E2 (below breakdown field Em) collision ionisation begins; but if the external ionising agent is removed the discharge weakens and stops.

1.20 Normal connection keeps the bridge at low potential: the upper arms CX and CN have very large impedance, so almost all the voltage is across them; R3, C4 that the operator adjusts are near earth: no HV danger. In the reverse connection (object earthed) all arms are at high voltage.

1.21 A damp wooden block acts like a large capacitor: C = εS/d (ε = ε0εr) is proportional to ε, and water’s relative permittivity is about 81.

1.22 Testing VTs with the QS1: keep the angle between the HV lead and the instrument transformer at least 90°: a lead close to the porcelain adds stray capacitance to the core and increases the positive error (reading > true value) caused by surface damp and dirt.

1.23 QS1 shunt positionTest-object capacitance CX
0.01below about 3000 pF
0.025below 8000 pF
0.06below 19 400 pF
0.15below 48 000 pF
1.25printed “below 40 000 pF”; presumably 400 000 pF (each step covers a larger range)

1.24 Raising QS3 bridge sensitivity: it depends on how much the potentials of points a, b change when R3 and C4 are set, i.e. on the voltage drops on them: increase the drops on R3, R4.

sections.h: AC withstand, induced tests, partial discharge (Q25–31)
sections.b:
QPoint
1.25 AC withstand methodsThree: (1) power-frequency (45–65 Hz) withstand; (2) induced withstand: power-frequency induced or multiple-frequency (100–400 Hz) induced; (3) impulse: switching impulse and lightning impulse
1.26 Regulator rating = test transformer ratingTo avoid burning out the voltage regulator
1.27 Where to measure the test voltageSmall-capacitance objects (oil breakers, porcelain insulators, insulating tools): may be measured on the LV side. Large-capacitance objects, or when amplitude and waveform matter: must be measured on the HV side, because of the capacitive voltage rise (容升): capacitive current through the transformer’s leakage reactance makes the HV voltage higher than the ratio suggests
1.28 Multiple-frequency sources(1) 2–4× frequency test generator sets, or thyristor inverters (limited output, complex: not widespread); (2) on site, a transformer over-excited to produce a large third-harmonic voltage
1.29 Why multiple frequency for induced testsE = k f B, k = 4.44 N S. To double the voltage at constant flux density B (core not saturated), double the frequency: so ≥ 100 Hz; since core loss rises sharply with frequency, usually 100, 150, 200 Hz, whole multiples of 50 Hz
1.30 Support transformerDesigned for induced tests (not needed if site conditions allow); usually single-phase, many closely spaced ratios over a wide range, so the support voltage can be in phase with the induced voltage of the object; support and intermediate transformers usually share one supply
1.31 Actual discharge quantityIn a partial discharge in a void, some gas is ionised; the total positive (or negative) charge produced in one discharge is the actual discharge quantity. (It cannot be measured directly; what is measured at the terminals is the apparent charge in pC: my note)
E = 4.44 f N B S

Worked use of 1.29 (my note): to induce 2 × rated voltage across a winding without saturating the core, feed it at ≥ 2 × 50 = 100 Hz; at 150 Hz the flux density would be (2/3) of normal, giving margin.

worked.q: A QS1 bridge (R<sub>4</sub> = 10 000/π Ω, 50 Hz) balances with C<sub>4</sub> = 0.008 µF, R<sub>3</sub> = 318 Ω, C<sub>N</sub> = 50 pF. Find tan δ and C<sub>X</sub>.
A 10 kV bushing has C<sub>x</sub> = 500 pF and tan δ = 0.6 %. What dielectric loss at 10 kV, 50 Hz?
worked.s: P = U²ωC tan δ = (104)² × 314 × 500 × 10−12 × 0.006 ≈ 0.094 W. (Tiny power: tan δ shows quality, not heating, at this size.)

worked.q: Two layers in series: C<sub>1</sub> = 1000 pF, tan δ<sub>1</sub> = 1 %; C<sub>2</sub> = 100 pF, tan δ<sub>2</sub> = 0.2 %. Overall tan δ?
worked.s: Neglecting tan² terms: tan δ = (0.01/1000 + 0.002/100)/(1/1000 + 1/100) = (1 × 10−5 + 2 × 10−5)/(0.011) ≈ 0.27 %. The lossy layer (large C, small voltage share) barely shows.
