tan δ is NOT done on cables in service because defects are mostly ___.
Multiple-frequency induced tests use at least ___ Hz.

topics.title: Electrical Testing II: Transformer Tests
topics.zh: 电气试验（二）：变压器试验

sections.h: DC bias, voltage regulation, insulation and tan δ tests (Q1–7)
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QPoint
2.1 DC bias increases vibrationA DC current in the winding becomes part of the magnetising current and biases the core, moving part of the working range into saturation; the total magnetising current becomes peaky, so vibration increases. (Sources include geomagnetic currents and HVDC earth-return currents: my note)
2.2 Voltage regulation modes at a pilot nodeReverse (逆调压): raise voltage at peak load (not more than +5 % of rated), lower it towards rated at light load. Forward (顺调压): allow it slightly low at peak (not below 97.5 %) and slightly high at light load (not above 107.5 %). Constant (恒调压): about constant at all loads, usually 5 % above rated
2.3 Why short and earth the windings not under test (insulation resistance, absorption ratio)Leads of the tested winding shorted together; others shorted and earthed. This measures the tested part to earth and to other windings, avoids errors from residual charge, and gives a smaller (more realistic) value than leaving them floating or guarded
2.4 Core earthed for tan δIf not, you measure the loss of the core-to-earth insulation, with local ionisation, so tan δ rises with voltage
2.5 Short all terminals of the tested winding (and the secondary)Measuring one phase only, without shorting, introduces large errors from winding inductance and no-load loss
2.6 Temperature and tan δModern insulation has relaxation-polarisation temperature Tm of several hundred °C; a good transformer’s overall tan δ hardly changes below 60 °C. Tests are done at 10–40 °C, the low-temperature region (long relaxation time, small and nearly constant tan δ)
2.7 Self-inductionA changing current in a coil induces an EMF that opposes the change of flux

2.8 Why other windings must not be earthed (or shorted) when measuring DC resistance of large HV transformers. With winding 1 under test (R1, L1) and winding 2 shorted (R2, L2), mutual inductance M:

R1i1 + L1 di1/dt − M di2/dt = u1 M di1/dt − R2i2 − L2 di2/dt = 0

Eliminating di2/dt shows the tested winding appears to have more resistance and less inductance (u1 = (R1 + R2M i2/(L2 i1)) i1 + (L1 − M²/L2) di1/dt, as I read the printed eq. 2-3); the true R1 appears only when i2 = 0 and di1/dt = 0. Even with the test current steady, R2i2 + L2di2/dt = 0 gives i2 = I0e−(R2/L2)t: a decaying current with time constant τ = L2/R2, very long because L2 ≫ R2. So the reading creeps towards the true value: measuring time several to tens of times longer, and errors.

2.9 Line-to-phase resistance conversion. Star without neutral: RAB = Ra + Rb etc., so

Ra = (RAB + RCA − RBC)/2 Rb = (RAB + RBC − RCA)/2 Rc = (RBC + RCA − RAB)/2

Delta (a-y, b-z, c-x connected): each line reading is one phase in parallel with the other two, e.g. RAB = Rb(Ra + Rc)/(Ra + Rb + Rc). With Rp = (RAB + RBC + RCA)/2:

Rb = (RAB − Rp) − RBCRCA/(RAB − Rp)
Ra = (RCA − Rp) − RABRBC/(RCA − Rp)
Rc = (RBC − Rp) − RABRCA/(RBC − Rp)

Check (my note): with all phases equal to R, each line reading is 2R/3, Rp = R, and Rb = (−R/3) − (4R²/9)/(−R/3) = −R/3 + 4R/3 = R. ✓ For balanced windings simply Rphase = 1.5 Rline (delta) or 0.5 Rline (star).

sections.h: Ratio mismatch, wattmeter, induced and impulse tests, frequency response, shielding, no-load test (Q10–17)
sections.b:
2.10 Why a 1 % ratio difference gives about 10 % circulating current. Two transformers, KA < KB, same primary voltage: secondary EMFs E2A = U1/KA > E2B. Paralleled at no load, the EMF difference drives a circulating current through both short-circuit impedances (referred to the secondary):

I2Y = (E2A − E2B) / (ZKA + ZKB)

Equal units with ΔU = 0.01UN and ZK = 0.05ZN each: I2Y = 0.01/(0.05 + 0.05) = 0.1 IN at no load: high copper loss, uneconomic. In the primaries, the balancing currents add to A’s load (smaller ratio, heavier loaded) and reduce B’s. So limit ratio difference to ±0.5 %.

2.11 Electrodynamic wattmeter multiplier: it cannot be read directly; the power per division

E = U I / F

U, I: rated values selected on the voltage and current knobs; F: full-scale divisions. At unity power factor full scale = UI, so E is the power per division; reading = divisions × E.

2.12 Induced withstand checks longitudinal (turn-to-turn, layer, section) insulation: enamel, oil, paper, varnish, compounds are never 100 % pure; impurities, bubbles, moisture, manufacturing damage concentrate the field; heat lowers breakdown voltage; partial discharge raises dielectric loss and heating, conduction increases, and a vicious circle leads to thermal breakdown (symptoms: higher no-load current and loss, overheating, arcing, vibration, howling). At rated voltage and frequency inter-turn voltages are too low to reveal defects, so a defective new unit looks normal. The induced test applies over 2× rated voltage at over 2× rated frequency (higher frequency also lowers solid-dielectric breakdown voltage) for the specified time, reliably revealing longitudinal defects.

2.13 Switching-impulse tests use negative polarity: polarity makes little difference to internal insulation, but external flashover voltage is much higher for negative impulses, so negative avoids external flashover during the test.

2.14 Terminal short circuit (出口短路): a short at the transformer’s secondary output terminals: outside the transformer, so not a transformer fault (though it stresses the windings: my note).

2.15 Transfer function (frequency-response analysis of winding deformation): at high frequency a winding is a passive linear two-port network of distributed parameters:

H(jω) = (a0 + a1jω + … + am(jω)m) / (b0 + b1jω + … + bn(jω)n)

Real-coefficient polynomials; the denominator is strictly Hurwitz (all roots in the open left half of the s-plane, else unstable); since H → 0 as ω → ∞, m ≤ n, usually m = n − 1; b0 = 1; n = order. In z-form H(z) = Σaiz−i/Σbiz−i. Roots of the denominator = poles (characteristic roots); roots of the numerator = zeros. A deformed winding shifts them.

2.16 Magnetic shielding (Fig. 2-6): a high-permeability shell (permalloy, iron-aluminium alloy) in a field carries most flux lines in its wall, few inside: flux lines refract at the boundary between media of different permeability. In transformers, shields on the tank wall make leakage flux pass through the shield instead of the tank steel, avoiding large losses and local overheating.

My note: the question mentions aluminium plates; aluminium is non-magnetic and shields by eddy currents that oppose the leakage flux (electromagnetic shielding), whereas the explanation given describes magnetic shunts of high-permeability material (in transformers usually silicon-steel packets). Both are used to protect tank walls.

2.17 No-load test at rated voltage: no-load loss is mainly iron loss, equal to the iron loss on load at rated voltage; since the core works near the knee of the magnetisation curve, no-load loss and current change sharply if the voltage deviates.

worked.q: Delta winding line resistances: R<sub>AB</sub> = 0.6400, R<sub>BC</sub> = 0.6400, R<sub>CA</sub> = 0.6600 Ω. Find R<sub>b</sub>.
Two equal transformers with 6 % impedance are paralleled; their ratios differ by 0.5 %. Circulating current?
worked.s: I2Y = 0.005/(0.06 + 0.06) ≈ 4.2 % of IN, at no load. (At 1 % it would be 8.3 %.)

worked.q: A wattmeter on 300 V and 5 A ranges has 150 divisions and reads 96 divisions. Power?

recap: Reverse regulation raises peak voltage by up to ___ %.
Shorted windings cause a decaying current with τ = ___ / R₂.
Ratio difference of paralleled units: within ±___ %.

topics.title: Electrical Testing III: Instrument Transformer Tests
topics.zh: 电气试验（三）：互感器试验

sections.h: Cascade VTs, open-delta winding, induced tests (Q1–6)
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QPoint
3.1 Terminal board of a cascade VTPrimary weakly insulated end X; secondary and tertiary terminals a, x, aD, xD; and 4 bolts fixing the board to the base, connected to the enclosure (earth)
3.2 Porcelain and terminal board affect conventional tan δA fairly high voltage (≤ the 2 kV test voltage) exists between X and a; if the porcelain or terminal-board surfaces are poor, surface current enters the measuring circuit and tan δ reads high
3.3 Conventional (bridge, reverse connection) vs self-excitation methodSelf-excitation gives lower tan δ because the voltage distribution along the winding differs: with the bridge reverse connection A is at 10 kV and X near 0; with self-excitation the whole HV winding is at 10 kV. Because the X end has lower insulation and surface leakage, the reverse bridge reads higher tan δ; capacitance differs for the same reason
3.4 Open-delta auxiliary winding (three-phase five-limb VT)Normally the three auxiliary voltages are symmetrical and the open-delta voltage is zero. With phase A earthed, the b and c auxiliary voltages rise to line values and the open-delta voltage becomes 3 times the auxiliary phase voltage (= 3U0, three times the zero-sequence voltage); a voltmeter or voltage relay across it signals the earth fault. (The 4th and 5th limbs give the zero-sequence flux a return path: my note)
3.5 Which instrument transformers get triple-frequency induced tests?Only graded-insulation VTs: the end insulation is low (about 3–5 kV) and cannot take the same test voltage as the line end. CTs and fully insulated VTs have small losses and need little source capacity: an applied power-frequency withstand test is enough
3.6 Why the induced test checks both endsThe VT end is earthed; a higher-than-power-frequency voltage applied on the secondary induces the test voltage in the primary with the same distribution as in service, but higher: checking longitudinal insulation

QPoint
3.7 Class 0.2 vs 0.2S CTs0.2S: metering circuits with small and widely varying load current (1–120 %); 0.2: measurement
3.8 Current (ratio) error and phase errorRatio error = (KnI2 − I1)/I1 × 100 %, Kn = I1n/I2n = N2/N1. Phase error: angle between the primary current and the secondary current phasor rotated by 180° (anticlockwise)
3.9 Expressionsf = (Im/I′p) sin θ × 100 %; δ ≈ (Im/I′p) cos θ × 3438′, where Im = magnetising current, I′p = primary current referred to the secondary, θ = angle between secondary current and magnetising current. (3438 = minutes per radian)
3.10 Rated burdenThe maximum burden that may be connected continuously
3.11 Error change at over-currentCaused by the magnetic properties of the core, which set the exciting current I0 (saturation)
3.12 Main causes of VT errorExciting current and the winding impedances
3.13 CT transient characteristicThe error behaviour of protection CTs during the primary current transient (with DC offset)
3.14 Peak instantaneous errors (TP-class CTs)Peak instantaneous error ε̂ = 100 îε/(√2 Ipsc) %: maximum instantaneous error current in the specified duty cycle over the peak of the primary AC component. Peak instantaneous AC-component error ε̂ac = 100 îεac/(√2 Ipsc) %

Why S class (my note): a 0.2S CT keeps 0.2 % accuracy down to 1 % of rated current, so a lightly loaded feeder is still metered accurately.

sections.h: Error testing, tan δ, magnetisation curve, graded VTs (Q15–22)
sections.b:
3.15 VT error test by comparison: a high-accuracy standard VT is connected with its primary in parallel with the VT under test; an error calibrator takes the difference of the secondaries. Circuit (book Figs. 3-3, 3-4): regulator TY → step-up transformer TS (a resonant step-up for capacitive VTs) → PT0 and PTX in parallel; burden boxes Y1–Y3 on the secondaries.

3.16 Check CT polarity first: to connect it correctly in series with the standard CT (subtractive or additive). Primary start L1, end L2; secondary start K1, end K2; L1 and K1 are like-polarity (dotted) ends, as are L2 and K2.

3.17 Actual error of the CT under test includes the standard CT’s error and the calibrator’s error:

Σf = f0 + fx − Δf Σδ = δ0 + δx·f/50 − Δδ

f0, δ0: standard CT; fx, δx: read for the CT under test; Δf, Δδ: calibrator; f: supply frequency.

3.18 tan δ of oil-paper capacitor-type CTs is generally not temperature-corrected: good oil is non-polar, its tan δ is conduction loss, rising with temperature; paper is polar, its tan δ (dipole relaxation loss) generally falls with temperature in 40–60 °C. Good oil-paper insulation free of conductive impurities and moisture shows no clear change there, so do not correct; and the correction factors for oil-filled equipment do not fit oil-paper.

3.19 Tap (last foil) to earth Cx and tan δ: not with the QS1 reverse connection: both connections give nearly the same tan δ, but the reverse connection gives Cx some tens of pF higher, because it adds the stray capacitance of the tap to earth in parallel. So use the normal connection.

3.20 Inter-turn short in a CT secondary: the volt-ampere (excitation, magnetisation) curve is slightly lower than normal in its initial part (book Fig. 3-6: curves for normal, 1 turn shorted, 2 turns shorted).

3.21 No-load test before and after the multiple-frequency induced test on graded VTs: an inter-turn breakdown during the test causes circulating current and higher no-load loss and current. Take no-load current at rated voltage before and after and compare (printed: “there should be a marked difference”; the sense requires no marked difference for a pass). A VT already shorted before the test would show no change either, so also compare with VTs of the same batch: no marked difference → acceptable.

3.22 Capacitive rise in multiple-frequency induced tests: capacitive current through the leakage reactance makes the primary voltage exceed the value from the ratio; larger leakage reactance and capacitance, larger effect. Neglecting resistance:

ΔU = ω U Cx Xk

U: voltage on the primary; Cx: VT capacitance; Xk: leakage reactance referred to the HV side; ω = 2πf. Different designs and voltages give different rises.

worked.q: A 10 kV system: phase VT secondaries 100/√3 V, open-delta windings 100/3 V each. What appears across the open delta for a solid earth fault on phase A?
worked.s: Each healthy auxiliary voltage rises √3 times and they add to 3 × (100/3) = 100 V (= 3U0), operating the earth-fault voltage relay. Normally it is 0 V.

worked.q: A CT reads I<sub>2</sub> = 4.99 A for I<sub>1</sub> = 600 A, ratio 600/5. Ratio error?
Graded VT: U = 66 kV induced at 150 Hz, C<sub>x</sub> = 500 pF, X<sub>k</sub> (at test frequency) = 40 kΩ. Capacitive rise?
worked.s: ΔU = ωUCxXk = 2π·150 × 66 × 103 × 500 × 10−12 × 4 × 104 ≈ 1.24 kV (≈ 1.9 %): measure on the HV side or allow for it. (Illustrative values, my example.)

recap: A graded VT’s end insulation is only about ___ kV.
Open delta during a single earth fault: ___ U₀.
0.2S class covers ___ % to 120 % of rated current.
CT terminals L1 and ___ are like-polarity ends.
The reverse connection adds ___ capacitance from the tap.

topics.title: Electrical Testing IV: Circuit-Breaker Terms and Tests
topics.zh: 电气试验（四）：断路器术语与试验

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QTermMeaning (book)
4.1Auto-reclosingThe breaker closes again a preset time after opening
4.2Recovery voltageVoltage across one pole’s terminals after the arc is extinguished: first the transient recovery voltage (TRV, marked transient character), then the power-frequency recovery voltage
4.3ContactTwo or more conductors whose touching completes the circuit; their relative motion opens or closes it; hinged or sliding contacts keep continuity
4.4PoleThe switch parts associated with one electrically separate conducting path of the main circuit (excluding parts that mount and operate all poles together)
4.5Break time (total)From the trip command to final arc extinction: tbreak = topen + tarc. Opening time: trip command to separation of contacts in all poles (inherent opening time). Arcing time: first arc initiation to final extinction in all poles
4.6Close–open time (metallic short time)During closing, from contact touch in the first pole to separation of the arcing contacts in all poles in the subsequent opening; must exceed opening time + pre-arcing time for the breaker’s self-protection
4.7Rated (short-circuit) breaking currentCurrent the breaker may break at rated voltage (kA)
4.8TravelDistance from start to end position: travel = contact gap + over-travel (wipe). Gap: insulating distance between open contacts; over-travel: further motion of the moving contact after touching (for butt contacts, the motion producing contact force)
4.9Synchronism (simultaneity)Time differences between the three phases on opening and closing; serious non-simultaneity connects or disconnects lines or transformers on fewer than three phases, causing overvoltages harmful to insulation

Example (my note): opening time 30 ms + arcing time 15 ms = break time 45 ms (about 2.25 cycles at 50 Hz).

sections.h: Arc chambers, wear, bounce, pollution terms (Q10–18)
sections.b:
QTermMeaning (book)
4.10Self-blast / external-energy interruptersArc chamber: device round the contacts limiting the arc’s position and speeding extinction. Self-energy: mainly uses the arc’s own energy; external-energy: mainly uses energy supplied from outside
4.11Oil-breaker chambers (all self-energy)Axial-blast (flow parallel to the arc), cross-blast (perpendicular), combined axial–cross blast
4.12Accumulated breaking current (SF6)Integral of breaking current over the number of operations: a wear indicator
4.13Contact gap (vacuum)Total clearance between the contacts of one pole, or connected conductive parts, in the open position
4.14Restrike rate (vacuum)Proportion of opening operations that produce restrikes
4.15BounceNumber: times moving and fixed contacts part and re-touch during closing; time: from first touch to final steady contact; maximum amplitude: the largest bounce
4.16Equivalent salt deposit density (ESDD)Equivalent amount of salt per unit insulating surface: wash the insulator with a set amount of distilled water, measure the conductivity, find the mass of NaCl giving the same conductivity in the same water, divide by the washed area: mg/cm²; it characterises pollution severity
4.17Specific creepage distanceCreepage distance of external insulation ÷ highest operating voltage (r.m.s.): mm/kV
4.18Break (断口)The part between moving and fixed contacts when open; single, double or multiple breaks

terms: Break time / opening time / arcing time
全开断时间/分闸时间/燃弧时间
金属短接时间（合—分时间）

worked.q: A 126 kV insulator string has 3150 mm creepage. Specific creepage distance?
Washing a 400 cm² insulator surface gives salt-equivalent 20 mg. ESDD?
Travel is 12 mm and over-travel 3 mm on a vacuum breaker. Contact gap?
worked.s: Gap = travel − over-travel = 9 mm.

topics.title: Electrical Testing V: Bushings and Capacitors
topics.zh: 电气试验（五）：套管试验与电容器试验

sections.h: Capacitor-graded bushings: tap earthing, structure, tan δ (Q5.1–6)
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QPoint
5.1 Capacitor-type bushingOil-paper or resin-paper insulation with capacitive grading foils that even out the radial and axial field
5.2 Why the tap (last foil) must be earthed in service110 kV+ bushings: many insulating layers on the conductor with aluminium foils between them form a chain of concentric cylindrical capacitors. The outermost foil (the tap, 末屏) is brought out through a small bushing for testing. If its earth is poor or open, the tap forms a small capacitance to earth in series with the much larger bushing capacitance; by series division a high floating voltage appears between tap and earth: discharges, burnt insulation, even explosion of the bushing
5.3 Core structure and testingConcentric insulating layers alternating with tin-foil layers round the tubular conductor, fixed at the flange. The test tap is connected to the last foil (for tan δ and partial-discharge measurement); the voltage tap to the foil next to it (for low-capacity supply). Old bushings may have neither; the last foil is led to the flange. Poor end seals let water in; moisture deep in the core is recognised, but early moisture only in layers near the tap is often missed: testers measure the core (R1C1, R2C2) but not the tap-to-flange insulation and oil (R3C3). Measure tap-to-earth tan δ as well; on old bushings, reinforce the tap lead or fit a test tap
5.4 Test loose bushings standing verticallyTheir capacitance is small, so stray impedances of the HV and measuring electrodes to nearby partly earthed frames, walls and floor have a large, position-dependent effect, giving scattered results. Stand them vertically on a well-earthed stand (least stray effect); not horizontal or hung on insulating slings at any angle
5.5 Bushings on a transformer: connect the windingsEnergising only the tested bushing’s conductor, other phases floating, other windings open, gives large errors, as when windings are not shorted for winding tan δ: magnetising inductance and core loss make the current differ in size and phase; it reaches the QS1 measuring arm through stray capacitance between winding and capacitor layers. Short each winding (and earth the others)
5.6 QS1 reverse connection must not be used on fitted bushingsThe flange is bonded to the tank, which is earthed. In the reverse connection the HV goes through the bridge to the test tap and back through the measuring lead and flange to earth: you actually measure the tap-to-earth tan δ, not the bushing (book Fig. 5-2, “wrong reverse connection”)

6.1 Breaking capacity (遮断容量): rated breaking capacity: the current (kA) and power (MVA) a breaker may break at rated voltage; three-phase:

Seb = √3 Ue Ieb

6.2 Grading capacitors across breaker breaks. A double-break breaker after clearing an earth fault (book Fig. 6-1): each open break acts as a capacitance Cc; the mid-point has stray capacitance Ce1 to earth. Without grading capacitors:

U1 = U(Cc + Ce1)/(2Cc + Ce1) U2 = U·Cc/(2Cc + Ce1)

With Cc = Ce1: U1 = 2U/3, U2 = U/3: the first break is much more stressed. With a grading capacitor C ≫ Ce1 across each break, C replaces Cc by C + Cc and U1 ≈ U2 ≈ U/2: even sharing improves insulation and breaking capacity.

QPoint
6.3 Coupling capacitorSeries-parallel capacitor elements sealed in porcelain; HV end to the line lead with a line trap; the other end out through a small bottom bushing to the coupling filter: part of power-line carrier communication (Fig. 6-3)
6.4 Insulation resistanceDC voltage between terminals ÷ leakage current through them
6.5–6.9 TermsElement: smallest unit of dielectric and electrodes. Unit: elements in one case with terminals. Bank: units electrically connected together. Collective (集合式): units assembled in one tank. Self-healing: capable of self-healing (metallised film clears local breakdowns: my note)
6.10 HV shunt capacitor installationCapacitors with primary and secondary equipment, connected in parallel to a three-phase AC system above 1 kV, able to operate independently
6.11 LV shunt capacitor installationSame for systems 1 kV and below
6.12 No terminal-to-terminal insulation test on siteDepends on electrode area (capacitance): no common standard; HV units are elements paralleled then series-connected, so a few healthy parallel elements mask many bad ones; the charging current is large, charging slow, readings unsteady, and the tester may burn. Measure terminals (joined together) to case with a 2500 V tester: generally above 2000 MΩ. If terminal-to-terminal must be checked, use the discharge method: crank a few turns (not over 5), then judge by the sound and spark when discharging across the terminals
6.13 Keep cranking until the tester is disconnectedThe tester voltage stays above the capacitor’s while charging; stopping suddenly leaves the charged capacitor at higher voltage, so it discharges back into the tester and may burn it
6.14 Shunt capacitors: no tan δ requiredOn small capacitors (coupling capacitors) tan δ finds local and distributed defects; on large ones (shunt capacitors) only distributed defects: a local defect is a tiny share of total loss, masked by the large capacitance
6.15 Oil leaksLong leakage lowers internal pressure so water gets in; less oil leaves the top short of oil, causing internal discharges
6.16 Compensating capacityThe reactive power supplied by the compensation

terms: 电容元件/单台电容器/电容器组

worked.q: A double-break breaker has C<sub>c</sub> = 10 pF per break and C<sub>e1</sub> = 15 pF. Share of voltage on each break? With 1000 pF grading capacitors?
A breaker is rated 12 kV, 31.5 kA. Breaking capacity?
Bushing capacitance 400 pF; the tap’s own capacitance to earth (if its earth link breaks) 4000 pF; line-to-earth voltage 127 kV (220 kV system). Floating tap voltage?
worked.s: Series division: Utap = 127 × 400/(400 + 4000) ≈ 11.5 kV: far beyond what the small tap bushing can withstand, hence discharge. (Illustrative values, my example.)

recap: A bushing’s outermost foil is called the ___.
Without grading, with C<sub>c</sub> = C<sub>e1</sub>, break 1 carries ___ U.
A coupling capacitor’s low end goes to the coupling ___.

topics.title: Electrical Testing VI: Surge Arrester Tests
topics.zh: 电气试验（六）：避雷器试验

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QPoint
7.1 Type letters FS, FZ, FCZ, FCDF valve type; S distribution; Z station; C magnetic-blow; D (rotating) machine
7.2 Main partsSpark gaps (“gaps”) in series with non-linear resistors (“valve blocks”)
7.3 Arc-quenching voltageIts rated voltage
7.4 Residual voltagePeak voltage across the arrester while discharge current flows
7.5 Power-follow currentSupply current that flows through the arrester after the discharge current
7.6 What makes flat-gap discharge stable (small scatter, flat volt-time curve)(1) Different permittivity of the mica washer and the air gap; (2) irradiation of the electrode surfaces and the gas between: both supply initiating electrons
7.7 Recovery speed of gap dielectric strengthToo slow → the gap re-breaks down as the recovery voltage rises. Measured by the cut-off ratio: the smaller it is, the faster the recovery. Shorter gaps recover faster
7.8 Volt-time and volt-ampere characteristicsGaps set the spark-over voltage; its dependence on time is the volt-time characteristic. Valve blocks set residual voltage and follow current; current vs voltage drop is the volt-ampere characteristic
7.9 Current-carrying (discharge) capacity of blocksThe limit of a specified number of specified-waveform current impulses passed without substantial damage
7.10 Heat capacityC = ΔQ/ΔT: heat absorbed (released) per degree of temperature rise (fall)
7.11 Why FS arresters need no leakage-current testThe DC test current is the conduction current of the parallel (grading) resistors across the gaps; only FZ, FCZ, FCD have them. Purpose: check sealing and broken resistors: moisture → current rises sharply; open resistor → current falls markedly. After transport, installation or removal a marked rise may mean displaced gap end caps or partly shorted resistors
7.12 Discharge counterRecords the number of arrester operations

sections.h: DC leakage test: where to put the microammeter (Q13)
sections.b:
In the DC leakage and withstand test (book Fig. 7-1) currents flowing include: I0 volume leakage through the arrester (what we want); I1 stray current from the HV lead (generator to meter) to earth; I2 stray from the screened lead; I3 stray from the arrester HV end; I4 stray from the HV output and terminal to nearby equipment; I5 surface leakage of the arrester to earth.

Meter positionReadsPros / cons
PA1: at the arrester HV endI0 + I3 + I4 (+ I5, removable with a guard ring): small errorAccurate, simple. But meter at HV: needs good insulation and screening; far from the tester, awkward to read and change range; some meters polarise in strong fields
PA2: at the tail of the HV transformer windingI0 + I1 + I2 + I3 + I4 + I5: largest errorMeter at low potential: safe, convenient (used in most packaged DC sets); but every stray current passes through it
PA3: at the arrester earth endI0 (+ I5, removable by screening the sheds): smallest errorLow potential, convenient, easy to screen; used when the arrester earth can be opened and its base is well insulated

sections.h: Zinc-oxide arresters, impulse terms, rectifier parts, monitoring (Q14–28)
sections.b:
QPoint
7.14 ZnO grain-boundary layerAdditive-rich oxide film about 0.1 µm thick round ZnO grains of about 10 µm diameter
7.15 Surface barrier of ZnO grainsAt a surface, atomic order is interrupted and oxidation and contamination alter electron energy states: the bands bend (upwards in n-type, downwards in p-type); the resulting potential difference is the surface barrier (what makes ZnO non-linear: my note)
7.16 Operating-duty testChecks the arrester can operate repeatedly and reliably under set conditions: high-current impulse duty (lightning) and switching-impulse duty
7.17 Impulse currentRises and decays within microseconds to thousands of microseconds
7.18 Nominal discharge currentPeak of an 8/20 µs current through the arrester; used to classify arresters (e.g. 5 kA, 10 kA: my note)
7.19 Virtual front time1.25 × the time for current to rise from 10 % to 90 % of peak (µs)
7.20 Impulse voltageRises and decays within microseconds to thousands of microseconds
7.21 Impulse spark-over voltageHighest voltage reached before discharge under an impulse of given shape
7.22 Cut-off ratioPower-frequency spark-over voltage ÷ rated voltage
7.23 Diode maximum reverse voltageHighest reverse voltage a diode can withstand; beyond it the PN junction is destroyed
7.24 Diode maximum working currentMaximum forward current allowed continuously
7.25 Silicon stackRectifier diodes encapsulated in resin as one block; an HV stack = many HV diodes in series, essential for HV rectification (acts as one diode)
7.26 Continuous operating voltage (Uc)R.m.s. power-frequency voltage that may be applied continuously between the terminals
7.27 Continuous currentCurrent at Uc: resistive plus capacitive parts, varying with temperature, stray capacitance and pollution, so a section’s may differ from the whole arrester’s; given as r.m.s. or peak
7.28 On-line monitorMonitors continuous current in service: changes reveal internal ageing or moisture; a pollution meter shows surface pollution; a counter records operations

Why watch the resistive part (my note): at Uc the current is mostly capacitive; ageing or moisture shows first as a rise in the small resistive component, so modern monitors separate it.

worked.q: A 10 % to 90 % rise of a test current takes 6.4 µs. Virtual front time?
An FZ arrester’s DC leakage current has fallen to half its previous value. Likely cause?
worked.s: Its parallel (grading) resistors may be open-circuited (broken). A sharp rise would instead suggest moisture or shorted resistors.

topics.title: Electrical Testing VII: Power Cable Tests
topics.zh: 电气试验（七）：电力电缆试验

sections.h: Cable types, corrosion cell, DC test basics (Q1–11)
sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QPoint
8.1 Level difference limits mass-impregnated paper cablesThe oil moves; with a large height difference between ends, oil collects at the low end with high static pressure, bursting terminations or the lead (aluminium) sheath and leaking; the high end dries out, insulation weakens, breakdown. Hence replaced by non-draining cables
8.2 “PVC is a thermosetting material”The book defines thermoset: once formed, cannot be reshaped or made to flow by heating. My correction: PVC is a thermoplastic (it softens when heated); XLPE is the cross-linked (thermoset-like) one
8.3 Low-smoke halogen-free (EPR cables)Compound contains no halogens (F, Cl, Br, At) and no lead, cadmium, chromium, mercury; burns without toxic smoke
8.4 Self-contained oil-filled cableUses continuous impregnation from an oil supply to eliminate voids in the insulation, allowing higher working stress
8.5 Induced voltage on a cable under testIf induced voltage exceeds the tester’s output, use a higher-voltage tester, to overcome it
8.6 Primary cell (and cable corrosion)A non-rechargeable cell converting chemical energy to electricity from the difference between two electrodes. Electrode potentials: Cu +0.334, Pb −0.122, Fe −0.44, Zn −0.76, Al −1.33 V (as printed). With the oversheath broken and water in, the galvanised armour sits about −0.76 V to earth; with the inner sheath also wet, armour and copper screen form a cell of about 0.334 − (−0.76) ≈ 1.1 V (less with much water): copper positive, galvanised steel negative. (Detecting these voltages reveals sheath damage; standard Al potential is −1.66 V: my note)
8.7 Ripple factor of a DC test setδU = (Umax − Umin)/2; Ud ≈ (Umax + Umin)/2; S = δU/Ud × 100 % (negative polarity taken as positive direction)
8.8 DC tests need little equipment capacityAC on a large capacitance draws large capacitive current; DC supplies only µA leakage. So for long cables DC withstand often replaced AC
8.9 Low loss and less damage under DCDC has only conduction loss (no polarisation loss). After a void discharges under DC, the space charge’s counter-field weakens the field in the void and suppresses further PD; under AC discharges repeat every half-cycle, decomposing organic insulation: DC testing is to some extent non-destructive
8.10 DC voltage distribution depends on core–sheath temperature differenceUnder DC the distribution follows insulation resistance, which falls with temperature: a temperature gradient strongly changes the distribution
8.11 DC breakdown hardly depends on timeSpace charge prevents prolonged ionisation in voids
S = (Umax − Umin) / (2Ud) × 100 %

sections.h: Phases, faults, capacitance; why not DC on XLPE (Q12–19)
sections.b:
QPoint
8.12 Phase colours (China)Yellow A, green B, red C
8.13 Cable fault types(1) earth; (2) short (parallel) fault; (3) open (series) fault; (4) flashover fault; (5) mixed
8.14 Open-circuit faults located with a capacitance bridgeA DC resistance bridge needs a DC path, which an open conductor lacks; use a capacitance (Schering-type AC) bridge
8.15 Cable capacitanceA cable is a cylindrical capacitor (core and earthed screen or sheath); charging current limits transmittable capacity and length; capacitance also checks quality and workmanship
8.16 Measuring capacitanceAC charging method: apply AC with no load, read voltage and capacitive current; or AC bridge (standard capacitor CN and the cable as two arms, RA, RB the others): C = (RB/RA) CN, for long cables, needs a standard capacitor; or a QF1-A cable fault tester
8.17 Capacitance locates faultsIt is distributed evenly and proportional to length: compare the faulted core’s capacitance with a healthy one
8.18 Not all HV cables are barred from DC withstandOnly extruded (rubber and plastic) cables: PVC, PE, XLPE, EPR
8.19 Can DC find mechanical damage in extruded cables?No: knife cuts in accessories, misplaced stress cones are not found even at very high DC
C = I / (ωU) × 103 µF (I in mA, U in V)

The printed factor reads “× 10”; with I in mA and U in V the factor must be 103 for µF (my check). Example: 50 Hz, 1000 V, 157 mA → C = 157/(314 × 1000) × 103 = 0.5 µF. Why not DC for XLPE (my note, consistent with Book 3 Ch 8): DC leaves space charge trapped in XLPE that can cause breakdown when the cable is re-energised on AC, and DC does not reproduce AC field distribution; hence 0.1 Hz or resonant AC tests.

worked.q: A cable core 1 has 0.45 µF, a healthy core 1.50 µF, and the cable is 3.0 km long. Where is the open circuit on core 1?
worked.s: Capacitance ∝ length: x = 3.0 × 0.45/1.50 = 0.9 km from the test end.

worked.q: A DC test set reads U<sub>max</sub> = 61 kV, U<sub>min</sub> = 59 kV. Ripple factor?
worked.s: Ud ≈ 60 kV; S = (61 − 59)/(2 × 60) = 1.7 % (generally required ≤ 3 %: my note).

topics.title: Electrical Testing VIII: Insulators; Insulating Oil and SF₆
topics.zh: 电气试验（八）：绝缘子试验；绝缘油和 SF₆ 气体试验

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QPoint
9.1 Flashover phenomenonSparks or arcs along the flashover path overheat the surface locally, carbonising and damaging surface insulation
9.2 Flashover vs breakdownFlashover: discharge along the surface; breakdown: through the body. Breakdown is usually far more serious: flashover is often ageing-type damage, breakdown is destructive
9.3 Dry arcing distanceShortest distance through air between the two metal fittings normally at operating voltage
9.4 Composite insulatorShort for rod-type suspension silicone-rubber insulator
9.5 Dry / wet / pollution flashover voltagesDry: clean, dry insulator: main rating for indoor insulators. Wet: clean insulator under rain: main rating for outdoor. Pollution: dirty insulator when damp
9.6 Hydrophobicity transferPolluted hydrophobic sheds pass their water-repellence into the pollution layer while staying hydrophobic themselves
9.7, 9.8 Fitting typesExternal (internal) fittings: metal fittings cemented outside (inside) the insulating part. Combined: one end inside, the other outside
9.9 KnurlingA rolled pattern on gripping or other surfaces (anti-slip); on the cemented surfaces of porcelain it raises bending strength
9.10 Multi-element insulatorTwo or more disc or bell elements cemented together and to the fittings
9.11 Why a good insulator has a sizeable voltage across itEach unit of a string carries a share (several kV) of the phase voltage; shares are unequal because of capacitances to the tower (Ce) and to the conductor (Cd) besides the unit’s own C: normally the unit next to the conductor carries the most, the middle ones the least, and the crossarm end slightly more
9.12 Rectifier / inverterRectifier: AC to DC (valves, ignitrons, silicon diodes, mercury arc); inverter: DC to AC
9.13 Point-contact germanium diodeA fine metal whisker (e.g. trivalent aluminium) on germanium, fused by a large forward pulse to form a PN junction; whisker = anode. Tiny junction: very low capacitance, but low reverse voltage and current: HF detection, switching, small rectifiers. E.g. 2AP1: 16 mA, 150 MHz
9.14 Live insulator testing in fine, dry weatherThe spark-gap fork method judges by the spark or sound; in damp weather leakage is larger, sparks and sound weak and hard to judge even with a smaller gap, and flashovers are more likely
9.15 Creepage distanceLeakage path along the external surface. Specific leakage distance λ = kL/U (k effective factor, L leakage distance, U line voltage)
9.16 Hydrophilic / hydrophobicHydrophilic: water forms a continuous film; hydrophobic: water forms separate droplets
9.17 Loss and recovery of hydrophobicityLong dry-band arcing, pollution, or treatments (plasma, corona, chemical oxidation, UV, X- and γ-rays) make silicone rubber hydrophilic; after discharges stop it recovers (low-molecular silicone migrates to the surface: my note)
9.18 Non-soluble deposit density (NSDD)Insoluble residue per unit surface; pollution = soluble part (ESDD) + insoluble part (NSDD)

sections.h: Insulating oil, gas analysis and discharge physics (Q10.1–19)
sections.b:
QPoint
10.1 Fractional distillationPhysical separation of crude oil into fractions of different boiling ranges by distillation; the first, indispensable refining step; compounds unchanged chemically
10.2 RefiningRemoving impurities and undesirable components from distillates to make base oils
10.3 Oxidation stabilityThe oil’s ability to resist oxidation by air or oxygen without permanent change: a key property
10.4 Water from oil oxidation2CnH2n+2 + 3O2 = 2CnH2nO2 + 2H2O (alkanes to acids plus water)
10.5 IonisationElectrons freed from atoms, leaving free electrons and positive ions. Forms: collision, photo-, thermal, surface ionisation
10.6 Light distillateFractions with fewer carbon atoms
10.7 Electrode gap 2.5 mm (breakdown-voltage test)Too small → breaks down early, result low; too large → result high
10.8 Raise voltage at 3 kV/sToo fast → breakdown voltage reads high; too slow → low
10.9 Stir and rest 5 min after each breakdownStir with a glass rod to clear free carbon from between the electrodes; rest 5 min so stirred-in bubbles escape
10.10 Parallel testTwo or more identical samples from one batch tested under identical conditions (temperature, humidity, instrument, reagents, person) to guard against chance errors; allowed differences set by standards
10.11 Same degassing device and oil volume (DGA)For repeatability of the degassing result
10.12 Reduce re-dissolution (gas from Buchholz relay)Gas left long in the relay partly re-dissolves (especially soluble components), changing concentrations in both gas and oil: sample promptly
10.13 Minimum detectable concentrationLowest concentration the chromatograph can detect for a given sample size
10.14 CrackingDeep thermal or catalytic breaking of chains into unsaturated small molecules (ethylene, propylene, butadiene). The book adds that cracked oil contains ions, so it conducts and insulation falls
10.15 Open-circuit voltage of a coreThe floating potential of an unearthed core in the strong field
10.16 Bundled insulation of LV windingsLarge transformers’ LV windings use transposed conductors: many small flat copper strands wrapped together
10.17 Electron avalancheAn initial electron near the cathode, in a strong enough field, ionises by collision; electrons multiply geometrically like an avalanche
10.18 Thermal inertia of an arcArc temperature lags the rapidly changing current because heating and cooling take time
10.19 Oil-flow electrificationIn large forced-oil transformers, oil flowing over insulating paper and pressboard becomes statically charged

Practical note (mine): the breakdown-voltage test is very sensitive to moisture and particles; a low reading usually means wet or dirty oil, which the next filtration or drying should fix.

terms: 油中溶解气体色谱分析

worked.q: A 4-unit string on a 35 kV line: why might a zero-value (faulty) unit go unnoticed by sight, and how is it found live?
worked.s: A punctured unit looks normal. Live testing with a spark-gap fork across each unit: a good unit carries several kV and sparks; a zero-value unit gives no spark. Do it in fine dry weather (Q9.11, 9.14).

worked.q: An oil sample gives breakdown values 42, 45, 39, 44, 41, 43 kV in six tests. Result?
worked.s: Mean = 254/6 ≈ 42.3 kV (the usual practice is to report the average of the six breakdowns: my note).

topics.title: Electrical Testing IX: Earthing Impedance, Overhead Lines, Arc-Suppression Coils
topics.zh: 电气试验（九）：接地阻抗、架空线路与消弧线圈试验

sections.b:
Source. Detailed notes on 《电气试验 223 问》 (223 Questions on Electrical Testing), ed. Wang Xuejun, Jiangxi Science & Technology Press, 2019: questions and answers from a substation test engineer’s work (Nanjing Longjiang substation), grouped by equipment. Written in my own words, keeping the book’s question numbers (Ch.Q). Test values follow Chinese preventive-test rules; in Singapore follow the equipment maker and the applicable SS/IEC standards. Where the printed text has an evident typo, I say so.

QPoint
11.1 Earthing impedanceImpedance at a given frequency between a point of a system or equipment and reference earth
11.2 Ground-surface potential measurementStep voltage, touch voltage and equipotential lines
11.3 Transferred potentialThe earth-grid potential carried away by a metal conductor connected to the grid at one end, when fault current flows into the grid
11.4 Isolating transformerUsually 1 : 1, with an earthed screen between windings, isolating high potential between primary and secondary circuits
11.5 Soil resistivityResistance between opposite faces of a unit cube of soil, Ω·m: drives earth resistance, surface potential distribution, touch and step voltages
11.6 Earth potential rise (EPR)Rise of grid potential relative to remote zero earth caused by fault current entering the earth through the grid
11.7 Too many grading conductors gain littleGrading conductors are horizontal electrodes at set spacing within the main grid (reducing step voltage); connections between two grids (at least 2) reduce total resistance. Beyond a certain number of meshes the maximum touch coefficient falls only slowly (saturation), so very small spacing is not worthwhile
11.8 Rounded grid corners (r = D/2)The highest step voltage of a rectangular grid appears just outside the corners along the 45° bisector; rounding the corners with radius D/2 (D = mesh spacing) lowers it by 5–10 %
11.9 ZC-8 earth tester uses AC; capacitor C1Soil conducts electrolytically; DC would cause polarisation EMF and large errors. The null detector is moving-coil, so a mechanical (or phase-sensitive) rectifier converts to DC for it. C1 blocks DC stray currents in the earth
11.10 Round, angle, flat steelRound: solid round bar; angle: two legs at right angles; flat: rectangular section, width 12–300 mm, thickness 3–60 mm
11.11 Spacing a ≥ 20 b (Wenner)To reflect the real current dispersion of the earth (b = electrode depth)
11.12 Depth sensed grows with aa is also called measuring depth; current penetration in the Wenner method is about 3a: small a measures only the surface layer; larger a sends more current deeper

Wenner four-electrode method (after book Fig. 11-2, redrawn): current I between C1 and C2, voltage U between P1 and P2; ρ = 2πa·U/I.

11.13 Derivation (a ≫ b): a point source I in soil of resistivity ρ gives potential ρI/(2πr) at distance r (half-space). At P1: from C1 +ρI/(2πa), from C2 −ρI/(2π·2a); at P2: from C1 +ρI/(2π·2a), from C2 −ρI/(2πa). So UP1 − UP2 = (ρI/2π)(2/a − 2/2a) = ρI/(2πa). With Rg = U/I:

ρ = 2π a Rg

sections.h: Overhead lines and arc-suppression coils (Q12.1–11, Q13.1–5)
sections.b:
QPoint
12.1 Phase coloursAC: A yellow, B green, C red, neutral black. DC: positive ochre (brown), negative blue
12.2 Single / double circuitOne supply circuit / two: single source with two circuits, or two sources with two circuits
12.3 Busbar, lead, conductorBusbar: collecting conductor at one voltage in a station connecting lines and equipment; lead: conductor brought out from equipment; conductor: main part of a power line
12.4 Joint resistance ratio by voltage dropSet the probe spacing equal to the compression sleeve length; read the drop U1 across the sleeve and U2 across an equal length of conductor: R1/R2 = U1/U2; valid only with a large current (the larger, the more accurate)
12.5 ThermocoupleConverts temperature into thermo-EMF (two metals in a loop with junctions at different temperatures); electrodes, insulating sheath, protection tube, terminal head; used with indicators, recorders, controllers
12.6 Phase-colour checkChecking that both ends of the same phase have the same colour
12.7 Positive-sequence impedance: far end three phases shortedEach phase’s impedance is then in series from start to end (series parameter)
12.8 Zero-sequence impedance: far end shorted and earthedZero-sequence current needs a conductor–earth return path; earthing the far end simulates it
12.9 Positive-sequence capacitance: far end openLittle current flows, so the whole conductor is at voltage U: all its capacitance is in parallel
12.10 Why short for impedance but open for capacitanceInductive reactance is a series parameter → series test circuit; capacitive susceptance is a shunt parameter → parallel test circuit
12.11 Phase-to-phase capacitance from C1 and C0For a transposed, symmetrical line: under zero-sequence voltage all phases are at the same potential, so there is no interphase effect: C0 = phase-to-earth capacitance. Delta-to-star: each C12 delta becomes 3C12 to the neutral P, which is at zero potential like earth, so C1 = 3C12 + C0
C12 = (C1 − C0) / 3
QPoint
13.1 Intermittent arcEarth-fault arc repeatedly extinguishing and re-striking; each extinction leaves charge on phase-to-earth capacitances, producing large intermittent arcing overvoltages
13.2 System capacitive currentEvery feeder has capacitance to earth; normally the capacitive currents balance; on a single-phase earth fault the healthy feeders’ capacitive currents flow through the fault point back to the bus
13.3 Tuning, detuning, dampingTuning (compensation) degree: how close the system is to resonance; detuning: how far from it; damping ratio: leakage conductance ÷ capacitive susceptance
13.4 Detuning not over 10 %Too large → larger residual current and faster rise of recovery voltage at the fault: the coil no longer extinguishes the earth arc
13.5 System splittingSeparating a power system into independent, non-synchronous parts to prevent loss of stability spreading; parts may lack power, so load shedding follows. Disabling out-of-step protection would prevent splitting even in severe faults: not acceptable for reliability
v = (IL − IC) / IC (detuning, my note)

Example (my note): IC = 40 A, coil set to IL = 43 A → v = +7.5 % (over-compensated, within 10 %); residual current at the fault ≈ 3 A plus the resistive component. Book 4 complete.

worked.q: Wenner test: a = 10 m, U = 2.4 V, I = 0.5 A. Soil resistivity? What depth does it mainly represent?
worked.s: Rg = 2.4/0.5 = 4.8 Ω; ρ = 2π × 10 × 4.8 ≈ 302 Ω·m; penetration about 3a = 30 m (book’s rule).

worked.q: A line has C<sub>1</sub> = 0.9 µF and C<sub>0</sub> = 0.6 µF. Phase-to-phase capacitance?
Sleeve drop U<sub>1</sub> = 0.9 mV, equal length of conductor U<sub>2</sub> = 1.0 mV at 300 A. Resistance ratio?
worked.s: R1/R2 = 0.9/1.0 = 0.9: the joint is better than the conductor (ratios above about 1.2 suggest a bad joint: my note).

topics.title: Electrical Accident Cases I: Lightning Accidents
topics.zh: 电气事故案例（一）：雷电事故

sections.h: Contents of the book, and the arrester and induced-charge cases (cases 4–6)
sections.b:
Source. Notes on 《电气事故的分析与处理》 (Analysis and Handling of Electrical Accidents), Shanghai Society of Electrical Engineering, editorial board of Electrical World (电世界), Shanghai Science & Technology Press: a collection of real accident case studies. The PDF supplied contains only the contents pages and book pp. 222–260 (end of Ch 6 “Lightning accidents” and all of Ch 7 “Other electrical accidents”), so only those cases are covered. Written in my own words; the cases are historical (1960s–80s, China), so some practices differ from today’s Singapore rules.

Chapter (from the contents)Topic
1Generators, transformers, instrument transformers (cases 1–24)
2Switches, contactors, relays, fuses (cases 1–19)
3Supply and distribution
4Electricity use
5Shock accidents (cases up to 33)
6Lightning accidents (cases 1–9; pp. 215–233)
7Other electrical accidents (cases 1–22; pp. 234–260)

Case 6.4, 220 kV substation lightning accident (only its end is in the PDF): the porcelain of an arrester stack cracked and broke; afterwards the measured voltage distribution showed the top three sections carried more than their share, confirming the analysis. Remedy: improve the voltage distribution of the 220 kV arrester, reduce leakage along the insulating pull rods with anti-pollution coatings (e.g. silicone grease) and raise their insulation level, so the top sections carry less and the parallel (grading) resistors no longer overheat; tests showed this worked.

Case 6.5, shocks from lines that are not energised. (1) 1962 summer: before reconnecting a jumper on pole 1 to restore supply to a mine, an old electrician “flicked” the conductor with a finger (an old habit to test for voltage) and felt a tingle; a test pen showed the line live. The mine’s diesel set was not running. Cause: a heavy thunderstorm at noon had left an induced charge (capacitive voltage) on the HV line through electrostatic induction from the thundercloud; discharging it to earth removed it. (2) Ten years later, with a black cloud approaching an HV line job, workers came down; one finishing off said “just a bit more” and was knocked off his seat on the crossarm with a crack, saved by his safety belt. No thunder or lightning: the charged cloud overhead induced charge and capacitive voltage on the line. Lesson: in summer field work, watch for induced charge before and after storms and short-circuit and earth all three phases. Editor’s note: a nearby cloud induces bound charge (opposite sign) and free charge (same sign), the latter partly leaking through insulators; after the cloud discharges, bound and remaining free charge do not fully neutralise, leaving charge on the line at a voltage too low to leak away but enough to shock: earth all lines being worked on, energised or not.

Case 6.6, FCD-10 arrester exploded by capacitively transferred voltage (Guangxi Luodong hydro station). After maintenance of main transformer No. 1 (15 MVA, 10/110 kV), with no HV breaker or disconnector, it was energised live, phase by phase at the HV bushings (to avoid splitting the system). The generator breaker was open; the FCD-10 arrester was on the LV side with only about 4 m of connection; the HV neutral was unearthed. Phase A was connected first and the A-phase arrester exploded at once. With one HV phase connected, the whole HV winding sits at the phase voltage Uφ, so the neutral is at Uφ (zero-sequence voltage), transferred to the 10 kV side through the inter-winding capacitance C12:

U1 = Uφ · C12 / (C12 + 3C11)

C12 and 3C11 (LV capacitance to earth) form a divider. With the generator connected, 3C11 is large and U1 small; with the generator breaker open and 4 m of lead, 3C11 is tiny and U1 large, exceeding the FCD-10’s power-frequency spark-over of 25–30 kV and lasting long, so it could not quench and exploded. Prevention: (1) when energising phase by phase, temporarily earth the LV neutral or any LV phase, removing it after all three HV phases are in; (2) add about 0.1 µF per phase to earth on the 10 kV side to raise 3C11; (3) fit a three-pole ganged disconnector on the HV side (since done); (4) avoid neutral displacement: ganged switches must close together, no unbalanced running.

Worked check (my note): 110 kV system, Uφ ≈ 63.5 kV. If C12 = 3000 pF and 3C11 = 3000 pF (short leads only), U1 ≈ 32 kV: above the 25–30 kV spark-over. With 0.1 µF added per phase, 3C11 ≈ 0.3 µF and U1 ≈ 63.5 × 3000/303 000 ≈ 0.6 kV. (Illustrative values.)

sections.h: LV overhead lines, mountain-top buildings, and line construction in storm season (cases 7–9)
sections.b:
Case 6.7, lightning on LV overhead lines. Four kinds: (1) direct or induced strokes on service drops; (2) strokes on the HV side of distribution transformers passing into LV services; (3) ball lightning on service drops or lighting lines; (4) strokes on buildings flashing back onto services or lighting. Most deaths occur in thunder-prone areas, on unshielded suburban LV lines, mostly wooden-pole lines (high insulation to earth), a few concrete-pole lines whose insulator pins were not reliably earthed. Findings: lamp-holder discharges to people killed mostly within 1.5 m (over 90 % of cases), injured mostly at 1.5–2 m (7 %), and beyond 2 m no casualties. Concrete poles act as natural earths. Lightning overvoltage on LV lines can reach 2000–3000 kV; accident rates in some areas reached 1.7–6.6 %; some cities lose dozens to hundreds of energy meters a year (one area over 1000 in a year). Where insulator pins were earthed (Jiangnan, North-east, Nanning), strokes caused no casualties; a Beijing scenic area with wooden poles and unearthed pins had bulbs exploding, TVs damaged, phone lines burnt. Patterns: more storm days, more accidents; suburbs worse than city; wooden poles worse than concrete or steel; strike-prone spots worse.

Protection (book)Details
1. LV arrestersOne set on the line about 50 m before the building (the book’s figure is marked 500 m), well earthed, and one set inside: costly, only for special important users
2. Earth the insulator pinsOn the last pole before the building: the pins act as a spark gap, greatly lowering the surge entering. Or earth the main line every 100–200 m; public buildings (offices, schools, theatres, hospitals) must have pins earthed; for ordinary users within 50 m of an earthed point, no extra earth. Earth resistance ≤ 30 Ω (≤ 50 Ω in rocky, high-resistivity ground). Keep 2 m from lamps during storms. Lines fully shielded by tall buildings or under eaves, and lines in low-thunder areas (< 30 storm days/year) with good experience, may skip it; concrete poles with natural earth ≤ 30 Ω need no extra earth
3. Energy meters in thunder-prone spotsGap protection of 1.5–2 mm; some use 500 V vacuum dischargers from telecoms, small LV or ZnO arresters; costly if applied everywhere

Case 6.8, Jiuxian Mountain weather station (Dehua, Fujian, 1650 m; 76.2 storm days a year, up to 102): ball lightning entered through the floor in 1967, stunning the operator and exploding in the corridor; in July 1969 an observer was killed on the observation platform (clouds overhead thin, storm on the opposite peak; he stood out like a good earthed conductor: probably an induced discharge, no rods then); after three rods were fitted in 1968 there were no strikes until 1976, but people felt tingles touching metal because incoming lines were unprotected; on 6 Apr 1976 a rod was struck and a ball of lightning ran down the down-conductor, entered the engine room through a crack and exploded, blowing a half-metre hole in a stone wall, wrecking the generator and burning wiring; the anemometer cable brought HV into the duty room and knocked the duty officer unconscious. Causes after rods were fitted: poor earthing, badly corroded down-conductors, unprotected incoming lines. Measures: (1) low earth resistance, large down-conductors; keep people out of a 5–10 m radius of rod earths in storms; (2) earth grid round buildings and grading grids where people walk, at least 5 m from free-standing rod earths, earthed at many points; (3) lightning fences round roofs and activity areas against side strikes; (4) no lines or stays above walkways or work positions; (5) incoming lines as armoured cable buried in the ground, sheaths bonded to the grid at several points, an arrester on every line; (6) metal cases of instruments well earthed; (7) metal doors and windows with metal mesh, earthed, kept shut in storms (ball lightning); (8) in high-resistivity ground, graphite powder (ρ = 1) and pottery clay (ρ = 10, units “Ω·mm²/m” as printed) as backfill: non-corrosive, not washed away; re-measure periodically.

Case 6.9, building lines in the storm season. (1) A 23 km 10 kV rural line (concrete poles, wooden crossarms, pin insulators, triangle): 15 km built in July, work stopped at a strain section with no slack conductor on the ground, so the line was isolated from earth; that evening a pole on a 650 m hilltop 200 m away was struck: a crossarm split, two pin insulators shattered, an LJ-35 conductor broke and fell. (2) A 35 kV line being strung by hand 24 km from a 110 kV substation (not yet connected to the breaker), distant faint thunder: a dozen workers pulling the conductor all fell together, silent for about 3 s, recovering after 4–5 s (“just felt a tingle, then nothing”). An induced overvoltage travelled along the line; the slack was coiled on the drum, not touching earth, so current went through people to earth; spread over many parallel paths, not fatal (two hurt in falling).

Recommendations (book)
1. Keep in touch with the weather service; do not work when storms may come, or fit temporary earths in the work area
2. Short-circuit the three phases at the start of the line and earth them reliably; remove only before energising
3. Finished lines not yet in service, arresters not yet in: short-circuit and earth
4. Lightning protection at crossings: earth concrete poles or fit gaps or arresters
5. When paying out and tensioning by hand, keep the slack conductor in reliable contact with earth
6. On long-span and angle poles (long work), short the three phases and bond them to the stay rod (buried 2–3 m: a temporary auxiliary earth), removed before coming down

terms: 感应电荷（束缚/自由电荷）

worked.q: Why did the FCD-10 survive with the generator connected but explode with the generator breaker open?
worked.s: The transferred voltage U<sub>1</sub> = U<sub>φ</sub>C<sub>12</sub>/(C<sub>12</sub> + 3C<sub>11</sub>) depends on the LV capacitance to earth. The generator’s large capacitance kept U<sub>1</sub> low; with only 4 m of lead, 3C<sub>11</sub> was tiny, so U<sub>1</sub> exceeded the 25–30 kV spark-over and persisted at power frequency, which the arrester could not quench.

worked.q: A crew finds a de-energised line “live” after a storm passed. What is it, and what should they do?
worked.s: Residual induced (bound/free) charge from the thundercloud. Prove dead, then discharge and short-circuit and earth all three phases before touching; keep earths on while working, and stop work when storms approach.

topics.title: Electrical Accident Cases II: Shock, Control and Fire Accidents
topics.zh: 电气事故案例（二）：触电、控制失灵与电气火灾

sections.h: Case 7.1 Shock in a park; case 7.2 tower-crane jib collapse
sections.b:
Source. Notes on 《电气事故的分析与处理》 (Analysis and Handling of Electrical Accidents), Shanghai Society of Electrical Engineering, editorial board of Electrical World (电世界), Shanghai Science & Technology Press: a collection of real accident case studies. The PDF supplied contains only the contents pages and book pp. 222–260 (end of Ch 6 “Lightning accidents” and all of Ch 7 “Other electrical accidents”), so only those cases are covered. Written in my own words; the cases are historical (1960s–80s, China), so some practices differ from today’s Singapore rules.

7.1 A near-fatal shock in a park (Kunming, 2 June 1983). An iron frame in a park shrubbery carried an iron-clad switch and a magnetic starter for a 17 kW centrifugal pump. A girl under 2 hugged the frame with her left hand and lifted her right foot to climb; she froze. Her 6-year-old brother pulled her by the skirt; she fell, face purple; the mother thought the boy had hurt her, then found a black wound on the left arm, two blisters on the left palm and four black marks on the abdomen; she was unconscious. A works clinic judged electric injury; on the way to hospital the girl was given mouth-to-mouth breathing; revived after over an hour.

Cause: for welding railings, a welder had taken power from the iron-clad switch with a much-used PVC copper flex; a barely visible damaged spot rested on the frame, putting 220 V on it. About 50 cm of the frame was buried, the path concrete: a fairly high-resistance earth path; the girl standing on concrete touching with her hand (and her raised foot) made a parallel path. With 10 kΩ body resistance about 20 mA flowed: enough to paralyse hands and feet so she could not let go, and make breathing difficult; a little longer would have been fatal. Had the boy touched her skin he might also have been shocked.

Lessons and measures (book)
1. Avoid electrical equipment wherever visitors can reach; if unavoidable, take safety measures
2. Check park wiring seriously; inspect reused appliances and materials carefully before use
3. New lines and temporary leads only by electricians; no unauthorised wiring, deal strictly with offenders
4. Make it a system with a person assigned to regular patrols

My note: an RCD (30 mA) on the supply to the temporary lead would have tripped; rescuers must free a victim with something dry and insulating, not bare hands.

7.2 TQ-60/80 rail-mounted tower crane: jib broken (autumn 1983). Day 1: power lost; a 75 A fuse in the main supply box had blown and the cable-reel slip-ring spring holder was broken, with no spare. The driver set the four universal changeover switches (travel, luffing, hoist, slew) to zero, covered the console with a rubber cover, closed the cab, but forgot to open the 100 A air circuit-breaker. Day 2: the electrician repaired the reel and closed the 150 A slate switch in the distribution box, and told the driver, who had no lifting work and did not go up to open his breaker: both controlling switches were closed. That night a storm with rain and wind: the hoist motor started by itself and lifted a steel formwork box; the limit switch failed, the hoist kept turning and pulled the 25 m jib back until it bent, caught on the counter-jib by the wire rope; the third section hung bent: jib written off. The box was flung out, broke a 10 kV line and hit a 180 kVA transformer, smashing a bushing; power failed (which stopped the hoist); the momentary overvoltage on LV burnt TVs in nearby homes.

Analysis (book)Measures (book)
(1) Important condition: the 150 A slate switch and the cab’s 100 A breaker were left closed while the crane was idle(1) Overhaul the crane, especially the electrics; re-check control circuits; replace sub-standard parts
(2) Direct cause: broken cab glass and ill-fitting windows let rain in; wires 123 and 106 in the panel terminal plug became conductive, shorting 111 and 106: with the switch at “0” it acted as if at “1”; the hoist contactor pulled in and self-held(2) A responsible person inspects site lines and equipment with records; separate power and lighting circuits; switch off site power after work every day and lock the boxes
(3) Indirect cause: poor discipline and safety training, lax inspection, late repair, poor maintenance(3) Use the case to train all staff, especially electricians and crane drivers

sections.h: Cases 7.3–7.8: wire on a stove, soot, a loose bolt, petrol fires, a threshing-ground fire
sections.b:
CaseWhat happenedCauseLesson (book)
7.3 Iron wire on a lamp lead electrifies a stove (Inner Mongolia school, early winter)A pupil adding coal felt a shock through the poker and shovel; another, thinking it a joke, tried and was jolted; no injury. Electrician: stove at 150 V to earthThe stove stood on bricks and porcelain shards 35 cm up (insulated from earth); the iron wire tying the stovepipe was tied at its other end to the wooden lamp rod, touching the lamp’s down-lead where the insulation had burnt through to bare copper (the phase wire): leakage via wire and tin chimney to the stove, then through a personInspected all 15 classrooms; another had chimney wire tied directly to a lamp lead: corrected
7.4 Soot causes a flashover short (12 Nov 1982)A three-phase air switch tripped twice within minutes; a 15 A three-phase knife switch for a 0.35 kW blower sparked; no marks on the blades, No. 22 fuse wire intact, but copper splatter under the handle and burnt blade endsThe switch was on the wall 120 cm from the furnace mouth at a 45° downward angle; when coal was added and the fan started, black smoke of conductive carbon particles, very hot, blew onto it and discharged under the handle where there was no bakelite cover. The operator then re-closed without clearing the fault: a second tripMove the switch away from the furnace mouth; train operators. (Never re-close onto an unexplained fault: my emphasis)
7.5 One bolt causes a shortThree running motors stopped within minutes; all thermal relays had tripped; all lacked the same phase: one fuse of the fuse-switch blownAn M8 × 45 mm terminal bolt of an unused RT0 fuse worked loose by vibration, fell and bridged the aluminium bar and the panel’s angle-iron frame: phase-to-earth short → single phasing → thermal trips(1) Bolts not too long, tightened; (2) clearances bar-to-frame and phase-to-phase above the minimum in the rules; (3) check fixing bolts front and back of panels, switches, fuses regularly
7.6 Isolate the battery before washing an engineA driver washed a muddy engine with a brush and half a basin of petrol; the iron basin touched the two starter terminals: sparks ignited the petrol; car badly burnt, driver’s arms and head burntConductive basin across live battery terminalsBefore working on battery-started vehicles, remove the battery earth strap; scrape off dirt with bamboo first, then wipe sparingly with petrol on cotton; never brush petrol about
7.7 Petrol-washed milling-machine control box catches fireAfter cleaning and repair, a loud bang and a large fire round the machine, spreading into another machine’s electrical box; put out with sand after tens of minutes; plastic wiring badly burntCleaned with petrol; to check the work, the operator jogged the machine while the bed was still wet and the control box under it uncovered: arcing of the AC contactor ignited the vapourNever wash machine electrical boxes or nearby equipment with petrol; switch off the main supply first when repairing; non-electricians must not press electrical buttons
7.8 Fire on a threshing ground (northern Jiangsu farm)Two drum threshers’ wooden frames and some straw burnt; hundreds of thousands of jin of grain nearly lost. A 7.5 kW motor drove six threshers; six lamps; a wooden pole 2 m away carried a makeshift outdoor wooden distribution box at 1.5 m; supply from 50 m away: three 10 mm² Al rubber-insulated power wires and two 4 mm² lighting wires; box with a 60 A porcelain-base knife switch and a 15 A porcelain plug-in fuse for lighting; leads dragged straight in through a large hole; box wrapped in PVC film against rain. Lamps flickered in the wind before 10 p.m.The electrician over-tightened the fuse terminal screw, damaging the conductor; the lead was not secured, swayed in the wind and broke at the terminal but stayed in the hole, making and breaking: arcs balled the aluminium end and burnt the screw; straw in the box caught fire, then the PVC film, whose burning drips lit the dry straw below and spread to the threshers(1) Keep temporary outdoor boxes clean, no straw; do not wrap them in flammable plastic film; (2) secure incoming and outgoing leads so terminals carry no strain; (3) tighten terminal screws properly without damaging conductors

worked.q: In case 7.1, estimate the current if the girl’s body resistance were 10 kΩ, and compare with typical thresholds.
worked.s: I ≈ 220/10 000 = 22 mA (the book says about 20 mA): above the let-go level for children and adults (about 10 mA), so she could not release, and near the level where breathing is affected; a longer exposure could cause fibrillation.

worked.q: List the three conditions that together caused the tower-crane accident in case 7.2.
worked.s: (1) Both supply switches (150 A in the box, 100 A in the cab) left closed while idle; (2) rain through broken cab glass bridged control wires so the hoist contactor closed and self-held; (3) the hoist limit switch failed, so the hoist did not stop at the jib tip. Underlying: poor maintenance and discipline.
